en: Preface:

Now, the One Great Treasury of Teachings branches into three: namely, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Śāstras. Although there are distinctions between the sudden and the gradual, the great and the small, they all issue from the Buddha’s own mouth;
through words he reveals the Way, and through the Way he establishes practice, all of which ultimately converge [upon the same goal].
This is merely the dharma-gate of the mind-ground. It is like the three legs of a precious tripod; if one is missing, it will tilt and overturn.
How, then, could it establish conduct and speech, cultivate virtue and morality, serve as a dam for prohibitions and precepts, and become the very foundation for transcending the world?
Therefore, the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra* is the key to the True Dharma. All Buddhas have realized it together, and all Bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattva practices this together [with others], and sentient beings possess this together;

taking precepts as its essence and precepts as its function, when its function is manifested, there is no conduct that is not established, and when its essence is clarified, there is no Way that is not complete.
Examining the strict purity and excellence of the Vinaya, both in principle and in practice, one must implement and actualize it without the slightest trace of pretense.
To sustain the world by means of the Dharma that tames and guides, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, has emitted the great perfect sound.
The various Bodhisattvas have widely proclaimed the *Prātimokṣa* to enlighten sentient beings of the Semblance Age: those who are deluded become ignorant, while those who awaken attain wisdom.
Truth and falsehood share the same source; self and others are universally enlightened—this extends even to the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding all causes and effects of karma—whether transgressions or blessings—there is nothing that does not fall within this scripture.

One must ensure that practice and understanding are in accord before establishing a model for the three realms and transforming and guiding devas and humans. It is the Vinaya Piṭaka alone that contains the most profound and wondrous principles;

this great collection of sixty fascicles is divided into four parts, hence it is called the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya). The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is contained within this great collection.

This is the essential compendium of the first division. Originating from the Venerable Upāli in the Western Regions, who personally received the Buddha’s entrustment, it was transmitted to the Eastern Land.
Thereafter, successive great masters—Nanshan Zhizheng, Chengzhao, Wuzhen, Yuankan, and Yuanzhao—propagated its teachings.
They were honored and praised by successive imperial rulers throughout the ages, as recorded in various grand ceremonies. During the Yuan and Ming dynasties...
When the True Dharma declined and became disordered, during the Qianzong and Zhengtong eras, the Elder Qianhua arrived by means of his wheel of vows.
For the southeastern quarter of the realm, those who came from all directions to receive the Vinaya teachings flocked together like swarms of bees and ants;
the flourishing of this transformative influence was already signaled therein.
The auspicious fortune of the Qing dynasty began to flourish. Following the legacy of Qianhua, the Monk Nanlai arrived; he magnified his lineage and expanded its model.
Those from the four quarters who received the Dharma from him were as numerous as stars surrounding the moon or birds flocking to the phoenix.
For forty years, he caused the transformation of the Dharma to thrive in the Southern Capital, and among the many thousands of followers, he found Master Dinggong.

There was one man. From his youth, he emerged as a preeminent talent. He extensively mastered both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) classics, examined and verified the entire corpus of the Vinaya Piṭaka, extracted the essence from the *Fayuan*, and elucidated the profound meanings of the various sūtras. He revealed the hidden treasures of former sages and continued the noble traditions of later initiators.
Having ascended from the stage of a student to the position of a teacher, though ten thousand disciples gathered like clouds, he never forgot [his roots].
With diligent effort and resolute intent, I have spent more than twenty summers in study until this essential work was completed.

This shall not only bestow great favor upon future students; even those contemporary masters of exhortation who are as numerous as stars scattered across the sky—those who neglect practice and realization while busily promoting a hollow form of the precepts for the sake of actual gain and sustenance—will, upon seeing this book, be able to immediately awaken their understanding.

Having cleared the reed-blockages, he ascended the broad royal highway; this is sufficient testimony that the Venerable Master Ding’s resolve to uphold the True Dharma was both sincere and far-reaching.
Alas! My life has been one of meager talent and coarse ignorance; how could my unrefined words suffice to add weight to this book?
Nevertheless, I privately rejoice that the Way of Nanshan accords between word and deed, and I further observe the integrity of Qiuanding.
Today, in order to remedy the pervasive decline of the Three Studies and to serve as a great banner of light for the Dharma in this final age, I have appeared at Mount Hua;
it is my good fortune that such an encounter occurs but once in a thousand years across the three periods of time.
Compiled by the younger brother Dazhen of Jia Shan in Runzhou, during the second month of spring in the Wuchen year of the Kangxi era.

Compiled by the Vinaya-studying śramaṇa Deqi of Baohua Mountain, Jinling, Qing Dynasty.

In order to explain this Vinaya, the major sections are divided into two: first, the explanation of the title; second, the entry into the text. The first, the explanation of the title, is divided into two:

first, the explanation of the title of the Vinaya; second, the explanation of the title of the author. The first, the explanation of the title of the Vinaya, is divided into two: first, the clarification... [text continues]
The Fourfold Division. Next, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is explained.
First, regarding what is called the "Fourfold Division": this major compendium of the Vinaya consists of sixty fascicles, which are divided into four parts. The first...
It is divided into twenty-one fascicles. Within it, the first part elucidates the origins, permissions, prohibitions, and the gravity of the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus.

The second part, consisting of fifteen fascicles, elucidates the three hundred and forty-eight precepts for bhikṣuṇīs, as well as the *khandhaka* on receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) and the *khandhaka* on the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). (As for the term *khandhaka*, it is translated here as "collection of dharmas," meaning...)

Because clusters of dharmas that are similar in nature are gathered together in one place, they are called "dharma-clusters" (*dharmaskandha*). In the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, they are named *khandhaka*; in the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya], they are called *varga*; and within the various sūtras, they are termed "chapters" (*parivarta*). Although these names differ, their meaning is no different.
The third division, consisting of thirteen fascicles, elucidates the sixteen *khandhakas* (sections on legal procedures).

These include the *Varsa* (Rainy Season Retreat), *Pravāraṇā* (Invitation to Criticism), *Carman* (Hides), *Bhaiṣajya* (Medicines), *Kaṭhina* (Robe-material), *Kauśāmbī*, *Campā*, *Pudgala* (Persons Subject to Censure), *Praticchanna* (Concealment of Faults), *Saṃghabhedaka* (Schism in the Saṃgha), *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (Settling of Legal Disputes), and the *Bhikṣuṇī* (*khandhaka*) sections, among others. The fourth division consists of eleven fascicles. Its...

The six *khandakas* (sections) elucidated therein—the *Vasana-khandaka*, the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, the *Pañcavargika-saṃgīti*, the *Saptavargika-saṃgīti*, the *Vinaya-skandhaka*, the *Vinayottaragrantha*, and so forth—constitute the various rules of Dharma.
This present *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is the first division (*prathama-bhāga*) within that great collection;
it specifically elucidates the two hundred and fifty rules of Dharma for *bhikṣus*. Thus, one should take this very sūtra volume.
It is named according to its numerical divisions; thus it is called the *Caturvarga* (Four-Part).
Next, I shall explain the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Regarding the term "Prātimokṣa": within the first division of the Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa, it clarifies only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the precepts, while also continuing with the seven...

The *Buddha-saṃkṣipta-śikṣāpada-sūtra* has been circulated in the world so that novice bhikṣus may recite and study it, enabling them to understand both the extensive and concise instructions and to maintain them with awareness, thereby not violating the essence of the precepts.

As for the fortnightly *poṣadha*, this code of precepts (*śīla-mātṛkā*) is recited as a constant rule; therefore, these two hundred and fifty articles have been separately compiled into this text. Thus [it is said].
This is called the *Sifen jiieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts). It possesses both general and specific names. First, the general name is explained; second, the specific name is explained.
That is to say, the entire body of disciplinary teachings within the Great Canon is generally termed "Vinaya. In Sanskrit, it is called *vinaya*, or alternatively *vinaya*.

This is translated as "skillful treatment" (śubha-vinaya). It is also translated as "discipline" (vinaya)—meaning the refinement of the three karmas and the subduing of transgressions. Refinement applies to both abstention and performance, whereas subduing clarifies only the cessation of evil.
Alternatively, it may be translated as "cessation" (*nirodha*). There are three meanings of cessation: first, the cessation of karma (referring to not killing, stealing, and so forth;

as stated in the Vinaya: "there is the *vinaya* for offenses, and there is the *vinaya* for disputes"); second, the cessation of afflictions (the Vinaya says: "to subdue greed and other defilements until they are exhausted, the Tathāgata established the training in higher morality"); third, the attainment of the fruit of cessation (as the Sūtra says).
"With pure precepts and possessing wisdom, one then attains the foremost path. Nanshan says: "The term *vinaya* is translated as 'subduing' (*tiao-fu*) and 'extinguishing' (*mie*).

These are names derived from its functional application; they are not the primary translations. The primary translation is 'law' (*lü*). 'Law' means 'dharma. This is a name derived from the teaching."
The determination of gravity and lightness, the opening and prohibition of precepts, and the maintenance or violation thereof are not fixed by what is non-Dharma;
they are like the codified statutes of royal law. Translating the term *vinaya*, it is called "Vinaya. The *Śīla-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: *Vinaya*:
*vi* in the Qin language means "to depart," and *naya* in the Qin language means "truth. Because one departs from various forms of error to proceed toward truth, it is so called.
It is indeed true. To subdue this mind, to still this mind, and to endure so that it does not arise—this is why it is called "true.
Subduing is precept (*śīla*); stilling is concentration (*samādhi*); enduring is wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus we know that when a single dharma is raised, the three trainings are fully encompassed.
Without the goodness of precept, concentration and wisdom do not arise. Furthermore, these dharmas of precept are of three kinds: first, the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*).
The first is the *śīla* (precept), also called the *prātimokṣa-śīla*. The second is the *samādhi-sahagata-śīla*, also called the *dhyāna-śīla*.
The third is the *mārga-sahagata-śīla*, also called the *anāsrava-śīla*. Regarding the *vinaya-śīla*: "Vinaya" means to restrain or prohibit; "śīla" refers to conduct or deportment.
Because it can restrain various evils within one's physical conduct, it is called "precept" (*śīla*). It is also termed "dignified deportment" (*airyāpathika*); here, "dignity" (*airya*) is—

Pure and solemn, he is awe-inspiring; his deportment serves as a model to be followed. He is also called the "Tamer" (*Vināyaka*), for he causes the activities of the mind to become harmonious and virtuous.
Concentration (*Samādhi*) is stillness and restraint; at the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes harmonious and virtuous, preventing all evils.
The Path is that which enables thorough penetration. After the realization of truth has arisen, one naturally refrains from transgressions;

this is like a plowman’s field where insects are cleared to a depth of four inches—this is the power inherent in the Path. Since these two types of precepts are the superior functions of the mind, they possess the power to give rise to the vows.

Because the Path (mārga) and meditative concentration (samādhi) arise simultaneously with the restraint of the Vinaya (saṃvara), they are termed "concomitant" (sahagata). Now, the *Vinaya Piṭaka* primarily elucidates...

The restraint (*saṃvara*) also encompasses meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*). Because pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) is maintained, meditative concentration and wisdom arise spontaneously;

thus, restraint is the cause and concentration and the Path are the fruit. Through the power of dhyāna and the untainted (*anāsrava*), both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) become entirely purified;
thus, liberation (*vimukti*) is the fruit and concentration and the Path are the conditions. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "This [restraint]..."
The *prātimokṣa* precepts exist when the Buddha is in the world, but do not exist when the Buddha is not in the world.
The dhyāna and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts exist at all times. The *prātimokṣa* precepts are obtained through instruction;
the dhyāna and outflow-free precepts are not obtained through instruction. It is even said that the *prātimokṣa* precepts belong only to the disciples of the Buddha.
Both śrāmaṇeras and non-Buddhists possess dhyāna-precepts. Now, that which can maintain the Buddha-dharma consists of the seven assemblies;
that the fruits of the three vehicles continue without interruption in the world is entirely due to the *prātimokṣa* being their root.
This is not the case for dhyāna-precepts or outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts. Therefore, among the three types of precepts, it is the most excellent. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* says: "The *vinaya*..."

The Vinaya Piṭaka is the life-force of the Buddha-dharma; as long as the Vinaya Piṭaka endures, the Buddha-dharma also endures. Having completed the explanation of the general name, we shall next clarify the specific distinctions.
The "Distinct" (Bie) refers to works such as the *Mahāsāṃghika*, *Pañcavargika*, *Sarvāstivāda*, *Daśabhāṇavāra*, *Sudarśana*, *Mūlabhikṣuṇīvinayamātṛkā*, and the *Vinayakāraṇasūtra*;
these are termed "Distinct. As for this present *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, it is generally referred to by the common name "Vinaya."
The specific [division] is called the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.

Having completed the discussion on the general and the specific, we shall further clarify the establishment of titles for the Sūtras and Vinayas. Their meanings encompass both single and compound forms, totaling seven types: namely, three single [titles] and three compound [titles].
The "single threefold" [classification] refers to those that establish their titles based on persons, such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra);

those that establish their titles based on dharmas, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Nirvāṇa*; and those that establish their titles based on metaphors, such as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. The "repeated threefold" [classification] refers to...
There are titles established based on persons (*pudgala*), such as the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others;

titles established based on phenomena (*dharma*) and metaphors (*upamā*), such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others; and titles established based on persons and metaphors, such as the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and others.
That which possesses all three—person, phenomenon, and metaphor—is exemplified by the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. Now, regarding this present *Prātimokṣa*:
Thus, the title consists of both the person and the dharma: the person is named Dharmagupta, and the dharma is named the *Caturvargika-vinaya*.

Alternatively, it may be stated that the title consists of the dharma alone, meaning the personal name is omitted and it is simply called the *Caturvargika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*. This concludes the explanation of the title.
Next, the title of the person [the translator] is explained.
Regarding the term "Yao-Qin": Qin is the name of the state, while Yao is the surname. This refers to the ruler Yao Xing; thus, it is called "Yao-Qin" to distinguish it from other Qin dynasties.
Regarding the name "Buddhayaśas," this is translated as "Awakened Brilliance" (Jue-ming). He was from the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There was a man of the Brahmin caste who left home at the age of thirteen. He was once traveling a long distance with his teacher when they encountered a tiger in the wilderness.
His teacher wished to flee to avoid it, but the teacher said, "This tiger is already full; it will certainly not attack us. Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed.

In his earlier years, he had some deficiencies in his studies. His teacher privately marveled at this. By the age of fifteen, he could recite two or three ten-thousand-word sections of scripture daily;
however, as he frequently went out for alms, his formal study and recitation were neglected. An Arhat, who highly esteemed his intelligence, [took note of this].

He constantly begged for alms to provide for him. He subsequently followed his maternal uncle and studied the treatises on the five sciences: (1) grammar (*śabdavidyā*), (2) logic (*hetuvidyā*), (3) medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), [4] arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), and 5. inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*).

He was proficient in all four branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and the fifth, inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*); there were no worldly arts or techniques with which he was not thoroughly familiar.
Later, he received the generous hospitality and offerings of the Crown Prince of the kingdom of Śākala. Kumārajīva arrived later and studied under him, treating him with great reverence.
When Kumārajīva returned to Kucha with his mother, Guṇabhadra remained behind. Shortly thereafter, the king passed away and the crown prince ascended the throne. At that time—
Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang and others to invade Kucha in the west. The King of Kucha urgently sought assistance from Kashgar;
the King of Kashgar personally led his troops to respond. Before the relief army had even arrived, Kucha was already defeated.
Kumārajīva was captured by Lü Guang. Daoxuan then sighed, saying: "Although I have known Kumārajīva for a long time, we have not yet fully expressed our innermost thoughts."
Suddenly becoming a captive, he did not expect to meet [Kumārajīva] again. After staying for more than ten years, he traveled east to Kucha, where his Dharma teachings flourished greatly.
While Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he sent a messenger to invite the Master; however, the local people detained him, and although he wished to depart, he was unable to do so.
He remained there for another year or so. Later, he said to his disciples, "I wish to seek out Kumārajīva. You should pack our things secretly and set out at night;
do not let anyone know. His disciples said, "We fear that if we are pursued tomorrow, we will be unable to avoid returning.
Thereupon, he ordered his disciples to take pure water and cast medicine into it, reciting several dozen words of dharani over it, and had his disciples wash their feet as they traveled by night.
The journey extended for several hundred *li*. At dawn, he asked his disciple Zhu to what he had perceived.
Zhu replied, "I only heard the sound of a violent wind. The people of the country pursued him but could not catch up. Upon reaching Guzang, Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an.

Hearing that Yao Xing had urged him to abandon the religious life (the term "unlawful" refers to Yao Xing’s admiration for Kumārajīva’s extraordinary talent and insight, leading him to advise him to leave the monastic path, which Kumārajīva refused), he sighed and said:
"Kumārajīva is like fine cotton; why have you made him enter a thicket of thorns? When Kumārajīva heard that [Sengrui] had arrived in Guzang, he urged Yao Xing to welcome him.
Yao Xing did not yet accept his advice. Shortly thereafter, Yao Xing commanded Kumārajīva to translate the *piṭaka*.

Kumārajīva said, "In propagating the Dharma teachings, one should ensure that both the phrasing and the meaning are perfectly integrated. Although I, this poor monk, can recite the texts, I am not yet proficient in their underlying principles."
"Only Buddhayaśas has profoundly mastered the subtle and profound meanings. He is currently in Guzang; I pray that you issue an edict to summon him.
Let his words be examined three times for detail before being committed to writing, so that these subtle teachings do not perish and may be trusted for a thousand years.

Emperor Xing immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him and presented him with generous gifts, all of which he refused. He then smiled and said, "Since your enlightened decree has been issued, I should indeed comply."
I gallop back in haste. However, since the Patron (Tányué) treats scholars so generously, were it to be as Master Kumārajīva was treated, I would not dare accept such an order.

This is because Xuánzàng had previously urged the concubines to pressure Kumārajīva (note: *yèng* is pronounced *yùn*; generally, women who accompany a bride to her marriage are called *yèng*). When the messenger returned with this report, Xuánzàng sighed at how close he had come to a transgression.
He sent messengers again with earnest letters to exhort him, and only then did [Kumārajīva] arrive in Cháng'ān. Xuánzàng went out in person to welcome him and invited him to the Xiāo Garden.
At that time, in the remote garden, Kumārajīva had produced the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra). For over a month, he remained hesitant and in doubt, having not yet set pen to paper.

Once Guṇabhadra arrived, they consulted together to resolve these difficulties, and only then were the words and principles finalized. He also produced the *Dīrgha-āgama* (Long Discourses) and other texts.
The śramaṇa Zhú Fóniàn of Liangzhou translated them into the Qin language, while Dàohán acted as the scribe. When [the work] reached...
In the tenth month, the session was concluded. This was because Buddhayaśas had previously recited the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in his native land but had not brought the Sanskrit original with him.
Yao Shuang, the Commandant of the Imperial Secretariat under the Qin, wished to invite him to translate it;

however, the Lord of Qin suspected there might be omissions or errors because no Sanskrit manuscript was available. Consequently, the Lord of Qin presented him with a scroll of medical prescriptions and a scroll of census records.
It comprised some ten thousand words. He was instructed to recite it, and one day, when the assembly of monks gathered, he was tested against the written text;

there was not a single character in error. The assembly marveled at his prodigious memory. Consequently, with Yaśas orally reciting the Sanskrit sounds and Fonian transcribing them into written Chinese, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was translated in the twelfth year of the Hongshi era, totaling forty-five fascicles (which are now divided into...).
[He] composed sixty fascicles. Śrīlāta was upright and elegant in person, with red whiskers; he was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā* and was thus called "Red-Whiskered Vibhāṣā" at the time.

Having served as Kumārajīva’s teacher, he was also titled "Great Vibhāṣā. Later, he returned to foreign lands and reached Kaśmīra, where he obtained one fascicle of the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*. He entrusted it to merchants to transmit to the various [monasteries] in Liangzhou.

[Seng]—later his whereabouts were unknown (according to the *Seven Patriarchs of the Lotus School*, in the first patriarch’s biography it states: "The Venerable One passed away in the eighth year of the Yixi era; he came to meet the Buddha.

When Master Huiyuan was by the Buddha's side, he bowed forward to the Master and said: 'Your honor’s will was set upon this long ago; why have you arrived so late? Master Huiyuan passed away on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era").

Zhu Fonian was a native of Liangzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth, and his aspirations and practice were pure and firm. Outwardly harmonious and inwardly luminous, he possessed a penetrating and discerning intellect. He recited and mastered many [scriptures].

His studies extended broadly to the non-Buddhist classics (*waidian*). He was particularly proficient in the *Cangjie* and *Yaya* glossaries. From his youth, he delighted in traveling abroad and became thoroughly conversant with various customs.

Born into a family from Xihe, he possessed a deep understanding of foreign languages; there were no Chinese or Sanskrit terms, nor their meanings and pronunciations, that he did not explain simultaneously.
Thus, although he lacked renown for his mastery of doctrinal studies (*arthaviniścaya*), his reputation for extensive learning was highly celebrated.
During the Jianyuan era of the Fu clan, Saṃghabhūti, Dharmanandi, and others entered Chang’an. Zhao Zheng requested that they translate various sūtras;

however, at that time, none of the famous and virtuous masters were able to transmit the translations. The assembly unanimously recommended Dharmarakṣa. Thereupon, Saṃghabhūti held the Sanskrit texts while Dharmarakṣa translated them.
He translated it into the language of Jin, resolving doubts and clarifying meanings so that the phonology and characters became distinct.

In the first month of the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, he again requested Dharmaratna to produce a translation of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Within the city of Chang’an, he assembled śramaṇas learned in the Dharma and invited Zhu Fonian to serve as the translator.
Through detailed exposition, analysis, and rigorous verification, the work was completed in two years. [This followed] the translations of An Shigao and Zhi Qian.

Thereafter, none surpassed [them] in their mindfulness (the śramaṇa Anqing of the country of Anxi, courtesy name Shigao, arrived at Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Zhi of the Eastern Han; he translated ninety-five scriptures.

The śramaṇa Zhi Qian of the country of Yuezhi arrived in Wu during the Three Kingdoms period; he translated eighty-eight scriptures). During the two dynasties of Fu Jian and Yao Xing, they were the preeminent masters among translators.

Consequently, the monastic community in Guanzhong all praised him. Later, he personally produced the *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa*, the *Daśabhūmi-saṃyojana-prahāṇa*, and the *Yao tai zhong yin jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State of the Womb), among other works.
As he began to edit and finalize them, his intentions were largely not yet fulfilled; he subsequently fell ill.
He passed away in Chang’an; both monastics and laypeople, far and near, could not help but lament his loss. The explanation of the title is now complete.

Second, the main text concerning the meaning of the precepts is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the introduction to the precepts (*śikṣāpada-nidāna*); second, the explanation of the specific precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the concluding exhortation and dedication of merit.

First, the explanation of the Preface to the Precepts (*śīla-uddeśa*) is divided into six parts: first, the recitation of verses of praise; second, the performance of preliminary preparations (*pūrvakaraṇīya*);

third, the formal execution of the *jñapti-karman*; fourth, the recitation of the Preface to the Precepts; fifth, the conclusion and inquiry; and sixth, the exhortation to uphold [the precepts]. The first section, the recitation of verses of praise, is further divided into six parts:
first, paying homage to the Triple Gem (*triratna*); second, the threefold admonition to listen and the benefits thereof; and third, relying upon the oral transmission of the masters.

Fourth, do not violate the four bases of morality (*śīla-pāda*). Fifth, the five precepts reveal completeness or deficiency. Sixth, the praise of the excellence of morality through metaphors. First, paying homage to the Triple Gem:
I bow my head in reverence to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
Commentary: At the commencement of any ritual practice, one must first pay reverent homage to the Triple Gem in order to seek their protective empowerment.

Bowing the head until it touches the ground represents the expression of reverence through the body-karma (*kāyakarman*). Reciting the sacred names aloud represents the expression of reverence through the speech-karma (*vākkarman*).
Maintaining visualization and contemplation within the mind represents the expression of reverence through the mind-karma (*manaskarman*). This is called the sincere offering of the three karmas.
[The Master] said: Why must one first pay homage to the Triple Gem when composing a treatise? There are seven reasons for this:
first, to manifest auspiciousness; second, to inspire faith; third, to make known [the Buddha’s] kindness and virtue; fourth, to establish a formal ritual.
Fifth, because the five types of manifest action (*vijñapti*) have a source from which they are received; sixth, because one requests the bestowal of majestic protection;

and seventh, because one follows in the footsteps of the former sages—there is this superior benefit in that one must first pay homage to the Triple Gem (*triratna*). Question: For what reason are these three called "gems"? Answer: According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, they are called gems because they possess six characteristics:
first, rarity; second, clarity and purity; third, power; [fourth, durability; fifth, being the basis for all virtues; and sixth, being the cause for the attainment of great bliss].
[The Three Jewels possess] power, fourfold adornment, supremacy, and immutability. Because these six qualities resemble worldly jewels, they are called the "Three Jewels" (Triratna).
Question: Why is the sequence of the Three Jewels as it is? Answer: It is according to the order of superiority and inferiority, namely: Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.

This is because there is a hierarchy of superiority and inferiority between the one who awakens to that Dharma, the Dharma which is awakened to, and those who follow and receive [the teachings]. If [considered] in terms of cause...

The sequence of results refers to the Saṃgha, the Buddha, and the Dharma; because the Saṃgha practices first, the Buddha subsequently attains perfection, and finally the fruit of the Dharma is realized.
The sequence of object and practice refers to the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the Buddha; taking the Dharma as the object, the Saṃgha cultivates superior practice, and the Buddha’s fruit is perfected.
The sequence of teacher and disciple refers to the Dharma, the Buddha, and the Saṃgha; the Dharma is the teacher of the Buddha, the Dharma comes first, and the Buddha comes next.

The Jewel of the Saṃgha is explained last. If following the order of faith, it is said: Saṃgha, Dharma, Buddha; that is, one observes the deportment of the Saṃgha, next gains faith in what they have realized, and only then takes the Buddha as teacher.
If following the order of manifestation, it is said: Buddha, Saṃgha, Dharma; for originally, the Buddha is the source.
Next, the Sangha is presented; the Dharma will be discussed later. For now, we shall follow the sequence of superior and inferior. Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are called the Triple Gem (*triratna*).
"Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language; its full form is *buddha*, which means "awakened. This awakening possesses three meanings: self-awakening, [awakening others], and... [awakening].
He has perfected both awakening and practice. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "How marvelous! The Great Teacher awakens himself and is able to awaken others. This is precisely that.
"Awakening oneself" means to realize and know all phenomena of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—such as the permanent and the impermanent;
to awaken to the true emptiness of nature and understand the false and illusory nature of delusions; and to achieve sublime wisdom through the perfection of one's merit. This is the Way.

Realizing perfect enlightenment is therefore called "self-awakening. Second, "awakening others" refers to exercising unconditioned compassion to deliver the realm of sentient beings (meaning that by means of equalizing wisdom, one does not intentionally fixate upon any sentient being, yet all sentient beings naturally receive benefit; thus, the *Fuxing* says: "Exercising this mind of compassion, it universally covers the Dharma-realm").

Therefore, it is able to spontaneously rescue beings from suffering and naturally bestow happiness; this is "unconditioned compassion" (*nirālamba-maitrī*). It is like a dragon king who raises clouds and pours down rain, moistening all equally and universally so that every being, according to its kind, attains growth.
[It] causes all to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa*; hence it is called "awakening others. Third is the perfection of the practice of awakening.

This refers to the complete purification of the three delusions, the full possession of all virtues, the realization of the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), and the perfection of practice and fruit;

therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Enlightenment and Practice" (the three delusions being those of views and thought, of the sands of phenomena, and of ignorance). This is what is meant by "Buddha.

As for "Dharma," it refers to the provisional and ultimate teachings expounded by the Tathāgata according to his nature and in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. If one considers this from the perspective of its meaning...
Explanation: There are two meanings. First, the meaning of sustaining its own essence (*svabhāva*). Second, the meaning of serving as a model to produce understanding in sentient beings.

Regarding "sustaining its own essence": this refers to the original, inherent essence which is truly immutable. It is not like the *paratantra* (dependent nature), which is provisionally established based on conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for [the former] has sustained itself without loss since beginningless time.

As the treatise says: "It is not empty according to reality, because it possesses its own essence and is fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of nature. Regarding "serving as a model to produce understanding in sentient beings": "model" (*niyama*) refers to a standard or rule; "beings" (*bhūta*) refers to sentient beings; and "understanding" (*avabodha*) refers to cognitive realization. This means that sentient beings possess the power of internal habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), and in relation to this...
From the Dharma, understanding and realization arise; from the objects [of the Dharma], understanding arises. Therefore, it is said that "it serves as a guide to produce understanding.

Regarding the term *bhikṣu* (monk): the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states that some say there is an equivalent translation, while others say there is none. As for those who say there is an equivalent translation:

To translate this: "Bhikṣu" means "remover of scarcity. Sentient beings have meager merit; because they lacked the Dharma as a means of self-sustenance during their causal stage, they now suffer from great want and deprivation.

Those who leave the household life and diligently uphold the pure precepts constitute a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); they can produce wholesome roots for sentient beings and thus eliminate the scarcity of cause and effect.
Regarding the term "no translation," its name contains three meanings. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: first, the destruction of evil; second, fear... [text continues].

Māra. Third, the mendicant who destroys evil: just as one is called a bhikṣu at the moment of first receiving the precepts, because through the three *karmavācanās* one gives rise to the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and destroys the unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*), he is said to "destroy evil. If considered comprehensively in terms of practice and realization:

The precepts can prevent what is wrong; meditative concentration removes mental distraction; and wisdom awakens one to the emptiness of conceptualization, enabling the destruction of the evils of views and afflictions;

therefore, it is called "destroying evil. Second, as for "frightening Māra": since he is able to destroy evil, Māra thinks to himself, "This person will not only leave my realm, but may also transmit the lamp of the Dharma to convert my followers and empty my palaces"; thus, fear arises.
Terror. Generally speaking, the three māras are also terrifying. (The three māras are: first, the *kleśa-māra*, which refers to all delusive afflictions within the three realms.

Because practitioners of the path have their minds disturbed by these delusive afflictions and are unable to achieve bodhi, this is called the *kleśa-māra*. The *pañca-skandha-māra* is also subsumed therein. Second, the *devaputra-māra*. This māra is the sixth heaven of the desire realm.

If a person diligently cultivates superior goodness and wishes to transcend the birth and death of the three realms, this *devaputra-māra* creates obstacles, initiating various kinds of disturbances so that the practitioner cannot achieve supramundane goodness.)

The faculties (*indriya*). This is called the celestial Māra (*deva-māra*). Third is the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), which refers to the dispersal of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the passing away of a celestial being. For a practitioner, this premature demise prevents them from prolonging the life of wisdom; this is called the Māra of death. Regarding the third, the mendicant (*yācanaka*):
"mendicant" (*yācana*) is a term for begging or seeking, while "person" (*śi*) is an appellation for one who is refined and pure. It refers to those who have left the household life.

To cultivate the virtue of inner purity and refinement, one must distance oneself from the four types of improper livelihood (*caturvidha-kuhaka-bhikṣā*): 1. **Downward-facing livelihood** (*adho-mukha-bhikṣā*): This refers to cultivating fields and gardens or compounding medicinal decoctions in order to seek food and clothing for one’s own sustenance;

this is called downward-facing livelihood. 2. **Upward-facing livelihood** (*ūrdhva-mukha-bhikṣā*): This refers to observing the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and storms, or studying the arts of divination and calculation in order to seek food and clothing for one’s own sustenance;

this is called upward-facing livelihood. 3. **Four-directional livelihood** (*tiryag-mukha-bhikṣā*): This refers to fawning upon those of power and influence, acting as a messenger between the four quarters, using clever speech to solicit much, and thereby seeking one’s own sustenance; this is called four-directional livelihood. 4. **Corner-facing livelihood** (*vidig-mukha-bhikṣā*): [The text here is incomplete.]

This refers to the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*). It means learning various incantations, divinations, and calculations of good and bad fortune to seek food and clothing for one’s livelihood; this is called "sustenance from the intermediate directions" (*vidiś-bhikṣā*).

To dwell in purity, to bring benefit and merit to sentient beings, to destroy the mind of arrogance, to be humble and self-effacing, and to request resources for the body in order to perfect the virtue of refined elegance—therefore, one is called a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*).
Because these three meanings are present within the causal stage, one obtains the three [results] upon reaching the fruit stage.
Regarding the title *bhikṣu*: first, "slayer of thieves," so named from destroying evil; second, "one who has attained non-arising," receiving this designation from terrifying Māra;

third, "worthy of offerings," achieving virtue through being a mendicant. Thus he is called a *bhikṣu*. As it contains many meanings, it is not translated [into Chinese] but remains in its original Sanskrit form.

Regarding the term "Saṃgha": "Saṃ" is a partial Sanskrit term; its full form is *saṃgha*. This translates as "harmonious assembly. It is a designation for four or more bhikṣus. There are two meanings of "harmony":
first, harmony of principle (*dharmasaṃgha*), which refers to collectively realizing cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*; here, "deliberation" means discernment).

Cessation is quiescence. This means that when sentient beings employ wisdom to discern the Four Noble Truths, they distance themselves from the fetters of views and afflictions, thereby realizing the principle of quiescent, true emptiness; this is called *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment). It is like a carriage drawn by an ox being called an "ox-cart.

There are six meanings of the harmony of two things: first, harmony in precepts through joint practice; second, harmony in views through shared understanding; third, harmony in body through living together; fourth, harmony in resources through equal distribution;
fifth, harmony in speech through the absence of contention; and sixth, harmony in mind through mutual joy.
Master Shi said: "To ensure harmony among the assembly, one must rely on six dharmas: first, to initiate physical action with a mind of loving-kindness;
second, to initiate verbal action with a mind of loving-kindness; third, to initiate mental action with a mind of loving-kindness;

fourth, when receiving food, to set aside a portion of the rice from one's bowl to offer to one person of higher standing and one person of lower standing; fifth, to maintain purity in the observance of the precepts; sixth..."

The wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*). It is by necessarily taking these six as its essence when dwelling together that the Sangha Jewel is revealed in its dignity as a field of merit for the world.
Furthermore, in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there are five kinds of Sangha: first, the shameless Sangha (*anapatrāpya-saṃgha*).

These are the monks who have broken the precepts. Second are the "ewe-monks" (*aurabhrika-bhikṣu*): ordinary persons of dull faculties and no wisdom, like a flock of ewes gathered together in one place.
They do not know the *poṣadha*; they do not know the *poṣadha-karman*; they do not know the *dharma-saṃnipāta*. (Regarding the *dharma-saṃnipāta*:

the *Mūla-nidāna* states that when sitting in assembly for the recitation of the precepts or the *pravāraṇā*, if visiting monks arrive, one should either continue the recitation or cease it, and one should listen according to the proper sequence. One should not follow the sequence... [text ends].

First, listen. A resident bhikṣu should exit the boundary and then depart; a visiting bhikṣu should do the same. Sometimes visitors arrive in small numbers, such that it would not be necessary to speak further. Even if a visitor possesses great virtue, if they are stubborn and capable of inciting strife, one should speak further, yet fails to do so.
Such a bhikṣu is said to be "one who does not know the assembly of the Dharma. Third, the division of the Saṃgha: performing formal acts (karmans) separately within a single boundary.
1. The fourfold pure saṃgha; 2. ordinary persons who observe the precepts; 3. ordinary victors (ordinary victors refers to the seven types of noble persons, both outer and inner ordinary beings:

first, those with a settled mind; second, those with mindfulness of specific characteristics; third, those with mindfulness of general characteristics—these are called outer ordinary beings; fourth, the stage of "heat"; fifth, the stage of "summit"; sixth, the stage of "patience"; seventh, the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma"—these are called inner ordinary beings); 4. the true saṃgha, consisting of those in training and those beyond training.
Among these, the salutation is properly directed toward the latter two types, because they are the true [saṃgha].
The Sangha can cause the ultimate True Dharma (the paths and fruits of the Three Vehicles) to endure for a long time;

because through the pure Sangha, the conventional True Dharma (the teachings of the Vinaya and instructions) can be made to endure for a long time. Those [members] of the aforementioned three types may perform illegal *karmavācanā* (formal acts).

Because they cause the True Dharma to be destroyed, they are not worthy of veneration. Furthermore, there are the Three Jewels of Sustenance (*pratīka-ratnatraya*) and the Three Jewels of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-ratnatraya*).
Regarding the Three Jewels of Sustenance: cast metal, molded clay, paper, silk, and pigments are called the Buddha Jewel;
yellow scrolls and red tablets containing the texts of the Great Canon are called the Dharma Jewel; and those with shaven heads and dyed robes are called [the Sangha Jewel].
These constitute the Sangha Jewel. Because these three abide in the world without interruption, they are called the "Abiding Three Jewels. As for the "Three Jewels of Identical Essence":
through the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent;

by simultaneously forgetting and simultaneously illuminating, the three types of knowledge reach perfect awakening—this is named the Buddha Jewel. The principle of the dharma-nature that is thus awakened to...
The complete fulfillment of the three truths is called the Dharma Jewel. Such awakened wisdom, in harmony with both principle and phenomena, is called the Sangha Jewel.
As for the term "all Buddhas," it refers collectively to all Great Teachers currently seated at the site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions;
because the essence of awakening is omnipresent, although they reside in other lands, they are able to act as benevolent protectors in this land.
This also refers generally to all the World-Honored Ones who appear successively throughout the three periods of time.
Because the nature of awakening is eternal, although they manifest in the past and future, they are able to bestow their responsive grace in the present; thus, they are called "the Buddhas.

Furthermore, the word "all" (zhū) applies universally to the Dharma and the Sangha as well, and may thus also be rendered as "all Dharmas" or "all Sanghas. This concludes the prostration to the Triple Gem.
Second, the benefits of heeding the admonition.
Now I shall expound the Vinaya dharma so that the True Dharma may abide for a long time.
Regarding the phrase "now I shall expound": this distinguishes it from what has already been said or what has not yet been said; it refers to the very moment when the precepts are being recited.
"Expounding" means the sense of proclaiming and disseminating. "The Dharma of Vinaya" distinguishes it from the two other teachings of Sūtra and Śāstra.
"Causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time": the True Dharma refers to the supramundane, untainted, noble Path.

When the True Dharma abides in the world, the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit are all fully present. This is because, by means of performing *karmavācanā* and the fortnightly *poṣadha*, [the True Dharma is maintained].
When the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) is perfected and concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) arise, the fruits of the śramaṇa’s path can then be expected.
If the *poṣadha* is neglected, the aggregate of morality becomes defiled, and the True Dharma will perish. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Vinaya is the life-span of the Buddha;
as long as the Vinaya remains in the world, the True Dharma will abide for a long time. The *Samantapāsādikā* asks: How is it known that the True Dharma...
"The Dharma abides for a long time" refers to the fact that the teaching of the precepts does not perish; hence it is said, "to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.

Regarding the statement, "The precepts are like the ocean, boundless," the *Śīla-kaṇḍa* (Exposition on the Observance of Precepts) states: "The waters of the ocean possess eight extraordinary qualities. For this reason, the asuras..."

The ocean is pleasant to dwell in for three reasons: first, all streams flow into it (the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 52, states that twenty-five thousand rivers from the four continents flow into the sea);

second, the tides do not miss their appointed times (the *Avataṃsaka* says that because the waters of twenty-five thousand rivers and eighty billion dragon kings' palaces enter the great ocean, they surge forth at the proper time, and thus the tides do not miss their limits);
third, when the five great rivers enter it, they lose their original names (*Saṃyukta Āgama*).

The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "The five great rivers merge into a single stream: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarayū; fourth, the Airāvatī; and fifth, the Mahī. These are called the five rivers.

Fourth, all river waters and rain from the heavens eventually flow back [to the ocean] without increase or decrease. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 51, states: "The ocean possesses four great jewels that can absorb all the waters so that the seawater neither increases nor decreases.

The first is named Sūryagarbha (Sun-Treasury); the second is named Ardratā-vigata (Free from Moisture); the third is named Jvālārcis (Flame-Light); and the fourth is named Aśeṣakṣaya (Exhaustion Without Remainder). If these four jewels did not exist, everything from the four continents up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) would be completely submerged."
5) It has a uniform salty taste; 6) it does not accept corpses; 7) it produces many precious jewels;
8) it is the dwelling place of beings of great form. Within my Dharma, there are likewise eight wonders by which I cause my disciples to find delight.
First, my disciples study the precepts progressively and all return to my Dharma, within which...
First, they study wholesome dharmas. Second, my disciples abide in the precepts and do not transgress them even unto death.

Third, members of the four castes who leave the household life are all called śramaṇas (the four castes being: first, kṣatriya, the royal caste; second, brāhmaṇa, the pure practitioners, analogous to the Confucian class in this land).

The *Huayan chao* states: "The Brahmins are the white class" means that according to the Brahmin dharma, those over seven years of age leave home to study the four Vedas; from fifteen years of age onward, they receive the Brahmin precepts and travel to various regions to pursue learning; at thirty, fearing the extinction of their lineage, they take a wife;

and at fifty, they enter the mountains to cultivate the Way. Within secular society, they may be called pure and white. The three Vaiśyas—also called Viśas—are the caste of merchants and traders. The four Śūdras are those whose occupation is farming and fieldwork. The *Kaiyuan lu* states:

"Before the Qin and Jin dynasties, those who left home generally followed the surname of their teacher. Later, the Dharma Master Shi Dao'an of Mitian declared: 'Having shaved one's head and donned dyed robes, one succeeds to the lineage of Śākyamuni; thus, there is no distinction of common surnames.'"

There is no one more venerable than Śākya; thus he took Śākya as his clan name. Later, when the *Ekottarika Āgama* arrived, it indeed stated: "When the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer bear their river names. Those of the four castes who leave the household life all abandon their original surnames and are uniformly called sons of the Śākyas.
Since this accords with the Sūtras and Vinaya, it has become an eternal standard; all are called śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas.

Fourth, within my Dharma, those who with firm faith leave the household life to study the Path enter the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, yet in the realm of nirvāṇa there is neither increase nor decrease. Fifth, likewise...

First is the taste of liberation. Sixth is the evil dharma of violating the precepts: although one sits among the assembly, one is always separated from the Sangha, distant from the Sangha, and likewise far removed from them.
Seventh is the abundant production of precious treasures, namely the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
Eighth is the assumption of a great form, namely the four stages of approach and the four fruits of realization. Furthermore, according to the Sarvāstivāda...
The treatise states: Of the two hundred and fifty precepts for a bhikṣu, each sentient being receives seven precepts.
When categorized by their underlying meaning, there are twenty-one precepts. For example, regarding the seven evils of body and speech that arise toward a single sentient being:
whenever these evils are committed, they arise due to the three causal conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion. Through greed, the seven [evils] of body and speech are incited.
If one commits [these], they constitute seven evils. Hatred and delusion are likewise. Thus, there are twenty-one evils—three times seven.
By reversing these evil thoughts, one attains the precepts; upon a single sentient being, one obtains twenty-one precept-matter (śīla-rūpa), and it is the same for all sentient beings.
It is as if, among five types of seeds, one were to break a single grain of wheat or millet, or sever a single fruit.
Plucking a single leaf, one likewise obtains twenty-one transgressions for each grain of wheat, each grain of millet, each fruit, and each leaf.
Just as with the precept against digging the earth, from the summit of Mount Sumeru above down to the adamantine foundation below,
extending horizontally throughout the entire dharma-realm, upon every single atom, one obtains twenty-one precepts.

Therefore, although the afflictions are not the objective conditions for the precepts, by turning away from evil one obtains the precepts and acquires a corresponding amount of the *rūpa* (form) of the precepts.
Furthermore, within each individual precept, there are ten benefits and merits, as well as three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices;
each instance of the pure *rūpa* of the precepts pervades the entire Dharmadhātu. Moreover, within every moment of thought, these are spontaneously accomplished.
The virtuous form of the Dharma of the precepts pervades the entire Dharmadhātu and is inexhaustible. As the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"The great ocean of the Vinaya has shores so vast they are difficult to know; its differentiated characteristics are infinite—how could I possibly detail them all?"
The Great Master’s ocean of Vinaya teachings is so profound that it is difficult to fathom; hence it is said, "Precepts are like an ocean without shore.
"Like a treasure sought without satiety":
the commentary explains that "treasure" refers to the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*). This jewel is able, in every moment of thought, to rain down [wealth] to fill Jambudvīpa.
It bestows all instruments of happiness, yet the essence of the jewel never suffers depletion. The precepts are likewise:

in every moment of thought, they give rise to all dharmas such as the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, up to and including the noble fruits of the three vehicles;
yet the essence of the precepts never undergoes change. Like that king of jewels, it grants its gifts without ever becoming weary.
Furthermore, wishing to protect the wealth of the noble Dharma, I shall explain it for the assembled multitude to hear.

As for what is called "the wealth of the noble Dharma," in its broad sense, it refers to the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and so forth, up to the factors of enlightenment and the path.

The seventeen categories of factors that assist the path. Briefly stated, these are faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and remorse (the seven treasures). These are called the supramundane treasures of the Dharma.

Just as worldly wealth can nourish the physical body and its lifespan, the treasure of the Dharma can nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. When all sentient beings practice these seven dharmas, they provide the sustenance for the realization of the fruit of the Path; therefore, they are called "treasures. First, the treasure of faith.

First is the wealth of faith (*śraddhā-dhana*). Faith is the mind of confidence; it means that faith enables one to resolutely accept and uphold the True Dharma as a requisite for attaining the Way. Therefore, it is called the wealth of faith. Second is the wealth of ethical discipline (*śīla-dhana*). Discipline refers to the precepts; it means that discipline is the foundation of liberation, capable of preventing transgressions of body, speech, and mind, and serving as a requisite for attaining the Way.

Therefore, it is called the wealth of ethical discipline. Third is the wealth of learning (*śruta-dhana*). Learning is the foremost of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). By hearing the Buddha’s teachings, one develops sublime understanding and practices according to what has been taught, thereby serving as a requisite for attaining the Way.

Therefore, it is called the wealth of learning. Fourth is the wealth of relinquishment (*tyāga-dhana*). Relinquishment refers to giving and charity; it means that if one can exercise a mind of equanimity, free from attachment to self or others, and bestow one's body, life, and material resources upon those who seek them, this serves as a requisite for attaining the Way. Therefore, it is called the wealth of relinquishment.

The wealth of generosity (*tyāga-dhana*): Thus it is called the wealth of giving material things. Fifth, the wealth of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā-dhana*): Concentration and wisdom are precisely *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Concentration gathers the mind so that it does not scatter and ceases all deluded thoughts. Wisdom illuminates and understands all phenomena, destroying all false views.

These serve as the resources for achieving the Way; thus they are called the wealth of concentration and wisdom. Sixth and seventh, the wealth of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya-dhana*): "Shame" (*hrī*) means to feel shame before the heavens; "remorse" (*apatrāpya*) means to feel shame before other people. This means that if one is capable of shame and remorse, one will not commit various evil karmas. These serve as the resources for achieving the Way; thus they are called the wealth of shame and remorse.
However, these spiritual riches cannot be guarded and protected without precepts (*śīla*). Precepts possess the power to prevent what is improper and cease what is evil.
It is like having strong soldiers and fierce generals who can subdue hostile enemies;
it is also like having sturdy walls and deep moats that can repel demonic armies, preventing them from finding an opportunity to invade and oppress.
Desiring to eliminate the four *pārājika* rules and to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, I shall explain to the assembled community as they listen the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

As for what is called "abandoning" (*pārājika*), herein, the violation of even a single precept constitutes an obstacle to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

They are abandoned by the Dharma; they are abandoned by the four fruits of the śramaṇa’s path; they are abandoned by all wholesome dharmas, including morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, it is like a person who has committed a capital offense and for whom there is no further way to live.
When a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense, there is forever no path for repentance; therefore, it is called "abandonment" (this merely explains the literal text;

the formal interpretation is as follows). The rules for saṃghāvaśeṣa and naiḥsargika-pāyattika are explained in the subsequent text. Now, although the precepts consist of five categories, only three are mentioned here.

By means of the heavy [precepts], the light are subsumed; thus, while the text is concise, its meaning is complete. One desires to avoid the four *pārājika* offenses so as not to transgress them, to forever sever the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, to remain free from obstructive hindrances, and to have no violation regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Therefore, when the assembly has gathered, listen as I recite the precepts. Through the merit of listening to them, one can truly distance oneself from these faults.
Third, relying on the oral transmission of the masters: Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda,
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni.

Commentary: Vipaśyin Buddha is also named Vīkṣin. In the language of the Flower [China], there are four meanings. Because his wisdom is full like the orb of the moon, he is called "Universal Vision" (Vipaśyin).
Because his dark essence is exhausted and delusions have perished, he is called "Pure Contemplation" (Vīkṣin). Since he is both perfect and pure, [he is so named].
It is thus called "Victorious Vision" (śeṣadṛṣṭi) and "Victorious Insight" (śeṣadarśana). In Sanskrit, it is *Śikhin*, also known as *Śikhi*; in Chinese, it means "Fire.

It is also called "Holding the Topknot" (*Dhṛtaśikha*), signifying that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is most supreme and resides at the crown of the mind. (Non-conceptual wisdom is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), as it is the root of all forms of wisdom.)
In Sanskrit, he is called Viśvabhū, also Suvidhi, and also Viśvabhū. In the language of China, this means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All.
It signifies that because his afflictions have been completely severed, there is no place where he is not sovereign (the afflictions being, namely, ignorance).

These three Buddhas above are the final three Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Eon). *Kalpa* is a Sanskrit term; in full it is *Kalpā*, which in the language of China means "differentiation" or "eonic period."
Regarding the time periods: as for the *Kṛta-yuga* (the Adorned Eon), it refers to this eon in which there is much adornment.

In Sanskrit, *Krakucchanda* is also called *Klūchin*; in the Chinese language, it means "that which should be severed," referring to the severing of all afflictions (*kleśa*) so that they are forever exhausted without remainder.
Within the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Eon), during the ninth *apakarṣa-kalpa* (decreasing eon), the human lifespan decreases until it reaches six years.
At the time of ten thousand years [per kalpa], he appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood, becoming the foremost of the thousand Buddhas.
In Sanskrit, he is called Kanakamuni; in the language of China, "Golden Silence. This means that "gold" signifies luminous manifestation, while "silence" signifies non-obstruction.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he is also named Kāśyapa-muni; in the language of China, "Golden Sage. This means—
This is because his body was golden in color. When the human lifespan had decreased to forty thousand years, he appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood.
"Kāśyapa" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in full, it is Kāśyapa. In the language of China, it means "Drinking Light.

This refers to the fact that the radiance of his body was so magnificent that it could "drink" (outshine) all other lights. When the human lifespan had decreased to twenty thousand years, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called Śākyamuni; this is translated here as "Nengrou" (Capable Sage). "Rou" (Sage) means gentle and harmonious. He is also called Śākyamuni. *Zhihuayan* states:
"This is translated as 'Capable Benevolence' and 'Silent Quiescence. Because he is silent and quiescent, he does not abide in saṃsāra;
because he is capable and benevolent, he does not abide in nirvāṇa. This auspicious title was established because his compassion and wisdom operate in tandem. *Fazhenyun* states: "The *Benqijing*..."
Śākyamuni is translated as "Able Benevolent" (Nengren). In the *Sūtra on Past Deeds* (*Pūrva-yoga-sūtra*), Muni is translated as "Silent Stillness" (Jimo).

"Able Benevolent" is his clan name (*gotra*); "Muni" is his title (*nāmadheya*). His clan name derives from his compassion for benefiting sentient beings; his title takes its meaning from his wisdom that penetrates the ultimate principle (*tattva*).

Because he benefits sentient beings, he does not abide in *nirvāṇa*; because he penetrates the ultimate principle, he does not abide in *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, "Silent" refers to the non-existence of manifested marks (*nimitta*).

As for the signs: silence demonstrates that there is no teaching to be taught; this is called the responsive manifestation of reality (this principle relies on the commentary). Furthermore, it is said:
"From the beginning of the kalpa until King Śuddhodana, my Buddha’s predecessors who established the royal line numbered eighty-four thousand two hundred and fifty-five kings in total.
Formerly, King Māndhātṛ was of the Ikṣvāku clan. His secondary queen had..."
The four sons were all intelligent and wise. The principal queen had one son who was stubborn, frivolous, and ugly.
Fearing that these four sons would usurp her royal inheritance, the principal queen used her influence to mislead the king and cause him to banish the four sons from the country.
The king acted according to her words and expelled them. At that time, the four sons obeyed the command; their mother’s sisters, born of the same womb, all wished to go with them.
The vast majority of the people delighted in following him. They reached the Śibi forest north of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*), where the terrain was level and expansive;
thereupon, they built a city and settled there. Admiring his virtuous influence, people returned like clouds, and it flourished into a great kingdom.
He then installed his younger brother as king, naming him Nīla. Several years later, the king asked about the whereabouts of his four sons. His attendants...

The minister answered in full detail. The King sighed deeply and said, "My son is Śākya; for this reason, he shall take 'Śākya' as his clan name. It is also said that it means "Straight Forest" (Zhílín).
Since he established his kingdom within a forest, he took the forest as his surname. Thus, Śākya is translated here as "Straight Forest. "Jìmò" (Silent Tranquility) is his personal name.
The *Sūtra of Past Deeds* (*Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra*) states: "As for the various Śākyas, their nature is arrogant and they speak much; yet when they see..."
The Crown Prince remained entirely silent. The King said, "It is fitting to name him Muni," for the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* refers to Śākya’s tranquility.
These four Tathāgatas appeared in succession in the world at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa (the "Auspicious Kalpa" is so called because many worthy persons appear within this eon).
The reason these names of the seven Buddhas are spoken of everywhere is, firstly, that they [appeared] within a hundred...

Because the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens have previously witnessed this within the intermediate kalpas; secondly, because our Teacher began his cultivation of the marks and signs with the Buddha Vipaśyin.
O Great Virtuous World-Honored Ones, please explain this matter for me; I now wish to explain it well.
Virtuous ones, all listen together to this explanation:
The World-Honored One (Bhagavān) is one who possesses the ten titles, whom the nine realms alike revere; he is the God among gods, the Sage among sages.
With causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, there is none equal to him in either the mundane or supramundane realms; therefore, he is named the World-Honored One.
The term "Virtuous One" (Mahābhāga) refers to one who equally rescues all sentient beings and possesses the virtue of great compassion;

one who subdues and transforms others through teaching and possesses great majestic power—hence, he is called a "Virtuous One. The phrase "speaking this matter for my sake" means that it was transmitted by relying on the teacher's oral tradition.

This demonstrates that it is not a mere speculative assertion. As for these matters, they consist of the four matters, the thirteen matters, and so forth, up to the seven methods for settling disputes.
I now wish to explain them well. To explain well means to act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings;
to have clear and lucid phrasing; to have the wording free from inversion, omission, or error; and to avoid illegal assemblies or incomplete requisites.
[This section is] missing. It is called "Well-spoken. "Virtuous ones" (bhadanta) is a term of respectful address.
From the bhikṣu who has first received full ordination (*upasampadā*) up to the elder bhikṣu of a hundred *saṃvatsara*, all should listen together.

Beginning from the *Śīlaskandha* (the Preface to the Precepts) and ending with the *Saptabuddhasamādānanirdeśasūtra* (the Sūtra of the Brief Instructions of the Seven Buddhas), one should listen attentively, focusing the ears on each part. Therefore, it says, "All virtuous ones should listen together."
Listen: Do not violate the four bases of virtue.
Just as a person whose feet are impaired is unable to travel anywhere, so it is with one who violates the precepts.

One shall not be born among gods or humans; yet if one desires to be born in the heavens or, if born among humans, one should always protect the feet of the precepts so that they suffer no damage or destruction.
(The first verse: the first two lines establish the metaphor, while the latter two lines apply the Dharma to clarify the obstruction to goodness.)
Exhortation on the Path. The first verse consists of two lines above that indicate birth in the happy realms (*sugati*), and two lines below that present both the Dharma and a simile.
A "simile" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a comparison; it employs familiar matters as comparisons so that profound teachings may be understood.
For example, if a person has feet, they can reach their destination as soon as they wish to go; but once the feet are destroyed, how could one proceed without them?

If one wishes to travel but lacks a boat, how could one hope to cross over? It is the same with the violation of the precepts: one cannot be reborn among devas or humans. "Devas" refers to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

"The form realm" (*rūpadhātu*) consists of the eighteen Brahma heavens; the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the four heavens. Together with the aforementioned six heavens of desire, these constitute the twenty-eight heavens.

"Humans" refers to those in the human destiny (*gati*) of the four continents. Since one has violated the pure precepts, it is difficult to expect the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), even as a human.
Those whose lot in heaven is severed, yet desire to be born among devas or humans, must always protect their precepts as they would their own feet;
only by not allowing them to be damaged can they be born there. Regarding the statement that upholding the precepts leads to birth among devas and humans, there are briefly two meanings:

first, the "feet" of the precepts must not be destroyed; if they are destroyed, one has no share even in the realms of humans or devas, let alone in nirvāṇa. Second, [the precepts serve as the foundation for all virtues].
These were spoken in accordance with the capacities of those present. To speak of *nirvāṇa* would have caused them fear; to speak of the human and celestial realms would have brought them joy.
For example, when the Buddha sought to deliver Nanda, Nanda was preoccupied only with his wife and children, having no desire or inclination for practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

The Buddha, knowing his intention, traveled together with him to the celestial palaces. There, Nanda saw the sons and daughters of gods everywhere sporting and enjoying themselves in bliss. Furthermore...
He saw a place where there were only goddesses and no deva-sons. Nanda asked the goddesses, "For what reason are there no deva-sons in this place?
They replied, "The Buddha has a younger brother named Nanda who has left the household life to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
He shall be born here to enjoy all manner of pleasures; we are waiting for his birth. Nanda felt joy arise in his heart.

Desiring to diligently cultivate the holy life, he later followed the Buddha into the hells. Only then did he realize that celestial pleasures had not yet been achieved while the fruits of evil were already manifest;

his heart was filled with terror. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he realized the fruit of the Path. Although it is now said that he was reborn among gods and humans, this was not the Sage’s true intention;
his actual goal was *nirvāṇa*. As it is said: "First one uses the hook of desire to lead them forth, and afterwards causes them to enter [the Way]."
Regarding the Buddha-wisdom, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "There are two perilous paths: first, that of humans and devas; second, that of the evil realms (*durgati*).

Although one may be born in the heavens and experience various supreme pleasures, when the retribution is exhausted, one falls back into the evil realms. Thus, the realms of humans and devas are not what should be desired.
Furthermore, as for the analogy of the precepts being like feet: there is no distant place they cannot reach. If one wishes to transcend directly to the pure realm, [the precepts are essential].
Regarding the highest grade of the highest birth: whether one wishes to ascend loftily beyond the triple world and forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra;

or wishes to serve the various Buddhas and hear the wondrous Dharma; or wishes for one’s nature to be tranquil and harmonious, and for the functions of illumination and application to be sovereign—none of these can be achieved without taking the precepts as the foundation.
If explained in terms of the complete observance of the precepts: if the observance of the precepts is complete, then body and mind...
Peace and happiness, because there will be no subsequent regret. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (in eleven fascicles) states:

"If a rākṣasa of craving and view begs for the entire life-buoy, it is like committing a *pārājika* offense; begging for half is like committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; one-third is like committing a *sthūlātyaya*;

as much as can be held in the hand is like committing a *pāyattika*; and as much as a speck of dust is like committing a *duṣkṛta*. Only when the buoy is complete can one cross the ocean; so too with the precepts."
One escapes the ocean of birth and death; even if concentration and wisdom do not arise, one will certainly not lose the body of a human or a deva.

It is like a charioteer entering a perilous path who, upon losing the axle-pin and breaking the axle, is filled with anxiety; so too it is for one who has violated the precepts—they harbor fear at the time of death.
Commentary: This verse takes birth and death as the perilous path. A *khaṭa* is the iron pin at the head of an axle; an axle is the rotating shaft within a wheel.

Transportation relies entirely upon the *khaṭa* and the axle. When one is actually entering the midst of the perilous path, if the *khaṭa* is lost or the axle breaks, it will be incapable of transporting one to the destination.
It is the same with the violation of precepts: the precepts possess the power of spontaneous functioning...

Merit: It transports one from the perilous path of birth and death to Nirvana, enabling one to attain peace and security. Having already violated the pure precepts, one is severed from any share in the fruits of the Path.
At the time of death, one harbors only fear; therefore, birth and death are likened to a perilous road, and the Dharma of the precepts is equal to the axle-pin.
When the precepts are violated, the signs of the evil realms appear at the time of death, just as within a perilous road.
The axle-pin is lost and the axle is broken; one is terrified and panicked, with no rescue from front or rear. As the Sūtra says:
"To close all gates to the evil realms and to reveal the correct path to humans, devas, and nirvāṇa is truly the merit of steadfastly upholding the pure precepts."
Fifth, the manifestation of the completeness or deficiency of the precepts:

Just as a person looking into a mirror feels joy or sorrow at their own beauty or ugliness, so it is with the recitation of the precepts; one feels grief or joy according to whether they are complete or violated.

Explanation: This means that it is like a person who looks at their own face in a mirror; if the features are handsome and fine, they give rise to joy, but if they are ugly, they give rise to sorrow and distress.
Therefore, the Vinaya says: "One observes oneself by means of the precepts, as a mirror reflects the image of the face."
The same applies to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). One should reflect within oneself upon what is defiled and what is pure.

If one's precepts are entirely pure, one will inwardly harbor joy and outwardly feel no shame before others. If the body of precepts is defiled, one will inwardly give rise to sorrow and distress, and outwardly feel ashamed before the Saṃgha.
Just as when two armies engage in battle, the brave advance while the timid retreat, so it is with the recitation of the precepts:
purity gives rise to peace, while defilement gives rise to fear.
Just as when two armies clash, the brave press forward and the cowardly flee in defeat, so it is for the practitioner who upholds the precepts.
When one battles against the demonic armies of the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), if one maintains a courageous and resolute will, one shall subdue those demonic hosts.

Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Just as a valiant general, well-trained in the arts of warfare, defeats his enemies regardless of death and with no regard for his own life, so too is the Son of the Buddha:
having mastered the training in the prohibitions and precepts, when the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are dispersed and destroyed..."
