○ First Precept on Sexual Misconduct:
Initial General Explanation.
Sexual misconduct is not the practice of brahmacarya. This is a shared precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. Brahma-...
The *Jālinīprabha-sūtra* states: "No woman shall intentionally commit sexual misconduct and so forth. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states:
"Due to delusion, and because of the affliction of desire as well as the objects of desire, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.

(According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, a training rule has seven meanings: first, the basis of self-benefit; second, the basis of benefiting others; third, the basis of the true meaning; fourth, the basis of majestic power; fifth, the basis of maturing sentient beings; sixth, the basis of maturing one's own Buddha-dharma; and seventh, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.)

Regarding the "bases" (*sthāna*): because ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not pure, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not manifest. Since wisdom (*prajñā*) can only arise by relying upon concentration, these [precepts] specifically receive the name of "points of training" (*śikṣāpada*). Because they are the fundamental source from which [the others] are produced, they are called "bases. These bases are what one should train in.
Therefore, it is called a *śikṣāpada* (precept). This precept is established through the conjunction of three conditions.

Second is the locus of its origin. At that time, the Buddha was in Vaiśālī (*Vaiśālī*; the *Mingyi ji* states it is also called *Viyali*, *Vyeśale*, or *Vaiśālī*; this is translated as "Extensive Splendor" [*Guangyan*]; according to the Western Regions...).

The *Record* states: "The kingdom of Vaiśālī was formerly erroneously transcribed as *Visheli*. Master Kumārajīva said: *Vai* means 'rice,' referring to what the soil is suited to produce; *śālīya* means 'vast and magnificent,' for its terrain is level, upright, and adorned. The *Jingming lüeshu* (Brief Commentary on the Vimalakīrti) says:

"This is translated as 'Vast, Adorned, and Pure. That country is broad and level, hence it is called 'Vast'; its cities and towns are splendid, hence it is called 'Adorned and Pure. Some masters translate it as 'Excellent Rice,' because it produces fine non-glutinous grain that surpasses that of other countries. Others say it means 'Excellent Path,' because the roads in the country are well-maintained and straight.

Still others say it means 'Excellent Path' because the people of that country delight in the Right Path, naturally cultivating benevolence and righteousness, requiring no sovereign, and with five hundred elders who together practice the Way and Dharma; among all the people throughout the land, there are none who do not [follow this]."
[He] returned with joy).
Third, the occasion concerning the person:

At that time, there was Sūdena-putra from the village of Kalandaka (Regarding "the village of Kalandaka," the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states it is the name of a mountain mouse). At that time, in Vaiśālī...

The king entered the mountains and slept beneath a tree. A venomous snake was about to emerge and harm him, but a rat came to that spot under the tree and screeched to wake the king. Grateful for its kindness, the king provided food from the village to this mountain rat;

consequently, the village was named Kalandaka Village. In that village lived an elder who possessed four hundred billion gold coins. Because of this village, the king bestowed upon him the title "Kalandaka Elder. This elder’s wealth was immeasurable, yet he had no children.
He prayed to the deities, and thus Sūdena (translated here as "Obtained") was born to him. In that village, there were many...
Possessing abundant wealth and jewels, his faith was firm and steadfast. He left the household life to pursue the Way.
At that time, grain was expensive and it was difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood through begging. Then, Sūdena thought to himself:
"I should now lead the bhikṣus to the village of Kalandaka to beg for food. Because of me, the bhikṣus will obtain great offerings and be able to cultivate the holy life."
He set out. "I shall cause my kinsmen to joyfully practice giving and perform various meritorious deeds.
Having formed this thought, he took the bhikṣu and went to the village of Kalandaka. When his mother heard that her son had returned, she went to where her son was and said to him:
"You may now abandon the path and return home. Why? Your father has already died; I am now alone, and I fear that our family wealth will be confiscated by the authorities.
He replied, "I cannot now abandon the path to practice such unrighteousness.
I now find great joy in the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and am cultivating the unsurpassed path. Although his mother thus exhorted him up to three times, her son refused her three times as well.
He then ordered that she be given to his wife so that the lineage of seed would not be severed. The son said to his mother, "This matter is very easy;
I am able to do it. At that time, before the Buddha had yet established the precepts, he did not perceive the faults of desire.

He then took his wife by the arm and led her into the garden, where they committed the three acts of impurity. At that moment, a ghost in the garden whose life had ended was immediately conceived in her womb.

In the ninth month, a son was born. He was given the name "Seed" (Bīja). [Question: For what reason do the three actions not become impure? Furthermore, why do they not abide in the second, nor reach the fourth? [Answer: The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

Because she was pregnant, his mother asked him three times; once he had obtained a son, she ceased her questioning. It was only after this had occurred three times that he finally obtained a son; thus, he committed the third act of impurity.

After Sudinna had committed this impurity, he was constantly filled with grief and anxiety. His fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), having learned the reason for his distress, went to inform the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. The World-Honored One asks when he knows [the answer], and does not ask when he knows;
he asks at the proper time, and does not ask when it is not the proper time; he asks when the matter is appropriate, and does not ask when it is inappropriate.
Knowing the time and the matter being appropriate, the World-Honored One asked: "Sudinna, did you indeed engage in unchaste conduct with your former wife? As...

"World-Honored One, I have committed an impure act [by speaking thus]. Second, in the Sanskrit *bhāranadina*, this is translated here as 'the former second,' because the wife follows after the husband."
[This is] the second [reason] for its name). At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Sūdena:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, nor is it the way of a śramaṇa. (Master Shi said: "In both the Buddha-dharma and the non-Buddhist paths, all who have left the household life are called śramaṇas. Master Zhao says: 'It is the general name for those who have left the household life.

In the language of Qin, the meaning is translated as 'diligent practice'—practicing diligently to attain nirvāṇa. The Āgama-sūtra says: 'Abandoning affection and love, one leaves the household life to cultivate the Way, restraining the sense faculties, remaining unstained by external desires, and possessing a heart of compassion toward all without exception...')"

They do not feel resentment when harmed; they do not rejoice in encountering pleasure, nor do they grieve upon meeting with suffering. Because they can endure all things like the earth, they are called *śramaṇas*. The "Treatise on Sacrifices" (*Jiaoshi zhi*) in the *Book of the Later Han* (*Hou Hanshu*) states: "*Śramaṇa* in the language of Han means 'one who has stilled the mind. They shave their hair and leave the household, severing worldly attachments and washing away desire."

"And thus one returns to non-action. The *Ruiying* [Sutra] says: "One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa. The original purpose of the text was for those who sever worldly attachments and wash away desires to leave the household life; now, if one instead engages in impure matters, one is not a śramaṇa.
It is not a pure practice; it is not a compliant practice (meaning it is not a practice that conforms to *nirvāṇa*). It is something that ought not to be done.
Sūdena, how can you, within this pure Dharma leading even to *nirvāṇa* through the exhaustion of craving, engage in impure sexual conduct with a former wife?

(Regarding "the exhaustion of craving and *nirvāṇa*: the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that it is because of craving for the three realms that sentient beings are unable to achieve liberation; they are bound and fettered by craving. When [craving] is exhausted...)

It is cessation. The exhaustion of craving is itself nirvāṇa. Furthermore, "nir" means non-arising, and "vāṇa" means non-ceasing; this refers to the meaning of neither arising nor ceasing. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"It would be better to place one's male organ in the mouth of a venomous serpent than to place it within the female organ. Why? Because one will not fall into the evil realms on account of that.
However, if one violates a woman, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will fall into the three evil realms. Why is this?"

Through countless skillful means, I have taught the Dharma for severing desire (that is to say, the Tathāgata has censured desire as impure and instructed all sentient beings to eliminate the craving of desire; once the craving of desire has withered away).

Then, exhausting this remaining physical form, one shall not undergo further existence. One must sever the perception of desire, extinguish the thought of desire, and dispel the fever of desire (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"The perception of desire" refers to the mind conceiving of a woman while the body and speech remain unmoved; "the thought of desire" means that regarding all sexual desires, one must not only keep the body, speech, and mental intentions unmoved, but must also bring them to a complete cessation; "the fever of desire" refers to the blazing fire of lust when two bodies unite, hence it is called the 'fever of desire').
I say that desire is like fire (if one does not touch it, one remains unharmed; once touched, one is scorched and consumed). It is like grasping a torch of straw—how could it fail to burn the body?

It is also like the fruit of a tree, which falls as soon as it ripens; so too is the commission of sexual misconduct. When the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) have ripened, one falls into the three evil destinies. Furthermore, it is like something borrowed; it is like a dry bone;

it is also like a piece of meat (referring to the physical forms of men and women, which are formed through the temporary borrowing of the combination of the four great elements. They are originally illusory transformations and not real. As for "dry bones" and "pieces of meat," this refers to the human form composed of skin and flesh enveloping the bones;

yet in a single day they may disintegrate, the skin and flesh fall away, and the appearance of white bones is revealed. Since such things are impure, how can one become stained by desire? It is like what is seen in a dream (that is, as in a dream...).

Regarding the things one perceives, one should not give rise to joy and yet falsely give rise to a joyful mind; one should not give rise to anger or fear and yet falsely give rise to anger or fear. Now, sexual desire is likewise thus: one should not give rise to defilement and yet falsely give rise to stained attachment.

It is like treading upon the edge of a blade (how could there not be the peril of wounding the body?). It is like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun (the sun and the new vessel can cause the water to evaporate;

lust is likewise able to destroy all wholesome dharmas). It is like the head of a venomous serpent, like a whirling wheel-blade, like standing upon a sharp spear-point, or like being pierced by a sharp halberd.

As for "the head of a venomous serpent" and "a whirling wheel-blade," these things must not be touched; if touched, they can destroy one's life. Lust is likewise: it can destroy the Dharma-body and wisdom.
"Life! To be pierced by sharp spears and halberds is a source of suffering and loathing; so too is lustful desire—it is deeply loathsome and utterly detestable.

Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "All wholesome dharmas are not called 'binding' (*saṃvara*);
why then is it said only that one 'binds the precepts'? The answer is: the precepts are the root of all virtues. To speak only of 'binding the precepts' is itself to encompass all bindings.")
It comprises ten points of meaning: first, it brings the Saṅgha together; second, it causes the Saṅgha to rejoice; third, it causes the Saṅgha to dwell in peace and happiness;
fourth, it inspires faith in those who have not yet believed; fifth, it increases the faith of those who already believe; sixth, it brings those difficult to discipline into submissiveness;
seventh, it grants peace and happiness to those possessed of shame and remorse; eighth, it cuts off the outflows (*āsrava*) of the present; ninth, it cuts off [the outflows] of the future.
The outflows. The ten principles for ensuring the long endurance of the True Dharma (within the two hundred and fifty precepts, these ten points are all collected; they are not repeated below).

First, gathering in the Saṃgha (this refers to the Tathāgata’s formulation of the various rules of training, subtle conducts, and dignified deportment, which he maintains with purity so that laymen and laywomen, upon seeing them, do not give rise to derision or slander;

when such derision does not arise, they spontaneously develop the aspiration for awakening; having developed this aspiration, they receive transformation; and having received transformation, they are gathered into and take refuge in the Jewel of the Saṃgha).

Second, causing the Saṃgha to rejoice (meaning that the Tathāgata’s formulation of the precepts causes the bhikṣus to abide within the discipline; they cleanse away mundane sentiments, so that wholesome dharmas flourish daily and the six points of harmony remain unimpaired, allowing them to dwell in supreme peace;
hence it is said, "causing the Saṃgha to rejoice").
Third, causing the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness (*saṃghasya sukha-sthiti*). (The Tathāgata instructs the bhikṣus: "This action incurs no offense; this action incurs an offense.

He prohibits and brings to an end all evil dharmas so as not to cause the bhikṣus to commit various evils, and he demonstrates the path of practicing good so that there may be no fear of the miserable realms. By ensuring they attain peace and happiness in both this life and future lives, it is called "causing the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness.")

Fourth, to cause those who have not yet gained faith to gain faith (because the precepts were established for this purpose: when bhikṣus carefully observe the Vinaya and their deportment is pure, those without faith, upon seeing them, will develop faith and say:).

The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are diligent and energetic; their observance of the precepts and their dignified deportment are all fully perfected. Having seen this, they give rise to faith. Therefore it is said: "Those who have not yet believed are caused to believe."

Fifth, causing those who already have faith to increase it (that is, when those who have left the household life hold their faith firmly and practice the various prohibitions and precepts as taught, people of the world see and hear of this, and their pure faith increases all the more).
This is called "great reverence" (and is termed the increase of faith).

Sixth, those who are difficult to tame are made compliant (referring to those who lack shame and remorse; when they commit unwholesome deeds and feel no sense of shame, the Buddha establishes the precepts, and if there are any who violate them, the Saṃgha disciplines them according to the Vinaya, ensuring they dare not do so again.
This is called "the ability to tame those who are difficult to tame").

Seventh, those possessing a sense of shame and remorse obtain peace and happiness (meaning that once the Buddha has established the precepts, he prevents shameless bhikṣus from entering the assembly for formal acts (*karmavācanā*) or reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, and prevents them from harassing bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma;
thus, those possessing shame and remorse are enabled to dwell in peace and happiness).

Eighth, the elimination of present outflows (this refers to sentient beings who do not restrain the three poisons and let loose the six sense faculties, giving rise to outflowing activities toward non-sentient objects;
the Tathāgata, based on these circumstances, establishes precepts to eliminate these outflows so they do not arise again—this is called the elimination of present outflows).

Ninth, severing future outflows (*āsrava*): (This refers to ordinary worldlings who do not sever the five sensual desires; yet by practicing unwholesome dharmas, they fall into the hells in subsequent lives and undergo various bitter sufferings.

It is not merely a single experience, but they transmigrate therein for incalculable eons. The Tathāgata proclaims this precept for them; by relying on and cultivating this precept, they cause them to realize the fruit of the Path and no longer receive a body in future existence. Therefore, it is called "severing future outflows.")

The Ten Ways for the True Dharma to Endure Long (The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "There are three aspects of the True Dharma: first, the endurance of the True Dharma through study; second, the endurance of the True Dharma through faithful acceptance; and third, the endurance of the True Dharma through the attainment of the Path.

What is meant by 'the endurance of the True Dharma through study'? It refers to the study of the Tripiṭaka. All that has been taught by the Buddha for its long-term endurance is called the True Dharma. Within the Tripiṭaka, the twelve dhūtas, the rules of decorum, the subtle practices, dhyāna, and samādhi—these are called 'the endurance of the True Dharma through faithful acceptance.

The four fruits of śrāmaṇya and nirvāṇa—these are called 'the endurance of the True Dharma through the attainment of the Path. Because the Tathāgata established the precepts, he caused the bhikṣus to follow and train in accordance with the Vinaya. Because [the Buddha] established the precepts, he caused the bhikṣus to conform to and train in the Vinaya. Due to...

Because one studies the precepts, the mind is rectified and the Vinaya is upheld. Because the Vinaya is upheld, one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because of meditative concentration, one attains the fruits of the Path and the True Dharma abides for a long time; therefore, study is the beginning.
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak thus: "If a bhikṣu commits an impure act, practicing the way of sexual desire, this bhikṣu is one of defeat (pārājika);
he is not to live in community. Thus, the Blessed One established the precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a Vatsiputra bhikṣu who became sorrowful and took no pleasure in the holy life (brahmacarya).
He immediately returned home and engaged in unchaste conduct with his former wife. He thought to himself, "I fear I have committed a pārājika offense. What should I do?
He then spoke to his fellow students, saying, "Excellent, elders! Please inform the Buddha of this matter for me, and act according to what the Buddha teaches."
"I shall practice these teachings. At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Foolish man! You have committed a pārājika offense; you may not dwell in communion.

(The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says: "The Buddha rebuked this foolish man. The Buddha possesses great kindness and great compassion, and he is never harsh in speech. Why then did he call him a 'foolish man'? The answer is: The Buddha’s words are spoken according to reality and are not harsh speech.

Because this sentient being is bound by all fetters and afflictions and is fully possessed of folly, the Buddha rebukes and subdues him out of his twofold mind of compassion—just as a current preceptor or ācārya instructs and admonishes a disciple.)
To call someone a "fool" is not considered harsh speech. If there is another person who does not delight in the pure life, one may listen to their request to relinquish the precepts and return home;
yet, if they later wish to go forth again to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should ordain them, allowing them to go forth and receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

Thereupon, he further established the rule against returning the precepts and against being lax in the precepts without repentance (this was the second establishment of the precept). At that time, there was a mendicant bhikṣu who relied upon...

Dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyaka*). According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun): "One who dwells in the forest does so because remaining among the assembly involves many affairs and much affliction, which obstruct the cultivation of wholesome dharmas. If one possesses an abundance of wisdom, however, one may remain among the assembly."

One who has heard much, seen much, debated much, and spoken much may have generated wisdom, yet lacks sufficient meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Such a person should dwell in a quiet place to cultivate the mind. Conversely, one who possesses abundant concentration should dwell among the assembly to seek extensive knowledge and insight. For this reason, [it is said].

[He] dwelt in the forest. There was a female macaque who had previously lived in that forest. At one time, a bhikṣu seeking alms went to the village for alms and returned to eat his meal in the forest.
Having finished eating, he gave the remainder of his food to this macaque. In this way, she gradually became tame and followed behind the bhikṣu;
eventually, she would not leave even when he tried to catch her with his hand. The bhikṣu then seized the macaque.
A monkey. While they were engaging in unchaste conduct, a large number of bhikṣus were inspecting their dwellings and arrived at that grove.
At that time, the macaque stood before the bhikṣus and displayed its lewd gestures. Then the bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"Could it be that another monk has committed this act of impurity? He watched him in a secluded place, and having seen him, he came and said, "Has the Tathāgata not prohibited it, saying that a monk must not commit an act of impurity?
[The other] replied, "The Tathāgata’s prohibition concerns men and women; he did not prohibit [it with] animals. The monks went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha, by means of countless...
Having thus rebuked him through skillful means, he entered upon the first *pārājika*. From this day forward, the precept should be recited as follows:
"Regarding the four established characteristics of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu shares the same precepts with other bhikṣus, yet does not return his precepts, nor confesses his weakness in the precepts, and commits an impure act..."
[Engaging in] sexual intercourse, even with an animal; this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in community.
Explanation of the Terms: Regarding "if a bhikṣu," there are eight kinds of bhikṣus. First, the *nāma-bhikṣu* (bhikṣu by name).

This refers to, for example, when people in the world wish to call out to a man or woman, they establish a name and address them as "bhikṣu. Or, when a donor invites a bhikṣu, even a śrāmaṇera who has not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is included within the number of bhikṣus; this is the "bhikṣu by name."

1) A bhikṣu [in the true sense]. 2) One who resembles a bhikṣu (referring to those such as non-Buddhists or laypeople who shave their hair and beards, wear the kāṣāya robe, and have received full ordination without a preceptor; they resemble bhikṣus only in physical appearance).

Yet in reality they are not bhikṣus; therefore, they are called "semblance bhikṣus. Third, those who call themselves bhikṣus (such as when the Elder Ānanda saw a precept-violating bhikṣu walking at night and asked, "Hey, who are you?
and the precept-violating bhikṣu replied, "I am a bhikṣu"; or likewise, a person living as a thief who is not a bhikṣu but calls himself a bhikṣu).

Fourth, the "Come-hither bhikṣus" (meaning that when the Tathāgata perceives that a person’s faculties have matured and they are capable of being converted, and they desire to leave the household life, the Buddha calls out to them, "Come-hither bhikṣu! In my Dharma, may you find joy.")

"Practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to reach the exhaustion of the source of suffering. Before the Buddha had finished speaking, his hair and beard fell away naturally; the *kāṣāya* robes were upon his body and the alms bowl was in his hand, as if he were a bhikṣu of a hundred years' seniority. 5. The Bhikṣu Who Seeks Alms:

This refers to one who does not accept invitations for meals but, for as long as he lives, sustains himself by begging for food. Because he remains far removed from wrong livelihoods, he is called a "bhikṣu who seeks alms.

6. The Bhikṣu Who Wears Cut-and-Sewn Robes: This refers to robes whose value might be hundreds of thousands or millions. Once a bhikṣu has obtained them, he cuts them up and wears them. By destroying their original value through sewing them together with needle and thread, he ruins their fineness and softness, thereby making them into coarse garments. He thus transforms the original [fabric] using tree bark.

"Color" refers to old cloth. One who is able to wear the *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (patchwork robe) is called a bhikṣu who wears the *khaṇḍa-cīvara*. Seventh, the bhikṣu who has destroyed the *saṃyojana-kleśas* (fetters and afflictions). "Fetters and afflictions" (*saṃyojana-kleśa*) refers to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*).

First, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-moha*) are clarified; subsequently, the delusions of thought (*vitarka-moha*) are clarified. The verse states: "The basis of suffering includes all [afflictions]; for accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), there are seven, eight, and two respectively. The view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are excluded from the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

In the higher realms, anger (*pratigha*) does not function; thus there are eighty-eight [delusions]. These are the delusions caused by the conceptual grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). In total, there are ten types of these delusions: namely, the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nivaraṇa*) and the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa*). "Dull" means sluggish or slow-witted. This refers to these five kinds of false delusions which arise through the investigation of the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

The five types of sharp afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; in contrast to the sharp, they are called dull afflictions. These are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. Regarding the five sharp afflictions: "sharp" carries the meaning of being quick and acute, meaning these five kinds of delusive confusion arise as soon as a thought moves, being constantly present even in moments of haste. They are:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Now, the severing of delusions does not go beyond the Four Noble Truths—namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). This causes one to know suffering, sever the origin, aspire to cessation, and cultivate the path.

Regarding the delusions that are grasped, there are those that obstruct the Truths and those that do not obstruct the Truths. Among the Four Truths, some [afflictions] are fully present and others are not. As for "suffering possessing all," this means that the ten afflictions are fully present within the category of the Truth of Suffering. [The same applies to] the Truth of Origin...

In the two truths of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), each possesses seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), excluding the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); thus it is said that three underlying tendencies are absent. In the truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are only eight underlying tendencies, excluding the two views of self-identity.

This is according to the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which together possess thirty-two underlying tendencies. Regarding the fact that anger (*vyāpāda*) does not function in the higher realms: this means that because the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*) is superior in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the underlying tendency of anger does not function.

Therefore, among the four truths, anger is excluded from each one; that is to say, under the truth of Suffering (*duḥkha*) there are nine, while the two truths of Origin (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*) have six, and the truth of the Path has only seven. Thus, it should be known that in the upper form realm there are only twenty-eight underlying tendencies, and the same applies to the formless realm. Across the three realms, there are a total of eighty-eight categories. Hence it is said:

There are eighty-eight *anuśayas* (proclivities). Once these delusions have been severed, one realizes the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Next, the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is explained; it is subtle and difficult to sever, and thus it is only through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that it is eliminated.

Regarding the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are four: namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), ignorance (*moha*), and pride (*māna*). In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), all four delusions are fully present. In the two upper realms, each excludes one—hatred—therefore, the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) has three: greed, ignorance, and pride; the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is likewise. Collectively, these are termed the "ten truths of cultivation" (*daśa-bhāvanā-satya*).

If one combines these with the aforementioned eighty-eight categories of delusions of insight (*darśana-heya*), they are termed the "ninety-eight proclivities" (*aṣṭānavati-anuśaya*). Furthermore, because the delusions of cultivation are difficult to sever, they provide the moisture for seven births. Now, the three realms are divided into nine stages (*bhūmi*). The single stage of the Desire Realm is called the "Stage of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies" (*pañca-gati-saṃkīrṇa-vāsa-bhūmi*).

The four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are: the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*), which is the first dhyāna; the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhija-prītisukha-bhūmi*), which is the second dhyāna; the stage of sublime bliss free from joy (*prītivirāga-sukha-bhūmi*), which is the third dhyāna; and the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣāsmṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*), which is the fourth dhyāna. As for the four stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):

First is the stage of the Sphere of Infinite Space; second is the stage of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; third is the stage of the Sphere of Nothingness; and fourth is the stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. Thus, it is said that there are nine stages within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Furthermore, these afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are divided into eighty-one grades. Within each stage there are nine grades, totaling eighty-one. This means that once a person who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has severed the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they enter the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to sever the nine grades of the afflictions of thought belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The reason they are the strongest and most difficult to sever is that the mind of the five desires of the desire realm is so powerful; they nourish seven births. Specifically, the highest-of-the-high grade alone nourishes two births: two births in the heavens and two returns to the human world. The high-middle [grade]...

The upper and lower grades of this category together moisten two births before they are severed; the middle and upper grades alone moisten one birth; and the middle-middle and middle-lower grades together moisten one birth. Only when these six grades are severed does one realize the second fruit, which is called the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakṛdāgāmin).

It is like the case of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*): because their afflictions have not yet been severed, the lower-upper grade alone moistens half a lifetime, while the lower-middle and lower-lower grades together moisten the other half. Thus, combined, they moisten one full lifetime. This refers to the exhaustion of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm; only then does one realize the third fruit, called the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Residing in the five heavens of the Non-returners, they do not return to be born among humans, as they have already destroyed all afflictions of the desire realm. Remaining are seventy-two grades of residual afflictions from the two upper realms.

Because the power of concentration increases when a sage of the third fruit cultivates the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), these are somewhat easier to sever. If these afflictions are completely exhausted, one immediately transcends the three realms and is called an Arhat; this means "no-birth," for they will never return again.

The three realms undergo *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death). Regarding the term "segmented": "segment" (*fen*) refers to a limit; "section" (*duan*) refers to a physical portion. This means that within the retributions of the three realms, there are limits to the length of one's lifespan, and there are physical portions consisting of large or small bodies;

none of these escape birth and death, which is termed "segmented birth and death. The two aforementioned delusions—the eighty-eight *anuśaya* (latent tendencies)—are called "delusions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). This refers to all views residing in the ground. Regarding the term "all": it encompasses the delusions of view throughout the three realms. "Upper guests and lower dust" refers to the delusions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*).

These all arise from sentient beings' failure to understand the objects of external dust, giving rise to various kinds of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). If one observes with wisdom, the essence of these delusions is fundamentally empty; thus, the Dharma...

When the principle of nature is manifest, how could delusion exist? Thus the Sūtra says: "That which does not abide is called a guest; this is the meaning of 'guest. As for the "two objects," they refer to subtle delusions that are able to defile the pure true nature, like rays of light streaming through a window crack.

The manifestations of various sensory objects (*dharmas*) can also disturb the nature of empty space. If wisdom is brought forth and one realizes that delusion is fundamentally non-existent, then the principle (*li*) manifests before one; how then could sensory objects exist? A sutra says: "Stillness and tranquility are called emptiness; agitation and movement are called sensory objects.

This is the meaning of "sensory objects" (*dust*). Regarding the afflictions of conceptual delusion within the three realms: the nine grades of the desire realm are called the "ground of abiding in desire-love"; the thirty-six grades of the form realm are called the "ground of abiding in form-love";

and the thirty-six grades of the formless realm are called the "ground of abiding in existence-love. Collectively, these are termed the "afflictions of the four grounds of abiding," which induce the fruit of segmented birth and death within the three realms. If one can eliminate the fruits of the three realms, the causes of the four grounds of abiding will perish, and one will realize *nirvāṇa with remainder*. These are the persons of the Two Vehicles.

This is the ultimate fruit (the bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters). A bhikṣu who has received the full ordination (*mahā-upasampadā*) through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma and has attained his status is a bhikṣu.

Among these, if one has received the full ordination through the formal procedure of the fourfold motion in accordance with the Dharma, has attained his status, and dwells within the dharma of a bhikṣu, this is the meaning of "bhikṣu" (here, the final sense is taken). [He is] a bhikṣu in common with other bhikṣus.

This refers to those who, like other bhikṣus, have received full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, have attained their status in accordance with the Dharma, and abide within the discipline of the bhikṣus;
this is called the meaning of "shared with the bhikṣus. What is meant by "identical precepts"?
After I have established the precepts for my disciples, they would rather die than transgress them; herein, they share the same precepts as the other bhikṣus (that is, the precepts).

Because their essence is non-dual, it is the "identical precept" (meaning that the characteristics of the precepts are not distinct). It is the "equal precept" (meaning that the conduct of a bhikṣu with a hundred years of seniority and a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts are equal in their practice of the precepts, with no difference between them).

This is called the identical precept. What is meant by "not abandoning the precepts"? Abandoning [the precepts] means returning [to the lay life]. [The following are cases where one does not abandon the precepts: abandoning the precepts due to insanity;...

One abandons the precepts through mental distraction; one abandons the precepts through physical pain and affliction; one abandons the precepts before a mute person; one abandons the precepts before a deaf person; one abandons the precepts before a person who is both mute and deaf;

one abandons the precepts before a person who is insane, mentally distracted, afflicted by pain, mute, or deaf; one abandons the precepts before a person from the Central Land (Madhyadeśa) who is from a Borderland (Pratyantajanapada);

Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Its shape resembles that of a vulture; for this reason, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Third, the person who initiated the occasion:
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Rājagṛha named Dhaniya, the son of a potter (a "potter" refers to a tile-maker; this bhikṣu...).
Kūṭadanta was the son of a potter. He lived in a secluded place, dwelling in a single thatched hut. Once, he entered a village to beg for food.
Later, some wood-gatherers broke his thatched hut and carried it away. When the bhikṣu returned from begging, he thought to himself: "I possess my own craft;
why should I not mix clay to build a complete, finished house of baked brick? I shall take wood and cow dung to fire it. Thus, he built a house.
It was red like fire. At that time, the World-Honored One descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and saw from afar that this house was red like fire.
Knowing [the reason] yet asking on purpose, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus about this matter. The bhikṣus reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked them: "From this day forward, you must not construct anything entirely red."
A tile-roofed house. The builder commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the bhikṣus: "Gather together and go quickly to break it down.

(The *Śāriputra-vinaya-saṃgraha*, or *Sudarsana-vinaya*, states: "The bhikṣu Dhanika built a house using his own materials. When the house was finished, why did the Tathāgata have it broken down? The answer is: It was broken because this house was impure;

it followed the methods of non-Buddhists. Furthermore, there is another reason: sentient beings who lack compassion build such tile-roofed houses. Dhanika was the son of a potter; he was skilled at mixing mud and constructing houses with windows and door-bolts.")

It was all constructed of clay, with only the door panels being made of wood. He took firewood, cow dung, and straw, and coated the exterior with red earth. After firing it until it was thoroughly baked, it became as red as fire; when struck, it rang out like the sound of a bell, and when the wind blew through the windows and doors, it was like the music of an orchestra.
When Sandhāna saw that the house had collapsed, at that time there was a timber-guardian belonging to the King of Magadha.
Being on intimate terms with Dhanika, he spoke to the wood-watcher, saying, "Do you know King Bimbisāra? Will he give me timber?
The man replied, "If the king gives it, you may take as much as you wish—good or bad, much or little—except for the essential timber reserved by the king.

The bhikṣu then immediately cut down [the trees] and carried them away. (The Sanskrit name Bimbisāra is translated here as "Mushi" [Model-Real]; this is because his physical form is full and substantial.)

[He was] called *Pariṇāha*, also known as *Chāyā-dṛḍha*. "Shadow" (*chāyā*) refers to his shadow [due to his height]. He is also called *Chāyā-jaya*, or *Bimbisāra*, which means "one with handsome features. All these names take the sense of being robust and excellent in appearance. His stature was tall and large;

his temperament and conduct were fierce and bold, and he constantly engaged in military expeditions himself. At that time, there was a high minister in charge of city affairs who, upon visiting the timber yard, saw the essential timber reserved for the King scattered in disarray after being cut and trimmed. Having learned the reason for this, he informed the King: "The bhikṣu Dhaniya..."
Later, he went to the king’s presence. The king said, "Venerable One, you ought to die. The king thought to himself, "Why should I deprive an ordained person of their life with such meager materials?
This is improper. Having rebuked himself, he released him. The ministers were indignant, and the laypeople of Rājagṛha censured him.
When the monks of few desires heard of this, they informed the Buddha. For these reasons, the Buddha [instituted the rule].
The Saṃgha of bhikṣus was assembled. Knowing [the situation], he asked intentionally: "Bhikṣu Dhanika, is it true that you have done this?
He replied: "It is indeed true, Blessed One. The Blessed One then rebuked him with countless skillful means. There was a bhikṣu named Kāru.

Originally a high minister of the king, he was well-versed in worldly laws (Kāla—sometimes rendered as Kāru or Kālu; in the language of Qin, "Black"). This bhikṣu had been an old minister of King Bimbisāra and was well-acquainted with the ways of the world;

therefore, the World-Honored One questioned him, and subsequently, the precepts were established according to the legal systems of the country. He was sitting in the assembly not far from the Buddha. Knowing [the answer], the World-Honored One asked nonetheless:
"According to the laws of the kingdom, for the taking of what amount of property does one deserve death? The bhikṣu replied: "If one takes..."
Five *kārsāpaṇas*, or an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, constitutes a capital offense. The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The foolish man Dhaniya (the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that he is called a 'foolish man' because, out of folly, he dug up earth, trampled mud, and gathered firewood to burn it, whereby many sentient beings died;

hence he is called a foolish man) has committed the first transgression of the precepts among the various bases for outflows (*āsrava*). From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for all bhikṣus."
Fourth, the definition of the precept: If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind, according to the nature of taking what is not given,
and is consequently seized by a king or a royal minister, or is executed, bound, or driven out of the country, being told, "You are a thief."
You are deluded; you have no understanding. This bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not dwell in communion.
Explanation of the Terms: There are four kinds of "villages" (*grāma*). First, those surrounded by walls; second, those with fences; third, those with incomplete fences or walls;

and fourth, those with houses on all four sides. (The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "A settlement" [*sanniveśa*] refers to that which contains lanes, streets, shops, and marketplaces; this is called a "settlement.")

"Those who have fallen" refers to households outside the village; they are called "fallen" (lao), and thus it is termed a "village settlement" (poluo). A "secluded and quiet place" refers to a tranquil location outside the village. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "An empty space."

Beyond the walls and enclosures, excluding the village boundary, all is designated as open space (*śūnyadeśa*). As for the village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*): it extends from the fence not far away to wherever the tracks of many people reach; this entire area is called the village boundary. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Outside the village, within the distance of an arrow-shot, where a person of conscience performs their bodily functions—that is called a village; the place where they walk is the boundary. Regarding "not giving": when another does not relinquish [the object], the one who takes it is a thief.

Regarding the offense of taking what is not given with a thieving mind: as for the legal standard of "five coins" or "the value of five coins" (according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, in Jambudvīpa, among all national laws, rites, and music, Rājagṛha is taken as the standard;

according to the laws of the kingdom of Rājagṛha, stealing more than five coins constitutes a grave offense. The Buddha, relying on this law, established that stealing to the extent of five coins incurs a *pārājika* offense.

Thus, wherever the Buddha-dharma currently exists within Jambudvīpa, the limit of five coins defines a *pārājika* offense. If a country does not use coins, the crime is established based on the equivalent of five coins). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: twenty *māsaka* make one *kākaṇī*.
*Kārṣāpaṇa*: One *kārṣāpaṇa* is divided into four parts; one part is five *māṣakas*. All Buddhas of the past and future have, by means of one part, established the *pārājika* offense.

All Buddhas do not differ in establishing the four *pārājikas*; they neither increase nor decrease them. Therefore, the Tathāgata established the second *pārājika* by means of one part. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One copper coin is worth sixteen small coins. As for the "king": [text continues].
He attains mastery. He is not subject to others (pervading the Three Powers, presiding over the myriad things, transforming through non-action;

when the Way prevails in the world, he bestows grace upon the people). As for "great ministers," they are various ministers who assist the king. "Seizing" (the *Saṃghāṭa-vinaya* says: the king’s agents seize him, either by grasping his hand or other parts of his body;

this is called seizing). "Killing" (depriving him of the life-faculty). "Binding" (the *Saṃghāṭa-vinaya* says: binding him with a house, or binding him with a city, or binding him with timber, or placing him in shackles and fetters, or placing him in stocks and manacles; this is called binding). "Expelling."

"Expelling from the country" means being expelled from the village, expelled from the city, and expelled from the kingdom; this is called "expelling. "You are a thief! You are deluded! You have no knowledge!"—these are words of reproach. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:

"You are a thief" is a general designation for delusion (*moha*). "Having no knowledge," and so forth, is a specific explanation of ignorance (*avidyā*). At the very time one performs the act of theft, because of delusion and a lack of knowledge, one employs the means of stealing. One lacks fear regarding the manifestation of the dharma or fear regarding the future;

it should be understood that these constitute the causes of theft. To commit such theft clearly defines the karmic act of stealing; whether by force or by stealth, provided one does not inform the owner, it is all termed "theft."
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense. If any condition is lacking, the offense is mitigated.

First, there must be the intent to steal; second, the object must belong to an owner; third, one must perceive the object as belonging to an owner; fourth, the value must be five coins or more; fifth, the object must be moved from its original location.

**Determination of the Offense:** Within this, there are seventy-two phrases concerning the commission of the offense. Now, removing the redundancies and retaining only the distinct cases, there are ten phrases in total:
taking with one's own hand; taking by watching over it; taking by dispatching another person; and taking while perceiving it as not being one's own property.

If one takes something not for temporary use, nor with the original intention of taking it (the character "ben" [original] is identical to "tong" [same]; this is likely a scribal error), but rather takes another's property while perceiving it as another's property;

if it is moved from its original place, and there is an owner, and one perceives there is an owner; and if one takes what is protected by another while perceiving it as protected by another—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

"Places" refers to: whether on the ground, or above the ground, or in a vehicle, or while carrying a load, or in open space, or in a tree, or in a village, or in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), or in a field, or at a site, or in a boat, or in water;
or crossing a pass or barrier privately without paying taxes; or taking another's entrusted property; or [taking] water or *śīrṣapāda* (willow twigs).

The fruits of trees, grasses, and shrubs; and footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed sentient beings—whether sharing in the same wealth and karma, or being sought after, or being waited for, or being guarded, or patrolling a narrow pass—these are called "locations.
Regarding "earth locations," these refer to treasures hidden within the earth that have not yet been extracted: the seven jewels, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, jade, and conch shells.

Agate; images made of gold or silver; clothing and robes; or whatever other items required for the earth that belong to an owner—if one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with a thieving mind, whether by dragging or pulling them away—("dragging" meaning to connect, "pulling" meaning to lead;

to drag and pull something from the ground and carry it away is called "taking by dragging and pulling")—or by burying them, or by lifting them and moving them from their original location—at the moment they are first moved, it is a *pārājika*.

*Yi*. If one employs skillful means with the intention to lift [the object] but does not lift it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). (The subsequent definitions of the offenses are all the same. Regarding "on the ground":

gold, silver, and even whatever items are required belong to the owner. Regarding "in a vehicle": there are four kinds of vehicles: elephant-vehicles, [horse-vehicles, carriage-vehicles, and palanquin-vehicles].
Horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, foot-vehicles, or whatever other vehicles there may be— all are called "vehicles. If upon these vehicles there are gold,
silver, the seven treasures, or even any necessary items that have an owner, and one takes such a vehicle from path to path,
from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from a pit to dry land, or from dry land...

Reaching up into the pit, as for those who carry loads—whether carried on the head, on the shoulders, on the back, or in the arms, or whatever other loads there may be—if upon these various loads there are gold, silver, the seven treasures, or even necessary items that have an owner; [one should not take them].
If one takes up a load, it may range from path to path, even into a pit. As for empty spaces,
they include places where the wind blows wool, or cotton, or *kucala*, or *cārapaṇi* (this is the name of a garment meaning "ash-water"),
or *kṣauma* (linen), or hemp, or silk-cotton, or *pāṭalambava* (in Chinese, "silk"), or *tūttura* (this means "fine cloth").
Whether it be a goose, a crane, a peacock, a parrot, a myna bird,
or any other possessed object located in a high place— such as an object placed upon a tree,
a wall, a fence, a peg, a dragon-tooth peg, a clothes rack, a rope bed, a wooden bed, or upon a large or small mat, or a pillow.
On the ground above, there are the seven treasures, gold and silver, and even all necessary items that have owners.

Regarding "village dwellings," there are four types of villages as mentioned above. If within a village there is gold, silver, or even various necessary items belonging to owners, one might attack and destroy the village by means of mechanical devices, or by flooding it with water, or by relying on close personal ties.
By force, or by means of eloquent speech and persuasion, one deceives others to obtain it. If it is obtained, it is a *pārājika*;
if not obtained, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. As for "a place": it is an unenclosed space with an owner located outside a village.

If there are gold, silver, the seven treasures, or even necessary items belonging to an owner within that empty space, and one uses some expedient means to damage or take that other person's unenclosed space, [it is a grave offense].
If one obtains [land] by flooding it with water, or through the influence of close relatives or powerful persons, or by means of eloquent speech and debate;
regarding fields— such as rice fields, wheat fields, sugarcane fields, or whatever other fields there may be— if within those fields there are gold, silver, the seven treasures,
or even any necessary items belonging to another, and one employs skillful means to destroy that other's field.
If it is obtained by means of water-sprinkling, or by relying on intimacy and power, or through eloquent speech and persuasion, or by deception;
as for the location, it may be a household residence, a marketplace, a fruit orchard, or a vegetable garden.
Whether in a pond, in a courtyard, behind a house, or in any other place, there may be gold, silver, and the seven treasures, as well as all necessary articles that have an owner. Regarding boats:

small boats, large boats, jar-boats (so named because their shape resembles a jar), single-log boats (made by hollowing out a large log to serve as a boat), *fang-chuan* (square boats), and oar-boats (*lu-chuan*; an *lu* is a tool for propelling a boat).

[These are] for the sake of names). Turtle-shaped boats; tortoise-shaped boats (meaning their shapes resemble turtles and tortoises); leather boats (made from hides); and bottle-gourd boats (the gourd is the same as the calabash).

Furthermore, the *hù* (gourd) is a ceramic vessel; both can be used to float objects. The *guǒchuán* (fruit-boat) is also named after its shape. The *xuánchuán* (suspended boat) refers to the practice common in temples today of hanging boats from the beams as offerings to the deities.
A raft or boat (Kuo Po says: wood is called *pí*; bamboo is called a *fá*. It refers to crossing objects by binding bamboo together).
Suppose there were further boats upon which there was gold, silver, the seven treasures, or even necessary items that had an owner.
Whether crossing from this shore to the other shore, or from the other shore to this shore; whether with the current or against the current; whether sinking in the water or moving onto the bank.

Above. Regarding the "shifting location" of water: if gold, silver, the seven treasures, or robes and coverlets are hidden and submerged in the water, whether it be otters, fish, turtles, or *śiṃśumāra* (the character *shou* is sometimes written as *shu*; the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states...).

The crocodile (*makara*) is over twenty feet long and has four legs resembling those of a *tadpole* (*tad*). Its teeth are extremely sharp; if birds or deer enter the water, it bites their waists, and they are severed instantly. It also turns back and kills its own offspring. It is found in Guangzhou.

As for the *utpala* flower (translated here as "blue lotus"), the *padma* flower (translated here as "red lotus"), the *kumuda* flower (translated here as "earth-delighting flower," also called *kumuda*;

translated here as "yellow lotus"), and the *puṇḍarīka* flower (translated here as "white lotus"): Master Rui states that when it has not yet blossomed, it is called *kumuda*, and when it is about to fall, it is called *kamala*.

The *ra* (lotus) is called *puṇḍarīka* when it is at its peak; because its substance changes with the time and its name follows the transformation of its color, it has these three names. Furthermore, there are other aquatic things that have owners.
If one uses a stratagem to damage another's water source, it is a *pārājika* offense if the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more; if less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the payment of taxes: a bhikṣu has no obligation to pay taxes. However, if there is an item belonging to a layperson (*avadātavasana*) that ought to be taxed...

If a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, causes another’s property to pass beyond a barrier—whether it be five coins or more than five coins—whether by burying it and then digging it up, or by deceiving through eloquent speech, or by means of incantations; [in all such cases, he commits an offense].

Regarding one who takes another’s entrusted property: having taken the entrusted property and departed with it, if they take five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with the intent to steal—whether by shifting it from the head to the shoulder, from the right hand to the left hand, from the left hand to the right hand, or by holding it in their arms or placing it on the ground—and thus lift it from its original location; or regarding water: if it is a large amount.
Small jars, as well as seeds, seed-vessels, or various scented waters, or medicinal waters—
if one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with a thieving mind; or regarding willow branches— whether one, two, or many, whether in a single bundle,
a single bunch, or a single load, whether scented with incense or smeared with medicine— if one takes them with a thieving mind for the value of five *kārsāpaṇas*.
If it exceeds five coins; if it is pulled or dragged; if it is taken away from its original location.
"Garden" refers to all grasses, trees, thickets, forests, flowers, and fruits that have an owner. "Footless sentient beings" refers to snakes, fish, and other footless sentient beings.
There are two-legged beings with owners: humans, non-humans, birds, and other two-legged beings who have owners.
There are four-legged beings with owners: elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, deer, sheep, and other four-legged beings who have owners.
There are many-legged beings: bees, *urucungas* (these insects have many hairs on their bodies and also many legs).

[This refers to creatures] similar to caterpillars). If it be a centipede, or any other many-legged sentient being that has an owner, and one takes it with a thieving mind—whether its value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*—in the case of "co-partners in wealth," those who share in the same business and obtain property together, they shall take five *kārsāpaṇas* or more together with a thieving mind.
In the case of "those who have made a pact," it means making a mutual agreement with another, instructing them by saying:

At such-and-such a time he will go; at such-and-such a time he will come. Whether by breaking through a wall to take property, or by plundering on the road, or by burning [a place] to obtain wealth from it—taking it together with a thieving intent, whether the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—if one waits in ambush, thinking, "I shall go to observe that village, or city, or ferry crossing, or mountain valley," or...
In whatever place people dwell— whether at marketplaces, shops, or workshops— if one takes with a thieving mind any property obtained there,
whether its value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, and if the guardian thinks, "When a person brings wealth from outside,
I shall guard it," yet all the property obtained is shared in common, and one takes it with a thieving mind for a value of five... [kārsāpaṇas].
Money. If it exceeds five coins, one should observe the path, thinking, "I shall observe the path.
If an army of kings comes, or an army of thieves comes, or an army of elders comes, one should inform them. Whatever wealth is obtained, all shall be shared.
If one takes with a thieving mind, whether the value is five coins or more than five coins, it is as described above in all respects.
If one initially removes it from its original place, it is a *pārājika*. If one employs the means to lift it but does not lift it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one employs the means seeking [an object] worth more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, whether one obtains more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*, or less than five *kārsāpaṇas*—or if one seeks [an object] worth five *kārsāpaṇas* and obtains more than five *kārsāpaṇas*—in all these cases, it is a *pārājika*.

If one obtains less than five *kārsāpaṇas* or does not obtain it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one employs the means seeking [an object] worth five *kārsāpaṇas* and obtains more than five *kārsāpaṇas*... [the text continues].
If one obtains five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense. If one obtains less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is not; it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one employs the means to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas* and obtains more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, or obtains exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense. If one obtains less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].

Thullaccaya. If he does not obtain it, it is dukkaṭa. If he instructs another by means of a stratagem to seek more than five coins, and [the other] obtains more than five coins, or obtains exactly five coins, both are pārajika. If [the other] obtains less than five coins, or does not obtain it, both are thullaccaya.
If he employs a stratagem to instruct another to seek five coins, and [the other] obtains more than five coins, or obtains exactly five coins...
If both [parties] obtain less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, they both incur a *pārājika* offense; if neither obtains [it], they both incur a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one employs a stratagem to instruct another to seek less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, and [the other] obtains more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, or obtains exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*, the one who takes it incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the instructor [urges someone] to steal less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya*. If [the amount] is not obtained, both are guilty of a *duṣkṛta*.

If one employs a stratagem to instruct another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, and the person following the instruction takes a different object, the taker commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*. [This applies when] employing a stratagem to instruct another to seek...
Five *kārsāpaṇas*. If it exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*, and the person being instructed takes the object from another location, the person being instructed commits a *pārājika* offense;

the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one employs a stratagem to instruct someone to seek five *kārsāpaṇas*, and if it exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*, and the person being instructed—thinking they are merely being sent to retrieve the object—takes possession of it without the intent to steal, yet obtains five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, [the] instructor... [commits a sthūlātyaya].

Pārājika. There is no offense for the one who receives the message. If one instructs another to take an object, and the one who receives the instruction understands it as an instruction to steal, then if the value obtained is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, the one who received the instruction commits a Pārājika offense; the instructor is not at fault.
If there is an owner and the perception that there is an owner, and one takes what was not given with a value of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, [it is a Pārājika offense].
If there is an owner and one suspects it, it is a sthūlātyaya. If there is no owner but one perceives there is an owner, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If there is no owner and one suspects it, it is a sthūlātyaya. If there is an owner and one perceives there is an owner, yet the value is less than five coins, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one steals less than five *kārsāpaṇas* from something with an owner, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one has the perception that something has an owner when it has no owner, or if one suspects it has an owner when it has none, and steals less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, these are all *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If one gives rise to a thieving mind and initiates the preparatory effort, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. Upon touching the object, it becomes a *sthūlātyaya* (i.e., a *sthūlatyaya*). Upon lifting it and moving it away..."
If the value at the place where it was left reaches five *māṣakas*, it is a *pārājika* offense; if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

If it is an object belonging to an animal and one touches that object, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). If one moves [an object] from its place and the value reaches five *māṣakas*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it does not reach that amount, it is an *dukkaṭa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who possessed many robes..."
The bowl. A disciple of Mahāpuṇya. Those disciples did not cultivate virtuous conduct and thought to themselves:
"We should go to the rooms of our preceptors and teachers and steal their bowls and robes; our own bowls and robes are also in the teachers' rooms. They then made an agreement among themselves:
"Whichever of you obtains clothing or requisites shall share them with me; if I obtain any, I shall likewise [share them]."
"I shall share it with you. Having said this, he enters the room and goes to the clothing rack;
if he takes hold of the robes of the Upādhyāya or Ācārya and shifts them toward his own robes, yet the robes do not leave their original position on the rack, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If he lifts the teacher's robe from the rack and places it among his own robes, it is a *pārājika* offense. This applies even if the teacher's robe is merely touching the edge of another robe or a thread of yarn.
As long as it has not been removed from the clothes rack, it is not a *pārājika* offense; once it has been completely removed, it is a *pārājika*.
If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*) suspects that this disciple might steal his robe or bowl, he hides his own robe and bowl elsewhere.
The disciple then enters the darkness and, by mistake, steals his own robe and bowl.

He speaks of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and praises the contemplation of impurity; he praises the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (also known as the nine perceptions).

When these nine types of methods for the contemplation of impurity are thoroughly mastered through mental recollection and the mind is no longer distracted, one immediately attains the accomplishment of *samādhi*. Natural sensual desire is eradicated, delusions and karma are extinguished, and one realizes the fruit of the Path. Although these nine perceptions are merely conceptualized objects used for meditation, [they lead to such results].

Nevertheless, when employed, it can accomplish great matters. It is like a corpse in the great ocean: a drowning person who clings to it will immediately be able to cross over. First is the visualization of bloating (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*): this refers to a practitioner who visualizes a corpse in their mind and perceives it as bloated.

1. The Perception of Bloatedness (*aughita-saṃjñā*): Just as a leather bag filled with wind differs from its original appearance, this is called the perception of bloatedness. 2. The Perception of Livid Discoloration (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*): Having already contemplated the bloated corpse, one further contemplates a dead body blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, its skin and flesh becoming yellowish-red and turning into dark, bluish-black lividity;

this is the perception of livid discoloration. 3. The Perception of Putrefaction (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*): Having already contemplated the livid corpse, one further contemplates a dead body transformed by wind and sun, its skin and flesh split and ruined, broken into six parts, its internal organs rotting and putrefying, with foul stench overflowing;

this is the perception of putrefaction. 4. The Perception of Blood-Smearedness (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*): Having already contemplated the putrefied corpse, one further contemplates a dead body from head to foot, with pus and blood overflowing and filth smeared all over the body; this is the perception of blood-smearedness. 5. The Perception of Pus-Rotting (*vipaḍumaka-saṃjñā*).

Having already observed the oozing fluids, one further observes the nine orifices of the corpse from which pus and blood flow out; the skin and flesh rot and decay, lying in a heap upon the ground as the stench increases ever more. This is the perception of putrefaction (*pūyabhijñā*). Sixth is the perception of being devoured by worms (*kṛmibhakṣaṇasaṃjñā*).

Having already observed the putrefaction, one further observes the corpse being nibbled by maggots and gnawed by birds and beasts, until it is mangled, stripped, and fallen apart. This is the perception of being devoured by worms. Seventh is the perception of scattering (*vidhvaṃsana-saṃjñā*).

Having already observed the devouring by worms, one further observes the corpse being consumed by birds and beasts, split open and scattered about, with tendons severed, bones separated, and head and feet strewn across one another. This is the perception of scattering. Eighth is the perception of bones (*asthisaṃjñā*). Having already observed the scattering, one further observes the corpse with its skeletal frame exposed, the skin and flesh entirely gone, leaving only...

Seeing white bones scattered about, like shells or like *ka* (agate), this is the contemplation of bones (*asthisaṃjñā*). Ninth, the contemplation of burning (*ādhyātmikasaṃjñā*): having already contemplated the bones, one further contemplates a corpse being burned by fire; it crackles and emits smoke and stench, until the white bones are all ablaze.
When the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, it becomes identical to ash and dust; this is the contemplation of burning.
