Having left the household life to enter the Way, because of his past conditions, he is destined to receive this Dharma.
Having passed away, he was reborn in the heavens. Descending from the heavens, he heard the Dharma from the Buddha and attained the fruit of the Path (sotāpatti).

For this reason, the Buddha is without partiality. Once, on account of a minor matter, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī gathered in one place. At that time, the Buddha observed that the assembly was diminished;
knowing the cause, he asked about it intentionally. Ānanda reported the aforementioned events in detail. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There is the Ānāpāna-samādhi, which is tranquil."
Joy. One is then able to extinguish all unwholesome dharmas so that they never arise again;
this is precisely the Dharma-gate of the Sixteen Special Victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*). *Ānāpāna* is translated here as "sending forth and sending away.
"Sending forth" refers to the inhalation; "sending away" refers to the exhalation. Regarding the Sixteen Special Victories: first, knowing the entry of the breath.

1. Knowing the exhalation of the breath; 2. knowing the inhalation of the breath; 3. knowing whether the breath is long or short; 4. knowing the breath pervading the entire body; 5. calming all bodily formations;
6. experiencing rapture; 7. experiencing pleasure; 8. experiencing all mental formations; 9. gladdening the mind; 10. concentrating the mind.
Eleventh, the mind produces liberation; twelfth, contemplating impermanence; thirteenth, contemplating emergence and dispersion; fourteenth, contemplating detachment from desire;

fifteenth, contemplating cessation; sixteenth, contemplating relinquishment. As for the term "special excellence" (*viśeṣa*), it is named according to its causes and conditions, such as how non-Buddhists and others are all able to cultivate and attain the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the four contemplations of non-contention.
Because one practices in this way, one does not arise within birth and death. These sixteen dharmas possess both *samatha* (calm) and *vipaśyanā* (insight);
they fully incorporate all dhyānas and are capable of giving rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore, they are called "Special Excellence" (*viśeṣa*).

If these sixteen dharmas are applied horizontally to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are four dharmas for each foundation, totaling sixteen; this is easy to understand. Now, we shall consider them applied vertically to the three realms.
This clarifies the characteristics of cultivation and realization. "First, knowing the inhalation; second, knowing the exhalation" corresponds to the practice of counting the breaths (*gaṇanā*).

The practitioner regulates the breath, maintaining a continuous and single-minded focus, following along with the breath. When inhaling, one knows it enters from the tip of the nose down to the navel.
When exhaling, one knows it exits from the navel up to the nose. In this way, one illuminates [the process] with a single mind.

The breath follows [the mind] without distraction. At that time, one knows the characteristics of the breath’s coarseness and subtlety. One knows that the wind-like gasping is coarse, while the characteristic of the breath itself is subtle (*Note:

There are four aspects of the breath: first, wind; second, qi; third, breath; fourth, gasping. *Zhi guan* says: that which has sound is called "wind"; if one guards it, it scatters. That which is constricted and stagnant is called "qi"; if one guards it, it becomes further knotted.

That which enters and exits without being fully exhausted is called "gasping"; if one guards it, it leads to exhaustion. That which is neither sounding nor stagnant, where entry and exit are both complete, is called "breath" (*xi*); if one guards it, one attains concentration). One regulates what is coarse.
Make it subtle, like a gatekeeper who knows who enters and leaves, and also distinguishes between good people and evil people; knowing the good, he admits them, and knowing the evil, he bars them.
Furthermore, he knows lightness and heaviness, smoothness and roughness, cold and warmth, and duration and proximity.

Moreover, he knows that because of inhalation and exhalation, there arise all manner of suffering and afflictions, the coming and going of birth and death, and the ceaseless turning of the wheel. The mind—
One should recognize this as fear. If one counts the breaths with a darkened mind, there will be no practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

At the time of correct cultivation and realization, many afflictions such as craving, views, and pride arise (craving refers to being attached to this counting of breaths; views refer to thinking "I am the one who can count"; pride refers to thinking "I can count" and thereby becoming conceited toward others).
Now, when following the breath, one immediately knows that this breath is impermanent. Life depends upon the breath; the breath constitutes life.

If even a single breath does not return, there is no more life. Knowing the breath is impermanent, one does not give rise to craving. Knowing the breath is not-self, [one does not give rise to grasping].

Thus, one does not give rise to views; awakening to impermanence, one does not give rise to pride. This constitutes the initial skillful means by which one is already able to shatter all fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).
It differs from counting the breaths, wherein one relies on the breath with single-mindedness to prevent the mind from scattering and thereby enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
for this reason, it is called "loving" (*anunaya*). Because it awakens one to impermanence, it is also called "exertion" (*pragraha*). Being in conjunction with concentration, it is named...

There is also the outflow-free (anāsrava). Because the practice of contemplation is unattached, it is also called outflow-free. (Knowing the entry and knowing the exit; it correctly relies on following the breath as its gateway.

Third, "knowing the length and shortness of the breath" corresponds to the concentration of the desire realm (kāmadhātu-samādhi). When an external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) realizes the concentration of the desire realm, they do not perceive any characteristics within the breath at all.
Now, in this context, when one first attains concentration, one immediately perceives the length and shortness within the breath.
This is the mark [of the practice]. Awakening to impermanence becomes increasingly clear, and one realizes the concentration of the desire realm; therefore, it is also called "Affection" (*anurāga*).

Because the contemplative practice awakens to impermanence, it is also called "Exertion" (*pragraha*). Fourth, "knowing that the breath pervades the entire body" corresponds to the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the threshold concentration).
When ordinary outsiders realize the *anāgamya*, they directly perceive that the characteristics of the body vanish and become like empty space. Thus it is said.
At that time, the body and breath truly exist; however, because the eyes are not opened, one is neither aware of nor sees them.

Now, when emerging from the "Special Excellence" (viśeṣa) stage and entering the "Not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) stage, one likewise enters samādhi in a state of total stillness, and immediately becomes aware that the body gradually emerges like a cloud or a shadow.

One perceives that the inhalation and exhalation pervade all the pores of the body, and also knows whether the breath is long, short, or equal. One sees that as the breath enters, there is no accumulation;

as it exits, there is no dispersion. It is impermanent, arising and ceasing. One realizes that the body is empty, provisional, and unreal, and further understands that arising and ceasing do not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Because these three factors combine, concentration arises; yet once these three factors are seen to be empty, then concentration [is likewise empty].
There is no dependence. One knows that emptiness is also empty and does not cling to emptiness; the aspects of affection and exertion are as previously explained.
Fifth, the "removal of bodily formations" refers to the factors of initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) in the first dhyāna. Regarding "bodily formations":

when the first dhyāna is attained within a body of the desire realm, the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) of the four great elements of the form realm comes into contact with the body of the desire realm. The desire realm...

The body-faculty gives rise to consciousness, which perceives these forms and tangibles. Because these two elements—form and consciousness—dwell together in mutual dependence, it is called "body" (*kāya*).

The body is itself a factor of awakening; from this bodily constituent arises contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), through which one knows the phenomena within the body that are subject to conditioned activity.

Therefore, it is called "bodily formations" (*kāya-saṃskāra*). Bodily formations are precisely the factor of "contemplation. Regarding the term "removal": because the breath has ceased throughout the body due to [the cessation of] discursive thought (*vitarka*), one attains the first *dhyāna*.
The mind-eye opens and becomes clear, and one perceives the thirty-six impure substances of the body as foul-smelling, filthy, and loathsome.

At that time, one realizes that these thirty-six substances exist by virtue of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and that each of the six parts, such as the head and so forth, is not the self. The four...
Within each of these "great" [elements], there is no individual body; this is what is meant by "removing the body of the desire realm.
Furthermore, within the body of the desire realm, the four great elements of the form realm cannot be found; this is called "removing the body of the first dhyāna. Why is this so?
If one says that there is a derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), does it come from the outside, go out from within, or abide in between?
When observing in this way, it is ultimately unfindable. It is only due to inverted conceptualization (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*) that one says "one experiences contact belonging to the realm of form.
When one observes truthfully and finds nothing, this is the removal of the body of the first dhyāna. Because the body is removed, the bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) cease.
This is precisely its cessation. Regarding "one who experiences joy in the sixfold reception": this is an antidote for the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*) in the first dhyāna.

Within the fundamental dhyānas, the factor of joy arises after the disappearance of tainted applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Since it lacks the illuminating discernment of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it gives rise to much affliction;
therefore, one should not experience it. Now, in the pure dhyāna, joy is born from within the factors of applied and sustained thought; because there is insight...

By practicing analytical deconstruction and realizing that the nature of vitarka and vicāra is empty, the joy that arises is likewise empty. Being unattached to this joy, one is free from all faults and transgressions;
thus it is said that one "experiences joy. This is like an Arhat who is unattached to all offerings, and is therefore called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
Seventh, "experiencing bliss" refers to the factor of bliss in the first dhyāna. In the fundamental dhyānas, there is [no such thing as]...

Regarding the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): because there is much defilement within pleasure, one should not accept it. Now, knowing that the nature of pleasure is empty and remaining unattached, there is no fault;

thus, the acceptance of pleasure is taught. Eighth, regarding the practitioner who experiences various mental states: this counters the factor of "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*) in the first dhyāna.
When entering one-pointedness in the fundamental dhyānas, the mind gives rise to defiled attachment; therefore, [that state] should not be accepted. Now, knowing...
This single mind is empty, deceptive, and unreal; this single mind is no-mind. Thus, one does not grasp or cling to it.

Being free from fault and transgression, it is precisely samādhi and right reception (*samyak-samādhi*). Therefore, it is said that one experiences all mental activities. Regarding "the nine minds producing joy":
Regarding the joy of inner serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) in the second dhyāna: the joy of the fundamental second dhyāna arises from inner serenity;

because it was not previously illuminated by wisdom, one frequently gave rise to attachment toward it. Now, by observing this joy, one knows it to be empty and deceptive, and thus does not give rise to attachment.
It is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Because true dharma-joy arises from the mind of right contemplation, it is said that "the mind produces joy.
Regarding the tenth, "the mind as a factor of concentration": this corresponds to the single mental factor (*citta-aṅga*) of the second *dhyāna*. In the second *dhyāna*, joy is mobile;
now, by reflecting back upon the nature of joy and knowing it to be empty and quiescent, the concentrated mind ultimately remains undisturbed and does not follow after the movement of joy. Ten.
"One who single-mindedly practices for liberation" refers to the overcoming of the bliss of the third dhyāna. In the third dhyāna, there is a bliss that pervades the entire body;
ordinary beings who attain it mostly give rise to the fetters of craving and thus fail to achieve liberation.

Now, by means of the wisdom of contemplation, one analyzes and deconstructs this, knowing that this bliss arises from causes and conditions, is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, and is deceptive and unreal. By contemplating this bliss without attachment, the mind...
One attains mastery. Regarding the twelfth contemplation on impermanence: it serves to counteract the immovability of the four *dhyānas*.

Because the third *dhyāna* is moved by pleasure, the fourth *dhyāna* is named the "immovable concentration" (*aniñjya-samādhi*). When ordinary people attain this, they often give rise to the notion of permanence and produce craving and grasping.

Now, by contemplating this concentration, one sees that it is subject to arising and ceasing, undergoing successive change, and being transmuted by the three characteristics; thus one knows it to be [impermanent].
This destroys the characteristic of instability. Regarding the thirteenth contemplation, "emerging from and dispersing": this is the antidote to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

"Emerging" means departing from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). "Dispersing" refers to dispersing the three types of form: (1) visible and resistant form; (2) invisible and resistant form; and (3) invisible and non-resistant form.
Furthermore, having departed from the realm of form, the mind relies upon space, dispersing with mastery so as not to be constrained by form.
Bound by phenomena, it is therefore called "emerging and dispersing. When ordinary beings attain this, they claim it is true emptiness; a sense of security arises, and they develop attachment to it.

Now, when observing the meditative concentration on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one knows that it exists as a combination of the four aggregates (*skandha*) and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and thus cannot be grasped.
Why is this so? If one were to say there is "emerging and dispersing," would it be that space itself is emerging and dispersing?

If it is the mind that wanders outward and scatters, then since the past mind has already ceased, the future mind has not yet arisen, and the present mind does not abide, how could there be any wandering?
If it is emptiness that wanders outward and scatters, then as a phenomenon devoid of cognition, what wandering or scattering could there be?
Since one does not attain emptiness-concentration, the mind has nothing upon which to fixate. 10.
The fourth contemplation on the departure from desire corresponds to the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*). All attachment to external objects is termed "desire.
From the desire realm up to the sphere of infinite space, all are external objects to the mind; even if empty space were considered an external object, it would still be so.
Consciousness comes to receive this emptiness and takes emptiness as its desired object; this is now the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Taking internal consciousness as its objective support while abandoning desire for external emptiness is called "detachment" (*vairāgya*).

When ordinary beings attain this, lacking the eye of wisdom to clearly discern it, they claim that the mind is in accord with the phenomenon of consciousness and that it is truly peaceful and secure, thereby giving rise to defiled attachment. Now, by means of the wisdom of contemplation...

Through analytical deconstruction, one knows that the consciousnesses of the three periods of time do not correspond with the present mind. Therefore, this consciousness is certainly nothing more than a mere name;
it is deceptive and unreal. Fifteenth, the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha*) corresponds to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This meditative concentration takes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as its object; the mind corresponds with the unconditioned, and thus it faces the object of unconditioned phenomena.
A slight degree of consciousness arises; ordinary people call this the extinction of the mind and, developing deep attachment, they are bound by it.

Now, one observes that even this slight consciousness is a composite of the four aggregates (*skandhas*), being impermanent, non-self, deceptive, and unreal—just as excrement, whether small or large, is equally foul-smelling—and thus one does not become stained by attachment. Regarding the "discarding" in the Sixteen Contemplations, it refers to...
It is neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). "Non-non-perception" is the antidote to both types of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

From the first dhyāna upward, there is only partial equanimity; there is no [simultaneous] dual equanimity. Now, in this concentration, one simultaneously abandons both [perception and non-perception], and it is the ultimate limit of equanimity;
therefore, it is called "abandonment. Ordinary beings who attain this take it to be *nirvāṇa*, yet they lack the discerning wisdom of realization.

[He] understood that he could not abandon [them]. Now he knows that this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is likewise composed of the combination of four aggregates (*skandha*), two bases (*āyatana*—namely, the mind-base and the phenomena-base), three realms (*dhātu*—namely, the mind-realm, the phenomena-realm, and the mental-consciousness-realm), and ten kinds of subtle mental factors (*caitta*, such as contact, attention, feeling, perception, volition, desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom).
It is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is deceptive and unreal, and should not be reckoned as *nirvāṇa*. Since...

Knowing emptiness and stillness, one does not undergo attachment. At that time, the practitioner deeply contemplates and relinquishes [the breath], thereby attaining the realization of the nirvana of the Three Vehicles.
However, it is not necessarily required that all sixteen [aspects] be complete; rather, one may attain awakening upon achieving three or two *viśeṣa* (special stages).
Furthermore, there are those of sharp faculties who, at the very first moment of following the breath, awaken to impermanence and immediately give rise to the [resolve for] the Unconditioned.
It is "with outflows" (sāsrava) because it initially arises together with the fundamental meditative absorption; thus it is called "also with outflows.

Within this state, when the wisdom of contemplation analyzes and deconstructs [phenomena] without attachment, it is called "also without outflows" (anāsrava). This, in brief, surpasses the six subtle gates.
Having rebuked the bhikṣus in the Pāvārika Garden with countless skillful means, he established the precepts for the bhikṣus;
these are the four formulated characteristics of the precepts.
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, provides a weapon to another, praises death, encourages death, saying, "Ho, man!

What is the use of this wretched life? It would be better to die than to live," or if he forms such a thought and employs various means to praise death and encourage death, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer to live in communion.
**Exegesis:** "Person" (*pudgala*) refers to the continuum from the initial consciousness until the final consciousness, wherein one's life is severed.

This consciousness is the eighth, the *ālayavijñāna*, termed the "store-consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*) because it contains no phenomena and encompasses no objects. It is also called the "active-maintaining consciousness" (*karmadhāraya-vijñāna*) because it can maintain all seeds of both good and evil.

As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When this consciousness first enters the womb at conception, it is like a magnet attracting iron; this is called the initial consciousness. Even until the time when life is about to end and the sensation of cold gradually arises, it is this consciousness alone that can maintain the body. If this consciousness abandons the body, the four great elements disperse."

This is called the consciousness at the end of life, also known as the "subsequent consciousness. It is what is said to be "the one who goes before and comes after, acting as the master. Furthermore, all sentient beings possess the continuity of the three—feeling, warmth, and consciousness—which links them together without interruption;

this is called the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*). Now, to cause those form and mind to be unable to continue in succession is called the "termination of life. Therefore, the phrase "with a deliberate mind" indicates that the act of killing was intentional and not accidental. "With one's own hand" means to carry out the killing with one's own hand, or to cause death by physically crushing or pressing down, using either the hands, the feet, the elbows, the knees, or other parts of the body;
or to kill a person by hurling a staff, a stone, or a brick from afar—all such cases are described as "with one's own hand. Regarding "giving a knife to another," the *Mūla* [text] states: "If..."

Knowing that the person intends to commit suicide, one places before them large knives, razors, spears, and the like, desiring to cause them to harm themselves. One praises death and encourages death (the *Mūla* states: "Regarding 'encouraging death,' one encourages three types of persons to die:

namely, those who have broken the precepts, those who uphold the precepts, and those who are ill. Going to the person who has broken the precepts, one says: 'Venerable sir, do you know? You have now broken the precepts and committed various sinful deeds; through body, speech, and mind, you constantly create manifold evils.

Venerable sir, if your life were to persist, your evil karma would increase, and you would long suffer the pains of hell. You should therefore cast off this body and take your own life. How does one encourage those who uphold the precepts?)?

[He] went to that person and said: "Venerable one, do you know? Since you have maintained the precepts, cultivated various wholesome dharmas, and are further able to extend your hand in giving—giving constantly, giving with joy, giving extensively, and giving distributively—you possess such merit that you will surely be reborn in the heavens.

The person who maintains the precepts asked: "Venerable one, what should I do now? [The other] replied: "You should abandon the body and take your own life. [This is how one encourages a sick bhikṣu to die:

He went to him and said: "Venerable one, do you know? You are currently gravely ill and suffering extreme pain. If you remain for long, your illness will only grow more severe and you will constantly endure hardship. You should abandon the body and take your own life. Thus he exhorted him in various ways. "Alas, man! [he cried].
"Son" (the term *tse* is an expression for alerting; "man" is a word for addressing) — one should form such a thought and contemplate various skillful means.
Praising death and exhorting death (to form such a mind is precisely to praise and exhort death; it is not for any other purpose). Regarding the conditions for the offense:
this precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense. If any condition is lacking, the offense incurred is minor.
First, there must be the intent to kill. Second, the object must be a human being. Third, one must perceive the object as a human being. Fourth, the life-faculty must be severed.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding those who commit this offense: whether one kills by one's own hand; or instructs another to kill; or dispatches a messenger to kill;
or sends a messenger back and forth to kill; or employs a secondary messenger to kill; or employs a succession of messengers to kill; or seeks out a man to kill;
or kills a man and then seeks another man to kill; or seeks out a man wielding a blade to kill; or kills a man and then seeks another man wielding a blade to kill; or...
Manifesting signs with the body; or speaking with the mouth; or manifesting signs with both body and mouth; or sending a letter; or instructing a messenger to write one;
or by means of a pitfall; or by means of a trap; or by giving poison; or by providing the instruments of death; or by killing oneself.
Whether by means of the hand, or with tiles, stones, swords, or staves, or even by other objects, one commits suicide; or one incites another to kill;

or at the time of killing, one personally supervises the victim being thrown into water or fire, or pushed from a mountain peak down into a valley, or causes an elephant to trample them to death, or causes them to be devoured by wild beasts, or causes them to be bitten by snakes, or employs various other such methods of inciting others to kill.

Regarding "sending a messenger to kill": a bhikṣu sends a messenger to take the life of such-and-such a person; the messenger goes and takes their life according to his instructions. Regarding "the messenger going and returning":
a bhikṣu sends a messenger to take the life of such-and-such a person; the messenger goes with the intent to kill according to his instructions, but before he can kill, he returns.
Immediately following the previous instruction, he goes again and kills. Regarding "sending a messenger repeatedly": a bhikṣu sends a messenger...
"Go and take the life of so-and-so. He sent a messenger again, and in this manner, up to four or five times.

That messenger went and killed him. As for these successive messengers—when a bhikṣu sends a messenger saying, "Go and take the life of so-and-so," and that messenger in turn dispatches another messenger, continuing even up to a hundred thousand messengers who go to take his life—who among them is the one seeking a man?

"Knowing that there is such a person who can use a knife, possesses skillful means, has practiced for a long time, is without fear or retreat, and is capable of taking the life of a certain individual"—the messenger then goes and takes that person's life.
Regarding the instruction to "seek out a man," it means instructing someone to seek him out.
Among these, who knows of such a person who can use a knife, possesses skillful means, and has practiced for a long time?
Without fear or retreat, he is able to take the life of such-and-such a person. That messenger then goes to take his life. He seeks out someone who holds a sword, asking:
"Who is brave and capable enough to hold a sword and take the life of such-and-such a person? That person then goes and kills him.
Teaching others to seek out one who holds a sword is also like this. As for manifesting signs with the body: he makes bodily gestures to kill, causing [the victim] to fall.

They are cast into water or fire; they fall from mountain peaks into valley bottoms; they are caused to be trampled to death by elephants; they are made to be devoured by wild beasts or stung by venomous snakes.
Because of these manifest physical conditions, they commit suicide. Or it is said: "The evil you have committed [will result in this]."
"You lack compassion; you harbor a poisonous mind; you do not perform any virtuous deeds. You provide no protection.

From the moment of your birth, you have incurred much demerit; it would be better for you to die. If one speaks thus, [the other should reply]: "I do not act with wicked violence; I possess compassion."
Do not harbor poisonous thoughts. You have already performed many virtuous deeds; you have already established merit; you have already provided protection.
Though you were born to undergo manifold sufferings, upon death you shall be reborn in the heavens. If, because of these words, he...
He then commits suicide. The manifestation of signs through body and speech is likewise. Sending a messenger:

if a messenger is sent to that person, [the messenger says], "The good and evil you have committed," as explained in detail above; the deceased hears this messenger’s words and dies. Sending a letter to kill:
holding the letter, one says, "The good and evil you have committed," as explained in detail above. Sending both a messenger and a letter: [the same applies].

It is also like this. Regarding those who fall into pits: having ascertained that they will certainly travel along a certain path, one should dig a deep pit in the middle of that road and place therein fire, or a sword, or a venomous snake, or a sharp stake, or a poisoned dart;
thus, should they fall into the pit, they will die.
"Triggering by leaning" (meaning: having set a mechanism and placed various lethal devices, it is triggered simply by leaning against them).

Knowing that a person will certainly lean against a certain spot—whether a tree, a wall, or a fence—and that outside of it there is fire, a blade, a stake, a venomous snake, or a poisoned dart, one sets the mechanism so that when they lean against it, they fall into it and die.
As for "medicine": knowing the illness of that person, one gives [it to them].

It is not medicine. If one provides various medicines mixed with poison, or administered in excessive doses, or provides instruments for killing, and if that person was previously known to have been weary of their own life and body and held this body in loathing, and one then places a knife, poison, a rope, or other means of death before them—if they die as a result of each of these aforementioned acts, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. However, if [the person] did not [previously possess such intent], it is not.

If [the victim] dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If [the victim] is a son of a deva, a son of a nāga, a son of an asura, a son of a gandharva, a yakṣa, a preta, or an animal that possesses the intelligence to understand human speech, or one who is able to transform its form, and one seeks to kill them through skillful means—if they die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if they do not die, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If an animal cannot change its form and one kills it, it is a *pāyattika*; if it does not die, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If it is actually a human being and one kills it with the perception that it is a human, it is a *pārājika*. If there is doubt regarding whether it is a human, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a human being but one perceives it as a non-human being, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
A *sthūlātyaya* [offense] for perceiving one who is not a human as a human; a *sthūlātyaya* for doubting whether one is not a human. The fourth section states:
"If one employs a means to cause another’s fetus to fall, it is a *pārājika*. If the mother dies but the child lives, there is no offense regarding the death of the mother;

one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (meaning that because the intent to kill was directed at the child and not the mother, there is no offense for the mother's death; since the original purpose has not been accomplished, the offense is established as a preparatory act). [End of] Assembly.
If many bhikṣus dispatch one person to take another’s life, all are guilty of a *pārājika* offense. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "To kill oneself is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
From the time of entering the mother's womb until the forty-ninth day, it is called 'resembling a human' (*manuṣyapratirūpaka*).
Beyond this period, it is entirely termed a 'human. Whether one kills a human or one resembling a human, it is a *pārājika*. [Regarding 'one resembling a human,' it refers to...]"

Entering the mother’s womb, one first acquires two faculties (*indriya*). At the initial stage of depending on conditions, when the father’s semen and the mother’s blood unite, consciousness arises from within them, acquiring the two faculties of body and life; this is called being "like a human. After seven weeks have passed, the six faculties are complete and the form of a human is achieved; therefore, it is called a "human.

If one writes a letter commanding someone to kill, for each character written, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. When the letter reaches the recipient and they die as a result, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one uses indirect or figurative speech to instruct someone to kill, and that person dies because of it, it is a *pārājika* offense.
*Pārājika*: Whenever one gives rise to the intent to kill, it is a *duṣkṛta*; when one employs the means [to kill], it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the person dies, it is a *pārājika*. There were two bhikṣus who harbored mutual resentment; later, while traveling together on a road, they struck one another, and one of them subsequently died.
The Buddha said: "Since there was no intent to kill, he does not commit a grave offense (*pārājika*). Striking a bhikṣu out of anger is a..."
Pāyattika. From now on, it is not permitted to travel together with one who is angry and has not yet repented; whoever violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

If one intends to kill that person but kills this person by mistake, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (meaning: if there is no intention to kill this specific person at all, but only the preparatory effort, it is a *sthūlātyaya*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one constructs pits, traps, snares, nets, or the like for the sake of another person, and that person dies because of it, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of it, it is also a *pārājika*. If they do not die as a result of it later..."
A *sthūlātyaya*. If one acts toward a non-human being and that non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a human or an animal dies, it is all *duṣkṛta* (meaning that there was no intent to kill regarding humans or animals).
If one does not aim at a specific individual but intends for whoever comes along to die, then if a human dies, it is a *pārājika*; if a non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is no death at all, there are two offenses: one is a *sthūlātyaya* and the other is a *duṣkṛta*.
To cut off one's own finger is a *duṣkṛta*. If, while nursing the sick, one becomes weary and sets them aside so that they die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one causes [the patient] to obtain medicine or food and they die upon taking it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. (*Mātṛkā*)

It is said: If one intends to kill an ordinary person but mistakenly kills an arhat; or intends to kill an arhat but mistakenly kills an ordinary person; or intends to kill one's father but mistakenly kills one's mother;
or intends to kill one's mother but mistakenly kills one's father—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

One does not incur the grave offense of violating the precepts [of killing]. [Question: If one mistakenly kills one's biological parents who are world-transcending sages (*ārya*), why is the precept not lost? [Answer: Regarding the two precepts of killing and stealing, the focus is on the intention (*citta*) and not on the actual outcome. In these cases, the act was directed toward the intended victim.

The intent was not fulfilled; although the sin was committed through expedient means, the one mistakenly killed actually lacked the intent to kill. Therefore, the gravity of the offense is not that of a *ānantarya* (heinous) crime. Yet, how could the retribution of the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*) be avoided? The Sarvāstivādins say:
"If, on account of a bhikṣu’s words, one leads an army to conquer a foreign land and thereby acquires both territory and treasures, one incurs both the *pārājika* offenses of killing and stealing.
If one grasps a sword with the intent to kill, from the moment one sets foot [on the path], every step constitutes a light *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), continuing until..."

If one returns before injuring a person, it is all a light *sthūlātyaya*. If the blade has struck a person, regardless of the depth of the wound, as long as life has not yet been severed, it is a heavy *sthūlātyaya*. If [the person] dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If one digs a pit for the purpose of killing a person, while it is not yet finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*; once completed, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*. If a person falls into it...
If one who is brave and capable manages to escape from the pit, one incurs a heavy *sthūlātyaya*. If one falls into the pit but does not die, one also incurs a heavy *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to setting snares or using shovels. If one sends a messenger to kill someone, at the time of giving the instruction, one incurs a light *sthūlātyaya*;
at the time the killing is actually carried out, one incurs a *pārājika*. If one sends a messenger to kill someone... [and instructs them...]
If a person comes and he kills them, yet receives the commission [for the killing], and the person goes away when he is killed, the bhikṣu incurs a light sthūlātyaya.
If he instructs one to kill with a sword, but [the killer] uses a staff to kill; or if he instructs one to kill this person, but [the killer] kills that person.
In all cases where one does not act according to the Teaching and employs a different means, it is entirely a light *sthūlātyaya*.

If, with a blade or a staff, one intends to kill a person, yet the victim does not die immediately upon being struck by the staff or stabbed by the knife—perhaps because death would have occurred ten days later—but then dies immediately from the blow after being struck by another person, the monk who originally struck him commits a *pārājika* offense for killing. As for the monk who struck him first...

If one commits *thullaccaya* [theft], [one asks: why does one incur a *pārājika* offense only for harming a human being? [The answer is: because among humans there exist the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the *prātimokṣa* precepts; furthermore, the four fruits of the śramaṇa are mostly attained among humans.

Buddhas and *pratyekabuddhas* necessarily arise among humans because they attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Therefore, harming a human being incurs a *pārājika*, whereas [harming] other realms of existence does not. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pārājika*;
for the three minor assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* requiring formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya*). This is called an offense.
Explanatory Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: if one throws a weapon, a staff, a tile, or a stone, and it accidentally strikes and kills another person;
if, while engaged in construction work for a dwelling, one accidentally causes a person’s death by falling a brick, stone, timber, rafter, or pillar;

or when supporting a seriously ill person as they are being raised up, or supported as they lie down or bathe, or when administering medicine, or moving from a cool place to a warm place. From... [text continues]
If one dies while moving from a hot place to a cool place, entering or leaving a room, or going to or returning from the toilet, with a mind entirely free of harmful intent, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as those occurring before the precept was first established.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states in detail: "Furthermore, among the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; yet if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world.
Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever killing, you will inevitably fall [into the lower realms]."
Regarding the Way of the Gods (Shendao): those of the highest grade become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like;
those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking rākṣasas.
○ Fourth: A General Explanation of the Precept Against Grave Falsehood.

To lie with a deceitful mind out of greed for profit is to act without truthfulness. This is a shared precept; the regulation for nuns is likewise the same. "Great" [refers to the gravity of the offense].
The same principle applies here. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "A bodhisattva should always produce right speech and also cause all sentient beings to produce right speech and right view;
yet, if one instead gives rise to wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions in all sentient beings, this constitutes a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This arises from delusion, due to seeking gain and worldly affairs..."
This training rule was established to restrain the affliction of seeking gain and offerings. It consists of two parts:
the conjunction of conditions and the origin of the rule.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the High Hall on the Monkey River in Vaiśālī; at that time, the price of grain was high.
The people were starving, and it was difficult to obtain almsfood. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Gather all the bhikṣus who are in Vaiśālī.
Once they had assembled, the World-Honored One addressed them: "You should know that at this time the world's grain is expensive and almsfood is difficult to obtain.
You all, according to those with whom you share the same upādhyāya or the same teacher, and following your close friends and acquaintances, should each [go together]..."
"To the left and right of Vaiśālī, you may observe the rains retreat as is appropriate; I too shall observe the rains retreat at this very place. Why?
Because food and drink are difficult to obtain, and I am mindful of the weariness and suffering of the assembly. When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s instruction, they [acted accordingly].
Each [monk] remained in retreat according to his assigned location. Regarding the third case concerning the person who initiated the dispute:
at that time, among the monks observing the rains retreat in a monastery by the Pārileyyaka River, a bhikṣu spoke to a lay devotee, claiming that he had attained [realization].

The Venerable Upatiṣya and others were honored with offerings by the lay devotees; they were not troubled by the lack of food and drink, their complexions were radiant and serene, and their physical strength was fully restored.
As for the other bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat at Vaiśālī, [they were otherwise].
Their complexions were haggard and their bodies withered; their clothing was tattered and worn out. When their retreat was concluded, they went to see the World-Honored One.
He greeted them and, upon hearing this, they reported the aforementioned matter in detail. The Buddha said, "You foolish people!
Even that which is true should not be spoken to others, let alone that which is untrue. Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are two kinds of thieves in the world. The first are those who are not actually practitioners of pure conduct, yet claim for themselves that they are practitioners of pure conduct.

The second are those who, for the sake of food and drink, speak falsehoods among the great assembly—though it is neither true nor their own—to claim for themselves that they have attained the states of superior men (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
Of these two, the one who claims to have attained the states of superior men for the sake of food and drink is the greatest thief of all. Why is this?

For this reason, because he takes the food and drink of others by theft (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* asks: "Since this has not been moved from its original place, why is it called 'theft'? It answers: It is named 'theft. Why?

Because one obtains great gain and support through false and deceptive speech, taking it by means of artifice. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "One who steals the food and drink of others is called a great thief, because of untruthfulness").
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked him with countless skillful means, established a precept for the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu..."
In truth, there was nothing known [by them], even regarding such things as empty, deceptive, and false speech.

At that time, there was a monk of overweening pride who said to others, "I have attained the Way. Later, at another time, he applied himself with diligence and without slackening, earnestly seeking skillful means.
Having realized the supreme and most excellent Dharma, he thought to himself: "Have I not committed a *pārājika* offense? What shall I do now?
He immediately spoke to the monks who shared his views, saying, "Please inform the Buddha on my behalf. Then those monks went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"Except for one who acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is no offense. The precept should be recited in this manner:"
The fourth is the characteristic of an established rule:
If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no knowledge, claims of himself, "I have attained the state of a superior person;
I have entered the sublime dharma of noble wisdom; I know this; I see this," and at a later time, whether questioned or not, he desires to clear himself...
[The Buddha said: "It is for the sake of purification that I say this: 'I truly did not know or see, yet I claimed to know and see; this was a false and deceptive lie.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), such a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer to live in communion."

**Exegesis:** "Truly having nothing known" means truly having no knowledge or vision. "Self-proclaiming" means self-asserting that one possesses faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, and eloquence.
"Human qualities" refers to the human aggregates (the five *skandhas*), the human bases (*āyatanas*), and the human elements (*dhātus*).

"Superior human qualities" (the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: these are the dharmas of the superior stream; that is to say, all the dharmas of the ignorant and foolish, such as the five hindrances and other base, evil matters, are not superior dharmas).

"The accomplishment of the essential means for transcending all phenomena" (the term "all phenomena" refers to what follows in the text; "essential means for transcending" means these phenomena are the essential methods for escaping the three realms;

"accomplishment" means realization—that is, "I have realized these phenomena"—hence it is called "the accomplishment of the essential means for transcending all phenomena. This sentence provides the general heading, while the following text offers the specific explanation).

He himself says: "Mindfulness is established in the body"; he himself says: "There is right mindfulness"; he himself says: "I maintain the precepts"; he himself says: "I possess desire [for the Dharma]"; he himself says: "I am not negligent."
The negligent one claims to be diligent; claims to have attained concentration; claims to have attained right reception (*samāpatti*);
claims to possess the Path; claims to be practicing; claims to possess wisdom; claims to have vision; claims to have attained [the fruits]; claims to have attained the fruits;

and claims that mindfulness is established in the body, asserting that mindfulness can lead one to transcendence. He becomes familiar with, attaches himself to, and cultivates this teaching, increasing its practice.

Extensive, as in the *Vinayavāha* (The Vehicle of Discipline), it is guarded and observed; one well attains equanimity, has attained certainty, and, being free from further difficulty, attains mastery.

This is called "one’s own declaration of having attained the foundation of mindfulness of the body" (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). As for the foundation of mindfulness of the body: the head and other six parts are a provisional combination of the four great elements and the five faculties;

therefore, it is called the "body. Within this, the wisdom that contemplates the body is "mindfulness. Clearly seeing the five kinds of impurity within the internal body and thereby destroying the inversion of purity—this is the "foundation" (*sthāna*). The five kinds of impurity are: first, [the impurity of the womb].

(1) impurity of the seed, (2) impurity of the dwelling place, (3) impurity of the self-body, (4) impurity of external appearance, and (5) ultimate impurity). One who claims to possess right mindfulness [should reflect on these].
There is mindfulness that can cause one to transcend [suffering]. One becomes familiar with, attaches oneself to, cultivates, and expands this dharma.
Like a well-trained mount, it is guarded and observed; one attains skillful equanimity, achieves certainty, and, free from further difficulty, gains mastery.
This is right mindfulness (to be mindful of all dharmas; seeing the Dharma and attaining the Dharma, the mind achieves concentration—this pervades all dharmas).

One claims to uphold the precepts (meaning to strictly maintain the disciplinary rules, carefully guard one’s dignified deportment, and sever all evil). One claims to possess desire; one claims to be non-negligent;

and it is the same for claiming to be diligent. *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "What is called 'desire' (*chanda*)? It is like the Buddha’s tireless and vigorous exertion; therefore, it is called desire. Desire is the root of the Dharma."

Because one seeks through desire, one attains all dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Root of Dharmas" (*dharmamūla*). It is able to give rise to all dharmas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha sometimes speaks of desire (*chanda*), sometimes of diligence (*vīrya*), and sometimes of non-negligence (*apramāda*).

For example, when a person wishes to travel a long distance, the initial wish to go is called 'desire. To set out and not stop is 'diligence. To be able to encourage and uplift oneself without lingering is 'non-negligence.

For this reason, we know that desire gives rise to diligence; because of diligence, there is non-negligence; and because of non-negligence, one can give rise to all dharmas, up until the attainment of the Buddha-way. [He] himself said he attained the concentration with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*).

The samādhi with vitarka and without vicāra; the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra. Regarding that which has vitarka and vicāra: when the initial mind enters dhyāna, it is called "vitarka" (applied thought).

When the first dhyāna is produced based on the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold), the pure material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) of the form realm come into contact with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of the desire realm. The mind is greatly startled and awakened; at that moment, bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises immediately, and one perceives this contact with matter as a hitherto unknown merit and benefit—this is the factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

The subtle mental discrimination is called "vicāra" (sustained thought). Having realized the merits of the first dhyāna, one uses the subtle mind to discriminate the material phenomena within this meditative concentration; the various sublime qualities and objects become distinct and clear, free from all [impurities].

Such qualities as these—namely, being covered and so forth—do not yet exist in the desire realm; this is precisely what is called the factor of *vitarka* (initial application). The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* asks: Are *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained application) one and the same dharma, or are they two distinct dharmas? Answer: They are two dharmas. The initial thought of a coarse mind is called *vitarka*;

the analytical discernment of a subtle mind is called *vicāra*. It is like striking a bell: when the first sound is loud, it is called *vitarka*; when the subsequent sound is faint, it is called *vicāra*. Question: According to the *Abhidharma*, from the desire realm up to the first *dhyāna*, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are associated within a single moment of consciousness (*citta*).

Why then do you say that the initial thought of a coarse mind is called *vitarka* and the analytical discernment of a subtle mind is called *vicāra*? Answer: Although these two dharmas exist within a single moment of consciousness, their two characteristics do not coexist simultaneously.

At the time of initial awakening (*vitarka*), observation (*vicāra*) is not clear; at the time of observation, awakening is not clear. It is like how the various stars do not appear when the sun rises. All mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) receive their names according to the occasion. Awakening is also like this. Regarding "without awakening but with observation" (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*):

when proceeding from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna, the mind that possesses awakening has already forgotten its discursive discrimination (*vikalpa*), yet the mindfulness of the flavor of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*) still remains. This is what is called the "intermediate state" (*dhyānāntara*) as explained in the *Samyukta Āgama*. The six heavens of Mahābrahmā are produced by the power of this intermediate concentration. Regarding "without awakening and without observation" (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ*):

from the second dhyāna up to the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), both the mind of awakening and the mindfulness of the flavor of dhyāna have been completely forgotten. Therefore, it is called the "concentration without awakening or observation" (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*).

The Samādhis of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), Signlessness (*animitta*), and Wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—that is, the three gates of liberation. These three are collectively termed "gates of liberation" because liberation is the gate to *nirvāṇa*. This means they are "passages"; that is, these three dharmas can serve as the path by which one enters *nirvāṇa*, and are thus called the "gates of liberation.

They are also called the "three samādhis," though "samādhi" is a name derived from the essential nature of the state itself, whereas "liberation" is a designation received based on its function as the means of passage.

Upon the realization of the fruit, the name changes to "liberation. What is called the gate of liberation of emptiness? There are six kinds of emptiness: internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). What is meant by "internal"?

Emptiness. One contemplates all internal phenomena as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and experiences them as empty. By what sense are they empty? They are empty of self; they are also empty of "mine. They are empty of permanence and empty of changelessness. What is external emptiness?

One contemplates all external phenomena as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and experiences them as empty. By what sense are they empty? They are empty of self; they are also empty of "mine. They are empty of permanence and empty of changelessness. Internal and external emptiness is also like this. What is the emptiness of emptiness?

It is when a bhikṣu, having accomplished the practice of the concentration on emptiness, contemplates all phenomena as the emptiness of emptiness, as previously described. Great emptiness is also thus. What is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)? The ultimate truth is *nirvāṇa*. As a bhikṣu contemplates...

Nirvāṇa is the knowledge of emptiness, the understanding of emptiness, and the experience of emptiness. In what sense is it empty? It is empty of self; it is also empty of "mine. It is empty of permanence and empty of immutability. By practicing thus without negligence, one attains concentration, and the mind abides in right abiding. This is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

To be able to penetrate [reality] in this way is called the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). As for the gate of liberation through signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*): taking noble nirvāṇa as its object is called the signless meditative concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).

While nirvāṇa is practiced as signless, conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) possesses signs. The three signs are arising, abiding, and ceasing. Nirvāṇa lacks these three signs; it is non-arising, non-abiding, and non-ceasing. Thus, conditioned existence has signs while nirvāṇa is signless. This nirvāṇa is tranquility, it is a dwelling place, it is protection, and it is a bright lamp.

This is the reliance; this is non-perishing; this is the refuge; this is the absence of feverish distress; this is the absence of sorrow and affliction. By contemplating nirvāṇa, one attains a concentrated state of mind; this is called the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*). Regarding the gate of liberation through wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*):

if one knows that all phenomena are signless, then there is absolutely nothing to be done; this is called "wishlessness. Why is this so? If one perceives anything as attainable within phenomena, one will have aspirations and cravings regarding the three realms, and because of this, one creates the karma of the three states of existence (*trabhava*).

Now, because no signs whatsoever can be apprehended, one has no aspirations or cravings regarding the three realms, and thus does not create any karma for the cycle of birth and death within the three states of existence. Since there is no karma, there is no retribution; this is the gate of liberation through wishlessness.

Regarding those who claim to have attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*): they conceive of the nine notions of meditative absorption (*navasaṃjñā-samāpatti*). First, the notion of bloatedness (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*); second, the notion of lividness (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*); third, the notion of putrefaction (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*); fourth, the notion of being smeared with blood (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*).

5. The perception of festering pus; 6. The perception of being devoured by worms; 7. The perception of scattering; 8. The perception of bones; 9. The perception of burning. Through such perceptions, one destroys the fetters (saṃyojana) and attains the path of the Three Vehicles. The ten perceptions are: 1. The perception of impermanence; 2. The perception of suffering; 3. The perception of non-self; 4.

The perception of the impurity of food; 5. The perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in; 6. The perception of death; 7. The perception of impurity; 8. The perception of cessation; 9. The perception of detachment; 10. The perception of exhaustion. By cultivating these dharmas, one severs all fetters.

Having attained the state of an Arhat, one enters the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). This occurs among humans or in the heavens; through the power of repeated cultivation based on the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists who loathe coarse mental formations, one suppresses and eliminates the defiled greed of the desire realm and the first three dhyānas.

Relying upon the fourth dhyāna, one causes the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) to cease manifesting. With the cessation of perception as its primary characteristic, it is called the "attainment of non-conception.

Once this attainment is achieved, it is neither lost nor regressed; at the end of life, one is immediately reborn in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*). There, the six consciousnesses do not function for the duration of four hundred and forty-nine great kalpas. Whether one was previously a Brahmin, sitting as a Brahmin did, or previously an unlearned bhikṣu, it is as before.

First, assume the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Next, practice "receptive concentration according to the Dharma" (*anuloma-dharmasamādhi*)—that is, the pure and unburdened methods of right practice such as the Noble Eightfold Path and various meditative contemplations that accord with the state of perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*);

thus it is called "according to the Dharma" (as cited in the *Vinayaviniścaya*). Then, practice "receptive concentration through mental visualization" (*manasikāra-samādhi*): this involves calming the mind with single-minded focus so that it does not scatter. Count from one to ten, neither more nor less. Some say that one should first count the exhalation;

when the breath is not hurried, the body does not become distended, and the body and mind become light and agile, making *samādhi* easy to achieve. If the mind is flighty, fix the mind on the *dantian* (lower abdomen) and count the inhalations. If the mind is dull or drowsy, fix the mind on the nose.

[The practitioner] should count the exhalations (it is not permitted to count both inhalation and exhalation together, for fear of giving rise to illness). One eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). This means that the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), by cultivating untainted pure meditation (*anāsrava-viśuddha-dhyāna*), attain the realization of this body;

Since there are no longer afflictions, the mind is pure; therefore, it is called untainted pure meditation. Third is the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*).

This means that the followers of the Two Vehicles, by virtue of cultivating untainted wisdom, attain the realization of this body; hence it is called the body of wisdom. "Untainted wisdom" refers precisely to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the contemplation of the four [noble truths].

It is the wisdom of the Truths. One who cultivates this wisdom is able to sever the afflictions of the three realms and emerge from the outflows of birth and death. Now, first:
Venerable sirs, these thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Commentary: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" means that this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there remains a residue within the Saṃgha.
Because one must repent before the assembly of monks, it is extinguished; thus it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The Root Text says: "As for the *saṃgha*, if one commits this offense, one must rely upon the *saṃgha* to perform the prescribed rite, and rely upon the *saṃgha* to obtain purification from the offense.
*Thullaccaya* (vaśiṣa) means 'remainder. If, regarding the four matters..."
If one commits even one of these, there is no further remnant [of the offense] that remains; one may not co-reside [with the Sangha].

These thirteen dharmas have remnants that can be remedied, and are therefore called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅgha-remnant). The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "Only through the observance of the community's instruction is the offense finally extinguished."
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "It is like a person who has been struck by another; if a portion of the throat remains, it is called 'residual' (*śeṣa*).
It is like two people who have entered together into the midst of a battle: one has been killed by another and his life has ceased;

the other has also been struck by another, yet a small portion of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) remains unsevered. If he obtains a skilled physician and excellent medicine, he may be cured; if not, he will not."
It can be cured. It is the same for those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; there is still some principle by which it may be repented.
If one obtains a pure assembly that performs the method for repentance and the removal of the offense according to the Dharma, this offense can be eliminated.
If it cannot be extinguished without a pure assembly, this is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
*Saṃgha* means "the community"; *āva* means "initial," referring to the initial *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (concealment) *karmavācanā* within the community;
*śeṣa* means "remainder," referring to the subsequent *ābṛhaṇa* (expiation) *karmavācanā*. Each of these offenses depends upon the Saṃgha.
Because it is removed through a formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), it is named after its object. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

"Since all four categories [of offenses] involve a remainder (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), why is this precept alone called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*? It answers: "Although all four categories involve a remainder, they are not entirely extinguished by the Saṃgha.
These thirteen matters are entirely dependent upon the Saṃgha; among the thirty matters, three are dependent upon the Saṃgha."
The others do not depend on it. Among the ninety matters, seven matters depend on the *saṃgha*; the others do not. Therefore, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṃgha-remnant offenses).

Regarding the three matters that depend on the *saṃgha*: the second, the *karmavācanā* for being separated from one's robe; the fourteenth, the *karmavācanā* for reducing the six-year period regarding bedding and furniture; and the twenty-second, the rule for using the alms bowl. Because the others do not depend on it, the Vinaya states:

"Whether by the *saṃgha*, by many people, or by a single person. Among the ninety matters, the seven matters that depend on the *saṃgha* are: the seventh, the appointment to proclaim a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); the twelfth, the rule for speaking irrelevantly (*anyavāda*) and the rule for causing provocation; and the twenty-second, the appointment to instruct.

The Rules for Bhikṣuṇīs: The sixty-eighth [offense] is the admonition against evil and heterodox teachings; the seventieth is the admonition against evil and heterodoxy. For śrāmaṇeras, two rules are established; the remainder do not apply.

○ First Precept: Manipulating the Male Organ and Emitting Semen.
General Explanation:
Regarding this matter of the absence of a female object—although the object is absent, one may still experience pleasure—this is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*).
The monastic rules for nuns differ, whereas in the Mahāyāna, the prohibition is uniform. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "It would be better to hack and chop one's own body with a sharp axe..."
The body: one shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily cling to pleasant tactile sensations. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:
"To give rise to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and fail to awaken from them is called an offense. This constitutes a multitude of offenses, which arise as defiled transgressions.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of delusion and a lack of wisdom, and based upon sexual acts and the afflictions of lust, this [precept] was established."
The training rule (*śikṣāpada*). This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.

Regarding the origin of the rule (*nidāna*): at that time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. [The *Vinayavibhaṅga-saṃgraha* states: "Traveling" is fourfold. What are the four? First, walking; second, standing; third, sitting; and fourth, lying down.]

These four modes of conduct are called "wandering. For example, as people of the world say, "The king goes out on a tour," whether he arrives at a place of amusement or is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the Buddha’s wandering through Śrāvastī was likewise so.

Śrāvastī is the name of a site where a practitioner once resided. In ancient times, there was a king who, seeing that this location was excellent, requested the practitioner to establish it as a kingdom; it was named after the practitioner and called Śrāvastī. It is like the city of Rājagṛha:

in the past, successive wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) resided in this city, and because of their names, it was called Rājagṛha. Śrāvastī is also like this. The *Mingyi ji* states: "In Sanskrit, Śrāvastī; in the language of China, 'Hearing Things' (聞物), also translated as 'Abundant Virtue' (豐德)."

This is because it possesses four virtues: First, the virtue of possessing wealth and treasures. This means that within the city of Śrāvastī, all manner of rare jewels abound, surpassing those of other countries; this is called the virtue of possessing wealth and treasures. Second, the virtue of exquisite fivefold sensual pleasures. This means that within the city of Śrāvastī, the five sensual pleasures are exceptionally sublime, such that they cannot be equaled by other countries;

this is called the virtue of exquisite fivefold sensual pleasures. Third, the virtue of being renowned for much learning. "Renowned" (rāo) means to benefit. This means that the abundance of wealth and treasures and the excellence of the five sensual pleasures in the city of Śrāvastī are heard of in the four directions;

this is called the virtue of being renowned for much learning. Fourth, the virtue of an abundance of liberation. "Abundance" (fēng) means flourishing. This means that among the people of the city of Śrāvastī, many cultivate the path of practice and thereby attain liberation; this is called the virtue of an abundance of liberation.

Regarding its virtue: the *Sudarsana* states that within the city of Śrāvastī there were five hundred and seventy thousand households. Outside the city, those belonging to the kingdom of Śrāvastī consisted of eighty thousand villages. The land was one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

A verse says: "Śrāvastī is most sublime; those who behold it never tire of looking. With the sounds of ten kinds of music, amidst which calls for food and drink resound, it abounds in many rare treasures, just like the palace of Śakra."

The occasion for this event involved a person. At that time, Kālodāyin (also named Udāyin; translated as "Black Radiance" or "Coarse Black," so called because his face was dark and his eyes were red) was of the Brāhmaṇa caste. He was born on the same day as the Buddha and was originally a high minister to the king.

Because the World-Honored One had left the household life and attained enlightenment, the father-king, longing to see him, commanded Kālodāyin to go and welcome him. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s location, the Buddha preached the Dharma to him and addressed him as "Welcome, Bhikṣu. Thereupon, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord.

He fell and attained the nature of a bhikṣu. However, his mind was full of desire. Later, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin woman who forced him into unrighteous conduct; the Venerable One did not comply. She harbored resentment and, maiming her own body, falsely accused the Venerable One.

She informed her father, who gathered an assembly of five hundred Brahmins. They attempted to drag the Venerable One away, but they could not move even a single foot because of the Venerable One’s great power. At that time, the Buddha perceived through his insight that this was the final instruction for him. The Buddha then diminished his power.

At that time, the crowd beat him until he was nearly dead and dragged him before the King. Although the King knew for certain that the matter was false, he still rebuked him three times. The Venerable One felt extreme shame and remorse, so he went to Śāriputra, prostrated himself, and related the events in detail. Śāriputra preached the Dharma and gave him instructions;

Kāḷudāyin aroused a mind of fierce diligence, whereby his fetters and delusions were all eliminated, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship. Having attained this fruit, he thought of repaying the Buddha’s kindness and proceeded to teach and transform others.

The Buddha said, "Among my śrāvaka disciples who teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to attain the noble fruits, Kāḷudāyin is the foremost. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he taught and transformed eight billion households, leading them to attain the noble fruits. His desire-mind was thus extinguished.
[The monk] was flourishing. His complexion was haggard and his body emaciated. Whenever he engaged in recollections or mental imaginings, he would emit impurity.
His faculties became joyful and his complexion radiant. When his fellow monks saw this, they asked him:
"Previously your complexion was haggard and your body was emaciated; now your complexion is harmonious, pleasant, and radiant. Is this because you have found a place of residence?"
"Are you at ease? Does food and drink cause you distress? Thus he questioned him to learn the reason for his condition.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One. On account of this incident, the Buddha rebuked Kālodāyin:
"How can you, having gone forth within my pure Dharma, engage in such defiled conduct? You foolish man, you stretch out your hand to receive the faithful offerings of others!"
Furthermore, with this hand, he fondled his organ and emitted semen. Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus:
"One must not fondle one's organ so as to cause the emission of semen. Once the precept was established, there was a certain bhikṣu who fell asleep with a distracted mind;
during a dream, he emitted semen. Upon waking, he remembered it and spoke of it to a fellow bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "There are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind:
first, having bad dreams; second, not being protected by the devas; third, the mind failing to enter the Dharma;
fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of dawn; and fifth, emitting semen in one's dreams. There are five merits in sleeping with a wholesome mind; these are the opposites of the above."
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak as follows:
"Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his own organ and emits semen, except in a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding intentional emission, there are six types of objects. As for intentional emission through a sincere mind, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Because the wind of deluded thoughts and improper recollections fans the fire of lust, the flesh, marrow, and fat flow; through heat, they transform into semen. There are seven kinds of semen: blue, yellow, red, white, black, the color of curd, and the color of curd-water.
What is semen of a blue color? It is the semen of a Cakravartin King. What is semen of a yellow color?
The semen of the crown prince of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is the essence. Why is that essence red? Because he has indulged much in female beauty.
Why is that essence white? It is the semen of a person carrying heavy burdens. Why is that essence black? It is the semen of the foremost minister of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Why is that essence the color of curdled milk? It is the semen of a *srotāpanna*. What is that curdled milk...?

The color of the fluid is like that of gruel; it is the essence of a *sakṛdāgāmin*. Regarding "emission": the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states, "The essence leaves its original location; the waist is considered the location.

It further says this is not so, for the essence exists throughout the entire body, except for the hair, nails, and dried matter, which contain no essence. If the essence leaves its original location—whether it reaches the [sexual] organ or not, and whether it is emitted or not—even if it is only enough to satisfy a single fly, one incurs the full offense.

This excludes cases occurring during dreams. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This refers to excluding those in dreams; all other instances constitute an offense. Although there is consciousness within a dream, it lacks fixed determination and no actual substance can be found. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Dreams are false and unreal."

If dreams were real, then those who practice the holy life within my Dharma would not attain liberation; because all dreams are unreal, therefore those who practice the holy life within my Dharma reach the end of suffering.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, the arousal of the intention to stimulate the organ;
second, the perception that one is stimulating the organ; and third, the emission of semen from its original location.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the one who commits this offense: if it is for the sake of pleasure, for the sake of self-experimentation (pleasure meaning a craving for the sensation of contact;

self-experimentation meaning [to determine] which of the seven types of semen it is), for the sake of merit, or for the sake of sacrificing to the gods (merit meaning playing with the genitals and emitting semen).

One attains great merit. Those who sacrifice to the gods do so by offering their vital essence (this belongs to the externalist Brahmin dharma). For the sake of being born in heaven (at that time, there was a Brahmin living in a secluded place who recited and maintained incantations.

According to the records of his scriptures, if one intentionally emits semen, he will be reborn in heaven at the end of his life. Desiring the path to heaven, he constantly stimulated his organ and emitted semen. At that time, another Brahmin who had left the household life to practice the Way heard these words;

for the sake of being born in heaven, he likewise stimulated his organ and emitted semen. He became doubtful and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "This is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. [It is also committed] for the sake of giving, or for the sake of seeds.)

[As for] "for the sake of giving": it may be that someone comes to beg for semen and one gives it. [As for] "seed": it may be that one has no offspring and emits semen in order to continue the lineage. [It is done] for the sake of arrogance and indulgence; for the sake of testing one's own strength;
