and for the sake of a fine complexion. [Regarding] "arrogance and indulgence": this refers to letting one's mind run wild, disregarding the Buddha’s teachings. [Regarding] "testing one's own strength": this means testing for oneself how much one can emit.

[Regarding] "for the sake of a fine complexion": being oppressed by the fire of desire, one's complexion becomes haggard; these causes and conditions are as explained previously. For such reasons, one plays with the organ and emits semen. First.
All *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. Regarding internal form, external form, and both internal and external form:

as for "internal form," it refers to that which is received; as for "external form," it refers to that which is not received; as for "both internal and external form," it refers to that which is both received and not received.

(Internal refers to what belongs to the internal body, namely the hands and other parts of the body; because one perceives cold, heat, roughness, and smoothness, it is called "internal form" that is received. External refers to what belongs to the insentient, namely vessels, lumps of clay, and so forth; since they lack perception, they are said to be "external form" that is not received. Internal...)

External forms refer to forms that are either received or not received (as understood by analogy with what precedes). Water refers to whether it is with the current, against the current, or sprinkled with water. Wind refers to whether it is with the wind, against the wind, or blowing from the mouth into the air.
As for "moving the body through the air," this means moving the body through empty space oneself. [Question: These are neither internal forms, external forms, nor both internal and external forms.

Why, then, does one incur an offense? [Answer: It is because one moves the body oneself that one incurs the offense. As described above, if one intentionally emits semen through such mental recollections, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

[If it is] emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if not emitted, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣu to use a means to stimulate [himself] so that the impurity is emitted—if it is emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if not emitted, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣu to use a means to stimulate [himself] so that the impurity is emitted—if it is emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if not emitted, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Excluding cases where a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī instructs another person to cause emission, there is no offense of loss;

[in those cases] it is all *duṣkṛta* (the "others" refers to the three minor assemblies). The fourth section states: If a woman grasps a bhikṣu and he moves his body before her and emits semen, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if he moves his body but does not emit impurity, it is *duṣkṛta*. Grasping [her] afterwards is also like this. Grasping...

The same applies to the time of performing prostrations. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one emits semen while asleep, and upon waking, arouses the intention and moves the body, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the body moves while asleep, and upon waking, one emits semen, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
To recollect the act of sexual intercourse constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:

If one initiates the preparatory effort while awake and emission occurs during a dream—or conversely—and one experiences pleasure with a conscious mind; or if one initiates the preparatory effort beforehand and subsequently ceases the mental intent.
If one employs a means such that the semen is about to move and immediately restrains the mind, in all such cases one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the phrase "about to move," this refers to when the semen has not yet left its original location. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu, by measuring his organ, forms the intention to experience pleasure and thereby causes the emission of semen, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; if there is no emission, he incurs a [lesser offense]."
This constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. It would be better to grasp a fearsome black snake with one's hand than to seize the sexual organ with a defiled mind;

for a *bhikṣuṇī*, this is a *pāyattika*. (The *Sarvāstivāda* school states that the term "*bhikṣuṇī pāyattika*" is used to establish a distinction between the two assemblies [of monks and nuns], and furthermore, because the afflictions of women are deep and heavy.)

It is difficult to restrain and difficult to control. If one were to impose a heavy regulation upon it, it would cause distress to sentient beings. Furthermore, for women, emission of semen generally requires a private, secluded place, much effort, and great exertion; for men, this is not so, as they can emit it according to the circumstances. Therefore, the two cases are not the same.
(3) Minor offenses of *duṣkṛta* constitute a transgression. This is what is called an offense.

The Opening of the Conditions: Those who do not commit an offense are as follows: if one loses semen while dreaming; if, having awakened, one fears it will defile the body, the clothes, or the bedding and mattresses;
if one discards it by placing it in a worn-out object, a tree leaf, or a vessel; if one discards it by pressing it with the hand; if one intends to emit impurity through desire;
if one sees a beautiful form but does not touch it and thus emits impurity; or if one [emits it] while walking.
If one touches both thighs; or if one touches the outer garment (*saṃghāṭī*) or the inner robe (*nirvāṇaka*);
or when passing urine or excrement; or when bathing with cold water or warm water; or while in a bathhouse using tree bark, fine medicinal powders, or clay for bathing;
or if one rubs and massages with the hands; or if one weeps loudly; or if one performs strenuous labor—in all such cases, [there is no emission].
If one produces an impure intention [but does not emit], there is no offense. Those who do not commit an offense are those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Sapoduo lun): "The Buddha established this 'precept against emitting semen' in order to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, and also because he wished to stop slander.
If one were to perform such an act, worldly people and non-Buddhists would say: 'The śramaṇas..."
The disciples of the Gate (Śākyaputrīya) engage in impure conduct, no different from worldly people.

Furthermore, because one wishes to inspire faith and reverence in devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits, if one performs such acts, even in private seclusion, the devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits will see them all.
Furthermore, it is the inherent nature of all Buddhas that sexual desire is a practice of unwholesome conduct and should therefore be restrained. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"One should conceive the notion of foulness and impurity toward sexual desire, such that not even a single thought of purity arises.
If one engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, upon waking one should feel remorse."
○ Second, the general explanation of the precept concerning physical contact with a female body.

This is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*). For nuns, it constitutes the fifth grave offense (*pārājika*). It is likewise proscribed in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "In accordance with..."
One intentionally seeks pleasure; because of being shrouded by delusion and due to the affliction of lust, this training rule was established.
Regarding the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Regarding the origin of this rule:

At that time, Kāḷudāyin, having heard that the Buddha had established the precept forbidding the manipulation of the genitals to cause the emission of semen, took a key in his hand and stood outside the door, waiting for women to come by.
When they arrived, he said to them, "Sisters, please come into the room and look."
Upon entering the quarters, they grasp [the monks], feel them about, and kiss their mouths. Those who find it pleasurable laugh at what they do;

those who find it displeasurable become angry, revile them, and leave the quarters. (According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*: "For what reason do women come into the monastery to look? There are three reasons: first, because worldly people have many distracting affairs, whereas the places where renunciants dwell are tranquil and peaceful;

second, so that they may associate with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and hear the Dharma; third, because the various quarters of the Saṃgha are adorned with colorful paintings on the walls and furnishings such as beds, couches, and bedding. Upon touching these things...)

"The eyes are delightful; therefore, we come to look. Question: "Why do these women follow the bhikṣus into the dwellings? Answer: "It is because those who have left the household life are pure and have severed desire;

out of faith and reverence, they follow them in without doubt. Question: "Why is it that some remain silent while others do not? Some say: "Those with much lustful intent remain silent, while those with little lustful intent do not remain silent. Others say: "Those who have no parents, brothers, husbands, or children, and thus have nothing to fear, remain silent.

Those who have parents, brothers, husbands, or children, and thus have something to fear, do not remain silent. For this reason, there are those who remain silent and those who do not. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One..."
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he established a precept for the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, makes physical contact with a woman— whether by grasping her hand, grasping her hair, or touching her body."
Regarding each individual part of the body: it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Explanation of the term:

"With a mind of lustful desire" means a mind defiled by craving. (*Śariputra-abhidharma-śāstra* [Sudarsana-vibhāṣā] states: "A mind transformed by sexual disorder" means that when lust enters the body, it is no different from a yakṣa or ghost entering the heart;

it is also like an old elephant sinking in mud, unable to extricate itself. A mind transformed by sexual disorder clings to whatever object it encounters and lacks shame or remorse. Either the mind transforms into desire, or desire transforms the mind; this is a mind transformed by sexual disorder. The mind is thus...

"Attachment" refers to [the desire for] women who are capable of engaging in sexual intercourse and who possess consciousness before death. "The body" refers to the physical form from the hair to the feet; "touching the body" means making physical contact with it.
If one grasps, rubs heavily, pulls, pushes, rubs against the grain, rubs with the grain, lifts up, lowers down, or presses;

as for "grasping and rubbing," it means rubbing the front and back of the body (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Grasping" does not mean rubbing; "touching" means neither grasping nor rubbing—this is called "touching";
"grasping" means pinching and placing [the hand] in one spot—this is called "grasping"). "Pulling" means pulling forward. "Pushing" means pushing away. "Rubbing against the grain" means from...
"From bottom to top" means from the lower part to the upper part. "Rubbing in the natural direction" means from the top to the bottom. "Lifting" means grasping and lifting up.
"Up and down" means, for example, if one is standing, grasping them and causing them to sit. "Grasping" means grasping the front or grasping the back; grasping the breasts or grasping the thighs.

"Pressing" means pressing the front or pressing the back; pressing the breasts or pressing the thighs (*The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Grasping the hand" begins with the upper arm and elbow, extending even to the fingernails). "Each individual limb" refers to [the various parts of the body].
(From the hair to the feet: all parts of the body). Conditions for the Offense:
This precept constitutes a full offense only when five conditions are met: first, there is a mind of lustful defilement; second, it is a human woman;
third, there is the perception that she is a human woman; fourth, there is physical contact between the bodies; and fifth, one experiences the pleasure of being touched by her body.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes physical contact with a woman—whether by grasping, rubbing, or massaging;
or by pulling, or pushing; or by stroking upward or downward; or by lifting, or lowering;

or by seizing, or pressing—then for every instance of contact, and even for every instance of pressing, each constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community). This applies whether it is a woman...
If a person touches a bhikṣu, for every instance of contact, and even for every instance of pressing, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a celestial female, an asura female, a naga female, a preta female, or a female animal capable of changing form touches his body, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a female animal incapable of changing form, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one touches a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one touches the body of one with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a woman performs a prostration and grasps one's feet, and one perceives the pleasure of the touch without moving the body, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, with a lustful mind, one touches a robe, an alms bowl, a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), a needle case, a straw mat, or even touches one's own body, it is all a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension). If it is a human female but one suspects it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If it is a human female but one perceives her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a non-human female but one perceives her as a human female, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
Thullaccaya for doubting whether she is a non-human female. Thullaccaya for the fourth case:
touching a male body while perceiving it as a female, or touching a female body while perceiving it as a male—both are thullaccaya.
Touching one woman while perceiving her as another, or touching another woman while perceiving her as this woman—both are saṃghādisesa. [The same applies to] touching a dead woman.

If one touches another whose body is not yet decomposed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If half is decomposed and more than half remains intact, or if one touches one whose body is fully decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a woman is being swept away by water and one takes her out out of affection, without experiencing the pleasure of touch, there is no offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is sitting when a woman comes to prostrate at his feet, and he feels a lustful thought arise, he should sit upright and say to her:

'Stand a little further away and prostrate. If the woman is deeply faithful and suddenly comes to touch his feet, he should bite his own tongue until it is painful, so as not to perceive the smoothness of the woman's body. If the woman...
When someone asks a bhikṣu for water, he should not personally hold the pitcher and pour it onto a woman’s hand; he should give it to her using a vessel.
If there is no vessel, he should have a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) give it. If there is no lay attendant, he should place the pitcher on a bed or similar high surface and have her take it herself.
If a woman falls into water and cries out for help, the bhikṣu should regard it as solid ground.
If one seizes and pulls her out, there is no offense. If one uses bamboo, wood, or rope to pull her out, there is no offense.
If one says, "I know that although you suffer, you must accept it as your past karma," there is no fault. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In general, regarding contact with a woman's body:
if she is capable of sexual intercourse and there is no cloth interposed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if there is a cloth, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If she is not capable..."
If one touches [a woman] who is without clothing, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); if she has clothing, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

However, if one sees a woman being swept away by water, or is about to commit suicide by hanging herself or ingesting poison, etc., there is no offense in touching her for the purpose of rescue. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"In the event of all dangers—whether from fire, water, weapons, venomous insects, malevolent spirits, or falling from a high place—if one rescues [her], there is no fault."
There is no offense. If one touches her by mistake without a defiled mind, there is no offense. If a woman is being swept away by water, one should rescue her;
even if a lustful mind arises, one should merely grasp her at one place and not let go. Once she has reached the shore, one should not touch her again. To touch her again constitutes an offense.
One incurs an offense. If a female embroiderer or painter touches [the monk] intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
If one touches a woman’s coarse or thick clothing, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one touches a human woman’s fine or thin clothing with the hand, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu has his hair touch her hair, or his body hair touch hers, or his nails... [and so forth].
If the fingernails touch one another, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Why? Because there is no conscious contact.
If a woman strikes a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu receives it with a mind of lustful delight, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a woman is dressed in male attire and a bhikṣu seizes her without knowing [her true gender], there is no offense. The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* says: Ānanda, for Mā...
One who is deluded by the *ḍomba* spell incurs no offense. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a mother comes to embrace one, or if a daughter sits upon one's lap, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pārājika*; for the three lesser assemblies [bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions. There is no offense in the following cases: if there is contact during the act of taking or giving; if there is contact while joking or laughing;
or if there is contact while explaining [the matter]. There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept had not yet been formulated at the outset.
The *Ahan jing* (Āgama Sūtra) states in detail: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people when he saw a mass of fire blazing intensely.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Suppose there were someone who grasped that fire and stroked it, and another who grasped a woman of one of the four castes, stroked her, and kissed her.
Of these two matters, which would be better? The bhikṣus replied, "Grasping those women, stroking them, and kissing them would be [better]."
It is better to act thus. If one were to grasp fire and cry out, one would be burned and scorched; skin and bone would be consumed until nothing remains, resulting in great agony that is unbearable.
The Buddha said: "It would be better to grasp fire and cry out until even the sinews and bones are consumed.

Why? Because by this cause and condition, one does not fall into the three evil realms. But as for those who are not śramaṇas yet claim to be śramaṇas, and so forth, even to the point of concealing..."
Committing offenses while dwelling in the monastic life, one’s interior becomes hollow and rotten while the exterior appears complete and pure;

thus, one fails to digest the offerings of the faithful and falls into the three evil realms, suffering for a long night. For this reason, one should maintain pure precepts when receiving the offerings of the faithful.

By doing so, all that is required will enable the donor to obtain a great karmic reward. Furthermore, having left the household life to become a śramaṇa, one shall likewise achieve fulfillment. *Sādhana*.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: The reason the Buddha established this precept against touching women is twofold.
First, because those who have left the household life are solitary and have no support, he now establishes this precept to provide them with a companion, so that they may have someone to rely upon.
Second, it is intended to stop strife and contention; for this [touching of women] is the root of such disputes. If one touches a woman, then [conflict] arises.

To prevent strife and disorder. Third, it is to eliminate suspicion; for if a bhikṣu were to take hold of a woman, people would not think he was merely grasping her, but would instead assume he was committing a great evil.
Therefore, this is prohibited. Fourth, it is to cut off the source of great evils. Desire is the precursor to all calamities;
if one takes hold of or strokes a woman, one opens the door to all manner of wickedness. Thus, one restrains the subtle to prevent the manifest.
Fifth, it is for the sake of protecting right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). If one associates with women, one loses right mindfulness. Sixth, it is for the sake of the superior Dharma.
A bhikṣu who has left the household life severs his tracks from the defilements of desire and dwells with his mind directed toward the transcendent; he serves as a model for the world.
If he were to grasp or touch a woman, he would be no different from an evil person, and would thus lose the respect and veneration of the people of the world.
○ Third, the general explanation of the precept against harsh speech.

This is a unique precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla). For nuns, it involves preparatory effort; in the Mahāyāna, it is likewise proscribed. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "It is common [to both vehicles]."

Vulgar speech; using a defiled mind to mock and tease; thereby inviting ridicule and disgrace; and due to doubt and lack of wisdom—based on these matters of sexual misconduct and the afflictions of lust, this training rule was established.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [is as follows].

At that time, Kāḷudāyin, having heard that the World-Honored One had established the precepts—prohibiting the manipulation of the genitals to cause the emission of semen and prohibiting physical contact—held the door-key and stood outside the door.
He waited for women to enter the room and addressed them with coarse and evil words born of lustful intent.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established the precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, utters coarse and lewd words of sexual desire toward a woman,
for every such coarse and lewd word of sexual desire spoken, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

Explanation of the Terms: Regarding "harsh speech" (*pāruṣya*), the *Mūla* states that there are two types of base and evil speech: first, that which arises from a *pārājika* offense; second, that which arises from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

There is that which is base by its own nature (*svabhāva-pāruṣya*), and there is that which is base due to its origin (*samutthāna-pāruṣya*). "Own nature" refers to the fundamental disposition; it is when the habituation to sexual desire is deep-seated and powerful. "Origin" refers to new conditioning; it is when external conditions are powerful.
Regarding "sexual speech," it refers to speaking of the merits and defects of the two [sexual] organs.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept constitutes a full offense when five conditions are complete: first, the intention of sexual desire; second, coarse and evil speech;
third, the object being a human woman; fourth, the perception that she is a human woman; and fifth, her clear understanding of the words spoken.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bhikṣu addresses a woman with coarse and wicked words even once, it constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
For every instance of coarse and wicked speech, provided that the words are spoken clearly and intelligibly, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for each.

If it is not clearly understood, there is a *sthūlātyaya* for each instance. If one provides a hand-seal (*aṅgulipratyaṅga*), sends a messenger, or makes a sign such that the woman understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If she does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Apart from speaking of the anus or the urinary tract, if one speaks of other parts as being "good" or "bad," it is a *sthūlātyaya*. [The same applies to] celestial women, *asura* women, or night-walking spirits...

If one causes a woman who is a *śakaṭī*, a *nāgī*, or a female animal capable of transforming her form, or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) who possesses a single organ, to utter coarse and evil speech, it is a *sthūlātyaya* if the person understands; it is a *duṣkṛta* if they do not understand.

If this is done by means of a sign with the finger, a letter, a messenger, or by manifesting a recognizable gesture, it is a *sthūlātyaya* if the person understands; it is a *duṣkṛta* if they do not understand.
A *duṣkṛta* offense: speaking harsh words to an animal that is unable to transform its form.
A *duṣkṛta* offense: speaking harsh words to a man. If one speaks harsh words while perceiving them as harsh words, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If there is doubt regarding harsh words, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If they are not harsh words but one perceives them as such, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If it is a human female and one suspects she is so, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a non-human female and one perceives her as a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one suspects a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The fourth section states:

if a woman is perceived as a man, or a man is perceived as a woman, and one utters coarse and evil speech, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If this woman is perceived as another woman, or another woman is perceived as this woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one is habitually inclined toward coarse and evil speech but lacks a lustful mind, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinayaviniścaya* says:

If there is a woman who speaks vulgar and evil words, and [the monk] receives them through his speech and takes pleasure in the matter, he incurs the full offense even if he himself does not speak vulgar and evil words. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bhikṣu, with a mind of desire..."
If one employs skillful means with the desire to accomplish this matter and uses a pretext by speaking of an incidental matter, and a woman understands these words, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; for the three lesser assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases. If, for the sake of a woman, one teaches the meditation on the impurity of the foul secretions, saying:
"Sister, you should know that this body has nine wounds, nine apertures, nine leakages, and nine flows. As for the nine apertures:
the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, and the passages for feces and urine. When teaching this impurity, if that woman considers it to be coarse and vulgar speech.
Regarding speech: if, while reciting the Vinaya, the words happen to reach this point, it is considered coarse speech;
likewise if one receives the scriptures from another, or if two people receive them together, or recite them together, or speak in jest, or speak to oneself, or speak very rapidly.

If one speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that, there is no offense in any case. There is no offense for those for whom the precepts have not yet been established, and so forth.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, the purpose of establishing the precepts is twofold: first, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time; second, to bring about cessation [of misconduct].
Third, because it prevents harming sentient beings and causes their faith and reverence to increase; fourth, because it leads to practicing the wholesome Dharma with few desires and contentment.
○ Fourth, praising the precept of renouncing the pursuit of sensual desires.
General Explanation:
This refers to employing alternative means out of a longing for sensual pleasure; this constitutes an unshared offense (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*).

The Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya prescribes the formal act (*karmavācanā*), which is likewise prohibited in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Due to delusion and ignorance, one engages in sexual acts and the afflictions of lust."
This training rule was established.
Regarding the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Regarding the origin of the rule:

At that time, Kāḷudāyin heard that the Buddha had established a precept stating that one must not toy with the male organ to cause the emission of semen, nor touch the body of a woman, nor use coarse and evil speech.
He then approached women, praising their bodies and soliciting their desires. The bhikṣus [reported this to the Buddha].
Having heard this, he reported it to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established the precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, in the presence of a woman, praises his own person, saying: 'Sister, I practice the holy life (brahmacarya).'"
"One who maintains the precepts with diligence and cultivates wholesome dharmas may offer this practice of sexual desire as an offering to me;
such an offering is the foremost and most supreme. This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
**Exegesis:** Regarding the self-praise concerning the body: it refers to praising one's own physical form as upright and handsome, and one's complexion as excellent.
One says, "I am of the Kṣatriya, householder, merchant, or Brahmin caste. The term "Elder Sister" (mahābhagini) is a designation for a female younger sibling.

When one says, "I practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," it means one diligently cultivates the state free from defilement—that is, being free from impurity and unwholesome dharmas; hence, it is called "free from defilement. To say "one who maintains the precepts with diligence" means... [not corrupt].

"Without breach, without perforation, without leakage, and without defilement. (Regarding "without breach": this is said in contrast to the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*). If one commits an offense involving expulsion (*pārājika*), one is like a broken vessel; since there is currently no transgression, it is "without breach.")

Therefore, it is said that it is "not deficient. Regarding "not perforated": this is said in contrast to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension). If one violates the precepts of this category, although one is not called a "broken vessel for the Path," there is a hole;

thus, one cannot increase the wealth of the sublime Dharma. Therefore, it is said to be "not perforated. Regarding "not leaking": "leaking" refers to seepage. This is said in contrast to the latter three categories [of offenses]. If there are violations of the latter three, although the vessel for the Path is neither deficient nor perforated, there is still seepage.

Because there is no violation, it is said to be "not leaking. "Without defilement" summarizes all five categories. Regarding "cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas": wholesome dharmas refer to the twelve *dhūta* practices. In Sanskrit, *dhūta* means "to shake off" (*dhunoti*), meaning to shake off...

Shaking off [the defilements] (because of the afflictions, karma, and retribution of the three realms). Delighting in secluded and quiet places (meaning to leave behind the clamor of crowds, dwell in an araṇya, and because the body is physically removed, the mind attains purity and is freed from the hindrance of desire).

Because it benefits all that is wholesome). When the time comes to seek alms (this refers to the regular practice of begging for food; that is, seeking alms according to the Dharma), one should restrain the six sense faculties so as not to become attached to the six sense objects, nor should one discriminate between the characteristics of male, female, and so forth.

Whether one obtains or does not obtain food, whether it is good or bad, one should give rise to neither hatred nor attachment. If one accepts invitations to eat, then whether food is obtained or not, greed and resentment easily arise. If one eats together with the *saṃgha*, the task of assigning others to serve the food will distract the mind, preventing entry into the Dharma. One wears rag-robes (meaning one gathers discarded refuse to patch together as clothing;
by covering oneself with this, one wards off cold and heat, remains free from greed, stays far from thieves, and avoids the peril of loss of life).

One practices the ritual of "leftover food" (*khalupaścādbhaktika*) and does not eat [further] (meaning that practicing the ritual of leftover food hinders the cultivation of the path, further increases greedy thoughts, and leads to a lack of contentment). One eats in a single sitting (meaning if one eats again [after rising], it is not permitted).

[This refers to] losing half one’s effort [by abandoning the practice of] eating at fixed intervals (*prāptapiṇḍapātika*). First is the practice of eating a single mouthful (*ekāsanika*; also called *mātrajñatā*, "moderation in food"). This means reflecting that there are eighty thousand families of worms within the body; these worms find peace and security through this food. I now sustain these various worms with food so that, when I later attain the Way, I may sustain them with the Dharma.

Furthermore, although one eats but once a day, if one indulges in greed and overeats until the belly swells and the breath is stifled, it will obstruct and ruin the practice of the Path. Whatever food one obtains, if one eats two-thirds of it, the body will become light and at ease;

this is called "eating a single mouthful. Second is sitting in a cemetery (*śmāśānika*). This means that in a cemetery there are always sounds of lamentation and corpses strewn about; because one contemplates impermanence and impurity, the path of realization is easily accomplished. Third is sitting under a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*).

Sitting on a low seat (meaning that it accords with the Dharma; for example, when the Buddha attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered *parinirvāṇa*, he did so all beneath trees.

Since there is no craving for dwellings, it is easy to enter the Path). Sitting in the open air (meaning that sitting under a tree is like being in half a house; attachment still arises, and crows cause clamor and impurity. If one is in an open space, light shines everywhere, causing the mind to become clear and sharp, making it easy to achieve profound contemplation).

Constantly sitting without lying down (meaning that whether walking or standing, the mind is difficult to restrain; however, one should eventually practice constant sitting. When drowsy, one does not let the side of the body touch the mat). Sitting according to circumstances (meaning that [one sits] according to the state of the mind...).

[He] attains [this], yet sits upon it; for he is free from attachment to what is loved and does not afflict others. He maintains the three robes (meaning that while laypeople keep various fine garments and non-Buddhists practice asceticism by remaining naked).

Now, the disciples of the Buddha should abandon the two extremes and maintain only the three robes. This is because they remain free from excessive seeking and the need for guarding [possessions]. Bhāṇaka (translated here as "tranquility," or "cessation," or "resting").

Because external conditions have thus ceased and been severed, at that time one may rest in tranquility and attend to the affairs of the Dharma. The *Fayuan* states: "Seeking the existence of *bhāṣya* (chanting) in the Western Regions is like the existence of *zan* (eulogies) in this Eastern Land.

A *zan* is composed of verses to form chapters; a *bhāṣya* consists of short stanzas to flow as hymns. Comparing their purpose and meaning, the names differ but the substance is the same. The *Vinayamātṛkā* says: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'I allow you to chant (*bhāṣya*). Chanting refers to the words of speech.

I allow you to cite essential phrases and sublime expressions from within the twelve divisions of the scriptures to directly reveal their meaning; therefore, it is called *bhāṇaka*. One who is widely learned can preach the Dharma; by upholding the *vinaya* and practicing seated meditation, one is complete in the three trainings."
Thus, one makes offerings to the foremost and supreme [being]. (The *Sudarsana* states: "Or, one praises their sexual requirements; this is the foremost offering. We who are renunciants... )
Other forms of offering are easily obtained; this offering of sexual desire is difficult to obtain, and is therefore called the "supreme offering.

Regarding the conditions for an offense: this precept constitutes a full offense only when five conditions are met. First, there must be a lustful intention. Second, one must praise one's own body and solicit desire.
Third, the object must be a human woman. Fourth, one must perceive her as a human woman. Fifth, she must clearly understand and accept the proposal.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, having thus praised himself, receives offerings but does not speak of sexual desire, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If he speaks of sexual desire, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community).
If he praises his own person before a woman, each instance of self-praise constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; this applies according to the number of times he praises himself.
If it is clearly understood, each instance constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if it is not clearly understood, each instance constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses hand gestures, written messages, messengers, or indicative signs to make another understand, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one does not know [the recipient], it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Except for the two [sexual] organs, if one further solicits another part of the body for offerings, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a goddess, an asura-woman, a yakṣa-woman, a preta-woman, or a female animal capable of transforming her shape, speaks in praise of her own body toward oneself and makes herself understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if she is not clearly understood, it is not.
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one sends a messenger, or if one speaks in praise of one's own body using manifest signs so that the other person understands, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;

if they do not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To a female animal who is unable to change form, if one praises one's own body to her, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To praise one's own body to a male, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If it is a human female and one has doubt regarding her identity, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If it is a non-human female and one perceives her as a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If it is a non-human female and one has doubt regarding her identity, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Vinayaviniścayasaṃgraha* states: "If one acts toward a woman capable of sexual intercourse, one incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*)."
If [the woman] is not capable [of understanding], the monk incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, the nun incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, and the three minor assemblies incur a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense. The exceptions:
There is no offense if a monk says to a woman, "This place is wondrous, supreme, and most excellent."
(This refers to praising the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-gate as being most supreme and peerless. This bhikṣu diligently upholds the precepts and cultivates wholesome dharmas.

"You all should make offerings through the kindness of bodily action (bowing with palms joined and lowering the head in prostration), the kindness of verbal action (uttering gentle words and praising their virtues), and the kindness of mental action (maintaining a heart of reverence and always cherishing them with longing). Those women thought to themselves:
"The bhikṣu praises his own body for our sake; when he speaks of the Vinaya, his words are similar [to those used for praise], yet he himself considers this to be praise."
Regarding the body: if one receives or recites the scriptures; if two people receive or recite them together; if speaking in a dream;
or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that—there is no offense. There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Fifth Precept on Brokering Marriages:
This refers to acting as an intermediary for sexual matters on behalf of others. This is a shared precept; the offense incurred by a *bhikṣuṇī* is identical. In the Mahāyāna, it is likewise.

The same applies to the regulations. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "One should give rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience, rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, and bestowing the pure Dharma upon others;
yet, on the contrary, one further gives rise to sexual misconduct and other such acts toward others. This constitutes an offense by prohibition (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This training rule was established because of base and evil matters."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha (Rājagṛha being the city of Rājagṛha). The person who gave rise to the occasion [is as follows].
There was a bhikṣu named Kāla who had formerly been a high minister to the king and was well-versed in worldly customs.
Whenever there were marriages in the city of Rājagṛha, everyone would consult Kāla to arrange the weddings.
Those men and women whose unions were pleasing would rejoice and offer praise; those whose unions were not pleasing would say: "We must cause Kāla..."
They constantly experienced suffering and distress. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows: "If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for others, conveying a man's intentions to a woman and a woman's intentions to a man..."
If one acts for the sake of establishing a marriage, or for the sake of a private liaison, even for a mere moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Explanation of the meaning: "Acting as a go-between for mutual coming and going" means causing those who ought to be united to do so (the *Vinayavibhaṅga* states:

"acting as a go-between" means conveying messages back and forth). There are twenty kinds of women; "protected by her mother" means she is under the guardianship of her mother (*Sudarsana-vinaya* states...).

The mother restrains her and does not permit her to go out or come in, fearing other matters; furthermore, she says, "I shall inspect and supervise her, not allowing her to play in other places, nor permitting her to walk about or enter and exit.
[She is protected by] the father, protected by both parents, protected by the elder brother, protected by the elder sister, or protected by both the elder brother and elder sister (the *Mūla* states:

if a woman’s parents and husband have all passed away, or have at some time been lost, and she stays in the house of her brothers, then the brothers provide protection). She protects herself and attains autonomy (meaning that parents, husband, and brothers are all...).

"Loss" (meaning she is alone). "Dharma-protection" (dhamma-rakkhā) means practicing the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—that is, having a pure heart, taking refuge in the Triple Gem, and receiving the five precepts; thus protecting her through the Dharma and the Buddha.

"Lineage-protection" (gotta-rakkhā) means not being given to a low-caste family. "Kinsman-protection" (ñāti-rakkhā) means being protected by her kinsmen, whether she herself wishes to be a slave or wishes to be a slave to another, or is given as a cloth-slave (a slave whose price is a garment).
"Cloth-protection" (vattha-rakkhā) means [being protected] by the price of a garment. "Giving" (dāna) means... [text continues].
A slave for wealth, even one obtained for the price of a single coin; a fellow-worker slave, who performs labor alongside [the master];
a slave rescued from water by one who was drifting in the river before they had become husband and wife;

a slave not subject to tax—meaning that although goods would normally be subject to a tax value, one does not take that tax value but instead makes them a slave; a slave released [from bondage]; or a slave purchased.
If born in the household; a hired servant who works for wages; one like a domestic laborer;

a protected slave who receives a flower garland as a pledge (meaning she is betrothed with a flower garland; once she has accepted the other's gift, she belongs to that person, hence "protected by another");

a slave obtained from border regions, meaning captured through plunder (meaning obtained when a general campaigns against a foreign land, or a bandit chief destroys a village or city—thus called "captured through plunder"). These are the twenty kinds.
It is the same for a man. Whether it be a woman protected by her mother or a girl protected by her mother, he dispatches a bhikṣu as a messenger to say to her:
"Become my wife," or "Have illicit relations with me," even for a mere moment (this excludes becoming his wife for life;
since the duration is not long, it is called "a mere moment"—there are thirty such moments in one day and night).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires five conditions to constitute the full offense. First, acting as a matchmaker for a human female; second, the perception that she is a human female;
third, receiving her message; fourth, going to deliver it; and fifth, returning to report the result.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, for each instance where one acts as a matchmaker and conveys the message clearly and receives a report back, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If the message is conveyed but not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If a bhikṣu receives the message, goes to the other party to convey it, but does not return to report;
or if he goes to the other party to convey it without having received the initial message, yet returns to report it—in all such cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

[This is] prohibited. If a bhikṣu receives a message but does not go, and the other party speaks but he does not return a reply; or if he goes without receiving a message, and the other party speaks but he does not return a reply—in both cases it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If he uses writing, finger-signs, or gestures to make himself known and the other party understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension from the community).
If the other party does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). [The same applies to] celestial maidens, asura maidens, and naga maidens.
If a female yakṣa, a female preta, or a female animal capable of transforming her shape [is approached], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a eunuch, one with two sexual organs, or a matchmaker speaks clearly [of the act], it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if not clearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one uses writing, finger-signs, or gestures to make oneself known to the other, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the other does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If [the partner] is an animal... [text fragment].

To act as a matchmaker for the transformation of forms (i.e., changing one's appearance) is a *duṣkṛta*. To act as a matchmaker for a man is a *duṣkṛta*. If one acts as a matchmaker while perceiving it as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one acts as a matchmaker while being in doubt, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one acts as a matchmaker while perceiving it as not being a matchmaking, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not act as a matchmaker while perceiving it as such, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one does not act as a matchmaker due to delusion, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one denies [the act], yet perceives a human female as a human female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If there is doubt regarding a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a human female as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one perceives a non-human female as a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If there is doubt regarding a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If a bhikṣu takes another’s letter and goes without reading it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one performs other services for a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a man has many wives, some who are mindful [of him] and some who are not, and a bhikṣu says to him, 'You should look after them equally and strive to treat them with impartiality,' and he replies, 'I shall do as my teacher instructs,' at that time the bhikṣu incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
If a monk encourages reconciliation between a husband and wife who are quarreling, he commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

However, if those husband and wife are not in harmony, or if there is a deficiency in matters concerning the Buddha or the Sangha, and the monk encourages their reconciliation for the sake of performing meritorious deeds, [there is no offense].
There is no offense. If there is a wife who has returned to her parents' home, and one encourages her to return early to her husband's house, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There were two *mahallaka* bhikṣus; one had a son and the other had a daughter, and they themselves arranged a marriage for them.
Both incurred a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If the act of matchmaking has already been completed, and a bhikṣu later comes to assist, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."
[The Vinaya] prohibits this. The *Mūla* states: "If a bhikṣu goes to a donor’s house and speaks thus: 'This girl has grown up; why does she not go out to marry?
or 'This boy is already grown; why does he not take a wife? or if he says, 'Why does this girl not go to her husband's home?
or 'Why does this boy not go to his wife's house?'—in all such cases, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If [he] points..."

If one acts as a matchmaker for marriages—whether it results in the birth of a son or daughter, whether both are male, both are female, or they are *paṇḍaka* (those who are neither male nor female)—it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says, "There is a daughter in that family; why do you not seek her? with the intention of acting as a matchmaker, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Even a single word that corresponds to the act of matchmaking results in a *duṣkṛta* offense.

An offense. If a disciple says to his preceptor, "I wish to act as a matchmaker for another," and the preceptor hears these words and gives silent consent, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (a grave offense).
[This means that the preceptor ought to have restrained him from this evil deed; yet, because the preceptor is unacquainted with the Vinaya rules, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* by giving silent consent.]

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If many women dispatch one bhikṣu to convey their words to many men, and he receives the message, goes there, delivers it, and returns with a report, [the offense] for the many [bhikṣus] is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding this precept, it does not matter whether one knows [the truth] or not."
If one merely accepts the message and delivers it, and upon delivery receives a reply, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

The *Śīla-nidāna-sūtra* states: "To release animals so that they may mate with their respective partners is a *saṃghāvaśeṇa* offense. [Question: Regarding the various schools' views on matchmaking for animals, why is it that the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) is not incurred? In the *Śīla-nidāna-sūtra*, the act of releasing animals to mate is uniquely classified as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Why is this so? [Answer: If one merely acts as a matchmaker, the impulse toward sexual misconduct is still remote. However, by releasing them to mate, one witnesses the illicit act with one's own eyes; therefore, even though the subjects are animals, the fundamental offense is incurred. *Bhikṣu* [End].
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa; for the three groups of minor followers, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.
Regarding the exceptions: there is no offense if the man and woman had previously engaged in sexual intercourse and later separated, only to reunite again.
If it is for the sake of one's parents who are ill, or if they are imprisoned and confined in a jail—take a letter and go to see them.
If it is for the sake of a faithful and diligent upāsaka who is ill, or if he is imprisoned and confined in a jail—take a letter and go to see him.
If it is for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or a stūpa; or if it is for the sake of a sick bhikṣu—take a letter and go to see them. In all such cases, there is no offense.
Offense. Non-offenses include cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Sixth Precept Regarding Excessive Size for Small Dwellings.
This is an unshared precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); nuns do not commit this offense together [with monks].

It is a common regulation in the Mahāyāna, as referred to in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* as "evil seeking" and "excessive seeking," and in the *Bodhisattva-pratimokṣa* as "having many desires and lacking contentment. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "To give a small amount and yet feel it is insufficient...")

To be called "having many desires" means to seek one thing after obtaining another; this is called "lack of contentment. Furthermore, to be insatiable regarding internal offerings is called "having many desires," while to be insatiable regarding external gains and support is called "lack of contentment.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "This training rule was established due to the base conduct and afflictions associated with matters concerning dwellings."
The setting for the origin of this rule:
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha. He permitted the bhikṣus to construct private dwellings.
This is the causal basis for the rule.
There was a monk in the country of Āṭavī who privately constructed a large dwelling. His labor was extensive (the *Mūla* states:

At that time, between the two kingdoms of Magadha and Kośala, in a vast wilderness, there were five hundred bands of bandits who slaughtered traveling merchants until the roads were cut off. King Bimbisāra then ordered his great general to go there to eliminate the bandits and subdue them by skillful means.

He immediately built a new city at the boundary between the two realms, gathered all the people together, and they resided therein; it was named Āṭavī City). This monk constantly went about begging for alms, which caused the householders to fear him.
[The tree spirit] avoided [the blow]. There was a bhikṣu who wished to build a dwelling and was about to chop down a tree.

The tree spirit thought of striking the bhikṣu, but fearing it would violate the principles of propriety, he went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha praised and comforted him. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was begging for alms in the city of Kalandaka.

The lay devotees saw him from afar and avoided him by entering the lanes (five households constitute a neighborhood; five neighborhoods constitute a *li*; a straight path is called a street; a curved one...).
[The Buddha] said, "In the lane. Kāśyapa asked about the cause of the matter and informed the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.
Regarding the characteristics of the rule:
if a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself where there is no owner, he must build it according to the prescribed measurement for his own sake. As for the measurement therein:
It shall be twelve spans long according to the Buddha’s span, and seven spans wide on the inside. A monk must have another monk point out the location;
that other monk shall point out a location that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a monk seeks to build a house for himself where there are difficulties or obstructions, without a patron and for his own sake, yet does not have another monk point out the location, and if it exceeds [the prescribed measurements]...
Regarding the measure of the offender: it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Explanation of the meaning:
"To seek for oneself" means to beg and solicit here and there. "A house" refers to a dwelling.
"Without an owner" means that there is no one there—whether one person, two persons, or many. "For oneself" means seeking and obtaining for one's own sake.
It is to be constructed according to measure. "According to measure" means the length is twelve *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha; the internal width is seven *vitasti*.

(*Vitasti* refers to the span of a fully extended hand. It is also called a "stretched hand. According to the Zhou measurement, one human *chi* equals two Buddha *chi*. During the Tang dynasty, two *fen* were added to each *cun* of the Zhou measurement, and two *cun* were added to each *chi*, making it equivalent to eight *cun* of the Zhou measurement.

One Buddha *vitasti* corresponds to one *chi* and six *cun* by Tang measurement. A length of twelve Buddha *vitasti* is the measurement for the depth of the room, which is exactly one *zhang*, nine *chi*, and two *cun*. An internal width of seven *vitasti* is... [the measurement for the width].)

The horizontal measurement is one *zhang*, one *chi*, and two *cun*. If it were too large, the labor required would be excessive; if too small, it would be difficult to accommodate the four modes of deportment. Now, the Buddha has prescribed this measurement as being precisely in the middle. Regarding difficult locations:
there may be tigers, wolves, lions, and various other predatory beasts, down to even ants.
If a bhikṣu is not troubled by these insects and beasts, he should cultivate and level the ground. If there are stones, tree stumps, or thorns, he should [remove them].
One should have people dig them out. If there are ditches, pits, ponds, or reservoirs, one should have them filled in.
If there is fear of being flooded by water, one should establish embankments in advance. If the land is claimed by others, one should settle the matter together so that no further disputes arise.
This is what is meant by "difficult places" and "obstructed places," where even a grass cart cannot pass through or turn around to come and go.

That is, a place that is obstructed. Having inspected a place that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions, that bhikṣu goes before the Saṃgha, removes his leather sandals, bares his right shoulder, places his right knee on the ground, joins his palms, and makes this formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen."
"Listen to me, [Name] Bhikṣu: you are begging for materials yourself to build a house that has no owner, for your own sake.

I now request from the Saṃgha that you be granted a site known to be free of difficulties and free of obstructions. When this has been requested three times, the Saṃgha should examine whether this bhikṣu is trustworthy.
If he is trustworthy, they should immediately grant permission for him to build. If he is not trustworthy, the Saṃgha...
The Saṃgha should go to that place to inspect it. If the entire Saṃgha does not go, they should dispatch a trustworthy person from among the monks to inspect it.

If that place is subject to both danger and obstruction, or if it is free of danger but obstructed, or if it is subject to danger but free of obstruction, in all such cases, one should not grant permission for the site.
Only if it is free of both danger and obstruction should permission be granted. Therefore it is said: "One should take a bhikṣu with them."
He shall point out the location. That bhikṣu must point out a location that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions (one should know that this precept has two origins;

there are two paths of prohibition for the precept: it should follow the majority regarding measurements, and if one seeks a site, the tree-deity becomes angry, thus resulting in a double offense). One should know the initial stages of constructing the dwelling:
whether it be stones, earth, brick, or clay lumps, up until the final stage when the plastering is finished. If...
If a bhikṣu builds [a hut] in a place where there is danger (which constitutes an offense against the established rule), the conditions for the offense are as follows:
this precept requires four factors to constitute the full offense. First, constructing it beyond the prescribed measure; second, not having obtained formal authorization (*anujñā*);
third, perceiving it as being beyond the measure and lacking authorization; and fourth, the completion of the hut.

**Determination of Offenses:** Regarding the offenses herein: if one builds in a location that has not been formally authorized by the Saṃgha, exceeds the prescribed measurements, and is both difficult and obstructive, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, it exceeds the measurements, but is difficult yet not obstructive, [there are likewise two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and two *duṣkṛta* offenses].

In cases where there is no difficulty but there is an obstruction: two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and one *duṣkṛta*. If the Saṃgha has not given its authorization and it does not exceed the prescribed measure:

one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In cases where there is both difficulty and obstruction: two *duṣkṛta* offenses. In cases where there is difficulty but no obstruction, or where there is no difficulty but there is an obstruction:

in both instances, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense. If the Saṃgha has given its authorization but it exceeds the prescribed measure: one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In cases where there is both difficulty and obstruction: [one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
There are two *duṣkṛta* offenses: if there is an obstacle but no hindrance, and if there is no obstacle but there is a hindrance, each constitutes one *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha’s formal authorization does not exceed the prescribed measure, yet there is both an obstacle and a hindrance, it is two *duṣkṛta* offenses; if there is an obstacle but no hindrance, [it is likewise].
If there is no difficulty but there is an obstruction, it is one *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for each case.
If the Saṃgha has authorized [the construction] but it exceeds the prescribed measure, and there is neither difficulty nor obstruction, it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension).

If a bhikṣu builds a house that exceeds the measure without authorization from the Saṃgha, and there is both difficulty and obstruction, if the house is completed, it is two *saṃghāvaśeṣas* and two *duṣkṛtas*. If it is built but not completed, it is two *sthūlātyaya*s (grave offenses).
Two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If he causes another to build it and it is completed, two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If it is built but not completed, two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If he builds a house for another and it is completed, two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses. If it is built but not completed, four *duṣkṛta* offenses. If he builds...
If one builds a house by marking the ground with cords, whether one makes it according to the prescribed measure or exceeds the measure, an offense is committed.

If a bhikṣu instructs another to build according to the cord-lines, and the person receiving the instruction builds it according to the dharma but exceeds the measure, that person who received the instruction commits an offense.
If the person who instructed them to build according to the cord-lines does so exactly according to the dharma but fails to inform [the supervisor] of this, the builder commits an offense.

If one instructs another to work according to the lines and measurements, and the work is done accordingly, the instructor is not at fault; however, if the instructor does not inquire whether it is being done according to the Dharma, the instructor commits an offense.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized the construction, yet one perceives that it has not been authorized, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the Saṃgha has not made a formal decision (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet one perceives it as having been decided; or if the Saṃgha has made a formal decision, yet one perceives it as not having been decided;

or if there is doubt regarding whether the Saṃgha has made a formal decision—in all these cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If [the object] exceeds the prescribed measure and one perceives it as exceeding the measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If there is doubt as to whether it exceeds the measure, or if one perceives it as not exceeding the measure when it does exceed the measure, or if one perceives it as exceeding the measure when it does not exceed the measure... [the penalty is a *sthūlātyaya*].
If one perceives it as being within the proper measure but it exceeds the measure, or if one has doubt regarding it exceeding the measure, these are all *sthūlātyaya* offenses.

If there is a danger and one perceives it as dangerous, or if there is a danger and one doubts it, or if there is a danger and one perceives it as not dangerous, or if there is no danger and one perceives it as dangerous, or if there is no danger and one doubts it—in all these cases, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. The same applies to obstructed locations. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When constructing a dwelling..."
If one receives bricks, lumps of clay, or piles of bricks and the like, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense in every case.
When the door and windows are completed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; when the construction is finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. All such uses constitute [an offense].

This constitutes a *vaiyāpṛtyakaraṇa-vinayātikrama* (an offense of improper conduct). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* states: "If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, 'Build a dwelling for me,' and having said this, he departs;
later, while the construction is not yet finished, he returns and it is completed—this dwelling was built improperly, and he commits an offense."
If one obtains [the site] before construction is completed, there is no offense. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If two or three people build a house together—such as one bhikṣu and one śrāmaṇera—there is no offense for either. Why? Because each person does not have a separate portion of the house."
If one divides a dwelling into sections and obtains a share of a single house, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. According to the Sarvāstivādins:

from the time the ground is leveled and marked with seals until two lumps of clay have not yet been finished, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*; once one lump of clay has been finished, it is a heavy *sthūlātyaya*;
when the construction of the room is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. These three cases concern the small group.
A *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This is called an offense; (regarding the *sthūlātyaya* for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it refers to the fact that she does not dwell in an *araṇya*).

**Explanations of the Exceptions:** There is no offense in the following cases: if one builds according to the prescribed measurements or less than the measurements; if one builds on land assigned by the *saṃgha*;

if one builds in a place free from danger and free from obstruction; if one builds according to the legal rules; or if one builds for the sake of the *saṃgha* or for a *stūpa* (this refers to a Buddhist shrine or temple). To preach...

Whether it be a hall, a grass hut, or a leaf hut—if one builds a small dwelling sufficient for one's own body, or a place for many people to reside (that is, for the sake of the community), there is no offense.
There is no violation for those cases where the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
The *Sārvastivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* explains in detail: First, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma; second, to stop slander;
third, so as not to afflict or harm sentient beings, but rather to increase their faith and reverence;
fourth, so that those with few desires and contentment may practice wholesome dharmas. It is for these four reasons that the precepts are established.
○ General Explanation of the Seventh Precept Regarding the Construction of Large Dwellings.
This is an exclusive precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla). For nuns, the formulation is the same as before. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna; the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The dhūta [practices]..."
One must not enter any such difficult locations, ranging from places where one practices the Path to those where one observes the summer retreat (varṣā).
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Because they obstruct the cultivation of wholesome deeds, give rise to disputes, and lead to the reproach of others, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established."
The setting of the origin:
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī (Kauśāmbī; according to the *Xiyu ji*, this is the kingdom of Kośala; the former name "Kauśāmbī" is an error.

It is located within the borders of Central India and is over six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is thirty *li* in circuit; the soil is renowned for its fertility, and the land is rich in cultivation. There is much paddy rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the winds... [are fierce].)

By nature he was firm and strong, fond of studying the classics and arts, and devoted to planting the roots of merit and goodness. "Ghoṣila" is the name of this elder; in the language of China, it means "Beautiful Voice. Because in a past life he was a puppy who, by barking with his voice, invited a pratyekabuddha.

Upon returning home, he made offerings; consequently, throughout his successive lives, he was rewarded with auspicious news. This elder was three feet tall, and the Buddha likewise manifested a body of three feet in order to convert him and lead him to the True Dharma.
The *Xiyuji* states: "Not far to the southeast of the city, there is an old monastery where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for several years."

The occasion for its arising concerns a person. At that time, King Udayana (also known as Uddayana or Udāyana; in the Tang language, "One Who Has Transcended Love") and the Venerable Channa were close friends and associates.

[Regarding King Udayana: When the Buddha was first born, the great earth shook and a universal radiance was emitted. At that moment, in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the Great King Śatānīka had just fathered a son. Seeing this radiance, he immediately formed a thought.

He said, "My son possesses the power of merit and has a great radiance; it is fitting that he be given the name 'Prabhāsa' (Radiance). *Chanda* means "to manifest" or "to reveal. *Sarvāsti* was the younger half-brother of the Buddha and the son of King Udayana’s sister.

He was born into a great noble family, left the household life to practice the Way, and resided frequently in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. By nature he was headstrong and self-willed, committing various transgressions and evils. Furthermore, because there were many opportunities therein to benefit sentient beings, he resided in this country for much of his time. Later, because he did not abandon his evil nature, the community of monks imposed the *brahmadaṇḍa* (the penalty of silence) upon him.

He fell to the ground in a swoon, but Ānanda preached the essentials of the Dharma for him, whereupon he immediately attained awakening and realized the fruit [of Arhatship]. [The Buddha] spoke, saying, "I wish to build a dwelling for you."
"Do as you please. Wherever there is good ground, you may build as you wish.
He replied, "Great King, near the city there is a Nyagrodha spirit-tree (Nyagrodha; also called *ni-juluo-tuo*; translated as 'knotless' or 'extensive';

the Āgamas state that its trunk is perfectly round and its leaves are green, smooth, long, and broad) where many people pass back and forth on foot, by elephant, horse, or carriage, and rest beneath it. Chandaka shall go and fell this tree."

The fruit resembles the *pippala* (emblic myrobalan), and its calyx supports it like that of a persimmon. However, this species is resilient to age and is the most capable of reaching great height among all trees. The lay devotee criticized and disparaged [this practice], whereupon the World-Honored One rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu wishes to build a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, he should take other bhikṣus with him to designate the site.
Those bhikṣus should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions. If a bhikṣu...
If one builds a large dwelling for oneself that has an owner, in a location that is difficult or obstructed,
and does not go with other bhikṣus to inspect and designate the site, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Exegesis: Regarding "a large dwelling" (*mahallaka*): it is one constructed using a great deal of wealth and materials, which has an owner—whether by one person, two persons, or many people (excepting cases where the size exceeds the limit;
otherwise, all other details are the same as previously stated).
○ A General Explanation of the Eighth Precept: The Precept Against Groundless Slander.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is identical. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "If a son of the Buddha..."

Out of a malicious mind, one groundlessly slanders a virtuous person, a good person, a Dharma master, a preceptor, a king, or a noble person, claiming they have committed the seven reversals, the ten grave offenses, and so forth.
If one speaks of these grave offenses to outsiders, it is a heavy offense; if one speaks of them to fellow practitioners of the Dharma, it is a light defilement.
This belongs to the category of natural offenses (*dharmāpatti*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Due to those who practice the same holy life (*brahmacarya*)..."
Out of compassion for sentient beings afflicted by defilements, this training rule was established.
Regarding the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain. The Venerable Trapusa Māra-putra, having attained arhatship, reflected to himself:
"This body is not firm. By what means should I now seek a firm dharma? It would be appropriate for me now to offer my services with diligence:
to distribute the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha, and to take turns receiving invitations for meals. He then went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately granted permission for him to be appointed through a formal ritual (karmavācanā). At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ascended the mountain toward evening. The Venerable...
From his hands, light radiated forth. Regarding the distribution of bedding (as for *Dharmaruci*: *Dharma* is the name of a bhikṣu; *Ruci* is a royal name. He was the son of King Ruci;

because he left the household life, he was called Dharmaruci. The Venerable One left home at the age of seven. When his hair was shaved and fell to the ground, he immediately became an Arhat. *Sudarsana* says: In the past, there was a Buddha named *Bhadrakāra*. This Dharmaruci was born into the family of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*).

The people of the kingdom and the towns held a great assembly together, inviting the Buddha to enter the country. He was surrounded by sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus, and the great assembly made offerings to him. Seven...

On a day of almsgiving, there was an Arhat who, amidst the great assembly, used his supernormal powers to arrange the seats and all the food and drink. When Trapusa (沓婆摩羅子) saw this, his heart was filled with great joy. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and said:

"I pray that in a future age when a Buddha appears, I may leave the household life to study the Way, quickly attain Arhatship, and distribute dwellings and food to the monastic community, no different from the supernatural power of the Arhat here today.

The Buddha said: "A hundred thousand kalpas from now, there will be a Buddha named Śākyamuni. At the age of seven, you shall leave the household life; as soon as your hair falls to the ground, you will become an Arhat named Trapusa. You shall surely obtain this vow. Now, from the world..."

"Venerable One, I beg these two vows in order to fulfill my original aspiration. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sa-p'o-to lun) asks: "For what reason does Dabba always emit radiance to manifest his own merit?

The answer is: There are two reasons for manifesting one's own merit. First, for the sake of gain and fame; second, for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings. If it is for the sake of the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings, he acts with mastery at all times without any hindrance. The reason Dabba emits radiance is precisely to stop slander.

For example, because the Buddha was slandered by the Brahmin woman Sundarī, he let out a lion’s roar, declaring himself to possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) to demonstrate his purity. It is like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana... [text continues].

Even when slandered by Kokālika, he uttered a lion’s roar, saying: "I possess the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga-ratna*). Just as in the storehouse of a wealthy householder there are various garments and various implements and weapons that may be used at will, so too do I possess the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment, which I may use according to my desire to manifest my purity.

Maudgalyāyana also uttered a lion’s roar, declaring of himself: "My birth has been exhausted; I shall not be born again. What was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been fulfilled," thereby manifesting his purity. Aniruddha, when slandered by others, declared of himself:

"I have entered the tower of wisdom and sport therein at will," thereby manifesting his purity. Just as Śāgata, when slandered by others for drinking alcohol, declared: "I am in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

Concentration can cause one to manifest purity by filling the fires from the Avīci hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); as Śūbhitā, when slandered by others, declared that she could know the events of five hundred eons in a single thought-moment to demonstrate her purity;
and as Dharmabhāṇaka (Dharmapāla), because he was slandered by Maitrībala, constantly emitted radiance to demonstrate his purity.
Regarding the origin of this matter:
