there was a bhikṣu named Maitrībala who, when his turn came to receive an assignment of lodgings, obtained a poor room and inferior bedding, whereupon he became angry.
The next day, when it was his turn to receive an invitation to a meal, the donor, hearing that it was Maitrībala’s turn, spread out a worn-out sitting mat outside the gate.
When he was given coarse and unpalatable food, Maitrībala’s anger redoubled. He then commissioned his sister, the bhikṣuṇī Maitrī, to bring false accusations against the Venerable One.

(The reason Maitrībala the bhikṣu constantly received such coarse and unpalatable food was due to the power of his past karma; furthermore, because this man lacked a pure mind day and night, devas, nāgas, and spirits created the conditions that caused all his undertakings to fail as he wished.
The Venerable One was not far from the Buddha, and the World-Honored One, knowing this, questioned him intentionally.
“Did you hear it? He replied, “I heard it, Blessed One; may the World-Honored One know this for himself. The Buddha said, “Now you should not answer me in such a manner.
If it is true, you should say it is true; if it is not true, you should say it is not true. The Venerable addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since my birth, I have never recalled dreaming of engaging in impurity, much less doing so while awake.

(Regarding the statement that "the World-Honored One knows this," the Sarvāstivādins say: Because he is truly pure, one cannot say it is so; because of the power of his past karma, one cannot say it is not. Why did the Buddha not state that Dharmapāla was pure?

First, because the Buddha’s mind of equanimity is free from partiality and attachment, he did not immediately declare one right and the other wrong. Second, because the fruit of Dharmapāla’s past karma had ripened: in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he served as a *karmadāna* [superintendent]).

[There was] a man-eater. A certain bhikṣu, an arhat, who was upright and handsome in appearance, was walking along a road. A woman saw him and conceived a lustful attachment; she followed him with her gaze, never letting him out of her sight. At that time, the man-eater saw her acting in this manner.

It refers to one who first engages in sexual intercourse with her and then says: "This bhikṣu has surely committed an evil act with this woman; because he slanders the noble ones, he shall fall into hell. Once his retribution is exhausted, he will emerge and, due to his original wholesome karma, encounter a Buddha and attain the Way.

However, by the power of his residual karma, he undergoes this evil retribution. On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala, saying: "There are two kinds of people who invariably enter hell:
those who do not lead a pure life yet claim to lead a pure life, and those who truly lead a pure life [but are falsely accused]."
To slander another by falsely accusing them of unchaste conduct without basis— these two are said to be those who invariably enter hell. Having rebuked [the offender],
he established the precept with its formal characteristics.
If a bhikṣu, being overcome by ill will, slanders another bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense,
desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct; and if at a later time, whether he is questioned or not,
it becomes known that this matter was groundless and that he spoke these words because he was motivated by ill will— if a bhikṣu speaks in such a manner, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
*Śaiṣa*. Explanation of the meaning: "Enveloped by anger" refers to the arising of anger one by one toward each of the ten unwholesome factors due to the causal conditions of the ten evil dharmas.

[The *Fashu* states: hatred, resentment, calumny, deception, arrogance, fury, wrath, parsimony, delusion, and envy. To be "enveloped by anger" means that the wholesome mind is overturned. The *Nanshan Chao* states: "A bhikṣu, by means of the six..."

The six points of concord (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) have loving-kindness as their essence. To say now that one is "enveloped by ill-will" means that this [state] directly envelops that essence, thereby contradicting the six points of concord and leading to slander and defamation. Regarding those who slander with groundless *pārājika* charges:
there are three grounds—seeing, hearing, and suspicion. As for the ground of seeing: it is when one has actually seen [the person] commit an act contrary to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
To see someone stealing five coins or more than five coins; to see them taking human life; or if another sees it and one hears it from them—this is called the root of seeing (*darśana-mūla*).

As for the root of hearing (*śruta-mūla*): if one hears that they have violated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), heard that they stole five coins or more than five coins, heard that they took human life, or heard them praising themselves for having attained superhuman states (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*)—if one says "I heard it from them"—this is called hearing.
Roots. Regarding the root of doubt (*vicikitsā-mūla*): there are two ways in which doubt arises—doubt arising from what has been seen and doubt arising from what has been heard.

Doubt arising from what has been seen refers to cases such as entering or leaving a forest with a woman, being naked and without clothing, having the male organ impure and defiling the hands and body, holding a blood-stained knife, or associating with evil companions; this is called doubt arising from what has been seen. From... [text continues]

Regarding "doubt arising from what is heard": if one is in a dark place and hears the sound of a bed, the sound of turning over on a grass mat, the sound of moving the body, the sound of conversing, or the sound of sexual intercourse;
or if one hears it said, "I have violated the holy life (brahmacarya)"; or if one hears it said, "He stole five coins or more than five coins";
or if one hears it said, "I have killed a person" or "I have attained the state of a superior man (uttarimanussa-dhamma)"—this is called doubt arising from what is heard.

Apart from these three bases, to slander another by means of other matters is called "baseless" [accusation]. (The Sarvāstivādins say: Regarding the faculty of the eye, it must be pure and free from disease; the matter seen must be precise and reliable, such that it may be depended upon and believed.

Only the physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is permitted as evidence, not the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Since the divine eye sees everything without exception, who among men is without fault? There are only degrees of magnitude. If the testimony of the divine eye were admitted, [there would be no way to refute anyone].)

In such cases, obstructive and chaotic matters will abound. As for the faculty of the ear, it must be pure and free from error; it is discerning, certain, and trustworthy. Furthermore, one does not employ the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*); its application is identical to that of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*). Doubt is not to be relied upon, for doubt is not definitive. One might, for instance, suspect that a transgression has been committed.

Some say there is no offense (because it cannot be relied upon). One who wishes to destroy that person of pure conduct (meaning one who destroys that person’s virtuous conduct of purity so that they no longer further cultivate the various superior dharmas, nor participate in the *poṣadha* and *karma* rituals in the same location) does so at another time (meaning after the [prescribed] time has passed), whether questioned or unasked (the *Mahāsāṃghika* says:

whether investigated or not investigated, one asks: "What did you see? Did you commit sexual misconduct? Did you steal five coins? Did you intentionally kill a human? Did you falsely claim superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*)? What did you see? By what cause did you see it? Where did you see it? This is called...).
Examination: If one does not inquire in this manner, it is called "failing to examine.

Knowing that these matters are groundless, yet saying, "I was angry," and thus making such a statement—this refers to subsequently repenting, reproaching oneself, and confessing the matter of false slander; thereby washing away faults and seeking purity of the precept-body. (The following statement concludes the offense committed.)

The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the presence of four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the presence of malice; second, that the three faculties [of the victim] are actually absent;
third, that the matter slandered is not a transgression of a bhikṣu; and fourth, that the speech is clearly articulated.
**The Formal Determination of the Offense:** In this context, regarding the one who commits the offense:

if that person is either pure or impure, and [the accuser] lacks the three bases of seeing, hearing, or suspicion, yet slanders them with a groundless *pārājika* charge—[if the accusation is] clearly articulated, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;

if not clearly articulated, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This excludes the four *pārājikas*; furthermore, if one slanders [another] with any other quality that is not the dharma of a bhikṣu, [the same applies].
If one says, "You have committed an offense of the extreme limit," and so on, up to "you have two sexual organs"—if this is stated clearly, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if not clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one uses a finger-seal, a letter, or a messenger to convey a sign that is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṓa*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Apart from these cases of non-monkhood, if one further slanders a monk with groundless charges, [it is likewise].

(These refer to the two hundred and forty-six rules in the following four chapters, as well as the rules concerning minor impediments (*paryantika*). This means that one incurs an offense by slandering another person according to the specific matter they have committed. For example: if one slanders someone with a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for what they have committed as a *pāyattika*, it is a *pāyattika*;

if one slanders them for what they have committed as a *dukkaṭa*, it is also a *dukkaṭa*. If one slanders them with the eight groundless charges of *pārājika*: if a bhikṣuṇī speaks and is clear in her meaning, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if she is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; the same applies if she uses a sign or gesture.)
If one writes a letter to cause another to understand the characteristics [of the offense] clearly, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if not clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the eight *pārājika* offenses, if one further slanders another with other groundless matters that are not *bhikṣuṇī*-dharmas, and speaks them clearly, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if not clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. (Regarding "other non-*bhikṣuṇī*-dharmas," these refer to the thirteen *duṣṭhulā* offenses. Excluding those that are not *bhikṣuṇī*-dharmas...
If one further slanders a bhikṣuṇī with another groundless charge (amūlaka-dharma), it is according to the offense previously committed.
Excluding the case of a bhikṣu, if a bhikṣuṇī slanders another person with a groundless charge, it is a duṣkṛta (the "other persons" refers to the three lesser assemblies).
The Sarvāstivādins say: If one wishes to slander another with groundless charges, one first speaks to those who agree, saying, "A certain bhikṣu has committed such-and-such an offense;
please assist me. [The offenses are] a heavy sthūlātyaya for a bhikṣu, and a saṃghāvaśeṣa for a bhikṣuṇī.

There are three minor offenses of *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If an *upāsaka* (i.e., an *upāsaka*) slanders a *bhikṣu*, one should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (the ritual of overturning the bowl) against him; this is what constitutes an offense."
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense if one speaks the truth based on the three criteria of having seen, heard, or suspected;

if one speaks in jest; if one speaks rapidly; if one speaks alone; if one speaks in a dream; or if one intends to speak of this but mistakenly speaks of that. There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, such as at the very beginning.
The *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka-sūtra) states in detail: "When a single thought of anger arises, eighty thousand gates of obstruction open.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Anger is not the dharma of those who have left the household life; the dharma of those who have left the household life is patience.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s appearance and attire differ from those of the laity while his mind for anger remains the same, it is not appropriate. If one practices patience, then...
To personally possess the merit of compassion, one must further cultivate patience (*kṣānti*), for this can accomplish one's own benefit.
Why is this so? It is because one who harbors hatred intends to harm others, yet in doing so, they instead harm their own body and speech;
by inflicting evil upon others, the evil they themselves receive is a hundred-thousandfold greater. Therefore, know that anger is a great self-inflicted loss. For this reason...
The wise person who desires to benefit themselves—seeking to escape great suffering and grave transgressions—should practice patience.
Master Kumārajīva said: "If one can practice patience, then internally one does not burden oneself, and externally one does not harm others; this is protecting both oneself and others.
When Master Wuzhuo traveled to Mount Wutai, he encountered Mañjuśrī, who had manifested as an old man. Furthermore...
The youth Kuṇḍadhāna spoke these verses to the Bodhisattva Aśoka:
"Absence of anger on the face is the offering; Absence of anger from the mouth emits wondrous fragrance;
Absence of anger in the heart is the precious jewel— Untainted and stainless, it is the true permanence."
Essentials of the Vinaya, Volume Five.
Compiled by the Dharma Master Deqi, a śramaṇa of the Vinaya Studies at Baohua Mountain in Jinling. Section Nine:
The Precept Against Slandering Based on Taking a Fragment from a Different Category.
The general explanation is the same as before.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Regarding the person who initiated the incident:
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra descended from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and saw a large ram (that is, a male sheep) engaging in sexual intercourse with a ewe.
He then compared the ram to Upatiṣya and the ewe to the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "Previously, I slandered Upavāṇa with groundless charges based on what I had heard.
Now, I have personally seen with my own eyes that Upavāṇa engaged in unchaste conduct with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrā.
When the bhikṣus questioned him and learned the facts, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the offense:

if a bhikṣu, out of malice, seizes upon a fragment from a matter belonging to a different category and, though the bhikṣu is not one who has committed a pārājika offense, slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy his pure conduct; and if, at a later time, he is questioned...
If he does not ask, yet it is known that he has taken a portion from matters belonging to a different category, and this bhikṣu himself says,
"I spoke these words out of anger," then for one who speaks such words, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

**Exegesis:** "Taking a portion from among the distinct categories" (*visabhāga-vastu*). (The *Daśabhāṇavāra* states: "Distinct categories" refers to the four *pārājika* offenses. If one commits these, one is no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya, and has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu;

therefore, they are called 'distinct categories. 'Non-distinct categories' refers to the thirteen matters up to the seven methods for settling disputes. If one commits these matters, one is still called a bhikṣu, still called a son of the Śākya, and does not lose the dharma of a bhikṣu;

this is called 'non-distinct category. A 'portion' refers to matters within the various modes of deportment. This means that when the Venerable Trapusa was beneath Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he stood together with a woman and conversed. This was a minor matter concerning deportment. [Cited from] Maitreya.

The earth saw this and, fearing that he would slander [the monk] by claiming it was not in accordance with the *bhikṣu* dharma, spoke of "matters among the various modes of deportment. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "As for 'other parts' (*avaśeṣa*): *Dabba* is a human being and the sheep is a non-human being; to substitute the sheep for *Dabba* is called 'other parts.

Alternatively, 'other parts' means that which is other than a *pārājika* offense; it refers to substituting a *pārājika* offense with a different matter. This is not a *pārājika* offense, as explained previously."
The conditions for the offense are the same as before.

Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, if a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense, yet he claims he has committed a pārājika offense, slandering him with groundless matters belonging to a different category, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa. If a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense...

That is to say: one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, up to and including an *adhikaraṇa-śamatha*, is accused with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category;

this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Or, if a monk has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, yet he claims to have committed a *pāyattika* offense, up to and including an *adhikaraṇa-śamatha*, and is accused with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category;
this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Or, if an impure person [is associated] with one who is not...
It is like a pure person resembling another pure person; or an impure person resembling a pure person; or a pure person resembling an impure person.
When one slanders another based on these matters—claiming they have the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance—it is a groundless accusation based on a partiality of facts.
Regarding the *pārājika* offense of slandering: all such cases constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one sees that [the person] while still a layman committed sexual misconduct, stole five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, or killed a human being, and then says to others, "I saw a bhikṣu commit sexual misconduct, theft, or murder";

or if one hears that [the person] while still a layman committed sexual misconduct, theft, or murder, and then claims for oneself to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), as follows:
Therefore, if one slanders another with a groundless *pārājika* offense, and the statement is clear, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. (The rest is the same as before, and thus is not set forth in detail here.)
○ General Explanation of the Tenth Precept: Causing a Schism in the Saṃgha.
This is a shared precept; the offense for a bhikṣuṇī is identical. It is likewise proscribed in the Mahāyāna. If the wheel of the Saṃgha has not yet been split, it constitutes an *āpatti* (offense).

This refers to a mind of hatred. It is subsumed under the training rule concerning perverse teaching. If the *saṃgha* wheel is split, it constitutes a transgression (*ānantarya*). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"On account of matters concerning the *saṃgha* and due to afflictions of false wisdom, this training rule was established."
The setting for the causal origin:
The Buddha was on Vulture Peak Mountain.
The person who gave rise to the causal occasion: [Name].

Devadatta (also known as Devadatta; this translates as "Heaven-Conceived," or "Heaven-Given," because his parents requested him from heaven; alternatively, it translates as "Heaven-Scorched," because when he was born, the hearts of humans and devas were all struck with alarm and heat; abbreviated as Tiāodá) desired to harm the Buddha himself and further incited King Ajātaśatru to assassinate his father. Consequently, his evil reputation spread abroad and his offerings and gains were cut off. He then took five of his own followers to beg for alms from house to house. (Devadatta... [is] the Buddha’s paternal cousin. Ajātaśatru... [is] the son of King Bimbisāra... [and] the grandson of King Śreṇika... [and] the nephew of the Buddha. His personal name is Ajātaśatru; this translates as "Unborn Enemy. Because he was born after his uncle, King Bimbisāra, had already been imprisoned, he was given this name. Furthermore, because he was born while his father, King Śreṇika, was still alive, he was given the name "Unborn Enemy" to signify that he would become an enemy before he was even born. The Buddha’s paternal cousin, Devadatta, being of a wicked nature, harbored malice toward the Buddha. He first plotted to kill the Buddha by means of a stone pillar, but the pillar split into two pieces and could not strike the Buddha. Next, he released a drunken elephant named Dhanapāla to trample the Buddha, but the elephant bowed its head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew. Subsequently, Devadatta climbed Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and hurled down a large rock, but it struck a boulder and shattered into fragments. Then, he caused the five hundred disciples of the heretical teacher Sañjayin to attack the Buddha, but they all fell prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and became his disciples. Finally, he conspired with King Ajātaśatru to imprison King Bimbisāra and starve him to death. Afterward, Devadatta went to the palace and, through various stratagems, incited the king to plot the murder of his father. When King Bimbisāra heard this, he said to the king: "I have committed no crime against you. Why do you wish to kill me? The king replied, "I have heard that you are a sage; I shall now test you. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of excrement and place it before the king. The king smelled it and spat it out, saying, "This is truly foul-smelling! Bimbisāra then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not smell this; if I am not a sage, I shall smell it. He then smelled it and did not spit it out. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not eat this; if I am not a sage, I shall eat it. He then ate it and digested it. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not die; if I am not a sage, I shall die. He then fasted for seven days and did not die. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by weapons; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring a sword and strike him. The sword struck his body and broke into pieces, unable to wound him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be burned by fire; if I am not a sage, I shall be burned. He then ordered his attendants to set fire to his body. The fire reached his skin but did not burn it. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by water; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to submerge him in water. The water reached his skin but did not drown him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by poison; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to give him poison. The poison entered his mouth but did not harm him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by hunger; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then fasted for seven days and did not die. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by cold; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to strip him of his clothes and expose him to the cold wind. The wind reached his skin but did not harm him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by heat; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to wrap him in furs and expose him to the midday sun. The sun reached his skin but did not harm him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by fear; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a fierce tiger and place it before him. The tiger approached him but did not harm him. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by sorrow; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to tell him that his mother and wife had died. The king wept and grieved, but his heart remained unmoved. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by joy; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to tell him that his mother and wife had returned alive. The king rejoiced greatly, yet his heart remained unmoved. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by pride; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a beautiful woman and place her before him. The king looked at her but felt no desire. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by anger; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a fierce man and provoke him to anger. The king felt no resentment. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by greed; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of gold and silver and place it before him. The king looked at it but felt no attachment. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by delusion; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of filth and place it before him. The king looked at it and felt no confusion. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by envy; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of food and place it before him. The king looked at it and felt no envy. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by stinginess; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of empty vessels and place them before him. The king looked at them and felt no stinginess. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by deceit; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of false weights and measures and place them before him. The king looked at them and felt no deceit. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by falsehood; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of lies and place them before him. The king looked at them and felt no falsehood. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by flattery; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of sycophancy and place it before him. The king looked at them and felt no flattery. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by slander; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of calumny and place it before him. The king looked at them and felt no slander. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by hypocrisy; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of pretense and place it before him. The king looked at them and felt no hypocrisy. The king then said, "If I am a sage, I shall not be harmed by arrogance; if I am not a sage, I shall be harmed. He then ordered his attendants to bring out a bowl of haughtiness and place it before him. The king looked at them and felt no arrogance.

Nanqin (Difficult-to-Approach) was the elder brother of the Buddha. He was extensively versed in both internal and external scriptures and possessed thirty of the marks of a great man. He was six inches shorter than the Buddha and was born on the seventh day of the fourth month. As for Ajātaśatru—whose name means "One Whose Enmity Has Not Yet Been Born"—his mother was pregnant with him before the day [of the Buddha's birth].

He already harbored an evil intent toward King Bimbisāra; thus, he was named Ajātaśatru (Unborn Enemy). In earlier translations, he was called "No Finger. At the time of his birth, a physiognomist declared, "This child will be an enemy to the king. The king ordered him to be thrown from a high tower, but he did not die;

only one finger was damaged, hence the name "No Finger. The *Puchao jing* (Sūtra on Universal Transcendence) states: "King Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī and attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience of conformity). At the end of his life, he entered the Raurava Hell, entering and leaving it immediately.

He was reborn in a Buddha-land in the upper direction and attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). When Maitreya appears, he will return to this realm as the Bodhisattva Acala (Immovable), and later he shall become a Buddha, titled Śuddhaloka Tathāgata (Tathāgata of the Pure Realm). Regarding the five people including himself: first is Śāriputra. This man possessed wisdom.

Cāṣa was first in rank. Second was Khaṇḍadravya, a close friend of Devadatta. Third was Kokālika, a disciple of Devadatta. Fourth was Kāṭhila; his sisters were seven in number, all of whom were bhikṣuṇīs and possessed great influence.
With Devadatta as their leader, they were thus known collectively as "the five. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, you must not eat apart from the community. I permit [only]..."
Three people eat together. The reason for this is that there are two benefits: to restrain those who are difficult to discipline, and out of compassion for the families of laypeople.
Why? Because one fears that such difficult-to-discipline individuals might form a separate faction on their own to trouble the Sangha.
Then Devadatta had this thought: "It is unprecedented; the Śramaṇa Gautama has indeed forbidden [this]."
[They] ate their food [in the village]. [Devadatta thought: "I should rather break that Saṃgha-wheel. After my own death, I shall gain a reputation, saying:
'The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power and unimpeded wisdom, yet Devadatta was able to break his Saṃgha-wheel.
We now possess five dharmas; we too practice the dhūta [ascetic practices], have few desires and are content, and delight in renunciation and excellence."
“Dharma! For the rest of our lives we shall beg for food; for the rest of our lives we shall wear rag-robes; for the rest of our lives we shall sit in the open air;

for the rest of our lives we shall not eat ghee or salt; for the rest of our lives we shall not eat fish or meat. With these five dharmas he instructed the bhikṣus, causing them to have faith and joy.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, “Today Devadatta has severed the four noble lineages.”
He rebuked him with countless skillful means, saying, "You should know that breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha is an extremely evil act.
It incurs a grave and heavy offense; one shall suffer its retribution in hell for an entire kalpa, from which there is no remedy. He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to admonish Devadatta so that he may relinquish this matter. Having performed the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, he established a precept for the bhikṣus.
Regarding the established characteristics of the offense:

if a bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in the Saṃgha and, through skillful means, adopts the practice of causing a schism, persisting in it and refusing to relinquish it, other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not, through skillful means, cause a schism."
"Reconcile with the Saṃgha! Do not accept the practice that causes schism in the Saṃgha; hold fast to it and do not relinquish it. Venerable one, you should be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

Being in harmony with the Saṃgha, you should live joyfully and without dispute, studying under the same teacher as one, like water and milk blending together. Thus, within the Buddha’s Dharma, there will be increase and you shall dwell in peace and happiness.
When that bhikṣu, being thus admonished, still holds fast and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should [admonish him] up to three times...
He is to be admonished. If he relinquishes this matter upon being admonished up to three times, it is well. If he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Explanation of the terms:
"In harmony" means performing the same *karma* and reciting the same *prātimokṣa* precepts together. "Saṃgha" refers to four bhikṣus.
Whether five or ten, even up to an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*). "Destruction" (*bhañjana*) means breaking. There are eighteen matters of such destruction:

[confusing] Dharma with non-Dharma (meaning that the Eightfold Noble Path is Dharma, yet claiming it is non-Dharma; or that the five dharmas are non-Dharma, yet claiming they are Dharma); [confusing] Vinaya with non-Vinaya (meaning that the Eightfold Noble Path is Vinaya, yet saying it is not Vinaya; or that the five dharmas are not Vinaya, yet saying they are Vinaya);

[confusing] an offense with a non-offense (not shaving the hair or clipping the nails, yet the Buddha says this constitutes a violation of the precepts; claiming that hair and nails possess life, and thus there is an offense in shaving or clipping them; whereas shaving the hair and clipping the nails is what the Buddha [prescribed]).

Regarding what is prescribed: the Vinaya states that one should shave once every half-month; this is the constant rule. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that for the hair on the head, beard, and nails to all be long and sharp is the mark of one who has broken the precepts. As for those who claim that "one who does not transgress yet speaks of transgression" [is at fault]:

the Buddha did not prescribe mental precepts, yet he stated that the arising of the three poisons within the mind constitutes a transgression of the precepts. Whether light or heavy, whether involving a formal residue (*sāvaśeṣa*) or no residue (*anavaśeṣa*), consider, for example, the Utpala Dragon King:

because he plucked a tree leaf, his offense was such that it could not be expiated. On this basis, some say that killing plants and trees is always a grave offense. Conversely, those who claim that a grave offense is light—citing cases such as Sudinna and Dhanika—argue that because they acted previously [under certain conditions], they did not incur a grave offense; thus they speak of offenses such as sexual misconduct and theft [as being minor].

Regarding "light" [and] "grave or non-grave": this refers to stating that the first two categories of offenses are grave offenses when they are not grave offenses, or stating that the latter three categories of offenses are grave offenses when they are not grave offenses.

(The above follows the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda). "Constantly practiced" means not "occasionally practiced. (The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Matters constantly practiced" refers to the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the distribution of the *kaṭhina*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the establishment of the fourteen persons for *karman*.
Regarding these fourteen persons, the *Śramaṇa-śataikakarman* states: 1. One capable of performing legal acts; 2. One capable of distributing bedding; 3. One capable of spreading bedding; 4.

One capable of distributing monastic cakes; 5. One capable of assigning and requesting [invitations]; 6. One capable of assigning novices; 7. One capable of distributing monastic gruel; 8. One capable of assigning gardeners; 9. One capable of distributing monastic robes; 10.)

11. One who distributes medicinal substances; 12. One who oversees monastic property day and night; 13. One who oversees coarse monastic goods; 14. One who maintains and guards the monastery site). Regarding what is prescribed and what is not prescribed (the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* states:

"If, regarding twelve matters—the Introduction to the Precepts, the four *pārājika*s, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*s, the two *aniyata*s, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*s, the ninety *pāyattika*s, the four *pratideśanīya*s, the *śaikṣa* dharmas, and the seven methods for settling disputes—a rule has not been prescribed, one should prescribe it;

if it has been prescribed, one should then relax it. This is called 'prescribing what was not prescribed. Regarding what is spoken and what is not spoken: the Eightfold Noble Path is that which was taught by the Buddha...)

To say that what was spoken by the Buddha was not spoken by the Buddha, and to say that the five dharmas not spoken by the Buddha were spoken by the Buddha—this constitutes the eighteenth basis for the schism of the Saṃgha. This is the method for breaking the Saṃgha.

To abide in these eighteen matters (this constitutes the method for accepting the schism of the Saṃgha through skillful means) and to firmly maintain them without relinquishing them (clearly explains the establishment of the precepts based on specific events).

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: Regarding the matter of schism in the Saṃgha, one who stubbornly clings to it and refuses to relinquish it does so because they have already intended to split the community, are gathering and converting disciples, maintain their own heterodox tenets, and seek out many evil associates;
thus, they persistently hold to it and do not relinquish it. That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu:

"Studying under the same teacher as water and milk blend" (this illustrates the excellence of harmony).

Furthermore, those who share the same teacher are those for whom the Tathāgata is their Great Teacher; though they have renounced the world from various lineages, they are all called sons of Śākya. They study the tenfold teaching together because there is no distinction in the essence of that teaching. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "There are two meanings of 'sameness':

first, sameness of mind; second, sameness of body. Sameness of mind means the mind is identical to the Dharma. Sameness of body means sharing one and the same harmonious assembly (*saṃgha*). The *Upoṣadha-sūtra* asks: "What does it mean not to be of the same body? Even if they are in the same place, if their minds and practices follow external dharmas, this is called being of the same body but different minds.

"Like water and milk blending" refers to the harmony of phenomenon and principle. When water and milk blend, they become of one characteristic and one flavor; when phenomenon and principle are one, they are without difference, and all equally attain liberation. Therefore, it is said to be like water and milk.

...it is appropriate). To "increase one's dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma" means that one is well able to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion; one is well able to practice diligently within the sublime Dharma so that the teachings of the Buddha may circulate;

and by abiding in the eightfold noble path, one is able to attain superior fruits by relying on this Dharma—therefore, it is said that one increases one's dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.

When that bhikṣu thus offers such admonition and [the other] stubbornly persists without relinquishing [the offense], this refers to the admonition offered in private. That bhikṣu should [then] three times...

One should admonish them to relinquish this matter (this refers to the formal monastic procedure of admonition within the Saṃgha). Up to three admonitions, it is well if they relinquish it (meaning they do not incur the fundamental offense).
"Does not relinquish" (meaning: a transgression is established upon defiance of the admonition).

Regarding the conditions for the offense: this precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, the intention to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; second, the undertaking of the methods for causing a schism;
third, the failure to relinquish [the position] after the Saṃgha has performed a formal admonition in accordance with the Dharma three times.

**The Formal Determination of the Offense** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, through skillful means, seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and having accepted the methods for causing a schism, persists in them and does not relinquish them, that bhikṣu should be admonished by others as follows: "Venerable sir, do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha through skillful means;
do not accept the methods for causing a schism and persist in them without relinquishing them. Venerable sir, you should instead act in harmony with the Saṃgha."
Be in harmony, rejoice together, and do not dispute; be like water and milk blended as one. Within the Buddha-dharma, there shall be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
Venerable sir, you should abandon this matter, lest the Saṃgha issue a formal reprimand and you incur a grave offense.
If you accept these words, it is well. If you do not accept these words, [the Saṃgha] shall further cause bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and...
Upāsikā: If a king, a great minister, or various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of heterodox paths (those of heterodox paths refer to those who have gone forth among non-Buddhist sects;

"śramaṇa" is a general term for those who have gone forth) should seek [counsel]—that is, seek to hear and accept admonition (this refers to admonishing in a private place)—and if monks from other regions hear of this person and find their words credible and worthy of being followed, they should request them. If the person follows their words, it is well; if not...
Regarding one who follows the instruction: one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having performed the announcement, one should further request:

"Venerable sirs, I have finished the announcement; there remains the formal act (*karman*). You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform a formal act against you and you further commit a grave offense.
If they follow the instruction, it is well. If they do not follow the instruction, one should perform the first formal act (*prathamā karman*). Having performed the first...

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should further request [the monk to desist]. If he follows the instruction, it is well. If he does not follow the instruction, a second *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Once the second *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should further request him. If he can relinquish [the offense], it is well.

If he does not relinquish it, the third *karmavācanā* is proclaimed, and it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If he relinquishes it after the first motion (*jñapti*) and the second *karmavācanā* have been completed, [it is likewise a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
There are three cases of *sthūlātyaya*: if one abandons [the offense] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā* have been completed, it is two *sthūlātyayas*;
if one abandons it after the motion has been completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya*; if one abandons it before the initial motion is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, while everything has not yet been formally announced, one employs expedient means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha and accepts the practice of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha, persisting in it without relinquishing it, it is all *duṣkṛta*.

If, when the Saṃgha is performing the formal act of admonition (*jñapti-karman*) against the person who is breaking the Saṃgha, there is a bhikṣu who instructs [the others], saying, "Do not relinquish [this]," that bhikṣu commits a *sthūlātyaya*. If not...
If she rebukes and admonishes [the nun], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If the bhikṣuṇī instructs her not to abandon [the offense], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If she has not yet been rebuked and admonished, yet the bhikṣuṇī instructs her not to abandon [the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Excluding bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, if there are others who instruct her not to abandon [the offense], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* (these others refer to the three minor assemblies). The third part states: "The *pātayantika*..."
Devadatta cast the voting sticks, saying: "Which elders among you who accept these five points as being the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teaching of the Buddha, please take a stick.
Thereupon, five hundred newly ordained, ignorant bhikṣus took the sticks.
He followed Devadatta away. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana preached the Dharma and, manifesting supernatural powers, were about to return.
The Buddha ordered them to perform a *sthūlātyaya* confession. He further stated: "There are two things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: false speech and similar speech (*sabhāga-vāk*).

As for false speech, it is to say what was not spoken by the Buddha that it was spoken by the Buddha. As for similar speech, it refers to the enactment of the five rules, which merely imitate the words of the Buddha. Furthermore, there are two other things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: performing a *karmavācanā* [against the community]...
If one, two, or even three bhikṣus take up the voting tally, they may employ skillful means, yet they will still be unable to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
nor can bhikṣuṇīs and others cause a schism in the Saṃgha. However, if this group consists of four or more individuals, [it is possible].

If those four members of the assembly exceed [the limit] and proceed to cast the voting tally (*śalākā*) to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), this constitutes the breaking of the harmonious Saṃgha.
One shall suffer punishment in the hells for one *kalpa* without remedy. One who is able to reconcile them attains the merit of Brahmā and enjoys happiness for one *kalpa*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "I do not see any other dharma that destroys the human aspiration for the Path as much as fame and profit."
Regarding "gain" (*lābha*): it is for the sake of gain that Devadatta split the Saṃgha. Because Devadatta accomplished eight unrighteous acts (*adharmas*), he split the Saṃgha.
These are: gain versus lack of gain; fame versus lack of fame; honor versus dishonor; delighting in evil and following evil associates.
There are four matters termed "splitting the Saṃgha. He preached five points, personally distributed voting sticks (*śalākā*), and separately conducted monastic business within the boundary (*sīmā*).
Furthermore, if a king, a great minister, or other members of the six groups cause the Saṃgha to be discordant but do not cause it to be split;
or if one bhikṣu, up to seven bhikṣus, are discordant, this is also not a schism.
If one performs Saṃgha affairs without consulting the elders, this constitutes discordance but is not a schism in the Saṃgha. Or if they do not eat together.
If, during a meal, they sit separately and engage in quarreling or verbal abuse, this is not yet termed a schism (*saṃghabheda*).

A schism occurs only when eight or more bhikṣus within a single boundary (*sīmā*) divide themselves into two factions and perform monastic affairs (*saṃghakarma*) separately; of these, the principal leader is—
One shall fall into the great hell for one kalpa, from which there is no salvation. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of schism in the Saṃgha:

the schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Regarding the schism of the *karmavācanā*: within a single boundary (*sīmā*), one performs the *poṣadha* and other rituals separately.
Regarding the schism of the Wheel of Dharma: the "Wheel" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path; it causes people to abandon the Eightfold Noble Path and enter onto false paths.

Regarding the term "Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*): its meaning is "to transport. This refers to transporting practitioners directly to *nirvāṇa* by means of the Eightfold Noble Path, thereby enabling them to attain the four fruits of the *śramaṇa*. Furthermore, "wheel" carries the meaning of "crushing and destroying.

This means that the Tathāgata, through the Dharma he has realized, turns it over and imparts it to the minds of others, thereby able to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings; thus it is called a "wheel. Just as the jewel of a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) is capable of both destroying and establishing, so too is the Dharma-wheel:

it destroys the enemies of the afflictions and establishes one in the principle of the Truths (*satya*). As for "entering into wrong paths": this refers to the five practices that are not the correct path leading to *nirvāṇa*. These are the teachings established by the teacher Devadatta, who gathered his disciples to cause them to lose right wisdom and increase their false views; therefore, it is said they have entered into wrong paths.
The Sarvāstivādins say: "What is the difference between breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha and breaking the Saṃgha through formal ritual (karmavācanā)? The answer is that there are various differences.
Both breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha and breaking the Saṃgha through ritual constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense;

however, breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha constitutes a heinous crime (*ānantarya*), whereas the *sthūlātyaya* for breaking the Saṃgha through ritual is not a heinous crime and is subject to confession."
Furthermore, one who breaks the wheel of the Sangha falls into the Avīci Hell and undergoes punishment for one kalpa. One who breaks the *karmavācanā* Sangha does not fall into the Avīci Hell.
To break the wheel of the Sangha requires at least nine persons; to break the *karmavācanā* Sangha requires at least eight persons.

In breaking the wheel of the Sangha, one person claims for themselves to be a Buddha; in breaking the *karmavācanā* Sangha, one does not claim to be a Buddha. This is the distinction between breaking the wheel of the Sangha and [breaking the *karmavācanā*].
All [monks] within and outside the boundary are completely split. To split the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) requires performing separate rituals within the boundary.
To split the wheel of the *saṃgha* necessarily requires a man; however, to split the *saṃgha* through formal ritual, both men and women are capable of doing so.

To "break the wheel of the Saṃgha" means to break the Saṃgha of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). To "break the Saṃgha through ritual" (karmāntika) means to break both the Saṃgha of conventional truth and the Saṃgha of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Breaking the wheel of the Saṃgha occurs only in Jambudvīpa; breaking the Saṃgha through ritual extends throughout the three continents.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; for the three smaller groups [of monastics], it is a duṣkṛta. This is defined as an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: One is not guilty of an offense if one relinquishes [the matter] upon the first admonition;
or if it is an illegal separate assembly; or an illegal harmonious assembly; or a legal separate assembly; or a legal-similar separate assembly; or a legal-similar harmonious assembly;
or if it is neither Dharma, nor Vinaya, nor the teaching of the Buddha; or if no formal censure or admonition has yet been performed; or if one is separating from evil friends and evil associates.
If one employs means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, they are to be restrained so that the schism does not occur.
If one assists in causing a schism through such means, two or three people may perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*).

This applies if they intend to perform an illegal and non-disciplinary formal act for the sake of the Saṃgha, for a stūpa, for an upādhyāya or his peers, for an ācārya or his peers, or for a spiritual friend.

Diminution. To make it a non-abiding place. One who breaks [the rule] does not commit an offense. One who does not commit an offense refers to those before the precepts were first established, and so forth (*The Samantapāsādikā* states:

"The first offender was Devadatta. Question: "If other precepts were not initially violated, Devadatta likewise should not have committed an offense. Answer: "Because he did not relinquish [his position] despite the three-fold admonition by the Saṃgha; therefore, he committed an offense").

the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.

(As detailed above). The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha directed the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for a reprimand, and having done so, he established the precept.
The characteristics of the established precept are as follows:
If there are one, two, three, or even countless bhikṣus who form a faction, and these bhikṣus say to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, do not admonish this bhikṣu. This bhikṣu is a speaker of Dharma;
this bhikṣu is a speaker of Vinaya. What this bhikṣu says, we delight in; what this bhikṣu says, we approve of."

That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. To say that this bhikṣu is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya, and that we delight in what this bhikṣu says and we accept what this bhikṣu says—this is not so.
For this bhikṣu is not a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, nor is he a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya. Venerable sir, do not seek to cause a schism."
"You have caused a schism in the Saṃgha. You should desire the harmony of the Saṃgha, O Venerable One;
let the Saṃgha be united, joyful and without dispute, studying under one teacher like water and milk mixed together, so that there may be increase and peaceful dwelling within the Buddha-dharma."
When that bhikṣu thus admonishes him, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

**Exegesis:** There are two kinds of compliance. First is compliance with the Dharma. This involves being instructed in the Dharma so as to increase virtue (*śīla*), increase the mind (*citta*), and increase wisdom (*prajñā*).

One recites and receives these [teachings] (these are called the three untainted trainings). Regarding the increase of virtue: virtue guards against the evils of body and speech; it purifies body and speech such that no fault remains. Regarding the increase of the mind:

the mind rests within impurity until nothing is left unperfected. Regarding the increase of wisdom: one clearly perceives the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and eradicates evil at its root. Furthermore, the increase of virtue refers to training in the Vinaya Piṭaka; the increase of the mind refers to training in the Sūtra Piṭaka; and the increase of wisdom refers to training in the Abhidharma Piṭaka. As stated in the Sūtras:

There are three trainings: the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*), the training in the mind (*citta*), and the training in wisdom (*prajñā*). By training in these three trainings, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of arhatship.

Therefore, it is known that training in these three trainings encompasses all training. Second, regarding those who comply with [providing] robes and food: one provides them with clothing, bedding, food and drink, seats and mats, and medical requisites.

Regarding their "companions": whether four or more than four (that is, even up to an infinite number). That bhikṣu says to those bhikṣus: "This is an unlawful faction that obstructs those who act according to the Dharma."

[They] should admonish and exhort [him]: "Venerable ones, do not admonish this bhikṣu. This bhikṣu is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma; he is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya" (The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states:

"One who speaks according to the Dharma" means one whose speech is complete and perfect. "One who speaks according to the Vinaya" means one whose words accord with reason without error and can lead to the true meaning; such is called speaking according to the Dharma. Uttering gentle words of admonition is called speaking according to the Vinaya).
We rejoice in what this bhikṣu says; we accept what this bhikṣu says (this clarifies the reliance [on him]).

Regarding the establishment of the precepts, the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "All that he has done accords with my own mind. That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sir, do not speak in such a manner; [he is] a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma."

...down to: "O Bhikṣu who speaks what is not Dharma, O Bhikṣu who speaks what is not Vinaya, [I] exhort you to follow the orthodox faction and abandon the heterodox school" (this indicates that breaking the Sangha is no small offense;

the merit of a harmonious Sangha is inconceivable, as explained previously). ...down to: "Venerable Sir, do not wish to destroy the harmonious Sangha" (this reveals that the crime of schism is not insignificant;
the harmony of the Sangha possesses merit beyond thought, the meaning of which was explained before).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, forming an unlawful faction;
second, upholding what is unlawful; and third, not relinquishing this behavior after being formally admonished three times by the Saṃgha according to the Dharma.

**The Formal Conviction:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu forms an unlawful faction and says to the other bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, do not admonish this bhikṣu," and so forth, up to "we approve of him," the bhikṣus should admonish them, saying, "...until [the community] increases in well-being and dwells in comfort;
you should relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses."
This is a grave offense. If he complies with what is said, it is well. If he does not comply with what is said, a formal motion (*jñapti*) must be made.
Having made the motion, one should say to that person: "I have made the motion; the rest of the *karmavācanā* remains.

You should relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense. If he complies with what is said, it is well. If he does not comply with what is said, the first [announcement] must be made.
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: once the first *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should say: "I have completed the motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā*;
two more *karmavācanās* remain. This continues in this manner until the third *karmavācanā* is concluded.

As for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the relative gravity of the remaining transgressions, these are all the same as in the preceding precepts. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one bhikṣu is expelled, and four [other] bhikṣus..."

If one follows him, it is called "schism-making. If there is a person of great knowledge, great renown, and great learning—a virtuous elder who clearly understands the meaning of the Tripiṭaka—one should not subject such a person to the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga*). If one does suspend them, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense, because this is in proximity to causing a schism.
Furthermore, it is said: if one person suspends another single person, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one person suspends two, three, or four people...
If one person follows two, three, or four [monks], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If two, three, or four people expel two, three, or four [monks] respectively, the resulting offense is likewise.

If the one who performs the *pravāsanīya* (act of banishment) acts according to the Dharma, then the offense belongs to the one being banished and those who follow in the banishment. These are common precepts; the offenses for *bhikṣuṇīs* are likewise the same. They are uniformly prescribed in the Mahāyāna as well. Specifically, seeking profit through profit and managing the affairs of laypeople and so forth are categorized under the precept of "defiling a family.
Engaging in wrong livelihood through improper mental activity and contemplation is categorized under the precept of "practicing evil conduct.
Speaking of the Saṃgha as having attachment, aversion, and so forth, is subsumed under the precept of "slandering the Saṃgha. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Due to..."
Because he engaged in vulgar conduct and defiled other families due to the affliction of *gehamacchariya* (household stinginess), the Blessed One established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*).
As for the setting of the origin (*nidāna*):

the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. When the elder Sudatta saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma, he immediately attained the first fruit [of the path]. He then built a monastery for the Buddha; wishing to select a suitable site, Prince Jeta...

It is said that Prince Jeta possessed a most excellent garden. The Elder [Anāthapiṇḍada] covered it entirely with gold coins to purchase it; however, one spot remained uncovered. The Prince said, "The area where the gold has not yet been spread must be returned to me; I shall use it to build a gate for the Buddha’s monastery.

When the World-Honored One arrived at the monastery and offered words of praise, he wished to perform a blessing. The Prince thought to himself, "I pray only that the World-Honored One will mention my name first. Knowing this, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the Prince's wish, declared: "This is the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma. (In the Sanskrit language, *Jeta*.)

This is called "Victorious in Battle" (Jetavana), named for the joy experienced at the time of his victory. Now, when it is simply referred to as "Jeta," it is for the sake of brevity in the text. "Anāthapiṇḍika" expresses his virtue; it means he constantly gave alms to the orphaned and the destitute. His original name was Sudatta. Because Jeta offered the trees and Anāthapiṇḍika purchased the grove, the two names were combined.

The name "Jeta" was used so that people from afar would know [the location], while "Anāthapiṇḍika's Grove" was used so that those nearby would know it. Thus, it is called "The Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Grove, in the Kingdom of Śrāvastī."
Regarding the origin of the persons involved:
at that time, there were two bhikṣus in the village of Kallavāḍa. One was named Aśvajit and the other was named Pūrṇaśas (Kallavāḍa is the name of a town in the kingdom of Kāśī;

according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is the land of Mount Kālaka; in Sanskrit, Aśvajit means "Master of Horses," and in Sanskrit, Pūrṇaśas means "Full Moon"). According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*:

Aśvajit (Horse-Teacher) was the most senior among the group of six; he had originally been a farmer who, together with his companions, had labored wearily in the fields. The setting of the origin:
The Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Park in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī (the commentary is provided in the preceding text).
The person who gave rise to the occasion:
The Venerable Channa was of a wicked disposition and would not accept the advice of others.
He said to the bhikṣus, "Do not speak to me of what is good or bad; nor shall I speak to the venerable ones of what is good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist."
"Do not say anything. Why should you instruct me? It is I who should instruct the venerable ones. Why is this?

Because my Holy Lord has attained Perfect Enlightenment. (Regarding the words "my Holy Lord": why is this? When Le-che and I escorted the Buddha into the mountains to study the Way, we did not see a single one of the elders attending upon the Buddha.

Yet, once the Buddha had attained the Way, he turned the Wheel of Dharma. Therefore, the Buddha is our family’s Buddha, and the Dharma is also our family’s Dharma. For this reason, I should instruct the elders; the elders should not, in turn, instruct me.)

If a bhikṣu is of a wicked nature and does not accept the words of others, and when the bhikṣus have admonished him in accordance with the Dharma regarding the rules of training, he himself does not accept their admonition, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me whether it be good or bad;
