The Bhikṣu Kāśyapa admonished that bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, do not yourself refuse to accept admonition. Venerable sir, you yourself should accept admonition.
Just as the venerable one admonishes the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, so too should the bhikṣus admonish the venerable one in accordance with the Dharma."
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase: they admonish one another, instruct one another, and confess their faults to one another.
When a bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should be admonished three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
**Exegesis:** "Having a wicked nature and not accepting the words of others" means being unable or unwilling to accept instruction.
Regarding the *śīladharma* (the discipline of precepts), after one has been admonished according to the Dharma—wherein the *śīladharma* consists of the seven classes of offenses (*āpatti-skandha*):
*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *sthūlātyaya*, *duṣkṛta*, and *durbhāṣita*—having thus been admonished according to the Dharma (meaning according to...).

The Dharma is as it is in the Vinaya, according to the Buddha’s teaching; that is to say, regarding the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) and seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*), one speaks in accordance with the facts and in accordance with the Dharma.

To not accept admonition personally means that when fellow practitioners admonish one in accordance with the Dharma, one still maintains a stubborn disposition and does not accept their words. One says: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me whether it be good or bad;
nor shall I speak to the venerable sirs whether it be good or bad. (This means: do not encourage one another in all matters of good, and do not obstruct one another in matters of evil.)

(This clearly demonstrates that one of an evil nature and arrogant disposition does not accept admonition). "Venerable sir, please desist; do not admonish me. (Regarding "please desist": this means to preemptively block [the speaker] so that what has not yet been said need not be said again. Regarding "do not admonish me":
this means having no desire to hear words concerning one's faults or virtues, and being unable to bear them in one's heart). That monk should admonish this monk, saying:

"Up to the point where you yourself must accept the words of admonition" (meaning he exhorts him to receive the admonition and to rectify his contrary disposition). "Venerable sir, you should admonish the other monks in accordance with the Dharma."

...up to the point of mutual confession (explicitly revealing the meaning of the benefit obtained through admonishing one another). By means of mutual admonition and confession, the disciples of the Buddha obtain increased growth and dwell in peace and happiness; by virtue of dwelling in peace and happiness, [they attain further progress].

Wholesome dharmas increase. Because wholesome dharmas increase, the Noble Teaching does not perish. Because the Noble Teaching continues in succession, the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles are transmitted without interruption.

All of this is due to the power of mutual instruction and repentance through successive transmission. Question: The *Sūtra on Brief Exhortation* later states: "One should simply observe for oneself whether one’s own bodily conduct is correct or incorrect. Yet here it says there is "mutual instruction through successive transmission. Are these two statements not contradictory? Answer: The Buddha established his teachings according to the specific circumstances of the time; thus, while the words may differ, their intent is consistent, and they do not contradict one another.

If a person harbors love or hatred in their heart, or if they are of dull faculties and lack wisdom, having heard little and seen little, their speech will be of no benefit. Furthermore, if one acts for the sake of gain and fame, or for the pleasures of the present life, or if one is newly ordained and remains attached [to worldly things]—[in such cases, mutual instruction would be ineffective].

Because of parents, brothers, wives, and children, it is said: "One should only observe one's own conduct. However, if one possesses a compassionate heart that benefits others, or if one has sharp faculties of wisdom, or is widely learned and far-sighted, or acts to guide and benefit sentient beings by propagating the Buddha-dharma, or desires to transform others through the Dharma so that they become like oneself, or has long been immersed in the power of the Buddha-dharma such that one’s ability surpasses that of others—then such a person should exhort and instruct others in turn. This is not a universal rule for all cases.
When this bhikṣu thus exhorts [another], he should do so in private; if [the fault persists], he should exhort them before the Saṃgha three times, as previously described.

The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, acting perversely according to one's own will; second, obstructing the instruction of others;
and third, not relinquishing the course of action after the Saṃgha has performed a formal triple admonition in accordance with the Dharma.

**Judgment on the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bhikṣu is of evil character and refuses to accept admonition—even to the point that he should abandon this matter—and further commits a grave offense after having been rebuked by the Saṃgha, the gravity of the transgression is the same as previously stated (without difference). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If various bhikṣus do not censure him and do not call him to mind for his own actions, yet he remains one with whom it is improper to converse, [he commits] a *duṣkṛta*."

*Ra*. This refers to that which should not be subject to formal admonition (*yao-chi*). "Should not be subject to formal admonition" means that one need not necessarily reprove or counsel him; rather, one immediately employs *morn-p'in* (silent exclusion).

The Buddha said that for a bhikṣu of evil character, one should employ the *brahmadanda* (the Brahma-penalty) method of governance. What is called the *brahmadanda* method? It means that when a son of the Brahma Heaven commits a transgression, a separate altar (*tan*) is established, and the offending son of the Brahma Heaven is placed within it.

None of the other sons of the Brahma Heaven speak with him. Since a bhikṣu of evil character is difficult to converse with, this method is used to punish him. All bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma do not speak with him; therefore, it is called the *brahmadanda* method. Regarding the term "to raise" (*ju*): [it refers to] a bhikṣu.

One should say: "Venerable sir, you have committed such-and-such an offense; you should confess it and not conceal it. You must eliminate it in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding "one who remembers":
the monk should say to the elder, "Do you remember committing such an offense at such a time and in such a place?
For a nun, this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; for the three minor groups, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exception for Opening [the Discussion]. There is no offense in the following cases: if one desists at the first word;
if it concerns that which is entirely contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not taught by the Buddha; if one has not yet been subjected to a formal reprimand or admonition;
or if, when being reprimanded or admonished by an ignorant person, one says to them: "The conduct of your own preceptors and teachers is also like this; you should learn further."
Question: Regarding the recitation of sutras, there is no offense if one speaks while joking, speaks too rapidly, speaks to oneself, or speaks in a dream;
nor is there an offense if one intended to say this but said that by mistake. There is no offense for those cases prior to the initial promulgation of the precept, and so forth.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states in detail: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "In a past age, there was a brāhmaṇa who constructed a charitable well in the midst of a wilderness. Herders and travelers would all come to the well to drink and bathe.
At sunset, a pack of jackals came to drink the remaining water. There was a leader of the jackals who did not drink from the ground."
[The jackal] went to the water and thrust its head into the jar to drink. Having drunk, it lifted the jar high and dashed it to pieces;
the shards of the earthenware jar remained pierced through its neck. The other jackals said to their leader:
"If even a moist leaf from a tree that can be used is something one should protect, how much more so this jar which benefits travelers? Why did you break it? The jackal [replied].
The master said, "I shall enjoy this pleasure; let my heart be content. Why should I concern myself with the affairs of others?
At that time, there was a traveler who said to the brahmin, "Your water jar has already been broken. You have replaced it, yet it will be broken by a jackal as before.
This continued until the fourteenth replacement. Though the jackals repeatedly admonished him, the brahmin still refused to listen. Then the brahmin thought:
He said, "Whoever it is that broke this jar, we must go and watch for them. It was indeed a jackal. He then thought, "This jackal is creating an obstacle for my meritorious well.
He then fashioned a wooden jar, sturdy and difficult to break, with a narrow opening for the head to enter but difficult to exit.
He placed it by the side of the well and, taking up his staff, waited in concealment. When the traveler had finished drinking, the jackal—acting as the master [of the situation]—[approached].
He entered first to drink. Having finished drinking, he threw himself to the ground; yet it could not be made to break. Then the brahmin seized his staff and beat him to death.
A deva in the sky spoke this verse: "The wise friend spoke words of compassion, But you were obstinate and would not accept the admonition.
By persisting in your stubbornness, you invited this calamity; Now you have lost your own life. Therefore, you are a foolish jackal."
Encountering such suffering as this wooden vessel.
Regarding the inquiry on the three fetters:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas; nine offenses are committed upon the first transgression, and four..."
Up to the third admonition: if a bhikṣu has committed any one of these offenses and knowingly conceals it, he should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*.
Once he has completed the *parivāsa*, he should be further granted six nights of *mānatva*. Having completed the *mānatva*...
There is a further method for the removal of offenses: one should remove this bhikṣu’s offense before an assembly of twenty monks.
If there is one person less and the assembly does not reach twenty, the bhikṣu’s offense cannot be removed; furthermore, the other bhikṣus may also censure him.
This is the proper time. Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? (Three times.)
The commentary states: "I have already explained" means that the matter has been fully clarified. It is said "already explained" because one wishes to cause the bhikṣus to re-examine their offenses.

Regarding the nine precepts where the offense is incurred upon the first transgression, from the rule against playing with the genitals and emitting semen to the rule against taking a morsel [of food] and slandering another: the offense is obtained as soon as the act is completed, and does not depend on the admonitions of others.

Thus it is said that this constitutes the "first offense. From the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha up to the offense of being obstinate and refusing admonition—these four root rules are not *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) offenses;
rather, it is only because one does not relinquish them after three admonitions that one incurs these specific offenses. Therefore, it is said: "four [offenses]...
up to three admonitions. "Each individual rule" refers to committing any one of the thirteen rules while knowing that one has done so and concealing it.
This refers to one who, knowing for themselves that they have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, conceals it with a mind of concealment.

If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but believes it to be a *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense, even though they harbor a mind of concealment, it is not termed "concealment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of concealment: first, concealment by night; second, concealment by mind. If one acts with concealment...

Concealing the mind until the appearance of light [at dawn] is called "concealment for one night. If one does not know or does not remember, even though the appearance of light has passed, there is no offense of concealment;

therefore, it is said that one must "know and yet conceal. Question: Regarding the four precepts, if one commits an offense and does not relinquish it after the three admonitions, the entire Sangha is aware of it. How can there be any concealment? Answer: Although the Sangha is aware of it...
To have no intention of revealing one's offense from the outset is precisely what is meant by "concealment" (*paticchādana*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "This bhikṣu enters the Saṃgha and proclaims: 'Venerable elders, I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

It would be well if I were to speak of it now; if I do not speak of it immediately, then from this moment on, the number of days shall be reckoned as days of concealment. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The Buddha rebuked the concealing bhikṣu: "Foolish man! This is an evil deed. You have violated the precepts yet feel no shame;
why then should you feel shame for failing to repent? He then spoke this verse: "That which is covered leaks; that which is opened does not leak.
Therefore, those who cover themselves should open up so that there is no leakage. [He] should be strongly admonished with the *pāyattika*.
*Parivāsa*. Regarding "forcibly granting": this means that because the person follows the Dharma, it refers to a person who has transgressed the Dharma bestowed by the Tathāgata;
they must rely upon and practice its conduct accordingly, hence it is called "forcibly granting.
*Parivāsa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "separate residence" (*bie zhu*). For what reason is it named "separate residence"? It means residing separately in a single room, not...
One may reside together with the Saṃgha; however, one must not dwell in the same room as those who have committed the same offense.
Even if one must stay together, one must inform the Saṃgha. One must sit and walk below all the members of the great Saṃgha and must not eat from the same grass mat.
Furthermore, although one has entered among the Saṃgha, one must not engage in questions and answers or conversation with the monks. For these reasons, it is called [the probationary period].

Separate dwelling. Next, the rules of conduct are explained. Regarding the seven groups of five practices that should not be performed and those that should be performed, the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
these include opening the doors, lighting lamps, sweeping and plastering the monastery buildings, cleaning the large and small latrines, removing filth, and providing earth and leaves;
giving fire in cold weather, fanning for coolness in hot weather, striking the *ghanṭā*, and making preparations.
Maintain the incense offerings and praise the Buddha. One should attend to the novices (śrāmaṇera) who are near full ordination, remaining below them in rank.

One should collect and put away the bedding of the Saṃgha and the implements for holding alms bowls. The stūpas and the incense halls should always be smeared and swept, and hot water should be provided.
One should wash the feet and apply oil for the virtuous bhikṣu. Regarding the offerings within the monastery, he should receive them last.
Practicing the dharma in this manner, one should do so throughout the entire period of the *saṃvatsara*. This is called the practice of *parivāsa*.
When the *parivāsa* is completed, one is further granted the six-night *mānatva*. "Further" means that it is added on top.
The Dharma of the Six-Night Practice. *Mānatva* is a Sanskrit term; in the Qin language, it means "joy of mind.
The person before [the community] rejoices in their own mind, feels shame and remorse, and causes the assembly of monks to rejoice as well.

As for the person’s joy, because they are granted a short period of time, they receive the name "joy" on account of those few days. As for the joy of the assembly of monks, it refers to observing the practice of this person as they carry out the prescribed dharma.
He shall not transgress again. The community of monks exclaims, "This person, through this [act], has reformed and repented;
he will no longer give rise to afflictions and has become a pure person. For this reason, he rejoices himself, and he also causes the community of monks to rejoice. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* says:
*Manatta* (摩那埵) is translated in the Han language as "subduing arrogance" (*zhéfú gònggāo*) and also as "lowering the mind" (*xià yì*). To "lower the mind" means to serve the community of monks.
Once the *manatta* has been performed, there remains the rite for the removal of the offense (*chu zuì*).

"Remaining" refers to the fact that after the *parivāsa* (separate dwelling) and the *manatta* have each been performed according to the Dharma, only the single rite for the removal of the offense remains. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, as cited in the *Shanjiàn*) states:

*Āpattipariśuddhi* (阿浮訶那) is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Han language, it means "calling in" (*huàn rù*) and is also said to mean "extracting from offenses" (*bá zuì*). What is meant by "calling in"?

It refers to being granted participation in the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts, and the *pravāraṇā*; because one shares in these ritual matters, it is called "calling in" and "extracting from offenses. The *Mātṛkā* states:
"To lift one from an unwholesome state and place them in a wholesome state is called *āpattipariśuddhi*. *Vibhāṣā*.
Nimu says: *Āpattipratikarman* (A-fu-ho-na) means that through pure precepts, one attains pure liberation; within these precepts, one is pure and free from transgression. Tandi-jemo says:
Because the offenses of the two categories [of the *Prātimokṣa*] are grave, it is necessary to perform the method of subduing (*vinayana*) within the Saṃgha.
This must consist of two parts: first, the rectification of the error; second, the rectification of the offense. First, he grants...
The *pārivāsika-karman* (the rite of concealment) is for the purpose of curing transgressions, not for curing offenses.

The *ṣaḍrātra-parivāsa* (six-night probation) and the *āvarhaṇa* (formal rehabilitation) are both methods for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), as they constitute the formal confession of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

One must remove this bhikṣu’s offense within an assembly of twenty monks. If even one person is missing such that the assembly does not reach twenty, the bhikṣu’s offense is not removed; it remains his offense.

It cannot be removed. Whenever one wishes to remove an offense, one must know five conditions. What are these five? First, by reason of the offense; that is, the offense committed. Second, by reason of the intention;
that is, knowing [the offense] and concealing it. Third, by reason of the penance; that is, granting *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth according to the number of days of concealment.
Fourth, by reason of having performed [the penance]; that is, causing the minds of the community to rejoice. Fifth, by reason of the person.
"Special" (*śu*) refers to the requirement of a full assembly of twenty members to determine the number. This is because the offense of this chapter is grave and unlike other rules;
it can only be eradicated by relying on the majestic power of the *karmavācanā* and the great strength of the Saṃgha.

If one attempts to complete the required number by including those practicing *parivāsa*, the number is not fulfilled. Likewise, if one includes those practicing *mānatva* to complete the number, it is not [fulfilled].
To constitute a quorum: if one uses a person under training (*śikṣamāṇā*) to complete the count, it does not constitute a quorum, as explained in detail in the section on "insufficient numbers.
By extension, one should know that a group of fewer than twenty is not a full assembly; it must consist of twenty monks who are in accordance with the Dharma and pure.
This is called being "full. If there is even one person missing or if the procedure is contrary to the Dharma, the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished, and the offense of that bhikṣu cannot be removed.
One should perform the ritual procedure anew. The bhikṣus may also censure it. "The bhikṣus" refers to the saṃgha that presides over the legal act.
If the procedure is performed improperly, they should censure its performance; one commits a duṣkṛta offense and must repent. This is the proper time [for such action].
This refers to the time for reciting the precepts, the disclosure of offenses, and the formal inquiry regarding purity (*pārisuddhi*).
Now, the inquiry regarding purity is made to the Venerable Ones. This constitutes the fourfold exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
Venerable sirs, because you are pure and silent regarding this matter, it shall be held as such.
The Three and Two *Aniyata* Dharmas are divided into four parts: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration of the precepts; third, the concluding inquiry;
and fourth, the exhortation to uphold them.
First: "Venerable sirs, these two *aniyata* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Regarding the explanation of the two *aniyata*s:
this precept consists of two articles, yet the essential nature of this offense lacks a fixed characteristic."

There may be many offenses, and it is impossible to speak of them with certainty. The Sarvāstivādins say that when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he had already determined the gravity, lightness, permissibility, and prohibitions of the five categories of precepts; there was no dharma that remained undetermined.

The reason it is called "undetermined" (aniyata) is simply that a trustworthy person does not recognize the characteristics or the relative weight of the offense, nor do they know the name of the offense. Even if...

He sees [the monk] sitting in one place with a woman, but does not know what he is doing with her—whether they are engaging in sexual intercourse, whether he is making physical contact, whether he is using coarse and evil speech, or whether he is speaking more than five or six words; therefore, it is called "undetermined."
Second, the detailed enumeration of the characteristics of the precepts has two parts.
First, a general explanation of the three initial indeterminate dharmas.
For a bhikṣuṇī, there are cases where [an offense] is shared and cases where it is not. If she enters a secluded place with a man, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To engage in impure conduct, or to have physical contact with him, is a *pārājika*. To speak coarse words is a *sthūlātyaya*. To preach the Dharma in more than five or six sentences is a *pāyattika*.
This is the same as in the Mahāyāna; these are offenses by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "This is because of the Upā..."
This training rule was established due to the affliction of sexual desire.
Regarding the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the person who provided the condition for its arising: when Kāḷudāyin was still a layman, he had a close female friend, a laywoman named Cāpā, who was beautiful in appearance;
Kāḷudāyin was also handsome in appearance, and they were mutually infatuated with one another. When the time arrived for the Venerable One [to go on his almsround],...
Having put on his robes and taken up his alms bowl, he went to the house of a lay follower (*upāsikā*) who was observing the fast, and sat with her in a secluded, private place.
At that time, Visākhā had some minor business to attend to; going there, she heard their voices from afar and thought to herself, "Perhaps they are preaching the Dharma.
She then leaned against the wall to listen. Hearing these words that were not in accordance with the Dharma, she peered inside and saw him sitting together with the one observing the fast.

The upāsikā sat together with [the bhikṣu] on a single bed. (According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*: Viśākhā was intelligent and of sharp faculties; she was a person of great virtue whom the Bhadanta respected. Knowing that the bhikṣu was sitting in a secluded place with a woman, why did she go there?

The answer is: This person had already entered the path of the fruits [of the śramaṇa]; she deeply delighted in the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha himself often said that there are five benefits in listening to the Dharma: first, hearing the Dharma not previously heard; second, purifying and strengthening what has already been heard;

third, eliminating wrong views; fourth, attaining right view; and fifth, understanding the most profound Dharma. For this reason, Viśākhā’s longing for the Dharma was so deep that she did not let suspicion hinder her. Viśākhā-mātā is translated here as Biézhī.)

This refers to the lunar mansion *Jyeṣṭhā*. She was named after the mansion under which she was born. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "She was the daughter of King Prasenajit’s younger brother, Dhanamahāśreṇi. Having fled from her country due to a crime, she settled in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā; there she married and gave birth to this girl. The girl was of exquisite talent and eloquence.

She was married as a wife to the seventh son of the minister Viśākhā-mitra of Śrāvastī. When King Prasenajit heard of her wisdom and eloquence, he appointed her as his royal sister. Later, she gave birth to thirty-two eggs, and from each egg emerged a son.

They were handsome and upright, possessing peerless courage and strength; the physical prowess of a single man could rival that of a thousand men. At that time, Viśākhā developed faith and understanding, and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them."

The entire family attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Later, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they immediately attained the stage of *anāgāmin*. Among the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*), she was foremost in wisdom and eloquence.
She went to inform the World-Honored One, who, after rebuking her with countless skillful means, established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed, or private place suitable for sexual intercourse,
and speaks improper words, and there is a faithful upāsikā who declares one of three matters— namely, that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, and the monk who was sitting there confesses himself, saying, "I have committed this offense," he should be dealt with one by one according to three rules: whether it is a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*.
As stated by a laywoman (*upāsikā*) of verified faith, that monk should be disciplined according to the Dharma. This is called [non-].
The Determined Dharma: Explanation of the Meaning. (*Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "In this context, the substance [of the offense] consists of the object, the location, the person, and the proof.
"A woman" refers to a human female who is of sound mind and not yet deceased (this constitutes the "object"). "Alone" means one bhikṣu and one woman. "A secluded place" means...
There are two kinds: first, concealment by sight, such as when one cannot see another due to dust, mist, or darkness;

second, concealment by hearing, such as a place where even constant speech cannot be heard. Regarding "obstructed places," this refers to obstructions such as trees, walls, fences, clothing, or other objects (this is due to the location).
As for "a place suitable for sexual intercourse" where one may sit: [the text continues with the specific conditions].

"A place where sexual intercourse can be accommodated" means within a distance of one *vyāma* (a fathom), where bodies may be in close proximity and one may sit or lie down; yet, that woman may either grant permission or not comply.

"Speaking unrighteous speech" refers to speaking of the dharma of lust (this being due to passion). "There is a laywoman (*upāsikā*) established in faith" means she has faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and does not kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or drink [intoxicants].
Wine. One who possesses good mindfulness and retention does not err regarding matters and speaks truthfully, never falsely. As the *Sarvāstivāda* school says:

"A laywoman (*upāsikā*) established in faith will never utter a falsehood for the sake of her own body or for the sake of wealth and profit. If someone were to say to her: 'If you speak falsely, it will not harm your life; if you do not speak falsely, your life shall be taken,' she would reflect to herself:

'I shall not speak falsely even if this physical body is destroyed and this single life is extinguished. If I were to speak falsely, immeasurable lifetimes would be extinguished, and furthermore, my Dharma-body would be harmed. Thus she vows not to speak falsely. Furthermore, if someone were to say: 'If you speak falsely, your parents, brothers, and sisters shall live...'"

"Sister, as for all my kinsmen, if I do not speak falsely, they will all be killed. Then I reflect: 'If I do not speak falsely, I shall harm these kinsmen of this single lifetime in the cycle of birth and death.

But if I speak falsely, I will wander through the three evil realms and forever lose the kinship and retinue of humans and devas over many lifetimes; furthermore, I will lose the supramundane retinue of the noble ones (ārya). I vow not to speak falsely. Furthermore, someone says: "If you speak falsely, I will give you precious jewels and various kinds of wealth and profit;

if you do not speak falsely, I will not give them to you. Then one reflects: "If I do not speak falsely, I will lose this worldly wealth; but if I speak falsely, I will lose the wealth of the noble Dharma (āryadharmanidhi). I vow not to speak falsely. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Even if it is..."

There are ordinary persons who possess faith and integrity; their words and deeds do not deviate from one another, and they act in accordance with what they say. Such a person is called a lay female devotee (upāsikā) who abides in faith. This is established by testimony. This is what the seated bhikṣu himself declares.
"I have committed this offense. Regarding these three matters, each should be dealt with accordingly (*The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"If this bhikṣu says of himself, 'I have committed this offense,' one should deal with him according to the bhikṣu's own words, not according to the words of the upāsikā. Why? Because what was seen or heard may not be accurate"). There was once a bhikṣu whose craving had been exhausted.

One day he went to the house of a donor and sat inside the room. The upāsikā stood outside, leaning against a separate bed, facing the bhikṣu. When ordinary bhikṣus entered the donor’s house for alms, they saw from afar that the bhikṣu and the upāsikā were sitting together on the same bed; they stared at them incessantly, [misconstruing the situation].

The monk who had exhausted his craving thought to himself, "This monk will surely say that I sat on the same bed with a woman. Each returned to his own quarters. The monk who was seeking alms, wishing to bring up the offense, went to the room of the monk who had exhausted his craving to request permission.

As he was about to enter through the door, the monk Vītarāga (the One Free from Passion) anticipated his thoughts through supernormal power and emerged from the ridgepole of the house, sitting in mid-air. After this monk had entered, he searched everywhere but could not find him;

seeing him sitting in the air, he said to the monk Vītarāga, "Venerable Sir, you possess such supernormal power! Why did you enter the house of a layperson and sit alone on the same bed with a woman? The monk Vītarāga replied, "Elder, this is the offense of entering the house of a layperson alone.

Elder, please protect me well. (Text) This refers to a case where one sees but does not verify the facts; one should adjudicate according to the monk's words. If he does not speak truthfully, then one should adjudicate according to the words of the female lay follower (*upāsikā*). For the Dharma is not fixed.
Therefore, no formal condition is established).

Determining the offense: In this context, regarding the offender—if a bhikṣu himself declares the place he is heading toward, declares the place he has reached, declares that he is sitting, declares that he is lying down, or declares that he is performing an action, he should be disciplined exactly according to what the bhikṣu has stated.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place he is heading toward, declares the place he has reached, declares that he is sitting, or declares that he is lying down, but does not declare that he is acting [otherwise], he should be dealt with according to the rules for an upāsikā; provided, however, that he does not declare that he is lying down.
One does not speak of having committed it oneself, nor even does one speak of the destination one has gone toward; all such cases are treated according to the words of the upāsikā.
The *Sudarsana* states: "If a bhikṣu wishes to enter a village and desires to sit in a secluded place with a woman..."
When putting on robes and taking up the alms bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he sets out and departs, for every step taken, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he arrives at the house of a donor and sits in a secluded place, it is a *pāyattika*. If he rises and then sits down again, it is a *pāyattika* for each instance.
If he sits together with many women, there are as many *pāyattikas* as there are women. If...
If a bhikṣu enters a secluded place first and a woman comes there to pay respects and inquire after his well-being, he commits no offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should question her regarding the matter she mentions with great urgency" (meaning one must ask promptly and not delay).
Once the bhikṣu has questioned her with such urgency, if she says, "I did not go," there is no offense; one should follow what is said by a trustworthy upāsikā.
Because the woman spoke falsely, this bhikṣu is subjected to the *yathābhūta-mṛṣāvāda-vinaya* (the formal act of seeking the truth regarding a false statement) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

Once the *karman* has been performed, he must comply accordingly; he shall not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others and so forth (as clarified in the section on the characteristics of the offense within the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* [methods for settling disputes]).
If he does not act in accordance with the Dharma, he shall not be released from this *karman* for as long as he lives (*karman-niḥsaraṇa* means "release"). Sarvāstivāda...

Generally speaking, if a bhikṣu initially says "yes" but later says "no," or says "I did not go" or "I did not commit this offense," one should follow the testimony of a reliable person and grant him the *yathābhūta-mṛṣāvāda-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for seeking the truth).

The reason for doing so is to cause the offender to subdue his evil mind, to ensure that he does not conceal his offense due to suffering and distress, and to protect those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
They shall dwell in peace and security. Furthermore, it shall be strictly enforced so that unwholesome dharmas do not arise.

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, if they confess their prior offenses, the *karmavācanā* should be lifted, and they shall be disciplined according to the gravity of the matter. If they do not confess, the *karmavācanā* shall not be lifted for as long as they live.
The *Huìxiáng lùn* (Treatise on Detailed Explanation) further states: "The reason for establishing precepts for the bhikṣus is threefold:

first, to stop slander; second, to eliminate strife and contention; and third, to increase the superior Dharma. A bhikṣu has left the household life, severing ties with worldly defilement, and is revered by humans and devas as one who transforms beings through the Way.
Yet, to engage in private, crooked, and base conduct with a woman in a secluded place—"

This is because: first, it would violate the intention of the Sage; second, it would cause the loss of the faith, respect, and devotion of humans and devas; third, [it would lead to] the fragmentation [of the community];

and fourth, it is for the sake of establishing the sequential method for severing evil karma. Since one might initially be secluded in private, gradually becoming habituated and entangled until there is no improper conduct one does not engage in, it is therefore necessary to prevent this.
Next, regarding the two dharmas for which the specific characteristics of the precept (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) are not fixed:
if a bhikṣu sits together with a woman in an exposed place that is unsuitable for sexual intercourse and utters coarse and wicked words.
If there is a laywoman who is established in faith, she may declare one of two offenses— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*—
regarding a seated bhikṣu. If that bhikṣu himself admits, "I have committed this offense," he should be dealt with according to one of those two rules—
either as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or as a *pāyattika*— exactly as stated by the laywoman who is established in faith.
That bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma. This is called an *aniyata-dharma* (the meaning is the same as before, so it is not explained again).
Third, the inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the two *aniyata-dharmas*. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?"
(Third inquiry). Fourth, the exhortation to uphold:
"Venerable sirs, since you are pure in this matter, you remain silent; thus it shall be held."

● The Four Groups of Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. This is divided into four parts: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration of the precept characteristics;
third, the concluding inquiry; and fourth, the exhortation to uphold them.
First, the general introduction:
"Venerable sirs, these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
Explanation: Regarding *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, the term *pāyattika* is translated as "falling.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Pāyattika" carries the meaning of being "burned," "boiled," or "fallen. This refers to one who commits this offense.
They fall into the evil realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, where they undergo the suffering of being burned and boiled.
Furthermore, if this offense is not diligently confessed and removed, it can obstruct all wholesome dharmas; because it has this meaning of "obstructing," it is called a *pāyattika*.
This precept consists of one hundred and twenty rules, the first thirty of which are listed here. Because...

Because it constitutes an offense regarding material wealth, the term *naiḥsargika* is added. According to the science of phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), *ni* is translated as "exhaustion" (*jìn*) and *sargika* is translated as "abandonment" (*shě*).
Because one is compelled to abandon [the object] into the midst of the Saṃgha due to greed for and pride in material things, it is called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
It is also called *shěduò* (abandonment-fall). These are Chinese terms, spoken here in abbreviated form.

Second, the individual enumeration of the precept characteristics consists of thirty articles in total. The first is named "keeping extra robes," and so on, up to the thirtieth, "seeking for oneself monastic property and taking it into one's own possession."
○ General Explanation of the First Rule: The Precept Regarding the Extra Robe Not Being Purified by Gift for Ten Days.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "First, if one pursues worldly benefit, spiritual benefit will not be accomplished; furthermore, one loses the patron (*dānapati*)."

With faith, reverence, and a pure mind, a bhikṣu never tires [of this practice]; yet it is no different from that of the laity, and thus violates the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) of the Buddha’s teaching.

This is a common precept; nuns are likewise bound by it. In the Mahāyāna, however, it is not the same: the Bodhisattva trains to universally benefit sentient beings, taking the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) as foremost.
Although the training differs, they must likewise perform the ritual of "purifying the goods" (śuddhaka-vastu). This is according to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.

It is said: This was established as a training rule (śikṣāpada) due to the matter of extra robes and the affliction of excessive greed. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions:
the location where it originated.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. He permitted the bhikṣus to possess three robes, but not more than that (this merely prohibited excess;

no formal precept had yet been established). The Cīvara-vastu states: The Buddha saw the bhikṣus traveling on the road carrying many articles and clothing. He thought to himself, "I should establish a regulation regarding the quantity of robes."

"One must not keep more than this. At that time, the Buddha was staying outdoors during the first watch of the night, wearing a single robe. During the middle watch, feeling cold, he put on a second robe. During the last watch, feeling cold again, he put on a third robe and then dwelt in comfort.
He then permitted the bhikṣus to keep three robes, but not more."

The occasion arose concerning people. At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: as for the "six groups," they are: first, Nanda; second, Upananda; third, Kālodāyin; fourth, Channa; fifth, Aśvaka; and sixth, Punarvasu.

Two of them attained the exhaustion of outflows and entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; two—Kālodāyin and Channa—attained rebirth in the heavens; two—Nanda and Upananda—fell into evil realms and were born among the nāgas; and one was Aśvaka).

The two *Pūrṇa* constellations—Nanda and Upananda—are skilled in mathematics, astrology, and the interpretation of signs; they are also adept at preaching the Dharma and debating its meaning, yet they are full of desire. The two *Aśvinī* constellations are proficient in music and various forms of entertainment, being capable in every such matter.

They were also skillful in preaching the Dharma and engaging in formal debate, and they were learned in the Abhidharma. Kāḷudāyin and Channa were deeply proficient in the art of archery and had a profound understanding of the Abhidharma. Indeed, these six men were not unversed in any doctrine; they were thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

Internally, they served as the pillars of the Buddha-dharma; externally, they acted as its great protectors. Five of them were of the Śākya clan and royal lineage, while only Kāḷudāyin was of the Brāhmaṇa caste.

All six were from noble families who influenced one another and became friends to propagate the Buddhist teachings; thus they were called the "Group of Six Bhikṣus. They would keep extra robes or wear robes early in the morning.
Whether it be robes for midday or robes for the late afternoon, he constantly busies himself with their adornment and storage.

(The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: Question: By what means does he obtain such various garments? Answer: Since he is of noble lineage, has many acquaintances, and furthermore possesses great desire, his clothing is abundant. Why does he thus accumulate so many robes? Answer: He was originally from a prominent clan;

while formerly living as a householder, he was attached to necklaces and various types of fine attire. Although he delighted in the Dharma and left the household life, because of his former habits he enjoys fine robes and alms bowls, and because of his great desire, he accumulates many.)
When the bhikṣus saw this, they went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

At that time, Ānanda obtained from a person a costly discarded rag-robe (pāṃśukūla) which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa, for Mahākāśyapa constantly practiced the dhūta austerities and wore such robes.
Mahākāśyapa was absent. Not knowing what to do, Ānanda went at once to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Mahākāśyapa, "When will he return? Ānanda replied, "He shall return in ten days. [Question: By what means did the Elder Ānanda know that Mahākāśyapa would return in ten days?

[Answer: The reason he knew is this: when Mahākāśyapa wished to travel through various countries, he went to Ānanda and said, "I wish to travel to such-and-such a country; I shall return on such-and-such a day. Alternatively, Mahākāśyapa might have sent a messenger to inquire after him.

"World-Honored One and Ānanda, on such-and-such a day I shall return. I know that I shall return in ten days. Question: For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the precept in accordance with Ānanda’s words? Answer: This is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense by formal rule), not a *prakṛti-āpatti* (a natural offense).
Therefore, he established it in accordance with Ānanda’s words. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I permit you to keep extra robes for up to ten days.
Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been withdrawn, he may keep an extra robe for ten days without having made it a formal gift;
if it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

**Exegesis:** "Having finished making the robes" means that the three robes are complete (that is, the three robes are sufficient; or, because the making of the robes is finished, it is called "having finished making the robes"). "The *kaṭhina* robe has been removed" (*kaṭhina* in Sanskrit;

here translated as "robe of merit," so named because one who has completed the summer retreat gains five benefits as a reward for their merit). These five benefits are: first, keeping extra robes; second, staying overnight apart from one's robes; third, eating in a group separate from the community; fourth, eating at successive meals;

and fifth, entering a village before or after the meal without informing others. These five are permitted such that no offense is committed. The *Vinaya-śīlopa* quotes the *Vidyāmātra-siddhi-śāstra*, which originally translates [the term] as "solidity" (*sāra*), as it is capable of inducing...

Indeed, it is because it can procure many robes. Furthermore, it is the opposite of "difficult to sustain" (*dussīlya*); for a poor person, sustaining life is difficult, yet by giving away even a small amount of wealth, one enters into the superior merit of this robe. It is like making an offering of a great mass of cloth as vast as Mount Sumeru.

What has already been mentioned as "exiting" refers to relinquishing [the *kaṭhina*]. Regarding those who enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat): the five months refer to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, at which point they exit the robe. Regarding those who enter the *paścimavārṣika* (later rains retreat): they do not receive the *kaṭhina* cloth, but are permitted only one month;

those who exit [at that time] are in the remaining seven months or the eleventh month). As for "keeping extra robes" (*atirekacīvara*): "extra" means having more than the three robes; as the *Book of Jin* says, "Throughout one's life, there are no superfluous possessions. [This refers to] the robe.
There are ten kinds [of robes]. First, *koseyya* cloth (the Master should translate this as "silk cloth," because it is made from the silk fibers of wild silkworms;

alternatively, it is called *kauśeya* cloth. In the eastern region of India there is the country of Oḍra; when the rice is ripening, the leaves transform into silkworms, and these silkworms eat the rice.

People harvest them, steam them, and turn them into cotton-like fiber). Second, *kārpāsa* cloth (this means "cotton flower"; it is a fine cotton cloth). Third, *kambala* cloth (this is a garment woven from wool, such as a coarse woolen blanket). Fourth, *kṣauma* cloth (this means...).
1. *Māyī* (Hemp Garment). The *Xiyu ji* states that this is a type of hemp; however, hemp is scarce in that land, so they mostly use grasses and sheep’s wool to weave it.

2. *Pañcamaka* (Coarse Cloth Garment). This is translated as "coarse cloth. 3. *Śāṇa* (or *Sana*) Garment. *Śāṇa* is the name of a tree; this tree is as tall as a man, its bark resembles hemp, and it is taken to weave garments whose texture is like coarse cloth.

This does not exist in this region. 4. *Māyī* (Hemp Garment). There are many varieties of hemp in the Western Regions, which are naturally blue, yellow, or red in color. 5. *Kṣaumika* (Fine Cloth Garment). This is translated as "fine cloth. 6. *Kauśeya* (Silk Garment). [Note: The source text lists this as "Jiuyiluo," which corresponds to *kauśeya*.]*

*Vastra* (also called *sūkṣma-vastra*, fine cloth). *Daśaka-māṣārddha-vastra* (a garment of ten *māṣa* and a half; the translation has not yet been seen). Regarding the "extra robe" (*atireka-cīvara*):

if it is eight fingers long and four fingers wide according to the Tathāgata’s finger measurement—wherein one Tathāgata finger measures two inches in width, making eight fingers equal to one foot six inches in length, and four fingers equal to eight inches in width, which is sufficient to serve as a robe-segment—it is called an extra robe.

Regarding "impure giving" (*aśuddha-dāna*) and so forth: there are two kinds of pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*): first, true purity (*bhūta-śuddhi*); second, indirect purity (*paramparā-śuddhi*). [In the latter part of the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga*...]

This is clarified within the fifty-ninth *pāyattika* [of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*]: "To perform neither of these two kinds of purification is called 'impure giving' (*aśuddha-dāna*). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Among the ninety-six types of heterodox teachings, there is no method for pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*).

Because of the Buddha’s great compassion and the power of his skillful means (*upāya*), he taught the practice of pure giving so that his disciples might be permitted to possess surplus wealth (*atireka-lābha*) without violating the precepts. Question: Why did the Buddha not simply permit the possession of surplus wealth directly?
Yet he forcibly established the precepts and devised this expedient means. He replied: "The Buddha-dharma takes few desires as its foundation;
therefore, the precepts were established so that one does not keep surplus wealth. However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ;
some may have much accumulated beforehand and yet later practice the Way and attain realization of the Noble Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata first established the precepts, and thereafter..."
He establishes skillful means so that there is no obstruction regarding the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings receive benefit.

Having performed the "pure gift" (*śuddha-dāna*), he is permitted to keep surplus wealth (*atireka-lābha*) without violating the precepts. Question: Does the monk who acts as the "pure master" (*śuddhādhiṣṭhātṛ*) not violate the precept against keeping surplus wealth? Answer: No.
There is no offense. This is because it was a skillful means of giving, as the object was another's property.

Regarding the conditions for an offense: this precept is completed as a full offense only when three conditions are met. If any condition is lacking, the offense is categorized as a preliminary transgression (*prayoga*).

The three conditions are: first, having a mind of greed or pride; second, possessing robes that exceed the prescribed measure; and third, failing to give them away by the end of the designated period.

**The Formal Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, and continues to obtain robes up until the tenth day, such that when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, he has committed a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture and confession). [In this context,] "obtaining a robe on the first day" refers to the day the robe enters his possession; it does not mean the first day of the lunar month.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day without having performed the *apariśuddha-dāna* (the formal relinquishment of ownership), and then obtains [robes] on the second day, and so on, up to the tenth day...
If a robe has been formally given away (*pariṇata*) or not formally given away, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

(In this context, from the time one obtains the robe on the first day until the tenth day—during which interval one may obtain it on some days and not on others—regarding those items obtained, some may have been formally given away and some not. Those that were formally given away involve no offense;

however, regarding those not formally given away, due to the influence of the robe obtained on the first day, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, they all constitute an offense of forfeiture. This same principle applies if [the robe] was sent to be given.

"Sent" (meaning dispatched; that is, given away). There are those who say "sent to another" refers to a case of indirect purification (*parivāsa*), which is incorrect. "If the robe is lost" (meaning stolen away). "If it is intentionally damaged" (meaning worn out, rotten, etc.).
"If it is made into something other than a robe" (meaning made for use as some other garment). "If it is taken with the intent of a close friend" (meaning taken away by one who is a close friend).
The same applies if one forgets to take it away (meaning: having placed the robe in this location, one departs on some business and forgets to retrieve it).

If one possesses a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe and, without relinquishing it, exchanges it for another robe, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense. This *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe should be relinquished to the Saṃgha.

Whether it be a multitude of people or a single individual, one may not perform the formal relinquishment apart from the assembly (meaning that it constitutes a valid, *yathādharma* act only when the entire Saṃgha within the boundary has assembled and no one fails to attend or provide their authorization).
The opposite of the above is termed "a separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*). If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When the time for presenting the relinquishment to the Saṃgha approaches, one should bare the right shoulder within the assembly, pay homage to the Elder (*sthavira*), kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak these words:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen to me. I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, intentionally kept this surplus robe for more than ten days; I have committed an offense involving forfeiture."
"I have now relinquished this robe to the Saṃgha; having relinquished the robe, my confession of the offense is complete. The Saṃgha should return this robe to this bhikṣu.

[The procedure for the confession of the offense and the method for returning it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* are explained in detail in the Vinaya. This bhikṣu, having completed the relinquishment of the robe within the Saṃgha...
If one does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If, when returning it, someone instructs one not to return it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one performs a *śuddhaka-dāna* (pure gift), or sends it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes a *pārihārika-cīvara* (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* says:
*culla-pārihārika-cīvara*; in Chinese, "miscellaneous small garments"), or intentionally destroys it (meaning intentionally damaging that garment), or burns it (meaning burning it with fire), or...

If one makes it into something other than a robe (meaning making it into another garment for use), and if it is worn until it is repeatedly damaged, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense in every instance (this refers to the monastic community capable of performing the formal act).

To return [the robe] when one ought not to return it is a violation of the Dharma, constituting a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one obtains a robe on the first day, one must perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*) on that same day;
likewise, if one obtains a robe on the tenth day, one must perform the purification on that same day; if one obtains a robe on the eleventh day, one must perform the purification on that same day."

One commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*. This is because there is no interval. An "interval" means: if one obtains a robe on the first day, one may keep it for nine more days; if one obtains a robe on the second day, one may keep it for eight more days;
if one obtains a robe on the third day, one may keep it for seven more days; continuing in this manner until, if one obtains a robe on the ninth day, one may keep it for one more day.
If one obtains a robe on the tenth day, one must perform the *paryodāna* (formal purification) on that very tenth day. If one obtains a robe on the eleventh day, [one does not].

It should be accepted; this is called "intermittent" [use]. If one seeks goods for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha or the Sangha and collects them in one place, there is no offense even if they are kept for a long time without being used. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"If one keeps robes for the sake of the Triple Gem, it is not an offense. Or, if a donor says, 'This is my property; you should use it,' even if..."
One should distinguish their application; there is no offense (as the fundamental part of the rule states that such distinction constitutes a pure gift). The root text says:

"If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), yet does not relinquish it, or even if one relinquishes it, does not confess and repent, or even if one confesses and repents, does not wait until the night has passed—whatever one obtains [in these cases]..."

This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense due to the prior defilement. If one relinquishes the robe and confesses the transgression after it has been kept overnight, there is no offense in either case.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "One must not relinquish it to another person or to a non-human being;

only after relinquishing it may one perform the confession of the fault (‘another person’ refers to the three types of minor assemblies). ○ Third: A general explanation of the precept concerning robes kept for more than one month.

This is a common precept; the violation by a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same. In the Mahāyāna, it is different: this is established as an offense of transgression (*prajñapti-āpatti*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"Because it obstructs the cultivation of the primary practice, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established."
The Setting of the Origin: The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park. There was a certain bhikṣu whose saṃghāṭī robe was old, worn out, and tattered. He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting the keeping of an extra robe for ten days; if one exceeds this period, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). Ten days..."
"In the meantime, we can no longer manage this. What shall we do? They then informed a like-minded bhikṣu, who in turn informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus to keep robes until they are fully satisfied."
The Originative Condition for Persons:
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had permitted the keeping of robes until they were complete.

They possessed some discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*) and other similar items, but these were insufficient; therefore, they took discarded rags from among them, washed and dyed them, and marked the four corners with dots on the heads.
Having performed the ritual purification (*viśuddhi*) and entrusted [the robes] to a monk friend, he departed for travel among the people.

Later, because the monk who had received the entrustment had not returned after a long time, he took out the robes and spread them in the sun to dry. When the other monks questioned him and learned the reason, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
