General Explanation of the Seventh Precept: Receiving Robes Exceeding the Allowable Limit.

This is a common precept; the formulation for nuns is the same. In the Mahāyāna, the regulation differs: one should accept according to what is offered. This is an offense of transgression (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
The underlying afflictions are the same as before; therefore, this training rule is established.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [text continues].
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, having encountered bandits and lost their robes, arrived at the Jetavana Monastery.
There was a lay devotee (upāsaka) who, hearing that the bhikṣus had encountered bandits and lost their robes, brought many fine robes and said, "Take as many as you wish according to your needs.
The bhikṣus replied, "Stop, stop! You have already provided for us sufficiently; we ourselves possess [the three robes]."
[The Buddha said: "The robe is not needed. The group of six bhikṣus said, "Why do you not take it and give it to us? Or why give it to others?
Yet the bhikṣus, though already possessing the three robes in full, took the householder's robe and gave it to the group of six as well as to others.
A bhikṣu of few desires, feeling resentment and reproach, reported this to the Buddha. After rebuking them, the Buddha established the precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept: if a bhikṣu has his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried off by water;

and if a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him at their own discretion and offers him many robes, that bhikṣu should accept the robes with moderation. If he exceeds this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Pāyattika. Explanation of the meaning: If one loses one robe, it should not be taken [as replacement].

If two robes are lost, the remaining one—whether it be double, triple, or quadruple thickness—should be torn down [to make others]. This applies whether it is a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, or an antaravāsaka.
...the *śrāvaka-saṃgha*. If a bhikṣu loses all three robes, that bhikṣu should accept clothing with contentment.
There are two kinds of contentment: the contentment of laypeople and the contentment of renunciants. Regarding the contentment of laypeople:

one accepts whatever clothing a white-robed person gives (meaning one should accept whatever is offered by worldly people; even if it is insufficient, one should not further beg for more). Regarding the renunciant...
"Contentment" refers to the three robes (meaning that once the three robes are sufficient, one should not accept more; thus it is said that those who have left the household life are content).

If a layperson freely invites a bhikṣu and gives him many robes (regarding "free invitation," the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: if a donor says to a bhikṣu, "If you have anything you need, take it as you wish," this is called a free invitation).
If a robe is fine, thin, or not durable, one should take it and make it double, triple, or quadruple-layered.

One should add borders and apply patches over the shoulders where stains and grease might accumulate. (The Vinaya-saṃgraha states: "If the shoulders of the three robes are stained with grease, one should [patch] the areas where they are worn on the shoulders.")

It should be replaced with a cloth measuring one cubit and a half in length and one span in width, sewn along its four edges; it shall be torn out and washed whenever soiled (text). According to the Vinaya regulations, this [patch] was originally intended to be applied on the inside. Nowadays, people place it over the shoulder on the outside, claiming it is a "Mount Sumeru" [patch]; this is an error. One should provide hooks and loops.
If there is any leftover material, one should ask the layperson: "What shall this remaining cloth be cut into?
If the donor says, "I did not give this because my robe was lost; I wish to give it to you, Venerable Sir," [then it may be accepted].

[The monk] hears this. If he wishes to accept it, he may do so [as a supplement for making robes]. He must inform the donor so that they are aware; this is called "accepting with contentment. If he accepts more than the minimum, he commits an offense.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, the robe is offered because it has been lost;
second, one accepts it with a mind of greed; and third, the material of the robe enters one's possession.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bhikṣu accepts robes beyond the limit of sufficiency, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If he forgoes the robe, performs the confession (*pratideśanā*), or fails to return it, the resulting offense is the same as previously described. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If a bhikṣuṇī loses her five robes..."
One may accept two robes. If one loses four robes, one may accept one robe. If one loses three robes, one may not accept any.
If a relative or a donor makes an offer at their own discretion, or if it is one's own property, one may accept them as one wishes.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the three minor groups [of practitioners], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances (Kāraṇa): There is no offense if one takes what is sufficient; or if one takes less than what is sufficient; or if a householder gives many robes;
or if the robes are fine, thin, or not durable; or if one makes a robe of two, three, or four layers; or if one provides borders, patches, or reinforcements for stained areas;
or if one provides hooks and fasteners; or if there are leftover remnants of cloth and one asks the householder, "What shall I do with these?"
If a householder says, "I am not giving this because my robes were lost; I wish to give it to you, Venerable Sir," and one accepts it, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, such as at the very beginning.
○ Eighth, the general explanation of the precept against seeking the price for robes.
This is a common precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. That is to say, it concerns seeking improperly and seeking excessively. And...

Lack of contentment. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of formal prohibition). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because of mutual physical contact and provocation, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. A certain bhikṣu who went on almsround entered the city to beg for food and heard a householder and his wife discussing together:
"Bhadananda is an old acquaintance of ours; we shall provide the price for such a robe and purchase such a robe for him."

When that bhikṣu who was begging for alms returned, he saw Baddhananda and immediately informed him of the matter above. Upon inquiry, he learned of the household and the person who had initiated the occasion.
The next day, Baddhananda went there and said: "If you wish to give me a robe, it should be one as vast as this."
[He] made [it]. It was new, beautiful, firm, and well-finished. "I shall accept it," he thought. "If it is not suitable for me to accept, what is the use of it?
The householder criticized and disparaged him. The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept. The wording of the precept is as follows:

except when one has not previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā* (invitation to a meal), if a householder later invites a bhikṣu for a *pravāraṇā* and says, "Venerable sir, what do you require?"...
Regarding robes: a bhikṣu was hesitant and did not dare to answer. Furthermore, there was a lay devotee who wished to provide a robe of high value;
the bhikṣu, being content with what he had, wished for one of inferior quality, yet he too was hesitant and did not dare to request it as he desired. The Buddha said:
"One who accepts an invitation of his own accord commits no offense. The precepts should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:

If a bhikṣu, when a layman or a laywoman has prepared the price for robes for a bhikṣu to purchase such robes and give them to a certain bhikṣu, that bhikṣu—without having previously received an invitation—goes to the house of the layman and speaks thus: "It is well..."
"O householder, buy such and such a robe for me for the sake of our friendship. If you obtain the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding "one who procures the price for such a robe," this refers to gold, silver, coins, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, necklaces, wrought gold, or unwrought gold.
Taking such a price for a robe, one purchases such a robe and gives it to a certain bhikṣu.

(Regarding "the price for such a robe": it may be from one coin up to a hundred thousand coins. Regarding "purchasing such a robe": the color refers to blue, black, and so forth; the measurement is either five cubits up to fifteen cubits; and the substance is coarse, fine, or otherwise. This is [the meaning].
A bhikṣu who has not previously accepted an invitation for *pravāraṇā* (an invitation from a layperson to accept offerings at will) goes to the house of a layperson and speaks thus:
"Excellent, layperson! ("Excellent, layperson" is a term of praise; it is an address to the layperson intended to cause the gift to become even more excellent).
Up to this point, there are two kinds of seeking for the sake of excellence: first, seeking the price; second, seeking the robe. Regarding seeking the price: the donor...
He causes [the donor] to provide a robe of great value, even seeking an increase of one-sixteenth of a *māṣaka* (in the Western Regions, sixteen *sheng* constitute a *dou*;

this is comparable to how sixteen *liang* constitute a *jin* here). Regarding the solicitor of robes, he says to the householder: "Make a robe of such width and length," even increasing it by one *māṣaka*.

[Regarding the phrase] "for the sake of making such and such a robe excellent," the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "To further seek what is new, fine, and durable—meaning that the price, color, and dimensions are all [superior]."
All are exquisite and refined). "If one obtains the robe" (meaning that the offense is established only when the robe actually enters one's possession).
The conditions for the offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a covetous intention;
second, one has not yet accepted an invitation to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; third, one seeks it for oneself; and fourth, the clothing or goods enter one's possession.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one first does not accept an invitation for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, yet goes to seek a costly and wide robe, and if such a robe is obtained, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). If one seeks it but does not obtain it, it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).

As for the forfeiture, confession, and non-returning [of the robe], the resulting offenses are the same as before. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To solicit something fine from a relative constitutes a *dukkaṭa*."

Regarding the offense: the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that if one asks for goods from a relative who possesses abundant wealth, there is no fault; however, if the relative is poor, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinayasamgraha* states that if one begs from devas and the like, or begs for thread, silk, small pieces of cloth, and so forth, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three lesser groups [bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is meant.
This constitutes an offense. Exceptions where there is no offense: having previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation), one goes to seek [alms];

seeking with contentment and in reduced measure; seeking from relatives; seeking from those who have left the household life; or seeking on behalf of another; or when another seeks on one's behalf; or...
Not seeking it, one obtains it spontaneously; there is no offense. One who has not transgressed refers to those for whom the precept was not yet established at the outset, and so forth.

○ The ninth precept concerning seeking to have robes made together follows the same circumstances as the preceding ones and is therefore not repeated here. The difference lies in "having them made together."
If a monk, when two householders or a householder’s wife have prepared the price for a robe and intend to purchase such a robe with that price to give it to a certain monk,
and that monk has not previously accepted an invitation from those householders, [he commits an offense].
He goes to the houses of two lay devotees and speaks thus: "Excellent!
Prepare such and such an amount for the price of cloth and make one robe together with me, so that it may be fine. If he obtains a robe [thereby], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
○ General Explanation of the Tenth Precept: The Rule Regarding Soliciting Robes More Than Six Times.
This is a shared precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna to prevent public censure and to maintain the purity of others.

This is an offense of formal prescription (*prajñapti-āpatti*). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because taking impure wealth and failing to protect the intentions of others leads to distress and confusion, this training rule was prescribed."
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a high minister who was a close friend of Upananda. He sent a messenger with the price for a robe to give to Upananda.
Upananda took the messenger into the city and gave the price for the robe to an old acquaintance, a householder, to hold for him.
At another time, the minister asked the messenger, "Has Upananda put on my robe? The messenger replied:
Not accepting his words, [the donor] immediately dispatched a messenger to demand the return of the price for the robe.
Upāli (Bhadanta) then hurried to the house of the elder and said, "I now require a robe. At that time, the elders of the city had assembled;
they had previously established a regulation that anyone who did not attend would be fined five hundred coins. The elder replied, "Venerable Sir, please wait a moment while I attend the assembly."
He returned, but Baddhālīta would not accept it. After the elder had finished making the robe for him, the assembly had already concluded its session.

Because he had not arrived, the crowd paid five hundred coins as a fine. The elder was universally criticized and disparaged. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu, or a king, or a great minister, or a brāhmaṇa, or a householder, or a householder’s wife,
sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu, saying, "Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu," and that messenger arrives...
To the place where the bhikṣu is, the messenger says to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, for your sake I have sent this price for robes;
please accept it. That bhikṣu should say to that messenger: "I should not accept this price for robes.
If I need a robe, at the proper time and when it is pure, I shall accept it. That messenger says to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, is there an attendant? [The bhikṣu replies: "Yes, he is needed."

The bhikṣu who has the robe-cloth should say, "There is. [He should say: "Whether it be a monastery attendant or an upāsaka, this person is the bhikṣu’s steward who constantly performs services for the bhikṣus.

Then that messenger, having gone to the place of the steward and delivered the price for the robe-cloth, returns to the bhikṣu and speaks thus: "Venerable sir, to the steward named so-and-so whom you indicated, I..."
"Venerable sir, the price for the robe has already been paid; you should know the time and go there, and you shall obtain the robe.
A bhikkhu who needs a robe should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them twice or thrice, should say: "I need a robe.
If, after reminding them twice or thrice, he obtains the robe, that is well. If he does not obtain the robe, [he may go] four or five times.
He stands silently before [the donor] six times. If he stands silently before him four, five, or six times, it is well if he obtains the robe;
if he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain a robe beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he may go himself or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was obtained and say: "Previously, you..."
"Send a messenger with the price for robes to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu. If that bhikṣu does not ultimately receive the robe, you should take it back;
do not let it go to waste. This is the proper course of action."

**Explanation of the Meaning:** Whether it be a king, a high minister, or even a brahmin, a householder, or a housewife (this clarifies the donor), they dispatch a messenger to deliver the price of a robe to a bhikṣu (the "price of a robe" refers to gold, silver, coins, precious gems, or wrought and unwrought gold).

Carrying such a price for a robe, [the messenger] gives it to a certain bhikṣu (this clarifies the recipient; "such a price for a robe" refers to amounts ranging from one hundred coins up to a thousand coins, etc.).

That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was. [The bhikṣu said: "I should not accept this price for a robe" (meaning that according to the dharma of a bhikṣu, one should not personally accept or store gold, silver, the seven treasures, and so forth; these are impure things and not the dharma of a bhikṣu, therefore they should not be accepted).

"If I require a robe at the proper time, I shall accept it when it is pure" (meaning in accordance with the time when a bhikṣu has need of it, or in accordance with the time when a bhikṣu is permitted to store one; hence it is called 'the proper time. 'Pure' means such as a woolen cloak made of camel hair and the like; because its substance is impure, it is unfit [to be used]).

[This refers to] robes; one must receive and maintain them in accordance with the Dharma and in a state of purity). That messenger says to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, do you have an attendant? [This continues] up to:

"He constantly serves as an attendant for the bhikṣus. (Regarding the term *saṃghārāmika*, it refers to those who serve as attendants provided by the Saṃgha. There are two distinct types: first, the *kappiyakāraka* [the pure person];)

The second is the garden keeper (*ārāmika*). What is a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible)? A bhikṣu tells the *kappiya-kāraka*: "Pure deeds should be performed; impure matters must not be done. Because he performs pure deeds, he is called a *kappiya-kāraka*.

If he merely guards the dwelling place, he is called a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*). He was originally given by King Prasenajit as a servant for the Saṅgha to constantly attend upon the bhikṣus. One who is called an *upāsaka* is, in meaning, a "faithful male layperson" (*śraddhā-puruṣa*), also known as a "pure person.

The direct translation is "male lay-attendant" (*upāsaka*). "Lay-attendant" (*upāsaka*) means one who approaches and serves the teachings of all Buddhas. It is also translated as "one who dwells near" (*upavasa*), meaning that by receiving and upholding the precepts, one is fit to dwell near the Saṅgha and perform various services for the bhikṣus; hence the term.

"He is always the steward for the bhikṣus. This refers to the bhikṣu indicating the person acting as the steward: "He is at such-and-such a city, such-and-such a village, at such-and-such a place, named so-and-so;

he is my steward. Then that messenger goes to the steward's location and delivers the price for the robe. [The text continues: "...until the Venerable One knows the time to go there, and shall obtain the robe" (meaning:

once that messenger has handed over the price for the robe and returned to report to the bhikṣu, saying, 'I have already given the price for the robe, Venerable One; you yourself should know the time—whether it be when you need to use it, or when it is appropriate to store it').
At that time, one should go to the person in charge of affairs; there one shall obtain such pure robes.
A bhikṣu who needs robes should go to the person in charge of affairs—whether that person is at home, in the market, or at a place of work—and speak to them two or three times.
"I now require a robe; please make one for me. This "making a reminder" means informing the other person so that they may remember it and not forget it;

hence it is called "reminding. If, after reminding them two or three times, one obtains the robe, it is well (meaning that one obtains it immediately upon request, without having to remain silent for six times;
hence it is called "well"). If one does not obtain the robe, one should remain silent before them four, five, or six times.

[The establishment of] this precept-substance (śīla-ātman) occurs precisely when one has gone to request [the robe] three times and remained silent for six times; if one obtains the robe within this period, there is no fault. Beyond this, one commits an offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When one has gone to request it three times and remained silent for six times..."

There may be a delayed deadline or an urgent deadline. When a bhikṣu goes to a donor’s place to request a robe and the donor replies, “Venerable sir, please come again in one month,” the bhikṣu shall go to request it after the full month has passed.

If the donor says again, “Please come again in one month,” the bhikṣu shall go to request it again after another full month has passed. If the donor says again, “Please come again in one month,” the bhikṣu shall go to request it once more after another full month has passed; however, once three months have elapsed, he may not request it further. If the donor says, “Please come in half a month,” he may not request it further once three half-months have passed.

If the donor says ten days, five days, four days, three days, two days, or one day—even down to three *muhūrtas*—he may not request it further once those three *muhūrtas* have passed. When he has gone there six times and remains in silence, the donor says:

"I know the Venerable One's purpose for coming. Wait one more month; let six months pass in this way, even down to six *muhūrta*s. Do not go again, but remain silent. *Sudarsana* asks: "What is meant by 'remaining silent'? [The answer is: "Not speaking with the mouth; standing and not sitting."

If a donor instructs one to sit, one must not sit. If they offer food or drink, one must not accept it. If they invite one to preach the Dharma or offer prayers of benediction, one must not do so in either case. If a donor asks, "For what reason have you come here? one should reply, "The householder should know for himself.

This is what is meant by remaining silent. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "To what extent is one said to remain in silence? It is like a person entering a storehouse to take goods and staying at the shop for a short while; or like wrapping up goods in a bundle for a brief moment—one should depart immediately.
If a bhikṣu utters one word, he breaks two moments of silence; if he utters two words, he breaks four moments of silence. If he...

Three verbal requests break six instances of silence (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one does not request verbally, one obtains twelve instances of silent seeking; if one makes one verbal request, it breaks two instances of silence, and so on up to six verbal requests breaking twelve instances of silence").
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, a covetous mind that desires to take possession;
second, requesting more than permitted in violation of the regulation; and third, the receipt of the clothing or goods into one's hands.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one solicits [the robe] by speaking more than three times, or remains silent for more than six times, and if the robe is obtained, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it is not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The procedure for forfeiture, confession, and non-returning, as well as the resulting offenses, are the same as previously stated.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "After this bhikṣu has spoken to the owner of the robe, if there is another circumstance, he goes to the place where it is held..."
Regarding the location of the matter: if asked why one has come, one should answer, "I have come because I have other business.
If told to take the robe and go, one should answer, "I have already informed the owner of the robe; you may go and settle the matter yourself. If told simply to take it away, [one should comply].
I myself understand the language. At that time, if the owner of the robe accepts it and takes it away, there is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu has sent a messenger to inform [the donor], and the attendant comes and says, 'Venerable sir, you may accept this robe.'"
One should reply: "I have already discarded this robe; you should return it to the place from which it was sent. If one replies in this manner, it is well.
If the recipient accepts the robe, he commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). If the attendant says, "Venerable sir, please accept this robe;
I shall consult with its donor to ensure his mind is made joyful," if it is done in this way, one may take the robe.
There is no offense for the [male] bhikṣu; it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for the bhikṣuṇī; it is a *duṣkṛta* for the three smaller groups. This is called an offense. The exceptions:
There is no offense if one obtains the robe after requesting it three times; or if one obtains the robe by standing silently for six times.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place where the price for the robe was received, either going himself or sending a messenger, and say:
"You previously sent a messenger to give a robe to such-and-such a monk; that monk has not obtained the robe at all. You should take it back so that it is not lost.
If the other says, "I have no need of it; I shall simply give it as a gift," that monk should, at the proper time, [accept it] with gentleness...

Seeking a robe through expedient means (*upāya*). [The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "If, when speaking to the owner, the owner says, 'I previously gave this to a bhikṣu,' one may seek it again by means of an expedient. At that time, one may speak three times as before and remain silent for six times.
If one receives [a robe] by seeking it at the proper time, by seeking with gentle speech, or by seeking through expedient means for the sake of making a *pārikkāra* (extra) robe, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Eleventh Precept: Regarding Bedding Made of Silk Cotton.

This is a precept not held in common [with the Mahayana]; for the Bhikṣuṇīs, the regulations differ. In the Mahayana, because it is for the sake of sentient beings, one may accept [such silk cotton], but...
It may be utilized; it has compassion as its essence. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:
"Because killing living beings increases greed and craving, causes one to neglect one's own wholesome qualities, and damages the right faith of others, this training rule was established."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Āṭavī.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
The group of six monks made new bedding out of mixed wild silk-cotton. They went to the silkworm-raisers' houses and said, "We need silk-cotton.
They were told, "Wait a moment; you must come when the cocoons are ripe. The group of six stayed nearby waiting.

While they watched the cocoons being dried, the silkworm pupae made a sound (a *pūpa* is that which the silkworm transforms into; the *pūpa* then transforms into a moth). The householders criticized them, saying they lacked shame.
[Feeling] shame [at having] harmed the lives of sentient beings, the bhikṣus heard of this and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked him and established the precept.
The formulated characteristics of the rule are as follows: If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using wild silkworm cotton, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
**Exegesis:** Regarding "various" (*miśra*): it refers to wool, cotton, *koccha*, *ulūka-pattra*, *kusha*, or hemp.

As for "wool" (*vāla*): this refers to the fine hair of animals. Regarding "*koccha* and *ulūka-pattra*": these have not yet been translated [into Chinese]. As for "wild silk-cotton" (*kauśeya*): the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that in this country, silkworms are raised according to the methods of the people of Qin;

when the worms mature, the resulting silk is called *kauśeya*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "*Kauśeya* is of two kinds: first, the natural (*jāta*), and second, the manufactured (*kṛta*). The natural is fine thread; the manufactured is spun thread."

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "As for 'mixed,' it refers to even if a single thread of *koseyya* (silk) is interwoven as either the warp or the woof, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. A 'single thread of *koseyya*' refers to the finest fibers within the silk. Regarding the making of a new bedding (*śayanāsana*):

the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states that there are two kinds of "new": first, newly manufactured; second, newly acquired. This refers to newly manufactured items. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In this country, the method of making garments from cotton has two types:

first, carding the cotton and spreading it out to store it, according to the method used for making felt; second, spinning the cotton into thread and weaving it to form a garment. These two types of garments are called 'bedding' (*pariṣkāra*). 'Bedding' is a general term for garments. As for 'making,' it may mean making it oneself."
If one causes another to make it, it is called "making new bedding.
Regarding the conditions for an offense: this precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, a mind of greed or pride;
second, seeking it for oneself; and third, the bedding having been completed.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one uses mixed wild silk cotton (*kośa-kaṭaka*) to make bedding and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one instructs another to make it and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one constructs it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one constructs it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This must be relinquished. Regarding this relinquishment: if one finely chops and minces it with an axe and mixes it with mud, or applies it as plaster on a wall.

Regarding the application of dye: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that even if one does not do it oneself, nor causes another to do it, but accepts what another has offered, it is still an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "Or, someone says to him: 'I shall make a *kauśeya* garment for you.'"
Because one desires to obtain it and does not desist, and because of this greedy mind, one incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*).
For the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense if one obtains pre-fabricated materials and chops them with an axe or hatchet to mix with mud for plastering walls or floors;
there is no offense. There is also no offense in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
In the *Zhimen jingxun* (Admonitions for the Black-Robed), the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* is cited as stating:

"If silks, cotton, furs, or other such items have been passed along from hand to hand until they are removed from the hands of one who has killed, and are then offered to a person who upholds the precepts, it is the dharma of a bhikṣu not to accept them.

If one were to accept them, it would not be out of compassion, yet it would not be called breaking the precepts. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Leather shoes and sandals [made of] *kauśeya* silk..."
Regarding clothing: such garments as these are not to be possessed at all; this is the correct sutra and vinaya. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If bhikṣus do not wear silks, cotton, or fine fabrics from the East, nor shoes, boots, furs, or woolen garments of this land, nor consume milk, curd, or clarified butter (*ghṛta*), then such bhikṣus are truly liberated in the world, have repaid their karmic debts from past lives, and do not wander within the three realms."
Why is this? Because by partaking of their physical remains, one becomes associated with them as a condition. As for the "East," this refers to the land of Zhendan (China) in the east.

Zhendan: in the east, the trigram is Zhen; it is the direction from which the sun rises, hence it is called Zhendan. The *Loutan jing* states: "To the east of the Sihe River is named Zhendan. It is so named because when the sun first rises, its radiance shines upon the eastern corner. As for "this land," it refers to the Five Indias of Western India.

"India" is a Sanskrit term; in the Tang language, it means "moon. The moon has many names, and this is one of them. This is truly because the sages and worthies have followed one another's tracks to guide ordinary beings and govern all things, like the moon shining down. For this reason, it is called India. [The East].

It is not that furs and wool do not exist; it is not that silk and cotton do not exist in the Western lands. These statements are made by way of what is most prevalent. As for the bodies of sentient beings, since one does not wear them oneself, those who have attained true liberation repay their past debts and do not wander through the three realms—know that this scriptural statement is quite profound.

Since they wear the bodies of others, all of which are due to their own conditions, how could they escape the three realms? It is like a person who eats the various grains from the earth; their feet never leave the ground. How much more so for sentient beings whose very bodies are consumed or worn—how could they possibly transcend the three realms?
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that the two masters Nanyue Daohui and Daohu did not wear cotton; both wore mugwort-filled絮 (*xù*). Thus, Nanshan said:

"Since the Buddha-dharma first flowed eastward for nearly six hundred years, only these acts of compassionate conduct on Mount Heng are worthy of our devotion" (referring to the Chan Master Nanyue Huisi.

From his youth, he was renowned among his neighbors for his kindness and forbearance. He frequently dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the secular life; he then took leave of his parents to enter the Way. Upon receiving full ordination, he constantly practiced seated meditation and attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives. Later, he realized the Dharma).

The *Huā-sānmèi* (Flower Samādhi), the Gate of the Supreme Vehicle. In the sixth year of the Guāngdà era of the Chen dynasty, he led forty monks directly toward Mount Nanyue. He then declared: "I shall lodge on this mountain for a period of ten years. My mind is set on distant travel; you, Master, should practice compassion and forbearance."

He upheld the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts. His clothing was made of coarse cloth, and in the cold, he added layers of mugwort and cotton wool. Master Daohui constantly took the dhūta practices as his vocation. Residing in the secluded valley of Mount Nüer, south of Fulu Monastery in Xinfeng, Yongzhou, he thatched together grass to form a hut.

He would sit in meditation for seven days at a time before emerging. Upon leaving the mountain to beg for food, he would preach the prohibitive precepts and instruct people in kindness and compassion. In this manner, forty years passed. During the summer of the third year of the Zhenguan era, he did not emerge from his retreat according to his usual schedule.

He passed away while sitting upright in meditation. Since Master Xiu left the household life, he had always worn only the three robes and never donned silk or cotton wool, for fear of harming living beings. The coarse cloth garments he wore had accumulated over many years; they were so dust-covered, decayed, and tattered that those who saw them felt a chill in their hearts.

Thus one knows that Xiu’s compassionate salvation was of the same spirit as that of Mount Heng. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "It is for the sake of stopping slander and for the sake of perpetually fostering faith and reverence."
Because practicing the Path leads to peace and happiness, and because one must not harm sentient beings, this precept is established.
○ A General Explanation of the Twelfth Precept: Regarding the Use of Black Sheep’s Wool.
This is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*). The offenses for nuns differ; it is uniformly prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states:

"Because of attachment to beautiful colors and further seeking what is fine and soft, one neglects one's duties and increases greed. To prohibit that which is unbeneficial, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is established."
The Setting: The Buddha was staying in a multi-storied pavilion on the banks of the Monkey River at Vaiśālī. At that time, many Licchavis were practicing sexual misconduct;
they would wrap themselves in blankets made of pure black sheep’s wool and travel about at night so that people would not see them. (Regarding the term "Licchavis": they are...)

Jian said: "In the past, the queen of the King of Vārāṇasī became pregnant and, when her months were full, gave birth to a mass of flesh that had neither hands nor feet. Fearing that the king would surely feel revulsion and contempt upon seeing it, she immediately took it and placed it in a vessel, then struck gold to make thin plates."

He wrote a title with vermilion ink stating: "This was born of the Queen of the King of Vārāṇasī. He covered the top of the vessel and sealed it with the royal seal, then sent someone to cast it into the river. Various spirits and deities protected it, ensuring that no wind or waves could cause it to drift or sink.

At that time, there was a Daoist practitioner who went to the riverbank at dawn to wash his face; seeing the vessel from afar, he approached and took it. Seeing the gold leaf and vermilion characters, and further seeing the royal seal impressed upon it, he opened the vessel to look inside and saw only a piece of flesh.

He thought to himself: "If this were dead flesh, it would surely have become putrid and rotten by now. There must be some extraordinary sign here. He immediately took it away and placed it in a clean location. After half a month had passed, it had formed into two pieces. Another half-month passed.

Each of the two pieces had five embryos. After another half-month, one piece became a male and the other became a female; the male was the color of yellow gold and the female was the color of white silver. When the Daoist saw this, he felt love and esteem for them as if they were his own children.

By the power of his mind of loving-kindness, milk spontaneously flowed from the thumbs of both hands to nourish his two sons. As the milk entered their bellies, they became transparent inside and out, like clear water passing through a *maṇi* jewel. The ascetic named the children "Licchavis.

Later, when a cowherd saw that the ascetic was exhausted from nursing the children, he asked for these two boys to provide him with sustenance. Subsequently, these two boys beat the cowherd’s son. The other sons told their parents, "This man who has no parents is beating us! The parents replied, "If someone beats you, you should simply avoid them.

In the Sanskrit language, "Licchavi" means "one who avoids going" (*parivarjayati*); it is also translated as "thin skin" or "similar skin. Later, when they were sixteen years old, they saw that the ground was level and vast, stretching far and wide...

It was one hundred *yojana* in extent. Houses were erected there; men were established as kings and women as queen-consorts. Later, as the number of princes gradually increased, each established his own residence; therefore, it was called the city of Vaiśālī, the dwelling place of the Licchavis.
Licchavi is his clan name; in the original language it is called *Licchavi*, which means "the lineage of King Rishi-datta.
As for the person who initiated this matter:
the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) then imitated him. The Licchavi said, "Venerable sirs, we remain within desire and engage in sexual intercourse."
"Out of desire you have acted; for what purpose did you do this? When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
He rebuked them and established the precept. The formulation of that precept is as follows:
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of new, pure black sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Explanation of the meaning: Regarding "new," the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "New" means not old. If one obtains worn-out black sheep’s wool to make a bedding, there is no offense. Regarding "pure black wool," it refers to either...

"Black" means naturally black or dyed black; "pure" means unmixed. "Goat wool" (*rāṅkava-ūrṇā*): *rāṅku* is the name for a wild mountain sheep. The *Tōngsùwén* states: "The curled wool of a sheep is called *rāṅku*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: [as cited above].

This wool is very precious; one may obtain one *liang* for a single coin, or even two, three, or four coins for one *liang*. However, this wool is extremely fine and soft; when it touches the eyes, no tears are shed. It is exceedingly difficult to obtain, which is why the use of pure black sheep’s wool is not permitted.

Regarding the making of new bedding (according to the *Sarvāstivāda*: the method for making robes from black sheep’s wool also has two types: first, by selecting and processing black wool to weave it into a fine felt).

The second is clothing woven from spun thread. These two types of clothing are both termed *śayanāsana* (reclining and sitting gear); this is the general name for such bedding and seating garments. These three robes made of wool are all to be formally accepted and maintained.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, acting out of a greedy mind for one's own sake;
second, being purely black and unmixed with other motives; and third, the completion of the act.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one makes a new bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool for oneself and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one instructs another to make it and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
It is not accomplished; it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes another to accomplish it, it is not accomplished; it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the forfeiture and confession (*pratyāpatti*) without returning the object, the offense is the same as before. The *Sarvāstivādins* say:
if one makes [a robe] by combining camel hair, ram’s wool, cow hair, or hemp, *karpāsa*, coarse cloth, or *kambala*, all are *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There is no offense if one makes [the robe] for a stūpa or for the Saṃgha. For the four assemblies, including the Bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
this is what constitutes an offense.
Explanatory conditions for non-offense: There is no offense if one obtains a pre-existing [robe], if it has been cut or damaged, or if it is thin and folded.

If it is made in two layers (folding it thinly to form a double layer; this constitutes a small sitting mat and thus does not constitute an offense), or if it is made into a cushion, or a pillow, or a small square sitting mat, or a lying rug, or a cloth to line the interior of an alms bowl, or a razor case, or a hat.
Whether one makes socks, or makes a cloth for removing heat, or makes a cloth for wrapping leather sandals, there is no offense in any of these cases.
There is no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, such as at the very beginning.
○ Thirteenth: General Explanation of the Precept Against Making Bedding with Mixed Colors.
This is a unique precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla). The offenses for nuns differ. It is a shared regulation in the Mahāyāna. It is a regulation of the internal Sangha and provides external protection.
Regarding the censure and the distress, the circumstances are the same as before.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The occasion arose regarding a person.

The group of six monks made new bedding out of pure white sheep’s wool. The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying it resembled that of kings or high ministers (in the Western Regions, white is considered the highest color;
as only kings and high ministers wear it, they said it resembled theirs). When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha, who rebuked them.
The formulation of the precept:
Regarding the characteristics of the established rule, if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts white, and four parts... [gray].
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Explanation of Terms: (The meaning of "black" is as stated above. "White" refers to either naturally white hair or hair that has been dyed white.

"Variegated" (*pāṇḍu*) refers to hair on the head, hair on the ears, or hair on the legs, or any other variegated-colored hair (*pāṇḍu* meaning mixed-color hair). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Coarse and foul" refers to hair on the head, feet, and belly.
The head, feet, and belly are the parts where movement occurs; the wool is coarse and of poor quality.
If one wishes to make a woollen bedding (śayanāsana) of forty *prastha*, twenty *prastha* shall be pure black, ten *prastha* white, and ten *prastha* variegated.
If one wishes to make a bedding of thirty *prastha*, fifteen *prastha* shall be black, seven and a half *prastha* white, and seven and a half *prastha* variegated.
If one makes a bedding (śayanāsana) of twenty *pātra* [of wool], ten *pātra* shall be pure black, five *pātra* white, and five *pātra* variegated (*kalmāṣa*).

(The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One *pātra* is four *liang*. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: 'If one makes a woolen mat of ten *jin*, five *jin* shall be pure black, two and a half *jin* white, and two and a half *jin* coarse.

If there is further increase or decrease, it should be calculated according to this text. That is to say, the ten *jin* of wool are divided into four parts; the pure black portion should consist of two parts, hence it is said "two parts black. The white portion consists of one part, which is the third of the four parts, hence it is so called.)

Three parts are white; the brindled portion also takes up one part, which is the fourth part. Therefore, it is called "four-part brindled" (made according to the regulations). If a bhikṣu does not use the lower [quality], he violates the regulation and commits an offense.
Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, acting out of a greedy mind for one's own sake;
second, exceeding the proper measure of black and white [materials]; and third, the completion of the article.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one makes a new bedding for oneself using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated [wool], it is completed as a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture);
if it is not so completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This applies equally if one causes another to make it.
If it is discarded, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one acts on behalf of another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding discarding, repentance, non-returning, and so forth, the offense incurred is the same as before. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Using black [wool] up to more than one *liang* constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; using white [wool] up to more than one *liang* is a *duṣkṛta*; using variegated [wool]..."
If it is reduced by even one *liang*, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding the two parts [of black wool]:
if one uses mostly black wool but conceives of it as equal, or if one conceives of it as less than equal and then adds more; regarding the third part [of white wool]:
if one uses mostly white wool but conceives of it as equal, or if one conceives of it as less than equal and then adds more; regarding the fourth part: if little inferior wool is used."

One forms the perception that it is equal [to the prescribed measure]. Whether one makes it oneself or instructs another to make it, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; its use constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.

The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Alternatively, if black [wool] is easily obtained while other colors are difficult to find, the number of *karṣa*s may be either reduced or increased, and in both cases the offense is established."
There is no offense [for the monk]. For the bhikṣuṇīs and the three lesser assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);
this is what constitutes an offense. **Exceptions:** There is no offense if: one makes it with two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated;
or if the white is insufficient, one completes it with the variegated; or if one makes it entirely variegated; or if one obtains a pre-made garment and cuts it up to destroy its original form.
If one makes it into a discolored item— whether as a pillow, a felt rug, a mattress, a bedding mat,
a small square sitting cloth, a bowl-cloth, a razor case, socks, a cloth for wiping away heat from tongs,
or a cloth for wrapping sandals— in all such cases there is no offense. There is no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Fourteenth Precept on Bedding and Requisites for Six Years.
This is an exclusive precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla); the offenses for bhikṣuṇīs differ. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna; there, bodhisattvas are required to have few desires and be content.

The mind should have no excessive seeking. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "In order to prevent the use of what is not desired, this training rule was established for those who receive new and fine [robes].
This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].
The group of six monks complained that their bedding was either too heavy or too light, too thin or too thick; they refused to relinquish their old bedding and instead made new ones.
Thus, they constantly sought out bedding and accumulated it in great quantities. When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.

The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept, with the sole exception of the formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma). There was a bhikṣu who contracted the disease of consumption (śoṣa); his excrement...
The bedding and requisites were extremely heavy. Due to a minor circumstance, he wished to travel through the human world, but he was unable to carry them while traveling.

He informed a fellow monk of his intention and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) for him.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat and uses it for six years or less than six years, and without discarding the old one, he makes another new one—
except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma)— it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Exegesis: Making new bedding and keeping it for six years (*Saṃghāṭī* says: "Making" means either making it oneself or having someone else make it; "new" means when first completed; *Vinayaviniścaya* says:

"Keeping it for six years" means that even if one does not wish to keep it, one must still fulfill the full six years). Except by *saṃgha-karman* (the *Sarvāstivāda* says: "Once the *saṃgha-karman* has been performed, one may request clothing and requisites from a donor to make robes;
the essence of this precept is to sever excessive greed and excessive accumulation).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, acting out of a greedy mind for one's own sake;
second, the garment being less than six years old; third, not relinquishing the old while making a new one; and fourth, the completion of the new garment.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one makes a new bedding while not relinquishing the old bedding for less than six years, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense of forfeiture and confession) once it is completed.
If it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If one causes another to make it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
It is not accomplished; it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one acts on behalf of another, whether it is accomplished or not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the forfeiture, confession, non-return, and so forth, the offense is the same as before. As for the essence of this precept:

once the robe has been made, within six years one must not beg from a donor for wool, thread, or various other requisites for making robes. One should make a robe of the proper measure, according to the weaving.

[End. Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture): the *Sarvāstivāda* school states that if one makes [a robe] from cloth and materials belonging to oneself, or if one makes it from cloth and materials purchased, there is no offense in either case.
The *Mahāsāṃghika* school states that one should personally record [the details], for otherwise the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) will be lost.

The Opening of the Circumstances; those who do not incur an offense: when the Saṃgha has granted permission, or when six years have been completed; when one discards an old [robe] before the six years are up and makes a new one;

This training rule was established to prevent a mind of contempt and disdain.

while the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he sent someone to accept an invitation for a meal. It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that the bhikṣus accept such invitations.

When a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he should take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and attach it to the top of the new one for the purpose of discoloring it;

"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and patch it onto the new one."

Above. Because it is a dyed color. If one makes a new sitting mat, one must not take a piece from an old one measuring even one span in length and breadth and paste it onto the new one for the purpose of achieving a dyed color; [if one does so], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one makes a new sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one must take a piece from an old one; to do otherwise constitutes an offense against the established rule.

If one acts on behalf of another, whether the work is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the forfeiture, confession, non-returning, and so forth, the offenses incurred are as stated above.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one takes [the material] less than half an inch, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If it has been separated for a night, there is no need for forfeiture; one should simply perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. This is comparable.
For a bhikṣuṇī and the three groups of novices, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

This is called an offense. **Exemptions:** It is not an offense in the following cases: if one cuts off a worn-out portion; if one patches a new piece over an old one because the original has faded in color;

If one acts [in this manner], there is no offense. One who commits no offense refers to those before the precept was first established, and so forth.
○ A general explanation of the sixteenth precept: carrying wool over three *yojanas*.
This is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*). The offenses for nuns differ; in the Mahāyāna, they are studied together. One should cease worldly censure and increase the pure faith of others.
The *Vinayaviniscaya* states: "Because of [the occurrence of] censure, this training rule was established."
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].

Bhadananda obtained some sheep’s wool, threaded it onto the end of a staff, and carried it along the road. A lay devotee criticized and disparaged him, asking, "How can the Śākya son, a śramaṇa, engage in the trade of selling sheep’s wool?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu traveling on a road obtains wool and there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three yojanas.
If there is no one to carry it and he carries it himself beyond three yojanas, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
**Exegesis:** If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road or at a residence and obtains wool, he may take it if he requires it.
If there is no one to carry it (meaning no *kappiya-kāraka* or lay follower, etc.), he may carry it himself for up to three *yojanas*.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, three *yojanas* consists of five-cubit bows; two thousand such bows make one *krośa*; four thousand bows make half a *yojana*; eight thousand bows make one *yojana*; sixteen thousand bows make two *yojanas*; and twenty-four thousand bows constitute three *yojanas*.
Carrying it oneself for up to three *yojanas*. If there is someone else carrying it, one should say to that person: "I now have this object;
you should assist me in carrying it as far as that place. During this interval, the bhikṣu must not assist in carrying it himself.
If there is no one to carry it and he lowers it [himself], he commits an offense by transgression of the rule.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, a greedy mind that carries a heavy load;
second, the wool being carried; and third, carrying it beyond the prescribed limit.
**The Determination of the Offense:** In this context, the offense for one who carries [wool] over three *yojanas* is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If someone assists another in carrying it over three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes any of the other four assemblies to carry it over three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This excludes wool; if one carries other *kuccara* materials, such as milk, leaves, grass, and so forth, there is no offense.
If one travels more than three *yojanas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, if one carries other objects attached to the tip of a staff while walking, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the forfeiture and confession (*pratyāpatti*) for not returning the object, the offense is the same as before. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:

"Once the [object] has been placed on the ground at the distance of three *yojanas*, if one moves it by flicking it with a staff or rolling it with the foot, once it has exceeded three *yojanas*, it is all forfeited."
It is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense [if one carries it] for two or three *yojanas*. If there is danger from tigers, wolves, or bandits, one may carry it out for three *yojanas*;

this constitutes a full relinquishment (*niḥsarga*). If, within three *yojanas*, one is robbed by bandits, and after being robbed, the item is returned to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu may again carry it for three *yojanas* without committing an offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) carry it. If...

If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), it is permitted to carry [the wool] oneself. However, one must not carry it on the head, wear it on the back, or bear it on the shoulders;

one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mātṛkā* states: "If a bhikṣu carries wool through the air, whether he carries it himself or has a *nirmāṇa-puruṣa* (an emanated person) carry it, in both cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī and the three lesser assemblies [of śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās], it is also a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is meant."
**Offense.** **Exceptions:** There is no offense if one carries it for three *yojanas* or less than three *yojanas*;

or if someone gives it to the carrier and instructs them to carry it as far as a certain place, provided that the carrier does not assist in carrying it further along the way; or if [the carrier is] acting as an agent.
The fourfold assembly of nuns may carry [these items] for a distance of three *yojanas*. This applies to woolen rugs (made of animal hair), woolen cords, or the hair from the head, neck, or legs;
as well as when making hats, tweezers, or hot-cloth headwraps, or when wrapping up leather sandals. In all such cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Seventeenth Precept Regarding a Bhikṣuṇī Dyeing Sheep’s Wool.

This is a precept not shared [with the bhikṣus]. The regulations for bhikṣuṇīs differ; it is studied in common with the Mahāyāna. As the Dharma-vehicle reaches the age of the Semblance and Final Dharma, one should appropriately...

To avoid the reproach of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and to sever all worldly contact with the dust of nunnery life, the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because the correct practice was being neglected, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The Setting of the Discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākya. (Śākya refers to the Śākya clan; this means "the abode of the Capable One.

Kapilavastu is a corruption; it should be called Kapilavāstu. *Kapila* here means "yellow," and *vāstu* means "place of reliance. In ancient times, there was a seer named Kapila who relied upon this [site].)

The Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*) states: "Kapilavastu. *Kapila* is also the name of a rishi. Because the rishi Kapila sprinkled water to establish a boundary and thereby founded a city, it is called *Kapilavastu*.

*Vastu* is a Sanskrit term meaning "city" in this language. It is also called *Kāpilavastu*, or *Kāśī*; the latter means "Red Marsh. Zhu Falan said to Emperor Ming of the Han: "Kāpilavastu is the center of the great trichiliocosm.

On the day of the summer solstice, there is still residual shadow in this land, whereas in India there is none; therefore, it is called the center of the great trichiliocosm. Regarding *Nyagrodha*: in the Western Regions, this refers to the *nyagrodha* tree, which is the willow or poplar of the Eastern Land (China). Although the names differ, the trees are the same.

Their substance is one and the same. Western monks pointed to willows to explain the intended meaning of the original term. Later, Eastern monks went there and recognized that the *nyagrodha* was the willow of the Eastern Land (China). Thus, the dialectical differences between the two lands were simultaneously and thoroughly understood. This garden is located three or four *li* south of the city of Rājagṛha.

After the Tathāgata attained enlightenment and returned to his kingdom, he sent a messenger to inform his father, the King, that the Tathāgata would not reside in the royal palace. Thereupon, he constructed sixteen great vihāras in this garden; including the smaller ones, there were sixty-four in total.

Within each courtyard, there were multi-storied pavilions, exactly like those in the Jeta Grove, without any difference. The Buddha resided therein and converted the eight princes as well as five hundred members of the Śākya clan. Because the name was derived from the trees, it is called [the Nyagrodha Garden].
At the Nyagrodha Park. Regarding the origin of the rule:
the group of six monks took sheep’s wool and made new sitting mats, having the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī [prepare them].

[The nuns] were stained; their hands were soiled with dye (some say *Gautamī*, which is her clan name; some say *Kauṭamī*; others say *Gopī*—all of these being feminine vocatives. If spoken in the masculine, it is *Gautama*, which means "Supreme on Earth").
She went to pay homage to the World-Honored One. The Buddha questioned her and learned the reason for this. He rebuked the group of six [monks] and established a precept.
"One must not have bhikṣuṇīs wash, dye, or card wool. The bhikṣus, being doubtful, did not dare to have their own relatives—bhikṣuṇīs—wash, dye, or card it.
The Buddha said: 'I allow that those who are relatives may wash, dye, and card it. The precept should be recited in this manner.'"
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Explanation of Terms: Washing, Dyeing, and Carding Wool. (As for "washing," it refers even to soaking once in water; as for "dyeing," it refers even to a single person's application of dye-liquid; as for "carding," it refers even to carding a single piece.)
Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, acting out of a greedy mind for one's own sake;
second, the nun being unrelated by kinship; and third, performing the act exactly as instructed.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one causes her to wash, dye, and card, but she only washes and dyes without carding; or if she only washes and cards without dyeing;
or if she only dyes and cards without washing—in all such cases, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*. If one causes [her to do so]...

Washing, dyeing, and carding: if one does not wash, dye, or card [the robe], there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses. If one causes a non-relative *śikṣamāṇā* or *śrāmaṇerī* to wash, dye, or card it, there is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding the forfeiture and confession (*pratyāpatti*) and the failure to return [the object], the offense is the same as before.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, if one causes a robe belonging to the Saṃgha to be washed or dyed, there is a *duṣkṛta*. [This applies to] a bhikṣu.
For a nun and the three groups of minor nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is what constitutes a transgression. Regarding the exceptions:
there is no offense if one causes a relative nun to wash, dye, or card [wool]; or if one washes, dyes, or cards for the sake of a sick person;

or if one washes, dyes, or cards for the sake of the Saṃgha, the Buddha, or a stūpa. There is no offense in these cases. Furthermore, there is no offense for those who have not yet received the precepts.

Regarding cases where the precepts have not yet been established (Question: When a nun washes or dyes monastic property, the *Śāstra* concludes that an offense is incurred, whereas the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states there is no offense. From which of these two principles should one follow? Answer: If she pretends to wash or dye monastic property for her own sake, she should be judged according to the *Śāstra* and the offense incurred.
If her mind is truly for the sake of the Saṃgha, one should follow the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which permits it).
The *Sārvastivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* explains in detail: "The formulation of the precepts is for the sake of the *adhikaraṇa-dharma* (the dharma of superior excellence).

If the community of bhikṣuṇīs were to persist in performing laundry and dyeing, they would neglect their primary duties; consequently, they would lack majestic virtue and destroy the *adhikaraṇa-dharma*."
Furthermore, this precept is established to cease unwholesome dharmas through their sequential causes and conditions, and to ensure that both divisions of the Saṃgha each maintain purity.
○ The Eighteenth Precept: Receiving Gold and Silver.

General Explanation: This is a common precept; the regulations for bhikṣuṇīs are likewise the same. In the Mahāyāna, the regulations differ: for the sake of sentient beings, it is permitted to accept [money].
However, a *śuddhakarmakara* (pure person) must handle and keep it. If no pure person is available, one may hold it oneself provided that the mind remains free from attachment.

If one greedily keeps [the item] for oneself, this constitutes excessive desire and a lack of contentment; this is termed a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*). This is a proscribed offense (*prajñapti-śikṣāpada*).
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because it gave rise to public censure and suspicion, this training rule was established."
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain. In the city, there was a high minister who was a close friend and acquaintance of Upananda.
Having obtained a large quantity of pork, he instructed his wife to set aside a portion for him. At that time, there was a festival in the city.
On that day, they performed various musical entertainments and did not sleep at all throughout the night. The minister’s son was also among them;
he too did not sleep at all through the night and, becoming weary, asked his mother, "Is there any meat remaining? His mother replied, "There is only the portion belonging to Baddhananda left.
The son gave money to his mother and instructed her, "Use this money to buy more meat for Baddhananda, and give me this [remaining] meat. His mother then...
He took the money and the meat.
Then, the man who had been incited rose up.
In the early morning, Baddhālī went to the house of a high minister. The minister’s wife fully informed him of the aforementioned matter. Baddhālī...
He said, "If you give me money for my sake, I do not need meat. [The man] then placed the money on the ground and gave it to him.

When Bhadanta received the money, he took it and went to the market. The lay devotees criticized and disparaged him. At that time, the king and his various ministers were assembled together and spoke thus:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are permitted to handle gold, silver, and coins; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not renounce gold."
There was a great minister named Muktika who possessed silver coins, precious gems, and pearl necklaces. He addressed the other ministers, saying:
"Do not speak such words, claiming that the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas may handle gold and silver coins or fail to renounce precious gems and pearl necklaces.
Why is this? I have heard directly from the Tathāgata that the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas must not handle gold and silver."

"Money! Having renounced precious jewels and pearl necklaces, the minister Maṇicūḍa, who possesses great power and is skilled in discourse, has caused all the ministers to rejoice, believe, and understand.
He went to inform the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One praised his words, saying they were of great benefit.
'Minister, you should know that the sun and moon have four afflictions: they are not bright, not pure, and cannot illuminate anything.'"
Nor do they possess majestic power. What are these four? They are the smoke, clouds, dust, and mist of the asuras. These are the great afflictions of the sun and moon.

(When the asuras fight with the devas, the devas use the sun and moon as their banners. By the majesty of the sun and moon, the devas always prevail over them. The asuras are constantly angry at the sun and moon and desire to destroy them.

However, due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, they cannot destroy them despite exhausting all their wisdom and arts; they can only obstruct them with their hands, causing them to temporarily vanish. There are likewise four [afflictions] for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
It is afflicted by being unclear, impure, unable to illuminate anything, and lacking majestic power. What are these four? Not abandoning the drinking of alcohol;
not abandoning sexual desire; not abandoning the holding of gold and silver in one's hands; and not abandoning wrong livelihood for one’s own sustenance.
These are the four great afflictions. A bhikṣu of few desires addressed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept. The formulated characteristics of the precept are as follows:
if a bhikṣu takes money in his own hand, or gold and silver, or instructs another to take them, or accepts them by placing them on the ground, [he commits an offense]. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sāgghi-pāyattika). Explanation of the meaning:
"To take money with one's own hand" (*saṃghī-vinaya*). [The *Mahāsāṃghika* states: "With one's own hand" means: either the body itself, a part of the body, or what is connected to the body.

"The body" refers to the entire body. "A part of the body" refers to the hand, foot, elbow, or knee. "What is connected to the body" refers to the *saṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, *antarvāsa*, *vraṇapaṭṭaka*, *saṃkakṣikā*, *varṣāśāṭī*, or within the bowl, sub-bowl, or *kañcaka*. This is called...

The continuity of the body is all called "one's own hand. As for the coin: upon it there are inscribed figures (the outer circle representing Heaven and the inner square representing Earth, with the name of the state situated between them, thereby embodying the three powers of Heaven, Earth, and Man).

Combined, they form an image; hence it is said that there are "inscribed images" above [the ground], which correspond to what is used in various lands). Regarding gold and silver: the *Fanyi jijing* states that the Sanskrit term is *suvarṇa*, or *suvarṇaka*, which translates here as "gold.

(The remainder is no different from the rules regarding extra robes.
If one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense but does not relinquish the bowl, and instead exchanges it for another bowl, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the abandonment of the confession without returning [the object], the offense is the same as before. The *Vinayasamgraha* states:

"If it is less than the prescribed measure, or if it exceeds the measure, or if one intends to give it to another person for their ordination (*upasampadā*) so as to provide for their needs—even if one does not specifically designate it as such—there is no offense.
The third section states: "A small bowl made of bronze (*kāṃsī*) and a secondary bowl are permitted to be kept without having to perform the ritual of pure giving (*pariśuddha-dāna*)."
The Sarvāstivādins say: If one keeps an extra white iron bowl or an unbaked clay bowl that is not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three junior groups [śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: if one performs a formal act of purification (*pariṣkāra-dāna*) within ten days;

if one gives it away to another; if one perceives it as having been plundered or lost; if one perceives it as broken or swept away; or if one takes and uses a bowl that has been seized, lost, burned, or swept away.

If another has already used it, or if the bowl was received as a deposit, or if the bhikṣu dies, travels far away, ceases his religious life, or is harmed by thieves or wild beasts, and thus does not hand it over to someone else, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-second Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Seeking a Fine Almsbowl.
This is a shared precept; nuns likewise incur the same offense. It is also established in the Mahāyāna. It serves to cultivate few desires and contentment, and to quell the world’s censure.

[This is] censured. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of a mind of greedy attachment, afflictions increase and one incurs the reproach of others; therefore, this training rule was established.
This is the origin story (*nidāna*).
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The occasion arose concerning Upananda:
his bowl having broken, he entered the city and begged for a bowl from various householders; he broke one bowl after another, seeking many more.
[The Buddha] permitted the keeping of many bowls. On another occasion, various lay devotees gathered in one place and each said, "I have now obtained immeasurable merit.

They asked one another [about their acquisitions], and all together they criticized and disparaged [the monks]. A monk of few desires reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept.
The established rule regarding the characteristics of the bowl:
If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five patches and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; the Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among those present and give it to him.
One should maintain it; even when it is torn, one should maintain it.
