This is the proper time. Explanation of the meaning: "Five patches" refers to the intervals between them being two finger-widths apart. One patch (a "patch" means a connection or mending). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Fewer than five patches..."

If there is one patch, and its size is less than five [finger-breadths], this is called "deficient. If there are two patches, up to five patches, and their size is less than five [finger-breadths], this is called "deficient. One who has five full patches means that the number of patches is already five and their size is also full; this is called "full.

If there are four, three, two, or one patch, or if there are no patches at all but the size is full, this is called "full five. Regarding the measurement of a patch: the distance between the openings of the patches must be sufficient for one thumb.

"Without leakage" means that the measurement of the patches is not deficient and furthermore, there is no seepage. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "It is permitted to use iron or copper for patching. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* says: "If a bowl is difficult to obtain, repair it as you wish. If it is easy to obtain, you may discard it and seek another good one. Seek again.

One obtains a new bowl for the sake of its excellence (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Or because one finds this bowl too large, too small, too heavy, too light, too coarse, or too rough; thus it is said 'for the sake of its excellence'").
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of four conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a mind of covetous desire for something fine.

Second, one must beg from a householder who is not a relative. Third, the amount requested must be less than the standard measure and not leak away. Fourth, the request must be fulfilled and the object obtained.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bowl has been broken and has fewer than five patches yet remains leak-proof, and one seeks a new bowl, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If it has five full patches and is leak-proof, yet one seeks a new bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This must be forfeited;
as for this forfeiture, it is to be forfeited before the Saṃgha at that residence. The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one begs..."
If one obtains many bowls, one should relinquish those that one is personally attached to or delights in; the remainder should be given to those of like mind.

Once they have been relinquished and the transgression confessed, the Saṃgha should return the bowls to that bhikṣu. If these bowls are of high value or of fine quality, they should be set aside, and the most inferior and substandard ones should be given to him.
Regarding the rules for relinquishment, confession, non-return, and so forth, the offense incurred is the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This..."

A bhikṣu who maintains the Vinaya and knows the *karmavācanā*, and who has accomplished five qualities, should be requested by the Saṃgha to be appointed as the person who distributes the bowls (*pātradhara*).
What are these five? He is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, without delusion, and he knows what has been given and what has not been given.
These are called the five. He should be appointed through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) with the following proclamation: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! [Name]..."
When a bhikṣu has accomplished five qualities, if the time is right for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha shall appoint such-and-such a bhikṣu as the bowl-distributor (*pātradhāraka*).
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*); the ritual procedure (*karman*) follows accordingly. The one performing the *karman* should announce it within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Let all those who possess bowls bring them here. If he does not so announce, he commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vyatikrama-vinayāpatti*). All...
The bhikṣus should each bring the bowl they themselves habitually use.
If a bhikṣu discards the bowl he previously used and instead brings a lower-quality bowl, he commits a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. The Vinaya states:
That bhikṣu’s bowl should be formally announced (*jñapti*) and presented to the Saṃgha. The announcement is made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. If..."
The Saṃgha’s time has come. May the Saṃgha listen with patience. This bowl shall be offered to the Elder in turn.
Having made this announcement, one should hold it out to the Elder. If the Elder wishes to take this bowl, he should give his own bowl to the next seat.
If it is given to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should accept it; he must not withhold it from the community.
The Saṃgha therefore did not accept it. Furthermore, one should not, on account of this cause, accept and keep the lowest bowl; if one accepts it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the second senior monk takes this bowl, he should take the bowl of the second senior monk and give it to the third senior monk.
If he gives it to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should accept it; he should not refuse it out of regard for the Saṃgha.
One must not accept it. Nor, for this reason, should one accept or keep a bowl of the lowest quality; if one accepts it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
In this manner, passing it along in succession until it reaches a junior monk, if that junior monk holds the bowl of this [original] monk, he shall return it to him.

If one gives [the bowl] by means of the very lowest-ranking seat-bowl, at the time of giving it, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). It should be given in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now give this very lowest-ranking seat-bowl..."
"I entrust this to Bhikṣu [Name] to receive and maintain it, until it is broken. The formal motion (*jñapti*) is thus; the ritual procedure (*karman*) follows accordingly.
That bhikṣu must guard this bowl: he must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it, nor should he place it beneath a leaning staff.
One must not place [the bowl] beneath a hanging knife, nor beneath a suspended object, nor in the middle of a path, nor upon a stone, nor beneath a fruit tree, nor on uneven ground.
One must not hold two bowls with one hand, except when the fingers are separated by the space between them.
One must not hold a bowl with one hand while opening both doors, except when doing so with focused mindfulness.
One must not place [the bowl] inside the threshold or beneath the door leaf. One must not hold the bowl and place it beneath a rope bed or a wooden bed, except for temporary placement.
One must not place it between a rope bed and a wooden bed. One must not place it on the corner of a rope bed or a wooden bed, except for temporary placement.
One must not stand and shake the bowl, even to the point of causing it to break. That bhikṣu...

One should intentionally break the bowl; one should not intentionally cause it to be lost. If it is intentionally broken, it must not be used for anything other than a bowl. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"This bowl should not be kept as a formal possession (*parigraha*), nor should it be formally designated (*paricchinna*). It should also not be given away. One should keep two bowl-sacks:
place the fine bowl in the long sack, and place the old bowl in the inferior sack. When going on alms-round, one should take them along."
Regarding the two alms bowls: if one obtains dry rice, it should be placed in the extra bowl; if one obtains moist rice, it should be placed in the old bowl. One should eat from the old bowl.
First, wash the extra bowl, dry it in the sun, and set it aside; in all matters, the extra bowl takes precedence.
When placing it in the storage case or when fumigating it with incense, always place the extra bowl first in a superior location. When traveling on a journey, send the old bowl ahead.
If one carries [the bowl], one should carry the extra bowl oneself. If there is no one to hold it for one, the extra bowl should be placed on the left side and the old bowl placed on the right side;
then one should go while carrying them oneself. This disciplinary rule applies until the end of one's life or until the bowl breaks; it should be properly maintained.
One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If this bhikṣu who carries the mended bowl..."

Therefore, to break it [the bowl] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Alternatively, if two teachers, spiritual friends, or others, out of pity for him, hide the bowl because they believe its washing hinders his progress on the Path, and he does not see it and subsequently begs for another one, there is no offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is what is called an offense.
The Explanatory Circumstances for Non-Offense: There is no offense if the bowl has five patches or more; or if it has fewer than five patches and one seeks a new bowl;
or if one asks for it from a relative; or if one asks for it from a renunciant; or if one seeks it for another; or if another seeks it for oneself; or if one obtains it without having asked;
or if one receives a bowl when it is being distributed to the Saṃgha according to seniority; or if one purchases and keeps one with one's own funds.
There is no offense in all cases. Those who do not commit an offense include those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.
○ A general explanation of the twenty-third precept: the precept against having a non-relative weave a robe.
This is a common precept; the formulation for nuns is likewise the same. In the Mahāyāna, because of [the concern for] sentient beings, the trainings differ.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because disturbing others and giving rise to censure, this training rule was established."
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
Desiring to sew a saṃghāṭī robe, Upāli’s brother, Bhadanta, entered the city and went to the houses of various lay devotees, where he begged for thread and obtained some.
He had much [thread] and thought to himself, "I might seek thread elsewhere to sew a saṃghāṭī.
The bhikṣu said, "Robes are difficult to obtain; one must prepare the three robes. I would rather weave the three robes myself now.
He then took the thread and went to a weaver. That weaver spun the yarn by hand and supervised the weaving himself. The laypeople criticized and disparaged him for his stinginess.
The monks who desired [to hear] heard this and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked them and established the precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows: If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave three robes for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Śaikṣa Dharma*: Explanation of the Meaning.
"Requests for oneself" means requesting [thread] from various places for one's own sake. "Thread" refers to ten kinds, as described above regarding the ten kinds of cloth-thread.
"The weaver is not a relative" means that the person who gives the thread is not a relative.
If the weaver is not a relative but the one who provides the thread is a relative; or if the weaver is a relative but the one who provides the thread is not a relative;
or if the one who provides the thread is not a relative while the weaver is a relative—in all such cases, there is an offense.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, one must personally beg for the material out of a greedy mind.
Second, a person who is not a relative must weave it. Third, the robe must be woven and completed.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one personally begs for thread and has a weaver weave it into a robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one supervises the weaving, or if one winds the thread by hand oneself, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. As for the confession of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika-pratideśanā*), the robe must not be returned [to the original owner]. Etc.
The offense is the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one personally goes to beg for thread, it is a *vyatikrama-citta-kaukṛtya* (an offense of transgression with mental regret).

If one obtains [the thread], it is a *vyatikrama-āpatti* (an offense of transgression). If it is woven into cloth, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If one pays a price for it to be woven, there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one weaves it oneself, or causes the five groups of monastics to weave it, in all cases it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."
If, for the sake of having no clothes, one begs thread from a person who is not a relative with the intention of making a robe, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has few clothes, one should properly beg for cloth; one should not beg for thread to make a robe. If thread is required to sew a belt, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three lesser groups [bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances for Non-offense: There is no offense if the weaver is a relative; if the one who provides the thread is a relative;

or if one weaves it oneself to make a bowl bag, a needle-case, or a felt mat; or if one makes a meditation belt (the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states: "The Buddha permitted sick monks in the waist region to possess a meditation belt, as was the case for the sake of Śāriputra").

It is permitted to keep three kinds of belts: belts woven from cord, braided belts, and belts made of woolen cord. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if made wide, it must not exceed eight finger-breadths; if made narrow, it should not be less than five finger-breadths. It should be made of a single color and not of variegated colors.

The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* states that, with the exception of brocade and high-quality white leather, all other materials may be used to make a belt. When sitting, one should use it to bind oneself. The method for making the belt is as follows: its width is one span (*vitasti*), and its length is according to the measurement of one's own body. It is also called the "leaning belt" (*niśraya-bandha*).
If one makes a waistband, a cap, socks, tongs, a cloth for wrapping, or a cloth for leather sandals, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept had not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.

The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Different Schools) explains in detail: This precept was established in order to eliminate unwholesome dharmas, to stop slander, and to perfect the noble lineage.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-fourth Precept: Seeking Fine Cloth from Weavers.
This is a shared precept; nuns are equally liable for its violation. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. It refers to seeking improperly or seeking excessively.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "This training rule was established because it incurs worldly reproach. This precept is formulated based on two conditions.
Regarding the setting of the origin: the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. There was a householder who was an acquaintance of Upananda; he brought out some fine thread.
He had a weaver weave it, intending to give such a robe as this to the person who provided the occasion.
The weaver said to Upananda, and Upananda replied, "If you weave for me, it must be vast and of the highest quality."
"It is firm and fine; I shall accept it myself. The weaver said, "The thread is insufficient. Upāli (Vaddhananda) went to the householder's home and asked for more thread.
The householder’s wife brought out a box of thread and selected the finest pieces at will to give to the weaver.
The weaver said, "The price is too low. She replied, "Just weave it for me, and I shall pay you further. The householder followed her lead.
Upon returning home, he saw that the robe was not the one he had previously ordered to be woven. When he inquired and learned the reason, he became critical and disparaging.

A bhikṣu of few desires heard of this and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept (the wording of which is as follows, except for the phrase regarding the invitation at the end of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony).

There was a householder who, having been invited at the *pravāraṇā*, offered a robe to a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu, being hesitant, did not dare accept it. The householder then wished to give the bhikṣu a robe of high value.
Regarding robes: if a bhikṣu is of few desires and knows contentment, and wishes to obtain one that is inferior [to what he already has], he may hesitate and not dare to ask for it. The Buddha said:
"If one has previously accepted an invitation for self-indulgence (pavāraṇā), there is no offense. The precept should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:

if a monk has a householder or a householder’s wife send a weaver to weave a robe for him, and that monk, having not previously received a formal invitation, goes to the weaver’s place and says, "Weave this robe for me; give it to me."
"It is very fine weaving; make it broad, large, and firm, and I shall give you a small amount of payment.
If that bhikṣu gives him payment—even the value of a single meal—and [the weaver] obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
**Exegesis:** "A householder or householder’s wife commissions the weaving of robes" (the following clarifies the donor’s motivation arising behind the scenes).
"That bhikṣu has not previously received a formal invitation" (this clarifies his fondness for luxury and excessive desire). "This robe is being made for me;

weave it for me with the utmost care, making it broad, large, firm, and dense. (Regarding "with the utmost care": this means requiring even greater refinement and luster; when weaving, one beats the threads extremely hard to make them firm, dense, and secure.)

"Extremely fine weaving" is the general heading; "vast, firm, and exquisite" is the specific explanation. "I shall give you a small amount of payment" (a small amount means from one coin up to ten or a hundred;

"payment" refers to gold, silver, coins, jewels, and so forth); "even down to the value of a single meal" (this signifies the absolute minimum; it means providing the laborer with the wage for even the least amount of work, namely one meal).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of four conditions to constitute the full offense. First, having much desire and a fondness for fine clothing;
second, the weaver being a householder who is not a relative; third, encouraging the weaving while promising payment; and fourth, obtaining the garment and it coming into one's possession.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one goes to seek robes without first having accepted an invitation for *pravāraṇā*, and if robes are obtained, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture);
if none are obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The offenses regarding forfeiture, confession, and non-returning are the same as previously stated.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one merely goes to exhort [the donor] and obtains robes without being permitted to pay a price, it is a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline)."
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; for the three smaller assemblies [of śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense. The exceptions: It is not an offense if one goes to seek [food] after having previously accepted an invitation to a *pravāraṇā*;

if one seeks with moderation and in reduced measure; if one requests from a relative; if one requests from a renunciant; if it is for the sake of another; if another acts on one's behalf; or if one does not request at all.
...and thus obtains [the robe], there is no offense. One who commits no offense includes those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-fifth Precept: Taking Robes Out of Anger.

This is a common precept; nuns likewise commit the same offense. It is equally prescribed in the Mahāyāna: for those on the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*), the mind of relinquishment is primary;

for those on the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is foremost. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "On account of the matter of taking robes, one cannot endure their neglect or deficiency."
This training rule was established due to the affliction of disparagement.
As for the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The person who initiated the occasion was Nanda’s disciple, who was skilled at exhortation and conversion (Nanda was the elder brother of Upananda. He had a core resident disciple named Dharma, who constantly harbored a sense of shame).

With a mind of remorse, he took delight in and respected the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), and was well able to exhort and transform others. When Upananda wished to travel through the human world together [with others], he first gave his robe to them.
Other bhikṣus said to him, "Upananda is a fool; he does not know how to recite the precepts, he does not know how to proclaim the precepts, and he does not know the *poṣadha* ritual.
Later, at another time, Upananda wished to travel through the human world together [with others].
He did not comply with his instructions and instead demanded back the robe he had previously given, refusing to return it. Baddhālīputra became enraged and forcibly seized the robe.
The bhikṣu cried out, "Do not do this! Other bhikṣus from neighboring rooms heard the commotion and gathered there;
having learned the cause of the dispute, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the offense:
if a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying, "Give me back my robe;
I will not give it to you," and that bhikṣu returns the robe and he takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Exegesis: Regarding "ill will" (the *Mahāsāṃghika* says: ill will is displeasure; it refers to the nine grounds for resentment). If one seizes [the robe] oneself, or instructs another to seize it, saying, "Give me back my robe;

I will not give it to you" (*seizing* means taking by force; whether seizing with the hand, seizing with the mouth, or seizing with both hand and mouth—this refers to when there was originally an expectation that the robe would be given, but because that intention was not fulfilled, one instead seizes it back).
If the bhikṣu returns the robe and the other takes the robe (the offense is established as soon as the robe enters his hand).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept is completed as a full offense when three conditions are met: first, the person has not been subdued;
second, one takes it away out of anger; and third, the robe is separated from that person's body and has been lifted up.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one seizes it oneself, or instructs another to seize it, and takes it to hide or store it away, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one seizes it but does not hide or store it away, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This applies equally if it is placed upon a tree or beneath a wall.
On a fence, on a stake, on a dragon-tooth peg, on a clothing rack, on a rope bed, on a wooden bed, or on small or large cushions;
or on a table, or on the ground—having taken [an item] and moved it from its place, there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one does not move it from its place, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the forfeiture, confession, and non-returning, the offenses are the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Taking by combining what was given separately; taking separately what was given combined; taking by combining what was given combined;
and taking separately what was given separately. Regarding "taking separately": one incurs numerous *pāyattikas*. Regarding "taking by combining": one incurs one *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, when giving a robe to another bhikṣu, says: "I will give it to you if you stay by my side; if you do not stay, I shall take it back."
If it accords with your wishes, I shall give it; if it does not accord with your wishes, I shall take it back. I shall give it to one who receives the scriptures;
I shall take it back from one who does not receive the scriptures. In all these cases, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu has sold a robe but has not yet received the payment, or if the price in money has not been finalized, and he takes the robe back, there is no offense. If he seizes the robe of a layperson, it is a *vibhaṅga* (offense of wrong-doing).
The nun felt remorse in her heart. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To seize the robes of the fourfold assembly constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

As for the essence of this precept: if a bhikṣu first gives his own robe to another and subsequently, out of a desire to cause distress, temporarily takes it back by force, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

If one gives away a robe and returns it to another, it is a *pāyattika* offense requiring confession. If one first gives a robe to another with the fundamental intention [of relinquishing it], and later takes it back with the fundamental intention [of reclaiming it], one must calculate its value;

if the value is reached, the offense of theft is established. (Regarding "giving with the fundamental intention": this means giving the robe to the other with a sincere intent, not giving it while harboring expectations. Regarding "taking back with the fundamental intention": this indicates taking it back, not merely seizing it temporarily for the sake of discipline.

Regarding "the offense is established by calculating the value": this refers to the value reaching five *kārsāpaṇas*, at which point the offense of theft is established. If one first lends a robe to another temporarily and subsequently takes it back, there is no offense.
It is an offense. If the preceptor temporarily seizes the robe from a disciple for the purpose of subduing them so that they may abandon unwholesome dharmas, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Exception: There is no offense in the following cases: if one does not speak with anger, saying, "I regret it; I will not give you the robe. Give me my robe back";
or if that person, knowing the other's heart has changed, immediately returns the robe; or if another person says, "This bhikṣu wishes to repent and return the robe to him";
or if one borrows another's robe to wear and there is no reason for the owner to take it back by force. If [any of these apply], there is no offense.

If there is fear that the robe will be lost; or if there is fear that it will be damaged; or if the person has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their decorum; or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*);

or if they have been expelled (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), or are subject to expulsion; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life—in such cases, taking [the robe] away without storing it or handing it over is not an offense.
It is not an offense in cases such as when the rule had not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-sixth Precept Regarding Medicines Stored Beyond Seven Days.
This is a common precept; nuns likewise incur the offense. Mahayana bhikṣus study this together [with the Hinayana]. This is an offense by formal decree (prajñapti-āpatti).
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "This training rule was established because of the affliction of greed regarding matters of medicine for illness.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. During the autumn months, the wind-disorders of various bhikṣus were aggravated, and their bodies became withered and parched."
A malignant ulcer developed. The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to take five kinds of medicine at both the proper and improper times;
these should be treated as food or medicine and not allowed to appear coarse.
This was the occasion for establishing the rule.

Pilindavatsa (translated here as "Vestiges of Habit"). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: This elder was constantly afflicted by eye pain. When he went to beg for alms, he would always cross the Ganges. Upon reaching the banks of the Ganges, he would snap his fingers and say, "Little maid, stop the flow!

The water would then part on both sides, allowing him to cross and beg for alms. A deity of the Ganges went to inform the Buddha that a disciple of the Buddha frequently reviled her, saying, "Little maid, stop the flow! The Buddha said, "Pilindavatsa, offer an apology to the deity of the Ganges."

He immediately joined his palms and said to the goddess Gaṅgā, "Little maid, I beg your pardon. At that time, the great assembly laughed at him, saying, "How can you apologize and yet still insult her?

The Buddha said to the goddess Gaṅgā, "Do you see how he joined his palms and apologized? This apology was free of arrogance; as for these words of his, you should know they were not malicious. For five hundred lifetimes, this man has always been born into Brahmin families and has always been self-conceited and noble, looking down upon others.

This is merely a habit of speech from his past, not a matter of a proud heart. The *Sūtra on Endowed with Virtue* says: "One who is able to practice compassion amidst suffering—this is Pindola Bharadvāja. He resided in the city of Rājagṛha and was widely known. Furthermore...
There was a large assembly of followers who obtained great quantities of ghee, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.

The disciples accumulated and stored these in such abundance that they overflowed everywhere, leaving the dwellings foul-smelling and filthy. The householders criticized and disparaged this, so the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. He rebuked them and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu is ill, he may consume leftover medicines—namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—for up to seven days.
If he consumes them beyond seven days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

**Explanation of the Meaning:** Regarding "the sick" (*bhikṣu*: the *Mahāsāṃghika* says there are two kinds of illness: first, primary illnesses, namely hunger and thirst; second, secondary illnesses, numbering four hundred and four.

There are one hundred and one illnesses caused by the imbalance of the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), one hundred and one caused by the imbalance of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*), one hundred and one caused by the imbalance of the water element (*ap-dhātu*), and one hundred and one miscellaneous ailments.

If it is a wind ailment, it should be treated with oil; a heat ailment, with clarified butter (*sarpis*); a water ailment, with honey; and miscellaneous ailments, by combining all these medicines). "Residual medicines" refers to clarified butter, oil, fresh butter (*navanīta*), honey, and rock sugar (*śarkarā*). [These may be kept] for up to seven days.

Regarding the oral reception [of medicine] (the *Sarvāstivāda* school says: this is the essence of the precept). If a sick bhikṣu requires seven-day medicine and has no attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) of his own, making it difficult to find one through solicitation, he should receive it from the hand of a pure person.

Having received it orally from a bhikṣu, he should keep it in one place and consume it himself within the seven days. Even if the illness is severe such that he cannot receive it orally, he may still consume it. Whether the attending bhikṣu receives it by hand or receives it orally, the formal act of reception (*paribhoga-vidhi*) is still accomplished. Having thus received it:

It is permitted to consume these leftovers after they have been kept overnight at one's discretion; hence they are called "leftover medicines" (*vighasa-bhaiṣajya*). Regarding *sarpis* (clarified butter): this refers to that from cows, sheep, and so forth. Regarding *taila* (oil): this refers to sesame, radish, *madhūka*, and so forth, as well as the five kinds of animal fats;

these may be taken after being strained according to the Dharma. Regarding *madhu* (honey): this refers to honey from bees. Regarding *phāṇita* (molasses): this is included within the category of cane sugar. Regarding the limit of seven days: this means the holy rule establishes the maximum duration as exactly seven days; exceeding this constitutes an offense.
The Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a mind that craves the taste;
second, it must be a seven-day medicine; and third, one must exceed the time limit without relinquishing it.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one acquires medicine on the first day and keeps it, continuing until the seventh day, and then the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine acquired during those seven days constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture). This is no different from the rules regarding extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*), with the sole distinction being the seven-day limit.
If one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and does not forfeit the medicine, but instead exchanges it for other medicine, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Once the confession of the offense has been completed after the relinquishment, the Saṃgha shall return the medicine to that bhikṣu.

Whatever that bhikṣu possesses that has exceeded seven days—such as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, or rock honey—he should give it to the park-keeper. If the seven days have been reached, he may eat the food relinquished to him by the bhikṣu.
If it is less than seven days, it should be returned to this bhikṣu; a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal motion and one proclamation) should be performed.
Grind it. Once this bhikṣu has taken it, he should use it to anoint his feet or to light a lamp.

If he discards it, confesses it, or does not return it, he incurs an offense identical to the previous case (this being one matter among these five rules concerning long items). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"One should wash one's hands clean before midday and receive the medicine from a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), speaking as follows: 'Venerable one, please attend to me.'"
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], have this medical condition. I now formally accept these pure medicines for myself to consume within seven days, as well as for my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Thus it is said three times. If one has consumed them for one day, one should immediately inform the fellow practitioners, saying:
"This medicine for my illness has been consumed for one day; six days remain. I shall..."
One should take [the medicine]. This should be announced [to others] for up to seven days.

Once the seven days have passed, if there is still remaining medicine, it should be given away to a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) or to a *śrāmaṇera* (novice). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
To seek a fine appearance, or to seek a delicious taste, or to seek corpulence, or to take various medicines with a deceitful mind—all these constitute an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). Five.
The commentary states: It should be relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall relinquish it to a layperson or a śrāmaṇera.

If it is used for lighting lamps, anointing the feet, or as discarded medicine, a bhikṣu must not use it; none of it may be consumed. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The three minor offenses constitute a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅). This is what is called an offense. Regarding the conditions for exemption:

those who do not commit an offense are as clarified in the preceding section on the confession of relinquishment (*pratyāśraya-pratideśanā*) in this Vinaya. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (十誦律) states: "If one has a serious illness, there is no offense."
When consuming the four types of medicinal sustenance (the four *catur-maṇḍa* medicines: ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar), one should form this thought:

"I consume these for the purpose of curing illness, not for the sake of delicious flavors. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If the ghee has not yet reached seven days [of its production], it may be given as a gift to a *śrāmaṇera*."
On the eighth day, if there is an urgent necessity, one may go to a śrāmaṇera to beg for food; this is without fault.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Twenty-seventh Precept Regarding Seeking the Use of Rain-Bathing Robes at Improper Times.
This is an uncommon precept; the offenses for bhikṣuṇīs differ. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Greedy seeking..."
Regarding gain and offerings: because begging for many rain-cloths contradicts the practice of renunciation, this training rule was established.
As for the origin of the rule:
while the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, the mother of Viśākhā invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, saying that the time for the meal would arrive tomorrow.
She sent a maidservant to the saṃghārāma to announce that the time had come. At that moment, it was raining heavily, and all the bhikṣus were bathing in the rain.
When the maidservant arrived and saw from afar that the bhikṣus were all bathing naked, she thought they were naked ascetics (nirgrantha) and returned to inform her mistress.
The mistress sent her out again to inform the Buddha and the bhikṣus. Upon their arrival and after the meal offering was completed, the mistress invited eight [bhikṣus].
The Buddha granted permission for all of these: the wish to provide food for visiting bhikṣus; food for bhikṣus traveling from afar;
food for sick bhikṣus; medicine for sick bhikṣus; food for those attending to the sick; the provision of congee for bhikṣus; the provision of rain-bathing robes for bhikṣus;
and the giving of bathing robes to bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the origin of this rule:

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of rain-bathing robes, they immediately sought rain-bathing robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and never relinquished their existing ones.
Consequently, they used them for other purposes; even when they actually possessed rain-bathing robes, they remained naked.
[The Buddha] bathed. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha [of this matter]. He rebuked them and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the spring season, he should seek a rain-bath robe; for half a month, he should use it for bathing. If a bhikṣu...
If one requests a bathing robe more than one month before the end of spring, or uses it more than half a month before the end of spring, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Explanation of the Meaning: "One month remaining until the end of spring" refers to the local custom of the Western Regions (which reckons a season as four months). It refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month until the tenth day of the fourth month.

Five days constitute one of the four months of spring. From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month constitutes the four months of summer. From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month constitutes the four months of winter; there is no separate autumn season.

When it is now said that "one month remains of spring," it means that the end of spring has already passed through three months, with one month remaining; hence it is called "residual. This "one month" refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month.
This is called the final month of spring. One should constantly seek a rain-bath robe (*varṣāśāṭī*). Regarding those who seek it: the World-Honored One permitted begging and soliciting for one.

When seeking, one should not go from small households here and there to obtain even a foot or two; rather, one should seek from wealthy and prominent families. Whether obtained from a single person or from many people, this is what is meant by "seeking a rain-bath robe. According to the Sarvāstivādins, there are generally two purposes for keeping a rain-bath robe:

first, when it rains, one uses it to shield the four sides while bathing therein; second, when the weather is hot, one also uses it as a screen while bathing. Furthermore, because there is much rain during the summer months, one constantly wraps the three robes (*tricīvara*) in it while carrying them on journeys.

One should seek and prepare a rain-bath robe for use during the half-month (that is, from the sixteenth day of the third month onwards), and one should use it for bathing and carrying it while traveling from the first day of the fourth month onwards.
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance, or uses it for bathing more than half a month in advance (seeking it more than one month in advance refers to...).

That is, one seeks [the materials] prior to the sixteenth day of the third month; using them for bathing more than half a month in advance means bathing prior to the first day of the fourth month. This is what is meant by "seeking beforehand and using beforehand."
**Conditions for Offense:** This precept constitutes a full offense only when two conditions are met: first, seeking with the fault of greed;
second, using with the fault of disregarding the instruction.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the commission of this offense: if one seeks [the item] before the sixteenth day of the third month and uses it before the first day of the fourth month, it constitutes an offense.
[If one] abandons [the robe], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Regarding the confession of abandonment and non-returning, the offenses incurred are the same as before.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This robe must not be accepted as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*). It must not be given as a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*). One must not wear it to enter a river or a pond to bathe.

One must not bathe while wearing it during light rain; one may bathe while wearing it during heavy rain. If the rain suddenly stops, [one must remove it]; otherwise, it will become stained with grime."
If one puts on [a garment] and bathes in other water, there is no offense. At other times as well, one must not bathe naked;
one should wear a *saṃkakṣikā* (i.e., a short skirt) or some other old garment. One must not wear a rain-cloak while performing various activities.
If one wishes to apply oil to the body, or if one is ill, or in a place where many people pass, one may tie it at both ends to form [a belt].
[This constitutes] an obstruction. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it must be relinquished. A single bhikṣu shall announce it within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe. This is to be said three times. If it is relinquished on the sixteenth day, [it is improper].
This constitutes a *vinaya*-offense. Having relinquished it, one may use it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), and it may also be subject to the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification).
Furthermore, one may enter other bodies of water to bathe and perform various crafts; there is no offense. The Sarvāstivādins say:

"A bhikṣuṇī may possess a bathing robe, but she may not possess a rain-bathing robe. Because nuns are physically weak and frail, it is difficult for them to carry [heavy garments]; for this reason..."

It is not permitted. If there is an intercalary third month, one should not seek to obtain a rain-cloak before the first three months; rather, one should seek to obtain a rain-cloak on the sixteenth day of the latter three months.
A bhikṣu incurs no offense if he does not keep a rain-bath robe. The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana*) states:
"The rainy season consists of four months, which together with the fifteenth day at the end of spring, amount to one hundred and thirty-five days of use. If...
If one bathes naked without using a rain-bathing robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions. There is no offense in the following cases: on the sixteenth day of the third month, seeking [the robe] for use on the first day of the fourth month;

or if, having already relinquished the rain-cloak, one subsequently puts it to other uses; or if one wears a bathing-cloth while bathing; or if one has no bathing-cloth; or if one makes a bathing-cloth; or if one washes or dyes it;

or if one has it dyed at a designated place (the character "gāi" here should be "shēn"; it was erroneously written as "rǎn"). In these cases, there is no offense. These are the cases where there is no offense. Most excellent.
First, the section on the original non-enactment of the precept, etc.
○ Second, the general explanation of the twenty-eighth precept concerning the acceptance and storage of emergency offering robes after the prescribed time.
This is a common precept; for nuns, it constitutes the same offense. In the Mahāyāna, however, because of [the concern for] sentient beings, the regulations differ.
Nevertheless, one must still perform pure giving in accordance with the Dharma. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), because of disputes arising from the communal distribution of robe-offerings, and due to the pursuit of robes exceeding the proper limits, leading to neglect, censure, and affliction, this training rule was established.

The setting for this origin story: The Buddha was at Piḷañña. Having accepted the invitation of a brahmin, he completed his summer retreat there. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "In the town of Piḷañña, there was a brahmin named Piḷañña;

King Prasenajit had granted him this town as a fief. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: 'His name was Ajita; he was a brahmin king. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: 'Ajita was one who maintained the sacred fire (*agnihotra*).')"
Therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda, "Go and tell the brāhmaṇa: 'I have completed my summer retreat with you;

now I wish to travel through the human world. When Ānanda went and delivered this message, the brāhmaṇa reproached himself, for during those ninety days he had failed to provide offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
(During these ninety days, the Buddha ate only horse-barley. The Buddha said: "In a past life, there was a Tathāgata named Vipasyin who resided at Bandhumatī.")

In the middle [of the assembly], he was together with a great multitude of bhikṣus. King Bandhumat, along with his ministers and subjects, invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for a meal offering. At that time, there was a brahmin in the city named Śaila who taught five hundred youths. When the king prepared the feast, he first invited the Buddha; the Buddha granted his consent by remaining silent.

Once the king had returned and finished preparing the food, he took up an incense burner and said: "I pray that you would deign to come and accept my offering. The Buddha commanded the great assembly to proceed to the royal palace. After the meal, they each returned.

At that time, a sick bhikṣu, having requested food, was returning home and passed by the place where the brahmin was. Seeing that the food was fragrant and delicious, the brahmin immediately gave rise to a feeling of envy and thought: "These shaven-headed śramaṇas should properly eat horse fodder; they should not eat such as this."
[The Buddha] also taught the young boys, saying, "These masters all eat horse fodder. At that time, the brahmin was none other than myself; the five hundred boys were the five hundred arhats.

Because I spoke at that time that others were eating horse fodder, I underwent various painful retributions, passing through the hells for countless thousands of years. Although I have now attained Buddhahood, due to these residual conditions, I and my assembly ate horse fodder in the village of Verañjā for ninety days to repay this remaining debt.
[They] went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. (The *Sudarsana-vaibhāṣa* says: "Withdrew" is like the turning of the sun.)

As for "at the side": it means being on one side. When a person of wisdom approaches a place where a person of long-standing virtue resides, they sit while avoiding six things. What are these six? First, being too far away; if one wishes to converse, the sound of one's voice will not reach them.

Second, being too close; this would cause offense to the person of long-standing virtue. Third, being upwind; this causes the odor of one's own breath to reach them. Fourth, being at a high elevation; this shows a lack of respect. Fifth, being directly in front; this makes it difficult to look upon them. Sixth, being behind; when the person of long-standing virtue is conversing with others, it is difficult to turn around to speak with them.
Having spoken thus, he withdrew and sat to one side, thereby departing from these six dharmas. The World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for him, causing his heart to rejoice.
The brāhmaṇa prepared an offering and bestowed robes; the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to accept summer robes.
Regarding the origin of the rule concerning persons:

the group of six monks constantly begged for robes at all times; they begged for robes even before their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) was concluded, and they accepted robes [before the end of the retreat].
Having completed his *varṣā* in one location, Upāli (Baddhananda) heard that the monks who had completed their *varṣā* in another location had obtained great gains.
The Upadhivāra went to that place and distributed the portion of robes; he obtained a great quantity of robes and brought them back to the Jetavana Monastery.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, using countless skillful means, rebuked him.

At that time, the people within the realm of King Prasenajit (Prasenajit, translated into Chinese as "Harmonious Joy"; the *Xiyu ji* states his formal name is *Bālāditya*) in the kingdom of Śrāvastī rose in rebellion.

Sena—translated into Chinese as *Shengjun* (Victorious Army)—the Dharma Master Jing translated as *Shenguang* (Victorious Light). The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "This King Prasenajit, in the past ten thousand kalpas, during the Dharma of the Buddha Nāgaprabha, was a king who was a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage."
The two ministers, Rishidatta and Punnaka (Rishidatta means "Bestowed by a Seer," also translated as "Gifted by a Seer" or "Given by a Seer," because he was obtained as a son from a seer;
Punnaka is sometimes called Pūraṇa, meaning "Old Friend" or translated as "Long-standing"; he was the elder brother of Rishidatta). These two brothers were the ministers of King Prasenajit.

In the kingdom of Kosala, he was of immense wealth, with no one equal to him; yet he was able to share his enjoyments equally with the Buddha and the fourfold assembly, without clinging to anything as "mine. In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, he himself spoke thus:

"When King Prasenajit wished to enter the park for an excursion, he had me mount a great elephant, carrying the foremost palace ladies—one before me and one behind me, while I sat between them. When the elephant descended the slope, the one in front would embrace my neck and the one behind would grasp my back.

When the elephant ascended the slope, the one behind would embrace my neck and the one in front would grasp my shoulder. Those court ladies, for the sake of entertaining the king, wore garments of fine silk and brocade, and were adorned with various exquisite perfumes, garlands, and ornaments; I was together with them."

While traveling, he constantly guarded three matters: first, he restrained the elephant, fearing it might lose its proper course; second, he guarded his own mind, fearing the arising of defiled attachments; third, he guarded his own body, fearing it might fall and be injured. At that time, I did not harbor even a single moment of improper thought regarding the king’s court ladies.

The Buddha praised the elder: "Excellent, excellent! You are able to skillfully guard your mind. However, Pūraṇa was solely devoted to the practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); he was free from desire and pure, unattached to perfumes and flowers, distancing himself from the vulgar and base, and his observance of the precepts was supreme.

Rishidatta was not solely devoted to the practice of the holy life, yet he was contented and realized the Four Noble Truths; his wisdom was supreme. Later, both passed away. The Buddha gave a prophecy for the two: one was superior in the observance of the precepts, and the other was superior in wisdom.

"Excellent! Both have been born together in the same realm and received birth in the same way; in a future life, they shall both attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner) and be born in Tuṣita Heaven, returning to this world only once more before reaching the end of suffering.
The King issued a decree for a military expedition. The two ministers thought to themselves: "We are going on this expedition; we do not know if we shall return.
We wish to provide food for the Saṃgha and offer robes as well. However, because the rainy season retreat had not yet concluded, the bhikṣus did not dare accept the robes and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I allow the bhikṣus to accept robes offered as urgent gifts (ātyayika-cīvara). This is the established rule for the formulation of the precept:
if a bhikṣu has not yet completed ten days of the final month of the three-month summer retreat, and the bhikṣus receive robes offered as urgent gifts, the bhikṣu shall know [the following]..."
This urgent robe-offering should be accepted. Having accepted it, one may keep it until the time for robes. If one keeps it beyond that period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Explanation of the meaning:

"The ten days before the end of the three-month summer retreat" refers to when there are still ten days remaining until the *pravāraṇā* ceremony—that is, before the sixth day of the seventh month has arrived.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month (as it is said that ten days remain before the end of the three summer months). Regarding "urgent robes" (*ātyayika-cīvara*): if one accepts them, they are obtained; if one does not accept them, they are lost.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Whether it be a king who gives, a queen who gives, a prince who gives, or a high official or general who gives—because the benevolent minds of such noble persons are difficult to encounter and difficult to see often—if a woman, when about to marry and go to her husband's home, gives things to the Sangha because she has now attained independence, or if a sick person gives things to the Sangha out of a virtuous heart so as to benefit both the living and the deceased—because these are given due to urgent matters, they are called 'urgent'."

[This refers to] the giving of robes. Regarding the "time for robes": it is one month after the *pravāraṇā* has concluded if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread; it is five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
When ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, if a monk obtains an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it.
Having accepted it, he should keep it for ten days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*. [If he exceeds this, he incurs an offense.]
The *kaṭhina* robe may be received for one month; the *kaṭhina* robe may be received for five months.
If, nine days before the *pravāraṇā*, an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) is obtained, a bhikṣu who recognizes it as an urgent gift of robes should accept it.
Having accepted it, he should keep it for those nine days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*. [If] the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread...

Regarding robes, [the period is] five months. If one day is added (in this manner, whether there are eight days, seven days, six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, or if only one day remains until the *pravāraṇā*, nine days are added accordingly).
If kept beyond [this limit] (meaning that exceeding one month or five months constitutes an offense).

The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the intention to possess out of greed; second, that the robe is not an urgent gift;
and third, possessing it beyond the prescribed time limits—either before the previous limit has expired or after the subsequent limit has passed.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, one may accept an *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robe). If one accepts it before the [prescribed] time or keeps it after the [prescribed] time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

"Before the time" means accepting the robe prior to the fifth day of the seventh month; "after the time" means keeping it beyond the end of one month or five months, even though it was not formally offered as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*).

As for the forfeiture, confession, and non-returning, the nature of the offense is the same as previously stated (it is one of the five cases concerning long robes). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Excluding the ten-day period, this applies to emergency robes. One.

Regarding all robes for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one must necessarily wait until the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. If one divides them during the *varṣā*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If it is during the summer retreat, or if a donor wishes to give with their own hands, there is no offense in taking [the robes]."

If one obtains extra robes, and a bhikṣu or a donor says, "When I return from my journey, I shall personally offer them," then even if they are kept beyond the prescribed time limit, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the three minor groups [bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense if one receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) that is neither before nor after the [prescribed] time.

There is no offense if the robes are seized, lost, burned, or washed away and one receives them after the [prescribed] time. There is no offense if one has the perception that they were seized, lost, burned, or washed away;
or if the road is impassable due to danger or hardship, up to the point of life-threatening danger or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if the monk who received the deposit...
If one dies, or goes abroad, or renounces the precepts, or if [the danger] such as being plundered by bandits or harmed by wild beasts has passed, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Twenty-ninth Rule: The Precept Regarding Separation from One’s Robe for More Than Six Nights.
This is a unique precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla) shared by Mahāyāna bhikṣus. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of failing to guard [the robes] properly..."
Because of the matter of being separated from one's robes and due to the affliction of prideful teaching, this training rule was established.
Regarding the origin of the rule:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. After the various bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat, the month of Kārttika was fulfilled.
While dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*), there were many dangers from bandits who plundered their robes and bowls and even assaulted the bhikṣus.

Consequently, the bhikṣus all fled to the Jetavana Monastery to live together in a community. When the Buddha inquired and learned the reason for this, he permitted them to leave one robe each inside the monastery.
Regarding the origin of the rule concerning persons:

When the group of six monks heard that the Buddha had permitted them to leave their robes inside a dwelling, they left their robes inside the dwellings and went out after entrusting them to a monk who was a relative or friend.
That entrusted monk then took the robes out and dried them in the sun. Other monks questioned him and learned what had happened.
Therefore, he informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu has completed the three months of the summer retreat and remains in an araṇya during the final month of kārttika, and there is cause for apprehension or fear...

Dwelling in a place of fear: if a bhikṣu dwells in such a place and wishes to leave one of his three robes inside a house, he may, due to certain circumstances, stay apart from that robe for up to six nights; if he exceeds this period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Explanation of the Terms: The End of the Summer Three-Month Period (referring to those who observe the *pūrvavārṣika* [early summer] retreat; having completed the three months of the summer retreat, it is the fifteenth day of the seventh month; hence, it is called "the end of the summer three-month period").
Later, when the month of Kārttika was full while staying in an araṇya—(note: *kārttika* is translated as "merit" (*guṇa*) and also as "the Pleiades" (*mṛgaśiras*).

Because the Pleiades govern this month, it refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month. This is the final month of the summer retreat; thus it is called "the latter month of Kārttika.

Regarding the phrase "staying until the month is full in an araṇya," it means that those who have undertaken the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*), although they likewise perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month like those of the earlier retreat, must still remain for a full three-month period to complete the term of the later retreat; hence it says "staying until the month is full in an araṇya location"). A...
An araṇya (forest hermitage) is five hundred *dhanus* from a village. In the country of Cāmara, one *dhanus* is four *hastas* long;

it is measured by the medium *hasta* (as explained in the *Nissaggiya-pācittiya* rule concerning the separation of robes). "One who has doubt" means one suspects there are thieves or robbers. "One who is terrified" means that within [the area] there are terrifying thieves or robbers.

"Keeping each and every robe" (The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Each and every robe" refers to the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsa*. One may not entrust the *saṃghāṭī* or the *antarvāsa*; one may entrust the *uttarāsaṅga*.
[Text] Without the *saṃghāṭī*, one must not enter a village to beg for food. Since the *antarvāsa* is worn against the body, one must not wear the *saṃghāṭī* alone).

"Within a house" means a village settlement. "Having a cause and condition" (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whether it be matters concerning the *stūpa*, matters concerning the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, or other matters"). "Six nights" (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: ...).

From the six nights following the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) is permitted to observe the rains retreat (*varṣa*) while staying apart from his robes. The reason this is permitted is that, in foreign lands, this period of six nights is the time when bandits emerge; therefore, it is allowed.
When those six nights have ended, before the appearance of dawn on the seventh night, if he relinquishes the robe, takes hold of the robe with his hand,

or goes to a place within reach of a stone’s throw (by "a place within reach of a stone's throw" is meant not the boundary of an araṇya, but the precincts of the village where the robe was entrusted; if he exceeds this distance, he commits an offense).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a mind of contemptuous disregard for the teaching.
Second, one must be separated from the three robes. Third, one must transgress the prescribed limit.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, once the six nights of being separated from one's robe have passed, if on the seventh night one does not relinquish the robe before the appearance of the dawn light, nor takes hold of it with the hand, nor remains within reach of a stone’s throw, then when the dawn light appears on the seventh night, one commits an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
With the exception of the three robes, to be separated from any other robe constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; [the robe] must be relinquished.

Regarding the confession for not returning [the robe], the offense is the same as before. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one stays for one night, two nights, or even up to five nights, and having finished the business, does not return, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Vinayasamgraha* states:

"Up until the seventh night, before the dawn has appeared, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This refers to intentionally not relinquishing the robe, or even [staying] within the range of a stone's throw, while harboring a mind of negligence regarding the instruction; therefore, one first incurs the offense of wrong-doing at the appearance of the dawn."

Upon departing, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Once the robe has been entrusted, one may go to check on it once every six nights; having seen the robe, one returns to the *āraṇya* dwelling.
If one continues in this manner, going to check every six nights, there is no offense. For the other four assemblies [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is what constitutes an offense."
Explanatory Circumstances: There is no offense if six nights have already passed; on the seventh night, before the dawn has appeared, one arrives at the place where the robe is kept;
or if one relinquishes the robe; or if one takes hold of the robe with the hand; or if one reaches the distance of a stone’s throw.

There is also no offense if the robe is seized, lost, burned, or swept away by water, such that one does not relinquish it, does not take hold of it with the hand, and does not reach the distance of a stone’s throw.

If a boat cannot provide passage, if the road is dangerous and difficult, or due to any such adverse circumstances, one does not abandon the robe, does not hold the robe in hand, and does not go as far as a stone could be thrown;
in all such cases, there is no offense. There is no offense for those who were previously unbound by the formulation of the precept.
○ General Explanation of the Thirtieth Precept: Taking Sangha Property for One’s Own Use.
This is a shared precept; nuns are equally liable for its violation. It is likewise established in the Mahāyāna. That is, taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself.
Section VI. The Vinaya-saṃgraha states: This training rule was established due to the affliction of greed. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
Regarding the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Origin of the Incident:
There was a householder who wished to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Sangha and to offer them fine robes.
When Baddhālī heard of this, he went immediately to him and said, "Householder, the Sangha possesses great benefit, power, and merit. Those who give to the Sangha receive much."
"Now, give the food to the assembly of monks and the robes may be given to me. The householder consented. On the following day, he invited the monks to his residence.
Seeing that the elder bhikṣu was fully endowed with dignified deportment, the householder uttered a loud cry of repentance.

The bhikṣu questioned him and learned the reason for this. He reported the matter to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept: "To appropriate monastic property for oneself constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. [The Buddha said: 'If various bhikṣus do not [act thus]...'"
If one knows that this is property belonging to the Saṃgha, yet it is not property belonging to the Saṃgha; or if one thinks it is permitted for the Saṃgha, yet it is not permitted for the Saṃgha;

and later realizes it is indeed property belonging to the Saṃgha, having already granted permission for the Saṃgha—some may perform the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* repentance, while others may feel shame and remorse. The Buddha said: "There is no offense for those who did not know.
The precepts should be recited in this manner."
The established definition of the offense:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, seeks to appropriate it for himself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Explanation of the meaning: "Property belonging to the Saṃgha" refers to that which was made for the sake of the Saṃgha—whether it has not yet been granted to the Saṃgha, has already been granted to the Saṃgha, or has already been relinquished to it.

Regarding "the Saṃgha" (the *Mahāsāṃghika* says: there are eight kinds of Saṃgha: the bhikṣu-saṃgha, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, visiting monks, departing monks, resident monks, monks in retreat, the harmonious Saṃgha, and the discordant Saṃgha). Regarding "objects":
Robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and down to drinking vessels (the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya* states there are eight kinds of items:

those for a limited time, those for a night, those for seven days, those for life, those corresponding to the object, heavy objects, impure objects, and pure-impure objects)—if one seeks these for oneself and takes them into one's own possession (seeking them by coming and going oneself, and thereby appropriating monastic property for oneself).

The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense. First, the intention of greedily seeking to take possession; second, that the object is property belonging to the Saṃgha;
third, the perception that it is property belonging to the Saṃgha; and fourth, that the object has already come into one's hand.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one knows that an object belongs to the Saṃgha and intentionally seeks to appropriate it for oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).

If an object intended for the Saṃgha is diverted to a stūpa; if an object intended for a stūpa is diverted to the Saṃgha; if an object intended for the Saṃgha of the four quarters is diverted to the present Saṃgha;
if an object intended for the present Saṃgha is diverted to the Saṃgha of the four quarters; or if an object intended for the Bhikṣu-saṃgha [is diverted to another], [it constitutes an offense].
To divert [the offering] to the community of bhikṣuṇīs; to permit the community of bhikṣuṇīs to divert it to the community of bhikṣus;

to permit it to be given to one place when it was intended for another—these are all *duṣkṛta*. If one has already permitted [the diversion] and perceives it as permitted, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one has already permitted it but suspects [it], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has not yet permitted it but perceives it as permitted, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has not yet permitted it but suspects [it], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
*Dūṣkṛta*. For those who abandon the confession without returning [the object], the offense is the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If there is someone wishing to give a gift, they ask the bhikṣu, 'To whom should I give? He replies, 'Give it to whomever your heart respects.'"
He asked again, "Where does the fruit of retribution become most abundant? He replied, "Giving to the Saṃgha yields the most abundant fruit of retribution.
He asked again, "What kind of Saṃgha is pure, observes the precepts, and possesses merit? He replied, "The Saṃgha is free from transgressions of the precepts; those who are not pure [are excluded].
If someone brings an object to give to a bhikṣu, he should say, "If you give it to the Saṃgha, you will obtain great fruit of retribution. If [the donor] says, "I have already [given to]..."
"It was given to the Saṃgha; now it is intended specifically for you, Venerable One. Accept it; there is no offense.

However, if one knows that the object was intended for the Saṃgha and diverts it to oneself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This object should not be returned to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha should use it.
If one diverts it to another person, it is a *pāyattika*. If one knows that the object was intended for this particular animal and diverts it to another animal, it is a *vinayātikrama*."
The mind feels regret. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a donor personally diverts property intended for the Sangha and gives it to oneself, there is no offense.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If property is directed toward the Sangha, one may preach the Dharma to the person [who would have received it] and cause the property to enter into one's own possession."
[If one] commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, the object is returned to the Saṃgha. If [the object] was directed toward three, two, or one bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one gives an object to this stūpa and dedicates it to another stūpa, the object enters that other stūpa; it need not be returned because the merit is identical.

If a bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta*, he must perform the confession for the *duṣkṛta*. If one gives an object to this *saṃghika* [monastery] and dedicates it to another *saṃghika* [monastery], the object...
If one enters another *saṃgha-kṣetra*, there is no need to return [the items], because the *saṃghas* are identical.
The bhikṣu should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession and give the *pravāraṇā* robes to this current *saṃgha*. The *pravāraṇā* items should be returned;
they must be given to this current *saṃgha*, because the ownership of the *pravāraṇā* items differs [from the original]. The bhikṣu should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession. If...
If it is not returned, one incurs an offense according to the value of the money. The same applies to the wax on the face.

If one knows that an object was intended for one person but has been diverted to another, one should take back this object and return it to its original owner, performing a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅) confession.
If one does not return that object, one incurs an offense according to its monetary value. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:

"If one sees another person giving an object to a group of shameless people, and observes that one's own merit is superior to giving it to them, and for the sake of benefiting the donor, one diverts the gift into one's own possession."
There is no offense [for the donor]. For the bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika; for the three smaller assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

This is what constitutes an offense. Exceptions: There is no offense if one does not know; if one has already consented but thinks one has not; if one consents to giving a small amount but is urged to give more;
if one consents to giving to a few people but is urged to give to many; or if one intends to give something inferior but is urged to give something superior.
If one speaks while joking or laughing, speaks by mistake, speaks while alone, or speaks in one's sleep; or if intending to say this, one instead says that—in all such cases there is no offense.
There is no offense for those who were not yet subject to the rule, such as at the very beginning before it was established.
The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) states in detail that there are two kinds of retribution for greed: First is having excessive desire.

This means that because one indulged in greedy desires in a previous life without restraint until the mind knew no cessation, this results in the present life. The habitual tendencies of karma are not forgotten;

they become even more intensified and superior, leading to the arising of greedy attachment. Second is insatiability. This means that because one’s greedy seeking did not cease in a previous life, it continues to expand...

They continue to pursue [their objects] with increasing speed; thus, they are moved by this present life. Their karmic habits remain unextinguished, their desire grows ever more intense, and they employ it without restraint, seeking without satiety.

Are you pure in this regard? (Three times.)
The fourth is the exhortation to maintain [purity]: "Venerable sirs, since you are pure in this matter, you remain silent;
thus it shall be held. *Vinayamukha*, Volume VIII.

Part Five: The Ninety *pāyattika* Dharmas. Divided into four sections: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration of the precept characteristics.
The three inquiries; the four exhortations to uphold [the precepts].
First, the general heading:
"Venerable sirs, these ninety *pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Śīla-sūtra*."

(If one discusses the categories of offenses, both belong to the third [category]. While the first thirty matters constitute offenses arising from wealth, these ninety matters are committed without such cause. Although the defilement of greed may be slight, the disregard for the teachings is no less. They differ only in that they lack the element of wealth;

even if one exceeds the prescribed measurements when making beds, robes, and so forth, it is merely a violation of the instructions. This does not resemble the [first] thirty [offenses], where one must cut and destroy the object before performing repentance. Furthermore, this *pāyattika* dharma, by its nature, encompasses all six categories of offenses.

Whenever an act is performed intentionally—whether light or heavy—at the stage of preparation (*upakrama*), there is always the *pāyattika* offense of disrespecting the holy teachings. Within all the categories of offenses, this particular category alone receives the designation "falling" (*pāyattika*).
