there is no offense. To dig the earth is a *pāyattika* offense. If it is half sand, it is a *vyatikrama* offense. If it is pure sand, there is no offense. The same applies to stones, gravel, or dung.
Ash is treated in the same way. According to the Sarvāstivādins, touching dry soil on top of ground where it has not yet been leveled constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if it penetrates down into moist ground, one commits a *pāyattika*. There is no offense at the base of a wall where the masonry is level, as this is distinct from ordinary ground.
Therefore, even if it has been built up and repaired, if it remains damp and waterlogged, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

Whenever one wishes to take vegetables, grass, or soil, one should speak from a distance, saying, "Bring clean [soil] from such-and-such a place where there is good [quality]. If one goes to the edge and points it out, one commits an offense.
When an anthill is wet with rain, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense, because it is not fundamental, solid ground. If there is grass growing within it, one commits an offense by touching that grass.
Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* (falling) and the offense of *dukkaṭa* (transgression) for enclosing earth: because there is a slight connection [to the structure], it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the ground beneath a roof: if the ground is covered throughout and earth is raised, it is a *dukkaṭa*; furthermore, regarding the ground below, it is a *pāyattika*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: To dig into ground where plants have not yet grown constitutes one *duṣkṛta* offense for each stroke of the spade;

to dig into ground where plants have grown constitutes one *pāyattika* offense for each stroke of the spade. If a bhikṣu acts as a master craftsman and, wishing to newly construct a Buddhist stūpa or a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), marks out a pattern on the ground, he commits no offense.
However, if other bhikṣus perform the marking, they commit an offense. This also applies to [digging] gold, silver, or mineral ores. If...
There is no offense for one who digs in places where realgar, red ochre, white plaster, stone-bearing ground, black stone, sand, or salt are found.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu engaged in construction wishes to establish the foundation, he should wait for an auspicious star."

When waiting for an auspicious day, if there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) available, one may personally drive a peg into the ground to mark the boundary; if it is four finger-widths deep, there is no offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *pāyattika*; for the three junior groups [of nuns], it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is what is called an offense.

The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense if one says, "Know this" or "Look at this"; if one is dragging timber or bamboo; if one is lifting and straightening what has fallen over;
if one is turning over bricks or stones; if one is taking cow dung; if one is taking soil from a collapsed bank or soil from a rat's burrow;
if one is removing soil from a walking path (*caṅkrama*) or soil from within a house; or if one is walking back and forth on the path.

Sweeping the ground, or striking the ground with a staff, or digging unintentionally—all these do not constitute an offense. There is no offense for those who were before the precept was established, and so forth.
○ The Eleventh Precept: Destroying the Village of Ghosts and Spirits.
General Explanation:
This is a common precept; the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same, and it is studied identically in the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition).

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "On account of the matter of seeds and the village of spirits (*bhūtagrāma*), this training rule was established due to the afflictions of censure and a lack of compassion."
Location: The Setting of Dependent Origination.
The Buddha was staying at the City of Vebhalinga.
The Buddha, arising from his seat, addressed the bhikṣus: "There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who, while repairing a dwelling, cut down a tree himself. When asked, "Is it true that you cut it down?
he replied, "It is true. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
The established definition of the precept:
"If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits (bhūtagāma), it is a pāyattika. Explanation of the meaning:

"Spirits" refers to non-human beings (*amanuṣya*). [The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Ghosts (*preta*) means 'those who are terrified' (*bhīta*); that is to say, they are empty and cowardly, possessing much fear. It is also said to mean 'majesty' (*vibhu*), for they can cause others to be afraid."

As for their majesty: furthermore, those who are characterized by constant craving are called *preta* (ghosts). This refers to those hungry ghosts who perpetually seek food and drink from others in order to sustain their lives. The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) states: "A *shen* (spirit) is that which possesses capability. Those with great power can move mountains and fill the oceans;

those with lesser power can manifest, conceal, and undergo transformations; therefore, they are called *shen*. As for a *cun* (village), it refers to all grasses and trees. There are five kinds of villages.

The root-propagated species (*mūla-bīja*) includes: *harīta* (i.e., yellow ginger), *uśīra* (i.e., fragrant root; this is called *maoxianggen* [cymbopogon root]; the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* calls it a cold-natured medicinal herb;

the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* calls it *xiangfuzi* [sweet flag]), *mūtaka-ṭha* (i.e., *nakha-gandha*, eaglewood), *rohiṇī* (i.e., *hānglián* [coptis]), and others produced from roots (they are called root-propagated because they arise from roots).
As for branch-propagated species (*skandha-bīja*), these include: *lośama* (i.e., the Bodhi tree) and *bālakhilya*.

*Tā* (referring to the *pāṭala* tree; these two types of trees are found in Jiǎo and Guǎng [modern-day Guangdong], but are not seen in other regions). As for "seed produced from branches" (*śākhā-praroha-bīja*), this refers to seeds generated from branches.

Regarding "seed produced from nodes" (*parvaja-bīja*): this refers to the *sumanā* flower (also called *sumanas*, translated as "well-gathering the mind"; it is also named *sumana* flower; its color is yellowish-white and extremely fragrant;

the tree does not grow very large, reaching only three or four feet in height, with branches drooping like a canopy; the fragrance of its flowers is similar to that of the *mallikā* flower); the *surabha* (unknown); and the *phullana*.

(*This is the name of a foreign herb.*) *Lèjiǎo* (*is the Jiǎo grass. Its taste is pungent and bitter. There are many varieties. Tiānjiǎo is also called Shuǐhóngcǎo; it mostly grows near water. Its stalks are over a foot tall, with large leaves that are reddish-white in color.

Mǎjiǎo has leaves largely similar to the former, and it also grows in low-lying, damp places. Shuǐjiǎo grows in shallow water; its leaves are large with black spots. Máojiǎo does not die at the roots in winter; there is hair on its leaves.
Báijiǎo, Hóngjiǎo, Xiāngjiǎo, Héjiǎo, etc., as well as those produced from joints, are of this kind. Fùluó seeds are seeds that grow within hollows.*) Sweet.
Sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, lotus roots, and other plants that grow from slips (the term *phala* [覆羅] is of unknown meaning; according to various schools, these are propagated by joints);
as for "seed-plants," these are those where the seed produces another seed (such as rice, wheat, hemp, beans, millet, and so forth, because the seed produces further seeds).

If one cuts or severs them, it is called "destroying a village of spirits" (*bhūtagāma*). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Village" has the sense of a collection; it refers to groves and thickets where various spirits, birds, beasts, and other sentient beings depend for their lives."

"Abiding" means like a village of people. "Destruction" is a general term for twisting, pulling, uprooting, digging, cutting, severing, crushing, and wounding. Regarding the conditions for the offense:
this precept constitutes a full offense only when four conditions are met: first, it must be living plants or trees; second, one must perceive them as such;
third, there must be intentional destruction; and fourth, there must be cutting, severing, or breaking.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one perceives something as a living plant among the five types of plants, and either cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, roasts it oneself, instructs another to roast it, or cooks it oneself, instructs another to cook it, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has doubt, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one perceives what is living as non-living, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one perceives what is non-living as living, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

*Duṣkṛta*. If there is no doubt that it is living, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the seven colors of plants and trees—blue, yellow, red, white, black, pale blue (a light shade of blue), and purple—if one cuts, instructs another to cut, roasts, instructs another to roast, or cooks, or instructs another to cook, living plants and trees while perceiving them as such, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one strikes living plants or trees with the perception that they are living, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one strikes what is not a living plant or tree with the perception that it is a living plant or tree, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one strikes what is not a living plant or tree with the perception that it is not a living plant or tree, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one strikes what is not a living plant or tree with doubt as to whether it is living, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one drives a wedge into a tree, it is a *pāyattika*. If one applies fire to living grass...
[Cutting] wood: a *pāyattika*. If one cuts most of a living plant or tree, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one cuts a plant or tree that is half-dry and half-living, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not say, "Look at this," or "Know this," it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* says: "If a bhikṣu has a specific need for something, he should say to the attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*): 'You know [this]...'"
It is so. If he does not understand, speak again, saying, "Look at this. If he still does not understand, speak again, saying, "Give this to me.
If it is burned by fire, broken, or cut, one knows that it will certainly not grow; there is no offense.
If grass grows in the courtyard of the dwelling place, it is permitted to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take charge of it. The *Mātṛkā* says: cover it with ashes, earth, or sand.
To pluck a living plant: a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). To say to another person, "Take this fruit; I wish to eat it": a *duṣkṛta*.
To swallow entirely a raw fruit that has not been purified: a *duṣkṛta*. To take dried mushrooms: a *duṣkṛta*. To strike a ripe fruit so that it falls:
a *duṣkṛta*. To strike a raw fruit so that it falls: a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Wood..."
Even if a bhikṣu were to be squeezed to death, though he held a sword or an axe in his hand, he would rather die maintaining his integrity than cut down trees or dig up the earth to save his life.
Why is this? Because by digging up earth or cutting down trees, one falls [into lower realms].

A person of wisdom would rather die while observing the precepts than live while violating them. If someone were to set fire to a monastery, [the bhikṣu] would protect it in order to remain [in that place].
In such a place, if one cuts grass or digs earth to extinguish a fire, there is no offense. If one overturns lotus flowers or duckweed in water, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If they are removed from the water, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). If one requires flowers or fruit, one may lift the branches of a tree so that a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) may take them;
there is no offense, provided the branches are not broken. If the tree is too high for the *kappiya-kāraka*...

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu takes hold of a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) while being carried away, he commits no offense. This arises from violating the precepts. When a tree oppresses a person, one may cut down the tree or dig up the earth, provided that the primary aim is to save the person; thus, one does not violate the prohibitions and both self and others are benefited.
This is in perfect accord with the intent of the Mahāyāna teachings. The Sarvāstivādins say: regardless of whether seeds are present or not, one must eat only pure fruit and never impure fruit.
If one swallows it whole, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one bites it open, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
The third section states: "One should not eat impure fruit; rather, one should consume it after performing the five kinds of purification methods:

first, purification by fire; second, purification by knife; third, purification by a wound; fourth, purification by bird-pecking; and fifth, purification by being unfit for planting. Among these, the first and last...
Once the seeds have been removed from the first three types of pure fruit, they may be eaten. One should not eat fruits or vegetables that are impure, nor should one perform the purification oneself.
One should not hold them in one's own hand while having another person perform the purification; rather, one should place them on the ground and have another person perform the purification.
Once purified, one must not eat them without having formally received them. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If it is grape..."

If various fruits and melons are gathered into a single heap, they are purified by applying fire to three or four places; this constitutes purification. However, if using a knife or fingernails, each individual item must be purified separately.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "In certain countries, when grain is heaped up, people fear that non-humans (*amanuṣya*) might steal it;
therefore, they mark it by burning the top with ash and fire. This is what constitutes purification. This is as in the case of the *māmaka*.

When the grain in the granary has not yet been purified, and fearing that young bhikṣus do not know the Dharma, one employs a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such matters) to purify it by fire.
When the grain in the granary is exhausted, the bhikṣu may always say, "Pound it away," and there is no offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
For the three junior groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This is what is called a transgression. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"The other three groups commit a *duṣkṛta* for killing plants and trees without a valid reason. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "The three groups are *śramaṇera*s; they do not commit an offense. [Question: Regarding these two Vinayas, from which perspective is their meaning derived? [Answer:

If one kills plants and trees without a valid reason, the offense must be adjudicated according to the *Pañcavargika*. If one acts for the sake of the Three Jewels during construction work, one relies on the *Sarvāstivāda*, whereby there is no offense. Thus, the permissions and prohibitions are appropriately applied.
The meaning is not erroneous.
Regarding the opening conditions for non-offense: it is said that one does not commit an offense if one knows [the plant] is dead; or if one cuts withered or dry grass and wood;
or if one drags wood or bamboo across living grass and plants; or if one uses a staff to clear away living grass covering a path in order to open it.

If one uses tiles or stones to prop something up and thereby cuts or injures grasses or trees; or if, while clearing the soil of a walking path (*caṅkrama*), or sweeping the ground where one walks to and fro, one inadvertently brushes against and cuts living grasses or trees;
or if one strikes the ground with a staff and thereby brushes against and cuts living grasses or trees—there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states in detail: Whenever an official in charge of affairs intends to fell a tree for the purpose of construction, seven days prior to the felling, he shall set out various sacrificial offerings beneath that tree, recite sūtras and incantations, and preach upon the ten paths of wholesome action.
One should praise their wholesome deeds and further address them, saying: "If there is a resident deity of this tree, you should seek another dwelling elsewhere.
At present, work is being undertaken for the sake of the Triple Gem; after seven days have passed, this tree shall be cut down.
When the tree is being felled, if any unusual signs appear, one should offer praises and speak of the merit of generosity and renunciation."
Regarding the fault of stinginess and greed: if it still manifests as a distinct sign, one should not cut [the tree]; if there is no such distinct sign, one may cut it. The Sarvāstivādins say:
those who establish the precepts do so for the sake of not afflicting sentient beings, for the sake of stopping slander, and for the sake of great protection of the Buddha-dharma.
There are three precepts that greatly benefit the Buddha-dharma; first, one must not...
1. One must not carry [loads]. 2. One must not kill plants or trees. 3. One must not dig the earth.
If these three precepts were not established, all kings would compel bhikṣus to perform various types of labor. Because these three precepts exist, all sovereign rulers restrain their minds.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: In the kingdom of Ti-ya-shi-lo (Tāmraparṇī), there was a physician who was the Nāga King Pa-la (Pala). He manifested...
Taking the form of a māṇava (here translated as "scholar-son"), he carried a full chest of gold and traveled everywhere, reciting verses and asking:
"Where is the king supreme? Who is stained by defilement while remaining unstained?
Who is the fool who remains unstained yet is stained? Where does the fool grieve? And where does the wise man rejoice?"
"Who can reconcile those who are separated? Such a person is said to be one who possesses true peace and happiness.

If there were anyone who could explain this, they were to be honored with a golden casket. However, no one was able to provide an explanation. He gradually traveled on until he reached the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
They proclaimed this once more. Someone replied, "There is a man of superior wisdom dwelling in an araṇya named Nārada;
he shall explain this meaning. Before long, Nārada arrived. The nāga questioned him with a verse, which he heard and committed to memory.
He said, "Twelve years from now, I shall explain it to you. The Nāga replied, "That is far too long. He gradually requested a reduction until it was seven days.
Then Nalada went at once to inform the five bhikṣus. The five bhikṣus replied, "You may ask the Buddha yourself.
He then proceeded to the Deer Park, prostrated at his feet, and sat down. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
He wished to seek ordination. The Buddha said, "First explain the meaning of the verses for the young brahmin (maṇava), and only then may you go forth.
He should answer thus: "The sixth king is supreme. Where there is defilement, attachment arises;
where there is no defilement, one gives rise to defilement. To speak thus is the mark of a fool. The fool grieves over this; the wise person [does not]."
This joy, which is capable of separating one from the objects of craving, is what is called true peace and happiness.
If he does not understand this, explain it further with a verse: "If a person hears sublime words and, having understood them, cultivates superior concentration;
yet if they hear them and do not comprehend the meaning, that person is due to their own negligence. If he still has doubts, you may address him as follows:
He cut the leaf with his fingernail. When asked whether the World-Honored One had appeared in the world, he replied, "He has already appeared.

When asked where he was, he replied, "He is at the Deer Park in the Place of Almsgiving. Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Nalada went to the Dragon King’s abode and answered everything as above.
That dragon transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King and went to the place of the World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "You are foolish."
"O man, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts but were unable to maintain them;
thus, you experienced this inferior body of a long-lived nāga. Why now do you again give rise to a deceitful mind? You should now restore your original form.
The nāga said, "World-Honored One, I am a nāga; I have many enemies and evils. I fear that sentient beings might cause me mutual harm."
The Buddha commanded the deity Suvarṇahasta to protect him. The Dragon King went to another place and resumed his original form;
he had seven heads, and the distance from head to tail was two hundred *yojanas*.
Upon each head grew a great *eḷā* tree, which, when shaken by the wind, caused pus and blood to flow, defiling his body with foul stench and impurity.
It was foul; flies and maggots were constantly present, and various insects covered his body, biting and feeding upon him day and night.

At that time, the Dragon King, assuming his true form, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at His feet, and stood to one side. He addressed Him, saying, “I pray only that the World-Honored One would grant me a prophecy:
on what day shall I cast off this dragon body? The Buddha said, “In the future, when the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years...”
In the course of time, there will be a Buddha appearing in the world named Maitreya. He will bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment, whereby you shall be liberated from your dragon body.
The Dragon King weeps with grief; tears flow simultaneously from the eyes of all his heads, forming fourteen rivers that rush and pour forth with startling force.

The Buddha ordered him to desist, saying, "Do not cause harm to the kingdom. The dragon prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished. The great assembly asked about his past causes and conditions.
The Buddha said, "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this dragon left the household life to practice within the Buddha-dharma.
He was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and fully cultivated the gates of meditative concentration. He practiced walking meditation beneath an Amla tree, exerting himself with self-discipline."

When a leaf struck his head, he endured it immediately. Later, becoming weary from fixing his mind in concentration, he arose from meditative absorption and began walking meditation with focused mindfulness.

When a leaf again struck his head, causing him extreme pain, he gave rise to a mind of anger and, using both hands, snapped off the tree leaves and threw them to the ground, saying these words: "What did the Buddha Kāśyapa see in an insentient object?"

Because of his transgressions, he was subject to this training rule (śikṣāpada) which caused him to undergo such suffering. Due to that fierce poison of a hateful mind and his violation of the precepts, at the end of his life he fell into this state as a nāga.
The twelfth [precept]: The precept against harassing others with discordant speech.

General Explanation: This is a common precept; the offenses for nuns are likewise the same, and it is studied identically in the Mahāyāna. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states:
"This training rule was established due to the affliction of anger arising from the matter of causing distress. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
The person for whom the discourse originated was...
The Venerable Chanda committed an offense. When the bhikṣus asked him, "Do you recognize that you have committed an offense?
he replied with an irrelevant matter, saying, "To whom were you speaking? What was it you said? What principle were you discussing? Were you speaking to me?"
"To whom are you speaking? Who has committed an offense? From what source does this offense arise? I see no offense; why do you say that I am guilty?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, who, using countless skillful means, rebuked him and authorized the Saṃgha to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of *anyavādaka* (speaking otherwise).
He then established the precept: "To speak otherwise [when one's words are not accepted] is a *pāyattika* offense. Subsequently, he proceeded to harass the community of monks.
When summoned, he does not come; when unsummoned, he comes. When he ought to rise, he does not rise; when he ought not to rise, he rises.

When he ought to speak, he does not speak; when he ought not to speak, he speaks. After the bhikṣus had reported this to the Buddha and rebuked him, the Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform a *saṃvāsanīya-karman* (act of causing discomfort) against Chanda. The precepts should be recited as follows:
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu falsely speaks otherwise to annoy another, it is a *pāyattika*.

Explanation of the meaning: "Falsely speaking otherwise" (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: if a bhikṣu sees Cchanna holding silver coins, the bhikṣu says to him, "Why are you holding silver coins? He replies...).

To say, "I am holding a tin coin, not a silver coin," when one has seen someone drinking alcohol and asks, "Why are you drinking alcohol? and replies, "I am drinking water"; or when asked, "Why are you sitting alone in a secluded place with a woman?
and replies, "There was a wise man [there]": these are called *anyavāda* (equivocation). At other times, one may remain silent and not answer. The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states:

Suppose a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu, "Have you seen such-and-such a bhikṣu, or laymen and women? and, with a malicious intent, replies, "I have never seen such people; I only saw two feet going away from here," or remains silent. This is called *anyavāda* used to annoy others.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the intentional desire to annoy another;
second, the act of annoying by means of equivocal speech; and third, having had the *saṃgha* perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against oneself.
The Formal Conviction (*Adhikaraṇa-śamatha*): Regarding the offense herein, while the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal motion (*jñapti*), one speaks evasive words, saying:
"To whom did you speak? What matter were you speaking about? What principle were you discussing? Were you speaking to me, or were you speaking to others? I do not see this offense."
If one speaks in such a manner after the formal motion has been made, it is all *pāyattika*; if one speaks in such a manner before the formal motion has been made, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, if one does not come when summoned, or comes when not summoned, or does not rise when one ought to rise, [it is likewise an offense].
If one rises when one should not rise, remains silent when one should speak, or speaks when one should remain silent, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has already been made, it is all *pāyattika*.

If an elder summons someone and they do not come, it is *duṣkṛta* (the offense is grave for disobeying the Saṃgha, and light for disobeying an elder). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one answers differently from what was asked within the Saṃgha, one incurs [an offense]."
*Pāyattika*. If, in the midst of many people, before one’s preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), or elders, one asks one thing and answers another, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If, toward the Saṅgha or those who are worthy of respect, one violates and disturbs them with a defiled mind regarding a teaching that is consistent with reason, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
however, if it is a teaching not consistent with reason, violating and disturbing it does not constitute an offense."
It is said: one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*. If one causes distress by acting contrary [to the rules] toward someone who does not understand them, it is also an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one has been appointed to oversee communal affairs and, with a defiled or malicious mind, fails to do what should be done or does what should not be done, one incurs an offense of *pācittiya*.
If there is no malicious intent, one incurs an offense of *dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one treats the precepts lightly..."

A *pāyattika*. If a teacher orders a disciple to sweep the floor and the disciple does not sweep it; or if instructed to sweep in one direction, they sweep in the opposite direction—in all such cases, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu sees hunters pursuing deer or other game entering the monastery, and they ask, 'Have you seen any deer pass this way?
he should not answer, 'I saw them. However, if it is a cold season, he should report..."
He said, "You may enter the warm chamber and go toward the fire. If it is a hot time, he should inform him, "You may enter the cool chamber and drink water.
If he says, "I am not fatigued," he should ask about the running deer; [the other] should examine his own fingernails and reply, "I see my fingernails.
If he asks again, he should look at the great void and reply, "I see the great void. If that person...
He said, "I am not asking about fingernails or empty space; rather, I am asking whether there is any fault in killing a sentient being.
One should then look in all four directions and reflect thus: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-satya*), no sentient beings exist among any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Then one should reply, "I do not see any sentient beings. In this case, there is no offense. However, if asked at other times, it is not so.
If one answers according to the facts, all incur an offense: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three junior groups [of nuns], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.

**Exceptions:** There is no offense if one does not understand because of hearing poorly; if there was a discrepancy in the preceding speech; or if one asks, "To whom were you speaking? and the matter is clarified.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one does not see this transgression; if one intends to perform an illegal or non-disciplinary *karmavācanā*;
if it concerns the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, or one's preceptors, teachers, relatives, or friends, and one intends to perform an unbeneficial *karmavācanā* against them;
if one does not grant consent for a formal act of reconciliation; if they do not come when summoned, or come when told not to come. If [it is] one...
Eating while seated; if one eats without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the "leftover-food" ritual); if one is ill and does not rise when called upon to do so—these do not constitute an offense.

Or if the dwelling collapses, or is burned, or a venomous snake enters the house, or even if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), if one is instructed not to rise and yet rises, there is no offense.
If, with a malicious intent, someone asks whether you have realized the "superior human states" (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*) and you do not speak of them, there is no offense.
If one performs an illegal or non-disciplinary *karmavācanā* (formal act);

or if, for the sake of the Saṃgha, a stūpa, a monastery, an upādhyāya, an ācārya, or a relative or acquaintance, one speaks despite being told not to speak when it would be unbeneficial; there is no offense.

There is also no offense if one speaks in a low voice, speaks hurriedly, speaks in a dream, or speaks to oneself; or if, intending to say this, one mistakenly says that instead. — *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* (The Vinaya Compendium).

It is said: If one has an ailment in the mouth and holds medicine in it without speaking, there is no offense. There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.

The Essential Points of the Vinaya, Volume Ten, Compiled by the Dharma Master Deqi, a Śramaṇa of the Vinaya School at Baohua Mountain in Jinling. Section Thirteen:
The Precept Against Slandering and Reviling.
General Explanation: This is a common precept; the offense for nuns is likewise the same, and it is studied identically in the Mahāyāna. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "This training rule was established due to the affliction of malice arising from the act of slander. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain. The Venerable Trapusa was appointed by the community of monks to oversee the bedding and seating of the Sangha as well as the food for the Sangha.
The persons who instigated this were the bhikṣus of the Maitrāyaṇīya school. Standing at a distance where they could see one another but not hear each other, they said to one another:
"This Trapusa-Malla has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. Other bhikṣus said to them: "Do not say that he possesses these."
[They accused him] with [the motives of] love, hatred, fear, and delusion. He replied, "We did not speak to his face; we were merely disparaging him in private.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who reprimanded them and established a precept: disparaging [a fellow monk] is a pāyattika offense.

Later, while Cidī was standing at the same spot as Trapuṣabhadra, he heard but did not see him, and said, "He has [the motives of] love, hatred, fear, and delusion. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who [reprimanded him and] established a rule.
Regarding the *pāyattika* offense of censuring through reproach, he replied: "We do not reproach you; this was merely an insult. The Buddha said:
"The precept should be recited in this manner. This is the established definition of the offense."
If a bhikṣu reviles or scorns [another], it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning: "Reviling or scorning" refers to either reviling while face-to-face or reviling behind one's back. Regarding reviling while face-to-face:

this refers to speaking within range of sight but beyond the range of hearing, [driven by] attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion. Regarding reviling behind one's back: this refers to speaking within range of hearing.
Regarding the statement "not seeing [the person]": there are the conditions for the offense of having love, hatred, fear, or delusion.
This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, having a mind of resentment or disparagement;
second, the person being one appointed by formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*); and third, the speech being clearly articulated.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one reviles a bhikṣu with contemptuous words and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This applies whether you were instructed by a senior elder (*sthavira*) to revile him, or if you acted upon such instruction to revile him.
Dukkata. According to the Sarvāstivādins: regarding this precept, if one first appoints fourteen people by the Sangha and then, out of anger, reviles such a person, it is a pāyattika.
If, after the *karmavācanā* has been relinquished, one reviles such a person out of anger, it is a dukkata.
If one sends a messenger or a letter, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: if one disparages a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one disparages another person, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three groups of minor followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances (Kāraṇa). There is no offense in the following cases: if the person actually possesses attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion;

if one speaks to cause them to confess out of fear that they might later feel regret; if speaking in jest; if speaking while alone; if speaking in a dream; or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that instead.
No offense. There is no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, such as at the very beginning.
○ A general explanation of the fourteenth precept concerning the failure to put away monastic bedding.
This is a common precept; the offense for a bhikṣuṇī is likewise the same. It is studied in common with the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Due to matters concerning bedding and furniture, and because of the affliction of disrespect, this training rule was established."
The setting for the origin of this account:
The Buddha was staying in the city of Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There was a householder who wished to invite the community of monks for a meal;
thus, the causal conditions arose.

The group of seventeen monks took the Sangha’s sitting mats and spread them out in the open air. They paced back and forth while waiting for the meal, but when the time arrived, they failed to gather them up and went directly to eat.
Consequently, the Sangha’s sitting mats were fouled by wind, dust, and soil, and damaged by insects and birds;
they became filthy and impure. When the bhikṣus returned and reported this to the Buddha, he rebuked them and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the offense:
if a bhikṣu takes a monastic rope bed, a wooden bed, bedding, a sitting mat, or a rug spread out in the open air, and having either laid them out himself or instructed another to lay them out,
departs without picking them up himself or instructing another to pick them up, it is a pāyattika.

Explanation of the Terms: Regarding "Saṃgha" (the Sangha), the *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "There are six kinds of Saṃgha: first, a Saṃgha of four persons; second, a Saṃgha exceeding four persons; third, the Saṃgha present before one's eyes (*pratyakṣasaṃgha*); fourth, the Saṃgha of the four quarters (*cāturdiśasaṃgha*);

fifth, the resident Saṃgha (*sthāyisaṃgha*); and sixth, the visiting Saṃgha (*āgantukasaṃgha*). Here, 'Saṃgha' refers to the property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters. There are five types of rope beds (*pīṭha*):
rope beds with curved legs, rope beds with straight legs, rope beds with bent legs, rope beds with notched legs, and legless rope beds. Wooden beds are likewise [of these same types].
Thus it is. Regarding bedding and cushions: they may be used for sitting or for lying down; a "cushion" (*ruò*) is used for sitting. *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

A sleeping cushion is four cubits long and three cubits wide, sewn together at the four edges and stuffed with wool or cotton. "Wool" refers to sheep’s wool; "cotton" refers to wood-cotton (*tūla*), reeds, *karpāsa* (cotton), *mṛdvīkā* (grape-vine fiber), *bhaṅga* (hemp), various mixed fillings, discarded rags, or refuse-rag robes (*pāṃśukūla*).

With such materials placed inside the cushion, one should beat them until even and level. Within it, lines should be sewn both crosswise and lengthwise to prevent the stuffing from gathering to one side. Alternatively, one may make a cushion by carding wool and then adding an outer and inner covering.
"Seated mat" refers to a small square sitting mat. "Spread out in the open air" means in a place without cover.

Whether one spreads it oneself or instructs another to spread it—"spreading" meaning to lay out and arrange—it should be said to the resident bhikṣu, the *māmāte*, or the manager who remains there after one has departed:
"I now entrust this to you; you must guard and look after it. This refers to instructing another to take it up. If there is no one at all...

One should lift it up, place it in a screened location, and depart. If there is no screened location, and one knows for oneself that this spot will certainly not be damaged, one should carry it securely, placing the coarse part over the fine part, and depart (that is, one lifts it oneself).
If one can return immediately, one should depart at once. If the rain is heavy, one should return quickly; if the rain is moderate, one may walk through it and return; if it is light...
If the rain falls lightly and one can travel and return, one who has not damaged their sitting mat (niṣīdana) should go.

A bhikṣu should proceed by employing such expedients in due order (even if he does not lift it himself nor instruct another to lift it, but simply observes the time and circumstances so that the mat remains undamaged, he may depart).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense. First, it must be the property of the Sangha of the four directions.
Second, one must intentionally fail to raise it [or report it]. Third, both feet must cross the boundary.
**Establishing the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one proceeds without employing such a method, at the moment the door is first exited, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot remains inside the door, and though intending to leave, one does not go but instead turns back in regret, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
If two people are sitting together on one bed, the junior person should fold up [the bedding] and depart. The junior person...
The person sitting there forms this thought: "The senior monk should collect [the bowl], yet the senior monk does not collect it;
the junior monk commits a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, because it is contrary to proper decorum, he commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.

On the other hand, the senior monk thinks: "The junior monk should collect [the bowl], yet the junior monk does not collect it; the senior monk commits a *pāyattika* offense. If neither of the two acts first...
If one does not put it away afterwards, nor puts it away simultaneously with others, both incur a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, regarding other empty rope beds or wooden beds, or ordinary bathing beds and bedding, or floor coverings, ropes, wool, and hemp—should these be left in the open air and one depart without putting them away, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one spreads out monastic bedding in the open air and enters a room to sit without putting it away, [it is likewise an offense].

To contemplate [this] is a *duṣkṛta*. According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, if one has spread bedding for the Saṃgha on an open space and wanders through the various rooms without entrusting it to someone else, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not lift up one's own bedding at the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The reasons for lifting it at the proper time are: first, to fear dampness from rain; second, to fear scorching by the sun; and third, to fear being blown away by the wind.
Even if there is a covering or obstruction, wherever the rain from the sun reaches, one incurs an offense. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"To fail to pick up another's private property constitutes a *duṣkṛta*; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three minor groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is what is called an offense."
The Exceptional Circumstances (Anāpatti): There is no offense if one takes a monastic rope-bed, a wooden bed, or a squatting bench;

or if one spreads ordinary bedding or cushions on an open space oneself; or if one instructs another to spread them and departs after having informed the resident monks, or even by employing a gradual method of departure as described in the text. There is no offense if two people sit together on one bed, provided the junior sits lower.

One should collect them. Any other empty rope beds or wooden beds, whether ordinary bathing benches or the outer and inner linings of bedding, or ropes, wool, and hemp spread upon the ground—if these have been laid out in the open air, one should collect them and depart.

If a monk’s sitting mat has been spread in the open air, having gathered it up and entered the room, one reflects that there is no offense. There is no offense for one who acted before the rule was first established.

Regarding the precepts and so forth, the *Vinayasamgraha* states in detail: "In all cases concerning the robes belonging to the Saṃgha, if one does not use another material as a lining or substitute, it is improper to use them;
nor should that substitute material be worn out or torn. If the bedding or furnishings of the Saṃgha have become damaged..."
If there are holes, they must be sewn and patched; if the fabric is torn or broken, it should be joined back together.
If it is beyond repair, it may be used as a lamp wick, or made into a broom, or cut up and mixed with mud to coat walls, fill crevices, and thereby increase the merit of the donor.
Furthermore, when listening to the Dharma, one should not sit together with bhikṣuṇīs or laypeople.
A śrāmaṇera or one undergoing training (śikṣamāṇā) may sit near [a fully ordained monk], provided there is a difficult circumstance; otherwise, it is an offense.

One who has no summer retreats (anupasaṃpanna) should not sit together with one who has three summer retreats. One who has completed one summer retreat must not sit together with one who has completed four summer retreats.
From the second summer retreat onwards, one may sit together with those who have completed three summers.
If the space in a layperson's house is cramped, there is no offense even if one sits together with one's upādhyāya. However, two persons should not lie down on the same bed.

There is no offense for one who possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame. If one is traveling on a journey, it is not an offense to lie down together provided they are separated by a large cloak or an intermediate robe.
The Sarvāstivādins say: "The establishment of the precepts is for the sake of the peace and happiness of those practicing the Path;
for the sake of nurturing faith and reverence; and for the sake of bringing the roots of goodness of the donors to fulfillment."
○ General Explanation of the Fifteenth Precept: Not Putting Away Bedding in a Sangha Dwelling.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise studied by those of the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of formal prohibition). *Vinayaviniścaya*.
It is said: This training rule was established due to the affliction of disrespect regarding matters of bedding and seating.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of this rule:
There was a visiting bhikṣu who spoke to a resident bhikṣu, saying, "I shall spread out bedding in a peripheral room and stay there overnight.

At another time, he did not inform him. The resident bhikṣu then departed. Consequently, the Sangha’s bedding became moldy and ruined; it was gnawed by insects and its color faded. At that time, the resident...
A resident bhikṣu did not see an incoming bhikṣu and assumed he had passed away or traveled far away. Upon entering the room to investigate, he saw that the bedding was rotten and ruined.
He reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha— whether spreading it himself or instructing another to spread it—
and when departing, neither lifts it up himself nor instructs another to lift it up, it is a pāyattika offense.

Explanation of the Terms: “Monastery quarters” (saṃghārāma) refers to the quarters belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions. “Quarters” (ārama) means that one may utilize them for the four modes of deportment (walking, standing, sitting, and lying down).

If one has spread out monastic bedding within the monastery quarters and then departs—whether by sitting or lying down—if there is a resident bhikṣu, a steward, or a *karmadāna*, one should say to them:
“Entrust this to me; keep it well and store it securely. (This refers to instructing another to put it away. If there is no one present therein...
One should entrust [the bedding] to another person. Without causing loss or damage, one should move the bed away from the wall and elevate its legs.
One should take the pillows, mattresses, and bedding, place them inside [the bed], cover them with other bedding, and then depart.
If there is fear that they might be damaged, one should take the bedding, woolen mats, and pillows and place them on a clothing rack, then stand the bed upright and depart (this is "self-lifting").
The conditions for the offense are the same as above.
Regarding the determination of the offense: herein, one who commits the offense does not employ such means and departs. If he goes outside the boundary, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot has gone outside the boundary and he returns in regret without proceeding further, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he intends to go...
If he does not depart, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If he returns immediately and does not remain outside the boundary for more than two nights,
and on the third night before the dawn has appeared, he either goes himself, sends a messenger, or informs his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the person in charge,
saying, "Please take care of this item"— if he does not do so, it is a *pāyattika* for a bhikṣuṇī.
A *pāyattika* offense; for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is what constitutes an offense.

Exceptions: There is no offense if one spreads bedding for the Saṃgha and, upon leaving after sitting or lying down, there is an original resident, a *māmaka*, or an administrator who says, "You must guard these items. If there is no such person... [text ends]
Regarding service to others: as described above, one should collect and depart. If the dwelling collapses, or is consumed by fire, or contains venomous snakes;
or if one is seized by thieves, tigers, wolves, lions, or those of great strength; or if one is bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If the time for his return is not long; or if he stays outside the boundary for two nights and departs before the dawn of the third night;
or if he sends a messenger to tell the resident monks, "Please take charge of this item";

or if the water or land routes are cut off due to all manner of difficult circumstances such that he cannot send a messenger by the third night—there is no offense in failing to take charge of the item. There is no offense in these cases.
Regarding the initial period before the precepts were established, etc.
○ A general explanation of the sixteenth precept concerning the forcible taking of lodging.
This is a common precept; the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same. It is studied in common with the Mahāyāna. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Out of self-conceit, one treats others with contempt, thereby giving rise to provocation and distress; due to matters concerning bedding and furniture, one gives rise to intolerance. For these reasons, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
The group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling on a road in Kosala.
Upon reaching a village where no bhikṣus resided, the group of seventeen said to the group of six, "You are our seniors; you should seek out a dwelling place first."
"We shall seek [a place] later," the group of six replied. "Go and seek; we will not seek a dwelling place.
Thereupon, the group of seventeen went to seek it and obtained a lodging where they spread out their bedding.
When the group of six learned of this, they went and said, "You should rise and stay according to the order of seniority. The group of seventeen did not consent, and the group of six...
While staying among the assembly, they spread out their sitting mats for the night. The group of seventeen [monks] spoke in a loud voice, saying, "Venerable sirs, do not do so.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept (the wording of which is as follows, except that the word "ignorant" is absent).

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether a place was one where others had already resided or not; later, they realized it was a place where others had already resided. Some then committed an offense of *pāyattika*.

Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense requiring confession): if there are those who are fearful and cautious, the Buddha said, "If one does not know [the rule], there is no offense. The precepts should be recited in this manner;
such is the established characteristic of the precepts.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, later arrives and forcibly spreads out bedding in the middle to stay overnight, thinking:
"If he finds it cramped, he will naturally avoid me and leave," and acts with such an intention for no other reason than this, it is an improper conduct; it is a *pāyattika*.
**Exegesis:** "Knowing that a previous bhikṣu occupies a dwelling place" means: a "previous bhikṣu" is one who was the first to spread out bedding and requisites;

it refers to a dweller who has been able to make use of a room or quarters throughout the four modes of deportment. "A latercomer forcibly spreads bedding and sleeps within [that space]" means: a "latercomer" is a bhikṣu who arrives after [the first].

The strong do not follow the wishes of others but instead bully them. As for those who are in the middle—whether lying at the head, at the feet, or at both sides of the bedding, such as a mat of grass, a mat of leaves, or even down to a simple ground-cover—one should reflect (forming this thought in the mind rather than speaking it):

"If they find it cramped or bothersome, they shall naturally avoid me and depart. (In that space, one should not sit or lie down recklessly, crowding others and causing them distress; if they find it cramped...)

One should withdraw of one's own accord; there is no need for verbal dismissal. Such causes and conditions refer to nothing other than [acts of] coercion, oppression, and disturbance (that is, creating causes and conditions of forceful harassment and disorder, rather than for any other purpose).
This constitutes improper conduct (*anairyāpathika*); whether sitting or lying down in a disordered manner, causing disturbance to others—all such acts fall within the category of improper conduct.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, knowing that another has already been residing there;
second, having a mind of intent to cause distress; and third, having forcibly spread out [the bedding] and finished.

**The Formal Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one knows that another has already obtained a dwelling place, yet later comes and forcibly spreads bedding within it, stays overnight, and lies down on their side upon the bed, it is a *pāyattika*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one comes later and sleeps upon another's bed, and that person is a senior elder (*sthavira*), one should say to them: 'Do you not know that the World-Honored One has established the precepts?'"
If a sleeping bhikṣu is of lower standing, he should be rebuked: "You do not properly understand the characteristics of the precepts;
how can you come later and sleep upon another's bed? If a bhikṣu is walking in meditation in another place and sees a bhikṣu coming first, he should move away.
When sleeping at night, even if one tosses and turns or speaks in one's sleep, one should not harbor a mind that causes disturbance.
There is no offense. According to the Sarvāstivādins: if one spreads [a mat] oneself, or causes another to spread it, for one who is able to spread it, it is a *pāyattika*;
for one who is unable to spread it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is the essence of this precept:

one must not forcibly contravene the wishes of another person when performing any action. If, for the purpose of annoying others, one closes a door or opens a door, or closes a window or opens a window... [and so forth].
To extinguish a fire; to extinguish a lamp; to chant *geya* or perform incantations; to recite scriptures or preach the Dharma;

or to engage in debate according to others' wishes—if one performs these acts without a desire to serve them, each constitutes a *pāyattika*. This offense is established solely because of the intention to annoy others.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; for the three junior groups [of nuns], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is what is called an offense. The exceptions: It is not an offense if one did not know beforehand; or if [the person] has already spoken and then stopped; or if the door was previously opened for them;
or if the door is wide and spacious so that there is no obstruction; or if a relative or old acquaintance says, "Just spread [your bedding] inside; I myself... [will take care of the rest].
One should inform one's master in the following cases: if one falls to the ground; if one turns over while ill; if one is overcome by a superior force; if one is imprisoned;

or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). There is no offense. There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, such as at the very beginning.
○ General Explanation of the Seventeenth Precept: Expelling Another from the Dwelling.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise studied in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Due to anger and resentment..."

Therefore, regarding the dwellings of the Saṅgha of the four directions, [the Buddha] formulated this training rule (śikṣāpada) on account of dragging others out [of their quarters], due to matters concerning bedding and furniture,
and the affliction of possessiveness.
This is the origin story (nidāna).
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There arose a certain occasion:
the group of six and the group of seventeen were traveling on the road in Kosala when they arrived at a small resting place. Seventeen.
The group of seventeen elders went to spread out bedding. The group of six replied, "Go yourself; what business is it of yours? The group of seventeen was delighted;
they entered the monastery cleanly and swept the rooms where wine was kept, making them pure, and spread out fine bedding for lodging.
When the group of six learned of this, they immediately entered and said, "Elders, rise and sit according to seniority. 10.
The group of seven was not yet satisfied. The group of six became angry and displeased; they forcibly dragged him out of the room. The group of seventeen raised their voices, crying, "Stop! Stop!
The bhikṣus in the neighboring rooms asked what was happening and learned the cause. They reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, does not wish for him to remain in the monastic dwelling, and either drags him out himself or instructs another to drag him out,
it is a pāyattika offense.
Explanation of the Terms: "Being angry with another and disliking them" means harboring resentment and displeasure toward someone with whom one shares a dwelling.

"Dragging [the person] out" means either pulling them by the mouth, or pulling them by the hand, or pulling them by both hands and mouth; this refers to doing it oneself or instructing another to do so.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, a bhikṣu who observes the precepts;
second, expelling him out of anger; third, within a monastic dwelling; and fourth, the person having exited the door.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one drags [the object] oneself, or instructs another to drag it, for every portion dragged, and according to the number of times it crosses the threshold, there is a *pāyattika* for each instance.
If one shuts another inside and leaves them outside the door, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one hurls an object outside the door, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one carries out another's belongings, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

*Dūṣkṛta*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: If one brings a person whom [the resident] dislikes to live in the same room with them, intending to cause that person to leave—whether they leave or not—it is all *duṣkṛta*. To drag out members of the other four assemblies is *duṣkṛta*.
If a *bhikṣuṇī* drags a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī* out, it is a *pāyattika*. To drag out members of the other three assemblies is [also a *pāyattika*].
It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one drags out a person who lacks shame or remorse, or if one drags someone out with the intent to subdue a disciple, there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda* school says: if one first forms the intention to kill and forcibly drags someone out, resulting in death, it is a *pārājika*;
if they do not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If one drags out a *bhikṣuṇī* with a lustful mind...

Regarding "grasping": it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one drags a bhikṣu out, and that bhikṣu clings to a pillar, grasps the door, or leans against a wall—if he is dragged away from each such place, there is a *pāyattika* for each instance.
If one scolds or rebukes him verbally to send the bhikṣu away, and he leaves each place in accordance with those words, there is a [pāyattika] for each instance."
*Pāyattika*. If one uses a means to drive [the person] directly out the door, one incurs one *pāyattika*.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a dwelling is on the verge of collapsing, there is no offense in pulling a sick person out.
If there is a bhikṣu who is quarrelsome and frequently violates the precepts, views, and proper conduct—if such a person is dragged out in anger, [there is no offense]. If...
If one lacks a virtuous mind, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If one drags out a pure *bhikṣu* from a place that is not a monastic dwelling, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If a person who has broken the precepts is driven out by the community, and he leans against a door or embraces a pillar, these parts should all be cut off and he should be pushed out.
Once the matter has been settled, the Sangha should [repair] the places where the limbs were severed.
If one repairs [the dwelling], or if it is done when a disciple or others pull [the offender] out of the room in hopes of reforming his evil ways, there is no offense.
However, one should not cause him to leave his place of residence. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pāyattika; for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions. There is no offense in the following cases: if one departs in due order without a mind of resentment;

if, after staying together for two or three nights, one sends away a person who has not received the precepts; if that person has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their dignified conduct;

if they have been formally accused by another; if they have been expelled by another; or if they are subject to expulsion due to a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and one drives them away.
For such persons as these, there is no offense. Regarding those who do not commit an offense, it refers to cases such as when the precepts have not yet been established.
As detailed in the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*: "If dragons or snakes should suddenly appear at one's dwelling place, one should snap one's fingers and say:"
"O worthy one, you should depart from afar; do not disturb the bhikṣu. If you do not leave, you should capture it with a soft object and carry it away;
do not bind it with hair-ropes or the like, lest it be injured. Release it calmly in a place overgrown with grass and weeds.
Wait until it has entered its hole, and only then depart. If you are discarding fleas, lice, or the like, you should do so upon old cloth."

Place it upon a cloth; observe its temperature and settle it accordingly. If such [a cloth] is unavailable, one should place it within a crevice in a wall or a hole in a pillar, allowing it to sustain itself naturally.
The Sarvāstivādins say: "This precept was established for the sake of not causing suffering to sentient beings and for the sake of extinguishing strife and contention."
○ General Explanation of the Eighteenth Precept Regarding Sitting on a Bed with Detachable Legs in a Multi-storied Pavilion.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise studied in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "Due to bedding..."
This training rule was established in response to the affliction of anger.
Regarding its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The origin of the incident:
Several bhikṣus were sitting on a multi-storied pavilion when the legs of their beds came loose.
As they sat uneasily, the legs of the thin beds beneath them gave way and fell upon a bhikṣu who was staying there. His body was injured and blood flowed; he lay looking upward.
[The Buddha] rebuked them with anger and abuse. When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. He rebuked them and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu, in a dwelling or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed that has removable legs, [he commits an offense].

*Pāyattika*. Explanation of the meaning: "Room" refers to either a communal monastic cell or a private room. Regarding "the upper story of a multi-storied building," this refers to standing such that one's head does not reach the ceiling.
Regarding "a bed with removable legs," the legs must be inserted into the frame (the legs being unstable; that is, having pointed legs shaped like pegs inserted into...).

"Descend from the middle. This refers to a bed with removable legs, known as a "bed with detachable feet. If one sits or lies down upon it (thereby completing the offense), the conditions for the violation are as follows:
this precept requires four factors to constitute the full offense: first, it must be a multi-storied building; second, the bed must have detachable legs;
third, there must be a person beneath the building; and fourth, one must sit or lie down upon the bed.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one sits or lies down on a bed with removable legs atop a multi-storied pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), such that the side of the body touches the bed as one turns over, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.

Excluding beds with removable legs, if one does so on a single-person sitting bench, a plank bed, or a bathing bench, it is in all cases a *dukkaṭa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* refers to this as a "pavilion."
If there is no one sitting below, there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda* school says: if the legs of the bed are not pointed, there is no offense;
even if they are pointed, if one sits or lies down without applying force, there is no offense. This precept must refer to a pointed-legged bed on an upper story.
If one sits on a bed or a seat in a place where the base is thin and sits or lies down with force, it is a *pāyattika*. Generally, regarding the method for a bhikṣu to sit:
if one is not careful in all respects, injury will inevitably occur, and furthermore, one’s dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) will be impaired; this constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; for the three groups of minor followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.

The exceptions (the conditions under which there is no offense): It is not an offense if one sits on a rope bed with curved legs, a rope bed with straight legs, a rope bed with bent legs, or a legless rope bed;
or if the supports of the bed are large; or if the legs of the bed have been removed and a crossbar (a horizontal strut) has been installed. Or...

If there is a wooden floor covering on that upper story, or if it is thickly covered, or if one sits with the legs of the bed tucked up, or if one sits having removed the legs of the bed, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept had not yet been formulated at the outset, and so forth.
○ A General Explanation of the Nineteenth Precept: Regarding Water Containing Insects Used for Sprinkling on Mud or Grass.
This is a shared precept; nuns are equally liable for its violation. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.
It is said: This training rule was established due to the affliction of a lack of compassion regarding the use of water. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions:
the locus of its origin and [the specific incident].
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
There arose a certain circumstance:
the Venerable Channa was constructing a large house and mixed the mud with water containing living insects; he then instructed others to do the same. The local elders were displeased.
[The Buddha] rebuked them, saying: "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack a heart of compassion; they harm the lives of sentient beings.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept. The bhikṣus did not know whether water contained insects or was free of insects;

later, when they realized it contained insects, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said: "If one does not know [that there are insects], there is no offense."
There is no offense. The precept should be recited as follows:

Regarding the established characteristics of the precept, if a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings, and he himself pours it over mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it, it is a pāyattika.

Explanation of the term *ti* (water). "Water" refers to water from ponds, rivers, or wells. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "Water (*shui*) means 'to level' (*zhun*); it levels objects. Its virtue is to moisten the myriad things; if settled, it is clear; if stirred, it is turbid;

if dammed, it stops; if breached, it flows. It possesses all eight kinds of merit. "With insects" (refers to the following): According to the *Vinaya-viniścaya*, one may perceive insects oneself, perceive them through another, or fail to perceive them. A guest... [text continues].

Living beings arise together with [the water]. There are generally two kinds of such beings: first, those seen with the eye; second, those caught by filtration. This applies even to the most minute living things. Water also includes fermented grain washes, vinegar, and other such substances; if they contain living beings, they must not be used.

Whether one personally applies mud or grass (as for "mud": it refers to grass-mud, *gao*-mud, elephant-dung mud, cow-dung mud, and so forth; as for "grass": this is a general term for the hundred species of plants, specifically referring to reeds, awns, and similar vegetation;
as for "applying" (*jiao*): it means to pour or drench, that is, to irrigate; whether acting on one's own behalf or instructing another to do so, all constitute an offense).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, that there are insects in the water; second, the perception that there are insects;
and third, personally instructing [another] to pour it out for use.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one knows that water contains living beings and throws grass or soil into it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Excluding water, if one pours worm-infested curd-milk, vinegar, or grain-soaking liquid onto mud or grass, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places soil or grass upon [water] containing living beings, it is likewise.

If one soaks [grain] in clear curd-milk, vinegar, or barley-gruel, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*. If there are insects in water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are insects in water but one suspects it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If there are no insects in water but one perceives them as such, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there are no insects in water but one suspects it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "By oneself..."
If one pours [water] over [an insect], it is a *pāyattika* for each individual [insect killed]. If one instructs another to pour [it], it is a *pāyattika* for each word spoken.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is a *pāyattika* for each individual insect that dies. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the three minor groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense in cases where one does not know there are insects; or where one perceives them as being without insects;

or where the insects are large and one removes them by touching the water with the hand; or where one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground—in all such cases, there is no offense. There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states in detail: "If a bhikṣu is constructing a dwelling and requires water—from a pond, a river, or a well—he must filter it until a vessel is full, and only after inspecting it to ensure there are no insects may he use it.
If there are still insects, he should use a double-layered filter and examine it closely. If there are still insects even after three layers of filtering, he should construct another well."

As previously observed with careful inspection, if there are still insects present, one should abandon the task at hand and go to another location. [One should consider that] the birth of insects is impermanent:
they may have been absent before and now exist, or they may exist now and later cease to be. For this reason, a bhikṣu should inspect daily;
only when no insects are found should he use the site. The Sarvāstivādins say: if one wishes to establish a place for dwelling, one should first...

Regarding the inspection of water: use fine cloth, one cubit in size, to make a water-strainer. Have one who is observant of the precepts and thorough in practice strain the water, and once strained, inspect it.
Hold the vessel toward the sun and examine it closely; if there are still insects present, one should make a water-strainer of triple-layered cloth.
If there are still insects present even after making a triple-layered water-strainer, one should not remain in that place.
○ A General Explanation of the Twentieth Precept Regarding Concealing a Transgression Beyond Three Days.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise studied by those of the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition). *Vinayaviniścaya*.
It is said: This training rule was established due to the afflictions of greed and pride regarding matters of dwellings.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Regarding the origin of the story: Channa was building a large house. After he had covered it once, there was still some straw remaining; he covered it again, yet more straw remained.

When he covered it for a third time, straw was still left over. Thinking that it would be difficult to search for more, he continued covering it without stopping until the roof collapsed. Thus it happened with the householder.
This was subject to criticism and censure. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.

The formulation of the rule is as follows: If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, including doors, windows, and other decorative furnishings, and directs others to thatch or roof it over; [he commits an offense].
[The construction] shall be limited to two or three layers. If it exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika*.

**Explanation of the Meaning:** Regarding "one who constructs a large dwelling": it involves the extensive use of materials (*sarvāstivāda* says thirty thousand coins; the *vinaya-vibhaṅga* says there are two kinds of "large" regarding a great residence:

first, large in physical dimensions; second, large in the value of the materials donated. This refers to being large in dimensions). As for the doors, panels, windows, and casements: a "door" (*hū*) is a place through which people enter and exit; one such opening is called a gate.

A *hu* (door). It is also said that the inner gate is called a *hu*. A *fei* (leaf) refers to a door panel. As for *chuāngyǒu* (windows), these are openings for the passage of light; those situated in a wall are called *yǒu*, while those in a roof are called *chuāng*. This also includes other decorative elements.

"Carved, engraved, painted, and decorated" refers to the instructions for covering [the roof]. There are two types of covering: longitudinal covering and transverse covering (*tshan* means a cover; it refers to thatching an object with woven *māṣa* grass).

According to the houses, towers, and pavilions constructed in the Western Regions, there are wooden-plank houses with flat roofs, walls plastered with lime, and roofs made of bricks, tiles, or thatched with *māṣa* grass, reeds, or wooden boards.

Their doors, windows, walls, and enclosures feature various marvelous designs and ornaments—paintings, carvings, and engravings—that are not of a single kind. The present phrase, "and other decorative implements," is a general designation for all these elements. Regarding "aligning the second and third joints": [this refers to the structural alignment of the thatch layers].

"Jie" (節) means "layers. However, one should stop at two or three layers of covering; exceeding this constitutes an offense. Therefore, it is said to be "two or three layers. There are slight discrepancies in the *Shiwén* (釋文) commentary on the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, which I suspect are errors in the translated text. The meaning is clear in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (五分律).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one reaches the fourth layer—whether covered with grass, tiles, or wooden boards—it is a *pāyattika* offense for each [layer].
(If one examines this meaning, there is no contradiction among the three sections; one incurs the offense upon reaching the fourth layer.)"
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the construction of a house is completed;
