second, the covering is not stopped; and third, the instruction for the completion of the covering is given.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, once two sections have been covered and the third section is not yet finished, if one does not go to a place where one is neither seen nor heard of, and the third section is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one leaves a place where one is heard of and goes to a place where one is seen, or leaves a place where one is seen and goes to a place where one is heard of, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūla* states: "If it is cooked..."
Whether using bricks, wood, or stone, or if the donor wishes for a rapid completion, there is no offense even if the weight exceeds the prescribed limit.
The Sarvāstivādins state: "In general, there are three grades of methods for constructing a dwelling—superior, middling, and inferior—and each has its own specific limit for the roofing method.
If one uses the roofing method of a middling or superior dwelling for an inferior dwelling, it is because of the excessive weight."
Because it is completed all at once (*sakṛt*). If one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika*.

If the upper chamber or above is covered according to the method [of construction], because it is likewise substantial, if one uses grass for the covering, for every blade of grass there is a *pāyattika*.
If it follows the method of covering according to the superior, middling, or inferior [grades], because it is completed all at once, there is one *pāyattika*. If it is not completed all at once...
When the wall of the enclosure is completed, there is no offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the three smaller groups, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
The exceptions: There is no offense if one has directed the work and two layers of thatching have been finished, and while covering the third layer, [the wall] has not yet been completed.

It is finished. If one reaches a place where there is neither sight nor hearing, where the paths of water and land are cut off, or due to all manner of difficult circumstances, and does not go to a place where there is neither sight nor hearing, there is no offense.
There is no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been promulgated at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Twenty-First Precept: The Rule Against Personally Going to Instruct Nuns.

This is an exclusive precept (asādhāraṇa-śīla); the formalities for its incurrence differ for nuns. In the Mahāyāna, bhikṣus study this together [with nuns], provided they necessarily observe the capacities of those to be trained.
One should know that there is great benefit in not committing this offense. Nevertheless, in these final ages of the Dharma, one must be especially cautious.
The Great Master Qingliang’s aspiration was that his feet should never tread upon the dust of a nunnery; he permitted it only when there was an urgent necessity, otherwise he did not allow it.

This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition). The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "This arises from a greedy desire for matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs, which invites public censure."
This training rule was established in anticipation of afflictions arising from specific conditions. Regarding the origin of this account:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. This was after they had completed their summer retreat.
Well-known to all, such as the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs headed by Mahāprajāpatī, were observing the rains retreat in the royal park at Śrāvastī.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to the place where the World-Honored One was and said to him:
I only pray that you will grant permission for the bhikṣus to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
When the World-Honored One grants permission for the senior bhikṣus to be appointed in turn to instruct the nuns and preach the Dharma, the Venerable Paṇḍa (also known as Śagata, or Paṇḍaka;
this means "born by the side of a small road," and is also translated as "Successor of the Path") shall go there. However, he has mastered only a single verse.
Those who enter into tranquility rejoice; seeing the Dharma, they obtain peace and happiness. In this world, freedom from ill will is the supreme joy;
not harming living beings is likewise so. In this world, freedom from desire is joy; renouncing craving and lust is so as well.
If one subdues the conceit of "I am," that is the foremost joy. Having spoken thus three times, he entered the four dhyānas three times. All the *arhats*...
The Chinese bhikṣuṇīs were all greatly delighted, while the group of six bhikṣuṇīs mocked and derided them with playful banter.
Thereupon, the Venerable One manifested supernatural powers and departed. This was the occasion for the arising of the narrative.
At that time, the group of six nuns went themselves to provide instruction, yet they did not preach the True Dharma;

instead, they spoke only of all manner of worldly treatises, even including jokes, dancing, and limping. The group of six nuns were greatly delighted, while the Arhat nun remained silent out of a spirit of reverence.
Mahāprajāpatī reported this to the Buddha, who then established the rule that the Saṃgha must appoint individuals to instruct the nuns.

At that time, the group of six [monks] said: "The Sangha has not appointed us to instruct the nuns. They then went outside the boundary and, appointing one another, went to provide instruction and admonition.
When the monks heard of this, they expressed their disapproval and reprimanded them, reporting the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha then established the rule: only those who have accomplished ten qualities may instruct the nuns. These are: (1) being fully endowed with the precepts; (2) being widely learned; (3) having recited the two... [the two codes].

(3) Profiting from the precepts of one's school; (4) Resolving matters with certainty and without doubt; (5) Being skillful in preaching the Dharma; (6) Having left the household life as a member of a noble clan.
(7) Her appearance is upright and handsome; when the community of nuns sees her, they rejoice. (8) She is capable of preaching the Dharma to the community of nuns and encouraging them to rejoice.
(9) Although she has not gone forth under the Buddha, she wears the dharma-robes and commits a grave offense.
(10) She is twenty years of age or older. Such as these may be instructed in the precepts for nuns; [the Buddha] established the precepts for the bhikṣus.
The established definition of the precept:
If a bhikṣu instructs or admonishes bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the *saṃgha*, it is a *pāyattika*. Explanation of the terms:

*Saṃgha* refers to those who share the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the same *karmavācanā*. "Without having been appointed" means that the *saṃgha* has not performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) [as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*].

This is called "not being appointed. If ten factors are not fulfilled, it is not called "appointing to the assembly"; it is not a valid *jñapti* (motion), it is not a valid *karman* (formal act), and because it is not valid, it is also not called "appointing. The *Mūla* states: One who possesses seven qualities should be appointed by the assembly to instruct the nuns:

(1) observance of the precepts; (2) extensive learning; (3) standing in the rank of seniority; (4) proficiency in the language of the capital city; (5) never having defiled a nun with one's body; (6) being well-versed in distinguishing the eight *pārājika* dharmas;

and (7) being able to skillfully explain the eight *gurudharma*s. Regarding the instructor, there are eight things that must not be transgressed. What are these eight? They are the nuns with eight hundred *varṣa*s (years of seniority).
(1) Upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, one should rise to meet him, inquire after his well-being, pay homage, and invite him to sit.
(2) A bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor must she slander him by saying that he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his dignified conduct.
A bhikṣuṇī must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu by saying, "What you have done is such-and-such," or "What you have done is improper."
In such cases, one may not state one's own case, nor may one obstruct another. One may not seek out offenses, nor may one obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Pravāraṇā*.
A bhikṣuṇī may not speak of the faults of a bhikṣu, though a bhikṣu may speak of the faults of a bhikṣuṇī (3).
Having trained in the training, a śikṣamāṇā shall request the full ordination from the Saṃgha (4). If...
(5) When a bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (saṃghāvaśeṣa), she must undergo *mānatva* for half a month within both communities (*ubhayasaṃgha*).
(6) Every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī must seek out a person to provide instruction from among the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).
(7) A bhikṣuṇī must not observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where there are no monks. When a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat, she must...
One should go before the community of monks and request three matters: [the confession of] what has been seen, heard, or suspected during the *pravāraṇā* (8).
These eight dharmas should be honored, revered, praised, and respected; for as long as one lives, they must not be transgressed. Why are these eight dharmas that cannot be violated taught?

It is because the Buddha’s maternal aunt and five hundred Śākya women requested permission from the Buddha three times to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*). When the Buddha did not grant it, fearing that the True Dharma would perish prematurely, Ānanda later petitioned him again and again until he finally consented. The Buddha then proclaimed the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*). Ānanda followed these regulations and disseminated them.

The women carried out these instructions; they are known as the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*). The bhikṣuṇīs honorably practice these eight dharmas. Because the True Dharma (*saddharma*) must not decline, the instruction is given every half-month. Furthermore, the Eight Rules of Respect are proclaimed so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sa po tuo lun) asks: "What is the difference between *anuśāsana* (instruction) and *avavāda* (teaching)?

It answers: "That which prevents what is unbeneficial is called *anuśāsana*; that which provides what is beneficial is called *avavāda*. Moreover, teaching one to abide in right mindfulness (*smṛti*) is called *anuśāsana*, while teaching one to abide in right awareness (*samprajanya*) is [called *avavāda*]."

Therefore, it is called "instruction" (*avavāda*). Even up to causing one to cultivate mundane wholesome dharmas, it is called "admonition" (*anuśāsana*); causing one to cultivate supramundane wholesome dharmas is called "instruction. This is merely the distinction between them.
The Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a mind of greedy seeking;
second, one goes uninvited; third, the words of instruction are clearly articulated.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: the bhikṣu should arrive at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇī should also go out to meet him at the appointed time.
If the bhikṣu does not arrive at the appointed time, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If the bhikṣuṇī does not go out to meet him when the time arrives, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If she hears that the instructor has arrived, the bhikṣuṇī should go out half a yojana to welcome him, provide for his needs, prepare bathing facilities, and offer him gruel and various kinds of food. If she fails to provide such offerings, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If she goes when the Saṃgha has not dispatched her, or on a day other than the designated day of instruction, she shall be given the eight points of non-transgression.
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If one goes to preach the Dharma when not appointed by the Saṃgha, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).
If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha is ill, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health.

If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha is not in harmony or the assembly is incomplete, one should still send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health. If one does not do so, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If...
If the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is ill, or if the assembly is not in harmony or incomplete, one must likewise send someone to pay respects and inquire after their well-being.

If one does not do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one does not dispatch someone to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, for every instance of failing to do so, it is a pāyattika offense.
To instruct other groups of two women is a duṣkṛta offense. If [the instruction is given by] the Bhikṣu Saṃgha..."
It is not permitted. To enter the dwelling place of nuns for the purpose of instruction, except when there is a valid cause, constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
A "valid cause" refers to the illness of a nun; this is called a valid cause.

If one enters the dwelling place of nuns for the purpose of instruction without being appointed by the Saṃgha, for every step taken inside, it is a *pāyattika*. If one foot has entered the door, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one does not recite the Eight Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) but first recites other dharmas, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one first recites the Eight Respectful Precepts and subsequently recites other dharmas, there is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"A bhikṣu should recite the bhikṣuṇī precepts so as not to let them be forgotten. Why? Because women are prone to forgetfulness and their wisdom is distracted. When I enter parinirvāṇa..."
After the Parinirvāṇa, the nuns shall inquire about the rules of training from the great assembly of monks. For the fourfold assembly to fail to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
this is called a transgression.
Exceptions: There is no offense in cases where the bhikṣus arrive at the appointed time and the nuns arrive at the appointed time to meet them, or even when they have prepared various offerings.
Various types of offerings. If the Saṃgha has appointed someone to deliver the eight rules that must not be violated;
or if the assembly of monks is ill, or the number of monks is incomplete, or the separate groups are not in harmony; or if one sends a messenger to pay respects;

or if a nun is ill, or the assembly is incomplete or not in harmony, she likewise sends a messenger to pay respects, inquire after the health of the Saṃgha, and offer greetings; or if there are obstacles on the water route, or any other such difficulties.

In cases such as these, there is no offense if one does not send someone else to pay respects or inquire after their health. There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one must not instruct nuns from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light. Not [to do so] is permitted.
One should go to a place that is secluded but not exposed; it should be a place that is neither too deep nor too exposed, such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree.
One must not go on the fourteenth, fifteenth, first, second, third, or fourth day of the lunar month;
one should go to provide instruction from the fourth to the thirteenth day. One must not instruct a community of nuns who are not in harmony.
Having arrived, one should ask whether the community of nuns is in harmony. If they say they are not in harmony, one should send a messenger to summon them.

If they cannot be brought, one should still provide the instruction; however, one must not provide the instruction in a partial manner, nor should one provide the instruction using long-winded speech.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-second Precept: Regarding the Instruction of Nuns Until Sunset.
This is an uncommon precept; it is not prescribed for nuns in the same way [as for monks]. It is studied by Mahāyāna practitioners alike to quell worldly censure and suspicion. Vinaya.
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: This training rule was established due to an incident involving censure.
As for the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The person who was the condition for his arising was the Venerable Nanda (the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: at that time, the cowherd Nanda stood leaning on a staff; hearing the Dharma taught by the Buddha from afar, he immediately attained realization and sought ordination from the Buddha, receiving full precepts.

At that time, he practiced with self-discipline in a secluded place and attained the fruit of Arhatship—this is not the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda). He was appointed by the Saṃgha to provide instruction.
The bhikṣuṇīs remained silent. Mahāprajāpatī said, "We wish to hear the Dharma; we pray that you will speak further for us.
After the Venerable One had taught them the Dharma, he remained silent. They requested him once more to teach the Dharma.
Nanda, with his beautiful voice, taught them the Dharma; the listeners delighted in hearing it, until finally evening fell. (From the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*)

The Saṃyuktāgama says: "The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra was dispatched by the Buddha to preach the Dharma and provide instruction to the community of bhikṣuṇīs. At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs heard the Dharma and attained the fruit of arhatship. The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya says:

"After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a king who erected a stūpa made of ox-head sandalwood, adorned with all manner of ornaments. This king had five hundred wives who made offerings to this stūpa, each making a vow, saying:

'In the future, may we attain liberation from this king. The king at that time was the present Nanda; the five hundred wives were the present five hundred bhikṣuṇīs. Due to the causal conditions of their original vows, they should attain liberation through Nanda. [Then] the bhikṣuṇīs departed from Jetavana.
The city gates were already closed, so they stayed overnight within the moats surrounding the city walls. At dawn, they entered the city ahead of the others.

The elders criticized and disparaged them, saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack pure conduct. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
The established definition of the offense:
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika. Explanation of the meaning:

"Appointed by the Saṃgha" means—as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*—that he has accomplished the ten qualities, the assembly is complete, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is accomplished, and the ritual procedure (*karman*) is accomplished; therefore, it is said that he has been "appointed by the Saṃgha. (From the Vinaya)

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Regarding the person appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, once they have been appointed, they shall instruct them for as long as they live; it is not necessary to appoint another.

To instruct the bhikṣuṇīs means to explain to them the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed, as well as other such dharmas. Regarding 'until sunset' (the *Vinayaviniścaya* states this indicates the limit: once the sun has set, it is called 'improper time.

Even if it is within the proper time, if the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs stands rather than sits, or if their busy activities have not yet ceased, or if their bodies are otherwise constrained, to preach the Dharma to them is also called 'improper time')."
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the person must be a fully ordained nun (bhikṣuṇī);
second, one must instruct her to recite the Eight Respectful Rules; and third, it must be past sunset.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one instructs a bhikṣuṇī until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*, except for the case of instruction.
If one receives, recites, or inquires about the meaning of the sūtras for her, or does so for other reasons, until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This excludes the case of a bhikṣuṇī; however, if one receives, recites, or inquires about the sūtras for other women, or inquires [about their meaning], [it is likewise a duṣkṛta].
[The meaning is as follows: If one arrives at another location due to other business until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:

regarding the cases of "sunset" and "perception of sunset," there are two heavy [offenses], two light [offenses], and two instances of non-offense. These are: if one preaches the Dharma throughout the night; or if the monastery gates are close together;
or if the city gates are not closed; or if both parties are within the same city; or if the community of nuns is in the house of a layperson. This...
None of these constitute an offense. For the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing);
this is what is called an offense. **Exceptions:** There is no offense in the following cases: if one instructs a *bhikṣuṇī* and stops before dusk;
except for women, if one recites, receives, or explains the meaning of the scriptures, or engages in other matters, for the sake of others; or at a ferry crossing.
Preaching the Dharma: It is not an offense for a nun to preach the Dharma while traveling with merchants at night; nor is it an offense if she preaches the Dharma within a nunnery;

nor is it an offense if she comes to a monastery to request instruction and happens to hear the Dharma being preached. There is no transgression in these cases. Those who are not guilty of an offense include those for whom the rule had not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-third Precept: The Precept Against Reviling and Slandering the Teaching for Nuns.

This is an exclusive precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); the regulations for nuns differ [from those for monks]. It is studied in common with the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of harboring..."
Out of a jealous mind, this training rule was established.
Regarding the origin of the rule:
while the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, a nun heard that her instructor was coming; she went half a yojana to welcome him and settled him in her quarters.
The vihāra, food and drink, bedding and seats, bathing facilities, and those who prepare the water for washing—
because the group of six monks did not assign these duties, they gave rise to a mind of envy and said: "There are no bhikṣus who instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
With a mind of truth, yet solely for the sake of food and drink, the bhikṣus heard of this and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus, "This bhikṣu teaches [the Dharma] for the sake of food and drink," [he commits an offense].
Regarding the term *bhikṣuṇī*: it is a *pāyattika* offense. Explanation of the meaning:

"For the sake of food and drink" (*Saṃghāṭi* states: "Food" refers to parched grain, flour, rice, fish, and meat; furthermore, there is food consisting of the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch).
"Instruction" refers either to the Abhidharma or the Vinaya.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the arising of a jealous mind;
second, speaking of providing instruction for the sake of food and drink; and third, speaking so that the meaning is clearly understood.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one says, "The bhikṣus teach the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," and so forth, up to:
"If they recite, receive, or inquire after the sūtras, and speak clearly, it is a pāyattika; if not clearly, [it is not]."

*Dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: If one says that [the instruction] was for the sake of making offerings, and thus instructs a bhikṣu or any of the other three assemblies, it is *dukkaṭa*.

If one says that a bhikṣu practices the twelve *dhūta* austerities, sits in meditation, recites sūtras, or performs various meritorious deeds—all for the sake of the benefit of making offerings—then for every such statement, it is *dukkaṭa*. (*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*)
It is said: If one says it was for the sake of medicine, one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the *vinaya*.
If one tells a bhikṣuṇī, saying, "That bhikṣu instructed you all for the sake of food and drink," one incurs an offense of *vyatikrama* against the *vinaya*.
If one says to the bhikṣuṇīs, "That bhikṣu instructs you for the sake of medicine," one incurs a *vyatikrama-citta-āpatti* (an offense of transgression involving mental regret).
For the four assemblies of nuns and others, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: when the matter is actually so; when it is for the sake of food and drink; when instructing a bhikṣuṇī;

when, for the sake of food and drink, one teaches the recitation or receiving of the sūtras; when speaking in response to a question; when speaking in jest; when speaking to oneself; when speaking in a dream; when intending to say this but mistakenly saying that.
There is no offense in the case of those who were not yet subject to the rule because it had not yet been promulgated at the outset.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Do not envy the offerings given to others; do not exalt your own gains; rather, within these circumstances, subdue your mind.
Constantly examine your own faults and do not speak of the shortcomings of others. Master Kumārajīva said: "Suppose there was a bhikṣu sitting in meditation in a forest.
When it was time for his meal, he took up his bowl and left the forest. On the road, he encountered wicked bandits who led him [away]."

He shot him with an arrow. The bhikṣu, having become angry, reproached himself for not having given rise to an evil thought. He then pointed to his belly and said to the bandit, "You should shoot this;
it was because of this that I led you out of the forest and caused you such distress. This is merely the fault of my belly.
To examine oneself and show leniency toward others is exemplified by this.
○ General Explanation of the Twenty-fourth Precept: Receiving Robes from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.
This is a precept not shared [with other classes]; it is not formulated for nuns, nor is it common to the Mahāyāna, because [in the latter] one trains for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Nevertheless, in the age of the Final Dharma, one must exercise careful scrutiny. The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "Because it leads to public censure, this training rule was established.
This precept is formulated through the convergence of three conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].

There was a bhikṣu who begged for alms and was fully endowed with dignified deportment. A certain bhikṣuṇī, upon seeing him, conceived a virtuous mind and repeatedly invited him [to her home], but the bhikṣu did not accept.
On another occasion, when the Saṃgha was distributing clothing and requisites, this bhikṣu took his portion and went out the door.
Seeing the bhikṣuṇī approaching, he gave it to her immediately, thinking that she would not accept it; however, the bhikṣuṇī took it nonetheless.
The bhikṣus repeatedly censured that bhikṣuṇī in the presence of others. When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha.

The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept, forbidding the giving of robes to bhikṣuṇīs. Consequently, all the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to give robes to their own relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to give robes to bhikṣuṇīs who are your relatives. He then added the three characters "non-relative" [to the rule], at Jetavana.
The two divisions of the Saṃgha were dividing the robes and articles together. The two groups mistakenly received the nuns' robes and attempted to exchange them, but the bhikṣus did not approve.
The Buddha said: "If they are being traded, it is permitted. The precept should be recited as follows:"
The established definition of the precept:
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for it, it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning (as in the thirty matters).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept is completed as a full offense when three conditions are met: first, the nun is not a relative;
second, it is not an exchange of goods; and third, she has already received the item.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, giving a robe to a nun who is not a relative—except in exchange for trade—is a *pāyattika*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one gives a robe to a relative nun who has broken the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
To give clothing to more than two nuns who are not one's relatives is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if one gives clothing of the proper measure, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if one gives clothing or articles that are not of the proper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "If a nun has been robbed by thieves and is currently lacking clothing, there is no offense even if one gives to her, provided she is not a relative."
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is what is called a transgression.
Regarding the exceptions: there is no offense for those who trade robes with kinsmen, or give them to a stūpa, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha.
There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been promulgated at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Twenty-fifth Precept: Making Garments for a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.

This is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*); nuns are not subject to the same regulation. It is studied in common with the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states that it was established because...
Out of censure and reproach, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
Regarding the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of this rule:
There was a bhikṣuṇī who wished to have a saṃghāṭī robe made. She went to the monastery and said to Kālodāyin, “Venerable Sir, please make a robe for me.
He replied, “You come here repeatedly and urge me on; therefore, I am unable to make it.”
The nun said, "I did not urge you; when it is finished, give it to me. She immediately cut the cloth for her and fashioned an image of a man and woman engaged in sexual intercourse.
When the nun came to collect the garment, she folded it and gave it to her, saying, "You must not rashly open it and wear it, nor show it to others.
You shall wear it when the time comes, walking behind the assembly of nuns. The nun followed these instructions and immediately put it on, walking behind.
When the laypeople saw this, they laughed loudly. Mahāprajāpatī asked about the reason for this and informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept, forbidding [bhikṣus] from making robes for bhikṣuṇīs.

Consequently, all the bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to make robes for their own relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha said: "In the case of a relative, there is no offense. One should..."
Thus the precepts are proclaimed.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense.
Explanation of Terms: "One who makes robes" (the maker refers to one who cuts and sews; the robes refer to the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsa*).
**Conditions for Offense:** This precept requires two conditions to constitute the full offense: first, that the nun is not a relative; second, that one sews it with one's own hands.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative, [the offense is incurred] according to the cutting of the fabric.
For every portion cut, it is a *pāyattika*. For every single stitch sewn, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if one spreads it out to inspect it, pulls it, irons it, rubs it with the hand, or grasps the corners to pull it straight and smooth it out;
or if one [uses] a border, a cord, or joins a thread—these are all *dukkaṭas*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "To take up the robe is a *dukkaṭa*."
Duskṛta. When cutting and when dyeing, it is all a pāyattika. When sewing, for every stitch it is a pāyattika.
For the four groups of nuns and so forth, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions: There is no offense in the following cases: if one makes [a garment] for a relative nun; if one makes it for the Saṃgha or for a stūpa;

if one borrows another’s robe, washes, dyes, or repairs it, and returns it to the owner—there is no offense. Those who have no offense include those for whom the precept has not yet been promulgated at the outset, and so forth.
○ A General Explanation of the Twenty-sixth Precept: Sitting in Private with a Bhikṣuṇī.
This is a precept not shared [with other vehicles]. The offenses for bhikṣuṇīs differ; it is studied equally by the Mahāyāna. It is to guard against worldly censure and suspicion. Vinaya.
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: This training rule was established because [the monks] incurred censure and slander.
Regarding the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of this matter:
Kāḷudāyin and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā both harbored lustful intentions. They sat together in one place outside the gate.
When the lay devotees saw them, they all felt resentment and said to one another, "Look at this!"
These two people sat together like a husband and wife, or like a pair of mandarin ducks. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept.
The characteristics of the established rule are as follows:
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense. Explanation of the meaning:
"Sitting in a secluded place" means one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī. "Secluded place" means a place hidden from sight or a place hidden from hearing.
A "place hidden from sight" refers to a place where there is dust, mist, smoke, clouds, or darkness.
"Not seeing" means not being able to see [the person]. "Hearing in a secluded place" refers even to a location where the sound of ordinary conversation cannot be heard.
Regarding the conditions for an offense: this precept requires three factors to constitute the full offense: first, a secluded place; second, the absence of a wise person;
and third, sitting with one's body in close proximity.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.
If she is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a duṣkṛta. If they remain standing, it is a duṣkṛta.

The *Saṃghīti* states: "If a nun invites a bhikṣu to a meal, and one nun sits together with the bhikṣu while another bhikṣuṇī comes and goes to serve food, when the nun serving food departs, the bhikṣu follows her; for each instance, he incurs a pāyattika.
The *Pañcavargika* states: "Sitting together with two other women [who are not nuns] also constitutes a pāyattika. The *Sarvāstivāda*...
If it is mostly cloudy, having walked for meditation (caṅkrama), one returns to sit; this is a pāyattika offense. For every time one rises and returns to sit, one incurs that many pāyattikas.
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion; or if there is a wise person present;
or if while walking he suddenly falls to the ground; or if he falls while suffering from illness; or if he is overcome by force; or if he is imprisoned; or if his life is in danger.
The Brahma-faring is difficult. There is no offense. One who commits no offense includes those for whom the precepts have not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.
○ The twenty-seventh [offense], traveling together with a nun, is explained in general as follows.
This is an unshared precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); nuns do not commit this offense together. It is studied equally by those of the Mahāyāna.

This is an offense of transgression (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because of the cause of public censure, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of three conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
The group of six monks and the group of six nuns were traveling through the human realm of Kosala. When the laypeople saw them, they all complained about them together.
The bhikṣus heard of this and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept, forbidding them from traveling with bhikṣuṇīs.
Consequently, the bhikṣus did not previously make an appointment with the nuns; when they encountered them on the road, they were apprehensive and did not dare [to travel together].
[They] traveled together. The Buddha said: "If there was no prior agreement, there is no offense. [The text] further adds the two characters "prior agreement" (*sāṃketa*).
Subsequently, many bhikṣus set out from Śrāvastī intending to go to Vaiśālī; at that time, many bhikṣuṇīs were also traveling there, wishing to travel with them.
Because the Buddha had established the precepts, they did not dare to travel together. The bhikṣus went ahead while the bhikṣuṇīs followed behind;
they were plundered by bandits and lost their robes and bowls. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "The precepts should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu travels along the same path with a bhikṣuṇī from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The "appropriate times" are: when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or dread; these are called the appropriate times.
At that time, regarding the explanation of the term "appointment" (*kāla*): it means making a mutual agreement to go together to a certain village, city, or country (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"As for a mutual appointment, it may be today, tomorrow, half a month, or one month"). They travel together along the same path (this is the general heading; the following is the specific explanation). As for "path": it refers to the space between villages.

There is a delimited range for travel (the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya* states: "The traveler" refers to three *yojanas*, two *yojanas*, one *yojana*, or one *krośa*). This excludes "other times" (which refers to permissions granted within prohibitions).

Traveling with merchants (merchants refers to those on a caravan; the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "A caravan" means that if one leaves this company, there is no way to proceed on the road; for this reason, the Noble One granted this exception, setting aside other circumstances.

Therefore, regarding the practice of traveling together: the *bhikṣuṇī*s' food should be carried by the *bhikṣu*s. When it is time to eat, they should pass it back and forth to one another. If there is a sick *bhikṣu*, they should carry him away together. If a person...

Regarding those who are young: the *bhikṣuṇīs* should also assist in carrying [the sick person], but they should remain at the head and not near the feet. If they reach a village, they should seek out medicine according to the needs of the illness. This should be understood to apply similarly if a *bhikṣuṇī* is ill.
This is called "at another time."
The Conditions for Offense: This precept constitutes a full offense when three conditions are fulfilled: first, there is a mutual agreement of intent;
second, they set out together on foot; and third, they reach the boundary of a village.
**The Determination of the Offense:** In this context, the offense is as follows:
traveling along the same path with a bhikṣuṇī, even up to the boundary of a village—according to the number of people or the extent of the boundary—constitutes a *pāyattika* for each instance.
If they travel through an uninhabited area outside a village for a distance of ten *li*, it is a *pāyattika*. If the distance is less than a village or less than ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one travels through the same boundary between many villages, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes preparations with the intention of going, such as arranging one's ornaments together, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* states:

"If traveling with a companion in a carriage, when stopping to rest or setting out, one calls for the nun to come so that she does not fall behind the group; one who speaks these words commits a *pāyattika*."
If one says, "Go, go," to a sister so that she does not lose her companions, there is no offense. A bhikṣu was traveling along a road with some merchants.
The merchants entered a village first, while the bhikṣu did not know the proper way to travel on the road. Seeing a bhikṣuṇī, he asked her:
If a sister says, "Show me the way," it is termed a mutual appointment (*sāṃketa*). If a nun raises one foot [to walk], she incurs a *vyatikrama* offense;
if she raises both feet, it is a *pāyattika*. As for saying, "Go and show me the road," there is no offense.

If, within a village, one is invited by a lay donor (*dānapati*) to eat but does not know the location of that donor’s house, and upon seeing a nun asks, "Do you know the location of such-and-such a donor’s house?
and she says, "Come and I will show you the way," this constitutes a formal appointment (*samaya*).

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept: "One is not permitted to travel on the same boat with a nun. The bhikṣus did not anticipate [this situation].

They were all traveling on a single boat and were all cautious and apprehensive. The Buddha said, "One should not expect to be free from transgression. Later, many bhikṣus wished to cross the Ganges River.
There were also many bhikṣuṇīs who likewise wished to cross the Ganges; however, because of the precept established by the Buddha, they did not dare to cross with the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs yielded to the bhikṣus, allowing them to cross first. Once the boat reached the opposite shore, a heavy rain fell and the waters rose. Before—
While they were returning, the day had already grown dark. The nuns stayed overnight on the bank, where they happened to be robbed by bandits.
The Buddha said: "There is no offense for those who cross directly; the precept should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī make an appointment to board the same boat together to travel upstream or downstream—
except in the case of crossing directly across— it is a pāyattika.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** "Upstream and downstream" (referring to going upstream against the current and downstream with the current; except for crossing over, it constitutes an offense).
**Conditions for the Offense:** This precept fulfills two conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be a mutual agreement;
second, both feet must enter the boat.

**The Determination of the Offense:** In this context, the offense occurs when one makes a mutual agreement to board the same boat for traveling upstream or downstream, excluding the case of merely crossing over.

If one enters the interior of the boat, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). If one foot is on the boat and one foot is on the ground, or if one employs the means to enter but does not actually enter, or if one agrees to adorn [the boat] together, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). *Sā* (End of section).
Bāhudantīya: To consult with a nun regarding boarding a boat is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one bhikṣu agrees with one nun to board a single boat together, it is a *pāyattika*; this applies up to boarding a single boat with four nuns.
Regarding the four *pāyattika* offenses: according to the number of nuns, one incurs as many *pāyattikas* as there are nuns.
If four bhikṣus board a single boat with one nun, each incurs one *pāyattika*; likewise, it is according to the number of nuns that one incurs as many *pāyattikas*.
[The same applies if] one makes an appointment to travel with a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī.

[Traveling] on the same boat. [Traveling] as a group (also a *pāyattika*). If a nun and a bhikṣu are each on separate boats, yet have made an appointment together and there is no layperson accompanying them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If they have not made an appointment, they must ensure that their voices cannot be heard by one another;
if they can be heard, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For the nuns and the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what constitutes an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: if there was no prior agreement; if one simply crosses to the other shore;

if the boatman loses control while going upstream or downstream; if one is held by force; or if one is threatened with danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these instances, there is no offense.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If the oars, paddles, or rudder break and one drifts with the current; or if one avoids a sandbank or shoal; or if the helmsman does not follow one's instructions—in all these cases, there is no offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one intends to cross straight across but is carried away by the water, there is no offense.
Those who do not commit an offense include those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.

If there is no second teacher, one should inform the senior monk (upādhyāya) and entrust all bedding and requisites to him for protection.
One should also announce this to all traveling companions so that no one abandons a sick person and departs.
When leaving the gate, they should say to one another: "Today we must not have any omissions; we should not be negligent regarding our caravan."

When traveling, one should promote both good and evil [awareness] so that neither is neglected or abandoned. Regarding one's own companions, if there is mutual attachment or if there is enmity between them, they should not travel together.
If there is a necessary reason for traveling together, one should first perform an act of *kṣamāpanā* (asking for forgiveness) and then go with them.
Whenever traversing a road, one should engage in discourse on the Dharma and must not utter evil words; alternatively, one may maintain noble silence.
Nevertheless, do not allow the mind to become distracted. If you arrive at a temple or shrine of a deity, recite a Buddhist verse (*gāthā*) and proceed while snapping your fingers.
A bhikṣu should not make offerings to deities. If you must pause briefly along the way, [act accordingly].

Whenever one goes to a spring or pond to fetch water, one should recite a gāthā. At the place where one stays overnight, one should recite the Threefold Salutation (Triskandhaka), adjust one's own deportment, and inquire about the location for lodging.

This is a precept not shared with the monks; the offenses for nuns differ [from those for monks]. It is likewise established in the Mahāyāna, as it constitutes a wrong livelihood.

She spread out a fine seat and prepared the necessary provisions.

The nun invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. She said, "The householder has invited men of low station.
Had he first spoken to me, I would have invited the 'Dragon among Dragons' for him. He asked, "Who is the Dragon among Dragons?
The nun replied, "Venerable Devadatta and others are such. At that moment, the two venerable ones arrived, and the nun spoke to the householder.
He said, "The dragon among dragons has arrived. The householder said, "Just now you called him a lowly person;
why do you now call him the 'dragon among dragons'? From this day forward, do not come to my house again.

After the two venerable ones had finished eating, they returned to the saṃghārāma. The Buddha, knowing this, asked them intentionally: "Today you accepted an invitation for a meal; did you obtain it?"
"Is it sufficient? He replied, "Although the food is sufficient, I am both a lowly person in the householder's home and a dragon among dragons.
When the Buddha questioned him and learned the reason for this, he rebuked the faction of Devadatta.
The precept has already been established: if one sends a bhikṣuṇī to solicit alms and thereby obtains food, it is a pāyattika offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether there had been solicitation or not; later they realized there had been solicitation.
Some performed the confession for a pāyattika offense, while others remained doubtful. The Buddha said: "If you did not know, there is no offense. In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great...
"Householder, this is a friend of Risi-datta. He has said:
'If Risi-datta comes to the city of Rājagṛha, I shall, for the sake of Risi-datta, provide offerings to the Saṃgha. A nun heard these words."
He remained silent within his heart. On another occasion, when the Venerable One entered the city, the nun heard of it and went to inform the householder.
He immediately sent a messenger to invite the Venerable One and the community of monks for a meal. Upāli asked, "How did you know that I had come here?"
The householder said, "This is what my family provides for our offerings. When the nun saw this, she said to the Venerable One, "If that is so, I should not eat.
The householder said, "I am not providing this meal based on the words of this nun; I have made a vow previously. The Venerable One said:
"Even though these words were spoken, I should not eat it either. He immediately desisted from eating and went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"If the donor had prior intention [to give], there is no offense. You should follow the rules as they have been taught."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause and condition of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise and exhortation, eats it—

Explanation of the Terms: Praising the Teacher and the One Who Converts Others.

These include those who dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*), those who beg for alms (*piṇḍapātika*), those who wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*), those who practice the ritual for leftover food (*khalupaścādbhaktika*), those who eat only once a day (*ekāsanika*), those who eat only a single morsel (*kavalikārāhārika*), those who sit at charnel grounds (*śmāśānika*), those who sit in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), those who sit beneath trees (*vṛkṣamūlika*), those who remain seated constantly (*naiṣadyika*), those who sit wherever they happen to be (*yathāsaṃstarika*), those who maintain the three robes (*traicīvarika*), those who recite verses of praise (*dharmakathika*), those who are learned in the Dharma (*bahuśruta*), those who uphold the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), and those who practice meditation (*dhyānin*). (From the *Śāstra*)

It is said: To praise their meritorious virtues is called *zan* (praise); yet even such praise is insufficient, and thus it is further termed *tan* (extolling). From dawn until midday, one may obtain food (there are five types of *bhojana*, or "proper foods," and five types of *abhyavahāra*, or "improper foods," which will be explained in the subsequent text).

This excludes cases where a donor has previously formed the intention (the *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: this means that if a donor first conceived the thought of preparing food and drink intending to give it to that person, even if one subsequently praises them for their observance of the precepts and great learning, there is no offense, as the praise was heard [after the fact]).
[He] sighed and subsequently refused to eat. Therefore, it is further stated: "Except when there was prior intent. Regarding the conditions for an offense:
this precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, a *mahābhikṣuṇī* must offer praise;

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one knows that food was obtained through the teaching of a bhikṣuṇī and eats it, for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*.
Apart from this food and drink, if one obtains other items—such as undergarments, lamp oil, or oil for anointing the feet (the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"The heels here are connected to the channels of the eyes; by pouring oil into the nose and anointing the feet, one can cause the eyes to become clear and bright")—all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs while perceiving that one is instructing, it is a *pāyattika*. If one instructs while suspecting that one is instructing, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one does not instruct while perceiving that one is instructing, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one does not instruct while suspecting that one is instructing, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargika* says:
If one obtains food by means of praising the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, even if one instructs [the donor] to place a small amount of ginger in the food and the bhikṣu eats it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding this precept, if one merely praises their virtues unilaterally, whether the eater is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or an *arhat*, eating the food constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. If not...

however, for the fourfold assembly including bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a duṣkṛta (offense of wrong-doing). This is what is called an offense.
