○ General Explanation of the Thirty-First Precept: Against Receiving Food More Than Once.
This is a shared precept; the regulation for nuns is identical. It is likewise observed by the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Because of staying overnight..."

Because [monks] accepting invitations for meals incurred public reproach, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated based on two conditions: the setting of the origin and the specific incident.
Regarding the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, there was a village without a permanent residence in the kingdom of Kośala, where a householder lived.
A dwelling was built for the bhikṣus, and they were constantly provided with food and drink. It was permitted for those residing there to eat only one meal per day.
A group of six bhikṣus went to that dwelling and stayed for one night; because they obtained excellent and delicious food and drink, they remained for a second [night].
He stayed overnight and again obtained fine food. He ate there repeatedly at that dwelling place, which caused the householder to criticize and resent him.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept. At that time, Śāriputra went to that same place for one night;

the next morning he obtained excellent food and fell ill there. Remembering the precept established by the World-Honored One, he immediately supported himself as he was ill and departed, but his illness subsequently increased.
[This was] a case of extreme urgency. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I allow sick bhikṣus to receive food in excess. The precept should be recited as follows.
This is the established formulation of the precept."
If there is a place where a bhikṣu is offered a single meal, a bhikṣu who is not ill should eat only that one meal. If he accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning: "A place where a single meal is offered" refers to eating at such a place for one night; this includes even [meals taken during] the proper time.

Regarding the sick person: it refers to one whose condition worsens upon leaving that village (the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states: "In the case of a sick person, even a wound caused by a bamboo leaf constitutes [an offense]; for one who is not sick, to accept [food] beyond [the limit] constitutes a transgression").
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the condition of being without illness;
second, receiving food in excess; and third, the food having already entered the throat.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a monk who is not ill accepts food at that single meal site beyond the permitted limit, for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
Apart from food, if he further accepts other items such as undergarments, lamp oil, or oil for rubbing the feet, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one stays overnight and does not eat, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one stays overnight in another place and eats here, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one stays overnight in another place and eats here, one incurs a *pāyattika*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the three groups of minor disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is defined as an offense."
The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: receiving food for one night; receiving food while ill;
or if a householder invites one to stay, saying, "I shall provide you with food; we have prepared this lodging and supplied these meals for the sake of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
Even if the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, do not arrive, I shall still give it to others. Or if a donor [invites them] in regular succession.

If one accepts an invitation to eat, or if children, daughters, sisters, or daughters-in-law invite one to eat in succession, or if one eats beyond the limit due to all manner of difficult circumstances or other such reasons, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Thirty-second Precept on Successive Eating (Paryāya-bhojana).

This is an exclusive precept; nuns do not commit the offense together with [monks]. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense by prohibition). According to the Vinaya...
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: "This precept was established due to the afflictions of excessive indulgence in food, neglect of duties, lack of tranquility, and public reproach;
it is formulated through the conjunction of three conditions."
The Setting of the Discourse:
The Buddha departed from Rājagṛha and traveled among the people. At that time, the world was suffering from a famine and grain was expensive; it was difficult to obtain almsfood.
There was a Śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa who, with five hundred wagons fully laden with food and drink, followed [the Buddha] through winter and summer.
They followed the World-Honored One, waiting for an opportunity to present offerings, yet there was not a single day that was free.
Ānanda informed the Buddha on their behalf, and the Buddha said to Ānanda, "You may go and tell the brāhmaṇa: 'Tomorrow morning, prepare gruel with these provisions.'"
After the meal, when it was time for the monks to receive their food, a brahmin observed that none of the offerings contained cakes.
He immediately prepared various kinds of gruel and cakes to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha. The Buddha said, "There are five benefits to eating gruel:
it effectively relieves hunger, relieves thirst, digests food from previous meals, regulates the flow of feces and urine, and alleviates ailments caused by wind. Thus he dwelt.
When the gentlemen heard that the Buddha had permitted the Sangha to eat gruel and cakes, they were all greatly rejoiced and became patrons.
There was one minister of little faith who, seeing the Buddha and the Sangha receiving such great offerings, spoke thus: "This is not right."
Regarding those with few fields of merit: they prepared rich and delicious food and invited the Saṃgha.
At that time, the various lay devotees of Ānapiṇḍada immediately prepared various kinds of gruel that very night and sent it to the monastery; the monks first ate the thick gruel.
Later, he went to the house of a high minister. He was unable to eat much, which the minister resented. "For the sake of the assembly of monks, I have prepared various kinds of fine food;
why do you first eat thick gruel before receiving my meal? The minister spoke thus in anger and resentment to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. There was also a minor musician in the city of Rājagṛha whose situation was the same.
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣus, he established a precept: "I do not permit successive meals (paryāya-bhojana).
However, at the places where sick bhikṣus were invited to eat, there was no food or medicine appropriate for their illnesses.

Even when such appropriate food and medicine were present, they feared and hesitated to eat it, worrying that they might commit the offense of taking successive meals. The Buddha said: "I permit sick bhikṣus to take successive meals. Hereafter...
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide a meal as an offering. Another householder also invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide a meal and robes as offerings.
The bhikṣus, being apprehensive and cautious, informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "There is no offense when giving robes.
The precept should be recited in this manner."
The established characteristic of the precept is as follows:
If a bhikṣu eats in succession (transfers his meal), except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense. The appropriate times are: when one is ill, and when robes are being distributed.
This is called "other times. Explanation of the meaning:

"Successive eating" (krama-bhojana) refers to being invited. There are two kinds of invitations: an invitation by turn of the monastic community (*saṃgha-krama*) and a private invitation (*pṛthak-nimantraṇa*).

Regarding "eating": it refers to rice, parched grain flour, dry cakes, fish, and meat. "Successive" means that having eaten at this house, one eats again at another place. This does not apply to those who are ill.
One is able to eat in a single sitting and ensure that food is sufficient. Regarding the gift of robes:

after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, there is a period of one month if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, and five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread. Furthermore, if there are other times when food and robes are offered as gifts...
If one receives many invitations for meals on a single day, one should accept one invitation for oneself and give the remainder to others, saying:
"Venerable sir, I shall go there; I now bestow this upon you" (this refers to giving only the food, not the robes).
The Root Text says: "Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a road, and the time of receiving robes.
These are the [permissible] times (this constitutes an exception to the general prohibition, specifically opening up these times).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, not relinquishing multiple invitations;
second, it being actual food; and third, the food having entered the throat.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one does not relinquish a prior invitation and accepts food from a subsequent invitation, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.
If one does not relinquish a subsequent invitation and accepts food from a prior invitation, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every swallow.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a sick bhikṣu cannot be satisfied at one place of invitation, he should accept a second invitation.
If he cannot be fully satisfied at the second place, he should accept a third invitation. If he is not yet satisfied at the third place, he should eat gradually after having accepted it;
however, until midday, he must not accept a fourth invitation. It is permitted to receive invitations repeatedly on festival days."
Regarding food: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that Ānanda had previously accepted an invitation from another, but he forgot it and did not remember it.
Later, while accompanying the Buddha, he accepted an invitation from King Prasenajit. As he was placing the food in his mouth, he remembered that there were two invitations.

Fearing that he would not give the other invitation to someone else, he did not dare to spit out the food out of respect for the Buddha; yet, fearing that he would violate his vow of upholding [the precepts], he did not dare to swallow the food either.
Because of his observance of the precepts, the Buddha knew that Ānanda’s heart was filled with remorse. He told him to keep it in mind and give it to another for them to eat.

Upāli asked the Buddha, "May others also do so? The Buddha said, "Except for five types of people: first, those practicing dhyāna (because they are single-mindedly absorbed in meditative concentration);

second, those living in seclusion (because there is no one present with whom to speak); third, those traveling on long journeys (because they are in haste on the road and may easily forget things, making it difficult to speak with them); fourth..."

Regarding those with chronic illnesses (those suffering from long-term ailments whose physical forms have become emaciated), they may reside with their kinsmen during the five periods of hunger (as no bhikṣus are present before them); all other cases are prohibited.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one has previously accepted an invitation for [monks] without robes, and subsequently accepts an invitation for [monks] with robes [it is not permitted]."
There is no offense. If one says to a bhikṣu, "Eat here; I shall seek clothing for you," there is no offense in eating.
If one says to a bhikṣu, "Eat here; you may go elsewhere as you please," there is no offense in eating. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

If, whether in a single dwelling, within a monastery, or in a forest hermitage (āraṇya), one eats frequently for the sake of seeking plumpness and vigor, or out of a fondness for fine food, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If one does not eat out of a spirit of contempt or with a mind of hypocrisy and deceit, one likewise incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
For the fourfold assembly of nuns and others, it is an offense of transgression (dukkaṭa). This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when it is the time for the distribution of robes;
if there are many invitations on a single day, one accepts one invitation and gives the others to others; if the invitation is for non-food; if the food is insufficient;

if there is no food provided at the invitation; if after having eaten one obtains more food; or if in a single location there is both a morning meal and an afternoon meal. In these cases, there is no offense.
Regarding the transgressor: this refers to the period before the precept was first established, and so forth.
○ A general explanation of the thirty-third precept concerning eating in a separate group.
This is a common precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise established in the Mahāyāna. This is an *āpatti* of transgression (*prajñapti-āpatti*).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This training rule was established because of Devadatta. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of eight conditions.
The setting of the causal origin:
The Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain. The person who gave rise to the occasion [is as follows].
Devadatta instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited King Ajātaśatru to kill his father.
His evil reputation spread far and wide, and his offerings and gains were cut off. He then went with five of his own followers from house to house to beg for food.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept forbidding eating in a separate group. At that time, there were sick bhikṣus who had been invited to a meal, yet [the rule] did not...

He obtained food and medicine appropriate for his illness; however, as there was excellent food and medicine suited to his condition, he was apprehensive and did not dare accept them, fearing he might commit the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*).
The Buddha said, "I allow a sick bhikṣu to accept food separately from the community.

After the bhikṣus had completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they began making robes during the month of Kārttika. The upāsakas feared that the bhikṣus would suffer from exhaustion due to a lack of food.
"Please accept a meal from us, monks. The monks said, "We request only three people; we may not accept a meal from a separate group (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
The Buddha said, "I allow you to accept a meal from a separate group when making robes. There was a householder who wished to give both food and robes and invited the monks for a meal.
Fearing they would commit the offense of eating with a separate group, the Buddha said, "I allow you to eat with a separate group when receiving robes. There was...
A large number of bhikṣus were traveling along the same road toward Kosala with some lay devotees (gṛhapati).
When the time for alms-round arrived and they wished to enter a village to beg for food, the lay devotees said, "We shall provide you with food.

Fearing that they might commit the offense of eating separately from the community (gaṇabhojana), the bhikṣus immediately entered the village to beg for food, while their companions proceeded ahead. The bhikṣus lagged behind and could not catch up, whereupon they were plundered by bandits. The Buddha...
[The Buddha] said: "I permit the acceptance of food from a separate group while traveling on dangerous roads.

Later, while traveling by boat downstream with a group of lay devotees, a large number of bhikṣus reached the time for alms-seeking. Desiring to enter a village to beg for food, the lay devotees said, "Just go;
we shall provide you with food and drink. The bhikṣus feared they would commit the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
Having disembarked, they entered the village to beg for alms. Their boat companions departed ahead, while the bhikṣus followed later;
they were then plundered of their robes by bandits. The Buddha said, "I allow bhikṣus, when traveling by boat, to eat separately from the community.
There were many bhikṣus who, wandering from the kingdom of Kośala, arrived at a small village. The local laypeople thought, "The Saṃgha is numerous, yet the village is [small]..."
[The portion] fell short. [The laypeople thought,] "We would rather prepare food for the community of monks so as not to cause them fatigue and distress.

They immediately invited the bhikṣus for a meal the following day. The bhikṣus, being cautious and apprehensive, informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit the separate meal of a distinct group when the great assembly has gathered.
Kāla, the nephew of King Bimbisāra, was providing food to the śramaṇas; he wished to [provide it] to the śramaṇas of the non-Buddhist paths.
Having gone forth from within the gate, he went to inform King Bimbisāra. The king asked, "Where do you wish to go forth?
He replied, "I wish to go forth among the Nirgranthas. The king asked, "Will you provide food for us śramaṇas?"
Kāla said, "Great King, who is a śramaṇa? The king replied, "The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, are they.
Kāla said, "I have never yet provided them with food. The king said, "Go now and provide food for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
He immediately went to the saṃghārāma and invited the bhikṣus for a meal. The bhikṣus, being cautious and apprehensive, reported this...
The Buddha said: "I allow monks to eat separately from the community when receiving a meal offering.
The precept should be recited as follows:
'If a monk eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense. Other times are: when one is ill, when making robes.'"

The times [when one may eat separately] are: when giving robes; when traveling on a journey; when traveling by boat; when a great assembly has gathered; and when śramaṇas are distributing food—these are the proper times.

Commentary on the meaning: Regarding "a separate group" (pṛthaggaṇa): it refers to four persons, or more than four persons (*Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If within a boundary, one separately invites four persons...").

This is called "eating in a separate group" (*pṛthag-bhakta*). If one is invited in succession, there is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Eating in a separate group means eating separately. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Eating in a separate group refers to not eating in the same place.

If four bhikṣus are within the same boundary, even if only one person does not eat together with the others, it is all termed 'eating in a separate group. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Separate group eating is prohibited for two reasons:

first, to protect and have compassion for the donor; second, to break the power and influence of those bhikṣus who harbor evil desires. Generally, there are two meanings of "separate group": first, a group is formed as a distinct assembly that constitutes a *saṃgha*, such as when Devadatta, including himself, five people went from house to house begging for food according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Second, [the other meaning is]...

[This practice] is distinct from the general rule. That is to say, although they reside together within the same fundamental boundary (*maṇḍala*), they eat separately. When receiving an invitation for alms, one must follow the order of the Saṃgha. According to the *Sarvāstivāda* and *Mahāsāṃghika*, pure food must be signaled by striking the *gandī* (wooden gong).

Inviting [monks] to eat in a private room is not permitted without a specific reason; the holy regulations are clear and must not be transgressed. As for "food," it refers to rice, parched grain, dry cakes, fish, and meat—these are called "primary foods" (*bhojana*), distinguished from other types of food.

Regarding "the time of illness," it extends down to those who are lame in their heels. Regarding "the time of making robes," it refers to the period after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded and before the *kaṭhina* robe has been removed.
The period for robes is one month; when the *kaṭhina* robe is spread, it is five months, up until a single "horse-tooth" stitch has been made upon the robe.
Regarding the time of giving robes: this refers to the one-month period, the five-month period, and other times.

As for the giving of food and robes during these "other times"—namely the seventh and eleventh months—even if food and robes are given then, it is still termed the "robe season. Regarding the time of traveling on a journey: it extends down to half a *yojana*, whether coming or going.

"Those who are traveling by boat" refers to those within half a *yojana* upstream or downstream. "When the great assembly gathers" means that when there are four people sufficient for a meal, having one person in excess constitutes a fault;
likewise, with five, ten, or even a hundred people, having one person in excess constitutes a fault (because the food is insufficient for the number of people).
The Sarvāstivādins say: "When the Saṃgha assembles—whether due to other circumstances or for matters of the Dharma—at least four resident monks are required, while the guest..."

"Four bhikṣus are called a great assembly. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Regarding the time for a great assembly meal: this refers to the 'Cūḍāmaṇi' (Top-knot) Great Assembly held by the World-Honored One, or the five-year Great Assembly, or the six-year Great Assembly.

On the day of such a great assembly, according to the donor's intention, food is prepared in various places; whether there are four or five [monks], they may divide the food as they please. As for the 'Cūḍāmaṇi' Great Assembly: when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he removed his top-knot at age five, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada held a five-year Great Assembly for the Buddha.

At age six, he restored the top-knot, and the householder held a six-year Great Assembly for the Buddha. Both are referred to as times of the Great Assembly. Regarding the giving of food to śramaṇas..."
Apart from these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, there are other renunciants who have gone forth from among the non-Buddhist sects.
If a bhikṣu has no legitimate reason for taking food separately from the community, that bhikṣu should immediately rise and announce:
"I have no reason for this separate meal; I wish to seek permission to leave. If another person likewise has no reason...
This is the formal cause (*nidāna*). It is also permitted for [two or three] to go out. If there are two or three people, they may eat as they please.
If there are four or more than four, they should divide themselves into two groups and enter to eat in turns.

If a bhikṣu has a reason for eating separately from the group (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*) and wishes to join them, he should immediately rise and say: "I have a reason for eating separately from the group; I wish to join."

Enter. You should listen and enter according to the order of seniority (the "causes and conditions" refer to the aforementioned seven conditions). This is the proper time (that is, the occasion when it is permitted for one to join the assembly separately).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, being without a formal invitation (*niyuta*) or being in a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*);
second, it must be a formal meal; and third, the food must have already entered the throat.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, it is eating in a separate group (*pṛthag-varga-bhojana*). For every swallow, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is a valid reason and one does not announce it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If three people eat and one does not eat, or if three are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and one is not fully ordained, there is no offense in all such cases. If food is sent to them, even down to a single grain of salt... [the same applies].
If one eats with that group from a single ladleful of food, there is no offense (this refers to a case where a donor within the boundary of the *poṣadha* invites the Saṃgha for a meal;

if they send even a single ladleful of food, down to a single measure of salt, to the monks within their own boundary, it does not constitute eating separately from the group). Or, if the donor says, "Whoever comes in, I shall give food to all," (this means there is no restriction against visiting monks);
or if the donor builds a separate room and gives it as a gift, saying, "To whoever stays in my room, I shall give food to all"—in these cases as well, [there is no offense].
There is no offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If three bhikṣus eat together in one place and a fourth person takes a portion of the food, there is no offense.
However, if traveling on a road or by boat, if one arrives today but eats today [having planned for tomorrow], or if one travels tomorrow but eats today, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "When eating from the communal store (*saṃghika*), one should act as follows..."

There are four kinds of signs: first, striking the gong; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum; and fourth, proclaiming the announcement. These four kinds of signs must be heard by those within the boundary so that they may know [the time for the meal].
One should perform only one according to the established rule; do not allow them to be confused, for this would fail to constitute the monastic rite.
If one consumes the food of the Saṃgha without performing these signs, the consumption is impure and is termed "stealing the property of the Saṃgha."
This is not called "eating in a separate group" (it is, rather, a high-grade *sthūlātyaya* offense).

If one eats by making a sign, even if there are bhikṣus within the boundary or no bhikṣus at all—whether many or few, whether they come or do not come—as long as there is no obstruction, there is no fault whatsoever.
If there is an obstruction, even if the *gandi* is struck, the meal is impure; it is called "stealing the property of the Saṃgha" (because of the obstruction).

[This refers to] a visiting bhikṣu; the offense is as previously stated). If within a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) there are two or three locations, each with its own beginning and end for the *saṃgha*, yet they perform only a single *poṣadha*:
at the time of the meal, they simply strike the *ghanṭā* (gong) at each location, and there is no restriction on anyone; being pure and without fault [is the rule].

(This means that while the Dharma is the same and the methods for the *poṣadha* and so forth within the boundary are common, the food and drink are separate. However, one must strike the *ghanṭā*; this is called acting according to the Dharma). If a *dānapati*...
One should invite four or more [monks] to eat within the boundary of the *poṣadha* (confession) area. One monk should be invited from the assembly to the place where the *poṣadha* is to be held;
if one portion of food is sent [to him], and this is not done, one commits a *pāyattika* offense. This is likewise if there are two or three locations.
If within a village there is no defined monastic boundary (*sīmā*), yet two donors invite four or more monks to eat at two separate locations, one should strike the *ghanṭī* (wooden gong).

One monk from each location should be mutually invited to the other; or, if a portion of the food is sent [to the other site], or if there are other bhikṣus present, they should enter according to the Dharma, down to even a single person. This applies unless there is mutual invitation or the sending of food.
Regarding "eating at the [wrong] time," it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. The *Mūla* states: there are five causes and conditions for this:

first, being invited to eat early; second, eating while staying in one's room; third, being a newly arrived guest; fourth, being about to depart on a journey; fifth, being afflicted by the suffering of illness; sixth, being a caregiver for the sick;
and seventh, being appointed to administrative duties (*karmadāna*). The *Muktaka* states: if one is a person in charge of supervision, they should...

If one first takes food for oneself from the *śīla* meal and eats it without transgression, it is a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī and a *dukkaṭa* offense for the three junior groups of disciples; this is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when making robes; when receiving robes as a gift; when traveling on a road; when traveling by boat;
when a great assembly has gathered; when śramaṇas are distributing food; or when three or four people eat in mutual exchange.
If one departs due to a specific cause or condition, there is no offense. Those who do not commit an offense include cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset.

According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, why did the Tathāgata establish the rule against eating in a separate group, yet permit three people to eat together in one place? The intention behind this was to protect all people and ensure they were not harmed.

[The number of monks] decreased. Furthermore, in order to subdue those bhikṣus with evil desires who, by severing their ties with many people and having numerous followers, called themselves "the Saṃgha," sought much for themselves, diminished the households [of the laity], and brought ruin upon the Saṃgha by causing it to split into two factions, he caused it to be made according to the Dharma.
Thus, bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma were unable to obtain offerings of robes, food, and drink, while unrighteous bhikṣus obtained much.

Regarding gain and offerings: because monks with evil desires, having obtained such offerings, engage in disputes and litigation with those who practice pure conduct, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that two benefits justify prohibiting separate meals for a group:
first, to protect and show compassion toward the donors; second, to break the power and influence of those monks with evil desires.
○ General Explanation of the Thirty-Fourth Precept: Receiving an Invitation for More Than Three Alms Bowls.

This is a shared precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise studied by followers of the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of formal prohibition). *Vinayaviniścaya*.
It is said: This training rule was established because of excessive greed regarding food. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. There was a woman named Gaṅgā, a woman from a large village, who came...

In the kingdom of Uddiyāna, she became the wife of a man. After several months had passed, she became pregnant. She returned to her parents' home, where she began to support herself by providing for those who came.
When bhikṣus arrived to beg for alms, she personally brought food to offer them. Later, her husband sent a messenger to summon her back. Because of this...
The bhikṣus ate all the food they had received and were just beginning to prepare more when the husband had already taken another wife.
Furthermore, outside the city of Vārāṇasī, a caravan of merchants was staying overnight. A certain bhikṣu seeking alms entered this merchant camp to beg for food.
A merchant who possessed faith and devotion took his bowl, filled it with excellent food, and gave it to him.
Not long after Kāśyapa had left the camp, another bhikṣu came to beg for food. In this manner, as they passed from one to another, all the other food was exhausted.
They then went to purchase grain in the market, but later they failed to catch up with their companions and were plundered by bandits. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept. Fearing and being cautious, the sick bhikṣus did not dare to accept food beyond their needs. The Buddha said, "I permit it;
the precept should be recited as follows.
This was the formulation of the precept.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who invites him with cakes, parched grain flour, or boiled rice, and if the bhikṣu wishes to accept it, he should accept two or three bowls.
Upon returning to the saṃghārāma, he should divide it to share with the other bhikṣus for their meal.
If a bhikṣu is not ill and accepts more than two or three bowls, and then carries it back to the saṃghārāma without dividing it to share with the other bhikṣus...
If a *bhikṣu* eats [such food], it is a *pāyattika*.
Explanation of the meaning: "A layperson's house" refers to a household with men and women (the *Mahāsāṃghika* says: the houses of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras).

If they invite a *bhikṣu* to receive cakes, parched grain flour, or boiled rice (cakes, parched grain flour, and boiled rice refer to various kinds of cakes, flour, and boiled rice made from wheat, barley, rice, beans, and so forth), he should ask them:
The Master said: "Is this food for women returning home, or is it provisions for merchants on the road?
If you say it is food for women returning home or provisions for merchants on the road, then after eating, you should go back to the monastery and inform the bhikṣus:
'In such-and-such a household there is food for women returning home and provisions for merchants on the road. If any wish to eat, they may do so. After eating, they should [inform the community].
He went out. If he wished to bring food back, he was permitted to take two or three bowls. "I shall not bring any food back now;
however, if I do bring one bowl of food, I will give it to the other bhikṣus so that we may share and eat it together. He should say to the other bhikṣus:
"In such-and-such a house there is food for a newly arrived wife and provisions for merchants on the road. If you go to that house to eat," [he should add].
One should eat right there at that house. If one returns with food, it should be from two bowls; I have already returned with one bowl.
If one returns with two bowls, one should share the food with the other bhikṣus and say to them:
"Even those who wish to eat, if they desire to take some from that house, should take only one bowl. I have already taken two bowls myself.
Return. If you return carrying all three bowls, divide the food among the bhikṣus and inform the other bhikṣus;
even those who wish to eat should eat at that house, and take care not to bring anything back. I have already brought three bowls.
If a bhikṣu requires them, he may accept two or three bowls. (The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: There are three types of bowls—large, medium, and small.

The large bowl may receive two *śrona*-measures of rice from the kingdom of Magadha, with room above for beans and vegetables; it is so large that one can hook the rim with a single joint of the thumb without touching the food.

This is the measure of the large bowl. The small bowl receives one *śrona*-measure of rice. The two between these are called medium. Regarding "two or three bowls": this refers to taking one large, one medium, and one small bowl; or simply two large bowls; or one large and two small bowls; or three medium bowls and one small bowl; or three medium [bowls], etc.)

One small bowl (two), or one medium bowl and three small bowls (three bowls; this refers to the maximum amount permitted to receive). Carrying these back to the monastery, he should distribute them to the other bhikṣus for food (*The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If he takes two bowls, he eats from one himself and gives one to the community of bhikṣus. If he takes three bowls, he eats from one himself and gives two to the community of bhikṣus.

He must not give them to acquaintances who are laypeople"). One who is not ill may not accept more than two or three bowls; however, if one is ill, there is no limit on the number. This was the Buddha’s regulation for those who are not ill.

Regarding the *Vinayavibhaṅga*: "Excessive receiving" refers to taking three large bowls, or two large bowls plus one medium bowl, or two large bowls plus one small bowl, or one large bowl plus two medium bowls. To summarize:

when receiving food from another, if it exceeds four and a half *śu* (measures) of cooked rice, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. However, if the donor permits one to take as much as desired, there is no offense.

Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, receiving food from a woman returning home or provisions for merchants on a journey;
second, receiving more than three bowls when not ill; and third, exceeding the limit of two feet [in taking the food].
**The Formal Determination:** Regarding the offense herein, if one who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls and carries them out through the gate, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, and one makes a movement to depart but then stops, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one takes food without asking whether the woman returning home has food or whether the merchant has provisions for the journey, it is likewise [an offense].

It is a *duṣkṛta*. If one carries [food] into a monastery and does not distribute it to other bhikṣus for them to eat, or if one does not inform the other bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

"If, while at this very seat, one eats more than three bowls' worth—excluding cakes and parched flour—or if one takes away only other items, or if the donor is pleased, one may take it away as one wishes."
There is no offense [for the donor]. For the bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the three junior groups, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense. Explanations of the allowance:
There is no offense in the following cases: receiving food in two or three bowls; a sick person receiving more than the allotted amount; or when inquiring after a woman returning from childbirth.
Having consumed the provisions for travelers on the road, he returns to the saṃghārāma and distributes them to share with the other bhikṣus.
He informs the other bhikṣus so that they may know the location of the village. If the traveler brings it himself to the saṃghārāma, it may be accepted;

if he brings it to the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra, it may likewise be accepted. There is no offense. One is not guilty of an offense in the following cases: if it is the first instance and has not yet been established as a rule.

Regarding the formulation of the precepts and so forth, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* (Lüshe) states: "There are three ways in which the faithful offerings of the laity are wasted and misappropriated:

first, when a donor with faith gives to one who maintains the precepts, but the recipient, having accepted it, gives it to one who violates the precepts; second, when a donor with faith gives to one who possesses right view, but the recipient, having accepted it, gives it to one who holds wrong views..."

A person with wrong views accepts food in three excessive quantities and does not eat it himself, even if he accepts as much as a single handful of food for a long time, except when the donor has previously granted him permission to do so at will.
These three matters are all termed the vain wasting of offerings made in faith.
This shall bring about an evil retribution.
○ Thirty-fifth: General Explanation of the Precept Regarding Not Performing the *Avaśeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* (the Ritual for Remaining Food).
This is an uncommon precept; the offenses for nuns differ. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (an offense of prohibition).
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because one eats again after being full, out of gluttonous greed and lack of satiety, this training rule was established."
The Setting: The Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park with the bhikṣus. He taught the practice of eating a single meal and praised the practice of eating a single meal.
The bhikṣus ate solid food (khādaniya), and if they drank liquids or took medicine, they would then observe the rule of eating only once; their bodies [became emaciated].
[The monks] became emaciated and their complexions grew haggard. The Buddha asked Ānanda to report these matters to him.

The Buddha said, "I permit the bhikṣus to eat until they are fully satisfied at a single sitting. However, some bhikṣus would eat *khañjaka* food, or drink gruel and take medicine, and then consider themselves satiated, refusing to eat further;
consequently, their physical appearance remained withered and pale. The Buddha again permitted [the eating of] the five [kinds of solid foods].
There are various kinds of food: rice, parched grain flour, dry cakes, fish, and meat; with these, one may be satisfied.

Although the sick bhikṣus obtained excellent food, they were unable to eat it all in a single sitting, and their bodies became emaciated. Furthermore, it was permitted for sick bhikṣus to eat repeatedly;
for a sick person, there is no rule regarding "finished eating. At that time, when a sick bhikṣu obtained delicious food, he was unable to finish it all.
After the attendant had finished his meal, he did not dare to eat [the patient's leftovers] and threw them away. Various birds came and scrambled for the food, crying out.
The Buddha said, "I allow the attendant to eat the patient's leftover food; there is no need for the formal procedure of 'no further food' (atireka-bhojana).
One morning, the bhikṣus received almsfood, set it aside, and entered the village to beg for more. Having eaten, they returned to take up the food they had set aside and gave it to others.
"Monks, when the monks have finished their meal and do not dare to eat more, they discard it, and the birds scramble for it, crying out.
The Buddha has permitted you to take the food you have received and, having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) procedure, eat it.
There was an elder monk of great renown who entered a village to beg for alms. Having obtained a large quantity, he ate together with others in one place and brought back the remaining food.
When [the Buddha] was with the bhikṣus, after the bhikṣus had finished eating their fill, they did not dare to eat more and consequently discarded it. Various birds then clamored over it.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] permitted the bhikṣus to take food from there and return; they should then perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (leftover-food) rite and eat it.
One should perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* rite by speaking as follows: "Venerable sir, I have already eaten my fill. Know this, look at this. This is how it is performed.
Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the practice of leftover food): he should take a small portion of the food and say to that bhikṣu, "I have finished;
you may take it. This is the person who provides the occasion.
There was a bhikṣu who was gluttonous and lacked moderation; he did not know what constituted sufficient food or insufficient food, nor what constituted leftover food or non-leftover food.
Whenever he obtained food, he ate it. When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu has finished eating his fill and subsequently receives an invitation, yet eats without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food),
it is a *pāyattika*.
**Exegesis:** Regarding "having eaten one's fill" (*pūrvabhakta*): there are five kinds of food—cooked rice, parched grain flour, cakes, fish, and meat.

Among these five kinds of food, if one eats any single one to satiety, it constitutes one of the five ways of having eaten one's fill. This involves: (1) knowing it is rice (meaning one knows the substance of the food is a primary meal;

if it is not a primary meal, it is not called "having eaten one's fill"); (2) knowing it has been brought [to one] (meaning one knows that a man or woman has brought the food and offered it); and (3) knowing the deportment [of the donor].

(This refers to knowing that one is receiving food while in the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—rather than while standing, sitting, or lying down. "Knowing the relinquishing of posture" means: (it refers to having received food while walking, and now being in the postures of standing, sitting, or lying down;
hence it is called "relinquishing"). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "One who has eaten to satiety makes a declaration of cessation and mentally abandons [the meal].
If the mind has not yet abandoned it, even if one utters the words of cessation, the act of cessation is not accomplished. If one eats again, one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense. If...
Having finished eating, one declares, "I have had enough. This constitutes the formal act of having finished eating (*kṛta-paryāpta*).

To eat without performing the *atirikta-bhakti* (the ritual for leftover food) constitutes an offense of falling into a transgression (*pācittiya*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The *atirikta-bhakti* is permitted for two reasons: first, for the sake of a sick monk; second, because a monk has a reason for which his food is insufficient.

The *atirikta-bhakti* in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is equivalent to the *yūshi* (leftover food) in our own Vinaya. Once one has finished eating, if one wishes to eat more, one must perform the ritual procedure before eating. To say that one eats without performing the *atirikta-bhakti* means that one eats immediately upon obtaining the food, without having performed this rite.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept fulfills three conditions before the full offense is established: first, having finished eating and abandoned the formal deportment;
second, not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) ritual; and third, swallowing the food after having eaten.

**The Formal Determination:** Regarding the offense herein: having finished eating and abandoned the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*), if one obtains and eats food without performing the *khalupaścād-bhakta* (remaining-food) rite, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.
As for "solid foods" (*khādanīya*): these include roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, oils, sesame, black rock-honey, and finely ground powders.
Having finished eating, if one obtains [such food] without performing the *khalupaścād-bhakta* rite...

If one eats it, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense. If, having already eaten one's fill, one performs the ritual of "leftover food" (*atirittakaraṇa*) for another, the ritual of leftover food is not accomplished;
it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one knows that another has already eaten their fill, yet performs the ritual of leftover food [for them], [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*].
If one takes food with one's own hand and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite; or if one places food on the ground and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite;
or if one causes a *kalpika-puruṣa* (pure person) to hold the food and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite;
or if one performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite before a *kalpika-puruṣa* by covering good food with inferior food and performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite; or if one receives from another...
Regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule on leftover food): if one takes it all away, in all such cases the *khalupaścādbhakti* is not established, and it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one has eaten enough and perceives that one has eaten enough, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). If one has eaten enough but suspects one has eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one has not eaten enough but perceives that one has eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has not eaten enough but suspects one has eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* says: "It is permitted."
When one person performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food), all other people may eat.

If a bhikṣu brings food and wishes to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa*, and he performs it over a bowl or within a vessel, it is validly performed only with respect to what is inside that vessel; the food remaining in the bowl is not considered to have been made into *kṛtapiṇḍa*.
However, if the liquid from the food in the vessel flows into the bowl, both are considered to have been made into *kṛtapiṇḍa*.

Regarding leftover food (*vighasa*): if two bowls are combined to constitute leftover food, and if the person before one is eating from exactly one bowl, then that single bowl may be designated as "leftover food.
If there are two bowls, and cakes or vegetables are placed across them covering both, then both may be designated as "leftover food.
It is the same for various other types of vessels. If this is the custom of the country...
When a small number of bhikṣus have finished eating, and a great donor arrives bringing various kinds of food and drink, and the bhikṣus have already risen and departed, what should be done?
If there is a *zhíyuè* (monthly supervisor) or a *weínná* (steward), or other administrators present at that place...
If one has not yet eaten to satiety, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leftover food) in the presence of that person.
If that person has already eaten to satiety, but the Elder has not yet eaten to satiety, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* in the presence of the Elder.

If the Elder is ashamed and unable to perform it among the people, the assembly should rise together; the Elder shall go to a secluded place and perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa*. If the Elder has already eaten to satiety...
When a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one should ask: "Venerable sir, has today’s *pravāraṇā* been completed?

If the visiting bhikṣu says, "I have not yet entered the summer retreat; how could the *pravāraṇā* be complete?", you should know that this person does not understand the characteristics of the Vinaya.
You should then ask him further: "Have you eaten? If he says, "I have already eaten," you should then ask: "Has the donor performed the *pravāraṇā*?"
Is it sufficient? If he says, "Venerable sir, where could there be enough food for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony?

Even water and vegetables are insufficient, let alone other food," one should know it is insufficient and should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover-food) rite with him. If he says it is sufficient, the Saṃgha should employ skillful means.
One should not disrupt the donor’s wholesome intention. If there is a senior śrāmaṇera among the assembly, he should be brought to the boundary (sīmā) and granted full ordination (upasampadā).
Once he has been instructed in the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-vidhi), only then should one eat. (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also employs this principle.

If all the gruel has just come fresh from the cauldron and does not form characters when written upon it, and if all fruits and vegetables are likewise [fresh], these do not constitute eating separately from the assembly (gaṇabhojana). Nor are they [forbidden].
"Eating at various places" does not constitute "having had enough to eat. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: There are five types of *pāsaṇṇika* (soft foods) that may be eaten:
first, rice; second, wheat and bean porridge; third, parched grain flour; fourth, meat; and fifth, cakes. Furthermore, there are five types of *khādaniya* (hard foods) that may be chewed:
namely, roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits. If one has already consumed the five types of chewable foods, as well as milk, curd, and vegetables...
...and so forth. If one subsequently consumes five types of edible food (*khādya*), there is no offense.

If, however, one has first consumed five types of edible food and then further consumes five types of chewable food (*bhojya*), as well as milk, curd, vegetables, and the like, it is called an offense. One should know that there are five expressions for "not yet finished":
when food is being served, if one does not wish to eat immediately, one should reply: "Wait a moment," "Go on," "Hold on," "Wait," or "Wait while I eat."
Furthermore, wait until I have finished. If one speaks while still [eating], it is called "not yet sufficient. If there is no sound of "finished" (*ca*), it constitutes a refusal of further food.

If the intention is not yet satisfied, even if one utters the word "finished," it does not constitute being finished; one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense because the speech does not accord with the Dharma.
If one eats the remaining food after performing the ritual of "having enough," one dwells in personal ease and causes the donor to dwell in ease.
One shall obtain merit. When wishing to perform the ritual, one should wash the hands and receive food.

Taking it with oneself, one approaches a bhikṣu who has not yet finished eating, or one who, though having finished, has not yet left their seat, and performs the rite in his presence. If he has not yet signaled that he is full, one should take two or three morsels of food.
If one has already finished eating, it is improper to eat; rather, one should press down on the food with the hand and say to him: "This..."
"This is your property; eat it as you please. There are five cases in which the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the formal act of making food 'leftover') is not accomplished:

first, when one is within the boundary while facing someone outside the boundary; second, when they are out of reach of one another (the *Śāriputrābhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states this means more than two cubits apart); third, when one is standing at the side."

Fourth, [the donor] stands behind [the recipient]. Fifth, the person ahead leaves their seat. If these conditions are reversed, it constitutes an offense for the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs; this is called a violation.

The Exceptional Circumstances: Those who do not commit an offense are as follows: one who perceives food as non-food; one who does not perform the *khalupaṭiggaha* (the ritual of receiving) for what is not food;
one who performs the *khalupaṭiggaha* for oneself regarding what is not food; one who performs the *khalupaṭiggaha* without placing it on the ground;
one who performs the *khalupaṭiggaha* even when it has reached the hand; or if another gives to him and he performs the *khalupaṭiggaha* for that which is given by the other. If...

If one is ill and does not perform the *yavaddhika* (remaining-food) rite, or if the food remaining from a sick person does not have the *yavaddhika* rite performed over it, there is no offense provided the *yavaddhika* rite has already been performed.

The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If it is northern fruit or the lotus root of the gods—such items that are difficult to obtain—or if it is a year of famine when food and drink are hard to find, one may eat them without performing the *yavaddhika* rite. There is no offense.
An offense. One who does not commit an offense refers to those before the precepts were first established, and so forth.
According to the *Vinayamātṛkā*, "If a bhikṣu receives a gift from others in an improper manner, he falls because of that gift."

There are two [types of such persons]. First, those who consume the offerings of others yet do not cultivate the Path according to the Dharma; they let their minds run wild and unrestrained, leaving nothing of merit to be recorded.

Second, those who give what has been offered to them, yet perform that giving improperly. Because of these two circumstances, they shall fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). As for those to whom one should give:
if they are one’s parents and are suffering in poverty, one should first cause them to receive the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions.
Only then should one give. If one is not poor, although they may have received the precepts of taking refuge, it is inappropriate to give to them [at that time].

Furthermore, there are other recipients for giving: those who repair stūpas, those who serve the Saṃgha, and those who maintain monastic dwellings; their labor should be calculated and they should be compensated with the appropriate wage.

If one gives them more than their due, one falls into the fault of improper giving. When giving food to the sick, one should act with a mind of loving-kindness and provide it according to what is suitable.

If one gives food to those who have committed errors, those fallen due to their transgressions, infants, those imprisoned in dungeons, or those who are pregnant, one should give it with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), without expecting any reward for its giving or receiving. To those who come to the monastery seeking alms, they should provide for themselves;
there is no need to give to them. However, if they have no provisions, there is no fault in giving to them. If a bhikṣu does not practice meditation, [he should likewise be supported].
If one does not recite the sutras, does not attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, yet accepts the offerings of others, one will fall because of that gift.
If the donor lacks these three qualities of action, and the recipient knows this yet still accepts the gift, both giver and receiver will fall because of that gift.

It would be better to swallow an iron ball and die than to eat the faithful offerings of others without observing the precepts. Furthermore, if one has already eaten to satisfaction, it is improper to force oneself to eat more.
This does not augment one's physical strength, but only increases one's afflictions. Therefore, one should not eat without moderation.
○ Thirty-sixth: General Explanation of the Precept Regarding Causing Others to Violate the Rule on Remaining Food (Vikṛti-śeṣa).
This is an uncommon precept (*asaṃvara-śīla*). The offenses for nuns differ; it is studied equally by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Because one wishes to cause another to commit an offense and then cross-examine them regarding their transgression, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
A certain bhikṣu was gluttonous; he did not know whether he had eaten enough or not, nor did he know whether there was more food remaining or not.
Having obtained it, he ate it. Another bhikṣu said to him, "It is truly unprecedented that you, such a glutton and lover of food, could act in this way."
He did not know whether he had eaten enough or not, nor did he know whether there was more food remaining or not; having received it, he ate it.

Later, upon hearing of this, he harbored resentment in his heart. At another time, he saw that bhikṣu having finished eating, yet not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of declaring the meal finished) regarding the remaining food.
He respectfully invited him to eat, and the monk accepted the food. The gluttonous monk said, "It is unprecedented!
Just as you are gluttonous, you do not know whether you have eaten enough or not, nor do you know whether it is leftover food or not.
You eat what you obtain without knowing satiety. He replied, "Although I have eaten, I am still not full. That monk said, "You..."
Having already eaten his fill, he asked, "Do you know that I have had enough? They replied, "We know.
When the monks heard this, they reported it to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept. At that time, the monks did not yet know what constituted having had enough and what did not;
only later did they realize they had eaten their fill. Some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha [instructed them...]
If one says "I did not know," there is no offense. The precept should be recited as follows:

Regarding the established characteristics of the rule—if a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has finished eating, yet [the latter] accepts an invitation and does not perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food) with earnestness...
"Please accept this food. "Venerable one, take this food. [If one says this] for this specific reason and no other, with the desire to cause another to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*.

Explanation of the terms: "Knows" means: either he knows by himself, or he hears it from another, or he knows because the person himself says, "I have already finished eating. "Food" refers to formal meal (bhojana), excluding other non-food items.

"Eating to satiety" (as explained previously). He earnestly invited him to eat. The Elder accepted this food—this being a term of address for an elder—and while harboring malice within, he outwardly manifested earnestness, desiring to repay a prior enmity by forcibly urging him to eat.

For this reason alone, and no other, he intended to cause another to commit an offense—that is, he desired to cause another to violate the precepts, creating a cause for affliction, and not for any other purpose.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute a full offense: first, harboring a mind of resentment;
second, knowing that the other person has already finished eating; third, giving food without performing the formal ritual; and fourth, swallowing the food after it has been eaten.

**The Formal Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if the recipient accepts the food and eats it, for every swallow both [the giver and the recipient] incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If the giver provides the food for him to eat and he does not eat it but discards it, the giver incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If the giver provides the food for him to eat and he does not eat it but sets it aside, or if the giver provides the food for him to eat and he gives it to another person... [the giver incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense].
If one gives food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of "leftover food"), yet the recipient eats it after performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa*;

or if one gives food to a sick person with the intent to cause another to commit an offense; or if one takes the leftovers of a sick person and gives them to another with the intent to cause that other to commit an offense;

or if one gives food to another after having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* oneself with the intent to cause that other to commit an offense—the giver in all such cases commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). This concludes the section.
If one has eaten enough and perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has eaten enough but suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If one has not eaten enough but perceives it as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one has not eaten enough but suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For the four assemblies, including the *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances. There is no offense in the following cases: if one did not previously know it was sufficient food; if one perceived it as insufficient food;
if one was given [food] and had it discarded before eating it; if one was given [food] and set it aside before eating it; or if one was told to have someone else take it away before eating it.

If one gives food that has not undergone the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (formal ritual of "leftover food") and causes it to be eaten after the *kṛtapiṇḍa* has been performed, yet the recipient eats it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa*, [there is an offense].
If one gives the remains of a sick person's meal, one must ensure that another does not commit an offense by having the *kṛtapiṇḍa* performed before giving it.
Not causing others to commit [an offense]. There is no offense. One who commits no offense refers to those before the precept was first established, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Thirty-Seventh Precept: Eating at Improper Times.
This is a common precept; it is likewise established for nuns. It is also regulated in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:
"Because it increases greed and invites public censure, this training rule was established."
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [is as follows].
Nanda and Upananda entered the city to watch musical performances; it was only toward evening that they returned.
Kālodāyin entered the city for alms at the close of day and came to the house of a pregnant woman. As the woman was carrying food out of the door, [he encountered her].
It happened that there was a thunderstorm. Seeing his face for a brief moment, she was terrified and cried out, "Ghost! Ghost! and immediately fell down. Kāḷudāyin said, "Sister, I am not a ghost;

I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya. The woman, filled with resentment, said, "A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya, would rather tear open his own belly than go out to beg for alms at night. The Venerable One returned and reported this to the bhikṣus.
[The Buddha] spoke. A monk of few desires informed the Buddha, who rebuked [the offender] and established the precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows: If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** "Time" refers to the period from the appearance of the morning light until midday.

According to this rule, it applies to all four continents in the same manner (meaning that for a bhikṣu residing on any of the four continents, the time for receiving food is defined by the local sunrise until midday). If it is sunrise in the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha), it is midday in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), midnight in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), and sunset in the Western Continent (Aparagoyānī).

If it is midday in the Eastern Continent, it is sunrise in the Southern Continent, midnight in the Western Continent, and sunset in the Northern Continent. If it is sunset in the Eastern Continent, it is midday in the Southern Continent, sunrise in the Western Continent, and midnight in the Northern Continent.

At night: when it is midnight in the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), the sun sets in the southern continent (Jambudvīpa), it is midday in the western continent (Aparagoyānīya), and the sun rises in the northern continent (Uttarakuru). When monks from Jambudvīpa go to dwell in the other three continents, they should eat only according to the time of those respective places, and must not let the meal pass until midday.

Therefore it is said that the same applies to the four continents. Regarding "improper time" (*akāla*): from midday until the appearance of the morning light (according to the *Sarvāstivāda*, from dawn until midday is called "proper time" because worldly people attend to their affairs and prepare food and drink;

from midday until the final watch of the night is called "improper time" because it is the time for social gatherings, games, and personal amusement, during which a bhikṣu wandering about might cause disturbance or offense).

Furthermore, from morning until midday is the time for begging food; one should enter the village and travel about during this period, which is therefore called "the proper time. From midday until the final watch of the night, one should remain silent, with hands folded, sitting upright to recite scriptures and practice meditation according to one's respective duties;

this is not the time for traveling or entering the village, and is thus called "the improper time. As for food, there are two kinds: *khajja* (solid food) and the five types of improper food (*bhojana*).
**Pūjanīya Food (The Five Principal Foods).

This is because the nature of all Buddhas eternally abides in the Middle Way, not adhering to either of the two extremes;

This indicates the preliminary preparations for attaining realization; it also causes the body and mind to obtain immediate benefit.
By not eating after midday, one sleeps little, avoids the ailment of undigested food, and experiences physical lightness and tranquility, making it easy to enter meditative concentration.
Because there are such benefits, one is instructed to eat at midday. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
There were certain donors who constructed monasteries and provided generous endowments to support the Sangha of future generations.

Among them was one who, though appearing to be a renunciant, went to the food steward at an improper time to request food. What kind of offense does the one who gives it and the one who eats it incur?
And what kind of merit does the original donor obtain? The Buddha said: "One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; this is an offense."

One who steals, one who gives at an improper time, and likewise one who violates the precepts, are all persons who commit theft. If one steals the property of a donor, it is not the intention of the donor;
thus the donor gains no merit because the object has been lost. There remains only the merit of the initial resolve to establish [the gift].

Śāriputra said, "If one accepts food at the proper time and eats it at the proper time, but then eats again at an improper time because it was not finished, or if one accepts it at the proper time but eats it at an improper time—would one still obtain merit?
The Buddha said, "One who is pure regarding food at the proper time is indeed a field of merit."
This is itself the renunciant life; this is itself the Saṃgha; this is itself the true friend of gods and humans; this is itself the guide for gods and humans.
Those who are impure are like precept-breaking, thieving hungry ghosts; they are the dwelling place of sin.

As for those who demand at improper times, whether it be the right time or not, they give food indiscriminately. Such a person in charge of food is called one who has retreated from the Path and is evil.
"Māra is called the 'broken vessel' of the three evil realms; he is a leper because he destroys the fruits of goodness.

Since even the Brahmins do not eat at improper times, and the non-Buddhist brahmacārins likewise do not consume food improperly, how much less should my disciples—who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma—act in such a way?
Anyone who does so is not my disciple; they are a person outside the Dharma, a thief. He gave [the bowl] to him.
If one steals and accepts even a single lump, a single handful, a slice of salt, or a bit of vinegar, one will die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines (*Jiao-chang*).

There, one must swallow glowing iron balls. Upon emerging from that hell, one is reborn among pigs and dogs, where one eats various impurities. One is then reborn as a malevolent bird, whose cries are regarded with dread by humans.
Finally, one is reborn as a hungry ghost (*preta*) within the monastic compound (*saṃghārāma*), dwelling inside the latrines and devouring excrement and filth.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, one will be reborn among humans as poor, destitute, and lowly; whatever they may say, people will not trust them.
This is worse than stealing the property of a single person, for whose sin is still relatively light, whereas this [act] seizes the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) of many people.
Because it interrupts the supramundane path. The *Vinaya-vastu* states: A sick bhikṣu took emetic and purgative medicines and experienced distress of mind after midday.

The Buddha ordered that he be given bamboo shoot juice. After it was given, he was not cured. The Buddha ordered that rice gruel be placed in a bag and squeezed to extract the liquid for him to drink. His illness still...
He did not recover. The Buddha ordered him to be taken to a secluded place and given rice gruel. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karman* states:
"There are five kinds of fruits that may be eaten at will, whether it be the proper time or not, and whether one is ill or not:

*Pippalī*, which is *jūjiàng* (vinegar made from the fruit of the *kōlā* tree). The *Neifǎchuán* states: "When food remains in the teeth and grease lingers upon the tongue..."

Until one has rinsed the mouth again with pure water, saliva and spittle must be discarded outside. If the designated time for eating has passed, one further commits the offense of eating at an improper time (*akāla-bhojana*).
