○ General Explanation of the Thirty-eighth Śeṣa-āhāra (Residual Food) Precept.
This is a common precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory offense). *Vinayaviniścaya*.
It is said: On account of this unlawful matter, this training rule was established.
As for the setting of the origin:
the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain.
Regarding the person who gave rise to this thought:
Venerable Kāla was constantly seated in meditation and reflection. When the time arrived, he entered the city to beg for alms.
He thought to himself, "It is wearying and painful to beg for alms every day. I would rather eat whatever I obtain first; as for the food obtained later, I shall carry it back. And so he did.
He acted according to what he had intended. On the occasions of both the morning and midday meals, the bhikṣus did not see Kāla; they suspected that he had either passed away or traveled far away.
Later, when they saw him, they questioned him and learned the reason for his absence, and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
The established characteristic of the precept:
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning: "Kept overnight" means that having received [the food] on this day, it reaches the next day; regarding all śramaṇas of the Śākya clan...

Regarding those who have received the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa-śīla*): all are impure [if they violate these rules]. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if a *mahābhikṣu* stays overnight with food that has not been personally received by hand, it is called "storing within" (*antar-upanidhi*).

To eat such food constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the food has already been personally received by hand, yet one stays overnight with it after having set it aside, it is called "leftover overnight food" (*vighasa-śeṣa-bhakṣa*). To eat such food constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. There are two kinds of food: formal food (*bhojana*) and non-formal food (*abhojana*).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the food must have been kept overnight;
second, one must perceive it as such; third, having eaten it, it must have entered the throat.
**The Formal Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one eats food that has been kept overnight, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow.
If one eats at an improper time or eats what has passed the proper time, it is a *pāyattika*. If one eats a seven-day medicine after the seven days have elapsed, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* offense: to consume medicinal substances for the rest of one’s life without a valid reason is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one has stayed overnight and perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has stayed overnight but suspects it (is not so), it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one has not stayed overnight but perceives it as such, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one has not stayed overnight but suspects it (is so), it is a *duṣkṛta*. According to the Sarvāstivādins, there are three types of staying overnight and consuming food.
If, having received food, one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself, whether it remains overnight with them or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
To eat it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). If one takes food with one's own hand, it is called "improper grasping" (*durgṛhīta*). At the moment of grasping, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and lets it remain overnight, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*. The same applies to eating it. If one eats...
If one does not receive or grasp [the food], yet forms the thought that it belongs to oneself and keeps it overnight, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

To eat it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense. It does not matter whether it was kept overnight with others or not; simply forming the thought that it belongs to oneself is termed "storing overnight" (*antar-śayita*).

If another bhikṣu eats it, there is no fault in its being kept overnight. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "First take the fruit for oneself; afterwards, have a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) accept it and eat it."
It is a *duṣkṛta*. There are two kinds of contact-food (*sparśāhāra*) that may be eaten without fault: first, when a pure monk touches it by mistake;
second, when a monk who has broken the precepts and lacks shame or remorse touches it. Heavenly food may be eaten even after midday (because it lacks substantial substance).
It may be accepted for seven days. The *Nidāna* states: "The remaining cakes and fruits should be given to the *śrāmaṇeras*; they are to be returned the following morning."
One may eat it. If one has a mind of expectation when giving it, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); at the time of eating, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).

If there is no mind of expectation at all, there is no offense. The *Mukhaḍaka* states: "If a sick person is poor, even if it is leftover or touched *ghṛta* (clarified butter) or oil, taking it is without fault.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If many bhikṣus are traveling together, and there is only one..."
When śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus each carry their own provisions, at the time of eating they each divide their portions.
Once a śrāmaṇera has received his share, he says to a bhikṣu, "I will now exchange my portion for yours, Venerable Sir.

Having received it, he exchanges it again with the second seat, continuing in this manner until many have partaken of the food; in all such cases, there is no offense. This applies provided the śrāmaṇera does not understand the rule.
If a bhikṣu carries his own portion of food and exchanges it with a śrāmaṇera so that they may obtain food from one another, there is no offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pāyattika; for the three junior groups [of nuns], it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.

The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases. If there is leftover food from what was received the previous night, and one gives it to one’s parents, those working on a stūpa, or those building a dwelling;
or if one gives it after having calculated its value; or if, while begging for alms at another time, one receives it from such a person;

or if there are holes or cracks in the bowl and food enters within, and the recipient picks it out, washes it, and repairs the damage according to the Dharma, provided that no further food remains; or if the food received the previous night is ghee.
If medicinal oil is used for nasal irrigation and the nose is pinched, causing the ghee or oil to exit with the saliva, it should be discarded; otherwise, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been promulgated at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Thirty-ninth Precept: Taking Food for Oneself.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise regulated for Mahāyāna bhikṣus. This is an offense of transgression (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "Because of this illegality, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
As for the place of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
The Originating Condition of Persons:
There was a bhikṣu who constantly went on almsround and wore robes made of discarded rags.

At that time, various lay devotees (gṛhapati) in the city, for the sake of deceased parents, brothers, sisters, husbands, wives, sons, or daughters, [prepared offerings] at a crossroads or at their gates.

[The Buddha] went down to the riverbank, beneath a tree, where he performed a sacrifice and made offerings. That bhikṣu took the food himself and ate it. The lay devotees (gṛhapati) criticized and disparaged this.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. [The Buddha] rebuked them and established a precept. The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to take water or tooth-sticks for themselves.
The Buddha said, "I permit it. The precept should be recited as follows:
The established definition of the precept:
If a bhikṣu eats food that has not been formally offered, or places medicine in his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a *pāyattika*.

Explanation of the meaning: "Not having received" (the offering) means, according to the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*, not receiving from a person under training (*śikṣamāṇā*), a bhikṣuṇī, a male or female novice (*śrāmaṇera* or *śrāmaṇerī*), or any layperson.
[It is] obtained). There are five ways of receiving: receiving hand-to-hand; or receiving by giving with the hand while holding an object;
or receiving by handing an object over to the hand; or receiving by handing an object over to an object being held;

or when an object is passed from a distance, such that both the giver and the receiver know [the transaction], and there is no physical contact or obstruction between them, yet it falls into the recipient's hand. These are called the five ways of receiving. Furthermore, there are five [other ways].
There are five ways of receiving food: if it is received by the body with the body; if it is received by clothing with clothing; if it is received by bending the elbow with the bent elbow;
if it is received by a vessel with a vessel; or if, for a specific reason, it is placed on the ground and received. These are called the five ways of receiving.

"Food" refers to *khajjaka* (solid food) and the five types of *bhojana* (principal meals). "Medicine" refers to *sāyaniya* (soft food)—this term has no direct Chinese equivalent, its meaning being taken as that which is consumed and digested.

As stated in the *Mūla-karman*: "Regarding *sāyaniya*, although one searches thoroughly through the Sanskrit manuscripts, this specific name does not exist [therein]. It refers to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.

The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, not receiving [the food] from another person; second, forming the perception that one has not received it;
third, having eaten it such that it has entered the throat.
**The Determination of the Offense:** In this context, the offense consists of taking food that has not been offered and placing it in one's own mouth.

With the exception of water and tooth-sticks, for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation). To eat at an improper time or to consume food past the proper time constitutes a *pāyattika*.
To consume a seven-day medicine after the seventh day constitutes a *pāyattika*. To consume a lifetime medicine without a valid reason constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one eats what has been received, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not receive [the food] but perceives it as not received, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not receive [it] but suspects [it], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one receives [it] but perceives it as not received, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one receives [it] but suspects [it], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Except for food that is to be eaten immediately, one must not swallow it; however, it is permitted to receive food from a nāga, from a deva, from a preta, or from a monkey.
One may receive food based on the donor’s verbal instruction, but one must not receive food by accepting what is thrown."
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: At one time, there was a donor who brought various offerings and arranged them before the assembly with the intention of giving them away.
However, a fire broke out in his house, and he abandoned the food to go and extinguish it. Since no one was present to hand over the food, the time for the meal was about to pass.

The Buddha said: "One should regard it as being from Uttarakuru and take and eat it oneself. If one receives the food, yet there is the fault of eating what has not been formally offered, one falls into transgression. If...

If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food), have them receive it. If there is certainly no one to receive it, push it aside and eat it. If liquid falls into it, remove the excess before eating.
If it has already been received and a child touches it, receive it again before eating. If one is ill and there is no one available to receive it, there is no offense in not receiving it. [Question:

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, throwing an object from a distance constitutes acceptance (*pratigraha*). However, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, one may not accept food that has been thrown. What is the meaning of this?

[The Buddha] replied: "In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it is stated that if one throws food from a distance due to a specific cause and condition, and does so without a disrespectful mind, it constitutes the acceptance of food. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, since there is no such cause and condition for throwing it across and giving it, and because the mind lacks respect, it is prescribed that one must not eat it.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a *pāyattika*; for the three lesser groups [of nuns], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is called an offense."

The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: taking water or *śīrṣaka* (mouth-cleansing sticks); or when food dropped by a bird falls into the bowl of a bhikṣu who is begging for alms;
or when food blown by the wind falls into his bowl. To remove such food—even down to the size of a fingernail—there is no offense regarding what remains.
There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been promulgated at the outset.

The *Huìxiáng* (Comprehensive Explanation) states that according to the *Sarvāstivāda*, there are four types of persons from whom one may receive food: men, women, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
Receiving food from non-humans or animals also constitutes a valid reception of food. Generally, the purpose of receiving food is twofold:

first, to sever the causal conditions for theft; second, to establish a witness. While receiving food from a non-human constitutes a valid reception of food, it does not [constitute a formal act of] receiving [in the ritual sense].
This is the proof. Therefore, regarding the permission to receive food from non-human beings: in remote and desolate places where no humans are present to receive the food, it is permitted.
However, if there are humans, non-humans, animals, or ignorant children present, it is not permitted in any case.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of stopping slander, for the sake of having few desires and knowing contentment, and to inspire faith and respect in others.
It is because of the mind. For example, in the past there was a bhikṣu who traveled with a non-Buddhist practitioner and stayed beneath a tree.

There were fruits upon the tree, and the non-Buddhist said to the bhikṣu, "Climb the tree and gather the fruit. The bhikṣu replied, "According to the dharma of us bhikṣus, one should not climb a tree that is taller than a man.
He further said, "Then shake the tree and take the fruit. The bhikṣu replied, "In our dharma, one must not shake [the tree]."
A tree fell its fruit. A non-Buddhist ascetic climbed the tree, gathered the fruit, and threw it to the ground for him, saying, "Take this fruit and eat.
The bhikṣu said, "In our Dharma, one must not eat unless it has been formally received. The non-Buddhist developed a heart of faith and reverence;
knowing the purity of the Buddha-Dharma, he immediately followed the bhikṣu and went forth as a monk within the Buddha-Dharma. He soon attained the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya).
○ General Explanation of the Fortieth Precept: Prohibiting the Solicitation of Fine Food When Not Ill.
This is an exclusive precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*). The regulations for nuns differ; it is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna. Even if a bodhisattva is ill, [they must not solicit fine food].
One must not eat fish or meat. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature;
therefore, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"Because it gave rise to public censure, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated based on two conditions."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].
Bhadanta had a merchant leader who served as his patron. [The merchant] went to him and said, "I now wish to obtain some mixed food.
The merchant asked, "What ailment do you have that you think of such food? He replied, "I have no ailment; I simply desire it.
The merchant said, "We merchants constantly buy and sell for our livelihood, yet even we cannot always obtain mixed food."
How much more so for those who have left the household life! When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.

All the sick bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to beg for food; even after receiving it, they did not dare to eat it. The Buddha said: "I permit you. You should recite the precept in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu obtains fine and delicious food and drink, such as milk, curd, fish, or meat, and if that bhikṣu, being free from illness,
seeks such fine food and drink for his own sake, it is a pāyattika offense.

**Exegesis:** If a bhikṣu obtains excellent and delicious food and drink without having requested them, there is no offense. (The following section concerns cases where one commits an offense by specifically requesting it.
"Excellent food" refers to milk, curd, fish, and meat. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: It is called "excellent food" because its price is high and because it is difficult to obtain.)

Because of the purpose of curing illness: there are things that are excellent food but not excellent medicine, such as milk, curd, and butter; there are things that are excellent medicine but not excellent food, such as raw butter and oil; there are things that are both excellent food and excellent medicine, such as clarified butter, meat, and dried fish;

and there are things that are neither excellent food nor excellent medicine, such as *harītakī* and other [medicinal fruits]. If one who is free from illness seeks [food] for oneself, [it is not permitted].

However, for a patient—such as one suffering from jaundice, festering abscesses, boils, hemorrhoids, loss of bodily control, jaundice, malaria, coughing, emaciation, wind-swelling (*vāta-sveda*), or water-swelling (*jala-sveda*)—and for whom various such illnesses require excellent food and drink in order to be cured, it is therefore permitted to beg for and eat such food. Regarding "for oneself," there are two types: either seeking it oneself, or causing another to do so for one's sake.
[The body is like a rope].
Conditions for the offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the condition of being free from illness;
second, delicious food and drink; third, obtaining the food and swallowing it.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one who is not ill solicits such fine food and drink for oneself, there is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) for every swallow.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one solicits while not ill and eats while not ill, one incurs a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If one solicits while not ill but eats while ill, one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) for the solicitation."

There is no offense when begging at mealtime. If one begs for food while ill but eats it while not ill, there is no offense at the time of begging, but one falls into an offense at the time of eating. If one begs while ill and eats while ill, there is no offense.

If, at the time of begging, one intends to obtain something else but another person offers food, one should reply: "Sister, my rice is already sufficient. If she asks, "What else...? [one should respond accordingly].

If one requires something, it is not an offense to beg for it according to one's own desire. If a donor says, "Whatever you require, you may ask for as you wish," then begging according to that is not an offense.
Or if one begs from devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or piśācas, there is no offense in any case.
For bhikṣuṇīs and the three lesser assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. This is what is meant by [the rule].
Offense. Exceptions:
There is no offense for one who is ill and begs for oneself, for one who begs on behalf of the ill, or for one who obtains it without begging.
There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Forty-first Precept: The Prohibition Against Giving Food with One’s Own Hand to Non-Buddhists.

This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. However, one should observe the suitability of the occasion; it may be permissible to give [in certain circumstances].

It may be so. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "This training rule was established because of the censure and suspicion arising from the matter of non-Buddhists appropriating long-standing property. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions:
the origin of the rule (*nidāna*) and the location of the event.
The Buddha, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, traveled from Kośala to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

(According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the one thousand two hundred and fifty people consisted of one thousand disciples from the brothers Uruvilvākāśyapa and his followers, and two hundred and fifty people including Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others; all were addressed with the "Come, monk" formula.

The reason they are always specifically referred to as "one thousand two hundred and fifty" is that these individuals were all ordained from among the Brahmins, because their following and teacher-group were so large, because they were all ordained by the "Come, monk" formula, and because they were all Arhats.)
[This was] the Buddha’s constant retinue.
Regarding the origin of the event:
various donors made offerings and obtained a great quantity of cakes and food. The Buddha commanded Ānanda, "Distribute the cakes to the Saṃgha. Having finished distributing them—
There was another [portion] which the Buddha ordered to be given to a beggar. There was a naked female ascetic of upright appearance;
Ānanda gave her a cake, but because the cakes were stuck together, he thought it was a single cake and gave it to this woman. The woman asked those nearby, "How many cakes did you receive?
They replied, "I received one cake. She then asked again, "And how many did you receive? He reported, "I received..."
"Two cakes. The woman said, "He has been having an illicit affair with you; how could he possibly give you two cakes?
Upon hearing this, Ānanda was immediately filled with sorrow, and when the bhikṣus heard it, they too were displeased.
There was a brahmin who, having finished his meal here, was heading toward Kosala. On the way, he encountered a highly faithful diviner-brahmin, who asked him, "Where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from Śrāvastī. He asked again, "Can alms-food be obtained? He replied, "It can be obtained. He asked, "From whom can it be obtained?
He replied, "It is obtained from the shaven-headed householder. He asked, "Who is this shaven-headed householder?
He replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama is he. The brāhmaṇa said, "Who are you? You eat the food of others!"
Having uttered these evil words, the bhikṣus reported these two circumstances to the Buddha, who then established the precept. The various non-Buddhists all complained, saying:
"One or two non-Buddhists have committed a transgression; what fault have we committed that we are not permitted to eat?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Those who wish to give food should place it on the ground to give, or they may employ another person."
It should be said for the recitation of the precepts as follows:
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept—
if a bhikṣu receives food directly from the hands of a male follower of another path or a female follower of another path, it is a pāyattika offense.
**Exegesis:** Regarding "male and female heterodox practitioners" (*tīrthika*): these are naked ascetics and followers of divergent teachings who have gone forth among these heterodox groups.

Because their minds do not penetrate the [true] principle and their minds wander outside of that principle, they are called "heterodox" (*tīrthika*). The Sarvāstivādins say: "The Buddha stated that, with the exception of the fivefold assembly of the Buddha himself, all other remaining renunciants are called heterodox.

This rule was established because of the incident involving the initiation of these naked ascetics; furthermore, one should not give food with one's own hands to any other heterodox practitioners. There are ninety-six types of heterodox schools, none of which fall outside the gate of the six teachers. Each teacher has fifteen types of doctrine. [End of excerpt]

The teachings bestowed upon disciples differ from one another; as disciples receive and practice these teachings, they each form distinct views. In this way, a single teacher gives rise to fifteen kinds of divergent views. Each teacher possesses a specific doctrine that differs from those of his disciples;

including both the teachers and their disciples, there are sixteen types in total. Thus, among the six teachers, there are ninety-six types. Regarding the doctrines employed by these teachers, when they are about to pass away, they invariably transmit them to a single disciple. In this manner, as the teachers passed the lineage to one another, there were always six teachers. The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states:

In immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there was a Buddha named Kuśundarabhadra. At the time when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu named Buddhajñāna. A donor offered him a priceless robe, which was subsequently plundered and torn by bandits.

His body was naked, and he had hung his hands from a tree before departing. A Brahmin gathering flowers saw him and gave rise to a false attachment, thinking: "The śramaṇa must know that the *kāṣāya* robe is not the cause of liberation.

From this, the heretics who pluck out their hair and go naked originated. Later, that bhikṣu managed to escape; he took tree bark and smeared it with red stone to cover himself, and he tied grass together to make a whisk to brush away insects. From seeing this, the renunciants among the heretics began their practice. In the evening, the bhikṣu entered the water to bathe.

He covered his body with the tattered rags discarded by cowherds. From seeing this, the heretics of the "Tattered-Rag Bathers" arose. Because monks had sores on their bodies that were being nibbled at by worms, they smeared their bodies with ash; from seeing this, the heretics of the "Ash-Smearers" arose.

Because monks cauterized their sores with fire, and finding the pain unbearable, threw themselves from cliffs to die; from this, the heretics of the "Fire-Worshippers" and "Cliff-Leapers" arose. Thus, the ninety-six kinds of heretics all originated from various appearances of these monks, imitating and following their practices.
Regarding "food": there are five types of formal food (*bhojana*) and five types of informal food (*abhyavahāra*).
The conditions for the offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, the recipient must be a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
Second, one must give the food with one's own hand. Third, the act of giving and receiving must be completed.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one gives food with one's own hand to a naked ascetic, whether male or female, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the recipient accepts what was given, it is a *pāyattika*. If the recipient does not accept what was given, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one attempts to give by means of an expedient but does not actually give, or if one desists after having intended to give, in all such cases it is a *dukkaṭa*. [End of Section] Sa.

Bāhu said: "If one gives food with one's own hand to any of the ninety-six types of those with heterodox views—whether they be householders or renunciants, naked or clothed—it is all a *pāyattika* offense. However, there is no fault if the Sangha gives food to non-Buddhists;
one simply must not give it with one's own hand. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a non-Buddhist comes to beg, one should..."
One should set aside one portion for oneself in a separate place and let the person take it themselves; one must not take the portion belonging to the Saṃgha and give it to them.
For the four assemblies, including the bhikṣuṇīs, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is what is called a transgression.
Explanatory Circumstances (Kāraṇa): There is no offense in the following cases: if one gives after setting it down on the ground; if one causes another to give; if one gives to one's parents;

if one gives to those working for a stūpa or those working in a separate room; if one gives as payment for labor or food; or if it is forcibly seized by means of power—there is no offense. The *Mūla* states:
"Alternatively, if one intends to remove someone's wrong views through the cause of food, giving it to them also constitutes no offense."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There is no offense if [the recipient] is ill, or is a relative, or is seeking ordination (referring to the period of four months during which the *parivāsa* probation is granted).
One must not give food to another before having first received it oneself; rather, after one has received it, one should subsequently give it to them.
In the case of those who are imprisoned, those in urgent need of food, or pregnant women, one should properly observe the appropriate amount.
Give it to them. One should give a single mouthful to an animal. There is no offense in cases such as when the precepts had not yet been established at the beginning.

(A detailed account is found in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*: Maudgalyāyana was leading the bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana along the ocean when he saw a great tree surrounded by many insects that were biting its trunk and even its branches and leaves, leaving not a single spot as small as a needle’s eye vacant.
At the very top [of the tree], there was a great outcry that shook the earth, sounding like the cries from hell. A bhikṣu asked Maudgalyāyana about it, and Maudgalyāyana replied:
"This is the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara) bhikṣu Śreṣṭha. He used the property of the Saṃgha—flowers, fruits, food, and drink—and sent them to laypeople.

He is now receiving this preliminary retribution (puṇyavipāka), and hereafter he will fall into hell as one of the insects that devour the trees. These very insects are the people who received his goods."
Also. ○ Forty-second: A general explanation of the precept against visiting other households without having informed [the host].
This is a shared precept; the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Because of the afflictions arising from worldly household affairs exceeding their limits and causing neglect, this training rule was established. This precept is constituted by the conjunction of six conditions.
The setting: The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park. There was a householder who was a close friend of Upananda.
He thought to himself, "If Upananda comes into the city, I shall provide a meal for the Saṅgha on his behalf."
Regarding the origin of the rule concerning persons:
On another occasion, when Baddhālī entered the city, the elder heard of it and immediately invited the bhikṣus for a meal.
When the bhikṣus arrived at the elder’s house, they waited for Baddhālī. However, at the time of the morning meal, Baddhālī went to another household. Just as [the meal] was about to begin...
He arrived late, causing the bhikṣus to have insufficient food. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who established a precept:

"It is not permitted to accept an invitation for light refreshment beforehand and then go to another household when the time arrives. At that time, there was a high minister who was a close friend of Upananda.
Having obtained many sweet fruits, he ordered someone to take the fruits and tell Upananda to distribute them among the Saṃgha. Upananda...
After having finished his meal, he went to other households and returned only when the time had passed, causing the community of monks to be unable to eat fresh fruit.
The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept: one is not permitted to visit other households before or after a meal. There were many invitations within the city.
The bhikṣus were all fearful and cautious, and did not dare enter the city. The Buddha said, "I allow you to enter the city after having entrusted yourselves to one another.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom they should entrust themselves. The Buddha said, "Entrust yourself to a bhikṣu.

If you are staying alone in a single room, you should entrust yourself to a neighbor who dwells nearby. Furthermore, he added the phrase regarding those who have not been entrusted, beginning with the sick bhikṣu.
He told the householder that he was making soup, porridge, and rice; fearing transgression, he did not dare enter the city.
The Buddha said, "I permit a sick bhikṣu not to announce his departure. Furthermore, I establish an exception for the time when one is not ill. A bhikṣu making robes may have various needs."
Everyone was fearful and cautious, not daring to enter the city. The Buddha said, "I permit you to enter without having made a formal entrustment (*anuddiṣṭa*) during the time of making robes.
Furthermore, during the time of making robes, when the time for receiving donated robes arrived, some had already secured a place to receive robes while others were still seeking them;
they were fearful and cautious, not daring to enter the city. The Buddha said, "I permit you to enter without having made a formal entrustment at the time of the gift of robes."
In the city, the precepts should be recited in this manner:
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts,
if a bhikṣu has already accepted an invitation and then visits other households before or after the meal without having entrusted himself to another bhikṣu.
Except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*. "Other times" refers to: when one is ill; when making robes; and when robes are being offered. These are called the "times. Explanation of the Meaning:

"Having first accepted an invitation" means having already accepted an invitation to a meal from a family of the four castes. "Before the meal" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for eating.
"After the meal" refers to the period from the time for eating until midday. "A family" refers to one that has a male member.
It refers to a place where women reside (other households refers to those not invited). Regarding "not having made an announcement":
if a bhikṣu makes an announcement with the intention of going to a village but returns on the way, he loses that prior announcement; if he wishes to go later, he must make an announcement again.
If a bhikṣu makes an announcement with the intention of going to a village but does not reach the place to which he announced, but instead goes elsewhere...
Regarding the household: if one loses the previous authorization (*anuśāsanā*), and wishes to go, one should receive authorization again before departing.

If, after receiving authorization, one goes to the house of a layperson and then further proceeds to a storehouse or a dwelling on the outskirts of the village, or if one goes from within a bhikṣuṇī monastery back out to the house of a layperson, one loses the previous authorization. One should receive authorization again before proceeding.
"Other bhikṣus" refers to those who dwell together within the same boundary (*sīmā*).
"When making robes" refers to the aforementioned periods of one month or five months, up to the point of making even a single "horse-tooth" stitch upon a robe.
"When robes are being offered" likewise refers to the aforementioned periods of one month or five months, as well as other times, such as when one encourages others to prepare food or offer robes.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, accepting an invitation from a group;
second, visiting another household without informing [the host]; and third, crossing the threshold with both feet.

**The Offense of Confession:** Regarding the offense herein: having previously accepted an invitation, if one goes to another household before or after the meal without informing a bhikṣu who has entered the village—except during the [permitted] times—it is a *pāyattika*. This applies even if one foot is inside the doorway.
With one foot outside the gate, though adorned with skillful means, he wishes to depart but does not; this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, even if it is within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) and near a layperson’s house close to the monastery, failing to inform them constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one returns late after having made a formal announcement (*jñapti*), thereby causing the Saṃgha to become vexed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for a bhikṣu;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three smaller assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is called an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when making robes; when robes are being offered as gifts;

when one has not formally entrusted the care of one's belongings to a monk; or if there is no monk to whom one can entrust them. This includes arriving at a storehouse, a village, or a peripheral dwelling; arriving at a bhikṣuṇī monastery;
arriving at the house of a layperson to whom one has entrusted one's belongings; or if one is held by force, or faces a threat to life or a threat to celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

It is difficult to practice; there is no offense. The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "If one says to the donor, 'Even if I do not come, you should provide food for the Sangha so that it is not neglected,' and the donor does not appoint this person as the primary representative, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept has not yet been promulgated at the outset."

○ General Explanation of the Forty-third Precept on Insisting on Sitting in a Layperson’s Home.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is identical. It is likewise studied by Mahāyāna followers. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Because of [entering] among the laity..."
Household affairs constitute the affliction of lust; this training rule was established [in response].
Regarding the origin of the setting:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of this account:
Kāḷudāyin and the laywoman Ciñcā were mutually infatuated with one another. While begging for alms, he arrived at her house and sat down upon a seat.
At that time, the laywoman Ciñcā had bathed and adorned herself; her husband was exceedingly fond of and respectful toward her. Her husband—
The husband asked, "What do you require? She replied, "I need food. He then sent his wife out to give her some.
After she had eaten, she remained seated and would not leave. The husband said angrily, "Since you still will not leave, what do you intend to do?
I am now abandoning you; go wherever you wish! Later, a bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard this and reported it to the Buddha.
Having rebuked him, he established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu sits down forcefully in a house where food is being prepared, it is a pāyattika offense."

**Explanation of Terms:** "Food" (*āhāra*): Men take women as their food; women take men as their food. (The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: This refers to the mutual enjoyment of men and women through sexual union;

thus it is called "food. "Jewels" (*ratna*): Mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver. (This precept concerns sitting forcibly in a household where food is being consumed. One incurs an offense by obstructing the sexual union of a man and woman.

It is not the presence of jewels that constitutes the transgression. "To sit down forcibly": (The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: Without asking the master of the house for permission, one follows one's own will...)
Because it accords with another's intention, it is said to be "forceful" (i.e., a violation of the established precept).
**Conditions for the Offense:** This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be a household possessing food;
second, it must not be in a public or open place; and third, one must sit alone and at ease.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one sits down by force where there is treasure while in a house where food is being served, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one is blind but not deaf, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one is deaf but not blind, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one stands but does not sit, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a woman has received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), and a man..."
If one does not accept [the precepts], and a man accepts the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*) while a woman does not, sitting within that household constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If both have accepted them, there is no offense. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"If it is a celestial maiden, a *paṇḍaka*, or the like, they all incur a fault; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three minor groups of nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
This is called an offense.
Regarding the exceptions where there is no offense: if one enters a house where food is being served and there is wealth [present], provided that the person extends their hand [to receive it];
or if one sits at the doorway; or if there are two bhikṣus as companions; or if there is a person capable of identifying [the owner]; or if there is a guest in the same place.
There is no offense if one is blind or deaf; if one passes through unexpectedly and does not stay; if one suddenly falls to the ground due to an illness;
if one is held by force; if one is imprisoned; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There is no offense if it is the house of those who have severed lust, the house of those observing the fast, or if there is another person of superior status seated there."
If many people enter and exit this house, there is no offense. One is not guilty of an offense in cases such as when the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
○ A General Explanation of the Forty-fourth Precept: Sitting in Secret with a Layperson in Their Home.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is likewise the same. It is also prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:
"This training rule was established on account of visiting the homes of others and the affliction of sexual desire."
The setting of the origin:
The Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].
It was also because a man and a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) were sitting behind a door panel conversing.
When a bhikṣu seeking alms arrived at that house, he heard the voice of Kāḷudāyin; he censured him and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established definition of the offense:
if a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place within a house where food is being prepared, and there is treasure present, it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning: "A secluded place" refers to a location shielded by trees, walls, fences, hedges, or screens such as clothing, or other objects that provide concealment.
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, being in a house where food is being prepared;
second, being alone with a woman; and third, sitting together in a secluded place.
The opening conditions for the determination of the offense are as previously explained and thus are not repeated here.
○ A general explanation of the forty-fifth precept: the precept against sitting with a woman in an open space.
This is a common precept; it is likewise established for the nuns. It is also prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The afflictions are as previously described.
This training rule was established based on the following origin story.
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There arose a certain occasion concerning a person who,
together with a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who had offered him a meal, sat in one place on the open ground while the alms-collecting monks were nearby.
The Bhikṣu Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked him and established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open, unsheltered place, it is a pāyattika offense."

Explanation of the Terms: “A woman” refers to one who possesses intelligence and whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed. “Alone” means a single woman; [the *Mahāsāṃghika* says: “A single woman with no other person present. Even if there are others, if they are asleep, deluded, insane, mentally deranged, in pain, infants, non-humans, or animals, it is also called ‘alone’. “A bhikṣu” [is as previously defined]. “In a village” means within the boundaries of a village. “In a forest” means outside the boundaries of a village. “Sits” means to sit down. “Lies down” means to lie prostrate. “Intentionally” means with a deliberate mind. “Embraces” means to embrace with both arms. “Takes hold of” means to grasp with one arm. “Grasps the hand” means to grasp the hand. “Grasps the hair” means to grasp the hair on the head. “Engages in sexual intercourse” means to engage in the act of sexual union. “In this way” means in such a manner. “A nun commits a *pārājika* offense” means she incurs a defeat. “Is not in communion” means she is excluded from the community of nuns. This is the meaning. If a nun intentionally embraces a man, takes hold of him, grasps his hand, grasps his hair, or engages in sexual intercourse with him, she commits a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. If she does so unintentionally, she commits an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). If she intentionally embraces, takes hold of, grasps the hand, or grasps the hair of a sleeping man, she commits an offense of wrong-doing. If she does so unintentionally, there is no offense. ○ General Explanation of the Forty-seventh Precept: Regarding Receiving Medicine Excessively.

This is a common precept; it is likewise established for the Bhikṣuṇīs, and those of the Mahāyāna study it together [with them]. If one seeks [items] for the sake of sentient beings, there is no offense.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because of the affliction of seeking excessively regarding matters given by others, this training rule was established. This precept is completed through the conjunction of six conditions.
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākyaśrī. Mahānāman of the Śākya clan (Mahānāman means "Great Name";

he was the son of the Buddha’s paternal uncle and attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin one month after the Buddha)—invited the community of monks and provided them with medicine, honoring them with respect.
The Elder gave the best [portion] to those who had initiated the occasion.
The group of six [monks] said among themselves: "He shows respect to the Elder and gives the best to him, but he has no respect for us."
With respectful hearts, they thought, "We should go to his house and seek out those medicines that are difficult to obtain and which he does not possess.
They went there and said, "We require such-and-such medicines. Mahānāman replied, "Whatever is in the house, I shall give it;
if there is nothing, I will go to the market and buy it to provide for you. The group of six said, "In your house, there cannot possibly be such-and-such..."
"This is medicine, yet you invite the Saṃgha and give them medicine; you have attachment, and furthermore, you speak falsely.
Mahānāma said, "I previously made a vow: 'Whatever provisions I have in my home, I shall provide for the invited Saṃgha;
if there is nothing, I shall go to the market and buy it to give to you. Now why do you say that I have attachment and am a person who speaks falsely? Elder, depart!"
"I have now departed; I shall no longer provide medicine for the Sangha. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept:
"When accepting an invitation for four months to receive medicine, one must not exceed that limit. The sick bhikṣus, being fearful and cautious, did not dare to accept medicine beyond that time.
The Buddha said, "I permit sick bhikṣus to accept medicine beyond that limit. Lay devotees frequently invited the bhikṣus.
Medicine was offered, but the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said, "I permit the bhikṣus to accept regular invitations for the provision of medicine.
Later, Mahānāma again thought to himself, "One should not let the medicine for the Saṃgha be cut off because of one or two individuals.
He invited the Saṃgha once more to provide them with medicine, but the bhikṣus were each individually apprehensive and did not dare [to accept].
[The monks] accepted [the medicine]. The Buddha said, "I permit you to accept it and request more medicine. The bhikṣus then calculated from the previous day's count.
The Buddha said, "You should not calculate from the previous day's count; rather, the count of days should begin from when the medicine was discontinued and resumed."
At that time, various lay devotees invited monks to share their medicinal herbs with them. The monks, being cautious and fearful, did not dare accept them.
The Buddha said, "I permit the monks to accept shared medicinal herbs. Furthermore, there were lay devotees who invited monks to accept medicines for life.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said: "I allow you to accept medicines for as long as life lasts.
The precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for four months' supply of medicine, a bhikṣu who is not ill may accept it; if he accepts beyond that, except for regular [medicines], he commits an offense.'"
To accept an invitation, a further invitation, a partial invitation, or an invitation for as long as life lasts constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

Explanation of the Terms: "Four months" refers to the four months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Regarding the invitation to provide medicine, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it may be during the four months of summer, winter, or spring;

the donor’s invitation is not fixed. Whether it be for four months, one month, or half a month, once the period has expired, one must not seek more. If invited to a morning meal, one must not request an afternoon meal; if invited to an afternoon meal, one must not request a morning meal. This applies to medicine as well.

The same applies to other items as well. If one says, "I shall provide you with the four requisites for the rest of my life," then at that time, one may request them according to one's wishes. The *Vinaya-chao* states: "To sustain one's life, do not exceed [the limits of] medicine. Although the term "medicine" is used generally, it must be divided into four categories.

First, *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the proper time) refers to those taken from dawn until midday; as permitted by the holy teachings, their use accords with the Dharma and should not give rise to karmic entangments. Second, *vikālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for improper times), such as various syrups and juices, are prescribed for specific illnesses and permitted for consumption outside the [proper] time, provided there is no violation of the established limits.

Third, *yāvaj-jīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for as long as life lasts) are governed by the rule of preparation; one must exhaust their allotted duration according to the time limit set for them, thereby providing profound benefit through their therapeutic use. Fourth, regarding medicines for the remainder of one’s life, because their potency is weak, they are permitted to be taken over a long period before they can eliminate afflictions. There are three types of "life" (*jīva*).

1. Exhausting the form of the medicine; 2. Exhausting the form of the illness; 3. Exhausting the form of the retribution. A healthy bhikṣu who should accept [an invitation] (meaning that the patient is not restricted;

if one invites them with a limit, it stops once the illness has healed; otherwise, if they are healthy, it constitutes an offense). "The sick person" refers to one who takes medicine as instructed by a physician.
"A regular invitation" refers to when a person says, "I shall always provide medicine. "A renewed invitation" refers to inviting again after the supply has been cut off. "An individual invitation."

As for "one who brings medicine to the saṃghārāma to distribute": regarding "one who invites [for as long as life lasts]," such a person says, "I shall provide medicine for as long as my life endures.
There are four types of invitations: there may be an invitation with a limit on the night but no limit on the medicine;
there may be an invitation with a limit on the medicine but no limit on the night; or there may be an invitation... [and so forth].

There are medicinal substances with a fixed limit for the night, and those with a fixed limit for the medicine; there are also cases where the night has no fixed limit but the medicine has a fixed limit.

What is meant by "the night has a fixed limit but the medicine has no fixed limit"? It is when one establishes a limit for the night but not for the medicine, saying, "I shall give you this much medicine for [this many] nights.
What is meant by "the medicine has a fixed limit but the night has no fixed limit"? It is when one establishes a limit for the medicine but not for the night.
He establishes a limit for the medicine, but does not establish a limit for the night, saying: "I give such-and-such medicine;
how can there be a limit for the night? The medicine has a limit. He then establishes both a limit for the night and a limit for the medicine.
He speaks thus: "For such a number of nights, I shall provide such medicine. How can there be no limit to the nights and no limit to the medicine?
He does not establish a limit for the nights nor a limit for the medicine, yet he says: "I invite you; please accept the medicine."

In this regard, there are cases where the night has a fixed limit but the medicine does not; cases where both the night and the medicine have fixed limits; cases where the medicine has a fixed limit but the night does not;

and cases where neither the night nor the medicine has a fixed limit—in these instances, one should accept invitations according to the season (referring to the summer retreat, which must have a fixed period and cannot be shifted).

Regarding these, there are cases where the medicine has a fixed limit but the night does not; and cases where neither the night nor the medicine has a fixed limit—in these instances, one should act according to the circumstances.
Regarding the reception [of medicine] (since it is unlimited, one should simply follow the donor's intention and need not fix a specific time limit).

Conditions for an offense: This precept requires three conditions to constitute a full offense: first, accepting an invitation for medicine; second, accepting further medicine after the limit has passed;
and third, requesting and obtaining it such that it enters the throat.

**Determination of Offenses:** Regarding the offense herein, if one accepts more than is permitted, there is a *pāyattika* for every swallow. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one solicits and obtains it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one solicits but does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one solicits bitter medicines such as *harītakī*, whether one obtains them or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "If, before the four months [of the rainy season] have concluded, one is invited to coarse food and further..."
If one requests fine food [when only coarse food was offered], it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). If one eats it, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If, after being invited to fine food, one further requests coarse food, the act of requesting it is an *dukkaṭa*, but there is no offense when eating it. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"When a donor offers medicine, it should be used as medicine; it must not be used as food. To ask for ghee when given oil constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
If a person offers medicine to the Saṃgha, the administrative bhikṣu should ask: "Is it to be kept within the village, or is it to be placed inside the monastery?
If he says it is to be kept within the village, [the administrator] must inform him when needed, saying: "I require such-and-such medicine;

prepare it for me so that there is no lack. If he says it is to be kept inside the monastery, he should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one subsequent proclamation) to appoint a person endowed with five qualities as the steward.
The Buddha does not follow after desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; he is one who knows what is medicinal and what is not, acting as the guardian of the Saṃgha’s medicine.
For a bhikṣuṇī [to act thus], it is a pāyattika; for the three minor groups of disciples, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.

Explanatory Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: accepting an invitation for four months; giving medicine to one who is ill; accepting regular invitations beyond the limit; receiving further invitations or specific invitations;
and accepting invitations for as long as one lives. There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Forty-eighth Precept on Viewing Military Arrays.

This is a shared precept; nuns likewise commit an offense if they violate it. It is similarly proscribed in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Because of viewing the military..."
The matter was chaotic and distressing, so this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
Regarding the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the subjects within the territory of King Prasenajit had rebelled, and the King himself...

He led the six armies on a campaign of conquest (one *jun* consists of twelve thousand five hundred men; according to the Zhou system, the Son of Heaven maintains six armies, while the feudal lords of great states maintain three, those of intermediate states maintain three, and those of small states maintain one).
The origin of the incident:
The group of six monks went into the midst of the army and observed King Prasenajit, saying, "Venerable sirs, you are here; what do you intend to do?
The group of six replied, "We have no business here; we have merely come to look at the military array. When the king heard this, he was displeased.
He asked again, "Where do you intend to go now? He replied, "I wish to go to Śrāvastī to see the Buddha.
The king said, "If you reach Śrāvastī, convey my name to the World-Honored One, pay homage, and inquire after his well-being.

Present this parcel of stone honey as an offering, and report these matters in detail to the World-Honored One. At that time, the group of six monks went there and, upon seeing the Buddha, reported everything in full.

Regarding the matter above: after the Buddha had rebuked them, he established a precept. Regarding the act of going to view military formations, it was at Pāveyya that there were two brothers who were high ministers;
the elder brother was named Likhita and the younger was named Puṇṇaka. The king commissioned them to lead an army for a campaign of conquest.
These two individuals were thirsting with longing to see him. The bhikṣu immediately sent a messenger to invite them. The bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious. The Buddha said:
"If there is an invitation to come, you are permitted to go. The precepts should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu goes to observe a military array, except when there is a specific cause or circumstance, it is a *pāyattika*.

Explanation of the meaning: "Array" refers to either a display or a battle. (*Vinayaviniścaya* states: There are four types of arrays: first, the spear-point formation; second, the chariot-axle formation; third, the half-moon formation; fourth, [the great array formation].)

The momentum of the Peng bird’s wings). As for the armies: the elephant army, the cavalry, the chariot army, and the infantry (the *Xiyu ji* states: "In the western lands, the most valiant warriors are all selected; fathers and sons pass down their craft, thereby perfecting military defense.

When at rest, they guard the palace and its precincts; when on campaign, they lead the vanguard. The elephants are clad in sturdy armor, their tusks fitted with sharp spikes. A single general rides securely upon them, granted the authority of command.

Two soldiers stand left and right to manage and drive them. The chariots are drawn by teams of four horses. Military officers ride in the chariots, surrounded by ranks of soldiers who support the rims and hold the shafts. The cavalry provides dispersed resistance, pursuing the defeated and rushing to their stations. The infantry are light and agile, chosen for their daring courage. They carry great [weapons]... )

Grasping a long halberd, or holding a sword or blade, he leads the vanguard of the battle array. Among all military weapons—namely the shield and spear, bow and arrow, sword, scimitar, axe, hatchet, *ge*, *shu*, long lance, wheel, and noose—all of which are mastered through worldly training—he may employ them when there is a timely cause and condition (*saṃvartanīya-pratyaya*).

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, "cause and condition" refers to cases such as when a king, a queen, a crown prince, a high minister, or a general dispatches a messenger to summon him; in such instances, there is no offense.

It is for the sake of stopping slander. If one does not go when summoned, one should say: "When the bhikṣu has something he seeks, he comes of his own accord even without being called; when he has nothing he seeks, though called, he does not come. This is for the sake of the fruits of the śramaṇa.

If he goes and preaches the Dharma, he may attain the stage of srotāpanna, up to anāgāmin. Furthermore, it is for the sake of increasing the roots of faith and reverence; and because the monastic and the lay community require one another, it serves to nurture the Buddha-dharma. For these reasons, going is permitted, so that through a joyful heart one may attain the fruits of the śramaṇa.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, there must be a military array;
second, there must be the intention to go and observe it; third, the object must be clearly perceived.
**The Determination of the Offense:** In this context, for one who goes and sees [the army], it is a *pāyattika* offense; for one who does not see it, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one makes preparations and intends to go to observe it but does not go, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a monk arrives after an army already on the march is in formation, he should leave the road to avoid it; if he does not avoid it, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Luo. Sārvastivāda says: If one does not go intentionally, but passes through the middle of the path due to the causes and conditions of coming and going, there is no offense.
If one stands still to watch, violating the rules of dignified deportment, it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅). If one looks around to the left or right, [it is likewise].
*Dukkaṭa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If an army comes to the monastery and one does not intentionally look at it, there is no offense.
If one intentionally looks at it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense. If one goes to look at people who are quarreling, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense. The *Vinayasamgraha* states:
If one observes the armies of devas, nāgas, asuras, and so forth, one also incurs *duṣkṛta*; this applies even down to intentional observation.

Watching the fighting of quails and the like constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all cases. However, if an enemy army is about to arrive and one must go to observe it in order to ascertain its distance, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "When seeing an army, one should not comment on its strengths or weaknesses."
The *Nidāna* states: "If there are those engaged in a fight, one should not go to look at them. If one sees a dispute, one must quickly abandon it and depart.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*; for the three minor groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is called an offense."
**Explanatory Circumstances (Kāraṇa):** There is no offense in the following cases: if one goes for a specific purpose; if one is invited to go; if one is taken away by force;

if one was already on the march in an army formation and subsequently descends to a lower path to avoid [the offense]; or if water or land routes are cut off, or due to other such difficult circumstances where avoidance is impossible.
There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset.

The assembly deliberated and declared: "Because the Buddha-dharma is most venerable, in order to extinguish slander, and to cause all unwholesome dharmas to cease and wholesome dharmas to increase, this precept is hereby established."

This is a shared precept; nuns are likewise bound by it, and it is studied in common by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "By observing the army..."
This training rule was established on account of the matter and the distracted mind.
As for the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of the rule: The group of six monks had a reason for staying overnight within an army camp.
When the laypeople saw them, they said to one another, "We are merely staying here because of our affection [for our kin]; why then are these śramaṇas also staying here? The other monks...
The Bhikṣu Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. Having rebuked [the transgressor], the Buddha established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason, he is permitted to go among the military for two or three nights. Should he exceed this limit, it is a pāyattika offense."

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding those who have a valid reason—such as being invited by a king, a queen, a crown prince, a high minister, or a general; or for the sake of the Saṃgha, a stūpa, or a private matter;
or when there is something to be formally announced—they may stay within an army for two nights. On the third night, they must depart before the first light of dawn appears.
One should remain away from places where [the army] is seen or heard (that is, one must strictly observe the three-day limit and not pass through until the dawn has appeared).
Regarding the conditions for an offense: this precept requires two conditions to be fulfilled in order to constitute the full offense. First, one personally enters the midst of the army;
second, one stays overnight without a valid reason.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one has stayed in the army for two nights and, on the third night, before the appearance of dawn, does not move out of the range of sight or hearing, then when the appearance of dawn occurs, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

If one moves from the range of sight to the range of hearing, or from the range of hearing to the range of sight, it is all a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Even if there is a valid cause."

If a matter can be settled by means of a letter, one should send a letter. If it is necessary to go in person, then after the business has been concluded, one should return immediately without staying overnight.
If the matter is not settled, one may stay for one night; if not settled after one night, one may stay for a second night; if still not settled, one may stay for a third night.
If, whether settled or not, one stays beyond three nights, it is a *pāyattika* offense. If the matter is settled [within those limits], there is no fault.
To stay overnight where one ought not to stay constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

If one is engaged in work for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha and has not yet finished, one may stay away from the army for one night; once that period has passed, one may stay longer. If the city or town is too distant to reach, one may remain.
One should stay overnight in a place where one can avoid seeing or hearing the army. When staying there, one should say to the sentries outside the camp:
"I intend to stay overnight at this location; do not mistake me for a stranger. If soldiers come to the monastery and take up residence there, [one should act accordingly].
One should not depart and leave her. Although staying for many nights involves no offense for the [other] nuns, for a bhikṣuṇī it is a pāyattika;
for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense if, after staying two nights, one leaves the range of sight and hearing before the light of dawn has appeared on the third night;
or if the path by water or land is cut off, or due to other such difficult circumstances; or if one does not leave the range of hearing and seeing;
or if there is no offense because the precept had not yet been promulgated at the outset.
○ General Explanation of the Fiftieth Precept: Against Observing Military Arrays and Engaging in Battle.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is identical. It is likewise proscribed in the Mahāyāna. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "If a disciple of the Buddha..."
One must not, out of a malicious intent, observe the fighting of men and women, military arrays and soldiers, or the combat of bandits and the like.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "This training rule was established to prevent causing armies to tremble with fear and to restrain the mind from agitation."
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].
There was a circumstance involving the group of six monks. They stayed within an army for two or three nights.
While they were there, they watched the military formations and the fighting. One of the six monks was struck by an arrow; his fellow bhikṣu wrapped him in his robe.
They returned in a carriage. The lay devotees asked, "What is this man's ailment? They replied, "He has no ailment;
he was merely shot by an arrow while observing the battle arrays. The lay devotees criticized and disparaged them. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them.
The formulation of the precept: Regarding the characteristics of the precept thus established—
if a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, or at any time observes military formations, combat, or troop maneuvers.
Regarding "the power and force of an army of elephants and horses":
it is a *pāyattika*. Explanation of the terms: "Army" refers to one type of army up to four types of armies; these may be royal armies or the armies of householders.
It refers to those who observe military arrays and battles, whether they be mock combats or actual engagements in battle. There are four [types].
Square arrays, circular arrays, or crescent-shaped arrays; or "tension-and-screen" (zhang-jian) arrays, or "box-like" (han-xiang) arrays.

If one observes the strength and momentum of a mobile army consisting of elephants and horses, there is first the power of elephants, first the power of horses, first the power of chariots, and first the power of infantry (*Saṃghāṭa* says:
when the strong and weak incline toward one another and one observes their circumstances and momentum, this is called "strength and momentum").
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, two armies engage in combat;
second, one has the intention to go and watch; third, one sees their formations.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if one goes and sees [the army], it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one prepares the means and intends to go but does not go, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one is already traveling on the road when the army arrives, and fails to avoid it when one ought to do so, it is a *dukkaṭa*. According to the Sarvāstivādins: [as stated above].

Regarding this essence of the precept: when a bhikṣu stays within an army for two nights, if he intentionally goes to see the troops donning their weapons, or the ivory standards, banners, and flags, or the two armies engaged in combat, it is a pāyattika offense.

Even if he is not staying within the army for two nights, if he intentionally goes to see them, up to the point of the two armies engaging in combat, it is likewise a pāyattika offense. If he sits down but does not look, [there is no offense]. Intentionally...
Standing to watch, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). Even down to watching the banners and flags of an army, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
The *Pañcavargīka-vinaya* states: "Watching birds and beasts fight is a *duṣkṛta*; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three minor groups [of novices], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is what constitutes an offense."
The Opening of the Conditions. There is no offense in the following cases: if there is a specific cause; if one has made a formal announcement; if one is summoned; if one is taken away by force;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Or, if one was previously on the front lines of an army and later arrives at a lower road to avoid [the offense];
or if the water or land routes are cut off; or if one does not avoid it due to various other difficult circumstances—there is no offense. This is the foremost case of no offense.
Regarding the initial non-enactment of the precepts, etc.
○ A general explanation of the fifty-first precept concerning the consumption of intoxicants.
This is a shared precept; it is likewise established for the nuns. It is also regulated in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"This training rule was established due to the affliction of censure arising from the matter of begging."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Cīda (alternatively called Ceti, or again, Cedī).
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].

The Venerable Sāgata (Sāgata means "Welcome" [svāgata]. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, on the day of his birth, his appearance was so lovely that his parents were filled with joy and cried out, "Welcome!

Thus he was named Svāgata). As stated in the *Guṇavat-sūtra*, among the śrāvakas, he was the one who possessed mastery over the fire-element (*tejodhātu*) supernatural power. He served as a provider of offerings for the Buddha.
Once, while seeking lodging at the home of a matted-hair brahmin, he sat cross-legged within the chamber of a venomous dragon. The dragon emitted fire and smoke, but the Venerable...
The dragon also released smoke and fire; the dragon, filled with wrath, again released the fire from its own body.

The Venerable One also released fire from his own body, immediately extinguishing the dragon’s fire and rendering it lusterless. Having thus subdued the venomous dragon, he placed it within his almsbowl.

At that time, the ruler of Kauśāmbī (who was King Udayana) was also staying there overnight. Witnessing this supernatural power, his profound faith increased further, and he desired to offer him worship.
He asked, "Venerable sir, what do you require? He replied, "Stop, stop! This itself shall suffice as an offering to me. Again he said, "Please tell me what you require.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks requested black liquor for him; the Venerable one became intoxicated and satiated, fell to the ground halfway along the road, and vomited.
Various birds cried out in confusion. The Buddha, knowing this, asked about it intentionally. Ānanda reported the matter in detail. The Buddha rebuked him, saying, "Fool!"
If people today cannot subdue even small dragons, how much less can they subdue great dragons? The Buddha said: There are ten faults in drinking alcohol:
first, one's complexion becomes ugly; second, one’s strength diminishes; third, one’s vision becomes unclear.
Fourth, they manifest signs of anger and hatred. Fifth, they ruin their fields, livelihoods, and means of subsistence.
Sixth, they increase their susceptibility to illness. Seventh, they augment quarrels and litigation. Eighth, their ill repute spreads abroad. Ninth, their wisdom diminishes.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the three evil realms. From this day forward, those who take me as their teacher shall [avoid these].
It was further determined that one must not place the tops of grass or wood into wine and drink it. Having rebuked [the offender], he established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika offense."
**Exegesis:** "Alcohol" refers to: wood-wine; wine made from *śāli* rice; wine made from other types of rice; barley-wine;
or any other substance that constitutes wine according to the rules for making it. Regarding "wood-wine":

this includes wine made from pear juice, wine made from *jambu* fruit (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that its shape is like a large watermelon and it is purple, sour, and sweet), wine made from sugarcane, wine made from *śāluka* fruit (which is the root of the lotus), wine made from *bījapūra* juice (the phonetic transcription is *zhì*), and so forth.
