The *rui* has thorns between its stalks; its fruit resembles an ear-ornament (*karṇikā*) and is purple-red in color. According to the *Bencao*, eating it stops nasal hemorrhage. If consumed over a long period, it lightens the body, benefits the vital energy (*prāṇa*), and prevents hunger.
As for wine made from grapes or pear juice, if honey or rock sugar (*śarkarā*) is mixed with them—even in the case of grape wine—it is likewise.

**Conditions for Offense:** This precept requires two conditions to constitute a full offense: first, the substance must be alcohol; second, one must greedily drink it so that it passes down the throat.

**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one eats or drinks anything that is actual alcohol, alcohol produced by fermenting alcohol, or a mixture containing alcohol, [an offense is committed].
A *pāyattika* offense. If one drinks sweet-flavored liquor, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one drinks sour-flavored liquor, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one eats yeast or dregs of wine, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
(According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*: "Regarding the offense of eating yeast: this yeast is made by mixing wheat and medicinal herbs with wine and letting them ferment.

Later, it is dried and carried about; when mixed with water and drunk, it causes intoxication. As for other types of yeast, there is no offense. If one perceives what is wine as wine, or has doubt regarding wine, [it is an offense].
If one has no perception of alcohol when drinking alcohol, it is a *pāyattika*. If there is no alcohol but one perceives it as such, or if one suspects there is no alcohol, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "In general, if one drinks that which possesses the color, fragrance, or taste of alcohol—even if one or two of these are missing—and it is capable of intoxicating a person, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If one drinks that which does not intoxicate a person, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*."
If the substance itself is not wine, yet possesses the appearance of wine, drinking it constitutes no offense. The *Mātṛkā* states:

"If medicinal substances—whether to be taken at specific times (*tatkāla-bhaiṣajya*), at improper times (*akāla-bhaiṣajya*), or for seven days (*saptāha-bhaiṣajya*)—are infused with wine, they may be consumed provided they lack the nature of wine."
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: If food or medicine has been boiled with alcohol, and it still possesses the aroma or flavor of alcohol, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if it lacks the aroma or flavor of alcohol, it may be eaten. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*; for the three junior groups [of disciples], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is defined as an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases. If a person suffers from such an illness that it cannot be cured by other medicines, and wine is used as medicine;
or if wine is applied to a wound—in all such instances there is no offense. There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, and so forth.
The *Sārvastivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one commits a transgression exceeding this [level of] sin, this wine is extremely grave;
one who drinks it can commit the four *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses—excluding the schism of the Saṃgha—because for the offense of schism, one must claim to be a Buddha oneself.
It can also destroy all precepts as well as other various evils. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "If one does not guard against it, one will abandon the abstention from drinking."
Regarding the precept against intoxicants, it constitutes a total violation of all other disciplinary rules.

It is heard that there was once a lay follower (upāsaka) of naturally benevolent character who had received and maintained the five precepts, observing them with single-minded devotion and without transgression. Later, on one occasion, his entire family, both great and small...
He was to serve as a guest for others, yet he alone did not go; instead, he remained behind to provide food for them.

When the time came to take his own meal, because it was very salty, he became thirsty in an instant. Seeing a vessel containing wine that looked like water, and being driven by his thirst, he took and drank it.
At that moment, he violated the precept against drinking alcohol. Then, a neighbor’s rooster entered his house and stole [some food].
He captured the chicken, killed it, and cooked it for food; thus, he further violated the precepts against killing and stealing.

A neighbor’s daughter, searching for her chicken, entered his room, whereupon he used force and coercion to commit sexual intercourse with her; because of this, he further violated the precept against sexual misconduct.
The neighbor became enraged and took him to the authorities. At that time, the judge questioned him regarding the circumstances, and he [related] all of them...
To refuse [the truth] and conceal it constitutes, for this reason, a further violation of the precept against false speech. Thus, all five precepts may be transgressed on account of alcohol;

therefore, among the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), the drinking of intoxicants alone is strictly regulated. Furthermore, alcohol causes the loss of mindfulness and increases shamelessness and lack of dread of wrongdoing;
because its faults are so profound and grave, it is singled out for specific prohibition.
○ A General Explanation of the Fifty-second Precept on Sporting in Water.
This is a shared precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise studied in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "It gives rise to public censure."
[The Buddha] was displeased and established this training rule.
Regarding the origin of the rule:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The occasion for the arising [of this teaching]:

While the group of seventeen monks was sporting in the waters of the Ajiravatī River (translated into Chinese as Wusheng, "Unconquerable"), King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā (translated as Shenglan, "Victorious Garland";
it is also the name of a flower; according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, this queen originally tended Mallikā’s garden and was skilled at weaving flower garlands) were there.

The Sūtra says: "Among my śrāvakas, there is one foremost in attaining realization, a laywoman (upāsikā) of firm and steadfast faith; she is Queen Mallikā. Standing atop a multi-storied pavilion, [the Buddha] saw her from afar and said to Queen Mallikā, "Look at those whom you serve.
The Queen replied, "These bhikṣus are youths who have only recently left the household life;
they have not long been in the Buddha-dharma. Some are elders who are dull-witted and know nothing. The husband—[the Buddha]—said:
The people immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sports and plays in water, it is a pāyattika offense."

Explanation of the Terms: "Playing in the water" means to let one's mind run wild and act according to one's own whims. One goes from this shore to the other shore; sometimes with the current, sometimes against it;
sometimes submerging here and emerging there; sometimes drawing patterns in the water with the hands, or splashing and drenching one another.
Even to the point of filling a bowl with water and playing with it:
the conditions for the offense. This precept requires two conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be within water; second, there must be the intentional mind of playing.
Determination of the Offense: Among these, the offense for playing in water is a *pāyattika*.
Excluding water, if one plays in curd-whey, clear curd-whey, fermented vinegar, or grain-liquor within a vessel, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: If one snaps one's fingers to make a sound as a form of play, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for all such acts of mind.
However, there is no offense for one who is learning to swim; as the Blessed One said, "A bhikṣu should practice swimming, lest he be unable to swim across due to some emergency.
If one plays with water or wine, at a later time, according to the number of drops [consumed], one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one sprinkles cool water for the sake of refreshing oneself, there is no offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To knead snow or play with dew on the tips of grass is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If there is water on a tray, or if there is water on a seat, to draw lines upon it with a finger is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If the water is deep enough to submerge the feet, to play within it by turning one's back [to the preceptor] constitutes a *pāyattika*."
If one rocks a boat or plays with the water, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the three groups of minor disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
**Explanatory Circumstances: Cases of Non-offense.** There is no offense in the following cases: if one is traveling on a road and crossing water from this shore to the other;
if one is dragging timber, bamboo, or reeds through the water, moving with or against the current; if one is gathering stones or sand;

if an object has been lost and has sunk to the bottom of the water, appearing at one spot and disappearing at another; or if one wishes to learn the art of swimming and extends one's arms to stroke [the water].
Splashing water on water: there is no offense in any of these cases. Those who do not commit an offense are those for whom the precepts have not yet been established, and so forth.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā*, it is for the sake of honoring the Buddha-dharma and for the sake of nurturing reverence and faith.
This precept is established so as not to neglect one's primary duties and to cultivate right mindfulness.
○ A general explanation of the fifty-third precept: the precept against striking or poking one another.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is the same. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"Because one tickled with a finger and laughed excessively, resulting in death, this training rule was established."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].

One person from among the group of six struck him with a wooden board, and one person from among the group of seventeen caused him to die (according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, he who struck him until he died was a young junior bhikṣu). The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
Explanation of the meaning: "Fingers" refers to the ten on the hands and the ten on the feet. (As for "strikes or tickles": using a finger, a toe, or any other object, he touches the other.)
It is because of taking pleasure in causing itching on the body.
Regarding the conditions for the offense: this precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be the intentional intent to tickle;
second, the hands or fingers must be used; third, they must touch the other person's body.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one strikes or tickles another with the fingers of the hand or foot, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) in all cases.

Excluding the fingers of the hands and feet, if one strikes or tickles another with a staff, a door-bolt, the handle of a fly-whisk, or any other object whatsoever, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a bhikṣu..."
Whether using one, two, or up to ten fingers, when tickling another, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
If both persons are paralyzed or insensate, and one tickles them, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

The Sarvāstivādins state that tickling a bhikṣuṇī, the three groups [of novices], the six types of offenders, or those who practice the five dharmas of Devadatta, as well as those with deranged minds or disordered mental illnesses, constitutes an offense.
A corrupted mind; being at home; having no teacher or Saṃgha—such cases as these all constitute *duṣkṛta*. Those who are blind, sightless, deaf, or mute [are ineligible];

those undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*; a *śrāmaṇera* who has received the precepts; one who does not see [the offense] or does not acknowledge it; and one whose evil and heterodox views have not been removed.

For those who perform the four types of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) based on [the aforementioned grounds], it is a *pāyattika* offense for all. If one instructs another to poke or prod [a person], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "To poke or prod a *śrāmaṇera*, or even an animal, is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mātṛkā* states:
"If one uses a finger to poke while the sense organ is impaired, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
For the group of three junior nuns, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is called an offense. Explanatory conditions for non-offense:
There is no offense if one does not intentionally poke or tickle; if one touches someone while sleeping to wake them; if one is entering or exiting, walking or coming; if one is sweeping the floor;
or if one accidentally touches with the tip of a staff. There is also no offense for one who has not yet committed the act at the time the precept was first promulgated.
Etc. ○ A General Explanation of the Fifty-fourth Precept: Refusing Counsel.
This is a common precept; the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"This training rule was established because of the inability to endure afflictions (*kleśa*)."
The setting for the origin of this account:
The Buddha was staying in the country of Kauśāmbī at the Ghoṣitārāma monastery. The individuals involved in the origin of this account were as follows:
Chanda intended to violate the precepts. The bhikṣus admonished him, saying, "Do not harbor such an intention; you should not do this.
Chanda did not comply and immediately committed the offense. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a *pāyattika*. Explanation of the meaning:

"Does not accept admonition" means (the commentary states: if that which is spoken by a person of honor should not be obstructed; if there is any instruction given, one should not oppose it, but rather remain silent and respectful).
One should dwell with reverence, free from envy and anger, having removed the mind of evil, and always remaining worthy of veneration.
Regarding the conditions for transgression: this precept constitutes a full offense only when three conditions are met: first, knowing that one's own conduct is contrary to the Dharma;
second, being admonished by a wise person; and third, refusing to accept such admonition.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: if another person forbids one by saying, "Do not do this;
it should not be done so," and the person knowingly proceeds to act as they did, committing the offense intentionally while fundamentally disregarding the words, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If the person knows that what they have done was indeed improper, yet commits the offense intentionally while fundamentally disregarding the words, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation). [This applies to] a bhikṣu.
For a nun, this constitutes a *niḥpātya* offense; for the three junior groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is what is called an offense.

**The Exceptions:** There is no offense in the following cases: if an ignorant person comes to admonish her, she replies, "You should first ask your two teachers about their learning, recitation of the scriptures, and knowledge of the methods of admonition; only then may you admonish me"; or if she speaks in jest; or if she is alone.

Speech. If one speaks while dreaming, or intends to say one thing but says another by mistake—all such instances are non-offenses. Those who are non-offending include cases where the precept has not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.

According to the *Vinayamātṛkā*, one should not accept the admonitions of five types of persons: first, those who lack a sense of shame; second, [those who lack a sense of dread of blame]; third... [text fragment].
1. Not studying extensively; 3. Constantly seeking out the faults of others; 4. Delighting in strife and contention; 5. Desiring to cast off the robes and return to lay life.
○ A general explanation of the fifty-fifth precept: not to cause fear in others.

This is a common precept; the formulation for nuns is the same. In the Mahāyāna, it is studied in common [with the Śrāvaka vehicle], though there may be no offense if one subdues others by observing their capacities.
The *Vinayaviniscaya* states: "This training rule was established due to the affliction of lack of tranquility arising from the act of frivolous play."
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra.
The person who gave rise to the occasion [was as follows].

At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Nāgapāla (translated as "Dragon Protector" or "Elephant Protector") was attending upon the Buddha and providing for his needs. It is said that this bhikṣu, during his present life, also realized the pure Dharma;
the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that he was the foremost bhikṣu among the Buddha’s śrāvakas in understanding the stars and predicting auspicious or inauspicious events—Nāgapāla is he.

When the World-Honored One was walking up and down on the path for walking meditation, it was the constant practice of all Buddhas that when they were walking, those who were making offerings would [attend them].
He stood at the head of the walkway. When the first watch of the night had passed, he invited the Buddha to enter his room; the World-Honored One remained silent.
When the middle and final watches of the night had passed, he again invited the World-Honored One to enter his room; at that time, the Buddha remained silent.
Nāgapāla, wishing to terrify the Buddha so as to compel him to enter his room, immediately turned back and was seized; he then made the voice of a non-human being to frighten the śramaṇa.
"I am a ghost. The Buddha said, "You should know that this foolish person’s mind is also evil. He rebuked him and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu causes fear in another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
**Exegesis:** Regarding "terror": if one uses forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects to terrify people, what constitutes terror by means of form?
It refers to manifesting the shape of an elephant, a horse, a ghost, a bird, a beast, or other such forms to terrify people.

[Question]: These are things commonly seen; why should they cause fear? [Answer]: Because they appear at an inappropriate time, they cause people to be terrified. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "As for 'form,' it appears in a dark place, causing one’s ears to prick up and one’s face to contort."
They protrude their eyes and tongues, even curling back a single finger, making terrifying gestures such as "he-he. As for sounds:

the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of donkeys, the cries of ghosts, and the calls of strange birds—through various such sounds they create terror. As for scents: root-fragrances, *sāla* tree fragrances (translated here as "birth";

if one says *sāragha*, it refers to resinous incense), and tree-resin fragrances (*vṛkṣa-niryāsa*; in Sanskrit *kunduru*, translated here as "xunlu"; its appearance is like peach gum; the *Xiyu ji* states...).

In the country of Aṭali in South India, there is the *kunkuma* (frankincense) tree. Its leaves resemble those of the *tánglí* (crabapple). The *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) states that it originates from the south of Tianzhu and Handan. The *Caowuzhuang* (Description of Plants and Objects) says it comes from the country of Daqin (Romania/Byzantium), growing on the sandy shores of the sea.

In midsummer, resin flows onto the sands; its form resembles white glue and is similar to pine resin. It is yellowish-white in color. That from India is white, while that from Handan is interspersed with green; their color and fragrance are not particularly strong. It is also said that "milk incense" (guggulu) is of the same category.

Whatever resin does not function as incense is collectively termed "glue-incense" (jiaoxiang). There are also fragrances from bark, fragrances from pith, fragrances from leaves, fragrances from flowers, fragrances from fruits, and beautiful fragrances;
there are also foul odors. By means of these various fragrances, they terrify people. As for tastes: whether sour, sweet, bitter, or astringent.
Whether it be salty, or the taste of a *kāṣāya*—through such various tastes, one causes terror. As for touch:

if it is hot (such as by using fire or a heated key), one says, "Fire has broken out," as it touches that person's body. If it is cold (such as by using a fan, a garment, water, or wine), one says, "It is snowing or raining. If it is light (such as covering them with a fine, thin garment), one says, "Clouds are falling.

If it is heavy (holding a heavy woolen blanket over them), one says, "The wall is collapsing. Whether it be fine or coarse, or smooth (such as the stem of an *utpala* lotus or a door-bolt)—one touches [them].
If he touches that person’s body and it is rough—as if it were the stem of a *padma* flower—he says, "This is a centipede. If it is soft, or if it is hard—in such ways does this touch terrify people.
As for the method: he says to the person before him, "I have seen your signs;

I dreamt you shall die," or "you shall lose your robes and bowl," or "you shall abandon the path," or "it is the same for your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*)," or "your parents will suffer a grave illness."
Sickness, or death. Using such things to terrify people (according to the Sarvāstivāda: if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Do not defecate or urinate upon living grass or vegetables;
you shall fall into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm"—this is called the characteristic of terrifying by means of the Dharma).
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be a conscious intent to cause fear;
second, one must employ the six categories of objects, such as visible forms and so forth; third, one must speak with clear articulation.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bhikṣu terrifies another person by means of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*), if he speaks and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*; if it is not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, if a bhikṣu himself uses these six matters to frighten others, or instructs another to do so, and the other bhikṣus are able... [to perceive it].
To cause [a bhikṣu] to be afraid; if one is unable to cause him to be afraid, it is all a *pāyattika*.

Apart from these six matters, if one further causes a bhikṣu to be afraid by means of other matters, it is a *duṣkṛta*. That is to say, if one uses such things as excessive sleep, excessive eating, or excessive talk.
One shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. If one causes fear in a bhikṣuṇī, the three groups [of monastics], or even any layperson, it is all *duṣkṛta*.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If, by means of something loathsome, one causes another to feel fear or distress—whether that fear actually arises or not—if the meaning of one's words is understood, one incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*). If, however, by means of something desirable..."
If one speaks of matters such as forms and sounds out of fear or annoyance, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

However, if one speaks of the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts with the intention of transforming and guiding them, there is no offense even if they become afraid. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *pāyattika*;
for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*. This is defined as an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: if one is sitting in a dark place without a lamp; or in a place for defecating or urinating;
or if, seeing something from afar, one says, "It is an elephant," "a thief," or "a wild beast," and consequently becomes terrified;
or if one is in a very dark room without a lamp, or in a place for defecating or urinating, and hears the sound of footsteps, the rustling of grass or trees, or the sound of coughing.
Fear. If one shows this to others by means of a physical form, it does not cause terror.

If such a thing were truly real, then upon seeing such a sign—whether in a dream or otherwise—if death were imminent, or if one were to leave the monastic path, or lose one's robes and bowl, or likewise with respect to the two teachers, or if one’s parents were gravely ill and about to die, or if one speaks in jest, speaks rapidly, or speaks to oneself in a dream.

[The Buddha] spoke in the Middle Indic language. If one intended to say this but mistakenly said that instead, there is no offense in any case. There is no offense for those who were first [in the community] before the precept was established, and so forth.
○ The fifty-sixth rule: The Precept Regarding Bathing Too Frequently.
General Explanation:
This is a shared precept; the offenses for nuns are likewise the same, as they study together in the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"This training rule was established due to excessive affliction arising from the act of bathing. This precept is constituted by the convergence of six conditions.
The Setting of the Discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. There was a pond belonging to King Bimbisāra, where he permitted the bhikṣus to bathe.
The occasion arose concerning a person.

During the latter part of the night, the group of six entered the pond to bathe. The king and his court ladies also arrived there and, hearing the sound of bathing, asked his attendants who they were.
Upon learning they were bhikṣus, the king said, "Do not make a great noise; do not let them depart before they have finished their bath."
At that time, the group of six monks washed one another with various fine medicinal powders until the first light of dawn appeared.

The king was unable to bathe at all and departed; the ministers then criticized and disparaged them. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept: "One should bathe once every half-month.
During the intense heat, however, the bodies of the bhikṣus became covered in sweat and filth, becoming foul-smelling and filthy; fearing the violation of the rule, they did not dare to bathe.

[Regarding] bathing: The Buddha said, "I allow you to bathe frequently during the heat. When various sick bhikṣus had their bodies smelling foul and filthy, or were soiled by excrement and urine, they feared [the rules] too much and did not dare to bathe. The Buddha said, "I allow you to bathe frequently when ill.

When various bhikṣus were sweating and becoming foul-smelling and filthy while working, the Buddha said, "I allow you to bathe frequently while working. Regarding various bhikṣus [during] wind and rain...
While traveling on the road, they became covered in dust and filth. The Buddha said, "I allow you to bathe frequently during times of wind and rain.

When the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, their bodies became hot and covered in sweat, grime, and dust. The Buddha said, "I allow you to bathe frequently while traveling on the road. The precepts should be recited in this manner.
Regarding the established rule for the observance of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill must accept this [limit] and may not exceed it, except during other times.

This constitutes a pāyattika offense. "Other times" refers to: the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of manual labor, the time of wind and rain, and the time of traveling on a road. These are the permitted times.

**Explanation of the Terms:** Regarding "bathing every half-month" (*ardhamāsa-snāna*): According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one bathes on the tenth day and the count reaches the fifteenth day, one must bathe again.

If one bathes on the fourteenth day, or even on the first day, the count shall begin from that bathing day; one must wait until the fifteenth day has been completed before bathing again. This is called "bathing every half-month. It does not mean that the period from the first day to the fifteenth day constitutes a "half-month.

Regarding "the hot season": The final forty-five days of spring and the first month of summer constitute the hot season. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: the remaining one and a half months of spring...)

The first month and the middle of the second month are called the "hot season. Because it becomes hot early in India, this is termed the "Indian hot season. Thus, wherever one may be, the hot season is determined by taking the first half of the second month as the standard; bathing during that time is not an offense.

Regarding "the time of illness": it refers to when, at the very least, the body becomes foul-smelling and filthy. This is called the time of illness (*Saṃghāṭī* states: "The time of illness refers to various ailments such as ringworm, scabies, sores, carbuncles, and pustules;

one must bathe for such illnesses, and bathing is permitted if it brings comfort"). Regarding "the time of work": it refers to when, at the very least, one sweeps the ground in front of a dwelling. (*Saṃghāṭī* states:

"The time of work refers to working with mud, repairing rooms or dwellings, clearing drainage ditches, drawing water from a well, plastering rooms or dwellings, sweeping the floor, or bathing one's *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, up to and including sweeping the stūpa courtyard or the monastic compound, even if it is only five or six strokes of the broom").

Regarding the term "when it is windy or rainy": this refers to when even a whirlwind or a single drop of rain touches the body (the *Sarvāstivāda* school states that during wind, dust and soil must surely settle upon the body;
during rain, the falling water must surely moisten one's clothes and defile the body; or when both wind and rain occur together, these constitute the time of wind and rain).

Regarding "when traveling on a road": this refers to traveling back and forth for at least half a *yojana*. As stated above, one must not take [the time] before or after [these specific conditions]. One should...

Taking the present as the temporal reference, the conditions for the offense are as follows: this precept requires three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, it is not a permitted occasion (*an-āpatti-pratyaya*).
Second, there is the intentional mind (*cetanā*) to bathe. Third, water has already been poured over the body.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, during the half-month [of the rains], one must bathe;
except for other times, if one exceeds this by pouring water over the body even once, it is a *pāyattika*. If water is poured over half the body, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.
If one prepares the requisites with the intention to bathe but does not go, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. The *Sarvāstivāda* school says: "If a bhikṣu..."
If one bathes today having come yesterday, or bathes today intending to depart tomorrow, it is a *pāyattika* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.

The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: bathing once every half-month; bathing during the heat of the season, when ill, while working, during wind or rain, or while traveling on a road;
bathing frequently for these reasons; or being compelled to bathe by force of another’s power. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
if there is a necessary reason, such as needing to cross a river or stream, or if one must go around a sandbank or rapids, or pass over a bridge or embankment, [the feet may be washed].
If one falls into water, or at times faints and others sprinkle water on them; or if one is learning to swim, or encounters rain—there is no offense in any of these cases.
If one must wash frequently during the [prescribed] period, one should maintain mindfulness before performing the bath. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one has already washed the body of a teacher or a sick person and becomes wet as a result, bathing thereafter does not constitute an offense."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there are no other [designated] times, one should follow the bathing method of potters.
First bathe the two thighs and the two feet; afterwards wash the head, face, waist, back, arms, elbows, chest, and armpits. There is no offense.

Those for whom there is no offense include those before the precept was first established, and so forth. (If on the day of performing repentance or consecrating a ritual altar, one must bathe; this originates from the holy word and is not an offense. It should also be done when the great assembly of the monastic community bathes en masse; this is likewise not an offense.)"
○ General Explanation of the Fifty-Seventh Precept: Lighting a Fire in an Open Space.
This is a shared precept; nuns incur the same offense. It is likewise studied by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Due to frivolous play..."
To remedy these afflictions, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated through the convergence of three conditions.
Regarding the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at the city of Kalandaka.
Regarding the origin of this account: the group of six monks said to one another, "We cannot speak as we please in the presence of the elders.
They immediately went outside the room and, standing on the open ground, gathered firewood, brush, and tree stumps to build a fire and roast themselves, using hollow tree stumps for fuel.
Within it was a venomous snake, driven out by the heat of the fire from a hollow in the tree. The bhikṣus were all startled and seized the burning wood, scattering and throwing it in all directions;
the flying sparks set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire. The World-Honored One rebuked them and established a precept, forbidding the lighting of fires in the open air.
A sick bhikṣu became fearful and hesitant, so the Buddha said: "I permit a sick bhikṣu to light a fire in the open air."
The bhikṣus wished to cook porridge, soup, or rice for a sick bhikṣu;

whether to fumigate their bowls, dye their robes, light lamps, or burn incense, they were all fearful and cautious, not daring to do so. The Buddha said: "In such matters as these, you are permitted to act."
The precepts should be recited in this manner:
regarding the established characteristics of the precepts,
if a bhikṣu, being free from illness, for the sake of warming his own body, intentionally kindles a fire in the open air or instructs another to kindle one— except [in cases of necessity].
The circumstances: a *pāyattika* offense. Explanation of the meaning:

Regarding "the sick" (if one has scabies, itch, or a rash; or a yellowing, suppurating wind-disease; if one knows that for such various ailments fire is necessary to obtain comfort, it is permitted and there is no offense).

If, for the purpose of warming one's own body, one lights a fire in the open air (meaning the precept applies when one is in an unobstructed place; if one lights it inside a heated room, a kitchen, or a bathhouse, it is not prohibited).

To blow [the fire] so that it flares up, or to turn over the firewood so that the flames become more intense—therefore, it is called "kindling. Regarding the exception for specific circumstances (*kāraṇa-vinaya*): if one cooks porridge, soup, or rice for a sick person;

if one is on duty as the month-steward (*māsa-pālaka*); if one is supervising meal services; if it is one's turn to maintain the fires or light the lamps; if one kindles fires in the kitchen, the heated room (*jantāghara*), or the bathhouse;

if one kindles fires for the sake of the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*; or if one kindles fires for fumigating the alms-bowl, warming water, or dyeing robes—for such causes and conditions, all are permitted. Therefore, it is called the exception for specific circumstances.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the absence of any covering or obstruction;
second, the presence of fire fueled by wood or brush; and third, either doing it oneself or instructing another to do so.

**The Formal Determination:** Regarding the offense herein: if one, being without illness, lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of roasting oneself, whether it be by burning the branches and leaves of trees, hemp, flax, or *kusha* grass, or cow dung, husks, or parched grain—this constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) in every case.
If one places fire among grass, wood, branches, leaves, hemp, flax, cow dung, husks, or bran and sets it alight, it is a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If something that has been half-burnt or scorched is thrown into the fire, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one burns charcoal, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one does not tell the person before them, "Look at this; know this," it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: To light a fire for roasting, such that the flame reaches a height of four finger-widths, is a *pāyattika*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When carrying a torch to shake off [insects], one must not do so over ground that has not yet been burned;
it should be done over ashes or on a tile. If the torch should fall to the ground by itself, shaking it over that spot incurs no offense.
The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: If one sets a wild fire, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*. Small [offenses].
For the three groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). This is what is called an offense.
**Explanatory Circumstances for Non-Offense:** There is no offense if one says to the person in question, "Look at this;

know this. Or if a sick person instructs another on their own initiative. Furthermore, there may be occasional circumstances where a caregiver, for the sake of the patient, cooks porridge, soup, or rice. If [the patient] is...
There is no offense in a kitchen, a greenhouse, or a bathhouse; likewise, there is no offense when fumigating a bowl, boiling dye for robes, lighting lamps, or burning incense.
The Sarvāstivādins say that there is no offense if it is extremely cold while traveling on a road.
Regarding "no offense," this refers to the initial period before the precept was established.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Huixiang) states in the fourth section: "There are five faults in sitting toward a fire: first, it causes one to lose one's complexion;

second, it causes a loss of strength; third, it causes the eyes to become dim; fourth, it causes many people to gather in a noisy crowd; fifth, it leads to much talk of worldly matters. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* further states:
"There are seven things that are of no benefit in lighting a fire: first, it ruins the eyes; second, it ruins the complexion; third, it weakens the body; fourth..."
1. The robes become soiled and ruined. 2. The five types of bedding and mats become ruined. 3. It gives rise to causes and conditions for violating the precepts. 4. It increases worldly discourse.
○ A general explanation of the fifty-eighth precept concerning the playful concealment of robes and bowls.
This is a shared precept; the offense for a bhikṣuṇī is likewise the same. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"This training rule was established due to the affliction of non-quiescence arising from frivolous behavior."
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Park. A householder invited the community of monks for a meal the following day.
Seventeen groups of monks took their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, and sat down on one side to practice walking meditation, awaiting the arrival of the time for the meal.

The originator of the offense was a group of six monks. While the other was turned away with his back to them, the six monks watched for the opportunity, seized [the object], and hid it. When the time came for him to search for it, the six monks stood before him and teased him.
Another monk, observing this, realized they had hidden it and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established the precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case— whether hiding them himself or instructing another to hide them—
even down to doing so in jest, it is a pāyattika offense.
**Exegesis:** Regarding the concealment of a bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case—these six items are the essential requisites of a śramaṇa and are objects that ought to be kept;
therefore, their concealment constitutes a primary offense (*pārājika*). As for items that should not be kept, their concealment results only in a transgression of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Whether one conceals them oneself or instructs another to do so (whether by oneself or through another, it is equally prohibited), even down to cases of mere joking (whether concealing them to annoy others or even out of playful mockery, they are all equally subject to this prohibition).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense. First, there must be the intentional intent to mock;
second, the six items must be concealed; and third, the act of concealing them must be completed.
**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one conceals [the robes] oneself or causes another to conceal them—even in jest—it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one conceals any one of the three robes, it is a *pāyattika*. If one conceals the *saṃkakṣikā* (also called *saṃghāṭī*;

in the language of Tang, 'armpit-covering robe'), or other such garments, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya*. (The *saṃkakṣikā* is used to cover the left shoulder, with the right side open and the left side closed.)

A young bhikṣu was begging for alms with his chest and armpits exposed, and he was desired by women. The Buddha therefore prescribed this robe to cover the chest and armpits. To conceal any of the three types of bowls constitutes a pāyattika offense;
to conceal a ladle or other utensils constitutes a vyatikrama-vinaya offense; to conceal a sitting mat (niṣīdana) constitutes a pāyattika offense.
To conceal spare bedding is a *vinayātikrama*. If there is a needle-case, it is a *pāyattika*; if there is no needle-case, it is a *vinayātikrama*.
According to the Sarvāstivādins, if one searches for it and does not find it, it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not search for it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one conceals a stone bowl, or a bowl made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or any other precious material, [the same applies].
If one searches for [the robes] and does not find them, it is all *duṣkṛta*. If one hides the five types of large, high-quality robes or other miscellaneous woolen garments, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
The *Pañcavargika* states: "To hide the property of the other four assemblies, or even the property of animals, is *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* to hide the property of two assemblies is a *pāyattika*; to hide the property of three assemblies is [a *pāyattika*] in all cases."
An *dukkaṭa* for a monk; a *pāyattika* for a nun; an *dukkaṭa* for the three minor groups [of trainees]. This is called an offense. Exemptions:
It is not an offense if one takes up and stores [the item] out of mutual care and concern; or if it is in an open space [and taken up] due to wind or rain.

If he picks up items that have been blown away or soaked, or if the owner is by nature negligent and leaves his robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case scattered and in disarray, one may take them up and store them away for the sake of admonishing him; likewise, if one borrows those robes from him.
If one leaves [an item] unsecured and, fearing it might be lost, takes it up;

or if, on account of this robe, bowl, or other belongings, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), and one takes them and hides them—in all such cases there is no offense. There is no offense for those who were not yet subject to the rule when it was first promulgated, and so forth.
○ A General Explanation of the Fifty-ninth Precept: Regarding the Wearing of a Pure-Gift Robe Without First Asking the Owner.
This is a shared precept; the formulation for nuns is identical. It is also studied by followers of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This [precept] concerns clothing..."
This training rule was established due to the matter of negligence and the affliction of defilement.
Regarding the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The origin of the rule:
After the group of six monks had truly given a robe to a close and dear bhikṣu, they later took it back and wore it themselves without informing the owner.
When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha rebuked them and established the precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the offense:
if a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī,
and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika.
**Explanation of the Terms** "Regarding the one who gives the robe": this refers to the *śuddhaka-dāna* (pure gift) of a robe.

There are two types of pure gifts of robes: first, the *bhūta-śuddhaka-dāna* (actual pure gift); second, the *paramparā-śuddhaka-dāna* (successive pure gift). As for the *bhūta-śuddhaka-dāna*, it is said:

"This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been purified (*akṛta-śuddhi*). Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir. This constitutes the actual pure gift. (Regarding the performance of this actual pure gift, see the *Samantapāsādikā*.)

It is said: "One may properly accept it as a safeguard, but one must not use it. How then may it be used? If the donor says, 'This is my robe; use it as you please, Venerable Sir,' and if these words are spoken, one may use it without fault.
Regarding the method of indirect pure gift (*parivartaka-śuddhi*): "This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*) which has not yet been purified.

Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to the Venerable One. The recipient should speak thus: "Venerable Sir, listen. You have this extra robe which has not yet been purified. Now [I receive] it..."
"I accept it for the sake of purification (*pariśuddhi*). Having accepted it, I shall ask: 'To whom do you wish to give it?
He should reply: 'To such-and-such a person. That person should speak as follows: 'Venerable sir, you have this long robe (*cīvara*) which has not yet been purified;
now I accept it for the sake of purification. Having accepted it, give this robe to such-and-such a person. This robe belongs to such-and-such a person.'"

There is. For the sake of [Name], you shall guard and maintain it for use as you wish. Regarding that which is a "pure gift through truth" (*bhūta-śuddha-dāna*), one should take and use it only after asking the owner's permission.
Regarding that which is a "successive pure gift" (*paramparā-śuddha-dāna*), one may take and use it as one wishes, whether or not the owner has been informed.

*Śikṣamāṇā* (translated here as "female trainee in the precepts"): according to the Vinaya, this refers to a girl of eighteen who trains in the precepts for two years; she is also referred to as "one of young age" or "one who was previously married at ten."

Regarding the granting of the six dharmas: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one must train the mind through the six dharmas; only when one is able to uphold these six dharmas may one be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*). For two years, one trains the body to determine whether or not there is fetal development [of a new embryo].

The *Shisao* (Commentary on the Essentials) states that a *śikṣamāṇā* must fully study three sets of dharmas: first, the study of the root precepts, which refers to the four grave offenses (*pārājika*); second, the study of the six dharmas, namely: sexual contact with a lustful mind, stealing four *kārsāpaṇa* coins or more, taking the life of an animal, speaking minor falsehoods, eating at improper times, and drinking alcohol;

third, the study of the rules of conduct, which includes all the precepts of a fully ordained nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) and must be studied as well. If one violates any one of the six dharmas, one must undergo another two-year formal ritual (*karma*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that [the seat of] the *śikṣamāṇā* is below that of the fully ordained nun and above that of the female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*). Female Novice.

Regarding the *śrāmaṇerī* (the *Nanshan bie xing pian* states: *śramaṇa* is translated as "ceasing affection" (*xici*), meaning to cease worldly, defiled emotions and to save all living beings through compassion. It further states: when first entering the Buddha-dharma, one often retains secular sentiments;

therefore, one must cease evil and practice compassion). Afterward, she must not speak to the owner regarding her wearing [the robe]; this refers to a truly pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) of clothing, for which one must necessarily ask the owner before wearing it.
This differs from a successively purified gift (*paramparā-viśuddha-dāna*), where one may wear it at will.
**Conditions for Offense:** This precept fulfills two conditions before the full offense is established: first, the robe is a truly pure gift;
second, one takes and wears it without informing the donor.
**Determination of the Offense:** In this context, the offender takes and wears a truly gifted robe without having informed the donor; this constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).

*Tī*. Regarding *sarvadharmāḥ*: this precept involves originally intending to deceive another regarding their robe, giving it to them for the purpose of making them work for one’s own ends, causing them to perceive it as their own;
once it has been made so, one then seizes it back—this constitutes a *pāyattika*. The reason it is not classified as a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*) is that it was not fundamentally given [as a gift].
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three minor groups of disciples, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called an offense. Regarding the exceptions:

there is no offense if it is a formal act of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) where one speaks to the owner regarding their attachment; or if it is a successive act of pure giving where one speaks [of the attachment] but does not speak [of the taking].
There is no offense. There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established at the outset, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Sixtieth Precept: Wearing Garments of Unaltered Color.
This is a shared precept; nuns also incur the same offense. It is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "One should instruct the body..."
The saṃghāṭī robes one wears shall all be dyed with colors that have lost their original luster. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"This training rule was established due to the affliction of public censure regarding matters of clothing. This is the origin story (*nidāna*).
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

A certain group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) wore white garments. Householders criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled royal ministers. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked him and established the precept. The characteristics of the precept are as follows:
if a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three kinds of disfigurement colors; within each color, he may choose whichever he prefers. If it is blue...
If one wears a new garment that is black, madder-colored, or not discolored (i.e., not dyed), it is a *pāyattika* offense.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** "New" refers to a new garment, or one newly obtained from someone that has not yet been discolored; it must be dyed blue-black or madder-color.

[Regarding "blue": the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: Take *harītakī*, either grind or pound it, mix with water to form a paste, apply it to an iron vessel, let it sit for one night, and then mix with warm water.

When dyed, the cloth becomes blue, yet it is not true blue. Regarding black: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "There is named mud and unnamed mud. Named mud refers to *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka* combined with iron in a single vessel.

Unnamed mud refers to actual earth, such as the mud of ponds or wells; all such earth is used to dye the cloth black. Regarding madder (*mūlana*): the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, "If one takes *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*, and grinds them upon raw iron to extract the juice for dyeing the robe, this is called madder (i.e., a purple-red color).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states, "If one obtains blue-colored cloth, one should apply mud and madder."

Regarding "pure" (the term *ni* refers to black; *qian* is the name of a plant, also written as *jian*, which is the color of murraya). If one obtains a garment made of *ni*, it should be blue; if one obtains a garment made of pure *qian*, it should be the color of *qian*.

It should be purified by blue mud; one may obtain yellow, red, or white robes. They should be purified by the three types—blue mud, madder, and [other dyes] (this refers to dyeing them with colors that alter their appearance according to the Dharma).
If they are not dyed to alter their appearance, it constitutes an offense against the established rules.

**Conditions for Offense:** This precept requires two conditions to constitute a full offense: first, that the garment is fit for wearing; second, that it has not been dyed with an altering color and is being worn as such.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a bhikṣu wears any other new garment without having altered its color, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one keeps heavy or light robes without having performed the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one keeps items that are not robes—such as bags for bowls, bags for leather sandals, needle-cases, meditation belts, hats, socks, tweezers, hot-towel wraps, or cloths for wrapping leather sandals—without performing *pariśuddhi*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one entrusts an undyed robe to the house of a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

*Dulva* (Vinaya) states: "It is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* says: "If one makes a *saṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, *antarvāsa*, rain-bath robe, wound-covering robe, or sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) from [unwashed] material, it is good if it is purified; if it is not purified, it is a *pāyattika* for that night.
The *Sarvāstivāda* says: "Regarding the five major colors, if one dyes them oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one makes a robe from them, it is not valid as a formal acceptance (*parigraha*)."

Whether it is of proper measure or improper measure, one must not wear any of them. If one first obtains a robe of the five primary colors and subsequently alters it into a color that conforms to the Dharma, it then becomes a properly maintained possession.
If one first makes it conform to the Dharma and subsequently ruins it with the five primary colors, it does not constitute a properly maintained possession.
If one performs the purification by means of the three dots, one may possess all [such robes].

If there are spots [on the cloth], unless they are purely blue, light blue, or green (*bì*), one may use them as *piṇḍoddhāra* (points for purification) and make them into the lining of a robe or a *saṃkakṣikā* (the Master Śīlādharma translates this as "inner garment," resembling the modern short skirt). If these spots do not appear on the outside, one may wear it;
however, if they appear on the surface, one must not wear the robe at all. The same applies if the color is yellowish-white and the impurities are large, with the exception of the case of wealth.
Leather sandals and all other clothing, bedding, and requisites, even down to the waistband, must all undergo the triple-dot purification (*tripuṇḍra-śodhana*).

Whether the robes are of a color that conforms to the Dharma or a color that does not conform to the Dharma, if one wears them without having performed this purification, it is an *pāyattika* offense.
If the original dots on a robe have worn away, it remains a purified robe and need not be purified again with new dots. If previously...
Regarding the purification (*śodhana*) of cloth: if one uses pieces of new material to patch ten or five locations, it is sufficient to perform the purification for only one location;
it is not necessary to purify each one individually. If it is leather sandals or boots that have been obtained, one should have a layperson (*avadātavasana*) wear them for five, six, or seven paces;

this constitutes the purification. If the material for the garment was already purified by marking (*tilaka*) at the time of acquisition, and it is subsequently dyed, [the purification remains valid].
Once the color has been applied, if it is not further purified, there is no fault, because it was already purified previously. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When performing the purification, it must be neither too large nor too small. At its largest, it should be four finger-widths; at its smallest, like a pea.
It may be one, three, five, seven, or nine [dots], but they must not be shaped like flowers. When washing the cloth..."
If mud falls upon it, or if a crow or bird steps upon it with muddy feet, it is immediately considered pure (*śuci*).
If one is making a *saṃghāṭī*, one should perform the rite of purification (*śodhana*) at one corner. This applies equally if it is a single patch or a half-patch;
the same rule applies to the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should mark it with three colors. If...
If one does not mark it, for every instance of wearing it, there is a *pāyattika* offense. If one does not wear it, for every night it remains [unmarked], there is a *pāyattika* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions; those who do not incur an offense: if one obtains a white garment and dyes it blue, black, or mūlāṇa;

or if it is a heavy or light garment, one may also keep it after performing the ritual of purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*). If it is not a robe or a bowl-bag, even down to a leather sandal-wrapping or a towel, one may likewise keep it after performing the ritual of purification.
If a garment has been dyed and then left at the house of a layperson, or if the color of the garment fades and is dyed again, there is no offense.
An offense. Those who do not commit an offense are those for whom the precepts have not yet been established, and so forth.

Clarifying errors: People today are unfamiliar with the Vinaya texts; having performed the "marking as pure" (*parikṣipta-śuddhi*), they fail to perform the "declaration of purity" (*śuddhi-vyāhāra*).

They claim that marking as pure is itself the declaration of purity. They do not realize that these two types of purification methods are distinct regulations within the precepts, and that the resulting offenses are incurred through two separate paths.

To perform *śuddhika* (purification by declaration) is to avoid the fault of keeping extra robes beyond the permitted limit; to perform *paribhogika-śuddhi* (purification by use) is to escape the transgression regarding new garments.
How could these be confused? For instance, when all kinds of gruel are purified with water, one is permitted to drink them; once fruits and vegetables have been purified, they may be eaten.
Once all new garments have been purified, they may be worn. How, then, could one perform *paribhogika-śuddhi* and yet treat it as *śuddhika*?
The adept explains this in detail.
○ A General Explanation of the Sixty-first Precept: Prohibiting the Killing of Animal Life.
This is a common precept; the offense for a *bhikṣuṇī* is likewise the same. In the Mahāyāna, it is likewise established as a grave offense (*pārājika*).
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "One must not intentionally kill any living being. This is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"Because of the matter of life and the affliction of a lack of compassion, this training rule was established. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of two conditions.
The setting for the origin of the discourse:
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
The person who gave rise to the occasion: [Name].
Kāḷudāyin was displeased; seeing a crow, he shot it with a bamboo bow, and it subsequently became a great heap [of feathers]. The lay devotee (gṛhapati) censured him with disdain.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept: "One is not permitted to take the life of an animal.
However, as the bhikṣus sat, stood, walked, or moved about, they frequently killed minute insects. Some performed the *pāyattika* confession for these acts, while others were fearful.
Regarding "carefulness," the Buddha said: "If one does not know, there is no offense. The precepts should be recited in this manner.
As for the established characteristics of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika (offense requiring expiation).
**Explanation of the Terms:** "Intentionally" means that one commits the act of killing with a conscious mind, and the manifest action (*vijñapti*) is not performed by mistake.

"Animals" (*tiryag-yoni*): In Sanskrit, this is *tiryañc*, which is translated here as "animal. Because they are born there due to karma characterized by deceit and crookedness, they are called animals. Furthermore, in Sanskrit it is *tiryag-yoni*, which means "moving sideways" (*tiryak*). They are also called "those who move sideways" (*tiryag-gāmin*), because their bodies are horizontal.

Since they experience the retribution of improper conduct, they move sideways across the heavens; thus they are called "those who move sideways. They are found throughout all five destinies (*gati*). Within them, there are hells; among them, there are those without feet, such as the *nāṅkuṭa* insects and others; and there are those with two feet, such as the iron-beaked birds and others.

Among those with four legs, there are such as black sly dogs and the like. Among those with many legs, there are such as centipedes and the like. Within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are those without legs, such as venomous snakes and the like;

those with two legs, such as birds of prey and the like; those with four legs, such as foxes, wildcats, elephants, horses, and the like; and those with many legs, such as six-legged insects and centipedes and the like. Within the three continents of the human realm, there are those without legs, such as all belly-crawling worms and the like;

those with two legs, such as wild geese and the like; those with four legs, such as elephants, horses, and the like; and those with many legs, such as centipedes and the like. In the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), there are those with two legs, such as wild geese and the like; those with four legs, such as elephants, horses, and the like; and the rest.

In the [heavens] of the Four Great Kings and the Thirty-three Gods (*Trāyastriṃśa*), there are two-legged beings such as birds of exquisite color; four-legged beings such as elephants and horses; and many-legged beings such as precious bees. There are none other than these.

In the [heavens] above those four, there are only two-legged beings such as birds of color; there are none other than these. There are three categories—those that move through water, on land, and through the air—and they possess all four modes of birth: viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born.
Regarding the method of killing, it is as explained in the *Pārājika* precepts and need not be recorded here at length.
Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the intentional killing of a sentient being;
second, the severance of the life-faculty; and third, the victim must be an animal incapable of transforming its form.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one employs the means to kill but does not actually kill, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "When one causes a person who is insane to carry out an act of killing..."

Although there is no offense for the one [who kills], the instructor incurs the fundamental offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Regarding 'animals,' this excludes nāgas; other animals are meant.
Although these nāgas are indeed animals, they are able to undergo transformations and possess supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). They protect the land and preserve the True Dharma;
their efficacy is comparable to that of the devas. Therefore, one who kills them commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. *Mahā*... [text truncated]

The *Lüechá* (Summary) states: If one intends to cut a vine but mistakenly cuts a snake, there is no offense. If one intends to cut a snake but mistakenly cuts a vine, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one intends to cut an insect but mistakenly cuts the ground, or intends to crush an insect but crushes soil, both constitute offenses of wrong-doing.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this is a *pāyattika*; for the three junior groups of disciples, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is what is meant by an offense.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in the following cases: if one does not intentionally kill;
or if one hurls a tile, stone, sword, or staff toward another place and accidentally severs life; or if, while working on a building, one loses a tile or stone from the hand and accidentally kills;
or if, while handling bricks, staves, wood, pillars, brackets, beams, or rafters, they fall due to a lack of restraint and cause death. These are the exceptions.
Regarding such matters, there is no offense for one who dies without a harmful intent. There is no violation for those for whom the precepts had not yet been established at the outset.
As detailed in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*: "The sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms."
If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness.
Thus, each of the ten unwholesome actions is fully present. First, regarding killing: for what reason does one undergo the suffering of hell?
It is because by killing, one causes suffering to sentient beings; therefore, when the body perishes and life ends, the manifold sufferings of hell all come to press upon oneself.
Second, as for why those who kill are reborn as animals: it is because their act of killing lacks compassion and contravenes human ethics;
thus, once their retribution in hell is exhausted, they receive an animal body. Third, as for why those who kill are further reborn as hungry ghosts:
it is because their act of killing is invariably motivated by a mind of stinginess and an attachment to flavors; thus, they further become hungry ghosts.
Fourth, as for killing living beings: why is it that one is born as a human yet obtains a short lifespan?
Because of killing and harming the lives of sentient beings, one obtains a short lifespan. Fifth, as for killing living beings: why is it that one also suffers from many illnesses?

Because killing violates the harmony of nature, various afflictions gather in competition; thus, one suffers from many illnesses. One should know that the faults and evils of killing are such as these.
The Sarvāstivādins say: It is for the sake of compassion, for the sake of severing evil deeds, and for the sake of increasing reverent faith that this precept is established.
