Your present reception of the precepts is the very foundation for the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). This is because the five [aggregates] are accomplished through the precepts;
if you were to sit upon your body without a sitting mat, then the fivefold concentration and wisdom would have no basis from which to arise."
○ General Explanation of the Eighty-eighth Precept: Making a Scarf for Covering Sores Exceeding the Proper Measure.
This is an uncommon precept; it is not prescribed for nuns. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Due to all..."
The Bhikṣus made [the robes] in excess of the proper measure; thus this training rule was established.
Regarding the origin of this rule:
while the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, various bhikṣus suffered from sores and scabs, and the flowing pus and blood stained their robes.
Regarding bedding and requisites: The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a wound-covering cloth. When the bhikṣus used this wound-covering cloth, it was coarse and hairy;
when they applied it to their wounds, lifting the cloth caused them pain. The Buddha said, "I allow you to use a high-priced, fine, soft cloth to cover the wound.
When wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment), if you go to the home of a layperson and are invited to sit, you should say, "I am suffering from an ailment. If the host says:
"Simply sit. You should pull up your inner robe (*nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*) and sit while covering the wound with this cloth.

When people began to do so, the group of six monks made many wide and long cloths for covering wounds. The other bhikṣus asked, "The Buddha has prescribed that there are only three robes; [is this not a violation?]"
He passed it by. "What kind of robe is this? they asked. The group of six replied, "This is a wound-covering robe. The bhikṣus felt resentment and reproached him.
They reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked him and established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
if a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. Herein, the measurement is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width.
If it exceeds these dimensions after being cut, it is a pāyattika offense.
**Explanation of the Terms:** Regarding the "wound-covering cloth" (*vaṇa-paticchādi*): there are various types of wounds and diseases. This cloth is held for use in covering the body.

Its length is four *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha, and its width is two *vitasti*. (The length is six feet and four inches; the width is three feet and two inches. This constitutes the standard measurement. If it exceeds these dimensions after being cut, it constitutes an offense.
**Conditions for Offense:** (As above, regarding making [an item] exceeding the prescribed measure while possessing full precepts.
**Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, it is no different from what was stated previously. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If ten days have passed since the healing of a wound, it constitutes 'storing' [the item], which is a *pāyattika* offense" (this should be treated identically to the offense of keeping an extra robe beyond the permitted period). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one folds the measurement or contracts the measurement..."
If one sprinkles water with the intention that it shall dry, yet makes it long and large, it is a *pāyattika*. If one uses it, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
For the four assemblies, including the nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
Opening of the Conditions: Non-offenses (are also as previously stated).
○ General Explanation of the Eighty-ninth Precept: Making Rain-Cloaks Exceeding the Prescribed Dimensions.
This is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*). It is not established as a common rule for *bhikṣuṇīs*. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"Because the *bhikṣus* constructed [buildings] beyond the prescribed measure, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established."
The setting for this account:
The Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park. Visākhā, the Mother of Migāra, had rain-bathing robes made and sent someone to bring them to the saṃghārāma to give to the bhikṣus.
The originator of the offense was the group of six monks. Having heard that rain-bathing robes were to be made, they produced many large and wide rain-bathing robes.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them and established the precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:

if a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. Among these, the measurement is six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width.
If it exceeds this, it must be cut down; [otherwise] it is a pāyattika offense.

**Exegesis:** Regarding the *varṣāśāṭī* (rain-bath robe): when the bhikṣus wear it while bathing in the rain, it should be six *vitasti* in length and two and a half *vitasti* in width (the length being nine chi and six cun;
the width being four chi). This constitutes the proper measurement. If it exceeds these measurements, one must cut it down and undergo repentance for the offense.
The conditions for the offense, the determination of the guilt, and the allowances for exemption are all as previously stated.

A detailed examination according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: Whenever a bhikṣu bathes—whether in an open space or a covered room—he must not do so in the company of laypeople, nor should he leave his upper body uncovered.
He must wear a *kaṣāya* (i.e., a *saṃkakṣikā*, which is an armpit-covering garment); first, he must maintain a sense of shame.
Shame. Second, because the arising of desire in others produces joy. Formerly, there was an Arhat bhikṣu who was bathing.
A certain bhikṣu, seeing his body fresh, pure, fine, and soft, immediately conceived a lustful mind. Not long thereafter, his male organ fell away and a female organ appeared.
He abandoned the path and returned to lay life, fathering a son. Later, they met by chance, and he recognized him as his former self.
Because he followed the Arhat’s instruction to repent and applied himself with single-minded devotion, he regained his male organ; therefore, one should not expose one's private parts.
To commit sexual misconduct with a great Bhikṣu who upholds the precepts or with a Śrāmaṇera is a sin equal to destroying a stupa made of the seven precious jewels.
To encourage others to leave the household life and practice with diligence brings merit equal to that of building a stupa.
○ General Explanation of the Ninetieth Rule: The Precept Regarding Making Robes Equal in Size to the Buddha’s.
This is an *asādhāraṇa* (unshared) precept; it is not prescribed for *bhikṣuṇīs*. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because it incurs..."
Regarding the censure of faults, this training rule was established.
As for the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Śrāvastī. Venerable Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha (this is translated as...).

Nanda was the Buddha’s own younger brother, born of his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī. He resembled the Buddha in body and possessed thirty of the marks of a Great Man; he lacked only the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) and the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet. He stood one *zhang*, five *chi*, and four *cun* tall. He was born on the ninth day of the fourth month.

After the Buddha, he was ordained and allowed to leave the household life; for him, the Buddha preached the *Garbha-sūtra*, through which he attained the fruit of Arhatship. Among the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, he was foremost in guarding the sense faculties and being able to ward off external objects.
When the bhikṣus saw him approaching from afar, they thought it was the Buddha and rose to welcome him; only upon reaching him did they realize it was Nanda.
"Ānanda, both [parties] should feel shame. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha prohibited the bhikṣu Nanda from wearing black robes.
This was the occasion for the rule.
The group of six bhikṣus made robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, or even larger than that. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, who rebuked them.
The formal enactment of the precept:

Regarding the characteristics of the rule established herein, if a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to that of the Tathāgata, or makes it exceeding that size, it is a pāyattika offense. In this matter:
Regarding the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s robe: it is ten *vitasti* (spans) in length and six *vitasti* in width;

this is called the dimension of the Tathāgata’s robe. **Explanation of the Meaning:** "Equal measure and exceeding measure" (below). [This clarifies the established rules for robes; the following clarifies the fixed dimensions of the robe.

Regarding the dimensions of the Tathāgata’s robe: it is ten *vitasti* in length and six *vitasti* in width. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states: "The Buddha’s body is one *zhang* and six *chi* [sixteen feet]; ordinary people are half that size. Therefore, the dimensions of the robe—both width and length—should both be halved. The Buddha’s younger brother...)

Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha; his robes should therefore be reduced by one chi in length and four cun in width compared to the medium size. Previously, Nanda wore the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) while the Buddha wore the middle robe (antaravāsaka); now, it is not permitted for [the disciple’s robe] to exceed [the Buddha’s] in size.

It is permitted to wear the lower robe (antaravāsaka); for an ordinary person, this refers to the lowest of the low grades. Furthermore, because the Buddha’s robes were like refined gold and were further applied with fine woolen fabric (*kambala*), their color was likewise so. Nanda’s robes should instead be covered with *pāṃśukūla* (rags from a dust heap), making them identical in color to the robes of other bhikṣus.

Regarding the term *pāṃśukūla*, this is translated as "dyed color" (*huài sè*). According to the measurements, the Buddha’s robe was one zhang six chi in length and nine chi six cun in width; this refers to the specific length and width used for dyeing the color distinct from that of the Tathāgata’s own robes.
The conditions for an offense and the exemptions for determination of guilt are the same as in the preceding precept.
A detailed examination of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When making it, one may make it less than the prescribed measure, but it must not exceed the measure;
it should be according to the size of one's own body. There are three types of this saṃghāṭī: the superior is five cubits long and three cubits wide; the middling is..."
The five-cubit [robe] is one *hasta* short in length; it is three cubits wide, one *hasta* short.
The inferior [robe] is four and a half cubits in length and three cubits wide, one *hasta* short. The *uttarāsaṅga* is likewise. The two middle types of the *antarvāsa* are also like this.
The inferior [type] is four and a half cubits in length and two cubits wide, one *hasta* short. (*Vinayaviniścaya*)
It says: "If one makes it less than this measure, there is no offense; if it exceeds five *hasta*, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The length of the *hasta* is not fixed; the Buddha commanded that it be according to the proportions of one's own body. The *Vinaya* says:
"Because the robe is measured according to the person."
The threefold inquiry on the formal questions:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this regard? (Three times.)
Fourth, the exhortation to maintain [purity]:
"Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus it shall be held as such.
● Sixth, the rules for the confession of offenses, divided into four parts: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration of the precepts; third, the conclusion.
Question: Regarding the four exhortations to uphold [the precepts], the first provides a general heading:
"Venerable sirs, these four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
Come. Regarding the term *pāṭidesanīya*, there is no direct translation for it. The *Shishi yaoyong chao* provides a translation based on its meaning:
it is named after the object of confession, which serves as the basis for its remediation. The *Vinayasamgraha* asks: "As for the other various offenses..."
[The Buddha] permitted the confession before another. Why is it called "confession before another" (*pratideśanīya*)? The answer is:
because one must go before each individual bhikṣu currently residing in the monastery and confess [the offense] one by one; since this differs from other offenses, it receives this specific name.

Furthermore, once the offense has been committed, one must confess it immediately and may not delay; this also distinguishes it from other offenses. (Examine these four dharmas: in substance, they are identical to the offenses of greed and affliction.)

The Buddha prohibited this because it gives rise to two faults: first, that food and drink increase one's own afflictions; second, that through lack of moderation, one causes others to lose their faith and respect. Although this section on remorse follows the chapter on the *pārājika* offenses, its transgression is greater than that of a *sthūlātyaya*.

Second, the detailed enumeration of the precepts is divided into four parts. The first begins with receiving food from a nun who is not a relative, and extends through to the fourth, taking food in a place of fear.
○ First: The Precept on Receiving Food from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative.
General Explanation:

This is an uncommon precept; it is not prescribed for *bhikṣuṇīs* in the same way. In the Mahāyāna, one simply considers whether something may be accepted or not, without distinguishing between a relative and a non-relative.
However, in this degenerate age, it is appropriate to maintain a distance from *bhikṣuṇīs*. (*Vinayaviniścaya*)
It is said: This training rule was established due to the affliction of censure arising from matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of four conditions.
First, the setting of the origin.
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from hunger; it was difficult to obtain alms.
On the third day, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā went out for alms and gave everything she had obtained to the bhikṣus. This continued for three days.
"One must not eat [in such a state]. A householder traveling in a carriage to visit the king cleared the way by driving people aside.
A *bhikṣuṇī*, while clearing the path, fell into deep mud and lay prostrate with her face pressed against the ground. The householder, moved by compassion, ordered his men to help her up.

Upon learning the reason for her fall, he censured her for her lack of propriety and yielding. When the *bhikṣus* heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha, who rebuked her and established a precept.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept food from a relative nun. The Buddha said: "I allow you to accept it when there is a sick bhikṣu.

They did not dare to accept food from a nun who was not a relative. The Buddha said: "I allow you to accept it. When a nun who was not a relative placed food on the ground, they did not dare to take it;
nor did they dare to take it even when someone else handed it to them. The Buddha said: "I allow you to accept it. The precept should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:

if a bhikṣu enters a village and, being free from illness, takes food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy offense."
[This] place should not be for me. I now repent before the Venerable One. This dharma is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the rule of confession). Explanation of the meaning:

Regarding "in a village" (*grāme*), [the offense is necessarily committed within a village]. The Sarvāstivādins say: "If one gives [food] in a temple of the gods, in a gathering of many people, or in a dwelling place of śramaṇas."

If one gives [food] outside the village or within the nuns’ quarters, there is no offense (provided it is not a non-relative, as previously stated). Regarding "the sick" (*sāṃghika* states: this does not refer to minor ailments; it refers to scabies, jaundice with suppuration, sores, carbuncles, and boils—conditions loathed and despised by others;

these are what is meant by "the sick"). Regarding "taking food with one’s own hand and eating it": "taking food with one’s own hand" clarifies that it is not placed on the ground for them or brought by another person.

It means receiving food directly from the nun’s hand; one incurs the offense only when it has entered the throat. Therefore, it is called "taking food with one’s own hand and eating it. This bhikṣu should then approach another bhikṣu...

The words of confession (*āpatti-deśanā*): "This bhikṣu who has committed an offense should confess his transgression before another pure and precept-observing person. Regarding the "words of confession": this refers to personally declaring the specific act that was committed (the following text constitutes the actual formula of confession).
"Venerable Sir, I have committed a censurable act (*garhya-dharma*), which is improper to do [as it was prohibited by the Blessed One and is not something a bhikṣu should do].
I now confess my transgression to the Venerable Sir [daring not conceal it, but revealing it openly]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The former person..."
One should ask, "Do you see your transgression? If he replies, "I see my transgression," one says to him, "Be careful not to commit it again.
He replies, "I shall receive and uphold this Dharma. This is called the method of repentance (the conclusion of the preceding text).
The Conditions for Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, it must be within a village; second, one must not be ill;
third, the person from whom the food is taken must not be a relative; and fourth, one must take the food with one's own hand and eat it.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if a monk enters a village and, being not ill, receives food with his own hand from a nun who is not a relative, there is a *pāyantika* offense for every swallow. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the monk is outside the village and the nun is inside, or if the monk is inside the village and the nun is outside... [and so forth]. If the monk is...

[The monk] is in the air; the nun is on the ground. Or, the bhikṣu is on the ground; the nun is in the air. Receiving food in such ways constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
When receiving food and drink with one’s own hands from a nun who is not a relative, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.

At the time of eating, one commits an offense requiring confession (*deśanā-dharma*). [This applies when] one is with a non-relative, yet perceives her as a non-relative, or she is indeed a non-relative.

If one suspects [the donor is not a relative], one commits an offense of confession (*pratideśanīya*). If one perceives a non-relative as a relative, or perceives a relative as a non-relative, or suspects whether they are a relative or not, one commits an offense of transgression of the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*). If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.

To receive [food] on behalf of another person constitutes an offense of transgression of the Vinaya. To receive [food] on behalf of a sick person involves no offense. This applies to the four assemblies, including the Bhikṣuṇīs.
This is called an offense of *dukkaṭa*. The exceptions:
There is no offense if one accepts food from a relative nun; or if one is ill; or if she places it on the ground and gives it; or if she causes another person to give it;
or if it is given within a monastery (*saṃghārāma*); or if it is given outside the village; or if it is given inside a nun’s dwelling (*bhikṣuṇī-ārāma*).

If [the food] is given [by the donor], there is no offense. The *Vinayaviniścayasaṃgraha* states: "If a nun receives food offered by a donor as an act of giving, rather than having begged for it, there is no offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when the precept had not yet been established at the outset."
○ Second, the general explanation of the precept against forbidding a nun from instructing on food.
This is an uncommon precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*); it is not established for nuns in the same way. It is studied by Mahāyāna practitioners alike. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of drinking..."
The training rule was established regarding the affliction of disparaging food.
As for the setting of its origin:
the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding the origin of this rule:
many bhikṣus were eating inside the house of a layperson together with the group of six. The group of six bhikṣuṇīs requested soup and rice for the group of six;
they gave them this soup and gave them this rice, but skipping those in the middle, they did not give to them, instead giving out of order. Six.
They ate together in a group. The bhikṣus, feeling resentment and reproaching them, informed the Buddha, who rebuked them and established a precept.
The formulation of the rule is as follows:
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson to eat, and there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who points out [the food], saying, "Give it to such-and-such a person."
[The donor] gives soup and rice to [a specific] bhikṣu. That bhikṣu should say this to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister, please wait;
you must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating. If not even a single bhikṣu says this to that bhikṣuṇī—"Sister, please wait;
you must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating"—that bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying: "Venerable sirs, I have committed a *deśanīya* offense..."
This is the procedure for the *paṭikarman* (act of confession). One should not act thus for me; I now confess my transgression before the venerable ones. This rule is called the *paṭikarman-dharma*.
**Explanation of the Terms:** "Within a layperson’s house" refers to a place where there are men and women present.

"Pointing out [food] for such-and-such a person's soup and such-and-such a person's rice" means instructing the donor to give food specifically to certain individuals. "Sister, please stop; the bhikṣu must eat first."

"Having finished" (a term used to address a sister; "cease" is a word of prohibition). One must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating—either saying, "Cease for a short while and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," or "Stay a little longer and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," or "Step back a moment and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
If they cease, it is well; if they do not cease, one should speak a second and a third time to make them cease. If there is not even one bhikṣu [who speaks thus], the offense is established.
The Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires four conditions to constitute the full offense. First, being in the house of a layperson;
second, a *mahābhikṣuṇī* specifically designating food for oneself; third, seeing or hearing [the designation] and not stopping it; and fourth, receiving the food and swallowing it.
**Judgment of the Offense:** Regarding the one who commits this offense: if there is not a single bhikṣu who says, "Sister, stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," and she nevertheless eats, for every swallow she incurs a *tishani* (pāyattika). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the other two groups of nuns instruct her to take more food and do not tell her to stop for a moment, it is a *duṣkṛta*. [The same applies if] a bhikṣu instructs her to take more food."
It is an act of inequality; it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika* says: "If one accepts [food] without speaking [to the donor], it is a *vinayātikrama* offense.
The one who eats commits an offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya-dharma*). If one eats without having received three admonitions, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense."
There is no offense if one eats after being stopped by three admonitions. There is no offense if all eat after one person has been admonished.
There is no offense if one eats while not seeing or hearing [the admonition]. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:
"If one eats outside the gate, one should ask whether there is no bhikṣuṇī inside the gate who is directing the food. If one does not ask, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing)."
If one sees a nun entering or leaving, one should also question her. If one does not question her, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for the four assemblies, including the nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense.
The Opening of the Conditions for Non-offense: There is no offense if one says, "Sister, please stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating. Or if the nun herself acts as the donor (*dānapati*); or if the donor has prepared the food and instructed the nun to distribute it;
or if it was not done intentionally, such as giving this to one person while setting that aside for another—in all such cases, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If the donor..."

She had never before invited the Saṃgha and was ignorant of the ritual procedures. At that time, the nun obtained [the opportunity] to instruct her on how to arrange the images and how to serve the food;
only after that should she sit down. There is no offense for those who were first [involved] when the precepts had not yet been established, and so forth.
○ General Explanation of the Third Precept on Receiving Food from a Family.
This is a unique precept (*asādhāraṇa-śīla*). It is not prescribed for the Bhikṣuṇīs, but is studied by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of begging..."
This training rule was established to restrain the affliction of disparaging others regarding their food. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of four conditions.
As for the origin of the narrative:
the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Regarding the origin of this condition:
there was a householder’s family where both husband and wife had attained faith and joy as disciples of the Buddha.

Having seen the Truths realized by the Buddhas, it is the constant practice of such disciples that they have no sense of attachment or stinginess toward the bhikṣus, even regarding their own flesh. If the bhikṣus...
Whenever [the layperson] came home, he would constantly provide them with food, drink, and various offerings; consequently, he fell into poverty.

His neighbors criticized and disparaged him, saying, "Previously he was great in wealth and abundance, yet by making offerings to the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, he has instead become destitute. When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha.

The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for the layperson to establish him as a *śaikṣaka* (one under training). There was a bhikṣu who had previously accepted such training.
When a household invited [the Sangha], they were hesitant and did not dare to go. The Buddha said: "I allow those who were first invited to go.

When a sick bhikṣu was hesitant and did not dare to accept food from a family under restriction (*śikṣā-dattaka*), the Buddha said: "I allow him to accept it when it is placed on the ground for him, or when someone else gives it to him.
When he was hesitant and did not dare to take it, the Buddha said: "I allow him to accept it; the precepts should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:

if a *kula-kamma* (formal act concerning a family) has previously been performed for a certain family, and a bhikṣu, without being invited by such a family and while not being ill, receives food with his own hands and eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying: "I have committed a blameworthy offense."

The Dharma Office. One should not act for my sake; I now repent before the Venerable Ones. This dharma is called the *pratideśanīya-dharma* (the dharma of confession). Explanation of the Terms: Regarding the *kula-karma* (formal act concerning a family):

this refers to a household where both husband and wife have attained the fruits of the Noble Path; such is called a "family" (*kula*). If even one member remains an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is not termed a "family. A "learner" (*śaikṣa*) is spoken of in contrast to the "one beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

If the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) is completely severed, then the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda-phala*) is realized; this is called "beyond learning. [As stated: "My births are exhausted. Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have already severed the death and rebirth of the limited realm (*paricchinna-bhava*); therefore, it is said, "my births are exhausted. [This concludes the section on] Brahma.

The holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; having attained the realization of the remaining fruits, it is said that "the holy life is established and what was to be done has been accomplished. That which ordinary persons and gods cannot accomplish, and which the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) have not previously performed—the cessation of deceptive afflictions—it is for this reason that it is said "what was to be done has been accomplished.

Because one will not undergo further existence, it is said "no further existence is to be undergone. Since there is no further dharma to be learned, they are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

If those in the first, second, or third fruits have not yet exhausted all delusions, there remains dharma to be learned and delusions to be severed; therefore, they are called "trainees" (*śaikṣa*). Because these trainees reside within the household, they are called "householder-trainees" (*gṛhastha-śaikṣa*), namely the four castes: Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* concerning families that have been "restricted": this refers to when the Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to perform a formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish a protective restriction for a family. Once such a restriction is in place, no bhikṣu is permitted to go to that house to receive food or drink.

This is because it would provoke the reproach of the world and cause the growth of the resolve for the Path. As for eating food with one's own hands when not ill: there are three exceptions to this rule. If one has previously accepted an invitation, or if one is ill, or if the food is placed on the ground and given by another person, these are all permitted.
To accept food outside of these circumstances constitutes an offense.

Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the fulfillment of three conditions to constitute the full offense: first, the formal ritual (karmavācanā) has been performed regarding a family under restriction;
second, one accepts food from them without a valid reason; and third, the food has already entered the throat after eating.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein, if one does not first request [food], and being without illness, accepts food with one's own hand from such a family and eats it, for every swallow there is a *tishaniya* (offense requiring confession). For the four assemblies, including the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
This is called an offense. Exceptions where there is no offense:
if one has previously received an invitation; if one is ill; if [the gift] is placed on the ground and given; if one receives it from another person;
or if it is given by a family of practitioners (*śaikṣa-kula*) and their wealth subsequently increases—there is no offense. This refers to the wealth of that family of practitioners.
The property has increased significantly. [The layperson] requests from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karmavācanā* for a "family under restriction. The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to revoke it. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-vinaya* (or *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*) states:

"If a householder's wealth diminishes and does not increase, whether he requests it or not, the *karman* for restricting the family should not be revoked. If his wealth increases, it should be revoked regardless of whether he requests it or not."
"And with relinquishment. If it neither increases nor decreases, one should relinquish it if asked; one should not relinquish it if not asked. The Vinaya states:
At that time, all the bhikṣus were doubtful and did not dare to accept food from a householder whose *kula-karma* (formal act concerning a family) had already been dissolved. The Buddha said:
It is permitted for the bhikṣus to accept food [from such families], and there is no offense. There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept had not yet been established at the outset.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*: "If the wife is an āryā and the husband is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or if the husband is an āryā and the wife is an ordinary person, one should not perform the *śaikṣa-kula-karman* (the formal act regarding a family under training) for them. If both husband and wife are āryas and are free from stinginess and greed..."
When their wealth and property were completely exhausted, he performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of treating them as those under training) for them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If the Saṃgha has already performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for a family, one must not avoid them like a bird avoiding an arrow-shot;

rather, one should cease going altogether only for a time, but should go from time to time to see them, preach the Dharma to them, and discuss matters concerning the Dharma. If the family wishes to give alms, one should speak to them [as follows]."

Set this aside for the time being; I myself know the proper time. If one first invites [a donor] and subsequently performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one must not accept items of great value or heavy weight;
one may accept only small, light items. If the members of a family of practitioners (*śaikṣakula*) should say, "Venerable sir, why do you not accept this offering?
Do you consider us poor? at that time one should reply: "You are not poor. As the Blessed One said, a *srotāpanna*..."
The people of the Hiraṇyavatī River achieve four dharmas, whereby they become the greatest among the wealthy of the śrāvakas. What are these four?
First, they give rise to a firm root of faith toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, which cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or humans.
Second, they give rise to a firm root of faith toward the Dharma. Third, [they give rise to a firm root of faith] toward the Saṅgha...

They develop a firm faculty of faith toward the Buddha; second, they develop a firm faculty of faith toward the Dharma; third, they develop a firm faculty of faith toward the Saṅgha, which cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, or worldly people;
and fourth, they develop a firm faculty of faith toward the precepts, which cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, or worldly people.
These are the four dharmas through whose accomplishment a Tathāgata’s śrāvaka is not poor among them, but is the most wealthy. Thus he spoke, causing joy to arise.
○ General Explanation of the Fourth Precept on Receiving Food in a Frightening Place.
This is an uncommon precept; it is not established for the Bhikṣuṇīs. It is studied by those of the Mahāyāna. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Because of its arising..."

Regarding censure and slander: this training rule was established due to the affliction of disparaging others over matters of food and drink. This precept is formulated through the conjunction of four conditions;
its origin is as follows.
The Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu.
At that time, there were women from the Śākyas— Śākya being their clan name and Koliya their lineage— who, together with various other women, took [the precepts].
While they were going to the monastery to make offerings of food and drink, various bandits harassed them on the road.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, you should tell the women not to go out onto the road, as there is fear of bandits.
If they have already left the city, you should tell them not to go to the monastery, as there is fear of bandits."
The Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣus. At that time, various donors, knowing beforehand that there was cause for suspicion and fear, nevertheless brought food.
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said: "First inform the donor and then accept.
When sick bhikṣus were likewise hesitant and did not dare to accept, the Buddha said: "I allow you to accept. At that time, there was a donor who placed food on the ground to give. If...
If one instructs another to give [it], one dares not accept it; the Buddha has declared that it may be accepted. The precepts should be recited in this manner.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
if a bhikṣu is staying in an araṇya, a remote place where there is suspicion or fear, or if a bhikṣu is in such a situation...

Dwelling in an araṇya, if one has not previously informed the donor, and does not receive food outside the monastery grounds, yet receives food with one's own hands while inside the monastery when not ill, one who eats such food should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have committed a blameworthy offense which should not have been done; I now confess it to you, Venerable sir. This rule is called...
The Method for Confessing Transgressions (*Pratideśanā-vidhi*). Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding dwelling in a remote *araṇya* (also called *aranyaka*) where there are doubts and fears:

(*Araṇya* is sometimes called *aranyaka*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translates it as "a place of seclusion. The *Sarvāstivāda* school translates it as "a place free from strife. Tiantai says: "Not performing communal affairs is called 'leisure' (*khan*); being free from clamor is called 'strife-free' (*keng*). Alternatively, it is translated as 'non-strife,' meaning that one's residence does not involve worldly entanglements.")

"Contention. This refers to departing for a village at a distance of five *li*. Master Zhaolun said: "Anger and agitation arise in the midst of a multitude; freedom from contention emerges in open space. Therefore, the Buddha praised dwelling in an *āraṇya* (forest hermitage).

"Remote and distant" means a place far removed from cities and towns, a secluded location. First, one does not inform the *dānapati* (the monk requests of the patron: "Do not go out further; there are robbers and terrors on the road"). If they have already left the city, one should say:

"Do not go as far as the monastery; there are doubts and terrors on the road. This is called "informing beforehand. A *dānapati* is a donor who is constantly able to practice giving; thus, they can personally cross over the ocean of poverty and suffering. If...
If one takes food with one's own hand and eats it when not ill, the offense is established. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"The transgressions of the first three training rules arise from village dwellings; the transgression of this one training rule occurs in the empty forest."

Conditions for the Offense: This precept requires the presence of four conditions to constitute the full offense: first, being in a forest hermitage where there is fear; second, not having informed the donor;
third, lacking a valid reason that permits [the action]; and fourth, swallowing the food after receiving it.

**The Determination of the Offense:** Regarding the offense herein: one who dwells in a remote forest hermitage (āraṇya) shall not, without first informing a donor, accept food outside of a monastery;
nor, being free from illness, shall one take food with one's own hand inside a monastery.
For every swallow of such food, there is a *pāyantika* offense. For the four assemblies, including the nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is defined as an offense.

The Exceptional Circumstances (*anāpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: if one has previously informed the donor; if one is ill; if the food is placed on the ground for one to take; if one instructs another to give it;
or when a person comes to receive instructions or listen to the Dharma, and the bhikṣu personally possesses private food and causes it to be given to them.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If food is given while a military force is passing through, or if a thief brings food himself..."
[If one acts] thus, there is no offense. There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precepts have not yet been formulated, and so forth.
[The formal inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have now recited the four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas. I now ask the venerable sirs: Is this so?"
"Regarding this matter of purity (asked three times).
Venerable sirs, since you are silent, you are pure in this matter. Thus, this matter shall be held as such."
