There was a householder who invited the community of monks for a meal. He personally served the soup and rice;
having given a portion of soup to one of the group of six bhikṣus, he recognized him and took more soup. The bhikṣu immediately covered it with rice.
The householder asked again, "Where is the soup? The bhikṣu remained silent. The householder censured him, saying, "He looks like a starving person. Therefore, it was prohibited.
[The monks] covered the soup with rice. Once the precept had been established, when the bhikṣus were invited to eat, the soup soiled their hands, their bowls, and their robes.
Fearing a transgression, they did not dare to cover the soup with rice. The Buddha said: "I allow you to cover the soup with rice. The precept should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must not cover the soup with rice while hoping to receive more; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if a bhikṣu receives food and fears it will soil his robes, he must not cover it entirely.
One side should be exposed. If everything is covered, when the person asks whether it has been obtained, one should reply, "It has already been obtained.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states that soup and rice must not be used to conceal one another; this is because one desires to obtain more and thereby increases the mind of greed.
One should cultivate a sense of detachment toward food and drink; this is what those who have left the household life ought to do—eating whatever is obtained as it comes.
To have few desires as one's mindfulness.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: One does not commit an offense if invited to a meal; or if at times one specifically requires soup, and at other times one specifically requires rice.
No offense. ○ The thirty-fourth precept: Regarding looking at the food of a fellow monk (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the occasion.
Among the group of six, one monk received a small portion of food. Seeing that his neighbor’s portion was large, he immediately said to the householder, "Your distribution of food is unequal;
you have favoritism. The householder replied, "I gave to everyone equally. Why do you say there is favoritism?
For this reason, the rule was established.
Regarding the established precept:
"One must not look into the bowl of one's neighbor; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: "Looking into the bowl of one's neighbor" means [inquiring], "Who has more and who has less?"
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Regarding the exceptions (*anāpatti*): there is no offense if one has such an illness; or if the neighbor-sitting monk is ill; or if one’s vision is dim;
or if one can see whether food may be accepted or not, whether it is pure or impure, and whether it has been formally received or not. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If..."
If one supervises the food, observing where it may be taken and where it may not be taken, there is no offense.
If a co-practitioner or a dependent disciple is ill, looking into their bowl to see whether the food is appropriate for their illness is without fault.
If one looks to see whether the Elder has received sufficient food, there is no fault.
○ The thirty-fifth precept: Eating while not keeping one’s bowl steady (the setting for the origin is the same). The individuals involved were the group of six.
Having received the soup and rice, they looked around left and right; then, taking the soup from their neighbors’ bowls, they hid it away for themselves. They themselves...
He could not see the soup. He asked, "I received some soup just now; where is it now? His neighbor replied, "Where did you come from?
He answered, "I was right here with the soup placed before me. I looked all around, and now it is gone.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who then established a precept.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
one should train oneself in the thought that the alms bowl is tied [to the body] while eating.
Explanation of the meaning: "The thought that the alms bowl is not tied" refers to looking around to the left and right. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not..."
Place the bowl before you and converse with your neighbor. If there is a cause or condition requiring you to speak with those to your left or right, stroke the top of the bowl with your left hand.
When the food distribution reaches the third person, you should first rinse the bowl and hold it up in anticipation of its arrival.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.

Exceptions: There is no offense in the following cases: if the neighboring bhikṣu is ill; if one receives [an offering] on his behalf because he is blind or to observe whether it is pure or impure, or whether it has been obtained or not;
or if one observes the time; or if there is danger to life, danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), or if one wishes to flee.
There is no offense in avoiding those looking on from the left or right.
A detailed examination of this is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "Reflect upon this food; the labor expended is immense.

If one calculates the sweat shed by the laborers to produce even a single bowl of rice, the amount of sweat is far greater than the food itself. Such is the bitterness of the toil required for this food."

As soon as it enters the mouth, it becomes impure; within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine. What was once a delicious flavor now becomes loathsome, such that one does not wish to behold it.
The practitioner reflects: "Such is this wretched food; if I were to become greedily attached to it, I would surely fall into the three miserable realms."
Contemplate food in this manner; you should thereby cultivate revulsion for the five desires.
○ The thirty-sixth precept on eating large mouthfuls of rice (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion:

The group of six monks ate their meals with such large mouthfuls that their mouths could not close. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying their manner of eating was like that of pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, oxen, crows, or birds. Therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept: one must not eat large mouthfuls of rice;
this is how one should train. Explanation of the meaning: "Large mouthful" means that which cannot be accommodated by the mouth. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It must not be large..."
Small [mouthfuls]. Like a lustful woman who eats two or three grains at a time; one should eat in a manner that fits the mouth.
The determination of the offense is the same as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The senior monk (*sthavira*) should eat slowly;
he must not finish eating quickly and then remain watching so as to cause the juniors to eat in a state of distress and fail to be satisfied."

Explanatory Circumstances: There is no offense in cases where the time for eating is about to pass, or where there is danger to life, danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or when eating hurriedly.
The Thirty-Seventh Precept: Eating While Holding the Mouth Open Awaiting Food (the setting of the origin is the same).

The originator of the offense was a person from the group of six. They received food, but before it had even arrived, they opened their mouths wide in advance. The householders criticized and disparaged them; for this reason, as before, the rule was established.
This is the formulated characteristic of the precept.
One should not open one’s mouth wide in anticipation of food; this is how one should train. Explanation of the meaning:
"Opening the mouth wide" means opening the mouth wide in anticipation before the morsel of food has even arrived. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When a bhikṣu eats, he should follow the manner of eating of the Elephant King of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*): once the food has entered the mouth, [he should eat] with his trunk."
This establishes the subsequent limit: once the preceding morsel has been swallowed, one should immediately place the subsequent ball inside; one must not keep the mouth open and wait.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "A 'ball' (*piṇḍa*) refers to a portion of rice scraped up with the hand, neither too large nor too small, which can be placed in the mouth;
it does not mean that the balls must be made to stick together."
The determination of the offense is the same as before.

Regarding the exceptions for non-offense: there is no offense if the time for the meal is about to pass, or if there is danger to life, danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if one eats quickly.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is a sore in the mouth, one may keep the mouth open in advance; there is no offense."
The thirty-eighth precept: Speaking while containing food in the mouth. (The setting for the origin is the same as before. Origin story:
The group of six monks spoke while their mouths were full of rice. Laypeople, as before, criticized and disparaged them. Therefore, it was established as a rule.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must not speak with food in the mouth; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: "Speaking with food in the mouth" means that when rice remains in the mouth, speech cannot be clearly articulated, causing others to fail to understand.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one is eating and is called by the upādhyāya, ācārya, or an elder bhikṣu, if one can respond without changing the sound of one's voice before the food has been fully swallowed, that is permissible; if one cannot, one must swallow first and then respond."
If the person before you objects, you should reply, "There is food in my mouth; therefore, I did not respond immediately. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"When food is in one's mouth, one should not speak, as that would be the same practice as that of laypeople (*avadātavasana*)."
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if one is choking and seeks water, or if there is a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). In these cases, there is no transgression.
○ The Thirty-ninth Precept: Throwing Food from Afar (The setting for the origin is the same).
Regarding the individuals involved:

the group of six monks took morsels of rice and threw them into their mouths from a distance. Householders criticized and disparaged this, saying it was like a magician; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not take a lump of rice and throw it into the mouth from a distance; this is how one should train.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
The Opening of the Precept: There is no offense in cases where one is bound and food is thrown into one's mouth.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Whether it be sour jujubes, grapes, or various other such things, even if one picks up and throws parched beans into the mouth to eat, there is no offense."
No offense. ○ The fortieth precept: Regarding the neglect of food (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the rule.
The group of six monks received food improperly; they took morsels of rice in their hands and bit off half of them to eat.
Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled pigs, dogs, camels, donkeys, oxen, crows, or birds. Therefore, this was established as a rule.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not let food fall [from the hand]. This is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: "To let fall" means that half [of the food] enters the mouth while half remains in the hand. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that this is not permitted.

Bite off half [a morsel] and place it back into the bowl; it should be eaten piece by piece so that each mouthful is of a suitable size. If a ball of parched grain (*maṇḍaka*) is too large, one should divide it with the hand until it is of a suitable size for a mouthful.
If it is a cake (*pūpa*), one should divide it into portions, making them equal and of a suitable size for a mouthful.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if one eats thin cakes, parched rice, melons, sugarcane, vegetables, various fruits, and the like.
There is no offense in these cases.
○ The forty-first precept: Eating with the cheeks full (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the offense was the group of six monks, who ate with their cheeks full. Laypeople criticized them, saying they were like monkeys; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must train oneself not to eat with puffed cheeks.
Explanation of the meaning: "Eating with puffed cheeks" refers to causing both cheeks to bulge out, resembling the appearance of a macaque. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Moving from one cheek to the other, chewing on one side and swallowing on that same side:
the offense is determined as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if the time for eating is about to expire, or if there is a threat to life, a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if one is eating quickly due to haste.
Eating. No offense. ○ The forty-second precept: Eating while making noise by chewing rice (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion.
The group of six monks made noise while chewing their food. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying it was like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, donkeys, crows, or birds.
Therefore, the following precept was established.
One must not eat making noise by chewing food; this is how one should train.
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: the *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states that "not eating by clicking the tongue" refers to when a donor provides food that is excessively sweet.
Therefore, one may click the tongue and feign an expression of sourness. As for those who do not savor food, if the food is actually sour, they savor it;
however, they make a sound with their lips to manifest an expression of sweetness. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When drinking gruel, one must not make a sound;
when eating roots, stalks, and the like, do not make a loud noise. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not swallow food whole so as to produce a gurgling sound."
If one makes a gurgling sound, there is no offense if it is due to a disease of the throat;
the determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense for chewing dry cakes, scorched rice, sugarcane, melons, fruits, and the like.
The forty-third precept: On eating with large mouthfuls (the setting for the origin is the same).
The individuals involved were the group of six who ate with large mouthfuls. Laypeople, as before, criticized and disparaged them; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must not take large mouthfuls of food; this is how one should train.

*Explanation of the meaning:* "Taking large mouthfuls of food" means opening the mouth wide and drawing food in from a distance. (The expulsion of air is called *chui*; the inhalation of air is called *xi*. Here, it refers to drawing food into the mouth.)
Laozi said: "If one wishes to contract it, one must first expand it. (This is correct.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if the mouth is painful; if eating soup; if eating curd, curd-water, ghee, or *sūpi*.

Ro-jiang (the method for preparing this liquor is as follows: first have a lay attendant pound large barley grains in a vessel, add water, and let it sit for two or three days until it becomes slightly sour; strain it thoroughly and drink it). Or *khu-chu* (this is vinegar;
because it has a bitter taste, it is colloquially called "bitter wine"). There is no offense [in consuming these].
○ The forty-fourth precept: Regarding eating by licking with the tongue (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion was the group of six monks who ate by sticking out their tongues. Laypeople, as before, criticized this with disdain; therefore, it was established as a rule.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not lick food with the tongue; this is how one should train.
*Explanation of the Meaning:* "Licking food with the tongue" refers to licking up morsels of rice with the tongue. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "to protrude the tongue."
Regarding eating: one should extend the tongue and place the food upon it, then close the mouth. One must not repeatedly lick the hands while eating;
one must not lick the hands while eating. If ghee, oil, or other substances are on the hand, one should gather them together by rubbing them against the rim of the bowl, and only then take the food.
The offense is determined as before. Exceptions:
There is no offense if one is bound; or if the hands are covered in mud, grime, or grease;
or if one takes food with the tongue. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One must not eat by counting on the fingers, nor [lick] honey, salt, and the like.

If one touches it with the finger and counts it, there is no offense. If the person on duty for the month or the food supervisor wishes to know whether the food is raw or cooked, salty or bland, sweet or sour, they may place it in the palm of their hand and lick it with the tongue;
there is no offense. If one is ill, they may place salt in the palm of their hand and lick it; there is no offense.
○ The forty-fifth precept: Regarding the rule against shaking the hand while eating (the setting for the origin is the same).

The originator of the rule was the group of six monks, who ate shaking their hands. Laypeople criticized them, remarking that they resembled kings or high ministers; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not shake the hand while eating; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that when shaking the hand, one must not shake it toward a neighboring seat. If food adheres [to the hand]...
The hand should be shaken forward before oneself. If one shakes out the bowl, the *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If there is food or water on the hand, do not shake it toward others.
Maintain focused mindfulness while eating, so as to sustain the body and advance upon the Path."
The offense is defined as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; when there is grass or insects in the food, or it is impure, and one wishes to shake them off;
or when food that has not yet been formally received is defiled by contact with the hand, and one shakes it off with the hand.
To leave [the food] is not an offense.
○ The forty-sixth precept: Regarding eating with scattered grains held in the hand (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the rule.
The group of six monks ate with their hands holding scattered grains of rice. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled chickens or birds. Therefore, the rule was established:
one must train oneself not to eat with the hands holding scattered grains of rice; this is the formulated characteristic of the precept.
Explanation of the Meaning: "Scattering rice" refers to discarding rice. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "One who does not scatter food with the hand must not eat like a cock scratching for food;
the determination of the offense is the same as before. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If food falls onto grass or leaves that have been accepted [as a seat], it should be eaten. If..."
If there is soil on it, one should blow away the soil and eat. Or, if there is much soil adhering to it, one may wash it with water and eat.
Exceptions where there is no offense: if at times there is grass or insects in the food, or if it is defiled by impurities.
If one discards food before it has been received, there is no offense.
○ The forty-seventh precept: Regarding handling a drinking vessel with soiled hands (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the rule:
The group of six [monks] held their drinking vessels with hands that were unclean and greasy. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled royal ministers.
Therefore, the rule was established; such is the character of the precept as it stands.
One must not grasp a drinking vessel with soiled hands;

this is how one should train. Explanation of the meaning: "Soiled hands" refers to hands that have rice mixed with grease adhering to them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣu is eating..."
One should protect the left hand; one should receive the drinking vessel with the left hand and drink while resting it against the lips.
One must not deeply insert the mouth into the rim of the vessel, nor allow the rim to touch the nose or forehead. One must not drink the contents entirely; a small amount should be left remaining.
One should discard it at the mouth and rinse it again with water before passing it down.

If there is a sore or wound on the left hand, one should place the right hand upon the rim of the bowl, wash it thoroughly to remove any grease, and rinse it with pure water; if it cannot be cleaned, one should catch the food with a leaf.
After drinking, proceed as above. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Whenever one wishes to eat or drink, one must always use earth powder."
Having purified oneself with soap powder and the like and washed one's hands, one may then grasp food vessels, drinking vessels, and pure water flasks.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Regarding the exceptions: there is no offense if one receives [the food] upon grass, or upon leaves, or if one receives it after having washed one's hands.
The *Wu bai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states in detail: Formerly, there was an administrative bhikṣu who was in charge of preparing food and drink.
He would constantly point his hand toward the vessels, saying, "Take this; use this. He did this every day without ever performing repentance.
When his life ended, he fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). One night, a bhikṣu named Wu-zhuo (Aśaṅka) went to the latrine and heard a voice calling out. He asked, "Who are you?"
"Who are you? He replied, "I am a hungry ghost (preta). He asked, "By what conduct in your former life did you fall into the realm of hungry ghosts?
He replied, "In this monastery, I served as an attendant for the Saṃgha. He asked, "Your former conduct was diligent; by what cause have you fallen into this state?

He replied, "I gave impure food to the members of the Saṃgha. He asked, "In what way was it impure? He replied, "The members of the Saṃgha had various jars and vessels in which they kept their food. With my finger..."

To take up a vessel [for food] while standing and to consume it [in that manner] constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*. If one does not repent after the third recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, the offense becomes increasingly grave.

For this reason, one falls among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). With both hands, they tear open their chests; the skin and flesh are pulled back to expose the throat, which is parched by wind. Question: Why do they tear open their chests? Answer:
Because the worms devouring their bodies cause them such agony. Question: Why do they groan and cry out? Answer: Because they are so overcome by hunger that they are on the verge of death.
He asked, "What do you wish to eat? He replied, "I wish to eat excrement, but I cannot obtain it; because other hungry ghosts push me aside, I am unable to move forward.
Venerable Aśvaghoṣa said, "I know what to do. The ghost said, "We pray that the Saṃgha will perform a prayer of blessing for us."
Asaṅga immediately returned and informed the assembly of requisites. The assembly offered prayers of blessing for him, and subsequently he obtained food from excrement and no longer groaned in pain.
Because of this testimony, it is known that a *mahābhikṣu* must not defile monastic utensils with his hands.
However, if it is not a monastic utensil, there is no offense in receiving it with one's hands and then giving it to the Saṃgha.
○ The forty-eighth precept: Discarding bowl-washing water at the house of a layperson (the setting for the origin is the same). The individuals involved were the group of six monks.
Having finished eating at the house of a layperson, they washed their bowls and discarded the water, leaving such a mess that even leftover food was strewn about.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged him, saying that he received food and drink like a starving person, yet discarded it in a messy heap like a royal minister;
therefore, this rule was established.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not discard the water used for washing the alms bowl inside the residence of a layperson;

this is how one should train. Explanation of the meaning: "Water for washing the alms bowl" refers to water mixed with rice. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "At the time of eating, one should attend to the capacity of one's stomach."

One should take [only what is needed] and must not accept too much. If a *karmadāna* (attendant) suddenly gives too much, before eating it, one should reduce the portion and give it to a neighboring seat-mate.
If the neighboring seat-mate does not take it, one should give it to a *śrāmaṇera* or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*). When washing the bowl, one must not pour even a single grain onto the ground;
if there are any, they should be picked up and placed on a wooden board or upon leaves. If they are very small grains, [one should handle them with care].
If the flour cannot be gathered, there is no offense; the determination of the offense remains the same as before.
Regarding the exceptions: one is not at fault if one receives it in a vessel or a basin, takes the water, and discards it outside. There is no offense.
[This constitutes] an offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one asks the owner [for permission] and discards it, there is no offense.
(Consult the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā*). The *Vinayasamgraha* states:

"There were some laypeople who requested water from the bowl of a bhikṣu for the sake of auspiciousness or to cure illness. At that time, Upānanda mixed the water from his food-bowl with the leftover rice."
If one were to give it [the bowl] directly, it would cause [the recipient] to feel disdain or contempt. Therefore, the Noble One established the ritual for bestowing the bowl-water.
One should first wash the bowl three times thoroughly, fill it with clear water, and recite the Noble Gāthā two or three times before bestowing it.

The Gāthā says: "Whether it be the pleasures of the five worldly desires, or even the pleasures of the various devas, compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, they do not equal even a thousandth part."
It does not even equal one [fraction]. Because the accumulation (*saṃskāra*) can give rise to suffering, and from suffering, accumulation arises again.
The Noble Eightfold Path can transcend to the state of sublime Nirvāṇa. That is to say, the giver will surely obtain its benefit; if one gives for the sake of profit as a form of pleasure.
In the future, one will surely attain peace and happiness.
○ The forty-ninth precept: Regarding the prohibition against defecating or urinating upon grass or vegetables;
the two conditions for the formal establishment [of this rule] (the locus of the originative narrative is the same).

The occasion for the rule arose when the group of six monks defecated, urinated, spat, and sneezed upon living grass and vegetables. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying they were like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, or donkeys.
Therefore, the rule was established. However, a sick bhikṣu was unable to avoid living grass and vegetables and became utterly exhausted. The Buddha said: "In the case of illness..."
A bhikṣu commits no offense. The precept should be recited as follows:
"Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
one must not defecate, urinate, or spit mucus upon living grass or vegetables, except in the case of illness. This should be studied."
Exegesis: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: One should stay on ground where no grass grows.
If, during the summer months, the grass is so lush that there is no bare space, one should stay where camels, oxen, horses, donkeys, or sheep have trodden.
If even this is unavailable, one should stay upon bricks, tiles, or stones. If even this is unavailable, one should stay upon dry grass or leaves. If even this is unavailable—
One should receive it with a wooden branch, so that the excrement falls first onto the wood and only afterwards onto the ground.

When a bhikṣu is walking for exercise (caṅkrama), he must not spit upon living grass. At the head of the walking path, one should place a spittoon made of pottery, stone, or leaves, and put fine ash or soil inside the spittoon;
only then should one spit upon it. This applies whether it be defecating, urinating, or spitting.

If saliva soils the hands or feet, one may wipe them on fresh grass. This applies to those who are ill—suffering from ailments of the lower body, cold disorders, wind disorders, or foot ailments—to the extent that they are unable to move about and avoid fresh grass, vegetables, and the like.

The offense is determined as before. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: If one is on green grass, beneath a fine tree, or at a flowering or fruiting tree where people rest, one must not defecate or urinate. There is no offense if it is in a thicket of thorns.

If traveling through a great forest where branches and leaves are densely interlaced, one should avoid areas frequented by people. If one traverses a field of living grass, [one should likewise avoid it].
There is no vacant space. One should carry dry leaves and spread them upon [the ground] when defecating or urinating; if none can be obtained, there is no offense.
For this nun, it is a *pāyattika*; for the three groups of minor followers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in cases where one is ill; or where, being in a place devoid of grass or vegetables, urine or excrement falls upon living grass or vegetables;
or when, due to the wind or being carried by a bird, it falls into living grass or vegetables. In these instances, there is no offense.
○ The fiftieth precept: Regarding defecating, urinating, spitting, or expectorating in water;
the two conditions combined for the formal establishment (the locus of the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion.
The group of six monks urinated, defecated, sneezed, and spat in the water. Householders criticized and disparaged them, saying they were like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, and donkeys.

Therefore, the rule was established. However, when sick bhikṣus became exhausted from avoiding the water, the Buddha said: "There is no offense for those who are ill. The precept should be recited as follows: [Insert the formal wording of the precept].
The established precept:
One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: "In water" refers to all rivers, streams, ponds, and bodies of water.
The offense is adjudicated as before. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate into water; one should do so on dry land.
If it is raining and the water has overflowed and filled [the area], one should do so upon a clod of earth.
If such is unavailable, one should do so upon a tile or stone, or upon bamboo or wood. First let it fall onto the wood, and only then into the water. If [it is] large or small... [text missing].
If one soils their hands or feet with saliva or mucus, they may wash them in water. Regarding the washing in water after defecating or urinating, there is no offense.
When a bhikṣu enters the water to bathe, he must not spit into it. If he is far from the bank, he should spit into his hand and then discard it.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If the water is not used by people, or if it is seawater, there is no offense. Water.
Although it may be used in moderation, it is not used by anyone at large or far away;
thus there is no offense. Regarding the exceptions for non-offense: one who is ill, or who voids excrement or urine on the bank and it falls into the water, commits no offense.
If [the excrement] is blown by the wind or carried off by a bird and falls into water, there is no offense.
○ The fifty-first precept: Regarding standing to urinate or defecate.
This is established through two conditions (the setting of the origin is the same).

The occasion for the rule arose because the group of six monks stood while urinating and defecating, which the householders criticized as being like cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, or camels; therefore, it was established as a precept.

When a sick bhikṣu was so exhausted that he was unable to squat, the Buddha said: "There is no offense for one who is ill. The precept should be recited in this manner: [One should not stand while urinating or defecating]. Exceptions apply in cases of illness.
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must not stand while defecating or urinating, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train.
*Explanation of the Meaning:* The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: The Buddha said, "Although these are my own regulations, they are not considered pure in other regions."

Regarding purification: none of these [local methods] should be employed. Although they are not my own teaching, for those practices prescribed in other regions that must necessarily be performed, one must not fail to do so.

(In this region, it is a matter of local custom for men to squat while urinating; since this is what the world censures and dislikes, one should follow the local custom as a form of purification. This does not contradict the Sage’s intent, as it accords with national customs and can be termed "pure observance of the precepts.

One must not arbitrarily adopt other external prohibitions and equate them with this standard. To do so would be to prescribe what was not prescribed or to permit what was prohibited; the sin of abandoning the Teaching would be difficult to avoid.)
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if one is ill, or if one is bound and restrained, or if the feet are covered with grime, oiliness, or mud.
In these cases, there is no violation.
Fifty-second: The precept on preaching the Dharma to one who has their robe draped over one shoulder;
two conditions combined for the formal establishment (the locus of the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the occasion.

The Group of Six and those who were disrespectful spoke the Dharma to people with their robes tucked up behind. The bhikṣus felt resentment and reproached them, and thus [the Buddha] established this rule.
When the bhikṣus were uncertain about whether it was an illness, they did not dare to speak the Dharma to those with their robes tucked up. The Buddha said: "There is no offense for one who is ill.
The precept should be recited in this manner."
Regarding the established characteristics of the precept:
one must not preach the Dharma to a person who has their robe draped over one shoulder in a disrespectful manner, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train.
*Explanation of the Meaning:* The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "To preach the Dharma" means to explain its meaning for the sake of another person, analyzing and expounding it in detail.
It is taught in order to cause one to practice in accordance with the Dharma. "Dharma" refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha and approved by the Buddha.
That which was spoken by the Buddha is what the Tathāgata himself spoke; that which was approved by the Buddha is what was spoken by the śrāvakas and praised by the Buddha as "well done.
This is called approval.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if one is ill, or if one speaks for a king or a royal minister. (The following cases are all the same).

○ Fifty-third: One must not preach the Dharma to one who has wrapped a cloth around the neck, except in the case of illness. This should be studied (the same as the preceding precept, with the difference being the wrapping of the neck).
Fifty-fourth: One must not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train.

*Commentary on the Meaning:* "Those with their heads covered" refers to those whose heads are covered by robes, leaves, or any other object whatsoever—all such instances are termed "having the head covered. In the Western Regions (India), it is considered a mark of respect to go bareheaded and barefoot.

In the Eastern lands, one shows respect through the neatness of one’s robes and cap; however, this follows the local customs. One must surely take reverence as the primary intention. Unless the person is bare-headed, one should not preach to those whose heads are covered by other items.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Regarding the exceptions: those who do not commit an offense are described in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* as follows:

if a bhikṣu goes before a king for the sake of a stūpa or for the affairs of the Saṃgha, or when he is in the presence of a landowner, he should stand at a distance where there is a pure attendant (*kappiyakāraka*). He should speak to the king with the intention of acting on behalf of that person. The king—

Listen. There is no offense. If a bhikṣu is traveling through a dangerous and perilous road while in a state of fear, and a guard says, "Venerable sir, preach the Dharma for me," he may preach it even though the person has their head covered; there is no offense (the same applies hereafter).
Fifty-fifth: One must not preach the Dharma to those who have wrapped their heads, except in cases of illness. This is a training to be observed.
*Commentary:* "Wrapping" (*gǒ*) refers to binding or wrapping around; it is distinct from "covering. The remainder is the same as previously explained.
Fifty-sixth: One must not preach the Dharma to one who has their hands placed upon their hips, except in the case of illness;

this is how one should train. Commentary on the Meaning: "One with hands upon the hips" (either with one hand or both hands) refers to someone who, out of self-conceit and arrogance, treats the Dharma lightly; therefore, one must not preach for them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
One must not preach the Dharma to those who are cradling their knees or sitting with their feet propped up, except in cases of illness.
(57) One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing leather sandals, except in cases of illness. This should be practiced.
**Explanation of the Meaning:** "Leather sandals" (革屣) refers to shoes made of leather (whether single-layered or double-layered).

**Conditions for Non-offense:** Regarding when there is no offense, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If it is a king, a landowner, or a guardian, even if they are wearing leather sandals, there is no offense in preaching to them.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If many people are wearing leather sandals, one cannot [make them... [remove them].
[He] was liberated. However, for those who do not cling, it is taught that there is no offense (the rest is the same as before).
According to the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*, Third Part: When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a son of a householder in Campā named Śrona.
His parents had only this one son and cherished him dearly; he had been so from birth.
He practiced austerities; he had never walked upon the ground, and hair grew on the soles of his feet.
At that time, the King of Magadha desired to see him and immediately issued a command to the Lord of Campā, ordering all the elders to bring their sons.
When the Lord of the City received the command, he, together with the elders, brought the sons there. He then requested of the King that a cloth be spread upon the ground for Śrona.

He went to the king’s presence and prostrated himself with his head at the king’s feet. Upon seeing him, the king was greatly delighted in heart and immediately bestowed gold and jewels upon him, saying, "I have already granted you benefit in this present life. The World-Honored One is on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
you should go there to see and pay homage to him. He shall grant you benefit in future lives. Rāhula followed these instructions, paid homage to the Buddha, and heard the Dharma.
He attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and received the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, becoming an upāsaka.

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa sought to leave the household life under the Buddha, but because his parents would not permit it, he fasted for five hundred days. Eventually, they allowed him to go forth.

He practiced the path with such diligence that as he walked in meditation, blood flowed and stained the ground like a place of slaughter. The Buddha then spoke to him using the analogy of the strings of a lute. Therefore...

It is permitted to wear a single layer of leather sandals while inside the monastery. If one is in a frontier region where there are many tiles and stones, two layers are permitted for the sake of protecting the body, the robes, and the bedding.
○ Fifty-eighth: One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, except in cases of illness. This is a training rule (*śikṣāpada*). Commentary:
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, there are fourteen kinds of clogs: gold clogs, silver clogs, jewel (*maṇi*) clogs, ivory clogs... [and so forth].
Sandals: wooden sandals, tāla-wood sandals, leather sandals, kṣaumaka-cloth sandals, corded sandals, reed sandals, tree-bark sandals, baka-wood sandals, and grass sandals.
These and others like them are called "sandals" (the remainder is the same as before).
Fifty-ninth: One must not preach the Dharma to those who are riding vehicles, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

Commentary: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are eight kinds of vehicles: elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, ox-vehicles, donkey-vehicles, [camel-vehicles, cart-vehicles, palanquin-vehicles, and foot-vehicles].
Vessel-vehicle; chariot-vehicle; palanquin-vehicle; sedan-chair-vehicle (the remainder is the same as before). ○ The Sixtieth:
The Precept Regarding Staying Overnight in a Buddhist Stūpa.
Two conditions combined for the formal establishment (the locus of the originative narrative is the same).
The origin of the rule concerning persons:
Six groups of monks stayed overnight in a stūpa. A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who established a precept.
Because the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to stay overnight in a stūpa for the sake of guarding it, the Buddha said there was no offense. "The precept should be recited in this way."
The established precept:
One must not stay overnight within a Buddha-stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it. This is how one should train.

*Explanation of the Meaning:* "Buddha-stūpa" (Sanskrit: *stūpa*; also transliterated as *fútú*, *tōubó*, or *sītōbǒ*—the latter being erroneous translations). This is translated as "square mound" (*fāngfén*). It is also...

It is translated as "reversed mound" (*yuǎnzhǒng*) and also as "high and manifest. In meaning, it is translated as "spiritual temple" (*língmiào*). A "temple" (*miào*) refers to appearance; it is the place where the physical appearance of one's ancestors resides. Furthermore, its Sanskrit name is *stūpa*. Xu Xuan’s *Xīn jiā* (New Additions) states that it is the *fútú* of the Western Regions.

As for the term *fútú*, here it is translated as "accumulated form" (*jùxiàng*). The *Jiètán tújīng* (Diagram Sutra of the Precept Altar) says: "The character 'tǎ' (tower/mound) in the Chinese script is merely a phonetic representation of an object; it was originally not a designation from the Western lands. According to the Sanskrit original, the place where the Buddha’s relics are interred is called a *stūpa*."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "That which contains relics is called a *caitya*; that which lacks relics is called a *stūpa* (the *Wenju* commentary notes:

a *stūpa* is one without a skeletal body; the present usage of 'Buddha-tower' [佛塔] is intended to distinguish it from other types of towers). Those who serve as guardians are excluded (referring to those such as the temple administrators and incense-lamp keepers who reside constantly within the tower)."
One should sweep away dust and filth, light lamps, burn incense, and guard the property of the stūpa; for this reason, the Noble One permitted staying overnight therein.
The determination of the offense is the same as before. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"Regarding various incense altars, halls, flagpoles, *caityas*, and the images or shadows of the Tathāgata, one must recite gāthās before stepping upon them; otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
The Exceptional Circumstances: There is no offense in cases where one stays overnight due to such an illness; or for the purpose of guarding [something]; or when seized by a powerful person;
or when there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, staying overnight is without offense.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its latter section, states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and the cremation has been completed, the fourfold assembly shall collect the relics and place them in a vessel of the seven precious gems" (*Shilao zhi* states: "Once the Buddha had passed away, his body was cremated with fragrant wood").

The sacred bones were crushed into fragments as small as grains; they could not be destroyed by striking them, nor could they be scorched by burning them, yet they possessed radiant and miraculous efficacy—these are called *śarīra*.

One should erect a seven-jeweled stūpa, thirteen stories high, within the city of Kuśinagara at the crossroads of the four main streets, topped with the mark of a wheel (*cakra*). (Regarding the "mark of a wheel,"...)

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "On the stupas of Buddhas, one should erect parasols, long poles, and the marks of wheels (*cakra*). In the sūtras, these are often referred to as 'wheel-marks' (*xianglun*), because people look up at them to observe these signs.
A stupa for a Pratyekabuddha should have eleven tiers; a stupa for an Arhat should consist of four tiers. These too are adorned with various precious jewels.
The stupas of a Cakravartin King are likewise made of the seven treasures, but they do not have tiered levels. Why is this? Because [the merit] has not yet...

Because they have been liberated from the suffering of existence within the three realms, the twelve-linked chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the eight kinds of stupas (*stūpa*) both possess the *harmikā* (the umbrella-like pinnacle).
A Buddha’s stupa has eight tiers; a Bodhisattva’s stupa has seven layers; a Pratyekabuddha’s has six layers; one who has attained the fourth fruit has five layers;

one who has attained the third fruit has four layers; one who has attained the second fruit has three layers; one who has attained the first fruit has two layers; a Wheel-Turning King’s has one layer; and for ordinary monks, there is only the *kadalī* (plantain) [canopy].
[It is] merely a leaf and a fire-jewel.
○ The sixty-first precept: Regarding the entrusting of wealth and goods within a Buddha-stūpa;
the two conditions for the formal enactment [of the rule] (the locus of the originative narrative is the same).
Regarding the origin of the rule:
The group of six monks stored their wealth and property within a Buddhist stūpa. A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
Because the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to store their goods in the stūpa for the sake of preservation, the Buddha said: "There is no offense. It should be done in this manner."
Regarding the recitation of the precepts:
one must train oneself not to conceal wealth or property within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of ensuring its security. This is the established characteristic of the precept.

Explanation of the Meaning: Regarding "wealth and goods" (this may refer to wealth offered to a stūpa or wealth offered to the Saṃgha; it is permitted by the Noble Ones to store such items within a Buddhist stūpa for fear of loss and to ensure their security, though this does not necessarily apply to private property).
The determination of the offense is the same as before. Exceptions: There is no offense if it is for the sake of preservation; if one hides it within a stūpa; if one is seized by a powerful person;
or if there is danger to life or danger to one’s holy life (*brahmacarya*). In these cases, there is no offense.
The sixty-second precept: Wearing leather sandals while entering a Buddhist stūpa (the setting, the occasion, and the person involved are the same as before).
The established rule of training is:
One must not wear leather sandals while entering a Buddhist stūpa; this should be studied.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or is seized by forceful persons.
○ Sixty-third [Rule].
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hands; this is how one should train.

[Commentary on the meaning: (In the previous precept, one was prohibited from entering and treading upon the ground of the Buddha while wearing them; this precept prohibits entering while holding them in one's hands, as it likewise lacks an attitude of reverence.)
64. One must not walk around a stūpa wearing leather sandals; this is how one should train. *Explanation:* There are two kinds of circumambulation:

first, circumambulation by way of passing through a path; second, circumambulation as an expression of reverence. When it says "walking around a stūpa," it refers to circumambulation by way of passing through a path. All other details are the same as before.
65. One must not wear leather boots when entering a Buddhist stūpa; this should be practiced.
66. [The following rule applies.]
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding footwear in one's hands;

this is how one should train. Explanation of the Terms: *Pura* (a transliteration of the Sanskrit term) refers here to short-topped boots. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The uppers should not be made too deep;
they are permitted to reach only above the ankles. They must not be like boots; rather, they should be open in the front and gathered at the back."
The sixty-seventh precept: Eating while seated on the ground and defiling it.
This is a combined formulation of two causal conditions (the locus of the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion.
After the group of six monks had sat beneath a stūpa to eat, they left behind grass and leftover food, defiling the ground before departing.

The bhikṣus expressed their disapproval and reprimanded them, and reported this to the Buddha when he was establishing the precepts. At that time, [the Buddha permitted] giving food after a stūpa has been built; likewise, giving food after a dwelling or a pond has been built.

Furthermore, when the assembly gathered and the seating area was narrow and cramped, they were uncertain whether the Buddha had yet authorized us to sit and eat beneath a stūpa. The Buddha [responded...]
[The Buddha] said: "I permit sitting and eating. One should not leave grass or food that has defiled the ground. At that time, there was a monk who ate while seated;
if he performed the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite of leaving food) and did not eat it, or if there was a sick monk, they did not dare to leave the leftover food or grass to defile the ground.
The Buddha said: "I permit you to gather [the leftovers] and place them by your side. When you go out, take them and discard them. It should be explained in this manner."

Regarding the precepts: as for the established characteristics of the precepts, one should train oneself thus: one must not sit to eat beneath a stūpa, nor leave grass or food waste that defiles the ground.

Exegesis: Regarding the statement that grass and food leave the ground defiled—this refers to the custom in the Western Regions (India) where, when receiving food, one spreads grass on the ground as a seat, as there are no chairs or benches. In ancient times, people sat upon the ground, and this is likewise the practice here [in China].
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if they are gathered in one place and carry them out for disposal when leaving.
○ The sixty-eighth precept: Passing under a stupa carrying a corpse (the origin of the rule is the same).
The origin of the rule:
Six groups of monks were carrying a corpse past the base of a stūpa. The deity protecting the stūpa became enraged, and for this reason, the specific formulation of the precept was established.
One must not carry a corpse past the base of a stūpa; this is how one should train.

*Explanation of the Meaning:* "Death" (*mṛta*) means "to be exhausted. When the vital breath has ceased and the spirit has departed, it is called "death. That which lies upon a bed is called a "corpse" (*śava*); that which is within a coffin is called a "coffin" (*kḷpta*).
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if one passes through this path, or if one is led away by forceful persons. These cases are not violations.
○ Sixty-ninth: One must not bury a corpse beneath a stūpa; this should be studied.
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*: When a bhikṣu dies, he should be cremated. If there is no firewood available...
It may be obtained. It should be discarded in a river; if there is no river, it should be buried in the ground.
Since the earth abounds with insects and ants, one should place it in a secluded thicket with its head pointing north and lying on its right side, supporting the head with a bundle of grass.
Whether with grass or leaves, one should cover its body and escort it away. A bhikṣu should have a capable person recite the Threefold Hymn of Impermanence.
He should recite the sūtras and chant gāthās to offer prayers for their welfare. Once the task is completed, he should return to the monastery and wash his body.

If he has touched a corpse, he must wash both his body and his clothes; if he has not touched one, he need only wash his hands and feet. Upon returning to the monastery, he should pay homage at the caitya.
Seventieth: One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this should be studied. Seventy-first.
One must not burn corpses beneath a stūpa. This is a training to be observed.
(72) One must not burn corpses within four paces of a Buddha-stūpa so that the foul odor enters it. This is a training to be observed.

(The Lotus Sūtra says: Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja thought to himself, "To offer worship through my supernatural powers is not as good as offering worship with my own body. He then poured fragrant oil over himself and burned his body as an offering to the Buddha Viśuddhaprabhāsa. This was his quest for the Great Dharma.)

"Those with deep feelings can perform what is difficult to perform; those with deep resolve can relinquish what is difficult to relinquish. Now, corpses are being burned on all four sides of the Buddha stupa, and the foul smoke and flames are polluting the sacred image. Therefore, I have established this prohibition."
○ The seventy-third precept: Passing under a stupa while carrying a corpse’s clothing or a bed.
This rule is established by combining two conditions (the locus of the origin is the same).
The person who gave rise to the occasion:
The group of six monks carried the clothes of the dead and passed beneath a stupa from its platform; the deity residing there became angry, and thus [the Buddha] established this rule.
Monks who wear refuse-rags (pāṃśukūla) were hesitant and did not dare to carry such clothes beneath a stupa. The Buddha said:
"I permit you to wash, dye, and fumigate them with incense before carrying them inside. This precept should be recited as follows:
Regarding the established characteristics of the precepts:
one must not carry a corpse’s garment or bed past the base of a stūpa, except when it has been washed, dyed, or perfumed; this is how one should train.

Explanation of the meaning: Regarding the phrase "except when it has been washed, dyed, or perfumed," the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one obtains a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe from a dust heap), [it should be] water..."
If it has been soaked for a long period, wash it clean using pure ash and apply *kṛṣṇāguru* incense upon it; only then may one wear it to enter the stūpa.
The determination of the offense is the same as previously stated.
The Opening of the Conditions. There is no offense in cases where one washes, dyes, or perfumes [the robes].

○ The Seventy-fourth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Defecating or Urinating Beneath a Buddhist Stūpa (The setting of the occasion, the person who initiated the rule, and so forth are identical to the preceding precepts and not different).
The established characteristics of this precept are as follows:
One must not defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha-stūpa; this is a training rule.
The offense is the same as previously defined.
Exceptions: There is no offense for one who is seized by forceful agents, or in similar circumstances.

The *Upabhaṅga-rāja-sūtra* states: According to the monastic law (*vinaya*), one who enters the boundaries of the saṃgha’s grounds for walking meditation, whether large or small, shall fall into the Arbuda hell for five hundred lifetimes.
Thereafter, for twenty minor kalpas, they shall constantly be made to embrace their own elbows and hands in that foul and filthy place of excrement and urine, reaching even unto the Yellow Springs.
75. One must not defecate or urinate toward a stūpa; this should be practiced.
76. [The following rule:]
One must not defecate or urinate on any side of a Buddha-stūpa so as to allow the foul odor to enter;
this is how one should train. ○ Seventy-seventh:
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecating or urinating; this is how one should train.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if the path passes through the center, or if one is held by force.
○ Seventy-eighth [Rule]
One should train oneself not to chew tooth-sticks beneath a Buddha stūpa.
(78) One should train oneself not to chew tooth-sticks facing a Buddha stūpa. (79)
The Eightieth Precept: Regarding the Prohibition Against Chewing Tooth-sticks Around the Four Sides of a Stūpa (the narrative context is the same as before).
The established precept formulation is:
One must not chew tooth-sticks around the four sides of a stūpa; this should be studied and practiced.

**Exegesis:** Regarding the chewing of the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick): The Vinaya states that there are five benefits to chewing the tooth-stick: first, the mouth is free from foul odors; second, one can distinguish flavors; third, it does not increase internal heat (*uṣman*); fourth, it promotes the appetite for food; and fifth, the eyes become clear.

To fail to chew it results in the opposite of these five benefits. The *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* states: "In the morning, chew the tooth-stick and rinse the mouth thoroughly for purification. As for the term *yángzhī* (楊枝), this is a vernacular expression. In the Western Regions, the specific type is not restricted;
whether it be the branches of the *karkaṭaka* (creeper), the *śiṃśapā* (acacia), the *aśvattha* (peepal), or the *āmra* (mango) tree—whichever possesses a bitter taste may all be used.

The offense is determined as before. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In the presence of the Buddha, in the presence of one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*), teacher (*ācārya*), or any senior elder (*sthavira*), in front of a Buddha-stūpa, or in front of a Śrāvaka-stūpa, one must not chew tooth-sticks (*dantakāṣṭha*). One who chews them commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
It is not an offense [to do so] before a bhikṣu of equal seniority. The *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Codes of Dignified Conduct) states:
"One must not turn one's back toward a Buddha stūpa, nor toward one’s upādhyāya or ācārya.
The exceptions (*an-āpatti*)—situations where there is no offense—are as follows: if one is ill; or if one is seized by force; or if one is bound in fetters.
...and so forth. ○ Eighty-first:
One must not spit or expectorate beneath a Buddha-stūpa; this should be practiced as a training rule.
82. One must train oneself not to spit or expectorate toward a stūpa. 83.
The precept against spitting or expectorating on the four sides of a stūpa (the causal context is the same as before).
Regarding the established precept: one must not discharge nasal mucus or saliva within four paces of a stūpa; this is how one should train. Explanation of the meaning:

"Nasal mucus and saliva" refers to what issues from the nose being called mucus (*si*) and what issues from the mouth being called saliva (*tuo*). Whenever discharging mucus or saliva, one must do so in a secluded place. As the *Water Repentance* (*Shuichan*) states: "Discharging mucus or saliva in the hall or chambers defiles [the sacred precincts]."
The ground of the Buddha and the Sangha is a place where the commission of faults is not light; one must surely be cautious regarding this! The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"At each of the four corners of the monastery, a spittoon should be placed beneath the pillars. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Place fine ash and earth inside the spittoon, and then spit upon it."
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or when a bird picks up the object and carries it away by blowing on it with the wind. These are non-offenses.
○ Precept 84: Regarding Sitting with Legs Extended Toward a Stūpa (The narrative context is the same as before).
The established rule of training is:
One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa; this is how one should train.
Exegesis: Regarding "stretching out the feet" (*śu-jia*): "stretching" (*shu*) means extending. One may stretch out one foot or both feet because of a lack of respectful faith.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.

Explanatory Circumstances for Non-Offense: There is no offense in cases such as when one has an illness like this, or when there is a physical barrier between [the monk and the stupa], or when one is held by forceful persons.
○ The Eighty-Fifth Precept: Building a Dwelling Beneath a Buddha Stupa.
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, traveling toward the brahmin village of Tundi (the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* calls it the brahmin settlement of Tudi;
according to this, the village is located more than sixty li northwest of the great city of Śrāvastī in Kośala, and was originally the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha).
The offense is incurred when, as in the case of the group of six monks, they place the Buddha’s stūpa in a lower room while they themselves reside in an upper room; thus was the precept established.
The characteristics of the rule are as follows:
"One must not occupy an upper room while placing a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room;

this is how one should train. **Explanation of the Meaning:** The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: The group of six monks stayed in the same room as the Tathāgata’s stūpa. The Buddha said: "This should not be done.
There was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of guarding it securely, was fearful and cautious and did not dare to stay overnight with it. The Buddha [permitted it].
[The Buddha] said: "It is permitted to place [the stūpa] upon a wooden peg or to sleep with it at the head of one's bed.
The group of six monks placed the Tathāgata’s stūpa in an inferior room while they themselves stayed overnight in a superior room. The Buddha said: "This should not be done.
One should place the Tathāgata’s stūpa in a superior room and stay overnight in an inferior room" (here, "superior" and "inferior" refer to quality). They then placed it...
[The monks] placed the stūpa in the lower room while they themselves stayed overnight in the upper room. The Buddha said: "This should not be done.
The stūpa of the Tathāgata should be placed in the upper room, and one should stay overnight in the lower room. (In this context, "upper" and "lower" refer to high and low positions.)
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense if it is due to a threat to life or a threat to one’s holy life (*brahmacarya*).
○ The eighty-sixth precept: Prohibiting standing while preaching the Dharma.
Second, regarding the combination of conditions (the details of dependent origination and so forth are the same as before):
One must train oneself in this precept:
when another person is seated and one is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.

Explanation of the Meaning: (The other person is seated while one is standing; the former lacks a mind of reverence, and the bhikṣu does not honor the Noble Teaching. Thus, he himself [addresses] another with what is contrary to the Dharma and speaks.)

The *Fanwang jing* (Brahmajāla Sūtra) states in detail: "If a son of the Buddha constantly practices teaching and transformation, giving rise to a heart of great compassion, and enters the homes of wealthy patrons (*dānapati*) or among all the assemblies, he must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
He should sit upon a high seat before the assembly of laypeople. A *dharmabhāṇaka* bhikṣu must not stand on the ground while preaching to the fourfold assembly."

A layperson (avadātavasana) may preach the Dharma. When preaching, the Dharma-preacher shall sit on a high seat, honored with offerings of incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners sits on lower seats.
They should be as filial toward their parents and respectful toward the teacher’s instructions as they would be when serving a fire-worshipping Brahmin.
If the one who preaches the Dharma does not preach in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka).
○ The Eighty-Seventh Precept: Teaching the Dharma to One Lying Down (The Buddha prohibited this because it involves pride of body and mind).
When another person is lying down and one is seated, one must not teach them the Dharma, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train.

Explanation of the Meaning: Excluding those who are ill. (At that time, Visākhā’s mother attained the three fruits [of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning] while on her way home. A sick bhikṣu went to visit her; his longing for the Dharma was so profound that he requested her to preach the Dharma for him.
However, because the Buddha had established the precepts, he did not dare to preach it for her. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and thus [the Buddha] granted permission for such preaching.)
○ Precept 88: Not Teaching the Dharma While Seated When the Listener is Not Seated.
If a person is seated and one is not seated, one must not teach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train.
The ninety-eighth precept concerning teaching the Dharma to one seated on a high seat:

The established rule states that if another person is seated on a high seat and oneself is seated on a lower seat, one must not teach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train.
**Exegesis:** The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of low beds: first, those that are physically low are called 'low';

second, those that are coarse and dilapidated are called 'low. There are two kinds of high [beds]: first, those that are tall and large are called 'high'; second, those that are exquisite and fine are also called 'high.'"
The *Sārvastivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (Huìxiáng) and the *Samantapāsādikā* (*Shànjiàn*) state:

The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a householder named Carpaṭa. His wife became pregnant and longed for āmra fruit (the āmra fruit is correctly called āmrapala)."

Master Zhaol’s commentary states: "Its fruit resembles a peach, yet it is not a peach. The *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) says: "The *nài* tree is certainly not a *nài* [tree]. Furthermore, it is translated as 'difficult to distinguish. Its fruit resembles a peach, yet it is not a peach; it resembles a *nài*, yet it is not a *nài*.
Moreover, its ripeness is difficult to discern, and its shape resembles a pear. [The text continues: He spoke to his son-in-law and asked him to find [the fruit].
Her husband replied, "This is not an *āmra* fruit. How could I possibly obtain it? His wife said, "If you do not get it, I shall surely die. The husband thought to himself: "Only..."
"In the king's garden there are out-of-season mangoes. I shall go and steal them. That very night he entered the king's garden to steal the fruit;
however, before he could obtain the fruit, the first light of dawn appeared, and he was unable to leave the garden. Thereupon, he remained hidden up in a tree.
At that time, the king and the brahmin entered the grove, intending to eat mangoes. The brahmin sat on the ground while the king sat upon a high seat;
the brahmin preached the Dharma for the king. A person stealing fruit was up in the tree, thinking to himself:
"I am now stealing fruit, and for this I ought to die. However, because the king is listening to the brahmin preach the Dharma, I shall now..."
"I am without fault; the King is without fault; the Brahmin is also without fault. Why is this?
It was for the sake of a woman that I stole the king's fruit. It was because of his pride that the King sat upon a high seat while his teacher remained below to listen to the Dharma.
And it was because of his greed for gain and offerings that the Brahmin sat upon a low seat while preaching to the King."
“Dharma! I and the king, the Brahmin, have no connection with the Dharma; I am now liberated.
Having formed this thought, he immediately descended from the tree, went before the king, and spoke these verses: “One person does not know the Dharma...”
One person does not see the Dharma; the teacher does not rely on the Dharma; the listener does not understand the Dharma.
For the sake of eating fine rice and various other delicacies—for the sake of such food and drink—I say this is "no Dharma.
For the sake of fame and profit, you have shattered the laws of your own house. I am but an ordinary person.
At that time, when people were above preaching the Dharma and those below spoke of it as being non-Dharma,
how much more so now, when I am high and you, my disciples, are below, as I preach the Dharma? At that time,
the one who stole the fruit was none other than myself.
90. One should train oneself thus:
"If a person is walking ahead and one is walking behind, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."

The Exceptional Circumstance: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu suffers from an eye ailment and another person holds a staff while leading him forward and speaks [the Dharma] for him, there is no offense (the rest is the same as the preceding precept)."
91. The precept on not preaching the Dharma to one walking in a higher place while one is in a lower place:
When a person is walking in a higher place for exercise and oneself is in a lower place for exercise, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
This is how one should train.
92. The precept on not preaching the Dharma to one on the path while oneself is off the path:
One who is on the path and another who is off the path should not preach the Dharma to each other, except in the case of illness. This should be studied.
The ninety-third precept on walking hand-in-hand:
The setting for the origin of this rule was when the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The occasion for the arising [of this rule] involved the group of six monks walking along a road holding hands, or obstructing other men and women. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying they resembled kings, ministers, or wealthy and noble elders; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the established precept:
one must not walk along a road holding hands; this is how one should train.
Explanation of the meaning: "Holding hands" means walking side by side while grasping each other's hands.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
Exceptions: There is no offense in cases such as when one has a similar illness, or suffers from blurred vision and requires assistance.
○ Precept 94: Climbing a Tree Higher Than a Person;
Combined with Two Conditions (the setting for the origin is the same).
The person who initiated the occasion.
There was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat atop a great tree. He voided excrement and urine upon the tree, which provoked the resentment of the tree deity.

The deity waited for an opportunity to sever his life-force; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. There was another bhikṣu traveling toward the kingdom of Kośala who encountered a fierce beast on the road.
Terrified and not daring to climb a tree higher than a man’s height, he was immediately seized by the fierce beast.
[The Buddha said: "It is harmful. The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "If there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), one may climb up a tree.
In such a case, the precepts should be recited in this manner, establishing the characteristics of the precepts separately."
One must not climb a tree higher than a person, except for reasons of necessity; this is how one should train. Regarding the exceptions:
there is no offense if it is due to a life-threatening danger or a threat to one's celibate practice (*brahmacarya*), and one climbs the tree higher than a person.
It is without offense for śrāmaṇeras and other minor groups to climb trees to gather branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit for the Saṃgha.

The second section of the *Aniyata-khaṇḍa* states: "If one wishes to take dry firewood from a tree, it is permitted to use a hook to take it, to use a ladder to take it, or to use a rope noose to take it;
if the entire trunk of the tree is dry, it is permitted to climb it."
○ Precept 95: On the Staff and Alms-bag (The setting for the origin of this rule is the same).
Regarding the person who initiated the offense:
Upananda placed his alms-bowl inside an alms-bag, fastened it to the head of a staff, and carried it on his shoulder. When the laypeople saw this, [they criticized him].
That is to say, when these officials all stepped off the road and watched him from a secluded spot, they realized it was Baddhālinda.
Because of their censure and reproach, the precept was established with its specific characteristics.
One must train oneself not to carry a bowl placed in a net-sack, suspended from the head of a staff over the shoulder while walking.
Regarding the exceptions: there is no offense if one is coerced by those using force, if one is bound, or if there is a threat to life.
The Brahma-faring is difficult; there is no offense.
○ Ninety-sixth: The precept against preaching the Dharma to one carrying a staff.
This is established by the conjunction of two conditions (the origin story and so forth are identical to those preceding).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who carries a staff and is disrespectful, except in the case of illness;
this is how one should train. Regarding the exceptions: there is no offense if, at that time, such an illness exists, or if a king or a high minister requests the teaching.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is traveling on a dangerous and fearful road, and the guards say..."
The Venerable One preached the Dharma for me. Although he was holding a staff, he preached the Dharma to him without fault.
97. The precept on preaching the Dharma to one who carries a sword:
One who carries a sword should not be preached the Dharma, except in the case of illness. This is how you should train.

Exegesis: Regarding the sword (*khaḍga*): it means "to restrain" (*jian*). It is for the purpose of preventing and restraining what is extraordinary or calamitous. Because it manifests a lack of reverence for the Dharma, its use is prohibited. Regarding those who remove illness:
if a sick person feels fear, they may use a sword to protect their body and ward off evil; therefore, its use is permitted. The meaning of the following three prohibitions is likewise the same.
98. The precept on teaching the Dharma to those carrying spears:
One who carries a spear should not be taught the Dharma, except in the case of illness. This is how one should train. 99.
The precept on teaching the Dharma to those carrying swords: [One who carries a sword should not be taught the Dharma. This is how one should train.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a knife, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule to be observed.
○ One hundred: The precept against preaching the Dharma to a person holding a parasol.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule to be observed.

**Explanation of Terms:** The *Saṃghīti* states: "Canopies" refers to canopies made of tree bark, canopies made of *tāla* leaves, canopies made of *tāli* leaves, bamboo umbrellas, folded umbrellas, and peacock-feather umbrellas—any such various items capable of shielding against rain and sun.

All are called "parasols" (chattra). This excludes those who are ill (such as those with sores on their heads from prolonged exposure to the sun, or those whose bodies suffer from disease and dread rain or heat, for whom a parasol is strictly necessary).
The inquiry on the three fetters:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the rules of training for the community. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard? (Three times.)
The fourth is the exhortation to maintain [purity]: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus shall this matter be maintained.

Compiled by the Dharma-teacher and Vinaya-student Śramaṇa Deqi of Baohua Mountain, Jinling. Section Eighty-seven:
The Methods for Extinction of Disputes (*Adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). Divided into four parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration of the precepts; third, the conclusion.
Question: Regarding the four exhortations to uphold [the Dharma], this is the first:
"Venerable sirs, these seven principles for settling disputes are recited every half-month from within the Sūtra of Precepts. If a bhikṣu..."
