When a dispute arises, it should be immediately resolved.

Commentary: There are four kinds of disputes: first, disputes concerning speech; second, disputes concerning investigations; third, disputes concerning offenses; and fourth, disputes concerning legal matters.
"Contention over speech" (*vāda-vivāda*) refers to debating the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) regarding what is right or wrong, correct or erroneous;

that is, citing eighteen matters—from "Dharma" and "non-Dharma" up to "what has been taught" and "what has not been taught"—where each person clings to their own view and thereby gives rise to contention. Because the contention arises from speech, it is called "contention over speech.
"Contention over seeking" (*anveṣaṇa-vivāda*) refers to when a bhikṣu commits a transgression and it must be rectified; there are three roots and five [factors] established for this.

As for the *adhikaraṇa* of accusation (*ucchedana-adhikaraṇa*): when one who has violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the deportment is brought before the Saṃgha, they are investigated for their prior offenses so that these may be eliminated.
Because a dispute arises from this investigation into prior offenses, it is called a "dispute of investigation" (*mṛga-adhikaraṇa*). As for the "dispute of transgression" (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*):
it refers to the seven classes of offenses (*saptāpatti-nikāya*) which, having been committed and remaining in the heart as faults, ought to be purified through confession. These are the offenses.

The characteristics [of these disputes] are difficult to distinguish, and their arguments are each diverse and confused, leading to the arising of contention. Because contention arises from transgressions, it is called a "transgression-dispute" (*āpatti-araṇa*).
As for a "matter-dispute" (*kicca-araṇa*), it is a dispute that arises from the matters within the aforementioned three types of disputes; thus it is named a matter-dispute.

Among these, a verbal dispute (*vāda-araṇa*) is settled by two *vinayas*: namely, by the presence of the assembly (*sammukha-vinaya*) and the majority decision (*yadbhūya-sammuti*), or it may be settled by only one *vinaya*.
That is to say, a dispute regarding litigation (*adhikaraṇa*) is settled by four *vinayas* through the presence of the parties:

namely, presence (*sammukha*), recollection (*smṛti*), non-delusion (*amūḍha*), and presence at the site of the offense (*tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*). A dispute regarding transgression (*āpatti*) is settled by three *vinayas* through the presence of the parties:

namely, presence (*sammukha*), confession (*pratijñākāraka*), or presence with the "covering over as with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*). A dispute regarding legal matters (*kṛtya*) is settled by all *vinayas*, according to the specific nature of the offense committed.
The Vinaya states: there is the violation of the *vinaya* and there is the dispute regarding the *vinaya*.

This means that the maladies to be extinguished are the four types of disputes (*caturvivāda*), while the methods capable of extinguishing them are the seven *vinayas*, namely the seven *vinayas* beginning with "presence before the assembly" (*sammukhavinaya*). These are capable of extinguishing the four disputes.
Therefore, it is said that there are seven methods for extinguishing disputes. The Vinaya states: "A bhikṣu who possesses ten qualities should be appointed to adjudicate matters impartially:
(1) being fully endowed with the observance of the precepts; (2) being learned; (3) having mastered the recitation of both divisions of the Vinaya with great proficiency;
(4) extensively understanding their meaning; (5) being skillful in speech, with clear eloquence and the capacity to engage in questioning and answering so as to cause [the opponent]..."
Joyful. Sixth, being able to extinguish the arising of the six grounds for dispute. Seventh, absence of attachment; eighth, absence of malice; ninth, absence of fear;
tenth, absence of delusion. The fourth section states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "By twenty-two kinds of conduct, one may know a person who adjudicates cases impartially.
They must fully uphold the two hundred and fifty precepts (1); they must be widely learned and well-versed in the Abhidharma."
13. A nun (2–3). She does not dispute with others (4). Nor does she persistently adhere to this matter (5). She should abide only after having censured those who deserve censure (6).
She should abide only after having instructed those who deserve instruction (7). She should abide only after having expelled those who deserve expulsion (8).
She is without attachment (9). Without hatred (10). Without fear (11). Without delusion (12). She does not accept the drinking [of water] from this faction.
(13) Not eating with them; (14) nor accepting food or drink from their faction; (15) nor accepting from this faction robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases;
(16) nor accepting from that faction robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases;
(17) not providing service to this faction; (18) nor providing service to that faction; (19) not entering a village together with this faction; nor [entering] together with that faction.
20. Entering a village in a group. 21. Not making a prior appointment or agreement [to meet]. 22. Nor arriving there later or sitting down later [than others]. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
A bhikṣu who accomplishes five qualities is able to extinguish disputes: he knows what is factual and what is not factual;
he knows what is beneficial and what is not beneficial; he finds companions and does not fail to find them; and he attains impartiality.
It is not that one does not obtain an equal companion; it is not that one obtains them at a time when they cannot be obtained.
There are two types of *thalatha*: first, guarding one's own mind. Upon seeing the right or wrong of others, one thinks: "The agent knows their own karmic actions. It is like a fire breaking out;
one merely saves oneself—how can one concern oneself with the affairs of others? Second, waiting for the proper time. This refers to seeing others engaged in disputes.
They say to one another, "We shall form this thought: 'This dispute and contention shall be adjudicated when the time comes. This is called the *dvitaraṭha*.
He partakes of the Dharma-food and flavor-food together with this assembly, and he also partakes of the Dharma-food and flavor-food together with that assembly.
Whether requested to adjudicate the matter or not requested, he adjudicates the matter. (It is also rendered as *talaṭha*. The Sarvāstivādins say: *tala* means "earth" and *ṭha* means...)
Abiding. With mastery over superior wisdom, one remains unshakable in the True Dharma, like a person standing on solid ground who cannot be toppled.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: When the bhikṣu Dharmadatta takes up a dispute, he should examine it through five matters: among these, who first arrived; who maintains pure precepts;
who is learned, wise, and well-versed in the Āgamas; who treats the teacher according to the Dharma; who has faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; and who does not disparage the Buddha.

Regarding the precepts: there are ten qualities by which the Saṃgha should appoint a monk as a mediator (according to the Sarvāstivāda, *u-vai* means "two," and *ku-la* means "equanimity" or "non-duality";

it refers to one who balances like a scale). He must know the places where disputes arise and their origins; he must be skilled in knowing disputes, capable of analyzing disputes, and understand the causes and conditions that give rise to disputes.
He must understand the meaning of disputes, be skilled in extinguishing disputes, and once a dispute has been extinguished, ensure it does not arise again.
Pure in the observance of the precepts, learned, and possessed of great wisdom—these are the twenty-two qualities of the bhikṣu Tāḷiṭa.
One should know that he is of sharp faculties and highly learned: first, he well understands the root from which phenomena arise; second, he skillfully distinguishes the characteristics of phenomena;
third, he well understands the distinctions between phenomena; fourth, he well understands the beginning and end of phenomena; fifth, he well understands the lightness of phenomena...

1. Gravity; 2. Skillfully knowing the matter of eradication; 3. Skillfully knowing that the matter of eradication will not arise again; 4. Skillfully knowing those who perform deeds and those who possess deeds;
5. Possessing the power of authoritative instruction; 6. Being able to cause others to receive [the teaching]; 7.
Possessing the power of skillful means and gentle speech; 8. Also being able to cause others to receive [the teaching]; 9. Possessing the power of self-subjugation.

Fourteen, they can also cause others to receive [the teachings]. Fifteen, they possess a sense of shame and remorse. Sixteen, their minds are free from arrogance. Seventeen, they have no arrogant speech.
Eighteen, their body, speech, and mind are without partial attachment. Nineteen, they do not follow the course of craving.
Twenty: not following the course of anger. Twenty-one: not following the course of fear. Twenty-two:

not following the course of delusion (this refers to one who is able to extinguish disputes). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: there are six roots of dispute (the Vinaya says that these six disputes constitute the roots).

First: harboring resentment and remaining silent. Second: having an evil nature and desiring to harm others. Third: greed and envy. Fourth: flattery and crookedness. Fifth: lack of shame and lack of remorse. Sixth: wickedness.
Sensual desire and wrong view (these six matters can give rise to disputes; therefore, they are called the roots of dispute). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:

"If a matter of dispute arises, one should employ the seven methods in accordance with the Great Teacher’s instruction to eliminate it according to the Dharma and the Vinaya" (this means that when a matter of dispute arises, it should be eliminated immediately).

Second, the detailed enumeration of the characteristics of the precepts, divided into seven sections: first, *sammukhavinaya* (settlement by presence) through seventh, *tṛṇaprastāraka* (the method of covering with grass).
○ First, a general explanation of the settlement of disputes through *sammukhavinaya*.
This is a shared precept; nuns are equally liable for its violation. In the Mahāyāna, monks study this together. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"One should give rise to a mind of compassion and skillfully harmonize those engaged in strife. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

"All these [precepts] were established because, when confronted by others with matters of inquiry, one cannot endure the affliction of being interrogated, censured, or disparaged. (The six precepts following this are all the same and will not be repeated)."
The setting for the origin of this discourse:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The person to whom the origin arose: [Name].
Kāḷudāyin and the group of six went to bathe in the river Aciravatī.
When Kāḷudāyin had finished bathing and stepped onto the bank, he put on the robes of the group of six, thinking they were his own; without checking, he departed.
After the group of six had finished their bath and stepped onto the bank, they did not see their own robes, but saw instead those of Kāḷudāyin. They immediately said, "Kāḷu..."
"Kālodāyin has stolen my robe. While the person was not present before me, you performed the *pravāsanīyakarman* (act of banishment).
Having heard this, Kālodāyin became doubtful and went at once to inform the Buddha. The Buddha asked him, 'With what intention did you take it? He replied:"
"This is my robe," he said, without any intention of theft. The Buddha declared that there was no offense. One should not wear a robe without first inspecting it.
One should not perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*), such as the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) and so forth, in the absence of the person concerned.
If one performs such an act in their absence, it is invalid, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. From this day forward, for the sake of all bhikṣus, I shall establish the *sammukhavinaya*.
The Bhikṣuṇīs settle disputes.
Regarding the characteristics of the precepts established:
those for which the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) is appropriate should be settled by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya*.
Explanation of the Terms: "Presence" refers to the presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, and the Saṃgha, as well as the boundary (*sīmā*).

What is the presence of the Dharma? It is that which is upheld by the Dharma to settle disputes; "upheld" means to receive and maintain (referring to the maintenance of the Sūtra-piṭaka). What is the presence of the Vinaya?

It is that which is upheld by the Vinaya to settle disputes (referring to the reception and maintenance of the Vinaya-piṭaka). What is the presence of the person? It is the exchange of words and meanings [between individuals].
This refers to the case where both parties involved in the dispute are present. What is meant by "the Saṃgha being present"?

It means that they have gathered together in one place for a formal act (*karmavācanā*), those who did not attend have granted their consent through proxy, and those present do not raise objections when they have the right to do so; such a harmonious assembly is called the Saṃgha.

To settle a dispute, the presence of the Saṃgha is required to perform the legal procedure; hence it is said, "the Saṃgha is present. What is meant by "the boundary being present"? It means that the formal act is performed within the defined boundary (*sīmā*) according to established restrictions.

This refers to the boundary established by marking it out and proclaiming its characteristics (i.e., the *sīmā*). Whenever one intends to perform a formal act (*dharmakarma*), the entire assembly of monks must gather within these limits to avoid the fault of a schism (*nānāsaṃgha*).

Since the settlement of disputes now requires that the assembly be present within the boundary to perform the ritual, it is called "the presence of the boundary" (*sīmapratyakṣa*). Disputes concerning speech (*vādavivāda*) are settled by two types of *vinaya*:

namely, by the presence of the assembly and by the majority decision (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*), or by a single type of *vinaya*, namely, the presence of the assembly alone. For example, if a single bhikṣu stands before another bhikṣu and speaks well...
Regarding verbal instruction: if it is in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, you should accept and approve it.
If a dispute is thus settled, this is called a "verbal dispute," which is resolved by a single means: the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties).
It is not necessary for many people to speak together. If one bhikṣu acts for two bhikṣus, or three bhikṣus act for a saṃgha, it is likewise.
Even up to the case where a saṃgha acts for one bhikṣu, or two or three bhikṣus act for a saṃgha, it is likewise.

(In this context, the meaning of "presence" [sammukha] is as follows: if the offense can be settled [by these means], it requires four or more persons. Regarding the five factors—dharma, vinaya, person, saṃgha, and boundary—if there is no presence [of any of these], it is not called the *sammukhavinaya*.)

If it can be settled, it may be by only two or three bhikṣus; even if only one bhikṣu is present, provided that the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the person are all present before him—though the Saṃgha and the boundary (*sīmā*) are not present—it is still called *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vibhaṅga* states: "There are two kinds of illegality regarding the settlement of disputes through *saṃmukha-vinaya*.
If it is illegal, one should command the illegal party to submit and grant them *saṃmukha-vinaya*. If it is illegal, one should command the legal party to..."
Regarding *tāḍana* (subduing) and the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence), there are two types that are in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmika*).

If it is in accordance with the Dharma, one instructs those who are in accordance with the Dharma to perform the subduing and grant the *sammukhavinaya*. If it is in accordance with the Dharma, one instructs those who are not in accordance with the Dharma (*adharmika*) to perform the subduing and grant the *sammukhavinaya*.
**Determination of the Offense:** If a matter of dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, yet it is subsequently reopened, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
(If one grants what should not be granted, or does not grant what should be granted, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.)
The *Mahāvinayavastu* (Mo de lü jia) states that there are ten types of *karmans* performed without the parties being present (*asammukha-karman*):

1. The bowl-covering (*pātra-ovadana*). 2. The removal of the bowl-covering (*pātra-ovadana-pratyuddhāra*). [This refers to when a layperson reviles or slanders a bhikṣu, and the Saṃgha performs the *pātra-ovadana-karman* against them, such that they may no longer interact with or receive food from the monks.

If the person recognizes their own fault and seeks to have it removed, the Saṃgha shall perform the *asammukha-karman* of release; this is done to punish the layperson by acting at a distance so as not to allow them to appear before the assembly. 3. The family under training (*śaikṣa-kula*). 4. The removal of the status of the family under training (*śaikṣa-kula-pratyuddhāra*).

(The third *pratideśanīya* dharma, as explained in the middle section). 5. Building a hut (*kuṭikā-karaṇa*): This refers to when a monk repairs an old hut for a layperson; the Saṃgha should grant permission through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and this is also performed without the person being present.

6. Śrāmaṇeras: This refers to the expulsion of a wicked or heterodox śrāmaṇera, placing him in a location where he can be seen but not heard; this is also performed without his presence. 7. Insanity (*unmatta*): Performing the *unmatta-karman*;

because the individual has lost their original mind and lacks discernment, it is unnecessary for them to be present. 8. Not prostrating; 9. Not conversing; 10. Not receiving offerings (*apratyuddhāra*). (These three...)

Regarding *karmavācanā*: it is said that when a bhikṣu has offended or harassed a bhikṣuṇī, the *bhikṣuṇīs* are permitted to perform these three kinds of *karmavācanā* for that bhikṣu; furthermore, it is permitted to perform them at a distance. One must not inflict disciplinary punishment upon a bhikṣu while he is present before the assembly.

Within the Vinaya, there are four cases where the person is not present: shaving the hair, ordination, living together with non-Buddhists, and bestowing the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts. Shaving the hair is the first step in entering the Saṃgha; when one intends to perform the single-announcement (*jñapti*), one shaves the person's hair and has them stand in a place where they are within sight but beyond hearing. The same applies to the single-announcement for ordination.

Regarding the four-month period of living together with non-Buddhists, one likewise sends them to a place where they are within sight but beyond hearing to grant it. Regarding the bestowing of the *śikṣamāṇā*...

The *śīla* (precepts) should likewise be received by sending [the candidate] to a place where they can be seen but not heard; therefore, this procedure is performed within the community of nuns. Combined with the preceding discussion, there are fourteen types of non-presence (*anabhimukha*). All other *karmas* must necessarily be performed in the presence [of the assembly].
The *Abhimukha-vinaya* (Resolution through Presence) is concluded (this extinguishes disputes regarding speech).
The second: the origin of the legal procedure for settling disputes through recollection (*sativinaya*).
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
Regarding the case of the person who initiated the matter: Upavāṇa did not commit a grave offense such as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, the bhikṣus all claimed he had committed a grave offense. They then asked him, "Do you recall committing a grave offense? and he replied that he did not.

He had committed a grave offense. He replied, "I do not recall committing such a grave offense. Although the bhikṣus continued to question him without ceasing, he thought to himself, "What should I do?

He informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I authorize the performance of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the purpose of restoring mindfulness to Dharmapāla."
Regarding the characteristics of the established precepts:
one who should be granted the *smṛti-vinaya* (rehabilitation through mindfulness) must be granted the *smṛti-vinaya*.
Explanation of the meaning: As for the *smṛti-vinaya*, that monk’s offense shall not be further raised; it shall not be [reproached].

One who practices *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline of recollection) refers to those monks who repeatedly interrogate another regarding their offense, yet that person does not recall having committed it; despite persistent questioning, they do not remember.

The Buddha therefore ordered the Saṃgha to apply *smṛti-vinaya* so that the individual may recall the offense, and to ensure that other monks shall no longer cause them to be reminded of it. Hence, it is called *smṛti-vinaya*. This constitutes a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) which is settled by two forms of discipline:

namely, *saṃmukha-smṛti* (recollection in the presence of the assembly), or *saṃmukha-amūḍha* (non-delusion in the presence of the assembly), or *saṃmukha-sthāna* (the place of the offense in the presence of the assembly). — *Sarvāstivāda* [Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra].

It is said: "This is the *śīlaviniścaya* (guarding discipline). All five groups [of practitioners] are given the *smṛtivinaya* (discipline of recollection); all five categories of offenses are given the *smṛtivinaya*.

It must be granted through a formal procedure of fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs must be present; the other three groups need not be present. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are three illegal ways of granting the *smṛtivinaya*... [The text continues with: "...there is [the case where] there is a comparison..."
The Venerable Kṣudraka committed an offense that does not entail expulsion, yet he claimed to have committed an offense that does entail expulsion.
This bhikṣu requested the *saṃmukhavinaya* (face-to-face settlement) from the Saṃgha; if the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on memory), this is called an illegal act. Why?

Because this person should instead be granted the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation). Furthermore, it is like the case of the bhikṣu Śreṇika, who, due to a state of madness, committed many impure acts.
This is an illegal purification of the dharma. One regains one's original mind, yet the offenses previously committed remain;

if the Saṃgha constantly discusses this matter [without resolving it], and that person asks the Saṃgha for the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness), and the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called illegal.

Why is this? Because such a person should be granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not deluded). Furthermore, it is like the case of the bhikṣu Hata, who was shameless and lacked a sense of remorse, having broken the precepts.
When there were charges against him based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, he himself declared: "I have committed these offenses."
If, after [the accused] says, "I have no such offense," the Saṃgha grants them the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called illegal. Why?
Because they should instead be granted the *tattvānusaraṇavinaya*. This is called the third instance of illegally granting the *smṛtivinaya*.
There are three ways in which it is according to the Dharma to grant the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection).

For example, when the bhikṣu Dharmadatta was falsely accused of a groundless *pārājika* offense by the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaśasī, and the Saṃgha constantly discussed this matter, that bhikṣu requested the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called being according to the Dharma. Why?
Therefore, this person should be granted the *smṛti-vinaya*. Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu commits an offense and confesses it, repenting according to the Dharma.
If the Saṃgha continues to discuss that matter, the bhikṣu requests the *smṛti-vinaya* from the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛti-vinaya*, this is called acting in accordance with the Dharma. Why? Because it ought to be granted.
Regarding the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection): Suppose a bhikṣu has not yet committed an offense, but it is certain that he will commit one.

Because of this matter, if the Saṃgha declares him guilty of an offense and that bhikṣu requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya* to that person, this is called being in accordance with the Dharma. Why? Because this person is worthy of receiving it.

Because of the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), this is called the threefold legal granting of the *smṛtivinaya*. [In the case of a dispute arising from a search, it is settled by two *vinayas*: the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and the *smṛtivinaya*.
It does not employ the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane) nor the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement according to the nature of the offense).]

**Conviction:** According to the Sarvāstivāda, regarding the practice of the *smṛtivinaya* (disciplinary procedure based on memory), other bhikṣus should not point out his transgressions, should not cause him to be reminded [of them], should not request a hearing, nor should they accept a request for a hearing from another bhikṣu.
If he requests a hearing from them, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if he accepts a request for a hearing from another, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If he does not listen, or if he brings up a transgression, or if one causes him to remember [the offense], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

(This refers to seeking out the grounds for a dispute by raising the faults and transgressions of another person, requiring that they be made to remember them. Once they have been made to remember, one must not cause them to remember them again. If one grants what should not be granted, or withholds what should be granted, the legal procedure is violated and the application of the Dharma is improper.)
One incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. (This is the settlement of a dispute through investigation.
○ Third: The origin of the legal procedure for settling a dispute through the "not-deranged" (*amūḷhavinaya*) rule.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a monk named Nandi who, due to a deranged and distracted mind, committed many offenses that were contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa. He said:
There was no limit to it; his coming and going, entering and exiting, did not accord with the rules of decorum. Later, he regained his original mind.
The bhikṣus asked him, "Nandiya, do you remember committing a grave offense? He replied, "Previously, when I was insane and my mind was deranged..."
"He has committed many offenses, yet it was not done intentionally; it was merely due to his insanity. Elders, there is no need to repeatedly confront and interrogate him.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to interrogate him without ceasing. That bhikṣu thought to himself, "What should I do? and informed the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "I authorize the Saṃgha to grant Nanda the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one who is no longer insane) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations)."
Polishing. Regarding the method for settling disputes through the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-delusion):
the established characteristics of the precept should be applied with the *amūḷhavinaya*; it must be applied with the *amūḷhavinaya*.
**Exegesis:** Regarding the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane):

it means that a monk should no longer be accused of this offense, nor should he be subjected to the formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (reproval for negligence). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha asked, "What is called the *amūḍha-vinaya*?

It refers to a case where a monk was formerly insane but is now no longer insane, yet his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) speak of his former acts of insanity. At that time, [the procedure] should be carried out swiftly.

The Saṃgha is quickly convened. Once the Saṃgha has been convened, according to the Sūtra and according to the Vinaya, the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is not insane) is granted to this bhikṣu in accordance with the facts of the case.
By means of the *amūḍha-vinaya*, the matter of the slander is settled. The Sarvāstivādins say: [as follows].

This is the *saṃvara-vinaya*. The five groups of practitioners are all granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for those who were not insane), whether it be *sammukhavinaya* (in the presence of the accused) or *asammukhavinaya* (not in their presence), as previously explained. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are four kinds of illegal granting of the *amūḍha-vinaya*:
there is a bhikṣu who is not insane but manifests the appearance of being insane. When the community of bhikṣus asks him among the assembly: 'When you were insane and deluded...'"
"Did you do something? Do you remember it now? He replied, "Venerable sir, I remember doing it out of delusion.
(1) Another person instructed me to do it; (2) I remember doing it in a dream; (3) I remember running here and there naked; (4) I remember standing while defecating or urinating.
This person requests the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not deluded) from the Saṃgha. If the Saṃgha grants this person the *amūḍha-vinaya*...
The Vinaya: these are called the four unlawful matters. As for the four lawful matters:

there is a bhikṣu who is actually insane and deluded, whose mind is inverted, and who manifests the appearance of insanity and delusion. When the other bhikṣus ask him, "Do you remember what you did while insane and deluded?
he replies, "I do not remember; others did not instruct me to do it" (1). "I do not remember doing it in a dream" (2).
"I do not recall running here and there naked (3). I do not recall standing while defecating or urinating (4). This person requests the *amūḍhavinaya* from the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha grants the *amūḍhavinaya*, this is called the four legal [procedures] (the rules of conduct are the same as before).
The Vinaya states: "If a dispute such as this is thus settled, it is a case of *vitaṇḍā-vivāda* (contentious dispute). It is settled by two methods of settlement:

*sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane). The *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) and *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement according to the nature of the offense) are not used. Ānanda asked again:

Is there a case of seeking a dispute (*paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*) that is settled by two forms of cessation—namely, *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *yadbhūyaḥ-sthiti* (determination according to the facts)—rather than by *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement through recollection) or *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one who was not insane)? The Buddha said: "There is.

For example, if a bhikṣu is fond of debate and, when debating with an outsider, encounters all manner of challenges and subsequently contradicts his own previous statements, and this is questioned within the community of monks..."
At that time, his speech was also contradictory from beginning to end; he had intentionally uttered a falsehood in the midst of the assembly.

The Saṃgha should grant this bhikṣu the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for the place of offense. If the dispute is thus extinguished, it is called a *vitanda-adhikaraṇa* (dispute concerning investigation). It is extinguished by two methods:

*saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *yadbhūya-vinaya* (settlement according to the facts of the offense). It does not employ *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection) or *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one who is no longer insane). What is [the case] here?

Regarding the locus of the offense: if that bhikṣu, while this offense is being addressed by one who performs the formal act of censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) or the formal act of reminding (*sāraṇīyakamma*), applies a legal procedure (*dhamma*) improperly, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The section on the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict for one not insane) is concluded; this settlement (*samatha*) is also [included in] the inquiry into disputes (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).
The fourth section: The origin of the legal procedure for settling disputes through self-acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*).
When the Buddha was staying at the Gaṅgā River in the city of Campā, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the *poṣadha* ceremony, the World-Honored One...
When the assembly was complete, they surrounded him on all sides. Sitting before the multitude in the open air, Ānanda, after the first watch of the night had passed, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The first watch has passed; may the World-Honored One recite the precepts. The World-Honored One remained silent. Ānanda then returned to his seat.
It was the same during the middle watch. When the final watch had passed and the light of dawn appeared, the community of monks remained seated.
"It has been a long time. We only wish that you would recite the precepts. The Buddha told Ānanda, "The assembly of monks is not pure.
It is impossible for the Tathāgata to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts within an impure assembly."
The one who causes [the monk] to rise:
The Elder Maudgalyāyana, having observed the assembly with his purified divine eye, saw that monk sitting not far from the Buddha.
He went to him and said, "You should rise now; the World-Honored One knows you and sees you. Depart!"
"Expel him! He should not remain here. Maudgalyāyana took that bhikṣu by the arm, led him outside the gate, and returned to inform the Buddha, saying, "The assembly is now pure;
may the World-Honored One recite the precepts. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "It should not be done in this manner."
If at another time, it should likewise not be done in this manner. Maudgalyāyana, one must cause the person to confess their offense first, and only then impose the penalty;

one should not impose a penalty without having them confess the offense themselves. From this day forward, for the sake of all bhikṣus, I shall establish the legal procedure for settling disputes through self-accusation (*pātimokkha-thapanā*).
Regarding the characteristics of the offense established: one should be subjected to *pāṭidesanīya* (confession); one shall be subjected to *pāṭidesanīya*.
Explanation of the meaning: What is "self-accusation"? It refers to one who confesses the name of the offense and the category of the offense. What is...?
To settle this: reproach your own mind and give rise to weary detachment (*saṃvega*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"The bhikṣuṇī Maitrābhūmi slandered the bhikṣu Dabba with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, saying, 'Dabba has defiled me. She was immediately subject to *pratyāśravaṇa-niḥsaraṇa* (expulsion by her own confession).

The Vinaya says: "Disputes involving offenses are settled through three types of *vinaya*: namely, *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *pratyāśravaṇa-vinaya* (settlement by confession)."

Regarding the method of treatment, it is like covering the ground with grass. If a bhikṣu has committed an offense and wishes to repent before another bhikṣu, he should go to a pure bhikṣu, bare his right shoulder, and—whether he is a senior or junior—prostrate at his feet, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and state the name and category of the offense.

(As for "name," this refers to the distinctions among the various sections [of the Prātimokṣa]; as for "category," this refers to the differing characteristics of the precepts, which are applied according to the individual's capacity.)

The *karmavācanā* states: (This differs from the thirty matters concerning the keeping of extra robes and being separated from one’s robes). He speaks as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess it before the Venerable One; I shall not dare to conceal it. Through confession there is peace and happiness;
without confession there is no peace and happiness. Recalling my transgression, I disclose it; knowing it, I shall not dare to conceal it. Long...
The Elder remembers me: that I was fully endowed with the body of pure precepts and maintained the purity of the *poṣadha*. This is stated for a second and third time. He should be told:

"Reproach yourself and let a sense of weary detachment arise in your mind. If he replies, "So be it," and the dispute is thus settled, this is a case of a dispute that has been settled by two methods of settlement:
*saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by confession). It is not [settled] otherwise.
[The ground] is covered with grass. If two or three people repent within the Saṃgha, it is also like this.

According to the Sarvāstivāda, the method of settling disputes through self-accusation (*pratijñākāraka*) extinguishes all matters involving the five groups of persons, as well as all matters concerning whether there has been an offense or no offense regarding the five categories of precepts (*pañcāpattinikāya*).
There are ten kinds of illegal [settlements]; if one commits a *pārājika* offense...
Saṃghāvaśeṣa, Pāyattika, Pratideśanīya, and Duṣkṛta—claiming not to have committed them; or, having committed the five categories of offenses, claiming not to have committed them;
or, not having committed the five categories of offenses, claiming to have committed them—these are called the ten illegal [cases]. As for the ten legal [cases]:

when a bhikṣu has committed the five categories of offenses, he says, "I have committed them"; or, when he has not committed the five categories of offenses, he says, "I have not committed them"—these are called the ten [legal cases].
[If one acts] contrary to the Dharma (this extinguishes disputes arising from offenses; transgressing this incurs guilt as described above).
○ Fifth: The Origin of the Method for Extinguishing Disputes by Seeking Out the Offense.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
There was a monk named Hastibala who delighted in debate; he would engage in discussions with non-Buddhists, and when faced with critical questions, [he would falter] from beginning to end.

There was a contradiction in his speech. When questioned within the Saṃgha, it was likewise so; his words were contradictory from beginning to end, and he intentionally uttered falsehoods in the midst of the assembly.
The non-Buddhists criticized and disparaged him. When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. After the Buddha had rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) against that bhikṣu for the offense of a place of punishment."

It shall be granted in this manner. The Saṃgha is to be convened; once the Saṃgha has been convened, the formal act of *ukkhepanīya* (suspension) is to be performed against him; once the *ukkhepanīya* has been performed, the formal act of *sativinaya* (reinstatement through recollection) is to be performed;
once the *sativinaya* has been performed, the penalty is to be granted. One capable of performing the *kamma* (formal act) should be appointed for this.
From this day forward, I establish for the bhikṣus the legal procedure for settling disputes by means of a verdict on the facts (*tassapāpiyasika*).

The characteristics of the offense established should be accorded with the characteristics for seeking out the offense (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* calls it "seeking the nature of the offense"; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls it "truly seeking the offense"; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* calls it "treatment by original statement").

**Exegesis:** What is the locus of offense? It refers to that monk who, regarding this offense, is subject to the formal act of *ukkhepanīya* (suspension) and the formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (restoration through recollection).
The *Lakṣaṇā-vibhaṅga-śāstra* states: "One who truly seeks out an offense" is one who, having previously committed an offense, confessed it, but later concealed it.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "This is the *tarjanīya-vinaya* (reprimand). This applies to all five categories of offenses (*pañca-pārājikādi*).

The *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya* (the discipline of seeking according to reality). This *vinaya* is granted to all five classes of monastics. There are five kinds of what is not in accordance with the Dharma (*adharma*).
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he first says he did not commit it, but later says he did.

If the Saṃgha grants this person the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya*, this is called "not in accordance with the Dharma. Why? Because this person ought to be granted the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment). Suppose there is a bhikṣu...

If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, yet first says he has not committed it and later says he has, and the Saṃgha grants this person a *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* (a formal inquiry for what actually occurred), this is called illegal. Why?
Because this person should be disciplined according to the offense he actually committed. There are five kinds of legal [procedures]. If a bhikṣu commits a *pārājika*...

O Āyuṣmān. First one says there is an offense, and later one says there is no offense. If the Saṃgha grants this person the *yathābhūta-veṣaṇā-vinaya* (the discipline of searching for the truth), it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why? Because this person should be granted the *yathābhūta-veṣaṇā*.

If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense down to a *duṣkṛta* (*dukkaṭa*) offense, and first says there is an offense and later says there is no offense—if the Saṃgha grants this person the *yathābhūta-veṣaṇā-vinaya*...
Nuns, this is called acting in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this? Because such a person should be granted the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (the discipline of searching for the truth).
Regarding the practice of the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya*: that bhikṣu should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others;
he may not receive dependence (*niśraya*) from others; he should not keep new or old śrāmaṇeras; he may not teach the Dharma to bhikṣuṇīs. If the Saṃgha...

One should not accept the *karmavācanā* (formal act) for the instruction of bhikṣuṇīs. One should not again commit a crime for which the Saṃgha has already granted a *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* (decision based on what was actually found).
If it is a similar offense, or if it is a more serious offense than that, one should likewise not commit it.
One should not criticize the *saṃghakarma*, nor should one criticize the person who performed the *karmavācanā*. One should not request permission from others. One should not...

One should not obstruct the *poṣadha*; one should not obstruct the conferral of ordination; one should not obstruct the *pravāraṇā*. One should not proclaim the faultlessness of a bhikṣu’s transgressions.
One should not engage in communal affairs [with him]. One should discipline one's own mind and conduct, remaining in accordance with the will of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
If one does not practice in this manner, one shall not be released from this *karma* for as long as one lives. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"This person must perform eight matters for the rest of their life: they must not ordain others; they must not grant others full ordination (*upasampadā*);
they must not provide others with formal dependence (*niśraya*); they must not accept the massage or services provided by monks; and they must not act as a monk."
He shall not receive appointments in succession, nor may he act as a Dharma-preacher or a Vinaya-preacher for the Saṃgha.
For the rest of his life, he should not be granted the *śikṣādattaka* (probation). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of original offenses:

first, those that can be expiated; second, those that cannot be expiated. If one has committed a grave offense and continues to conceal it, he should undergo the *yāvajjīvam apratikarmārhata* (the lifelong penance)."

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for confession (this also extinguishes disputes arising from contention; it is extinguished by two methods of settlement, namely: presence before the assembly and the investigation of the nature of the offense. The transgression incurred due to discord is as previously described).
The sixth: the origin of the legal procedure for settling disputes by means of a majority vote.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Regarding the "arising through persons":
at that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī were disputing. The Saṃgha settled the dispute in accordance with the Dharma.

Those bhikṣus who had been disputing could not accept the Saṃgha’s resolution of the dispute. After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "One should seek out many people."
Seeking out the offense; using the words of many who know the Dharma; for the sake of the bhikṣus, establishing the method for settling disputes through the decision of the majority;
the characteristics of the formulated precept.
One should apply the *yadbhūyasikīya* (decision by the majority); one must apply the *yadbhūyasikīya*. Explanation of the meaning:

One should employ the words of many who know the Dharma; one listens as the counting sticks (*śalākā*) are distributed. A formal act of double announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is performed to appoint a person to distribute the *śalākās*.

(If a dispute arises among the bhikṣus and cannot be settled, one should seek out many bhikṣus who know the Dharma to settle it by distributing counting sticks. The majority is indicated by the abundance of the sticks. What is "the words of the majority"?)*

Those who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātikā are called Sarvāstivādins. Regarding "seeking much" (bahv-arthika-vinaya): it is so called because one seeks many causes and conditions for a decision, seeks a decision from many sources, and reaches a decision based on what is found in many places.

There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*): being possessed of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion; and not knowing whether the distribution has already been carried out or not.
One should be appointed if they possess the opposite of these five qualities. There are three ways of distributing the counting sticks: first, openly; second, [secretly]; third, [by whispering].

Concealment. Three ways of whispering. What is meant by "openly"? Even if among the assembly there are many bhikṣus who speak contrary to the Dharma, if those two teachers, or the elders, or wise persons all speak according to the Dharma, one should proceed openly by distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*).
Two kinds of sticks should be made: one broken, the other whole. One should announce: "Those who speak such words shall take the unbroken stick; those who speak such [other] words..."
Those who speak thus shall take and break their voting sticks (*śalākā*). Once the voting sticks have been distributed, they should be counted in a separate place.

If those who speak according to the Dharma are in the majority, a formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made; by doing so, the matter of dispute is settled. If those who speak according to the Dharma are in the minority, they should pay their respects and depart.
They should then send a messenger to the dwelling place of the monks, where he makes this report within the Saṃgha: "That dwelling place is contrary to the Dharma."
There are many bhikṣus. Excellent, Elder, you should go there. If the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma are numerous, the dispute will be settled and the merit will be great;
hearing this, that bhikṣu should go. If he does not go, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

What is the procedure for the distribution of voting tickets (*śalākā*) by concealment? Even if those who act according to the Dharma are numerous among the assembly, if those two teachers and the *sthavira* [know...]

The assembly is not acting according to the Dharma. Fearing that the voting sticks (*śalākā*) might be cast openly, the bhikṣus should follow the lead of the senior monk (*sthavira*) among the assembly and cast the voting sticks in secret.

(According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, "casting the voting sticks in secret" means that because the person casting the sticks perceives the assembly as consisting of those who act contrary to the Dharma, they expect that many will take the illegal sticks;

if it were done in public, those who assist the illegal faction would feel ashamed to take an illegal stick. How is the voting stick cast by whispering? Even if the assembly is acting according to the Dharma...
There are many such cases. When those two teachers—the Elder and the Wise One—speak what is not Dharma, one should conduct a vote by whispering.
When conducting the vote, the seating should be spaced so that there is room for one person between each individual, with their bodies slightly obscuring the view. That bhikṣu shall then whisper.
[The proponent] says: "Your two teachers and close associates have already taken the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
Excellent! You too should take one out of compassion. If the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma are numerous, the dispute will be settled and much merit will be gained.
Having distributed them, they count them on one side. The Sarvāstivādins say: "The reason for distributing the voting sticks is that the matter is difficult to resolve."
If one were to say that "this is right" or "that is wrong," it would inevitably increase their malicious intent;
therefore, voting sticks (*śalākā*) are distributed before the assembly so that preferences for good or evil subside naturally and the principle remains impartial. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

Once the distribution of voting sticks is complete, if the number of illegal sticks exceeds [the legal ones] by even one, one should not proclaim that "the illegal persons are in the majority. Just as when legal persons are few, one should employ skillful means.
When the sitting is dissolved, if those who wish to come for the morning meal arrive, one should announce that it is time for the morning meal.
Likewise, at the time of the afternoon meal, the time for bathing, the time for preaching the Dharma, or the time for reciting the Vinaya, one should make the announcement as appropriate.

If someone perceives that the proceedings are contrary to the Dharma, they may say, "We are superior; for our sake, the sitting has been dissolved. We shall not rise now; we must resolve this matter right here on these seats."
At that time, if there is a small hut near the vihāra that is free of insects, one should have a *karmadāna* set fire to it and shout, "The fire is rising!
The fire is rising! Then, while everyone scatters to extinguish the fire, one should go and seek companions who act according to the Dharma.
The Vinaya states: When deciding a matter by means of voting sticks (*śalākā*), the entire Saṃgha must assemble; one may not accept *kṣānti* (consent/proxy). Why?
Because many bhikṣus might speak what is contrary to the Dharma; thus, no bhikṣu should accept *kṣānti*. This is like the procedure for distributing alms bowls (*pātra*).
If the matter cannot be decided [by the initial assembly], then even if there are three, two, or one person present in that monastery...

A bhikṣu who upholds the Tripiṭaka and is esteemed by the fourfold assembly should go to that place and speak to one of the bhikṣus there, recounting the matter in its entirety according to the sequence previously described. That venerable bhikṣu should speak as follows:
It is impossible for two people to speak to one another such that both are victorious; among them, one must necessarily be victorious and the other defeated.
Speech of this kind is called speaking in accordance with the Dharma. If it is not spoken in this way, it is called speaking contrary to the Dharma.
Regarding the determination of the offense: if these various signs refer to a bhikṣu, and after the matter has been settled according to the Dharma, he initiates it again, it is a pāyattika.
If he merely censures them, saying, "This legal proceeding was not according to the Dharma," he commits a duṣkṛta.

Regarding those who possess virtue, they are such that the multitude submits to them and there are none who do not heed their words. Even if there were someone who did not follow them, they would feel shame and be ridiculed by others;
thus, they must accept what is said. When people transmit matters, they generally speak of the facts and not of individuals.

Great Virtuous Bhikṣus likewise speak directly of the right and wrong of the matter at hand, rather than speaking of the person involved in the matter. Thus, both parties come to know the truth within themselves.
When one submits, then victory and defeat become manifest. To "re-raise a *pāyattika* offense" means to seal each individual transgression so that neither party may speak further thereafter;
thus the offense is established. (This *vinaya* rule also extinguishes disputes through speech.)
The seventh: the origin of the legal procedure for settling disputes by covering over with grass.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Origin of the Person:
At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī were disputing with one another. Many of these bhikṣus violated numerous precepts;
they both practiced and spoke things that were not the dharma of a śramaṇa. Their coming and going was without restraint. Later, the bhikṣus thought to themselves: "We have committed many offenses."
Regarding the various precepts, they both practice and preach what is not the way of a śramaṇa. Their coming and going is without restraint.

If we, among ourselves, were to inquire well into this matter, it might cause this dispute to become even deeper and more serious, persisting for months and years, so that the dispute could not be extinguished in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teachings, thereby preventing the Saṃgha from attaining peace.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "This matter of dispute should be settled by the method known as 'covering over with grass' (tṛṇaprastāraka).
For the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the legal procedure for settling disputes by covering over with grass."
Regarding the characteristics of the established precepts:
they should be like "covering the ground with grass," and they ought to be like "covering the ground with grass.
Explanation of the meaning: "Covering the ground with grass" refers to a case where there is a dispute among monks, and among those monks, many have committed offenses against the Saṃgha.
It is a transgression; it is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa. Our speech lacks restraint, and our coming and going, our movements and conduct do not accord with the rules of decorum.
We should reflect thus: "In this matter of dispute, we have committed many offenses; these are not the ways of a śramaṇa, and our speech lacks restraint."
"In their coming and going, they do not act in accordance with the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*).

If we were to investigate this matter among ourselves, we fear it would cause the offense to become grave and heavy, preventing the dispute from being settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, and causing the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort. Within that assembly, there is a wise and capable bhikṣu who..."
Rising from their seats, they bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, spoke these words:
"Venerable Elders, regarding this dispute of ours, we have committed many offenses that are contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa.

Our speech has been unrestrained, and our movements and conduct have not conformed to the rules of decorum. If we were to investigate this matter thoroughly, we fear it would cause our transgressions to become even more grave."

When a dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, yet it causes the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort, if the elders will forgive me, I now perform a *trṇaprastāra* (grass-mat) confession of this offense for the sake of the elders.
This should be said a second time among the assembly. Those bhikṣus should then make a formal announcement (*jñapti*).
The *tṛṇaprastāraka* (grass-covering) confession is announced as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha permits, this matter of dispute shall be confessed by the *tṛṇaprastāraka* method. Having thus announced it, one performs the *tṛṇaprastāraka* confession.
Then, from among that assembly, one who is wise and capable rises from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and...
Placing the right knee on the ground and joining the palms, he makes this declaration:

"Venerable Elders, regarding these matters of dispute and the offenses I have committed—excluding the *garukāpatti* (grave offenses) and the *pratisedha-gṛhapati-kula-karmavācanā* (the formal act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople)—[I declare them]. (Regarding the exclusion of grave offenses:

by means of this *tṛṇaprastāraka-dharma* [method of covering with grass], all light offenses such as *pāyattika* and *dukkaṭa* are entirely extinguished. However, if one has committed a *pārājika*, one must still undergo expulsion (*pravāsanīya*); if a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one must again perform the *parivāsa* and other such rites; and the same applies to *sthūlātyaya*."
This is removed by means of the *tṛṇaprastāra* (covering with grass) rite; it prevents one from going to the homes of laypeople, yet it does not result in full absolution because of this.
If the elders consent, for the sake of the elders and oneself, one performs the *tṛṇaprastāra* confession. The second assembly should also speak in this manner. What is the *tṛṇaprastāra*?
It is that which consists of confessing without specifying the name of the offense or its category. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "Grass..."
The *tṛṇaprastāra* (covering the ground with grass) has two meanings. First, when disputes arise frequently, the disputants are numerous, and the matters become increasingly manifold;

if one traces them back to their origin, it is difficult to determine the source. The Buddha permitted the *tṛṇaprastāra* to extinguish such conflicts, just as tangled grass that is difficult to arrange is simply discarded when it becomes disordered.
Second, when virtuous elders exhort and persuade the disputants, causing them to turn toward [reconciliation].
The two groups [of monks] spread out four sheepskins as a means of repentance (the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "They all stretch out their hands and feet and prostrate themselves on the ground;
thus they are like sheepskins"). As for the two groups, each has its own assistants; therefore, they are made to remain in separate locations. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If there are bhikṣus who engage in quarreling and mutual abuse, committing evil karma of body, speech, and mind, and later wish to remove their offenses within the Saṃgha, they shall perform the 'grass-covering' (*tṛṇapraticchādana*)."

One should repent on the ground. After having made the three requests, one should extend the hands and feet, prostrate upon the ground, and listen with single-minded attention to the *karmavācanā* from the *karmadāna* (the master of the ritual).

He then performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. This is called the settlement of a dispute arising from an offense through the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* and the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (spreading grass on the ground).
What is meant by "spreading grass on the ground"? It means that those bhikṣus no longer speak of the origins of the quarrel; the Saṃgha...
Nor does one further inquire into the root of the matter (this is a *vinaya-vinīta*; it is a comprehensive settlement for both disputes over offenses and disputes over matters).
According to the *Mūlakalpa*, there were two bhikṣus who became estranged and engaged in various kinds of discordant speech.
They slander one another. Regarding these two persons, one should trust the one who maintains the precepts; if both maintain the precepts, one should trust the one who is learned;
if both are learned, one should trust the one who has few desires; if both have few desires, [one should trust the one who is content].
One should have faith that those who possess extremely few desires will never give rise to discord if both parties are indeed free from excessive desire;
such a thing is impossible. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Those who employ anger and resentment do not extinguish anger and resentment; only the power of patience can extinguish them.
There are five matters of dispute that are difficult to extinguish: not seeking resolution through the Saṃgha, not complying with the Buddha’s words, and not acting according to the Dharma."

[The monk] says: "The two assemblies' contentious minds do not cease; they do not seek purification for their transgressions. Those who act contrary to the five aforementioned matters are easily extinguished.
This is the third formal inquiry.
Venerable sirs, I have already recited the seven rules for the settling of disputes. Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
(Three times. The fourth [section] is the exhortation to uphold [the precepts].
"Venerable sirs, since you are pure in this matter, you remain silent; thus I shall hold it so.
● Next, the section on the final summary has two parts: first, the summary of the titles; second, the exhortation to study other dharmas.
Now, first of all:
Venerable sirs, I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have already recited the four *pārājika* rules;
I have already recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules; I have already recited the two *aniyata* rules; I have already recited the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.
The *Pāyattika* Dharmas. The ninety *pāyattika* dharmas have been explained; the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas have been explained;
the *śaikṣa* dharmas have been explained; the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas have been explained. These were spoken by the Buddha;
they are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Second, the exhortation to study other dharmas.
If there are further other Buddha-dharmas, one should study them all in harmony with these.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if there are further other Buddha-dharmas," there are two meanings. First, the Vinaya; [the second is] the dual...

These clarify the rules for cessation and action, as well as the *Khandhakas* concerning monks and nuns. This present *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, however, clarifies only the two hundred and fifty training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for the great monks (*bhikṣu*).
There are further dharmas that should all be studied and practiced. As the *Mūla-prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"If there are further other dharmas and secondary dharmas (*anudharma*)," the *Vinayavibhaṅga-ṭīkā* explains:
"If there are further others" refers to the seventeen *vargīyas* (in Sanskrit, *varga*; in the original Vinaya, *khandhaka*; in its correct pronunciation, *vaggu*;

here translated as "dharma-aggregate," because dharmas of similar category are gathered together in one place). All the prescribed rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) should be practiced. Regarding "dharmas and secondary dharmas": the dharma...
This refers to the Dharma of the pure, unburdened, and correct practice that is nirvāṇa.

Because the Eightfold Noble Path and other such factors accord with that state of perfect stillness (parinirvāṇa), they are called "conformable to the Dharma" (anudharma). The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There may be matters concerning which I have neither previously prohibited nor permitted; yet regarding those matters, if one acts contrary to them, it is impure, whereas acting in accordance with them is pure."
That which is pure is indeed purity; it should be practiced. If one violates purity and follows impurity, that is impurity and should not be practiced. One should train in accordance with this.
You, sirs, should assemble together, rejoicing without dispute, with a single mind and a single teaching, blending like water and milk, and should diligently bring this into full manifestation.
The Great Master’s teachings bring about peaceful dwelling; do not be negligent.
Second, this refers to all the Sūtras and Abhidharma, for the wisdom-life of the Buddhas is entrusted to the Tripiṭaka. By studying them, one causes the Buddha-dharma to endure long;
when the Way is bright and virtue is complete, one does not defile the Saṅgha-ratna. Since the Way is propagated by people, it can only be inherited and made flourishing through such means.
The seed of the Buddha: if one does not study, the True Dharma will remain hidden, the eye of the world will perish, and one will further incur the fault of being as ignorant as a sheep.
One must therefore strive diligently in study so that the lamp of the Dharma may be transmitted in succession, ensuring that the True Dharma abides long and is not extinguished.
● Ninth, the *Sūtra on Briefly Relating the Buddha’s Teaching*, which consists of seven parts. From the first, Vipaśyin Buddha, down to the seventh, our original teacher Śākyamuni.
Now, the first part is divided into two: first, the Dharma taught according to the capacity of the audience; second, the person who teaches it.
Hereafter, all [sections] follow this same pattern.

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "When the first Buddha, Vipaśyin, appeared in the world, many of his śrāvaka disciples delighted in the practice of mortifying the body as their correct conduct.
Furthermore, various false teachers, following their own perverse desires, preached false doctrines to them."
To counteract that, this verse was spoken:
"Patience is the supreme path; the Buddha has declared the unconditioned to be foremost. One who goes forth and vexes others is not called a śramaṇa."
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "patience is the foremost path," why does this verse specifically praise patience?
It is because while those who observe the precepts are not necessarily able to practice patience, those who practice patience certainly never fail to observe the precepts.
The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* states: "The virtue of patience is such that it cannot be equaled by the observance of precepts or ascetic practices. In Sanskrit, this is called *kṣānti*.
This is translated as "patience" (kṣānti). The *Fajie Cidi* states: "In the language of Qin, it means 'endurance' (rén'ǔ).

It refers to the ability of the internal mind to peacefully endure external objects of insult; hence it is called 'endurance. There are two kinds of endurance: first, patience toward sentient beings (*sattva-kṣānti*);

second, patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). What is meant by patience toward sentient beings? Patience toward sentient beings also has two types: first, [enduring] respect and offerings..."

In the midst of these, being able to endure without attachment, one does not give rise to arrogance or negligence. Second, being able to endure amidst anger, verbal abuse, beating, and harm, one does not give rise to resentment or vexation;
this is called patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*). What is meant by patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*)? Patience toward phenomena is also of two kinds.
The first is non-mental phenomena, namely cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, illness, old age, death, and so forth. The second is...
Mental phenomena refer to such things as anger, sorrow, doubt, sensual desire, pride, and various false views.
To be able to endure these two types of phenomena without being moved is called "patience regarding phenomena" (*dharmakṣānti*).

If one perceives an insult that could be endured, even if one does not retaliate through body or speech, it is difficult for the mind to achieve complete liberation. If one has not yet attained this single thought-moment of liberation, then—
To strive for cessation alongside the śramaṇas is for name and reality not to correspond. One should only deeply contemplate the nature of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*);
since neither the arising of beings nor the arising of dharmas can be apprehended, there is not even humiliation—whom could one call "patient"?
Therefore, it is called the foremost path of patience (*kṣānti*). When the Buddha says that the unconditioned is supreme, he means that among unconditioned dharmas, patience is supreme.
Therefore, "the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely *nirvāṇa*. The two phrases beginning with "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*) are words of contrastive clarification.

They serve to exclude those among the heterodox outsiders who, under false views, leave home and falsely proclaim divergent teachings to instruct others. Such people needlessly afflict their bodies and compel others to follow their own practices;
thus, both self and others suffer, and in the end there is no fruit or benefit. Why is this? Because the dharma of a śramaṇa is patience (*kṣānti*).

Do not harbor anger toward those who insult you. Diligently cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom to thoroughly realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Those who have left the household life for the sake of the unconditioned dharma are called true renunciants."
This is the *Śīla-sūtra* spoken by Vipaśyin Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. [Explanation:
The Sanskrit term *Tathāgata* is also rendered as *Tathāgaja*. During the Later Qin period, it was translated as "Tathāgata" (如來).

This means that ordinary beings do not come as they truly are (*atathā āgata*), and those of the Two Vehicles come as they truly are (*tathā āgata*) but do not return; only the World-Honored One is both...
"Thus Come" (*tathāgata*) may also be explained in terms of the three bodies (*trikāya*). The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Thus Come One. This refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (in the context of the turning of the wheel of Dharma) states:

"The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is called 'thus' (*tathā*), and perfect enlightenment is called 'come' (*āgata*). This explains it in terms of the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Riding upon reality as it is..."

The Way. Coming to achieve perfect enlightenment—this is explained in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Because he differs from ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, he is called the *Tathāgata*. In the Sanskrit language, *Arhat*;
this is translated here as "one who is unattached" (*amuktaka*), and also as "one worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because he is worthy of receiving the offerings of all sentient beings, both noble and ordinary, throughout the nine realms. In the Sanskrit language, *Samyaksaṃbuddha*.

It is also called *Samyak-saṃbodhi*; in the language of Qin, it means "Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. It is also called "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*), because one universally knows all phenomena within the dharma-realm.
Master Kumārajīva says it is "Perfect Universal Awakening": it is called "perfect" (*samya*) because the dharmas have no discrepancy;

it is called "universal" (*saṃ*) because wisdom is all-pervasive; it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*) because one has emerged from the dream of birth-and-death. The *Miaozong* (Exquisite Commentary) states: this...
These three titles are precisely the names of the Three Virtues (triguṇa). Now, in terms of their referents, they correspond in meaning to the Three Truths (trisatya):
"The One of Right and Universal Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) is the True Truth (paramārthasatya) of Prajñā; "The Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat) is the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛtisatya) of Liberation;

and "The Tathāgata" is the Middle Truth (madhyamasatya) of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Ānanda, if I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases extensively, you would require an eon..."
One cannot exhaustively receive [the teachings] due to the brevity of life; this cites three of the ten epithets of the Tathāgata (hereafter, all follow this pattern).

Second, when the Tathāgata Śikhin appeared in the world, many of his śrāvaka disciples practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for the sake of rebirth in the heavens. To counteract this, that Buddha spoke this verse.
"Just as a person with clear vision / Can avoid dangerous and evil paths, / So too a wise person in this world / Can distance themselves from all evils.
The first two lines present a simile. Just as a person who possesses sight is able to avoid perilous difficulties and ultimately attains safety and peace, so it is here.
In this context, "eye" refers to the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*). This eye possesses luminous illumination and is associated with wisdom; it is able to see the Dharma and attain the Dharma.
Just as one with clear vision avoids dangerous paths and can reach a place of safety, so too within the three realms there is nothing that is not perilous or evil.
Yet the foolish, lacking wisdom, do not contemplate the methods for escape; thus, when their sublime celestial rewards of pleasure are exhausted, they fall.
They fall back into the various evil realms, undergoing saṃsāra for a long time without liberation; therefore, they are collectively called "evil paths.
Among those in the world who possess intelligence and are able to distance themselves from all evils—being intelligent, they are able to hear the Way;

being clear-sighted, they are able to see the Way—they believe in the Buddha’s wondrous Dharma, deeply recognize the causes of suffering, and thoroughly understand the three realms as if they were water.

The moon in the sky and flowers in water are empty by their very nature; they are like illusions and transformations. All evils, without being sought after for abandonment, naturally distance themselves from one.
Having abandoned all evils, one does not summon bitter fruits and forever cuts off saṃsāra, reaching the ultimate stage.

It is peace, security, and constant bliss. "All evils" refers to the three delusions—view-delusion, affliction-delusion, and the delusion of dust-like sands and ignorance—including all their active manifestations and seeds.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Śikhin, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

The third Tathāgata, Vipaśyin, appeared in the world. Among his many śrāvaka disciples, there were many who were content with merely maintaining their moral discipline and did not cultivate other dharmas; furthermore, they constantly observed the faults of others and caused them distress.
To counteract this, he taught this brief instruction.
Do not slander, nor be envious; you should practice the precepts with devotion. Know moderation in food and drink, always delighting in solitude;
with a concentrated mind, take joy in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
(The first two lines: "Not slandering" means that the intent of this verse clarifies the initial restraint of verbal transgressions by not disparaging others.

He is not envious and guards his mental karma, desiring not to harm others. While the slanderer utters evil words with the mouth, the envious person harbors evil thoughts in the mind; being free from these two faults, he practices the precepts. Thus, when all three karmas are pure, one is called a true upholder of the pure precepts. The following clarifies the method of counteractive cultivation. The two lines concerning "knowing moderation in food and drink" [are as follows]: [The text continues: "Knowing moderation in food and drink, one attains the bliss of tranquility. This means that by knowing the proper measure in eating and drinking, one does not become intoxicated by flavors, and thus the body and mind remain light and at ease. Because the body and mind are at ease, one can cultivate the path without hindrance. This is called the practice of the first dhyāna. Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows moderation in food and drink is like a wise person who guards a treasure. This means that just as a wise person guards a precious jewel against loss, so too does one guard the body and life through moderation in food and drink, ensuring they do not perish. This is called the practice of the second dhyāna. Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows moderation in food and drink is like a physician treating a patient. This means that just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to the illness, so too does one regulate food and drink according to the needs of the body, ensuring that the four elements are balanced and the body is healthy. This is called the practice of the third dhyāna. Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows moderation in food and drink is like a farmer tending the fields. This means that just as a diligent farmer sows seeds and waters the fields according to the season, so too does one nourish the body with food and drink according to the proper time, ensuring the body is strong and capable of practicing the path. This is called the practice of the fourth dhyāna. Therefore, one who knows moderation in food and drink is able to attain the bliss of tranquility. This is the meaning of the verse. Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows moderation in food and drink is like a king governing the realm. This means that just as a wise king governs the realm with justice and does not oppress the people, so too does one govern the body with moderation in food and drink, ensuring it is neither too indulgent nor too austere. This is called the practice of the *samādhi* of the cessation of perception and feeling. Furthermore, it is said: "One who knows moderation in food and drink is like a sage dwelling in seclusion.
